item.title: Anthropic S-1 Shocker, Greatest Business Ever? Google’s $500B Wipeout, Midterm Predictions
item.description: Anthropic reported $16.3 billion in first-half revenue, up 14× year over year, and is targeting a $100 billion IPO. Cheaper tokens alongside roughly 10× annual efficiency gains support about 85% incremental gross margins, but customer returns remain unproven. AI financing demand equivalent to roughly 30% of Treasury issuance through 2027, plus power access, remain key constraints.
item.content:encoded:
All-In · Chamath Palihapitiya、Jason Calacanis、David Sacks、David Friedberg · 2026-10-30 · 86 min · 原语言 EN

Anthropic reported $16.3 billion in first-half revenue, up 14× year over year, and is targeting a $100 billion IPO. Cheaper tokens alongside roughly 10× annual efficiency gains support about 85% incremental gross margins, but customer returns remain unproven. AI financing demand equivalent to roughly 30% of Treasury issuance through 2027, plus power access, remain key constraints.

TL;DR

  • Anthropic is targeting a $100 billion IPO after producing $16.3 billion of first-half revenue, up 14× year over year. Calacanis cites a November 16 listing under ANT at a $1.5–$2 trillion valuation, while Sacks calls the six-year-old company potentially “the biggest venture outcome of all time.” The $100 billion year-end ARR projection remains ambiguous between recurring revenue and annualized revenue run rate.
  • The strongest bull case is that cheaper tokens are expanding margins rather than exposing a business dependent on subsidies. Sacks calls the reported $80 billion loss a “phantom number” arising from convertible-note accounting, against roughly $9–$10 billion of capital consumed. His mechanism is 10× annual efficiency improvement permitting substantial price cuts while retaining savings; Friedberg specifies approximately 85% incremental gross margins, with baseline compute costs still present.
  • Enterprise penetration leaves substantial runway, but demonstrated customer returns remain the critical test. Customers spending at least $100,000 reached 11,900, approximately 1% of Friedberg’s estimated eligible global customer base. Chamath wants evidence that experimentation converts into multimillion-dollar commitments, while Friedberg acknowledges his assumed 2–10× customer return is unsupported: “I have no idea.”
  • A remarkable business can still arrive at a fair valuation inside an increasingly concentrated funding market. Chamath’s revised IPO midpoint is $1.5 trillion; around $1.4–$1.6 trillion, “there’s no deal.” His larger concern is AI financing demand equivalent to roughly 30% of Treasury issuance through 2027: either higher corporate borrowing costs pressure the AI ecosystem, or higher Treasury yields raise borrowing costs throughout the economy.
  • Power availability and government influence could become more binding constraints than customer demand. Chamath reads compute infrastructure as Anthropic’s dominant risk and argues that slowing permits could become a political weapon; Calacanis counters that Democrats could instead champion Anthropic’s expansion. Friedberg predicts government allocation of compute capacity, while Sacks warns that an exceptional business makes regulatory protection especially objectionable.
  • Lower prices strengthen the adoption thesis while leaving open-model competition and recursive self-improvement unresolved. Calacanis revises his earlier commoditization call “in the face of new evidence” and imagines 500× token usage as workers acquire multiple agents. Sacks still sees cheaper open models threatening important markets such as coding, while Anthropic’s reliance on recursive self-improvement could collide with its safety constituency.
  • Google’s $500 billion selloff divides concerns about search monetization from evidence that diversification is working. Search revenue still rose 12% to $63 billion, while Cloud doubled to $30.7 billion and operating income exceeded $11 billion. Friedberg questions the timing of a consumer AI replacement; Chamath wants auction-manipulation allegations addressed; Sacks sees the stock as somewhat oversold, and Calacanis buys more during the show.
  • The central midterm disagreement concerns the Senate, with broad agreement that a Democratic House would unleash investigations. Chamath expects a Democratic “spritz”: a narrow House majority with Republicans retaining the Senate. Calacanis backs Polymarket’s Democratic probabilities of 68% for the Senate and 92% for the House; Sacks distrusts both polling narratives and prediction-market certainty, expecting potentially “a more normal midterm result.”

Digest

1. Anthropic’s IPO combines record ambition with concentrated control

  • Calacanis says Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are targeting November 16 for an ANT listing raising $100 billion at a $1.5–$2 trillion valuation. That would exceed SpaceX’s $85 billion June IPO; he cites a 78% Polymarket probability of raising at least $95 billion. Sacks calls the six-year-old company potentially “the biggest venture outcome of all time,” emphasizing the speed of value creation.
  • Revenue, in Calacanis’s rundown, reached $16.3 billion in H1 2026, up 14× year over year; Q2 contributed $11.6 billion, roughly 30× the level five quarters earlier. Anthropic projects $100 billion of year-end ARR against a $40 trillion TAM, whose derivation he says he does not know. He also leaves unresolved whether ARR means recurring revenue or annualized revenue run rate.
  • The seven founders would retain 50.1% of voting power through a single class of F shares. Calacanis also describes an optional arrangement directing 80% of their shares into a nonprofit-type entity, while explicitly acknowledging uncertainty over its form: “Who knows what it’s gonna be structured as?” His question is how that concentration of wealth and control changes technology and politics.

2. Compute multipliers undermine the cash-burning narrative

  • Sacks argues the much-discussed $80 billion loss is a “phantom number”: convertible notes issued to infrastructure partners, including Amazon, generated accounting losses as Anthropic’s valuation rose. “If they had just issued equity, that loss wouldn’t be there.” Against roughly $110 billion raised, he says the company consumed only about $9–$10 billion, substantially changing his assessment of capital efficiency.
  • His operating explanation separates raw compute from “compute multipliers”: better algorithms, curated data, and architectures such as MoE. Delivering a given capability becomes roughly 10× cheaper annually; cutting customer prices by, say, 50% still leaves substantial efficiency gains for Anthropic. Alternatively, those savings can buy greater capabilities. His rebuttal to commoditization is that falling token prices and improving margins can occur together.

3. The productivity stack looks profitable, but customer returns remain assumed

  • Friedberg tracks customers spending at least $100,000 from 200 at year-end 2024 to 1,500 at year-end 2025 and 11,900 by September. He estimates roughly 200,000–300,000 US businesses, and more than a million globally, could spend that amount while keeping it below 1% of total spending. On that definition, Anthropic has penetrated only around 1% of potential customers.
  • Friedberg’s illustrative stack turns $1 of NVIDIA cost into $4 of chip revenue at 75% margins. For SpaceX’s Colossus 1, he uses $10 billion of capex, depreciation over five years, and $1.25 billion monthly revenue to derive roughly 83% margins. Anthropic’s approximately 85% margin is incremental, with baseline compute costs remaining; the original dollar ultimately supports $18 of Anthropic revenue.
  • Chamath challenges the final box: how much value customers actually receive. Friedberg concedes, “The last box I made up,” explaining that he assumed customers make 2–10× what they spend: “I have no idea.” His evidence is experiential—Claude lets his teams accomplish more, faster—even after installing their own open-source cluster. He allows that early exuberance could instead be masking poor returns.
  • Chamath supplies Microsoft as a concrete productivity example: revenue increased from $198 billion to $332 billion over four years while staff increased by only 2,000. He interprets this as more output from approximately the same human input. Depending on uptake of an exit offer extended to 60,000 people, he says headcount could fall below 200,000.

4. Million-dollar budgets separate experimentation from enterprise conviction

  • Chamath’s estimated customer distribution comprises approximately 40 million individuals and small businesses spending below $100,000, 10,000 customers spending $100,000–$1 million, 1,650 spending $1–$10 million, and 250 spending above $10 million. Expansion within existing accounts—“negative churn”—plus new customers could support hundreds of billions in revenue over three to seven years without approaching full penetration.
  • His sales explanation: directors and VPs can experiment within delegated budgets of around $1 million, signing up for several products. Larger commitments require cross-functional approval and an explicit ROI or total-cost advantage. About 1,900 customers exceed $1 million, but stripping out venture-funded AI natives might leave only a couple hundred Global 2000-type companies. “The ROI case is still a little speculative.”
  • The quarterly test is whether the 10,000 customers below $1 million graduate into single-digit millions and then tens of millions, supported by defensible use cases and analyses. Chamath hopes a listing after November 11 will require disclosure of Q3 figures. He reports whispers that growth moderated to around 50%, while leaving Q4 explicitly “TBD.”

5. A stronger balance sheet changes the IPO pricing calculation

  • Chamath revises his earlier funding and valuation call: he had assumed only $30–$50 billion of cash and wanted pricing nearer $1 trillion. “I was wrong.” He says Anthropic had $125 billion entering June and estimates an $80–$120 billion raise would bring it toward the roughly $250 billion cash buffer he wants.
  • Sacks adds approximately $80 billion of debt-facility capacity and puts prospective dry powder above $300 billion after the IPO. His answer to bears questioning future compute commitments is that Anthropic now has capital to support them, potentially through around 2030. Chamath agrees that the smaller necessary equity raise materially improves the offering’s prospects.
  • Chamath’s revised valuation range is $1.3–$1.7 trillion, centered on $1.5 trillion. Raising less improves pricing power and control over the float. Nevertheless, at approximately $1.4–$1.6 trillion, he calls the stock “kind of priced fairly”: “There’s no deal,” although investors receive an entry into the company’s future.

6. Data centers turn power policy into an economic battleground

  • Chamath begins his S-1 analysis with a word cloud of risk factors, treating management’s allocation of words as evidence of priorities. Compute dominates, especially data centers, financing commitments, and power. Regulation follows, then privacy, data retention, IP, and safety. Customer traction receives comparatively little attention. His conclusion: “As goes data centers, as goes power.”
  • His partisan inference is that Democrats seeking an economic slowdown before 2028 could obstruct power and data centers, while Republicans must accelerate them. Calacanis challenges the incentive: why wouldn’t Democrats champion Anthropic as an ideological ally and prospective source of political funding? Sacks doubts that today’s party would do so, describing proposed model approvals as “a DMV for models.”
  • Sacks cites GDP growth of 2.5% in the first half and tracking around 3.7% in Q3, against AI build-out spending near 3% of GDP; he argues the build-out effectively accounts for economic growth. Calacanis accepts AI’s importance but disputes the broader prosperity claim, emphasizing inflation, war, tariffs, and dissatisfaction among people without equity holdings. Sacks rejects calling the economy a disaster.

7. AI borrowing creates a risk that company analysis cannot settle

  • Chamath says major AI companies collectively owe roughly $340–$400 billion, with Microsoft an exception for halving its debt. Calacanis checks Meta’s figures and reports $80 billion of cash and short-term investments against $82 billion of debt. The broader issue: anticipated AI financing through the end of 2027 equals approximately 30% of Treasury issuance over the same period.
  • If investors prefer government debt, hyperscalers must offer higher coupons. Those financing costs then cascade through neoclouds and other infrastructure providers, bringing default risks forward and potentially creating a negative feedback cycle. This is why Chamath thinks a strong operating business can still face substantial market risk.
  • If AI companies obtain attractive financing instead, Treasury may have to pay more. Because borrowing elsewhere is linked to government yields across two-, five-, and ten-year maturities, higher rates then affect the broader economy. Chamath says he has never seen this market risk before; Calacanis says he has not seen anything this close to the GFC in 15–20 years.
  • Chamath calls the complex “too big to fail” but says, “I’m generally bullish.” Calacanis counters that exceptional American franchises could attract sufficient global capital. Conditional on Anthropic meeting its targets, he says its cumulative first seven years could exceed the comparable combined revenues of the iPhone, Google paid search, and Amazon retail, excluding AWS.

8. Government influence could become a constraint on private AI power

  • Friedberg views companies, nonprofits, and governments as competing organizations accumulating resources for their constituencies. AI’s capital, productivity, and influence threaten governmental power. His prediction extends beyond blocking construction: governments could regulate the actual compute layer after production, allocating who receives how much capacity. He expects the conflict to develop regardless of which party governs.
  • Calacanis wants Anthropic’s founders publicly championing candidates as visibly as Sacks supported Trump. Sacks pushes back that Anthropic already has substantial PAC funding and a large government-affairs operation, hiring former Biden officials and, increasingly, former Trump officials. He distinguishes his individual political activity from a corporation pursuing regulatory advantage.
  • For Sacks, an IPO would clarify that Anthropic is a major technology company deserving the same suspicion as its peers—an “800-pound gorilla,” rather than an innocuous startup. He pairs his “best business ever” thesis with opposition to regulatory capture: an AGI monopoly or duopoly should receive stronger competition, not additional regulatory moats.

9. Cheaper intelligence expands usage while open models and RSI test the lead

  • Calacanis revises his earlier open-model call “in the face of new evidence”: competition is “not slowing them down yet.” Sacks stresses that Q3 remains undisclosed; the claim that Anthropic eliminated 99% of distillation, lost revenue, then reaccelerated after token-price cuts is “scuttlebutt on X,” rather than an established explanation.
  • Sacks’s demand argument is “Jevons paradox”: cheaper tokens unlock uses, and agents consume far more than prompts. Calacanis imagines 100–200 million white-collar workers each running five agents and predicts 500× token usage. His adoption forecast is conditional: once cyber constraints ease, daily workplace use could rise from roughly 10% to 60–80%; large enterprises currently restrict connections to email and internal knowledge.
  • Sacks still sees open models commoditizing valuable applications such as coding without necessarily matching the frontier. Anthropic’s defense increasingly uses its own models to discover algorithmic efficiencies. He cites an August chart showing recursive self-improvement used in 26% of tasks involved in developing subsequent models; he does not know October’s share.
  • He suspects a split between Anthropic and safety “Doomers”: the company must accelerate RSI to stay ahead, while its allies fear exactly that. He reads Dario’s pacing letter as “almost like creating an alibi in advance for themselves.” Sacks does not fully endorse their RSI-risk story, and leaves unresolved whether safety pressure could slow research enough for open models to catch up.

10. Google’s search slowdown obscures a rapidly improving cloud franchise

  • Calacanis reports a 10–15% Thursday decline erasing approximately $500 billion of market value after Q3 earnings. Overall revenue grew 25%, but search missed expectations for a second consecutive quarter, growth slowed from 17% to 12%, and free cash flow was negative. Searches themselves are increasing; monetization is the concern as AI supplies answers and agents complete tasks.
  • Sacks disputes the implication that search is already deteriorating: quarterly revenue increased from $56 billion to $63 billion. Its share fell below 50% because other businesses grew faster. Cloud doubled to $30.7 billion; Friedberg notes its operating income increased from approximately $3.5 billion to more than $11 billion. Sacks regards diversification as something Alphabet has long wanted.
  • For Friedberg, roughly 21× operating income requires reliable future cash flows. The question is whether consumer AI can replace search monetization quickly enough as the legacy engine flattens. He also floats an explicitly uncertain internal resource conflict: Google may earn more renting compute externally than allocating it to its own model researchers.

11. Google’s auction controversy complicates the diversification story

  • Chamath highlights advertiser Max Anderson’s allegations, explicitly saying he does not know whether they are true. Anderson describes spending more than $500,000 monthly and claims changes to Google’s ad auction. Chamath explains the traditional Vickrey mechanism: the highest bidder pays the runner-up’s price. Abandoning that mechanism could, in his view, let Google overearn temporarily.
  • Friedberg’s concern is that advertisers eventually recognize weaker economics and reduce spending. Chamath urges investor relations to address the allegations before “pulling money from the future into the present” becomes the prevailing interpretation. Separately, a more balanced mix of Search, YouTube, Cloud, and other bets could improve diversification while requiring a transition to investors comfortable owning a conglomerate.
  • Chamath’s talent priority is blunt: “How do you keep Demis at Google?” He also says to pay Thomas Kurian whatever he wants. Sacks calls the stock a little oversold; Calacanis buys more during the recording. Friedberg notes Alphabet’s approximately 6% SpaceX and 15% Anthropic stakes, while Calacanis says he thinks it owns 85% of Waymo.

12. The midterm split concerns the Senate and the next two years

  • Chamath still expects a Democratic “spritz”: Republicans retain the Senate, Democrats obtain a narrow House majority. He anticipates subpoenas and document releases creating “FUD” before 2028. He also thinks an economic slowdown benefits Democrats, returning the conversation to state and local control over power permitting and data centers.
  • Sacks distrusts polls after hoax firms entered averages and cites Patrick Ruffini’s finding that three-quarters of polls across three elections erred toward Democrats. He also challenges prediction markets, citing misses on Bolsonaro—though he allows Bolsonaro may have been robbed—and Netanyahu. His forecast is modest: the governing party normally loses midterms, and the outcome might be “a more normal midterm result” than the advertised bloodbath.
  • Calacanis backs Polymarket’s 68% probability of Democrats taking the Senate and 92% for the House. His reasoning combines anti-Trump turnout, disillusioned moderates, and an America First constituency angry over inflation and another war. He expects a Democratic sweep and presents that as analysis rather than his personal political preference.
  • Calacanis predicts subpoenas, renewed impeachment fights, and legislation designed to force damaging Republican votes before 2028; he expects new Republican leadership beyond JD Vance and Marco Rubio. Sacks agrees that investigations would return but argues Democratic overreach could revive the political pendulum. Their disagreement is chiefly over the electoral outcome and eventual political beneficiaries; both expect confrontation if Democrats take the House.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/anthropic-s-1-shocker-greatest-business-ever-goo

item.title: Episode 201 - October 30, 2026
item.description: Pharma buyers remain active in early-stage assets and China, though term sheets do not guarantee Q4 closings. Amvuttra sales fell to $81 million from $129 million in Q2 as Alnylam cut franchise guidance for a second time this year. AI may reduce data-gathering costs, but a 10,000-patient cardiovascular study still takes five years and $300 million.
item.content:encoded:
Biotech Hangout · Chris Garabedian、Graig Suvannavejh、Sam Fazeli、Brian Skorney、Yaron Werber · 2026-10-30 · 61 min · 原语言 EN

Pharma buyers remain active in early-stage assets and China, though term sheets do not guarantee Q4 closings. Amvuttra sales fell to $81 million from $129 million in Q2 as Alnylam cut franchise guidance for a second time this year. AI may reduce data-gathering costs, but a 10,000-patient cardiovascular study still takes five years and $300 million.

TL;DR

  • Pharma’s deal appetite remains intact, with early-stage assets and China firmly in the sourcing mix. Sam highlighted Lilly’s continued early/clinical-stage strategy, Bristol Myers’ $13 billion in cash and securities, and Novartis’ preference for bolt-ons below $2 billion. Sanofi’s emphasis on “faster translational efficiency” reinforced China’s attraction, although active term sheets do not guarantee Q4 closings.
  • Alnylam’s commercial disappointment shows how quickly clinical success can lose its valuation cushion. Graig cited Amvuttra sales of $81 million in the quarter, down from $129 million in Q2, and a second franchise guidance cut; shares were down about 30% over the week and 60% year to date. Sam separately corrected his BeiGene comment: Brukinsa revenue was $1.13 billion, and he had mischaracterized U.S. demand in the quarter as declining.
  • AI’s demonstrated workflow gains have not removed the clinical-development bottleneck. Sam described replacing two or three data-gathering contractors, but Brian’s counterexample remained a 10,000-patient cardiovascular study taking five years and $300 million: efficiencies would “not accelerate things by 90%.” Yaron pointed to Amgen’s 16-month trial enrollment, crediting AI-assisted patient and site identification.
  • A reopening IPO market still requires discrimination between financing access and investment returns. Graig counted approximately 31 biotech IPOs, including renewed appetite for phase 1 companies, but estimated at least half traded below issue price; Eikon had fallen from $18 to about $5. Chris hoped biotech “might be seen as a safe haven” from tech’s AI-spending concerns, while Sam warned that hypothetical geopolitical escalation and renewed tariffs could lift rates.
  • Rare-disease regulatory flexibility offers encouragement without solving the funding problem. Chris welcomed FDA efforts to “codify the flexibility” around small trials, evidence standards and manufacturing. Plowshare’s $7 million philanthropic/angel round illustrated community support, but substantial institutional capital would still be needed; Palvella’s review timeline provided another concrete positive.
  • IgA nephropathy supplied unusually strong evidence of disease modification. Brian highlighted Voyxact’s two-year VISIONARY results: essentially flat eGFR, one composite kidney event versus 28 on placebo, and no kidney-replacement cases versus five. He described this as having “stopped disease progression,” while distinguishing those mature results from programs still awaiting longer-term kidney-function data.
  • ESMO strengthened Amgen’s small-cell franchise and Genmab’s answer to its royalty cliff. Sam called DeLLphi-304 “practice-changing”; the Genmab discussion framed three pipeline readouts as potential foundations for growth through the 2029–30 Darzalex royalty decline. Genmab shares had doubled in three months, with three prospective blockbuster launches envisaged by late 2027/early 2028.
  • Strong combination efficacy does not eliminate development and partnering risk. Yaron argued that Tango’s PRMT5 inhibitor tripled exposure to Revolution Medicines’ RAS drug, creating dose, labeling and pricing complications. BMS’s formal collaboration and expected absence of that interaction made it a formidable competitor. Sam said he had intended to discuss Tango and PRMT5 inhibitors, but the conversation ended before he did.

Digest

1. Pharma buyers remain active without promising imminent closings

  • Sam’s reading of pharma earnings was continued engagement: Lilly remained focused on early and clinical-stage deals, particularly immunology, neuroscience and oncology. Bristol Myers stayed agnostic on transaction size, prioritized business development and cited $13 billion in cash and marketable securities, plus debt access. Its approach was to transact “as things come through,” rather than wait for one particular opportunity.
  • Novartis still preferred bolt-ons below $2 billion, with larger transactions selective; Sam did not think the Avidity trial news had changed that philosophy. One VC had described four or five companies at term-sheet stage, supporting Chris’s optimism approaching Jefferies and JPMorgan. Sam retained the timing caveat: “whether those deals close in Q4, who knows?”
  • Sanofi’s China commentary mattered because it made the operational argument explicit. Sam highlighted its description of a “thriving hub for scientific advancement” and R&D’s emphasis on “faster translational efficiency.” An established regional commercial presence also supported manufacturing and drug-development partnerships: this was pharma explaining China’s advantages directly.

2. Alnylam and IPO dispersion expose the limits of market optimism

  • Graig said Amvuttra sales were $81 million in the quarter, versus $129 million in the second quarter—a meaningful decline in a competitive landscape. The CEO called the results unsatisfactory despite underlying growth demand, and the franchise received its second guidance cut of the year despite an expanded sales force. Separately, Sam corrected his BeiGene comment: Brukinsa revenue was $1.13 billion; he had erroneously described U.S. demand in the quarter as declining.
  • With Alnylam shares down about 30% over the week and 60% year to date, Graig distinguished scientific accolades from commercial execution: “the rubber hits the road.” Chris relayed chatter on X that the company had not used its stock currency and position of strength to acquire pipeline diversification.
  • Graig’s unofficial IPO count reached 31, approaching a previously discussed forecast of 50. Protein-degrader company Lycia Therapeutics rose about 60% intraday on debut before finishing roughly 30% higher. The day’s phase 1 offerings, Bamboo Therapeutics in immunology and Aspen Neuroscience in Parkinson’s cell therapy, suggested investors would still finance earlier development.
  • That appetite coexisted with weak aftermarket performance: Graig estimated at least half the year’s offerings traded below issue price. Eikon, which he covered, had fallen from February’s $18 IPO to about $5 despite a good update at ESMO and more than $500 million in cash. Chris noted that some believed its platform-led valuation had been high, distinguishing it from product-driven offerings.

3. AI improves execution while human studies retain their time cost

  • Brian highlighted Anthropic’s S-1 emphasis on life sciences, its April acquisition of computational biology company Coefficient Bio, and its acquisition of Methyl Medicine, a one-person biotech run by Cody Tranbarger, who revealed himself as “Professor Oak.” Chris connected this with an existing operating shift: venture-backed companies reaching pivotal studies with around 20 employees, and one approaching phase 2 with a single full-time CEO. AI could reinforce smaller teams rather than create that trend.
  • Yaron described Bruce Booth’s distinction between generating molecules against validated targets and understanding novel human biology: more discovery output could crowd the entrance to clinical development, though infrastructure could absorb more assets. Chris added that clinical-trial capacity remains limited. He also reconsidered the maxim that “chemists with computers are going to replace chemists without computers.” For finding new IP around scaffolds and targets, he was beginning to question whether computers might replace chemists themselves.
  • Sam already found AI could displace two or three contractors gathering and sifting data, while retaining human quality control. Population and biobank data offered potential biological insight. Yaron said AI could help identify protein–protein interactions, understand protein structure and movement, and find undruggable targets, while emphasizing the need for wet-lab work at scale. Brian’s warning was “garbage in, garbage out”: fast information processing still produces mistakes, and claims to “cure all diseases in 10 years” invite skepticism.
  • Chris also emphasized the lack of good translational models: for new targets, success still has to be tested in human clinical studies. Brian’s bottleneck was a 10,000-patient cardiovascular outcomes study taking five years and $300 million: efficiency would “not accelerate things by 90%.” Graig hoped better patient selection could improve probability of success, while study duration remained fixed. Yaron pointed to Amgen’s lipoprotein(a) study, enrolled in 16 months versus about a year and two months longer at Novartis, crediting AI-assisted patient identification and site mapping.

4. A biotech rotation remains vulnerable to higher rates

  • Chris saw a possible rotation as big tech funded an “unproven AI buildout.” He cited Amazon’s $220 billion in expenses for AI data-center buildouts, Alphabet losing 13% of its market value—about $500 billion—on an earnings disappointment, and Microsoft announcing layoffs or offering packages to 27% of its workforce. He also cited a roughly $6.3 billion crypto heist involving Bitcoin taken from Binance hot wallets. Chris said tech was facing an “existential crisis” as investors questioned whether AI spending would produce better revenue and profits, and suggested biotech “might be seen as a safe haven.”
  • Chris also cited more than 50 novel FDA approvals and 10 potential remaining decisions as grounds for an unusually strong approval year despite leadership churn. Sam’s pushback was conditional: rumors of a post-midterm attack on Iran could imply retaliation, higher oil prices and higher rates; renewed tariffs could add inflation. “I know nothing,” he stressed, attributing the scenarios to others. His investment mechanism was straightforward: sufficiently high risk-free returns make parking money in a Treasury more attractive, and biotech cannot assume immunity.

5. Rare-disease flexibility still needs financing and successful trials

  • Chris welcomed FDA’s rare-disease pathway meeting and a more standardized, “fit-for-purpose” approach across CDER and CBER. The agenda included small-sample statistics, enrollment constraints, real-world evidence, patient and expert input, and flexible manufacturing requirements. The aim was to “codify the flexibility that they’ve always signaled”; the open comment period ran through December 12.
  • Plowshare’s $7 million angel/philanthropic round illustrated both community commitment and the capital gap. Its maple syrup urine disease program addressed a condition in the Amish-Mennonite Plain community in Pennsylvania. CEO Kevin Strauss led the Clinic for Special Children and had ties to the Lancaster community, where he had helped with access to Zolgensma for SMA. Chris saw potential across concentrated inherited disorders, but emphasized that institutional investors would ultimately need to finance clinical development “through the finish line.”
  • Graig highlighted Palvella’s QTORIN rapamycin for microcystic lymphatic malformations: approximately 30,000 U.S. patients by the company’s estimate, potentially as many as 95,000, with no FDA-approved therapy. Its 505(b)(2), non-new-molecular-entity application had roughly six months from filing to decision, or four months after acceptance. Graig said “there’s going to be an approval here,” and cited potential across three other indications.
  • Acumen supplied the opposite outcome: its phase 2 Alzheimer’s antibody, which targeted beta-amyloid oligomers rather than necessarily plaques, failed, and shares fell 80%. Graig said the result might underscore whether sponsors need a brain shuttle, especially for antibodies; this candidate had not used one. Chris’s enthusiasm remained conditional: shuttles could open disease areas “if we can get it to work.”

6. IgA nephropathy moves from surrogate improvement toward kidney outcomes

  • Brian described a field transformed from relative neglect: roughly 200,000 diagnosed U.S. patients, with IgA-driven inflammation causing progressive scarring. His strongest interest was in reducing the causative antibodies. Voyxact’s two-year VISIONARY results extended its proteinuria-based interim approval with essentially flat eGFR against steady placebo deterioration: “basically this drug stopped disease progression.”
  • The newly disclosed composite kidney-event result carried a hazard ratio of 0.029: one event on treatment versus 28 on placebo. Kidney-replacement therapy occurred in no treated patients versus five controls. Brian also emphasized the apparently favorable safety profile and low-dose, once-monthly subcutaneous administration; his enthusiasm concerned the observed two-year course.
  • Vera’s atacicept also improved outcomes and slowed eGFR loss. Vera’s povetacicept showed similar interim proteinuria results, with an approval decision about a month away but longer-term eGFR still outstanding. Whether BAFF inhibition adds benefit to APRIL inhibition remained debated. A co-host who covers Climb Bio noted that its earlier-stage CLM-116 data were consistent with those of Chinese partner Mabworks, but it had neither proteinuria nor eGFR results yet.

7. ESMO’s strongest small-cell result contrasts with exploratory vaccine signals

  • Sam treated Moderna’s pancreatic vaccine poster cautiously: only around 19–20 patients, and comparison with BioNTech’s early study lacked rigor. Still, about half generated 34 new antigens despite pancreatic cancer’s low mutation burden. A 17% tissue-insufficiency rate matched melanoma. The antigen yield gave him more hope for upcoming studies in generally higher-mutation-burden tumors.
  • Yaron emphasized that BioNTech’s platform differed: 20 rather than 34 new antigens, unmodified mRNA and delivery without Moderna’s lipid nanoparticles. Its shareholders were split over retaining cancer vaccines versus reducing spending and concentrating on the broader pipeline. He favored pipeline focus, highlighting PD-1/VEGF, CTLA-4 lung-cancer data and a HER2 ADC.
  • Amgen’s DeLLphi-304 was Sam’s clear “practice-changing” result. He cited 21.1 months in the overall-survival data while noting approximately 16 months’ median follow-up and substantial censoring after month 12. He was “pretty convinced” DeLLphi-312 would also succeed, resetting the first-line small-cell lung-cancer setting and raising the competitive bar for subsequent drugs.
  • Yaron described the CD3 bispecific tarlatamab’s “long survival tail.” DLL3 ADCs had higher response rates, with durability and tolerability the concern, although newer results looked encouraging. Amgen’s collaboration testing Zai Lab’s ADC, which binds a different epitope, suggested a possible combination strategy as tarlatamab became entrenched.

8. PD-1/VEGF gains support as Genmab builds beyond royalties

  • Sam welcomed China’s first-line biliary-tract-cancer results for ivonescimab plus chemotherapy: overall and progression-free survival improved against the Imfinzi control, which itself performed well. It was another “tick in the box.” He expected Western benefit but left the patient groups unresolved ahead of HARMONi-3. Yaron anticipated tumor-specific outcomes: some standards of care, others “a bit of a wash.”
  • In the Genmab discussion, the speaker described frontline Epkinly’s 51% reduction in progression or death as a “complete home run.” Rina-S then beat Elahere in ovarian cancer, with a claimed “60 to 70% reduction in the risk of death,” activity across expression levels and activity after Elahere failure. The speaker expected second-line leadership and a race with Lilly into frontline treatment.
  • Genmab’s Merus-acquired head-and-neck program added another phase 3 “home run.” The speaker cited a 50% reduction in the risk of death and activity regardless of HPV status, while noting only topline data were available. Shares had doubled in three months. The speaker argued the three programs could bridge the 2029–30 Darzalex royalty cliff, with three prospective blockbuster launches by late 2027/early 2028 and growth continuing through that transition.

9. Tango’s combination promise meets pharmacokinetic and partnership constraints

  • The opening assessment of Tango’s vopimetostat PRMT5–RAS combination data in pancreatic cancer was positive. Yaron said efficacy was “phenomenally good,” but argued that Tango’s PRMT5 inhibitor increased exposure to Revolution Medicines’ RAS drug threefold, creating a separate problem: using roughly one-third of the RAS drug’s dose raises pricing and labeling questions. Tango also lacked a formal supply arrangement and would need to purchase the partner drug.
  • Yaron contrasted this with BMS’s PRMT5 inhibitor and formal partnership: BMS would co-develop the drugs globally, had a supply agreement, and was not expected to have the same drug-drug interaction. He also cited BMS’s pace, its more advanced lung-cancer monotherapy work and its own RAS agents in phase 1. Sam said he had intended to add comments on Tango and PRMT5 inhibitors, but the conversation ended before he did.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/episode-201-october-30-2026

item.title: Illia Polosukhin On The Future Of AI, Crypto, And How Near Is Going To Win
item.description: NEAR Intents processes about $4 billion monthly, with near.com contributing 10–20% of volume depending on the week. Protocol fees convert into NEAR purchases, while perps and Earn also direct fee shares toward buybacks, but Illia gave no cumulative buyback figure. Adoption and integration security remain tests after a partner-built BSC connection suffered a $3.8 million exploit.
item.content:encoded:
1000x · Avi Felman、Illia Polosukhin · 2026-10-30 · 50 min · 原语言 EN

NEAR Intents processes about $4 billion monthly, with near.com contributing 10–20% of volume depending on the week. Protocol fees convert into NEAR purchases, while perps and Earn also direct fee shares toward buybacks, but Illia gave no cumulative buyback figure. Adoption and integration security remain tests after a partner-built BSC connection suffered a $3.8 million exploit.

TL;DR

  • Illia says NEAR Intents processes about $4 billion monthly, with protocol fees converted into NEAR purchases. near.com contributes 10–20% of volume, depending on the week; perps and Earn also direct fee shares toward buybacks. His framing is that “every product is effectively generating revenue and then buying back NEAR,” although he supplies no cumulative buyback figure.
  • NEAR’s strategy now includes building the consumer finance product itself. Launched in February at NEARCON, near.com combines cross-chain assets, swaps, payments, stocks, perps and Earn with biometric login and a private shard running inside secure enclaves. Illia describes the broader business as “a vertically integrated stack for the AI and blockchain future.”
  • Illia thinks the larger opportunity is bringing $20–40 trillion of business commerce on-chain through AI agents. Agents would find counterparties and negotiate, while blockchain supplies escrow, settlement and dispute infrastructure for businesses that do not trust each other. “AI is a front end, blockchain is a back end”: the target is commercial relationships burdened by legal friction, while consumer grocery purchasing is already highly optimized.
  • Illia argues that agents handling money need verifiable inference and explicit spending limits. An arbitrary model endpoint—especially a router or free model, but also some actual providers—could substitute models or return malicious instructions: “you have no idea what's running behind it.” Near ID’s stated answer is signed GPU, model and software provenance; a financial agent’s policy engine requires approval before exceeding its permissions.
  • A $3.8 million exploit of a partner-built BSC connection exposed gaps in NEAR’s integration testing. Illia reports systems restored within an hour and “100% recovery” after identifying the attacker, while acknowledging that the connection had been insufficiently tested. NEAR is accelerating verification across interacting contracts; he claims a 100-fold cost reduction compared with what he phrases as “using OpenAI, like Sol or Astra”—a comparison that is unclear in the transcript.
  • Avi’s central commercial challenge is that strong technology alone does not bring users or distribution. Illia says NEAR now works “sales first,” citing wallet integrations, Venice’s end-to-end encrypted mode, Brave’s agent using NEAR as an option, and non-crypto, non-AI design partners. The concrete agent-commerce example is an event company monetizing its venue database through bookings: the intended business model is “paying for outcome.”

Digest

1. The AI ambition preceded NEAR, and compute determined its pace

  • Illia’s case for decentralized money starts with his grandparents’ Sberbank savings becoming worthless after the USSR dissolved. In post-Soviet Ukraine, he recalls bread prices rising, he thinks, 100× within roughly a year: “the currency didn't work yet.” Separately, competitive programming convinced him at 14 that “machine should write this code.”
  • A Google experiment around 2012–2013 supplied the next opening: an unsupervised model learned the concept of a cat from unlabeled internet pictures. Illia identifies it as a paper by Jeff Dean and Andrew Ng, trained across, he thinks, about 600 machines. He attributes the broader neural-network breakthrough to Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun getting multilayer networks and backpropagation to work, with the math and compute catching up. Illia wanted the equivalent for language; animals could see, but people tested intelligence by asking questions. He joined Google to work on question answering.
  • At Google, the obstacle was algorithmic: recurrent neural networks read one word at a time, trained slowly and could forget a long document’s beginning. His early answer projected words into vectors and summed them by paragraph, producing a fast, simple question-answering model on google.com around 2015–2016. Transformers extended that parallelism so GPUs could train larger models on more data.
  • To explain attention’s layers, Illia uses “cat sat on a wall”: first connect cat with sitting, then connect that combined concept with the wall. He describes KV cache as retaining processing so later questions can reuse it. OpenAI’s next move was to “scale the hell out of this,” through GPT-1 and GPT-2 toward ChatGPT; the architecture also worked for images, sound and video.

2. A micropayments problem became a two-year blockchain build

  • In 2017, Illia and co-founder Alex were training transformers on GitHub, aiming to replace separate applications and SaaS with computers that simply did what users requested. Limited compute constrained them. They recruited students in Eastern Europe, Southeast Asia and China to write code and explanations, then discovered that paying contributors across fragmented banking and payment systems was its own problem.
  • Crypto was supposed to solve global micropayments, but in 2018 transaction fees exceeded what they were paying students. The intended detour was an easy blockchain with cheap transactions whose prices would not rise with usage. Sharding, account abstraction and WebAssembly followed from those requirements. “It's gonna be six months,” Illia recalls; an August-to-January pitch became an October 2020 launch, a little over two years later.
  • The underestimate was permissionless coordination, despite both founders’ distributed-systems experience. Sharding raised routing and data-availability problems; they implemented, he thinks, five consensus designs. Illia says they broke liveness in the original Avalanche design, noting that Avalanche has since changed substantially. Their Whiteboard Series continued that approach: engineers explaining mechanisms deeply enough that flaws, including Loom’s exit game, could emerge on camera.

3. Chain abstraction now connects a consumer app to NEAR purchases

  • Avi challenges whether infrastructure can itself be consumer friendly. Illia’s answer starts with interviewing roughly 300 crypto companies in 2019 and testing onboarding themselves: buying a CryptoKitty from a new machine took 92 steps and 12 hours, with what he describes as 99.99% drop-off. Better wallets, smoother onboarding and meta-transactions could remove requirements such as acquiring gas before using an application.
  • That evolved into chain abstraction: restricting users to one chain resembled making Netflix viewers pay another currency because the next video lived on another server. With Intents, users specify an outcome—10 ZEC at a shielded address, funded with Solana USDC—and solvers choose the route. Asked whether this is just a bridge, Illia says solvers may use LayerZero, Binance or whatever achieves the outcome.
  • After waiting for others to build the consumer experience, NEAR launched near.com in February at NEARCON. Illia describes Face ID or fingerprint login, assets including Bitcoin and Zcash, payments, swaps, stocks, perps and Earn without juggling wallets or gas. Its private NEAR shard runs inside secure enclaves: encrypted transactions decrypt and execute there. He calls trading privately and paying out across ecosystems “privacy in motion.”
  • Illia puts Intents volume at about $4 billion monthly; near.com contributes 10–20%, depending on the week. The protocol’s take varies by asset, with less charged on stablecoins, and fees convert into NEAR. Perps and Earn also contribute fee shares toward buybacks. Avi presses for cumulative NEAR purchases, but Illia supplies no figure, pointing instead to revenue.near.org: “every product is effectively generating revenue and then buying back NEAR.”

4. Agent commerce targets the friction between businesses

  • Avi’s bigger objection: give an AI agent an Ethereum private key and it should already transact, regardless of the underlying chain—so what makes AI × blockchain distinctive? Illia accepts that commerce can happen without blockchain. His proposed division is “AI is a front end, blockchain is a back end”: agents find counterparties and negotiate, while markets execute transactions.
  • The concrete ambition is an agent arranging delivery of 50 tons of steel to the Port of LA, supported by escrow and dispute resolution. Illia argues that businesses’ lack of trust creates lawyers, long agreements and redlining; blockchain rails could reduce that friction. He initially describes a $20–50 trillion annual market, later describing $20–40 trillion of economy he thinks AI can bring on-chain.
  • He draws the boundary at business relationships, rather than grocery buying: consumer purchasing is already highly optimized. NEAR’s agent market begins with digital work because outcomes are easier to verify, then aims at broader commerce. Hiring agents also introduces a privacy requirement: an agent running on somebody else’s machine could expose your trading relationships and private information.

5. Inference provenance and spending policies address different agent risks

  • Illia’s inference warning is concrete: an API endpoint could substitute a smaller or quantized model, or fabricate a tool response instructing an agent to run a Bash command that infects the machine and steals private keys. He says this risk applies especially to routers and free models, but also to some actual providers. Avi expects OpenAI safeguards; Illia says the vulnerability sits with the agent and whichever endpoint it uses. With Hermes pointed at an arbitrary API, “you have no idea what's running behind it.” He also warns that browsing the internet and reading news can be another attack route, and says NEAR has an attack bench for this.
  • Illia names Near ID as the source of signed provenance identifying the GPU, exact model and software hashes, plus every node routing traffic. He calls it “full end-to-end verifiability and privacy.” Decentralizing GPU access is another benefit. He also sees a compute-market opportunity in replacing today’s bilateral supplier haggling—availability in two months, competing price quotes—with blockchain-based markets.
  • The planned near.com financial agent adds a separate control: a policy engine constrains execution, with explicit approval needed outside the policy. Illia compares it to hiring a money manager with restrictions, rather than handing over every dollar. Users could authorize even a memecoin strategy, but the agent should not choose one unilaterally. The same policy system is also a developer product for other applications.

6. The BSC exploit accelerated verification of the whole system

  • Discussing the previous week’s exploit, Illia says a BSC connection used by NEAR Intents lost $3.8 million. Shield detected the activity, the team paused and patched it, and systems were back online within an hour. He describes Shield as scanning NEAR and other chains for anomalies and suspected laundering. He says the concern started with the Bitget hack, where North Korea was effectively trying to move money around.
  • Shield’s data then helped identify the attacker, Illia says: “we got all the money back,” with “100% recovery” and an on-chain apology. Avi asks whether NEAR engineers built the link. It came from an ecosystem partner, but Illia concedes that it “wasn't tested to the level that we should be testing on.”
  • The response is to accelerate formal verification across the whole interacting system of contracts, alongside stronger monitoring. Illia says work had already been underway for months, claims number-one results on multiple benchmarks, and claims a 100-fold verification-cost reduction compared with what he phrases as “using OpenAI, like Sol or Astra.” The comparison is unclear in the transcript.

7. Distribution starts with customers and charges for outcomes

  • Avi’s go-to-market challenge is blunt: good technology has failed before, even when Turing Award winners built it. Illia says NEAR now works “sales first,” finding customers or design partners before building.
  • Distribution includes Trust Wallet, Ledger, LI.FI and SwapKit; Shield partnerships include Binance and ZeroShadow. Illia says Venice uses NEAR for its end-to-end encrypted mode, while Brave uses NEAR as an option for its agent. Robotics companies are also using NEAR on the back end for inference and agents.
  • The non-crypto, non-AI example is Philosophia’s venue-finding agent. Its accumulated internal database can answer a request for an institutional side event in Singapore for 50 people, replacing an email and an employee searching the records. The offering combines that database with an agent and charges for the outcome—actually booking the venue. Illia presents this as automating an existing commercial relationship.
  • The product he is most excited about is the financial agent operating on users’ existing near.com assets. The longer-term ambition is an agent market expanding from digital tasks into paid real-world actions: “paying for outcome,” and ultimately moving “real GDP” on-chain.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/illia-polosukhin-future-ai-crypto-near-is-going

item.title: What Robert Caro learned about power after studying it for 50 years
item.description: Caro says Moses overcame construction opposition through political will and Depression-era workers who were cheap and available. Popularity and overlapping offices with different terms made Moses hard to remove as his public purpose hardened, exposing democracy’s unresolved execution-versus-displacement tradeoff. Johnson’s persuasion rested on control of assignments, legislation and campaign money; Caro still cannot explain Vietnam’s escalation.
item.content:encoded:
Dwarkesh Podcast · Robert Caro、Dwarkesh Patel · 2026-10-30 · 61 min · 原语言 EN

Caro says Moses overcame construction opposition through political will and Depression-era workers who were cheap and available. Popularity and overlapping offices with different terms made Moses hard to remove as his public purpose hardened, exposing democracy’s unresolved execution-versus-displacement tradeoff. Johnson’s persuasion rested on control of assignments, legislation and campaign money; Caro still cannot explain Vietnam’s escalation.

TL;DR

  • Caro argues that exceptional political operators can break infrastructure deadlocks even when safeguards appear to make construction impossible. Property owners blocked roads in the 1920s, too; Moses nevertheless connected New Yorkers to Jones Beach, 27 miles away. Asked how democracies balance execution against displacement, Caro offers no easy institutional fix: “I’m not sure there is a good spot.”
  • Execution capacity can become difficult to discipline once popularity and institutional control reinforce each other. Moses’s overlapping offices and different terms protected him against removal, while his early public purpose hardened into disregard for opposition. Caro’s unanswered question for him: “Did you realize you were changing?”
  • Moses’s construction achievements also depended on an unusually favorable labor market. The Depression supplied unemployed architects and skilled workers who were available cheaply and had few alternatives. Caro emphasizes that “more than the wages, they were available”; political will operated alongside material conditions.
  • Johnson’s persuasion worked because he controlled resources that other politicians needed. Committee assignments, legislation and campaign money gave requests consequences beyond personal charm. “Behind his persuasion was the power,” Caro says; Johnson could do things “to you or for you.”
  • Caro credits Johnson’s domestic breakthroughs to a determination Kennedy did not share, while leaving Vietnam’s escalation unresolved. Teaching poor children in Cotulla helped shape Johnson’s drive for education, civil rights and anti-poverty legislation. Vietnam destroyed the presidency’s promise, but Caro resists a finished explanation: “I’m still trying to figure that out.”
  • Faster access to information does not necessarily accelerate work whose bottleneck is reading and judgment. Digital searches help Caro locate Vietnam oral histories, but he doubts his earlier books would have been completed faster. His discipline for sustaining years of work is to define the book’s purpose in one sentence, or at most a paragraph.
  • Caro’s unpublished research is a substantial resource for future scholarship. He recalls cutting 350,000 words from The Power Broker and preserving detailed notes from roughly 700 interviews for that book alone. He accepted “a great deal less money” to place his archives in New York, prioritizing accessibility and the possibility that others will recover what publication left out.

Digest

1. Political genius can break construction deadlocks

  • Patel challenges Caro with the Second Avenue Subway: roughly 50 years of construction, 1½ miles opened and more than $4 billion spent. Caro rejects the assumption that earlier builders faced an unobstructed system. In the 1920s, property owners could block roads and people were already saying, “Government can’t build anything.” Exceptional operators nevertheless found ways through.
  • Jones Beach supplies Caro’s example: Moses saw a magnificent beach only 27 miles from New York City and determined to make it accessible. The connecting road required crossing properties whose owners opposed it; Caro notes that Moses initially lacked eminent-domain power. Overcoming those obstacles was “an act of political genius,” alongside the will to insist, “I’m going to build it.”
  • Patel contrasts stalled construction with China’s tens of thousands of miles of railway over 10–20 years, accompanied by displacement and recklessness. Asked for a middle ground, Caro answers, “I’m not sure there is a good spot.” He wants someone capable of building despite opposition, while rejecting Moses’s ruthlessness and disregard for public opinion.
  • The Depression materially helped Moses: unemployed architects lined Fifth Avenue, while workers had few alternative jobs. “More than the wages, they were available,” Caro stresses; Moses could hire cheaply and fire ruthlessly. Cheap skilled labor also helps explain architectural ornament: Caro describes elaborate stone carving opposite his 15th-floor apartment, visible to almost nobody. Builders could afford such work because “people came cheap.”

2. Moses’s idealism hardened into power resistant to correction

  • Caro rejects the reading that everything Moses did was bad: “You didn’t read the book.” His early subject was an idealist pursuing merit-based civil-service promotion and recreation for city residents. The change matters: building to improve lives became building because Moses wanted something built, regardless of hardship. Caro describes a “hardening,” hesitating to call it corruption.
  • The Cross Bronx Expressway is Caro’s decisive example: tens of thousands evicted without relocation provisions, followed immediately by “the world’s longest traffic jam.” When Bronx politician Henry Epstein argued that moving the route two blocks south would displace only “a couple of hundred people,” Moses exposed his affair and, in Caro’s account, effectively destroyed him. He learned to find opponents’ weaknesses and use them.
  • Could earlier governors and mayors have dismissed Moses, as Rockefeller eventually accepted his threatened resignation? Caro first says yes: Moses was unelected. His practical answer is different: popularity made dismissal politically prohibitive, while overlapping offices with different terms and removal rules protected him. Only after “cracks appeared in the armor” could someone prepared to withstand public and newspaper criticism remove him.
  • Caro witnessed decline through an office’s silence: earlier interviews ended with a secretary bringing requests and telephone messages; one late interview ended with none. “There had been no calls.” Loyal aides still deferred to Moses, and Caro thinks he expected persistence to win again. Granted one more question, Caro would ask, “Did you realize you were changing?” He thinks Moses did not.

3. Johnson’s persuasion rested on leverage and an overriding purpose

  • For Caro, Johnson’s celebrated personal persuasion cannot be separated from institutional control. A senator asked for a vote knew Johnson could grant or deny a committee assignment or help pass a desired law. The arm around the shoulder carried consequences: “Behind his persuasion was the power.”
  • Asked whether he wished Coke Stevenson had won the 1948 Senate election, Caro answers yes. He regards Stevenson as an idealist who also accomplished things as Texas governor and believes he would have been “a great senator.” The tragedy was not simply defeat: Stevenson never fully grasped that Johnson would employ the methods used against him.
  • Caro rejects Patel’s counterfactual that Kennedy, with Johnson remaining majority leader, could have delivered Johnson’s domestic breakthroughs earlier. Kennedy was “a good president,” particularly in foreign policy, but lacked Johnson’s “overriding desire” to change America, shaped by teaching poor children in Cotulla. Caro credits that drive with civil rights and anti-poverty laws America otherwise would not have had. Why did Johnson keep escalating Vietnam? “I’m still trying to figure that out.”
  • Patel asks whether Johnson’s and Moses’s 16-hour days reflected unusual physical reserves. Caro attributes them to will: “A lot of people have their energy.” Fatigue barely entered their calculations. Johnson called one senator at 5 a.m.; the reply was, “Oh, Lyndon, I was just lying here waiting for your call.”

4. Relentless interviewing connects documents to decisions

  • Patel sees Caro sharing his subjects’ refusal to accept obstacles; Caro hopes he does not share their ruthlessness. His reporting imperative is narrower: some witnesses possess knowledge nobody else can supply. Johnson’s first secretary accompanied him across Texas. “There’s no other human being on earth” who could explain those hours, making an honest interview indispensable.
  • John Connally illustrates how documents sharpen questioning. Caro knew Connally collected and distributed campaign money under Johnson’s instructions. Requests for $1,500 might receive $1,500, $500, “No,” or “No, never.” Connally explained that the last meant the congressman would never receive Johnson’s money. Asking why a particular man received that judgment opened the revealing stories about how Johnson allocated political support.
  • On sustaining a book through five or ten years without public feedback, Caro’s first answer is candid: “You’re not” sure you are on track. His safeguard, learned after The Power Broker, is to think through the whole book and reduce its purpose to one sentence, or at most a paragraph. Otherwise, three years later, he risks asking, “What am I trying to do?”

5. Faster discovery leaves the hardest work intact

  • Digital resources now help Caro locate soldiers’ oral histories and documents for a detailed account of the Battle of the Ia Drang Valley. Whether they would have accelerated earlier books produces a wavering answer: they “might’ve made things faster,” but he ultimately doubts completion would have been faster. He would still read the documents; “finding them is a small thing” compared with reading them.
  • Caro recalls giving editor Bob Gottlieb a 1,050,000-word Power Broker manuscript. Keeping it to one volume meant reducing it to about 700,000 words: 350,000 words removed. He still regrets material readers never encountered. Yet anticipating cuts did not stop him writing what he thought belonged: “I don’t seem to have the ability not to write the stuff.”
  • The unpublished record includes detailed typed notes for roughly 700 interviews for The Power Broker alone, and extensive Senate research. Caro placed his archives with the New-York Historical Society despite substantially larger offers elsewhere. He accepted less money—an amount that mattered to him—because he wanted accessible material in New York rather than somewhere researchers would have to fly to reach.
  • Sam Rayburn exemplifies what those cabinets could yield. Caro included only a brief chapter, although Rayburn ran the House and helped pass many Roosevelt bills. Caro says there is “no good biography of Sam Rayburn.” His hope is that another researcher uses the underlying material to recover consequential history his own books could not accommodate.

6. Loneliness shaped both Johnson’s world and Caro’s working life

  • Patel asks whether an ordinary person’s biography could illuminate an era as powerfully. Caro’s frontier research suggests the richness: witnesses discussing Johnson also recounted their grandparents’ lives. Loneliness especially struck him. One elderly interviewee directed him 22 miles out of Austin, then another 22 miles along a dirt road; he passed neither house nor person. He doubts America fully understands the “heroism” of enduring such isolation.
  • Caro’s own solitude is deliberate and costly. He turns off his telephone each morning and expects to speak to nobody all day, despite considering himself friendly. Calling someone would “break the concentration.” He returns calls only at day’s end; some friends understand, others do not. The demands of sustained attention, he says, have “impacted my entire life.”

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/robert-caro-master-biographer-reflects-at-91

item.title: What Happens When Both Sides of a Case Use AI?
item.description: AI could make previously uneconomic plaintiff cases viable: Eve CEO Jay Madheswaran says firms need at least $5,000 in fees, while 96% of labor-and-employment cases are rejected. One Los Angeles firm raised capacity from about 100 to 500 clients per attorney using Eve across intake and casework; however, Madheswaran says end-to-end autonomous case completion remains unfinished.
item.content:encoded:
The a16z Show · Jay Madheswaran、Alex Rampell · 2026-10-30 · 52 min · 原语言 EN

AI could make previously uneconomic plaintiff cases viable: Eve CEO Jay Madheswaran says firms need at least $5,000 in fees, while 96% of labor-and-employment cases are rejected. One Los Angeles firm raised capacity from about 100 to 500 clients per attorney using Eve across intake and casework; however, Madheswaran says end-to-end autonomous case completion remains unfinished.

TL;DR

  • AI could make previously uneconomic plaintiff cases worth taking. Eve CEO Jay Madheswaran says lawyers generally need at least $5,000 in fees to accept a case, while 96% of labor-and-employment cases get rejected. Automating intake, qualification, and legal work could unlock that demand; Alex Rampell’s framing is “revenue expansion,” because firms can represent more people.
  • One Los Angeles firm increased capacity from about 100 to 500 clients per attorney. Madheswaran credits intensive adoption across intake, handoffs, and settlement preparation. Rampell calls this a “shadow labor market”: the opportunity extends beyond historical legal-software spending into work that previously required additional employees.
  • The defensibility argument rests on workflow context and legal information absent from public datasets. Madheswaran says fewer than 1% of cases produce opinions, leaving settlement outcomes and effective tactics largely inaccessible to general models. Even Albert Einstein dropped into a firm “will not be productive for quite some time”; Eve supplies context while, he says, never training on privileged client-case data.
  • Small firms could become much larger businesses through specialization and consolidation. On a $25,000 settlement, Madheswaran estimates roughly $8,000 in attorney fees, with half consumed by labor and 30% by marketing. He expects proprietary datasets to help firms look “more like software companies,” expanding narrow expertise nationally or integrating acquisitions faster.
  • Outcome pricing fits contingency law, but broader adoption requires predictable delivery costs. Eve shifted away from its initial “tall, grande, venti” subscription approach after learning that customers valued additional clients and outcomes. Madheswaran expects savings to fund more compute and legal work, while preserving a hedge on hourly billing: “I don’t think it’s going to die completely.”
  • Stronger plaintiff firms could change defense tactics and reshape how disputes are resolved. One customer answered holiday-timed discovery requests the same day using an Eve agent, defeating a workload-pressure tactic. Madheswaran expects routine exchanges through “agents talking to agents” and, in some areas, automated dispute resolution that assists human judgment.
  • Fully autonomous case resolution remains a development target. Asked whether Eve has completed an entire case without intervention, Madheswaran answers, “Not yet, but we’re close.” Cases involve “probably 10,000 back and forths”; engineers are the constraint, and his claim of hundreds of billions of dollars in vehicle-accident value depends on delivering that end-to-end capability.

Digest

1. Labor costs exclude clients even when lawyers charge on success

  • Madheswaran’s starting point is “legal AI for real people”: contingency firms collect only when clients win, making representation possible without an open-ended $500–$600 hourly bill. More legal work can improve outcomes, but someone must finance that work. Eve aims to cover the path from the first call to settlement, “giving David a slingshot to take down Goliath.”
  • Rampell’s market-failure example is a client with $1,000 of damages: a lawyer taking one-third cannot cover the necessary paralegal and attorney work. Contingency removes the client’s upfront bill without making the case economical. As Rampell puts it, “even if I win, I lose,” because carrying costs can exceed the potential return to the firm.
  • Madheswaran says lawyers do not take cases yielding less than $5,000 in fees; even at that level, many lose money, with a few big wins carrying the portfolio. His example is a fender bender below the deductible: even if that deductible is $3,000–$4,000, “no lawyer in America will touch that case.” For an individual, he notes, that can mean a lost paycheck.
  • In employment law, he describes a 30–45-minute intake call followed by roughly 10 hours researching whether alleged misconduct fits a cause of action. Only then might counsel discover the case cannot produce $5,000; he says 96% of labor-and-employment cases are rejected. Eve answers calls, qualifies prospects against the firm’s criteria, and can begin a demand or preliminary work immediately, changing that screening equation.

2. Revenue expands when the whole workflow gains capacity

  • Rampell’s central distinction: “if I use Eve, I make a lot more money for my firm,” because it can accept more cases. “It’s actually revenue expansion.” Madheswaran describes bottlenecks moving from a solo attorney returning calls to an intake team overwhelmed by successful marketing; automating one task is insufficient if work simply piles up at the next handoff.
  • One Los Angeles firm increased its load from about 100 to 500 clients per attorney, Madheswaran says. He credits the firm with working hard and using Eve “up to the max”: intake, qualification, agent-managed handoffs, and mediation preparation, including settlement outcomes and previously successful tactics. He pictures the lawyer as “almost a data scientist and engineer,” improving a continuously advancing process.
  • Historically, he says, a plaintiff practice needed little more than a cellphone and email; some solos avoided even Microsoft Word. Software had not solved the labor constraint, while institutional defense buyers attracted development budgets. Rampell calls the opportunity a “shadow labor market”: outcomes run into hundreds of billions of dollars, so historical software spending understates the addressable work. His 12-cent-an-hour paralegal is a hypothetical illustrating labor AI could supply.

3. Private case knowledge makes general intelligence useful

  • Rampell’s application-layer challenge is direct: why won’t ChatGPT, Claude, or their developers absorb this business? Madheswaran welcomes better models, but “if you drop Albert Einstein into a law firm today, he will not be productive for quite some time.” Intelligence still needs the firm’s working context and the information required to act effectively.
  • Madheswaran says less than 1% of cases actually settle and get turned into case opinions; most settle before litigation, leaving essential information outside scrapable public data. Rampell makes it concrete: knowing GEICO actually paid $29,000 on an injury claim matters. An insurer dealing with 100,000 firms sees patterns fragmented plaintiff practices cannot. Rampell points to insurers’ Colossus software as an existing information advantage.
  • For Madheswaran, the missing knowledge is practical: an effective demand against State Farm for soft-tissue injuries, the local courts, and opposing counsel’s behavior. His organizing question is “what is the best thing I can do at this particular moment?” That decision repeats throughout a case; Eve is meant to make the context usable at every step.
  • Rampell presses on sharing data across separate firms. Madheswaran distinguishes privileged cases—“we don’t train on that data ever”—from tactics attorneys already exchange through continuing legal education. Eve hires attorneys and tracks case success; its Auditor reviews every page of every case overnight for issues an ideal attorney would catch. He says “almost every single case has missed information,” explaining the value of comprehensive review.

4. Stronger plaintiffs change tactics and expose court bottlenecks

  • Rampell’s pushback is that insurers and defense firms will acquire AI “superpowers” too. Madheswaran accepts a world where 99%, maybe 99.9%, of representation work is AI, while retaining a human difference in client understanding, local relationships, and advocacy. Institutions still have money and time as weapons. He thinks routine exchanges will become “agents talking to agents”; some Eve customers already spend more time preparing for trial.
  • One observed change is tactical: a defense firm repeatedly sent discovery just before Thanksgiving or another major holiday, expecting the plaintiff team to rush or sacrifice vacation. The plaintiff firm created an Eve agent that answered the same day. Madheswaran’s reading of the defense reaction: “this is what happens when the other side has resources.” He says defense still largely bills hourly and has not matched plaintiffs’ pace.
  • Rampell’s court-capacity concern comes from his own Wells Fargo dispute: after four hours of frustration, he told Codex/ChatGPT, “Sue Wells Fargo.” He says four hours later it had filed the suit and found a process server, but the court date was in February. Lowering the cost of initiating legal work leaves adjudication as a bottleneck.
  • Madheswaran thinks it is “inevitable” that more disputes move outside courts, extending existing channels such as veterans’ committees, the EEOC, mediation, and arbitration. In “some pockets,” he expects “ADR, automated dispute resolution,” using AI-assisted neutral parties to assemble historical facts and accelerate decisions. He does not think judgment itself will be replaced; people must still address biases that might exist in those comparisons.

5. Software economics could support specialists and rollups

  • Rampell asks whether a firm handling 100 cases per lawyer, then 500, perhaps eventually 5,000, could become a billion-dollar business. Madheswaran thinks firms will look “more like software companies.” On a $25,000 settlement, he estimates roughly $8,000 for the attorney: about half goes to labor, 30% to marketing, and the remainder may be profit. That structure makes reinvestment difficult when improvement means hiring a better attorney.
  • The prospective change is a proprietary dataset that improves results in a narrow field. Madheswaran expects specialization to deepen from employment or intellectual property into soft-tissue injuries with particular fact patterns. Targeted advertising might then beat Morgan & Morgan’s broad billboards. Rampell draws out the expansion path: get good locally, then take that competence nationwide; Madheswaran agrees.
  • The opposite path is consolidation. Madheswaran says customers on the scale of Morgan & Morgan are buying other firms because Eve can shorten integration around the client’s desired legal outcome. By handling operational and workflow changes, the platform reduces painful reintegration and can accelerate the point at which an acquisition becomes worthwhile.

6. Outcome pricing requires knowing what delivery will cost

  • Rampell notes that contingency firms already sell the outcomes SaaS vendors are now trying to price. Madheswaran admits Eve initially copied the “tall, grande, venti” subscription model: “we didn’t know any better.” Customers cared about serving more clients, forcing an early shift toward outcome-based pricing, roughly a year and a half before the conversation.
  • Rampell’s defense of hourly billing is information asymmetry: clients may not articulate their needs, and scope can change. Madheswaran agrees that a new case might require 10 or 100 hours before anyone knows. His broader requirement is to infer, from the facts, how much compute an outcome needs—through better data and better execution—so legal work can be priced and delivered more predictably.
  • Madheswaran’s hedge matters: “I don’t think it’s going to die completely,” he says of the billable hour. Some legal work reveals its value only years later. Elsewhere, predictable outcomes permit amortized costs, and labor savings can fund more tokens and more useful work. The intended cycle is better outcomes and more revenue, with savings reinvested in serving clients.

7. End-to-end autonomy remains an engineering problem

  • Asked what limits growth, Madheswaran says benchmarks grading whether one task went “mostly okay” miss the problem. Eve needs reliable outcomes across long-horizon workflows, built separately for each case type. There is still “a decent amount of human touch needed per case,” although he says that is falling month over month. The main constraint is engineers.
  • Rampell asks the essential test: has Eve autonomously answered the phone, onboarded a client, and obtained the insurer’s check end to end? “Not yet, but we’re close.” Madheswaran estimates a single case involves “probably 10,000 back and forths.” Earlier, he describes matters lasting six months to a year, making reliability over extended sequences central.
  • His concrete example is medical-record collection: outbound calls to insurers and healthcare providers take two weeks today, he says. Eve’s voice agents make those calls, sometimes encountering other agents and learning to get past them. Record collection, document creation, and opposing-party conversations are being automated, but some human intervention remains; early versions of the broader workflow are live with customers.
  • Madheswaran says completing vehicle-accident cases end to end would unlock value in the “hundreds of billions of dollars,” conditional on delivering that capability. He says Eve has helped “a couple hundred thousand clients” so far, against an aspiration to reach hundreds of millions.
