item.title: I Got Interviewed! The Story Behind Sourcery, Alex Karp, Sam Altman Clip..
item.description: Sourcery grew from O’Shea’s internal funding tracker into a public research archive, with LinkedIn bringing most subscribers. She favors broad promotion over exclusives, estimating 90% of interview work happens afterward; announcement timing helped early podcast traction. Behind Genius has backed over 60 companies across three funds, emphasizing “technical storytellers”; Doherty says Knox Metals’ visibility drives orders and investor interest.
item.content:encoded:
Sourcery · Paige Finn Doherty、Molly O'Shea · 2026-10-30 · 66 min · 原语言 EN

Sourcery grew from O’Shea’s internal funding tracker into a public research archive, with LinkedIn bringing most subscribers. She favors broad promotion over exclusives, estimating 90% of interview work happens afterward; announcement timing helped early podcast traction. Behind Genius has backed over 60 companies across three funds, emphasizing “technical storytellers”; Doherty says Knox Metals’ visibility drives orders and investor interest.

TL;DR

  • Sourcery grew from an investing workflow that compounded into a research archive and media business. Molly O’Shea began by collecting funding rounds, acquisitions, exits, IPOs and new funds for colleagues, then published the newsletter publicly. Investor identities, round sizes and time between financings supplied signals; years of tracking Stripe, Coinbase, Flexport and Figma built familiarity. Her honest exception: “Definitely not OpenAI.”
  • O’Shea approached X as a distribution system she could learn through repeated experimentation. After Elon Musk’s takeover, she saw the platform as a game and used her writing and creativity to grow while working at an RIA that restricted what she could post about. Paige Finn Doherty—not O’Shea—described reading summaries of the published algorithm and practicing 140- or 280-character storytelling, especially the first line. O’Shea’s assessment of “breaking” remains tentative: “I think I get penalized every now and again for it.”
  • Funding announcements need sustained distribution and company participation to earn attention. O’Shea credits announcement timing with early podcast traction, but argues that exclusives which shut out other coverage are “shooting themselves in the foot.” Her billboard analogy requires repeated exposure, and her production estimate puts “maybe 10%” before the interview: “90% is afterwards.”
  • A public wish list converted audience goodwill into access to difficult guests. O’Shea thinks she has interviewed “probably over 20%” of her original 100 dream guests. Adding an initially omitted Alex Karp prompted an introduction; earnings and the biography Philosopher in the Valley supplied the reason to interview him. She read the book in roughly two days and had to reach New York within about five.
  • O’Shea recalls Karp’s sword moment as unexpected and important to Sourcery’s walking-interview lore. The conversation also cites roughly 4.3 million views for the sword clip, 4–4.5 million for the interview, and Paige’s estimate of 50 million-plus wider views. Paige says the interview is pinned to her profile; the transcript does not clearly reconcile that with O’Shea’s account of her Karp interview. The Jack Altman exchange about Sam being his brother was Paige’s; whether it was a bet remains unresolved.
  • O’Shea is prioritizing guest selection and interview quality over adjacent investing opportunities. Despite describing annual reach in the hundreds of millions of impressions and views, she has declined fund, advisory and public-company board opportunities to preserve focus. Factory and headquarters tours attract substantial YouTube audiences, although she admits, “I actually can’t really think very well when I walk.”
  • Paige Finn Doherty’s investing thesis connects technical execution with the ability to explain it. Behind Genius has backed over 60 companies across three funds, emphasizing “technical storytellers.” Her example is Knox Metals, whose public presence she says drives customer orders and investor interest; its new 75,000-square-foot Detroit facility also supplies material for her next phase of video storytelling.

Digest

1. O’Shea used her creative advantage to preserve career options

  • Growing up in Westport, Connecticut, O’Shea watched her mother build and design homes and her father run a marketing agency. Business ownership was the working life she understood. A beachside lemonade stand with her sister supplied an early pricing experiment: “No, I think we’re going to raise prices. $5 a cup.”
  • Her creative training began with drawing houses, teaching herself dimensions and filling sketchbooks with imagined towns. Commissioned paintings for her mother’s clients and graphic-design work connected that ability to revenue. She enjoyed “making it, refining it, and selling it,” then using the money to finance the next project.
  • Asked why she studied art at NYU, O’Shea answers: “‘Cause it was gonna get me in.” At a competitive school where classmates accumulated academic credentials, art was her differentiated strength. “If you know your asymmetric advantage, you have to pour into that,” she says; additional art classes and a strong portfolio supplied her route into college.
  • Architecture faced a different calculation. A USC summer intensive meant roughly nine studio hours daily, while professional education could take five to six years; the eventual compensation did not justify the commitment for her. She wanted “an efficient ROI” and alternatives if the career proved unsuitable. NYU’s examples of theater students entering finance and other crossovers offered that flexibility.

2. Paige’s route to venture differed from O’Shea’s fund-side career

  • The Google 30 Weeks and Blue & Tuck story belongs to host Paige Finn Doherty. As a project manager at the designers’ incubator, she was also building a sports-bra company with a phone pocket. She describes using NASA-derived, silver-ion-plated fabric that blocked radio frequencies. Her research into material science led from thinking they needed to invent a fabric to finding existing suppliers.
  • Doherty says meeting a venture capitalist made the job look easy. She was young, at NYU, living in expensive New York and working many jobs; she lacked the money and risk appetite to build a company without income. VC seemed like a way to learn from companies and potentially use those lessons to start one in her 30s.
  • O’Shea’s own route was different. She worried firms would not hire someone with an art degree, finished her credits early and shifted toward entrepreneurship and business classes. She joined a growth-equity fund doing pre-IPO investments, including spreadsheet modeling, decks and research, which she found “a really satisfying intellectual journey.”
  • The first few funds she worked for were emerging managers, and she says she probably changed funds every year or so. One could not raise another fund, and she was let go from her first job out of college—a “harsh reality check.” She learned that “you can’t depend on the world” and that she had to stay ready to apply her skills to the next opportunity.
  • Finding companies, understanding trends and packaging research helped her identify gaps and overlooked opportunities for her teams. She says she was particularly good at finding companies and diligencing them.

3. Sourcery’s first product was curated information for an investment team

  • At TMV, O’Shea tried to make herself useful by taking work off the partners’ plates and helping them see ahead. Sourcery began as an internal newsletter aggregating financings, acquisitions, exits, IPOs and fund activity. Initially she spent perhaps an hour before work compiling it daily; the workload eventually pushed her toward a weekly cadence.
  • After moving to New York Life Ventures, she published it publicly, and friends spread it through word of mouth. She cannot reliably date that launch: “I have zero clue.” Later, posting on LinkedIn—particularly around her time at Upfront—became a substantial acquisition channel. She says most newsletter subscribers came from LinkedIn.
  • The value was curation: investor names, amounts raised and time between rounds supplied observable signals, while constant exposure built a mental bank of companies. She had followed businesses including Stripe, Coinbase, Flexport and Figma for years before interviewing them. Asked whether she spotted emerging winners, she immediately qualifies the record: “Definitely not OpenAI.” Stripe, by contrast, seemed “really obvious” to her.

4. O’Shea’s X growth and Doherty’s algorithm study were distinct

  • O’Shea dates her serious commitment to X to Elon Musk’s takeover. Having studied his companies and operating habits, she expected a system she could learn: “Game on.” Her writing and creativity were useful, while employment at an RIA restricted portfolio-related commentary. She built a professional posting playbook within those constraints rather than starting with a newsletter revenue target.
  • Doherty—not O’Shea—described reading summaries of X’s open-sourced algorithm and studying how it weighted content. She said she practiced psychological hooks and storytelling in 140 or 280 characters, “more specifically in the first line,” connecting that craft to startup fundraising and sales.
  • O’Shea says she does not know where the recurring “breaking” opener came from, but has “obviously abused that.” Her assessment remains tentative: “I think I get penalized every now and again for it.” She says X had indicated excessive use could lead to downranking, so she would save it for funding announcements, though she sometimes uses it jokingly.

5. Announcement coverage depends on repetition and reciprocal promotion

  • Timing interviews around announcements helped the podcast break out. Doherty points to companies directing promotional resources toward launch coverage; O’Shea adds the surrounding “media storm.” Funding news offers novelty, numbers and FOMO, particularly among investors checking which rounds happened without them. But competing announcements mean a financing still needs a reason for people to care.
  • Her strongest disagreement with conventional launch management concerns exclusives that close off other media opportunities: companies are “shooting themselves in the foot.” She allows that a Bloomberg exclusive may be worthwhile, but says, “The internet doesn’t work like that.” Her recommendation is broader coverage, ideally with distinctive angles, while maintaining quality and avoiding spam.
  • Repetition explains the mechanism. Her analogy is a billboard: “you won’t notice that billboard until you’ve seen it 20 times”; perhaps the 50th exposure prompts someone to read it. Investors, founders and employees sharing a story contribute to that repeated visibility. She wants authentic participation from the team, rather than paid partnerships or repetitive posts that feel manufactured.
  • Her frustration is companies requesting interviews and then failing to engage when they appear. Production involves scarce slots, travel, editing and equipment; she also supplies files and offers custom clips. A repost or reply helps reach investors, LPs, family offices, operators and prospective employees. Agreeing with Doherty about promotion’s workload, she estimates “maybe 10%” comes before an interview: “90% is afterwards.”

6. A public guest list supplied both introductions and a reason to interview Karp

  • O’Shea’s dream-guest list expanded from 20 names to 100 and appeared around October of the preceding year. People tagged candidates and volunteered introductions because the request was visible and concrete. She now thinks she has interviewed “probably over 20%” of it, and wants the list to become an annual exercise.
  • Karp was initially missing. A friend at Palantir challenged the omission, prompting a revision that placed him at “1B” alongside Ivanka’s “1A.” The friend forwarded it, and Karp reportedly liked its ordering, including Palmer Luckey ahead of Marc Andreessen. O’Shea’s takeaway is that people can help when they know what she wants.
  • “Maybe three days later,” the friend called with an opening. Palantir’s earnings and the biography Philosopher in the Valley supplied the occasion: “There has to be some sort of novelty or uniqueness to the interview and a reason to do it.” She read the book in approximately two days and needed to reach New York within about five.
  • The day before, she learned that Palantir would provide production but wanted a walking interview—her first. Karp was “not the best at sitting still,” she explains. A preliminary 15- or 20-minute conversation helped him understand who she was. The format subsequently changed Sourcery’s direction; she credits that interview with substantial impact and reach.

7. The sword and Altman clips made personality part of distribution

  • O’Shea says the sword sequence was unexpected. She thought they would take a photograph afterward; instead, Karp began demonstrating with the sword while the crew kept filming. In her account, she wore a dress and heels for a public-company CEO interview while he wore a ski outfit. Her reaction was visible: “What’s going on?” Nobody present had expected the performance.
  • O’Shea says the first walking interview “literally cascaded” the Sourcery walking-interview lore. The conversation later cites roughly 4.3 million views for the sword clip and 4–4.5 million for the interview. Paige says the interview is pinned to her profile and estimates the video’s wider circulation at 50 million-plus views. The transcript does not clearly reconcile those profile and view-count references with O’Shea’s account of her Karp interview, so the figures cannot be confidently assigned to her interview.
  • The Jack Altman exchange was Paige’s interview, about his podcast Uncapped. She asked whether Jack was nervous to interview Sam Altman; Jack said Sam was his brother and asked her to keep the exchange in. Asked whether the discovery was a bet, Paige first says they will leave it unanswered, then says, “Maybe.”

8. Guest selection requires turning down opportunities that could perform well

  • O’Shea describes Sourcery’s annual reach in the hundreds of millions of impressions and views, yet says the work is still unfinished. Scheduling requires frequent rearrangements and sometimes sudden cross-country or European travel. She concedes that announcement interviews can generate better immediate metrics because attention is already concentrated around them; that does not automatically make them her priority.
  • Her goal is an intentional “archive” of people and perspectives. “The goal is not to be busy and full,” she says. She could fill the calendar with announcements, but that would crowd out the guests she most wants. The same focus explains declining fund, advisory and public-company board opportunities that would conflict with her current work.
  • Jenny Johnson of Franklin Templeton illustrates the kind of interview she values. Johnson had just returned from Uzbekistan and warned that she was not thinking clearly; O’Shea found her references and historical knowledge unusually strong anyway. Encounters like that reinforce the need to return to the central project: refining the guest mix and capturing substantive stories.

9. Walking tours expand the format while making the interview harder

  • O’Shea still defines herself as an investor. Research, diligence, market maps and data shape her interviews: “Does it actually have longevity?” She wants to understand how a business grows, whether its underlying model is durable and what happens when ten competitors appear. Improving the show means delivering better information while expanding the audience intentionally.
  • The Karp interview required neither an earpiece nor note cards; she credits memory and intense concentration. Stage work initially felt different: she recalls taking a shot before a morning Citadel Securities conference appearance because she was so nervous, despite rarely drinking. Now she reduces the task to “asking questions and listening,” and says she enjoys moderating live.
  • She calls walking footage “10, maybe 100 to 1000x more dynamic.” Factory and headquarters tours supply changing surroundings, tools and demonstrations of how things are made—material she thinks suits YouTube particularly well. Those interviews have attracted hundreds of thousands of views. She predicts the Figure AI tour will “probably” reach a million views “pretty soon.”
  • Doherty asks whether they should be walking during this interview. O’Shea’s candid answer: “I actually can’t really think very well when I walk.” The format is demanding for some investors and public-company CEOs, too. Platform comparisons also require care: she considers million-view outcomes easier on X because of its social-network effects, while Instagram remains something she is learning.

10. Behind Genius connects technical storytelling to business development

  • Turning the interview around, O’Shea asks Doherty about Behind Genius. Doherty traces her interest in venture to watching Silicon Valley, then posting what she was learning on Twitter without an existing VC network. She also wrote a children’s book about venture, published a year after college. Behind Genius grew from that path and now backs “technical storytellers.”
  • Doherty has invested in over 60 companies across three funds. Her example is Knox Metals: its founder’s presence in the reindustrialization movement, she says, has materially helped customer orders and inbound investor interest. She recently toured its new 75,000-square-foot Detroit facility, providing a physical setting for explaining what the business does.
  • Doherty experiences walking interviews differently from O’Shea: objects make questions concrete—“this block of metal or this saw.” The conversation is also her 100th Seed to Harvest episode. Her next ambition is to invest more heavily in video storytelling and stronger guests, potentially borrowing O’Shea’s public top-100-list approach.

item.title: Will Druck Kick Off The Next Phase of Crypto's Bull Market?
item.description: Druckenmiller’s tweet about TradeXYZ and ICE’s involvement could make onchain markets useful first as institutional price data, before large trades can be absorbed. Anthropic’s $17 million open interest, with less than $4 million hedgeable, shows the gap between pricing and execution. ICE may widen Hyperliquid’s U.S. reach, but KYC, separate order books and incumbent resistance leave access and liquidity unresolved.
item.content:encoded:
Empire · Jason Yanowitz、Santiago Roel Santos · 2026-10-30 · 58 min · 原语言 EN

Druckenmiller’s tweet about TradeXYZ and ICE’s involvement could make onchain markets useful first as institutional price data, before large trades can be absorbed. Anthropic’s $17 million open interest, with less than $4 million hedgeable, shows the gap between pricing and execution. ICE may widen Hyperliquid’s U.S. reach, but KYC, separate order books and incumbent resistance leave access and liquidity unresolved.

TL;DR

  • TradeXYZ’s market data could make onchain price discovery institutionally useful before the markets can absorb institutional-size trades. Druckenmiller tweeted about TradeXYZ; Santos described him as making a strategic investment, while the discussion also identifies ICE as the investor. Yanowitz calls the moment “a defining moment for the industry,” comparing it with Paul Tudor Jones’s May 2020 Bitcoin endorsement and expecting roughly 8–10× onchain-volume growth over the next year. The immediate use case is pre-IPO and weekend price discovery: Santos cites $17 million of Anthropic open interest, with less than $4 million hedgeable.
  • ICE could give Hyperliquid regulatory muscle, but U.S. access faces litigation and fragmented liquidity. Santos expects resistance from competing exchanges and says injunctions and court involvement are possible. The Dragonfly guest explains that regulated markets would need KYC and separate order books from offshore TradeXYZ liquidity, likening the fight to “King Kong versus Godzilla.” HYPE had rallied to around $94–$95; Yanowitz raises the multiyear question of whether it could grow from roughly a $100 billion valuation to $200 billion–$500 billion.
  • Google’s MPC offering strengthens its crypto infrastructure business without yet supplying a complete custody application. Yanowitz warns that crypto-native firms’ time to scale is running short; Santos initially questions whether the product has been formally announced, and the Dragonfly guest explains that Google Cloud appears to provide enclave-based cryptography, not a turnkey custodian. Fireblocks-style asset support, signing workflows and approval interfaces would still need to be built.
  • The strongest bull thesis in the discussion centers on perps and distribution. Santos welcomes YC’s renewed interest in crypto but warns that many listed startup ideas have been tried and failed: he notes that 99.8% of stablecoins are dollar-denominated and says, “Don’t tokenize random assets.” He favors backing proven products. One lending founder’s planned Base deployment, which Santos recounts, illustrates the pull of Coinbase’s idle capital and Base’s onboarding.
  • AI’s capital requirements could turn a funding contraction into an incumbent advantage. Santos warns that Instinct’s compute costs, losses per user and apparent unwillingness to charge could force punitive financing. Yanowitz endorses the view that “AI structurally favors incumbents,” while Santos agrees that hyperscalers have the balance sheets to weather a contraction. Yanowitz rejects an easy crypto-rotation trade if AI bursts: “we’re coming down with it.”
  • Crypto’s institutional allies strengthen its lobbying position while midterm politics threaten its reputation. Santos points to ETFs, stablecoins and financial institutions as reasons crypto gained allies; Yanowitz says ICE’s involvement could add powerful lobbyists. Santos reads Jeffrey Sprecher’s account of seeing Hyperliquid mentioned in Trump’s White House script as a sign of political support. The hosts discuss odds of roughly 94% for Democrats to win the House and 70% for the Senate; Yanowitz predicts two years of scrutiny over Trump-family business interests.
  • Consumer AI’s political upside depends on usefulness spreading beyond unusually busy early adopters. Santos argues that personal assistants can improve ordinary lives immediately; he cites Muse’s roughly 2.5 million daily active users and 30% seven-day retention, despite 10 million downloads, and says, “I’m so atypical.” Yanowitz contrasts his six upcoming flights with a friend who will not fly this year.

Digest

1. TradeXYZ makes onchain price discovery institutionally relevant

  • Druckenmiller tweeted about TradeXYZ, and Santos describes him as making a strategic investment. The discussion also identifies ICE as the investor in TradeXYZ. Yanowitz calls the moment a “defining moment for the industry,” recalling Paul Tudor Jones calling Bitcoin the “fastest horse in the race” in May 2020. Bitcoin was around $9,000 then and later reached $60,000, $65,000 and $70,000; Yanowitz says the endorsement removed career risk for other managers. He expects comparable 8–10× growth in onchain volumes over the next year.
  • Yanowitz’s proposed use case is price discovery, especially before IPOs, with weekend trading secondary. In his framing, markets are downstream of what happens to Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX. Historically, pre-IPO pricing relied on illiquid markets and reports that offerings were five or ten times oversubscribed. A liquid market now gives investors a reference point.
  • Santos cites $17 million of Anthropic open interest on TradeXYZ, with less than $4 million hedgeable. He says this is not enough for a major fund to hedge meaningful size, but the price itself can still inform decisions. Yanowitz compares the data opportunity with Polymarket: prices may be useful even when liquidity cannot absorb meaningful geopolitical hedges. Santos offers weekend oil pricing during the Iran war as another example of a signal investors can use in real time.
  • Yanowitz’s inference—explicitly “reading between the lines”—is that ICE can sell market data before U.S. hedge funds of meaningful size can participate. CoreWeave bonds, for example, could be priced downstream of expectations for Anthropic’s IPO. Yanowitz puts ICE’s trading fees and services revenue at about $5.5 billion and its data business at $2.5 billion.

2. ICE brings distribution and a fight with incumbent exchanges

  • The Dragonfly guest says CME’s Terry Duffy opposes perps and 24/7 markets, and that CME sued to stop the CFTC from treating perpetuals as futures rather than swaps. Santos expects Nasdaq and CME to resist what he characterizes as a regulatory backdoor for NYSE to secure a monopoly on a product. He says injunctions are possible and courts may have to decide whether the products are allowed. The guest likens the ensuing fight, with ICE involved, to “King Kong versus Godzilla duking it out over the city.”
  • U.S. regulation also changes liquidity: the guest says KYC and market surveillance mean a domestic venue cannot simply reuse TradeXYZ’s offshore order book. He expects two books, as with Polymarket. He also says more than 40 companies have forced tokenized-stock listings to be delisted, noting that under SEC rules a company can elect not to allow its stock to be tokenized and traded.
  • Yanowitz thinks ICE may offer Hyperliquid through hundreds of participating brokers. He contrasts that with the Kraken-Bitnomial arrangement, which he says routes trades through Kraken’s broker NinjaTrader, acquired by Kraken. Yanowitz—not Santos—calls ICE’s resources, reputation and “muscle” a major advantage for entering the U.S.
  • Santos cautions that HYPE had already rallied and that the move may be baked into the price by the time listeners hear the episode. Yanowitz says HYPE is around $94–$95 and asks whether, over several years, a roughly $100 billion valuation could grow to $200 billion, $300 billion, $400 billion or $500 billion. Santos separately asks whether it could reach $500 or $1,000 per HYPE. Yanowitz sees ICE as bullish for cementing Hyperliquid’s leadership, while noting regulatory uncertainty, fragmentation and liquidity as important factors.

3. Google supplies a cryptographic building block

  • Google’s MPC key-security offering leads Yanowitz to warn that crypto-native firms’ time to scale enterprise sales and international expansion is running short. He recalls a conversation about six months earlier in which someone at Google claimed the company had better MPC technology than crypto custodians. Santos initially questions whether the product is formally announced or based on a CoinDesk report; Yanowitz points to a public post from Google Cloud’s crypto lead.
  • The Dragonfly guest distinguishes Google Cloud infrastructure from a custody application. As he understands it, Google supplies cryptography running inside enclaves, not Fireblocks’ asset support, contract-signing workflow, approval interface or mobile app. A competitor could build a custodial product on top of the technology; Google is supplying a component.
  • The guest compares it with Amazon KMS: securely storing keys does not by itself produce a turnkey application. Yanowitz accepts the distinction as “super important to call out.” The exchange narrows his initial competitive warning: an infrastructure offering does not automatically mean Google is delivering the complete service institutional customers use.

4. Dragonfly preserves dissent inside shared governance

  • The Dragonfly guest explains that VC titles are “totally made up”: analysts and associates were once common titles, while general partner usually implies investment authority, a role on the investment committee and significant carry. Managing partners often manage the firm and can be designated key persons; if a key person leaves, LPs may have the option to shut down a fund. The guest says Rob and Tom’s promotions make Dragonfly a four-person partnership with joint decisions and no reporting lines among them.
  • Investments require a majority, so one dissenting vote does not block a deal. For exceptional conviction, a GP has a “gunslinger budget” once per fund: one GP who supports a deal can push it through even if nobody else does, provided that GP also invests personal money. There is no separate dollar limit, though each GP has risk parameters. The mechanism permits contentious investments without requiring consensus.

5. YC’s return revives a debate over startup ideas and cycle timing

  • YC’s renewed crypto request covers AI capital raising, stablecoins and stablecoin-based neobanks, tokenized trading infrastructure, and agents as prolific traders. Yanowitz jokes, “It always comes back to ICOs.” Santos welcomes YC’s renewed commitment and credits Neil with revitalizing its crypto program, but warns that “VCs have terrible ideas for startups.”
  • Santos’s example is non-dollar stablecoins: he says 99.8% of stablecoins are U.S. dollars, reflecting demand rather than founders simply overlooking other currencies. Yanowitz admits his own first startup idea was “Bloomberg for crypto,” before discovering it was a repeatedly tried cliché. Santos’s warning on indiscriminate tokenization is categorical: “Don’t tokenize random assets.”
  • Santos reads YC’s return as a possible late-cycle sign, recalling renewed enthusiasm around 2021. Yanowitz instead places the market around “mid stage two”: Bitcoin roughly tripled in 2023 with little public attention; then prices improve while layoffs and bear-market scars persist; later fundraising gets wild; finally, celebrity NFTs arrive. Santos says, “We’re probably in mid-stage two,” while Yanowitz notes Justin Bieber is not launching NFTs.
  • Yanowitz defends startup requests as “generative prompts” for founders, not literal instructions to build the listed ideas. Santos says he cannot recall a good crypto company coming out of a crypto request for startups. He favors proven perps over broad tokenization lists: “back the fastest horse, back the killer product.” Santos also doubts anyone can systematically time markets.

6. Distribution and separable risks offer paths for DeFi innovation

  • Santos points to Vitalik’s writing on Uniswap and prediction markets as earlier ideas that helped inspire builders. He recalls Hayden Adams teaching himself Solidity to build Uniswap. Santos’s present criticism is that Vitalik has become hostile to DeFi and financial infrastructure, contributing to Santos finding Ethereum “deeply uninteresting.”
  • Santos recounts meeting a founder of an up-and-coming lending protocol that built on Ethereum mainnet because the founder believed institutions trusted it more. The founder said much of the relevant TVL was on Base and that Base had done well at onboarding; the team plans to deploy there and later on Robinhood. Santos stresses this is “one anecdote,” but says it illustrates the pull of idle capital sitting in Coinbase.
  • Asked for a new primitive beyond perps, Santos recalls a paper he had not fully read: tokenize a 24/7 perp and split overnight exposure from daytime exposure. He says the paper claims stocks perform about 100 times better overnight than during market hours, while admitting, “I have no understanding of why this would be true.”
  • Yanowitz challenges the paper’s claim that fees make buying at the close and selling at the open impractical, noting that high-frequency firms trade despite fees and that his overnight fees were unchanged. Santos suggests the issue may instead be slippage when opening and closing large positions daily, which could erase the effect. He qualifies his explanation: “I think that’s what was implied. I don’t know.”

7. AI’s funding model favors strong balance sheets

  • Instinct raising at a $30 billion valuation prompts Santos to say it is “very plausible” the company blows up. He points to compute-heavy losses per user, the expense of building a large capital stack, and the apparent unwillingness of Noah to charge customers. If investor appetite seizes up, Santos says the company could have to sell half the business in a massive down round.
  • Yanowitz cites a Microsoft employee’s thesis that “AI structurally favors incumbents”: capex already committed becomes a cost and scale advantage across consumer products. Yanowitz says he agrees; Santos also agrees, pointing to Nvidia, Microsoft and Amazon as major beneficiaries of the buildout. Santos expects a contraction and says startups unable to fund capex without selling equity could be frozen out, while large companies can weather the storm and issue debt.
  • Santos says Anthropic, OpenAI and Cursor show that venture-backed startups can still achieve extraordinary growth. But he contrasts value capture: in crypto, almost all the value went to startups; in AI, startup successes are small beside market-cap gains at Nvidia, Amazon and Google. Yanowitz adds that BlackRock and JPMorgan captured little compared with the crypto industry, and emphasizes backing teams with product-market fit, real demand and reasonable valuations. If AI bursts, Santos says crypto will come down with it.

8. Institutional allies coexist with a looming political threat

  • Santos asks whether incumbents need enough upside from a disruptive technology to help clear regulatory resistance. He says crypto gained “actual allies” around 2023, citing ETFs, BlackRock and financial institutions, followed by stablecoins aligning with U.S. interest in internationalizing its debt. Yanowitz argues that ICE’s potential benefits from prediction markets and tokenization could make major financial firms powerful advocates for access.
  • Santos reads an account from ICE founder Jeffrey Sprecher: after earlier discussions about Hyperliquid, Sprecher saw Trump’s White House script mention it and concluded, “the US wants this platform to come and be regulated in this country.” Sprecher said ICE then redoubled efforts to bring TradeXYZ and Hyperliquid together.
  • Santos predicts a post-midterm “vibe shift” and says MAGA is likely to lose the House and Senate. The hosts cite odds of roughly 94% for Democrats to win the House and 70% for the Senate. Yanowitz—not Santos—predicts two years of news about Trump’s and his family’s business interests, saying crypto is the easiest shorthand for the story even though other interests are involved. Santos also says AI has become more unpopular than crypto.

9. Consumer AI’s broad appeal remains contested

  • Santos argues that useful consumer AI could shift sentiment: even a free executive assistant might visibly improve ordinary lives. Yanowitz says the political inflection may depend on bigger breakthroughs, such as AI helping cure cancer, rather than booking flights. Santos pushes back: “Don’t underestimate the small things”—a personal assistant can offer a concrete quality-of-life improvement before healthcare advances.
  • Santos cites Muse at about 2.5 million daily active users and 30% retention after seven days, despite 10 million downloads. He says most people do not need a personal assistant and reflects, “I’m so atypical,” given how busy he is. Yanowitz contrasts his six flights in the next two and a half weeks with a friend who will not fly this year.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/will-druck-kick-off-next-phase-crypto-s-bull-mar

item.title: Are We in an A.I. Bubble? We're About to Find Out.
item.description: Anthropic’s possible $100 billion IPO at a $2 trillion valuation would put its AI economics under public-market scrutiny: first-half 2026 revenue reached $16.3 billion, up 14X, while operating losses narrowed to roughly $600–700 million. Griffith estimates third-quarter growth at 44%; the key test is whether the slowdown reflects competitors catching up or broader demand weakness, as non-cancellable compute commitments leave the company exposed if usage falls.
item.content:encoded:
Hard Fork · Kevin Roose、Casey Newton、Erin Griffith、Mike Isaac、Jasmine Sun · 2026-10-30 · 54 min · 原语言 EN

Anthropic’s possible $100 billion IPO at a $2 trillion valuation would put its AI economics under public-market scrutiny: first-half 2026 revenue reached $16.3 billion, up 14X, while operating losses narrowed to roughly $600–700 million. Griffith estimates third-quarter growth at 44%; the key test is whether the slowdown reflects competitors catching up or broader demand weakness, as non-cancellable compute commitments leave the company exposed if usage falls.

TL;DR

  • Anthropic’s IPO will test whether AI’s extraordinary growth can justify its capital demands. Kevin Roose frames it as a possible $100 billion raise at a $2 trillion valuation; Erin Griffith calls public scrutiny a “demystifying moment.” First-half 2026 revenue reached $16.3 billion, with 14X growth and operating losses narrowing to roughly $600–700 million from over $2 billion. Griffith explains an $8 billion net loss as a convertible-debt accounting quirk; the transcript earlier says $80 billion, so those figures conflict.
  • The decisive question is whether Anthropic’s slowdown reflects competition or weaker demand across AI. Griffith estimates third-quarter growth at 44%, following Claude Code’s surge, as competitors caught up and customers restrained “token maxing.” Competition alongside continued market growth means “party on”; a broader retreat would expose the debt-financed infrastructure ecosystem and Anthropic’s often non-cancellable compute commitments.
  • Public shareholders will enter a company designed to preserve founder control and unusual safety commitments. Seven founders hold 50.1% voting power across a structure with five stock classes, an independent trust and approved successors. Kevin’s example of the commercial implications: “model welfare” considerations may delay retiring older models, while Griffith says investors generally approach Anthropic as an enterprise software business.
  • AI’s political backlash is affecting local infrastructure decisions while remaining a relatively low national voting priority. Jasmine Sun calls opposition an “80/20 issue,” but says AI usually ranks around 22 out of 39 issues and only roughly 1–5% of voters in some affected states name it their top concern. Close rural races could still turn on data centers, and a Republican midterm defeat could create room for tougher regulation.
  • California’s proposed 5% billionaire wealth tax has drawn a $333 million opposition campaign. Prop 40 would reach unrealized gains, including private startup stock; opponents contest its design, durability and precedent. Healthcare groups including Planned Parenthood also oppose it, but a co-host challenges the recurring defense that a tax is simply “poorly written.”
  • AI-driven vulnerability discovery is creating a race between faster attacks and faster repairs. Mike Isaac expects “the old internet breaking much faster,” while Kevin Roose cites an intrusion into Anthropic’s own systems as evidence that sophisticated AI companies remain vulnerable. Casey Newton relays a qualified counterargument from Joshua Saxe: a “defender-dominant window” may allow repairs before ordinary cybercriminals adapt, although nation-state attackers remain a different threat.
  • Big Tech is cutting staff while reconsidering how it measures AI-assisted work. Microsoft offered buyout packages to 60,000 people, although Griffith cites expected take-up of 3–5% and probably at most 3,000 departures. Separately, an Amazon memo rejects token consumption and lines of code as performance measures in favor of “long-term outcomes”—leaving unresolved how managers make quarterly employment decisions.
  • An Anthropic experiment suggests expert oversight can become unacknowledged deference to AI. Sun reports that experts followed AI recommendations over 80% of the time and reused its arguments over 70% of the time, while only 15% acknowledged its influence. Her concern is that humans become “wrappers on AI agents,” outsourcing decisions without recognizing the transfer.

Digest

1. The IPO opens AI’s economics to public scrutiny

  • Kevin Roose frames the offering as a referendum extending beyond Anthropic: it might raise $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation and support companies struggling in debt markets, or raise much less and send the stock market “into a tailspin.” Griffith describes it as the first pure-play large language model company to open its books publicly after four years of investment and economic reorientation.
  • The operating figures surprised Griffith positively, though she stresses that the assessment is arguable: “the business looks kinda healthy.” Kevin cites $16.3 billion in first-half 2026 revenue; Griffith describes 14X growth. Operating losses for that half narrowed to roughly $600–700 million, compared with over $2 billion in the same period last year.
  • The net-loss figures are inconsistent in the transcript. Griffith first says Anthropic posted an $80 billion net loss, then explains that an $8 billion net loss reflects convertible debt issued to shareholders being counted as a loss. She says that accounting effect will clear in the next quarter or by the offering, and is “not a reflection of the health of their actual business.” Infrastructure spending remains enormous.
  • Griffith’s “demystifying moment” is the move from valuations set by a handful of venture investors to financial modeling by public-market managers and pension investors: is the company worth $2 trillion, or perhaps $1.5 trillion? Her caveat survives: Wall Street also buys “hype and momentum,” so listing alone does not guarantee a sober verdict.

2. Slower growth makes fixed compute commitments the central risk

  • Griffith’s central mechanism is capacity planning on a “knife’s edge,” borrowing Dario Amodei’s description. Anthropic signs expensive infrastructure contracts anticipating future usage, many of them non-cancellable. If demand disappoints, the obligations remain; if it buys insufficient capacity and demand materializes, it loses business. Current demand does not settle how much capacity to reserve.
  • Claude Code drove the first-half surge, but Griffith says OpenAI is catching up, cheaper and open-source alternatives are competing, and customers are reducing token spending after “token maxing got out of control.” The filing lacks third-quarter results, although investors have received previews and reporting indicates slower growth.
  • “I think in Q3, they grew 44%,” Griffith says: a move from “gangbusters growth” to “just great growth.” The explanation matters more than the slowdown alone. A market-wide pullback would threaten the ecosystem’s investment and debt assumptions; competitors taking share while total demand keeps growing means “great, party on.”
  • Griffith expects the roadshow, probably beginning in a week or so, to supply the next growth story: biological research, drug development and legal technology beyond coding. Her image of the exercise is bankers flying executives to investors such as “insurance companies in Iowa” and “telling them about the machine god.” The company needs those audiences to believe expansion continues.

3. Safety commitments coexist with permanent founder control

  • Griffith traces Anthropic’s origins to founders who believed OpenAI was insufficiently concerned with humanity’s future. Early funding came from safety-oriented backers such as Sam Bankman-Fried and Jaan Tallinn; mainstream venture investors initially saw a science project, then embraced its enterprise business. Kevin’s pushback: the same choices also fit an efficient software company whose founders want control. Griffith says later investors generally do not share the stranger philosophical commitments.
  • Kevin highlights the 93-page risk section’s catastrophic and existential warnings; Griffith, crediting Matt Levine, notes the distancing phrase “Concerns have been raised.” Another disclosure says safety and “model welfare” considerations may delay retiring older models. Kevin interprets that as concern that models might be alive, likening it to Apple saying “the iPhone 12 is alive” and continuing to make it.
  • The governance provisions limit shareholders’ ability to challenge those priorities. Griffith describes five stock classes, seven founders retaining 50.1% voting power and authority to elect directors, alongside an independent trust controlling a majority of board seats. Founders also approve a “secret list of successors.” Her conclusion: “They don't wanna lose control of the AI or of the company.”
  • Sun adds the founders’ pledge of 80% of their equity to charity and an employee culture interview asking, “Hey, would you work here if your equity went to zero?” Mike Isaac sees a different adjustment for public investors: the filing foregrounds cancer cures and promising drugs before the darker possibilities. “Someone told him to jazz hands a little bit at the top, right?”
  • Kevin also cites a Wall Street Journal headline pitching the investor “bull case” for a 10% extinction chance as a 90% portfolio win; Erin jokes, “Die rich.” This is headline framing, not a company forecast.

4. Data-center opposition is locally potent but nationally less salient

  • Sun distinguishes widespread dislike from electoral priority. AI and data centers are an “80/20 issue” with bipartisan negative sentiment, yet AI usually ranks around 22 out of 39 issues. Even in states such as Ohio and Pennsylvania, she says roughly 1–5% of voters name it their leading concern. Mayoral races, recalls and council changes are clearer channels than major Senate contests.
  • Kevin challenges whether Senate campaigns wasted resources opposing data centers. Sun says close races can mobilize rural Republicans and infrequent voters when construction reaches their backyard; Sherrod Brown might benefit in Ohio. She also attributes Greg Abbott’s “pseudo-moratorium” on approvals and electricity-grid connections to pressure from electoral opponents and rural Texans. Concrete power lines motivate people more readily than abstract AI debates.
  • Isaac is watching companies reposition their Washington teams if Democrats gain power: “these are corporations that don't necessarily believe in anything except self-preservation a lot of the time.” Joel Kaplan’s announced departure from Meta provides one reference point. Griffith doubts this means a broader cultural reversal; venture investors’ relief at escaping expectations around issues such as DEI appears more durable.
  • Sun’s conditional forecast concerns the 2028 Republican primary: if the party suffers in the midterms, JD Vance, Marco Rubio or others might depart from Trump’s AI positions. She sees tension between libertarian deregulators and New Right figures, including people at American Compass, considering rules around children, jobs and safety. Republican voters, she says, generally prefer slower development with safeguards over an abstract “beat China” argument.

5. The wealth-tax fight combines donor self-interest with design objections

  • Griffith describes Prop 40 as a proposed one-time 5% wealth tax on California billionaires, including unrealized gains in private startup stock. Building a Better California has assembled $333 million, principally from Sergey Brin, with John Doerr and Stripe founder Patrick Collison also involved. A wider network includes wealthy founders and investors who are not themselves billionaires.
  • Opponents argue that the measure is poorly drafted, its spending insufficiently specified and its supposedly one-time nature unreliable. They fear California could establish a precedent copied elsewhere and discourage founders from moving there. Their messaging documents acknowledge that “Billionaires are seen as having a net negative impact across issues,” explaining why donors prefer other organizations to make the public case.
  • Planned Parenthood and other healthcare groups also oppose it: Griffith says a one-time replacement for Trump administration cuts would not establish sustainable funding. Some opponents support a wealth tax in principle. A co-host challenges whether they would always say a particular bill was badly written; Griffith agrees the defense can resemble “I agree with your message” but reject how it is delivered.

6. AI exposes security weaknesses faster than the internet can coordinate repairs

  • The PHP vulnerability labeled “Black October” illustrates distributed exposure. Isaac describes old infrastructure containing longstanding holes; Kevin explains that a flaw in a widely used programming language requires fixes across many websites. His concrete example is Clues by Sam: he could not record a puzzle score while its operator repaired the PHP problem.
  • Isaac preserves the optimistic counterargument: the vulnerabilities already existed, and AI can also find repairs and accelerate defense. But he calls that outlook “a little rosy.” His expectation is more frequent disruption and “the old internet breaking much faster” as automated discovery increases the workload for security teams.
  • Kevin cites Cathedral, a startup involving former DOGE staff, accessing Anthropic’s Slack and IT systems and obtaining trade secrets. Anthropic is supposed to be developing exceptionally capable internal cyber-defense models that it cannot release publicly, yet its own systems were penetrated. Kevin’s concern expands from under-resourced municipalities to “the best and most AI forward companies in the world.”
  • Casey Newton relays a qualified alternative from former Meta AI researcher Joshua Saxe: a “defender-dominant window” may exist because cybercriminals take time to organize and operationalize new capabilities. Defenders could use that interval to lock systems down. The limitation is nation-state actors, which already possess resources and motivation to attack infrastructure; this is not, Casey stresses, a wholly positive story.

7. Staffing cuts and failed productivity metrics reveal unresolved workplace economics

  • Microsoft offered buyout packages to 60,000 people out of roughly 230,000 employees. Griffith distinguishes eligibility from departures: she cites expected take-up of 3–5% and probably at most 3,000 exits. Still, “rolling layoffs” have eroded the prospect of a comfortable 30-year technology career. She finds Microsoft’s framing especially dark: giving employees “more control over their future.”
  • Isaac attributes much of the pressure to AI and infrastructure spending, suggesting companies without such enormous capital bills might cut less. His proposed example, Accenture, immediately draws objections from Griffith and others that consultants themselves are exposed to AI replacement. He concedes the example fails; the exchange leaves both infrastructure financing and substitution risk in view.
  • An Amazon vice president and distinguished engineer’s memo rejects token consumption and lines of code as measures of engineering performance. Isaac explains the latter failure: more generated code can simply leave systems full of material someone must eventually delete. The memo instead prioritizes “long-term outcomes,” which Isaac accepts as the relevant objective.
  • The unresolved problem is judging those outcomes quarterly when deciding who remains employed. Griffith says the token-maxing trend reversed almost before her first story could appear. Isaac’s verdict: “spending billions of dollars to find out something is a terrible idea.” Casey recognizes the familiar workplace cycle of fulfilling a metric, then being instructed to optimize its opposite.

8. Expert judgment can become an unacknowledged wrapper around AI

  • Sun describes an Anthropic randomized controlled trial giving professional statistical analysts AI advice about a scenario, with recommendations split half-and-half. “I think over 80% of the time,” experts chose the same answer as the AI; over 70% used its arguments to justify their decisions. Only 15% said the AI agent had influenced them.
  • Her worry is humans becoming “wrappers on AI agents”: supplying the face and typing while outsourcing judgment without noticing. That offers a quieter route to lost control than rogue systems—“a lot of the times we're just gonna let the AIs take over.” Casey’s joke about repackaging other people’s opinions reinforces the uncomfortable familiarity. He adds that people say AI makes everybody a manager; Sun agrees.

9. Crypto investors broaden their mandate as builders move to AI

  • Griffith flags Andreessen Horowitz’s change to the branding and name of its a16z crypto fund. Given its longstanding blockchain advocacy, including Chris Dixon’s earlier Hard Fork appearance, the change looks consequential. Kevin jokes, “It’s just all Frontier now.” Griffith estimates that “something like 80, 90%” of venture dollars are now going to AI, while crypto is deeply out of fashion.
  • The firm’s stated position remains “We're not backing away from crypto” and “We're just expanding our mandate.” Griffith offers a practical explanation: there may simply be too few investable crypto startups to absorb billions. “Without the hype, without the number going up,” fewer people want to build in the industry, while entrepreneurs gravitate toward AI.
  • Paradigm provides the precedent: removing some crypto language from its website in 2023 attracted immediate attention and backlash. Griffith’s broader explanation is that venture capital is also a marketing business because “all money's kind of the same.” Funds need a distinctive statement of interest to attract founders, but must change mandates when opportunities shift.

Verification Notes

The transcript first says Anthropic posted an $80 billion net loss, then describes an $8 billion net loss and its accounting explanation. These figures conflict, so neither has been normalized.

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/are-we-i-bubble-we-re-about-find-out

item.title: The Numbers Behind Anthropic's IPO, AI Bubble Questions, Meta's Spending Continues
item.description: Anthropic’s subscriptions and API are profitable, yet training R&D exceeds serving costs and rose in the first half; cloud fees booked as sales and marketing may flatter margins. Thompson says the $80 billion first-half 2026 loss reflects Amazon loan repricing, while 2027–2028 customer revenue must catch industry capex; Meta’s Muse likewise makes training spend strategic, though Sharp questions its necessity.
item.content:encoded:
Sharp Tech · Ben Thompson、Andrew Sharp · 2026-10-30 · 98 min · 原语言 EN

Anthropic’s subscriptions and API are profitable, yet training R&D exceeds serving costs and rose in the first half; cloud fees booked as sales and marketing may flatter margins. Thompson says the $80 billion first-half 2026 loss reflects Amazon loan repricing, while 2027–2028 customer revenue must catch industry capex; Meta’s Muse likewise makes training spend strategic, though Sharp questions its necessity.

TL;DR

  • Anthropic’s strong operating business does not remove the cost of staying at the frontier. Thompson says subscriptions are profitable and the API is more profitable, but training-related R&D exceeds serving costs and increased more during the first half despite exploding usage. Competition determines spending whose pace is “out of their control.” He expects a bubble and painful reset, while explicitly declining to identify this IPO as the top.
  • The headline loss and headline margins require different accounting adjustments. Thompson attributes the reported $80 billion first-half 2026 loss to repricing Amazon’s loan liability, which could be repaid in shares: “It’s not money out the door.” Conversely, about half of revenue comes through cloud platforms, whose roughly 30% cut—with estimates around 37% also cited—is classified as sales and marketing. He thinks that treatment overstates gross margins, although the underlying business still looks excellent.
  • The hyperscalers could capture more of AI’s upside by financing the industry’s funding gap. Google, Amazon and Microsoft have the greatest capacity across free cash flow, debt and equity: the “girders of the bridge” until customer revenue catches spending. Existing shareholders fund equity issuance through dilution, and distressed labs could eventually accept worse terms. The hyperscalers that help finance the bridge could also gain power to develop competing chips and press Nvidia’s prices.
  • The demand question is about timing, even for an AI believer. Craig Moffett’s test is whether final customer payments can support the entire value chain in 2027–2028, excluding transactions between suppliers. Thompson says current Anthropic revenue comes nowhere close to industry capex, but that infrastructure serves demand two to five years ahead. “Multiplying humans” into new businesses could create that demand; the difficulty is that such transformations usually take longer.
  • Frontier labs need customer attachment to escape competition based solely on model quality and price. Microsoft and Palantir want customers to keep models replaceable, while Thompson argues the labs eventually need to own applications, workflows and interfaces. Cloud workspaces and accumulated habits make switching harder than changing an API endpoint: “Lock in is an important part of making money.”
  • Meta’s Muse strategy makes heavy training expenditure integral to the investment case. The discussion cites up to $95 billion of stock offerings and shares down roughly 10% over a week; Sharp says dilution is a reason the shares should be down. Thompson says companies like Meta may be able to get away with dilution. Meta must control Muse’s underlying model, so the coherent objection is that “Meta doesn’t actually need Muse.” He also sees an indirect threat to Netflix: AI funding pressure pushes Meta to maximize Reels engagement and advertising.
  • Government power remains a constraint on private AI and communications infrastructure. Thompson’s argument is conditional: if AI becomes as powerful as Anthropic predicts, governments will assert authority because “they have the guns.” Both hosts describe the Ukraine Starlink episode as opaque; Thompson guesses Musk acted in alignment with Washington, while Sharp guesses Washington requested the action. Neither presents those guesses as established facts.

Digest

1. Anthropic’s profitable products sit inside an expensive race

  • Asked whether Anthropic’s IPO could mark AI’s peak as Coinbase’s listing did for crypto, Thompson answers, “I don’t know.” He considers a bubble, painful collapse and eventual recovery inevitable, but cannot identify the timing. His concern is investment arriving faster than useful ideas can be absorbed, rather than a belief that the technology lacks value.
  • Sharp’s reading of the S-1 is that Anthropic looks like “a rock-solid business.” Thompson agrees about the operating core: subscriptions are profitable, and the API is more profitable still. That distinction matters because an attractive business serving existing models can coexist with a much harder economic proposition in developing their successors.
  • Sharp notes that subscriptions also create distribution advantages. Having already paid, customers use Claude, develop habits and advocate for it inside their employers. Thompson thinks paying for both competing services is worthwhile, but doubts many customers will. The subscription therefore purchases recurring exposure to the product as well as revenue.
  • The catch is R&D: training spending is larger than serving costs and increased more during the first half even as usage exploded. Better competing models force further investment. “The speed with which they need to spend money on that is out of their control.” Sharp emphasizes that this is an ongoing expense, rather than a problem solved once.

2. Cloud distribution improves access and complicates margins

  • Amazon’s early investment forced Anthropic onto Trainium, something Thompson doubts it initially wanted. That constraint proved useful: starting with Nvidia, then supporting Trainium, TPUs and an AMD deal required hardware flexibility. Anthropic built “a layer of abstraction” across chips. Amazon benefited too, because a demanding frontier customer improved Trainium’s capabilities and tooling for other customers.
  • Availability across AWS, Google’s cloud and Microsoft also helped Anthropic win enterprise customers while OpenAI was tied to Microsoft. Thompson’s concrete example is straightforward: a company whose data already lives on AWS would rather consume AI there. About 50% of Anthropic’s revenue comes through those three providers.
  • Thompson challenges how that revenue is recorded. If a customer pays Amazon $100, Anthropic recognizes $100, then books the platform’s roughly 30% share—about 37% in estimates cited—as sales and marketing. He argues for recognizing net revenue or treating the payment as cost of revenue. Either would reduce the headline margins under discussion; he still calls the business’s margins excellent.

3. The $80 billion loss exposes the mechanics of dilution

  • Thompson explains the reported $80 billion first-half 2026 loss through Amazon’s financing. Amazon supplied money as a loan that Anthropic could use for compute; Amazon could receive repayment or take shares. As fundraising rounds increased Anthropic’s valuation, its obligation was repriced and the increase booked as a loss. Thompson believes Amazon will receive shares at the IPO: “It’s not money out the door.”
  • The corresponding investment appreciation appears in Amazon’s income. That creates a broader earnings-reading problem: hyperscalers’ reported profits can swing with investments unrelated to their operating performance. Thompson contrasts Amazon’s Anthropic gains with a decline in Google’s SpaceX holding and advises focusing on operating income.
  • The economic bill survives the accounting adjustment through dilution. Thompson identifies outstanding share obligations involving Broadcom, Google and roughly two-and-a-half additional Amazon arrangements. He also describes a provision permitting issuance of 2% of outstanding shares after roughly 50% stock appreciation. “The people who are paying are existing shareholders”: their ownership funds the compute purchased with those arrangements.
  • Equity financing shares upside with new investors, which Thompson considers healthier than relying entirely on debt. Sharp prefers public access and disclosure to permanent private ownership. Still, Thompson questions the opportunity available to buyers at illustrative valuations of $1.5 trillion or $2 trillion. His caricature of the pitch: “We’re going to dilute you endlessly, but we’re going to control the world.”

4. The IPO snapshot may conceal a changing growth trajectory

  • Sharp suspects, without claiming certainty, that insufficient compute made first-half financials look better. Thompson explains that Anthropic did not have enough capacity: because compute is a major cost, the shortage kept costs lower even as customers experienced outages. Sharp jokes that those customers “did your part for Anthropic’s IPO” by helping make the margins look better.
  • The S-1’s numbers stop at June 30. Thompson asks whether spending indicators such as Ramp’s index showed growth slowing, given OpenAI’s push and Astra’s arrival, or whether it reaccelerated after Opus 5.5. Sharp argues that Opus 5.5 could restart growth. If model improvement is what restarts demand, however, that reinforces the need to keep funding the training race. The growth slowdown remains uncertain, and Thompson notes that extraordinary growth cannot simply repeat indefinitely.
  • Thompson says the financial information becomes stale on November 12, while reporting points to a mid-November listing. Whether Anthropic lists before that threshold or supplies an update could materially change the picture.

5. Owning the interface offers an escape from replaceable models

  • Thompson describes a second battle beyond OpenAI versus Anthropic: frontier labs versus the surrounding software industry. Microsoft and Palantir tell customers to build around models that remain interchangeable. Satya Nadella and Alex Karp emphasize flexibility, better prices and protection against handing a future competitor the details of one’s business.
  • That proposition is uncomfortable for labs whose largest expense rises with frontier competition. If customers can switch by changing an API, pricing power stays limited. Thompson argues that, “in the fullness of time,” labs need to move up the stack and own the customer experience. Sharp sees potentially enormous software revenue; Thompson emphasizes the resulting attachment.
  • Their own usage shows why interfaces matter independently of model rankings. Thompson compares Codex to people who organize email into folders: projects and threads suit structured work. Sharp, a former lawyer, calls Codex “the associate” and Claude “the partner.” Thompson says Claude handles varied incoming tasks, while Sharp has done most of the concrete building on his GeckoBot project in Codex, with Claude powering it.
  • Cloud workspaces deepen that relationship. A convenient virtual machine that remembers work also means, as Thompson puts it, “you’re now stuck in their cloud.” Applications and familiar workflows make switching progressively harder. That is the commercial purpose of climbing the stack: “Lock in is an important part of making money. Like, what’s your moat?”

6. Anthropic’s moral positioning raises a governance question

  • A listener compares Dario and Daniela Amodei’s criticism of OpenAI during their Walter Isaacson interview to “someone badmouthing their ex during their wedding vows.” The complaints span advertising, sycophancy, government dealings and honesty. Thompson’s objection is strategic as well as personal: defining decisions through opposition lets OpenAI set the agenda. “Who’s actually setting the agenda here?”
  • Thompson says he has never taken Anthropic’s claimed moral authority seriously. Sharp, by contrast, says he believes they are trying to act as moral arbiters. His concern is concentration: “There is no small collection of people that get to decide it for everyone else.” Thompson agrees that teaching Claude morals is not the right approach.
  • Thompson connects the governance concern to the S-1’s unusual structure: roughly seven share classes and special voting arrangements he describes as a “magic share.” He prefers conventional corporations with understandable profit incentives. Those incentives have problems, but give counterparties a predictable framework for decisions and investment. Public buyers receive disclosure; they also knowingly accept dilution and governance that is not simply organized around maximizing profit.

7. Final demand must eventually finance the entire chain

  • A listener brings back Craig Moffett’s question about 2027 and 2028: are customer payments entering Anthropic and ChatGPT sufficient to cover the whole system? Transactions among Nvidia, TSMC, clouds and labs can distract from that test. Moffett’s formulation, quoted by Sharp: “All that really matters is enough money coming into the system to support the system.”
  • Thompson says current Anthropic revenue comes nowhere close to aggregate capex, but that spending also builds capacity for two, three, four or five years ahead. The uncertainty is timing. Strong revenue growth makes investors tolerate dilution and unusual governance; slowing growth makes those same features suddenly salient.
  • Google, Amazon and Microsoft have the greatest capacity to supply free cash flow, borrow against diversified businesses and issue shares. They are the “girders of the bridge” across the funding gap. If labs require repeated rescues, the hyperscalers could acquire substantial ownership and control. Sharp imagines Amazon offering a distressed Anthropic terms even less favorable than its early financing.
  • Nvidia’s support for neoclouds reflects the risk that funding runs out before revenue catches up. Thompson’s railroad analogy preserves the distinction: useful infrastructure can survive a financial crash. But a successful bridge financed by hyperscalers creates another problem for Nvidia. Those customers gain negotiating power, develop competitive chips and push pricing; the entities sustaining demand can also weaken its supplier’s position.

8. Multiplying people creates demand on a slower clock

  • Drawing on his exchange with Palantir’s Shyam Sankar, Thompson distinguishes improving the bottom line by replacing people from improving the top line by “multiplying humans.” The latter creates workflows, opportunities and businesses that did not previously exist. It also usually takes longer and often comes from new companies. AI-native challengers may displace incumbents that struggle to bolt AI onto unsuitable software structures.
  • Thompson could scarcely be more bullish on AI. Sharp says he is in the middle ground and does not think AI will replace everyone. Thompson argues that the economy is not purely utilitarian: a huge portion of it involves status, pleasure and things people want but do not need. Infrastructure spending happens now; the businesses and cash flows required to repay it may arrive much later.
  • His defense of advertising follows the same optimism about new demand. Meta can show people things they did not know they wanted: “It’s manufacturing human desire.” Economic activity includes expensive World Series tickets, not merely necessary tasks AI can perform efficiently. Thompson calls Anthropic’s criticism of advertising evidence of misunderstanding humanity. His answer to claims that people cannot invent valuable new activities: “I bet we can.”
  • Thompson’s timing example is the internet: 1993 preceded search advertising around 1999–2000 and the feed in 2006. Discovering a powerful technology’s interface, businesses and monetization takes time. Sharp says AI will be good but does not think it will replace everyone; Thompson says he is an unequivocal believer in AI while emphasizing that monetization and adoption take time.

9. Muse makes Meta’s training expenditure a strategic commitment

  • Sharp cites Meta shares falling about 10% over a week after increased AI spending plans and a new nonvoting share class. The report discussed potential stock offerings of up to $95 billion. Sharp says dilution is a reason the shares should be down; Thompson notes that companies like Meta, Google and Microsoft may be able to get away with it.
  • Anthropic’s disclosure clarified the debate for Thompson by exposing training’s share of costs. Muse could become the “aggregator of aggregators,” owning the interface between users and other services. But Meta must control a sufficiently good underlying model; outsourcing that dependency to a lab seeking the same interface would be dangerous. “If you believe in Muse, you should be happy they’re spending money.”
  • Sharp says Muse’s model is not good enough; Thompson replies that he does not really experience that limitation. Sharp instead highlights 1Password integration as a major improvement. He explains how an agent-specific vault can supply API keys and passwords without awkward terminal files or secrets pasted into chat. Thompson sees 1Password’s unpopular transition toward cross-platform enterprise software as prescient: businesses pay, Apple pressures consumer password tools, and agents need credentials.
  • The training-versus-serving distinction also changes the discussion of Anthropic’s enterprise push. Sharp says the S-1 gives him some sympathy for it: enormous training bills create pressure to sell the resulting models somewhere. Thompson notes that serving enterprise customers consumes relatively little compute compared with training, easing the concern that those customers necessarily take capacity away from other products.

10. Meta’s cash engine funds ambition and pressures Netflix

  • Thompson says Sharp wrote the most compelling investor objection: “Meta doesn’t actually need Muse.” Its advertising business remains formidable. Investors seeking straightforward optimization would prefer the behavior of professionally managed Google or Amazon. Meta instead has a founder, Mark Zuckerberg, pursuing another platform opportunity. Sharp considers this direction more promising than some of Meta’s previous detours.
  • Thompson views Amazon’s infrastructure and inference focus as rational for a company already built around lower margins and logistics. It can serve Anthropic and OpenAI without spending billions to lead frontier development itself. The hosts defer their discussion of Google to the next episode.
  • Thompson’s Netflix thesis is indirect. AI expenses pressure Meta to produce cash, encouraging more ads and more engagement. Earlier restraint over feed ad loads and video consumption gives way to “all the dials turned to 11.” Someone spending an hour watching Reels has less time for Netflix. Sharp initially doubts familiar AI-video displacement arguments, then accepts this cost-pressure mechanism as more persuasive.

11. State power shapes AI access and military infrastructure

  • Responding to a listener who understood him as demanding Anthropic serve the government, Thompson clarifies his argument. If AI becomes civilization-altering, governments will assert authority over its deployment: “They have the guns.” He is describing power and inevitability. The separate normative debate over surveillance or weapons targeting does not resolve whether a private supplier can dictate terms to a state possessing overwhelming coercive power.
  • Thompson distinguishes commercial Starlink from military Starshield. “As I understand it,” the US military controls Starshield’s use; he acknowledges uncertainty about the precise boundaries of Musk’s authority. On Ukraine, he notes that the country was using commercial Starlink rather than Starshield and raises the possibility that Washington asked Musk to enforce the service’s terms.
  • Both hosts stress how little they know about the reported Ukraine slowdown. Thompson guesses Musk was in close alignment with the Trump administration; Sharp guesses the US government asked him to do it. These remain hypotheses. Their shared point is that Ukraine has less power than Washington or the infrastructure supplier it depends on.
  • Thompson’s industrial argument is that consumer demand supplies military scale. Defense primes serving one government customer tend toward expensive, low-volume systems; drones and missiles increasingly require volume. His analogy is car factories repurposed for wartime production. His proposed route to domestic drone capacity is categorical: “Ban all foreign drones and completely legalize drone delivery across the US.” Sharp embraces the commercial-volume argument.

12. Persuasive filmmaking can carry a disputed premise

  • Thompson calls You Can See Everything “the Zootopia of documentaries”: excellent craft carrying a premise he finds untenable. He rejects a sympathetic reading of Elizabeth Holmes as someone manipulated by men and interprets her relationships differently. His concrete objection is the theater’s alarm at Holmes granting Billy Evans power of attorney, which Thompson regards as normal when someone enters prison and a partner cares for the children.
  • Sharp’s defense rests on the film as commentary about media and truth, rather than as an Elizabeth Holmes documentary. He sees multiple layers of construction and interpretation and thinks it should win best picture. Thompson grants the filmmaking’s persuasive power while remaining frustrated by what that persuasion accomplishes.

13. The Brewers’ title rewards an outlook built around the season

  • Thompson had made peace with the Brewers’ small-market limitations and learned to enjoy summer evenings without expecting a World Series. Basketball with Giannis felt different: a real chance creates relentless pressure. The Brewers’ victory initially produced surprisingly little feeling because he had “cauterized the postseason in my heart.” He then becomes emotional explaining the unexpected reward of enjoying both the season and its championship ending.
  • The connection back to AI is uncertainty and control. Thompson objects to people depressing themselves about an unknowable future while missing the life they can live now. “Be nice to people around you. Learn new things. Explore new things.” His sports lesson is that outcomes lie beyond a fan’s control; his broader advice is, “Figure out the future when it gets there.”
