item.title: Octav Founder Shares His DeFi Playbook: Options, Uniswap LPs, and Tokenized Stocks
item.description: Tokenized equities let retail users borrow against one NVIDIA share, pairing familiar collateral with DeFi composability. Baril says scarce Uniswap liquidity at Robinhood’s launch earned roughly $75,000–$80,000 in two weeks at 3–5% fees, until competitors undercut them at 1%. Falling prices increase LP risky-asset inventory, so fixed-premium puts help only when pool fees cover their cost.
item.content:encoded:
The Edge Podcast · DeFi Dad、Nomatic、Mathieu Baril · 2026-10-30 · 73 min · 原语言 EN

Tokenized equities let retail users borrow against one NVIDIA share, pairing familiar collateral with DeFi composability. Baril says scarce Uniswap liquidity at Robinhood’s launch earned roughly $75,000–$80,000 in two weeks at 3–5% fees, until competitors undercut them at 1%. Falling prices increase LP risky-asset inventory, so fixed-premium puts help only when pool fees cover their cost.

TL;DR

  • Baril’s tokenized-stock thesis combines traditional trading tools with collateral access at retail scale. Borrowing against one NVIDIA share is his example of the “best of both worlds”: familiar assets, smaller position sizes and DeFi composability. He has moved beyond simply lending USDC at 3–4% into S&P 500 exposure and USDG on Robinhood.
  • Baril says his Robinhood launch trade made roughly $75,000–$80,000 in two weeks by supplying scarce Uniswap liquidity at 3–5% fees. He gives two approximate capital figures—close to $300,000 and about $200,000. Arbitrage against Rialto generated flow until competitors undercut his fees. He expected the window to last only one or two weeks and withdrew as returns deteriorated.
  • LP hedging is an inventory problem because falling prices leave the provider owning more of the risky asset. An initial 50% short therefore does not cover every subsequent inventory state. Baril prefers fixed-premium puts without liquidation risk: his example leaves $50 from $150 in LP fees after a $100 option premium, with tokenized-stock hedges initially executed through a traditional broker.
  • He takes profits through wide LP ranges and sometimes replaces spot holdings with leveraged exposure. His range illustration is +200%/–66%; another tactic uses roughly 33% of the Derive position value for a 3x long on Lighter, freeing about 66% for other positions, including Paradex’s DIME. “Same exposure” depends on continuing to manage liquidation risk.
  • Around $1 billion FDV, Baril wants to reassess conviction against revenue and traditional-company valuations. DeFi Dad raises the difficulty of adding HYPE at roughly $90 billion FDV versus a recent Derive entry around $0.40. Baril’s secondary options bet is Paradex: he estimates Derive takes about 90% of on-chain options volume, while Paradex offers stock options and often cheaper premiums—potentially supported by incentives.
  • Ethereum is Baril’s store-of-value holding, while Derive, Tread and Kinetiq are his largest liquid bets. Despite his mining origins, he says, “I think I have 1” Bitcoin as a memory, citing greater upside elsewhere and concerns about its community’s resistance to change. He rejects ETH at $30,000 in 10 years but believes $5,000, $7,000 or $10,000 can come “over time.”
  • His capital follows new-chain activity, while his institutional observations favor Ethereum mainnet’s staying power. He has moved his activity from Base to Robinhood for now and is bullish on Kinetiq’s Elysium ecosystem, helped by Hyperliquid’s reputation. But the constraint he hears from funds is the “Lindy effect”: they will use mainnet while saying, “Don’t ask me to go on an L2.”
  • Octav and Tactical turn wallet activity into a more usable picture of positioning. Tactical visualizes and helps users copy multi-leg options, while Octav can connect hedges across venues using GLM-5.3 on its own systems. Historical API snapshots cost $30 per address annually versus $150 for Lite, with transaction data available through Pro. DeFi Dad cautions that copying does not guarantee profit; Baril’s tax boundary is equally clear: “Data alone won’t work” without an accountant.

Digest

1. Octav’s data work creates early access to protocols

  • Baril’s route into DeFi started with Bitcoin mining in 2013 while studying robotics engineering in Canada. He bought ASICs in batches of 50 to resell, met future Octav co-founder Luc as a customer, and mined through 2022; their Ethereum operation reached roughly 500–600 GPUs. Using mined ETH in DeFi let them do more with those assets.
  • After biotech work in California and a strategy role at Zapper, he left in 2022 to build Octav around tracking DeFi profits and Canadian tax liabilities, including assets in his Cayman Islands hedge fund. It has become a data platform for hedge funds and family offices, with ConsenSys among its clients. The original requirement was simple: “I need to understand where the money is.”
  • Clients request integrations, often to track early-investor vesting, giving Octav access before wider attention arrives. The team meets founders, reads contracts and tests the flow with small amounts such as $100. Contracts they cannot see on InterScan or teams that will not talk to them are red flags; integration does not guarantee Baril will invest. Nomatic presents founder interviews as accessible diligence, but warns people can be “really good actors.”

2. Tokenized equities give traditional tools a new role onchain

  • For Baril, the compelling innovation is bringing traditional-market tools into DeFi. He finds many protocol FDVs overvalued and views borrowing against NVIDIA or the S&P 500 as safer than borrowing against AAVE. That preference underlies a move from USDC into S&P 500 exposure and USDG on Robinhood, seeking more than 3–4% lending yields.
  • His concrete example is the wealthy shareholder borrowing against Tesla stock: tokenization lets a retail user borrow against one NVIDIA share. Add composability and smaller position sizes to traditional-market tools and the result is the “best of both worlds.” His framing of traditional finance’s migration: “We have the tooling, but now we have the infrastructure, and the infrastructure is on-chain, so let’s move on-chain.”
  • Options needed market makers because strikes, time and other factors make liquidity difficult; a Uniswap-style AMM was insufficient in his account. Derive, which he has held since Lyra, opened the market once it attracted enough market makers. Tread supplies another missing piece: professional market-making tools spanning Hyperliquid, other perp venues and centralized exchanges. He sees this tooling bringing greater capital efficiency and stability.

3. Robinhood’s launch fees offered a short window

  • At Robinhood’s launch, Baril saw tokenized-stock volume on Rialto but none on Uniswap. He opened NVIDIA, Tesla and S&P 500 pools at 3–5% fees: “If you want to pass through my pool, you’ll pay the fee, and that’s it.” Arbitrageurs balancing prices between venues supplied flow even when his pools were expensive.
  • He says he moved close to $300,000, then describes the amount as about $200,000; he reports making roughly $75,000–$80,000 in two weeks. He knew the window would be one or two weeks, not four or six months. Competitors opening 1% pools predictably eroded returns, so he withdrew.
  • His next search borrowed from Aerodrome’s model on Base, where voting directs liquidity incentives and, in his view, aligns token ownership. He deployed into the small DEX he calls Allendale, at roughly $1 million TVL, after meeting the team and checking contracts. Its anonymous team remains a red flag: he says they are ready to get out if something happens.
  • He initially thought launching with USDG would be Robinhood’s “nail in the coffin.” Instead, users bridged in for tokenized stocks and expanded USDG’s TVL relative to USDC. He explicitly says USDG is not decentralized; its appeal is competition and another stablecoin alongside USDC and USDT. Launch volume has already normalized, but he remains interested in Robinhood’s traditional-finance focus.

4. An LP hedge must follow the changing inventory

  • DeFi Dad asks how a SPY/USDG LP was hedged. Baril starts with ETH/USDC: as ETH falls, an AMM position accumulates ETH and can end entirely in ETH, leaving no stablecoins. A static short of the original 50% allocation therefore misses the growing inventory exposure. Hedge size must reflect what the LP can become.
  • He prefers buying puts because the premium is fixed and the purchased option has no liquidation price. In his example, $150 of LP fees less a $100 option premium leaves $50. Perp shorts can sometimes pay funding, but rates move and liquidation must be managed. “That’s the beauty of options.” He frames the broader task as market-maker inventory management that smart contracts can automate.
  • For tokenized stocks, he initially bought hedging options through a traditional stockbroker because suitable on-chain options were scarce; Paradex’s stock options could bring the complete strategy on-chain. LP fees must cover the premium. He considers SPY/USDG less volatile than ETH pairs—SPY will not lose 25%, “hopefully”—while stressing correct calculations as the LP shifts into one asset.

5. New chains attract his capital, while mainnet retains institutional trust

  • Asked whether Robinhood has displaced Base, Baril says he moved “100%” of his activity to Robinhood for now, following volume and new opportunities. The chain had been his focus for roughly six or seven weeks. He expects a gradual return to Base or other chains as tokenized-stock markets develop, including possible arbitrage in the same stock across chains.
  • He still uses Hyperliquid for trading and hedging, alongside Derive, and says he bought a big bag of Kinetiq early. He is bullish on its Elysium ecosystem because he knows the team and expects a stronger DeFi, trading and tokenized-stock focus than HyperEVM delivered. He is unsure how to classify its layer structure, but stresses that it starts with Hyperliquid’s reputation behind it.
  • On the airdrop, his position is affirmative: airdrops have become a full-time job for people extracting money instead of rewarding early contributors who grow the product. He thinks selling the airdrop was a good choice because those extraction incentives do not align with a company’s goal of developing power users.
  • New chains create arbitrage and liquidity gaps before markets settle, but he does not think 25 L2s make sense long term. Lower Ethereum mainnet gas costs and the “Lindy effect” matter to institutional clients. His summary of fund responses: they will deploy on mainnet, but “don’t ask me to go on an L2.” He does not expect Elysium to displace mainnet.

6. Wide LP ranges and leverage change how he takes profits

  • For taking profits, Baril prefers wide Uniswap V3 or V4 ranges over waiting to press the sell button. His illustration widens a typical +100%/–50% range to +200%/–66%, avoiding a full range’s poor capital efficiency. In a Derive/ETH pool, he collects fees in both assets and sells fee income while keeping the underlying LP position.
  • If Derive rises 2–3x and the LP ends up fully converted out of it, he accepts that as an exit on strength. The reverse risk remains: a falling token leaves the LP holding the bag. “It’s hard to take profit,” he says, because a double encourages the belief it can double again.
  • His other tactic replaces spot with leveraged exposure. Using 100,000 Derive tokens as the illustration, he says to sell 66% and put 33% into a 3x long on Lighter, freeing the remaining 66% in USDC while maintaining similar exposure. “You just need to manage your liquidation price” is the condition he attaches to that capital efficiency.
  • He used freed capital to buy Paradex’s DIME, keeping Derive exposure while adding a second options venue. He describes this as spreading project-failure risk across the theme. It follows his preference for a “beta play”: owning a credible follower that might benefit from the category leader’s growth without necessarily being the better product.

7. A $1 billion FDV triggers a fresh valuation review

  • DeFi Dad’s question is how to stay long for the next 12 months while taking profits and avoiding vaporware. His hesitation: HYPE at roughly $90 billion FDV is harder to add to than Derive, which he recently bought around $0.40. Baril’s response centers on revenue, valuation and whether conviction survives a higher price.
  • Around $1 billion FDV, Baril wants to reassess, contrasting crypto valuations with companies worth $50 million or $100 million that have real revenue. Emissions and tokenomics complicate the comparison; it is a review threshold rather than an automatic exit. His behavioral warning is closing winners and doubling down on losers: “You should do the opposite” and double down on a winner. He still sees room for Derive because of its revenue, attention and creation of an options market in crypto.

8. Ethereum is his reserve, with options tokens carrying active risk

  • Despite the Bitcoin sweater, Baril says, “I think I have 1” Bitcoin as a keepsake. He sees greater upside elsewhere and dislikes what he calls a toxic, change-resistant community. He acknowledges Bitcoin’s fixed gold-standard identity, but asks whether its community would adapt to quantum risks: “Do we need that? I don’t know.”
  • Ethereum is his store of value, but the valuation thesis is restrained. He sees it as internet infrastructure whose applications capture value, and does not believe in ETH at $30,000 in 10 years. He does believe it will reach $5,000, $7,000 or $10,000 “over time,” while expecting that to take time and arguing that very high ETH prices complicate gas economics.
  • His largest liquid exposures are Derive, Tread and Kinetiq; the leaders can change roughly every year. He gives no percentage allocation. His watchlist includes Venice’s VVV and Interfold, but VVV remains conditional: “If it makes sense over time.” AI tokens attract hype, and his own DGX Spark setup means he does not need to buy private inference. He also expects perhaps four or five other options projects to take a little of the market.

9. Paradex offers a second bet on options growth

  • The Paradex thesis is explicitly a secondary bet, analogous to his Lighter purchase alongside Hyperliquid. Baril estimates Derive takes about 90% of on-chain options volume and sees Paradex as the next venue already taking share. He is also watching Hypercall, which he describes as built by the team behind the former bridge Synapse.
  • His evidence is product activity and team access: he has met Paradex’s team, interviewed them for Tactical and seen them launch stock options that Derive does not have. The bet is that options remain a small market with room for several projects. Derive remains his primary position.
  • Tactical can compare premiums when the user has money on both venues. “If they can quote you,” Paradex often offers a better premium, he says. He leaves the subsidy question open: “Are they incentivizing this? Maybe.” The concrete change is competition over option pricing as additional venues arrive.

10. Tactical makes options positions easier to understand and copy

  • Tactical grew out of Baril’s attempts to explain options to two Octav developers who were deep in DeFi but did not understand options. One developer built an initial version in a weekend; Baril says the product had been live for about two weeks. Users can follow traders such as CoolCrypto, receive Telegram alerts and copy a position at a different size. Baril says platform use can generate revenue; he traces the idea to Derive’s builder-code system.
  • The interface groups multi-leg positions and makes strategies easier to inspect instead of leaving users to reconstruct them across accounts. A capped call sells an upper call to reduce the premium while limiting upside; an iron condor earns if price remains within a range and loses outside it. DeFi Dad’s caveat stays explicit: copying another trader does not guarantee a profit.
  • An AI flow can use a view—Ethereum above $4,000 by March, for example—to suggest an options strategy. Baril says Octav and Tactical’s AI runs on GLM-5.3 on their own systems, including multiple DGX Spark machines, and that they are trying to keep it private. Leaderboards, trade theses and daily winning or losing trades give users more context about positions they might copy.
  • Execution remains awkward because Derive and Paradex operate on separate chains, requiring funds on both before users can copy trades. The team is considering a single deposit that funds both accounts. That remains a proposed simplification; the current product is still being developed, with more explanations and clearer wording planned.

11. Octav connects cross-venue hedges with usable wallet history

  • Baril’s hypothetical pairs show why cross-venue data matters: a 5x Hyperliquid long may be hedged by a Derive put, while a Lighter long plus Hyperliquid short may collect funding in a delta-neutral position. DeFi Dad highlights the shift from manually combing dashboards to asking an AI what changed, which positions were closed and how much exposure remains.
  • Historical snapshots run daily at midnight UTC. Lite costs $150 per year for one address and includes snapshots, premium widgets and exportable value reports; Pro adds transaction-level inflows and outflows. AI is free for now, but its answers depend on accessible data: Lite unlocks historical snapshots, while Pro enables transaction questions such as when a token was bought.
  • Users who skip the frontend can pay $30 per year per address in API credits for daily snapshots. Octav offers an API, CLI, MCP and skill, allowing users to connect their own AI, including a private Venice setup. Baril attributes the usefulness to structured protocol data and historical changes that a model would otherwise have to reconstruct from explorers and other platforms.
  • On taxes, Baril draws a boundary: “Hire an accountant, because data alone won’t work.” Octav supplies DeFi data to Cryptio and was built to explain positions and transactions, not produce a 1099. DeFi Dad pushes for year-round ballpark estimates because accountants struggle with current DeFi data; Baril says Pro can support a good understanding of annual liabilities.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/octav-founder-shares-his-defi-playbook-options-u

item.title: WHOOP CEO, Will Ahmed: 50B Hours of Health Data, a 4 Million Member Data Moat, & the FDA Fight
item.description: WHOOP shifted from a $500 purchase to $15–$30 monthly subscriptions as membership grew from one million to three million in 24 months; Ahmed expects around four million at year-end. Its just-over-50-billion-hour data set supports emerging AI, but biomarker prediction remains preliminary; after an FDA warning letter, Ahmed says WHOOP’s case helped drive blood-pressure wellness guideline changes.
item.content:encoded:
All-In · Will Ahmed · 2026-10-29 · 56 min · 原语言 EN

WHOOP shifted from a $500 purchase to $15–$30 monthly subscriptions as membership grew from one million to three million in 24 months; Ahmed expects around four million at year-end. Its just-over-50-billion-hour data set supports emerging AI, but biomarker prediction remains preliminary; after an FDA warning letter, Ahmed says WHOOP’s case helped drive blood-pressure wellness guideline changes.

TL;DR

  • WHOOP’s accelerating membership growth makes retention and recurring revenue the central business story. Ahmed says reaching one million members took 12 years, two million another 18 months, and three million another six months; he expects around four million at year-end. Replacing a $500 purchase with subscriptions now priced at $15–$30 monthly lowered the entry barrier and made WHOOP “really obsessed with” existing members.
  • WHOOP’s data advantage combines continuous measurement with context for interpreting it. Members wear the device 23.6 hours daily, generating just over 50 billion hours of physiological data; blood tests, medical records, and journal feedback add context. Ahmed says WHOOP is developing its own foundational models, but biomarker prediction remains preliminary: physiological signals “might” identify an abnormal result without directly measuring it. He also says 80% of members interact with the AI.
  • Personalized coaching is already useful, while the journal’s examples show why correlation needs scrutiny. Jason reports an apparent 7% recovery benefit associated with warm baths, but his apparent 3% penalty from vitamin D prompts questions about travel and missing observations. The assistant describes that result as “a correlation, not evidence”; the newer GLP-1 tracker turns personal context into activity, hydration, and protein goals.
  • The FDA dispute centers on whether blood pressure can serve wellness purposes without a medical diagnosis. Ahmed says WHOOP received a warning letter, maintained its position, and kept Blood Pressure Insights available after guidelines changed. He thinks WHOOP’s case helped drive that change; its ECG feature separately has FDA 510(k) clearance.
  • WHOOP’s expansion strategy favors controlling the health experience while replacing some adjacent hardware. Jason proposes branded cuffs and scales, citing a $10 billion valuation and illustrative revenue arithmetic of four million members paying $250 annually. Ahmed calls cuffs commoditized and says the longer-term ambition is to “replace the cuff”; he also says WHOOP does not sell member data.
  • LeBron James’s ambassador deal formalizes an existing customer relationship rather than creating one. Ahmed says James has worn WHOOP for 11 years and was among its first 100 users. The original principle still matters: “you want people to love your product authentically.” Some athletes later invested, and WHOOP developed name, image, and likeness agreements.
  • The closing discussion flags company approval and broker claims as checks in private-market secondaries. Ahmed advises building a relationship with the company CFO and getting their blessing for an SPV or secondary transaction. Jason says some brokers claiming to have shares are “trying to create a market”; Ahmed describes his own inquiries going quiet when he asks for details.

Digest

1. Subscriptions changed WHOOP’s growth curve and incentives

  • Founded in 2012, WHOOP took roughly 12 years to reach one million members, another 18 months to reach two million, and another six months to reach three million. Ahmed expects around four million at year-end. The company now employs 1,200 people: an “overnight success” that took a long time.
  • The consumer product launched in 2017 at $500 upfront. Over the following year, Ahmed observed unusually persistent usage but insufficient purchases. The subscription experiment addressed that mismatch: lower the entry price, let customers discover the value, and earn revenue over time. He credits the change with growth in 2018–19; current plans range from $15 to $30 monthly.
  • The deeper change was organizational. Subscriptions made WHOOP “really obsessed with” existing members, engagement, effectiveness, and behavior change. Ahmed contrasts that with hardware businesses needing another sale every 12 months: WHOOP wants new hardware when it is “a step function better,” while continually improving products already in members’ hands.
  • That commitment extends beyond the original purchase proposition. Ahmed lists ECG monitoring, AFib detection, Advanced Labs blood testing, the Healthspan longevity feature and WHOOP age, and Blood Pressure Insights as capabilities members might not have anticipated 18 months earlier. Jason’s endorsement is that WHOOP assumes responsibility for explaining when an upgrade is worthwhile.

2. Continuous baselines make small physiological changes visible

  • WHOOP organizes its interface around sleep, recovery, and strain; recovery becomes a red, yellow, or green score from 0–100%. Continuous measurement shapes the hardware: a 14-day battery and a charger that slides onto the device during wear. Ahmed says members consequently wear WHOOP an average of 23.6 hours daily.
  • Ahmed describes heart rate variability as a lens into autonomic regulation, with sympathetic and parasympathetic activity working together. His typical age benchmarks fall from 80–100 in one’s 20s to around 70 in the 30s, 50 in the 40s, and 30 or below in the 50s and 60s. Keeping HRV flat over years, he argues, can itself indicate good fitness and longevity.
  • Jason’s example is an early warning rather than a specific diagnosis. His respiratory rate rose about two breaths above normal and skin temperature about 2° for two consecutive days before Sunday-night chest pain sent him to the emergency room. He says testing found inflammation rather than a heart attack; the earlier readings had put him “on high alert.”
  • Ahmed recalls another member with close to a decade of baseline data whose HRV fell from about 100 to 50. Subsequent medical testing found testicular cancer. Jason asks whether HRV was previously known as a leading indicator for that cancer. Ahmed’s answer preserves the uncertainty: “I don’t think so.”

3. The AI opportunity depends on combining different kinds of data

  • Continuous wear has produced just over 50 billion hours of physiological data, which Ahmed calls “one of the largest health data sets in the world.” WHOOP is developing its own foundational models and combining sensor information with uploaded blood tests, Advanced Labs results, and medical records.
  • Ahmed says WHOOP is “starting to see indications” that physiological signals “might” predict whether a biomarker is out of range without measuring that biomarker directly. His hypothetical next step is a targeted recommendation to test cortisol.
  • Self-reported context supplies another layer. Just over 50% of members journal daily across more than 100 behaviors, supplements, drugs, and lifestyle choices. Mood entries could, for example, supply information for predicting happiness. Ahmed also cites members opening the app eight times daily and 80% of the membership interacting with the AI.
  • Jason’s assessment of the coach has changed: initially “pretty dumb,” it now earns seven and a half out of 10. He describes receiving flight-specific advice about sleep and caffeine when traveling to Japan. Asked whether the system inferred that capability independently, Ahmed explains that WHOOP created a dedicated travel team because the use case was so popular.

4. Journaling turns personal observations into coaching, with confounding still visible

  • Jason thinks behavioral insights become available after five “yes” and five “no” entries. He reports an apparent 7% recovery improvement associated with warm baths and a –9% association for alcohol. Ahmed says alcohol has a hugely negative effect for many people. He also says eating within three hours of bedtime is detrimental across the WHOOP population, explaining that digestion interferes with quality sleep during the first hours in bed.
  • Jason challenges his apparent 3% recovery penalty from vitamin D: “I don’t know if that’s accurate or not.” Ahmed suggests travel might explain the association. The coach adds that Jason has not logged vitamin D during the latest 14-day stretch and calls the result “a correlation, not evidence” of causation.
  • GLP-1 tracking adds medication context to the same coaching system. Ahmed says that typically about half the weight lost is fat and half muscle, making strength work and protein priorities in WHOOP’s response. He describes reports of creatine helping as “anecdotal success,” while emphasizing activity—even bodyweight training—to limit muscle loss.
  • Jason says he lost 43 pounds, moving from 213 to 170, and now takes a maintenance dose. His agreed plan includes 9,800 steps, two strength activities weekly, daily hydration, protein, and logging his GLP-1 dose. Ahmed checks that the AI discussed the plan and Jason confirmed the goals, illustrating how the assistant translates personal circumstances into commitments.

5. The FDA fight challenged a boundary between wellness and medicine

  • Ahmed says WHOOP began pursuing wrist-based blood pressure monitoring four years earlier. A stress, sleep, and blood pressure study enrolled 70,000 people, with participants uploading cuff readings daily over several weeks. Pairing those readings with existing physiology created training data. WHOOP’s stated ambition was accuracy “as accurately—or within similar accuracy—as a medical device.”
  • His regulatory argument concerns intended use. Heart rate monitoring for exercise or sleep falls under wellness, while AFib detection or heart attack prediction requires medical regulation. Blood pressure, he says, historically faced a blanket medical-device requirement. WHOOP believed research connecting blood pressure with stress, sleep, and well-being justified a corresponding wellness application.
  • WHOOP launched Blood Pressure Insights and received an FDA warning letter. Ahmed says the company “stuck to our guns” through a public disagreement. He reports that the FDA subsequently updated guidelines to recognize blood pressure wellness applications, “I think based on our case” and industry feedback. The feature remains available; he describes the current FDA relationship as positive.
  • Ahmed distinguishes that dispute from WHOOP’s regulated products. Its wrist ECG feature has FDA 510(k) clearance. Depending on the application, WHOOP either pursues clinical trials and medical clearance or seeks a faster wellness launch. His position is that both approaches belong in an innovative company’s relationship with the agency.

6. WHOOP wants control of the experience without making every accessory

  • Jason asks for WHOOP-branded scales and cuffs, citing a $10 billion valuation and estimating $1 billion revenue from four million members paying $250 annually. Those figures come from the host’s framing. Ahmed says WHOOP often favors building or acquiring over partnering, but regards cuffs as commoditized technology: people can calibrate WHOOP with a cuff, after which WHOOP can measure blood pressure without one. “At the end of the day, we kind of want to replace the cuff.”
  • Ahmed links the right to accumulate health information to strong data policies: “we do not sell data,” and “you are not the product, Jason.” He also resists Jason’s dismissal of Apple, calling its watch the most successful smartwatch and respecting its hardware and software. He notes that the wearables field had more competing products 10 years earlier than today.

7. Athlete marketing follows authentic adoption, while access rules lag

  • LeBron James is becoming a global ambassador after 11 years wearing WHOOP without a formal relationship. Ahmed says James was among the first 100 users, making his adoption unusually validating for an unknown company. He joins an ambassador roster that includes Cristiano Ronaldo, Patrick Mahomes, and Lewis Hamilton.
  • Jason presses whether paid partnerships reverse WHOOP’s earlier reluctance to pay athletes to wear the product. Ahmed says companies not yet doing large-scale advertising should be careful about paying people to use their products. “You want people to love your product authentically”; because WHOOP must be worn 24/7, he says, paying an athlete who dislikes it would not work. Some athletes later invested, and WHOOP developed name, image, and likeness agreements to advertise those relationships.
  • Competition access remains unsettled: Ahmed says NBA game usage is still under review. At the Australian Open, players were asked to remove WHOOP despite International Tennis Federation approval, while other majors subsequently said wearables could be worn. Ahmed describes a “natural evolution” toward acceptance. Jason instead suspects sponsorship pressure, joking that a $10 million advertising commitment might change organizers’ opinions.

8. Secondary-market demand creates another verification problem

  • Jason says he started a late-stage practice after members of his 4,000-member syndicate asked for access to later-stage companies, with deals including Zipline and ICON Homes. He notes that when he knows a founder, the CFO approves transactions. Ahmed advises building a relationship with the company’s CFO, getting their blessing, and accepting a refusal.
  • Jason says some secondary brokers claiming to have shares are “really just trying to create a market.” Ahmed describes his own experience: brokers claim to have shares at a certain price, but when he asks who the transaction is with and offers to coordinate with the company CFO, they go quiet. He calls it a “fishing expedition” and says these situations arise when a company is doing well as well as when it is failing.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/whoop-ceo-will-ahmed-50b-hours-health-data-4-mil

item.title: How an unelected man ruled New York for 30 years
item.description: Moses made Triborough’s temporary charter durable through refinancing and toll-contract powers; by 1946 it could borrow $360 million, versus New York City’s $150 million headroom. Fast delivery and beneficiaries from banks to unions made resistance costly; Johnson similarly built power through committee control, campaign-fund access and agenda-setting. His 1957 civil-rights compromise avoided a Southern filibuster but retained jury-trial protections for Southern election officials.
item.content:encoded:
Dwarkesh Podcast · Dwarkesh Patel · 2026-10-29 · 25 min · 原语言 EN

Moses made Triborough’s temporary charter durable through refinancing and toll-contract powers; by 1946 it could borrow $360 million, versus New York City’s $150 million headroom. Fast delivery and beneficiaries from banks to unions made resistance costly; Johnson similarly built power through committee control, campaign-fund access and agenda-setting. His 1957 civil-rights compromise avoided a Southern filibuster but retained jury-trial protections for Southern election officials.

TL;DR

  • Moses turned a temporary bridge authority into a durable financial and legal power base. The 1933 act let him refinance 40-year bonds “from time to time,” borrow “for any other corporate purpose,” and entrench toll powers in bond contracts. By 1946, Triborough could borrow $360 million, while New York City could borrow $150 million before hitting its legal debt limit.
  • Execution created dependence that elected officials struggled to unwind. Moses completed 1,700 park renovations in four months and controlled the engineering plans that helped New York secure 1/7 of national Depression-era work-relief funding by 1936. Mayors faced his projects or nothing; at his peak, 12 government posts made him a “hydra with a dozen heads.”
  • Moses made construction reward the interests capable of blocking it. His “concentrated faction for YIMBY” combined discounted bond purchases for banks with union jobs, legal fees and politically brokered insurance. Beneficiaries pressured opponents, while newspaper relationships and resignation threats raised the political cost of removing a personally “money honest” operator.
  • Control over scarce favors and procedure gave Johnson power his office did not formally possess. The majority leader’s sole formal power was recognition first on the floor; Johnson controlled committee assignments and access to legislation, and could connect colleagues to campaign funds through Texas oilmen. He protected private bargains through restrictions on debate. As Patel quotes Senator Paul Douglas, “all the action takes place offstage before the play begins.”
  • Johnson’s 1957 civil rights deal linked unrelated concessions to bridge an apparent legislative deadlock. Over seven months, a dam vote, jury protections for striking workers and eligibility for Black citizens to serve on federal juries brought together competing factions. The jury-trial guarantee for Southern election officials remained, leaving the bill weak enough that Southern senators agreed not to filibuster it and advancing Johnson’s hopes for the 1960 presidential nomination.
  • Patel reads Moses and Johnson as opposite trajectories between ideals and power. Caro’s Moses began as a reformer before power became “a drug”; Johnson’s opportunism preceded his presidential leadership on the 1964 Civil Rights Act and 1965 Voting Rights Act. Patel also disputes blaming Moses for New York’s decline, arguing that larger structural forces mattered more.

Digest

1. Moses made a temporary authority financially permanent

  • Patel starts with the 1933 Triborough Bridge Authority Act: an institution intended to disappear after repaying its construction bonds. Moses inserted permission to refinance “from time to time” and borrow “for any other corporate purpose,” resetting a maximum 40-year term. Authority over connecting roads and related facilities stretched a two-bridge mandate into jurisdiction over much of New York.
  • The financing advantage was measurable: in 1946, Triborough could borrow $360 million; New York City could borrow $150 million before hitting its legal debt limit. Toll revenues financed expansion and supported further borrowing.
  • Moses also wrote toll-setting and surplus-retention powers into bond contracts. In Patel’s account, constitutional protection against impairing contracts made those powers irrevocable short of a constitutional convention, lasting throughout bond lifetimes that refinancing could continually extend.

2. Delivery and patronage made Moses costly to remove

  • Removal required “stated charges after a formal hearing,” while Moses was personally “money honest.” At his peak, 12 simultaneous posts, divided between mayoral and gubernatorial appointments, made removing him from one office dangerous: the other heads of the “hydra” survived.
  • Moses was reappointed every six years because no mayor or governor wanted to fire him. He was popular for delivering beaches, parks and pools within election cycles; in his first four months as city park commissioner, he completed 1,700 park renovations. By 1936, his prepared plans helped New York capture 1/7 of national Depression-era work-relief funding. Without independent engineering capacity, mayors could choose his projects or build nothing.
  • Resignation threats put unfinished projects, funding and public approval at risk. Relationships with newspaper owners, including the Sulzbergers, meant mayors also anticipated hostile front pages.
  • Patel calls Moses’s beneficiaries a “concentrated faction for YIMBY”: banks bought discounted bonds without competitive bidding; unions gained jobs; connected lawyers collected fees; party bosses brokered bridge insurance. These beneficiaries pressured officials obstructing construction.

3. Power complicates the verdict on both men

  • Caro’s Moses began as an idealistic reformer defeated by Tammany Hall; power initially served his dreams, then became “a drug that creates in the user a need for larger and larger doses.” Patel disputes blaming him for New York’s 1970s crisis: in his opinion, structural forces mattered more, with Detroit and St. Louis suffering worse collapses without him.
  • Johnson followed the opposite trajectory in Patel’s telling. Southern senators saw an ally: asked whether Johnson showed sympathy for Black people, Herman Talmadge answered, “None indicated.” Yet as president, Johnson spearheaded the 1964 Civil Rights Act and 1965 Voting Rights Act, acting on ideals few knew he held.

4. Johnson concentrated favors and controlled the agenda

  • The majority leader had exactly one formal power: recognition first on the floor. Johnson became his party’s leader at 44, in a Senate averaging around 60, then built leverage by controlling bill scheduling and committee assignments, and by connecting colleagues seeking campaign money to Texas oilmen. “Johnson could give and Johnson could withhold.”
  • His control of the steering committee displaced seniority for many seats. After Estes Kefauver opposed him on an important 1957 motion, a coveted Foreign Relations seat Kefauver expected went that same week to the more junior John F. Kennedy.
  • Johnson required unanimous consent agreements limiting debate and amendments before bills reached the floor, protecting privately negotiated deals from public persuasion or surprise changes. Patel cites Senator Paul Douglas: “all the action takes place offstage before the play begins.”

5. Information control made the 1957 compromise possible

  • Johnson’s third tactic was information brokerage: committee staffers and aides reported to him while he listened and cajoled colleagues. Knowing each senator’s demands let him connect unrelated votes and ensure deals left him ahead.
  • Passing some civil rights legislation in 1957 mattered to his hopes for the 1960 presidential nomination. Northern liberals rejected Southern demands for jury trials: Southern jurors had to be registered voters, producing all-white juries that, Northerners argued, would never convict white registrars for excluding Black voters.
  • Over seven months, Johnson assembled the bargain: Western senators received a vote on a federal dam between Idaho and Oregon; Midwestern Republicans secured jury trials for striking workers; moderates won eligibility for Black citizens on federal juries. The jury-trial guarantee for Southern election officials remained, keeping the bill weak enough that Southern senators agreed not to filibuster.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/what-i-learned-about-power-from-lbj-robert-moses

item.title: Hacking Just Got 1000x Cheaper
item.description: Attack costs may have fallen “probably 100, maybe 1,000 fold,” while defenders spend 10–1,000 times more; compromised trust infrastructure lets one entry point seed further attacks, a panelist says the demand is “very bullish compute.” Anthropic’s cash and no customer exceeding 10% of revenue ease near-term financing fears, but open-source commoditization and whether demand absorbs efficiency gains remain unresolved.
item.content:encoded:
Delphi Digital · Kevin、Jason、José、Yan、Ceteris、Jake Sylvestre · 2026-10-29 · 73 min · 原语言 EN

Attack costs may have fallen “probably 100, maybe 1,000 fold,” while defenders spend 10–1,000 times more; compromised trust infrastructure lets one entry point seed further attacks, a panelist says the demand is “very bullish compute.” Anthropic’s cash and no customer exceeding 10% of revenue ease near-term financing fears, but open-source commoditization and whether demand absorbs efficiency gains remain unresolved.

TL;DR

  • The discussion estimates cyberattack costs have fallen “probably 100, maybe 1,000 fold,” while defenders may spend 10–1,000 times what attackers spend. Compromised trust infrastructure can turn an old device into a starting point for further attacks. The exchange argues that better defensive models do not remove the attacker’s advantage: finding one entry point can suffice. One panelist calls the resulting demand “very bullish compute.”
  • Anthropic’s S-1 eases near-term financing fears without resolving the long-term economics of frontier models. Ceteris highlights cash reserves and no customer exceeding 10% of revenue; open-source commoditization remains unresolved. The compute trade still depends on demand absorbing efficiency gains: a panelist warns that Jevons’ paradox taking five years would still be a problem.
  • Jake expects SpaceX and Elon to “clean up this market in the next 12 months,” particularly through stranded compute and weaker operators. Execution speed, diversified revenues, and financing advantages underpin the call. Another panelist points to the cloud business’s short-notice contracts and spot-price exposure as substantial downside risks.
  • Hypercall’s options thesis rests on making underwriting and hedging cheaper through Hyperliquid’s existing liquidity. Jake reports roughly $250 million of associated perp volume over 30 days and estimates equivalent Binance hedging would cost 10–15 times more under generous fee assumptions. Around-the-clock trading, fractional contracts, and composable collateral are the customer proposition; retail distribution remains the execution problem.
  • Bitcoin’s quantum tail risk produces the episode’s sharpest disagreement, particularly over whether a fork could preserve value after compromised coins move. José argues holders would choose the fork that protects value. Other panelists warn that a fork or compromised coins could be damaging; one estimates roughly 90% downside. Jake expects quantum cracking eventually and stresses that compromised Satoshi keys would imply a much wider migration problem.
  • Large IPOs and AI financing could drain public-market liquidity while recycling exit proceeds into venture. A panelist sees exceptional conditions for agile early-stage funds, supported by mega-fund demand and scarce investable companies. Yan warns that weak Anthropic trading could reset private marks quickly, while Kevin wants retention evidence behind startups reaching $100 million ARR before they have meaningful cohort histories.
  • The crypto stance is patient rather than aggressively leveraged, with Bitcoin around $80,000 and a possible retest of the $70,000s still inside the bullish framework. Jason holds previously raised cash because “if I don’t have a read, I don’t play the game.” Ceteris remains constructive on 2027, while Yan sees on-chain financial activity and debasement—not a single treasury buyer—as the cycle’s underlying drivers.

Digest

1. Cash remains a position while crypto lacks follow-through

  • Jason expects little surprise from the Fed meeting and admits his claim that the 10:30 seller had disappeared immediately failed. He holds cash raised during the earlier on-chain trading surge because his market read keeps reversing: “If I don’t have a read, I don’t play the game.”
  • Ceteris does not think the cycle is over and expects 2027 to be good, but sees “no follow-through.” Bitcoin is around $80,000, Zcash between $1,100 and $1,300, and HYPE around $80. Midterms the following Tuesday might change conditions; meanwhile, patience beats pushing leverage on the first breakout. He acknowledges possible complacency.
  • Yan expects chop followed by a stronger year-end, though Bitcoin could retest the $70,000s from roughly $80,500. His cycle thesis is TradFi activity moving on-chain through RWAs, stocks, and perp DEXs such as Hyperliquid and Lighter, potentially with institutions providing front ends. Debasement adds longer-term support; midterms could constrain Trump-related policy risk.

2. Anthropic’s balance sheet buys time for the AI trade

  • Ceteris reads Anthropic’s S-1 as materially better than feared: substantial cash extends the runway, and no customer accounts for more than 10% of revenue. José notes that this counters speculation about extreme dependence on Meta or Jane Street. Ceteris thinks removing those near-term concerns helps money return to adjacent AI names.
  • The distinction is between working capital and eventual business value. Cash “kicks the bucket down the road massively,” but cannot answer whether open-source competition commoditizes models. That remains unresolved; an S-1 could not have settled it anyway.
  • José describes SK Hynix’s quarter as “absurd,” estimating “60 billion, something like that” in earnings. He sees some mechanical downside support when memory stocks trade around three times forward earnings, while acknowledging cyclicality. Neoclouds have also rebounded, but remain “very hard to understand businesses.”

3. Efficiency gains can redistribute value across the AI stack

  • Jake questions why the whole stack trades together. He cites a Google paper he thinks was called TurboQuant cutting memory requirements by 80–90%, and SanDisk’s prospective high-bandwidth flash alternative to high-bandwidth memory. Advances across memory and fiber could “really nuke the value out of these neoclouds”; he expects greater dispersion.
  • Ceteris sees upside in the roughly $500 billion of compute commitments being discussed because much of that capacity was secured below spot prices, which he says rose about 44% this year. José identifies the correlated downside: take-or-pay obligations leave unused capacity precisely when resale prices collapse. He cites telecoms in 2001 and SemiAnalysis’s 50-gigawatt forecast for the following year.
  • Jake asks whether a sudden tenfold reduction in training and inference costs could expose finite demand, as cheaper blockspace did in crypto. José thinks AI demand is more real, but warns that Jevons’ paradox taking five years would still be a problem. Over half the Fortune 500 reportedly spend above $100,000 annually with Anthropic, yet that represents only 0.1% of the Fortune 500 companies’ overall expenses.
  • José describes the frontier-lab CFO’s trap: underbuy compute and competitors undercut or out-train you; overbuy and a downturn can blow you up. Yan expects cheaper compute to deliver multiple expansion for beneficiaries outside AI. He cannot determine how much of Microsoft’s cited 60K layoffs reflects AI and rejects a neat layoffs-equal-spending explanation.

4. Cheap attacks compound through compromised trust

  • Jake calls the PHP issue “kind of a nothing burger,” since hosting providers or Cloudflare can intercept many attacks. The scarier issue concerns an intermediary certificate provider whose name he tentatively gives as eMudra. Older devices retaining compromised certificate trust could accept impersonated services—for example, a gas meter receiving a malicious software update and becoming permanently difficult to patch.
  • The discussion estimates attack costs are down “probably 100, maybe 1,000 fold,” and describes how one compromise can seed another: vulnerable devices become botnets and create further entry points. A panelist speculates that Railway’s problems might connect to the certificate compromise, explicitly noting the absence of a postmortem. Its GitHub build connections illustrate how stolen credentials could propagate damage downstream.
  • A panelist asks whether defenders’ access to better models and more compute should give them the advantage. Another responds categorically: “No, not at all.” Attackers need one opening, potentially beneath an otherwise secure application. The discussion puts defensive spending at 10–1,000 times the attacker’s expenditure and raises the hope of an eventual equilibrium favoring defense.
  • A panelist argues AWS and Google Cloud are safer than smaller hosts on scale grounds and points to national-defense data as potentially richer targets. José counters that cloud-hosted stablecoin minting keys could enable enormous issuance. Another panelist asks how much value an attacker could actually realize, even with access to massive holdings.

5. Bitcoin’s quantum risk divides the panel over recovery

  • José says he considers Satoshi’s vulnerable coins less threatening than a few months earlier. He expects any breakthrough to involve a lab tied to the U.S. or China and doubts a government would destroy the holding’s value. Another panelist calls governments historically paper-handed; Yan says a Democratic administration “would just dump this to zero.” José replies: “No, they wouldn’t.”
  • José thinks holders would favor a fork removing stolen coins over one allowing an attacker to dump them. Other panelists warn that a fork itself would be damaging; one estimates Bitcoin could fall roughly 90% in the adverse scenario. Jake adds that even burning compromised coins would be bearish because the underlying message is that someone accessed supposedly secure keys.
  • Jake expects quantum computers eventually to crack Bitcoin and stresses that cracking Satoshi’s keys would mean other keys also need migration. Ceteris estimates moving everyone’s UTXOs could consume half a year to a year of block space, while new signature schemes introduce risks. José questions the appeal of governance that is extremely slow to change; Yan distinguishes immutability from security.
  • Jake offers an explicitly unlikely, non-quantum scenario discussed with core developers around 2019–2020: an early Windows XP random-number configuration might expose one experimental key, allowing 50 BTC to move without compromising everything else. “I don’t think this happens,” he emphasizes. The point is that a nonfatal technical event could initially look fatal; the others expect severe market panic.

6. Synapse’s bridge economics explain its options pivot

  • Jake says “bridging was dead” economically by 2022–2023 as Across started getting traction: margins fell roughly 100-fold in a year. On some chains, a million messages generated about $1,000. Demand was not expanding enough to offset that compression. Interoperability work—such as using bridged GLP as lending collateral—suggested a different application: improving options collateral efficiency.
  • A perp market maker can operate with leverage and an ADL backstop; an option writer might post 10–100 times the premium received. Jake calls full collateralization “crazy.” Earlier Dopex work with GMX showed the concept, but fees and liquidity were inadequate. Hyperliquid supplied the missing liquid on-chain hedging venue and made building the product compelling.
  • Keeping SYN reflects Jake’s preference for founders pivoting with their existing investors, rather than repeatedly launching tokens. He compares startups raising $5–10 million and still pivoting with one or two months of cash left. Hyperliquid also inspired him by refusing familiar crypto games and winning anyway. Ceteris subsequently discloses that he recently bought SYN.

7. On-chain options compete on access and capital efficiency

  • A host asks what remains distinctive if Robinhood offers comparable assets. Jake identifies 24/7 trading, particularly when Middle East events drive volatility outside market hours, and fractional contracts. A one- or two-week at-the-money S&P 500 call can require a ticket of several thousand dollars; fractional options could keep even year-out contracts accessible for a few dollars.
  • Jake says Hyperliquid delta-one positions can offset option risk, while purchased volatility can also support margin. Vaults add options to existing spot and perp strategies, enabling covered calls, basis trades, and more aggressive structures. His composability example: deposit Nvidia, write a covered call, collect premium, then borrow against the position and loop it. Yan also sees vaults supplying structurally needed volatility sellers.
  • Hypercall generated roughly $250 million in Hyperliquid perp volume over the preceding 30 days, mostly taker flow from delta hedging, Jake says. Under generous Binance fee assumptions, his team calculated equivalent hedging would cost 10–15 times more there. Competing options venues therefore need competitive perp execution too—a harder undertaking than simply shipping options infrastructure.

8. Retail distribution and perp partnerships shape adoption

  • Jake expects short-dated retail options first, with flows eventually supporting longer maturities; RWAs look like the clearest opportunity. “No one trades options” strikes him as “one of the dumbest takes,” given Robinhood usage and India’s daily notional. He anticipates a HIP-3-like trajectory: months of flat activity followed by a liquidity flywheel.
  • A host presses on distribution: working infrastructure does not automatically attract traders. Jake’s practical answer is user-generated TikTok content, citing FOMO, plus builder codes and wallet integrations. His bridge background informs the warning: bridging looks seamless in quiet markets, then liquidity disappears when a price move makes everyone want to trade simultaneously.
  • Jake sees Robinhood as a closer competitor than another crypto options protocol, with Polymarket or Kalshi potentially entering through a DCM. Structural difficulties remain, but they have substantial dry powder. He expects an oligopoly of two or three major players, each partnered closely with a major perp DEX, because managing both products together is difficult.
  • Outside options, Jake favors new lending models. He mentions 3Jane’s loans against Binance accounts, while noting he has not reviewed it for several months. Non-overcollateralized credit remains underexplored; crypto-card providers can build repayment and spending profiles. “They’re credit card companies, right? They should extend credit.”

9. IPO supply could tighten public-market liquidity

  • A panelist expects potentially the largest public-market liquidity drain in history over the next 12 months. Yan adds AI capex and tightening debt access, citing Paul Tudor Jones’s caution about 2027 despite a constructive year-end view. Kevin thinks markets can initially absorb Anthropic, but worries about later issuance turning equity supply positive after roughly 10–15 years of contraction.
  • Yan would avoid Anthropic initially because other investments could benefit if it succeeds. Depending on pricing around a possible $2 trillion valuation, Ceteris expects a better entry after listing, potentially resembling SpaceX’s initial drawdown. Staggered vesting and unlocks matter. The balance-sheet reassurance does not make the opening public-market price automatically attractive.

10. Venture’s financing advantage still depends on exits and retention

  • José thinks early-stage private markets have “never been in a better spot.” Mega-fund demand resembles index flows into scarce qualifying companies, amplified by “low float, high FDV”: companies sell perhaps 10% each round, while existing holders cannot freely sell. Few businesses can absorb nine-figure checks. He favors a small, agile early-stage fund over roughly five years.
  • Ceteris finds private markets “spooky.” Yan warns that weak Anthropic trading would establish a lower clearing price, remove markups, and tighten funding throughout the stack, as in the previous venture cycle. José acknowledges that Instinct at $30 billion looks extreme. Yan’s qualification is blunt: “It works until it doesn’t,” and the reversal can travel downward quickly.
  • Kevin questions what extraordinary revenue ramps actually prove. Startups now reach $100 million ARR so quickly that some lack usable retention cohorts. What does Instinct’s retention look like 12 months later? Fast growth followed by churn in intensely competitive AI products could force more disciplined underwriting and spread caution through private markets.

11. SpaceX’s operating advantage comes with spot-price exposure

  • Jake expects consolidation among stranded compute and weaker neoclouds in 2027. The premium shifts from promised data centers to installed, working capacity earning revenue now. He cites companies paying substantially higher prices for compute secured into 2027 and says SpaceX and Elon are positioned to “clean up this market in the next 12 months.”
  • Yan emphasizes financing: diversified revenues, scale, and lenders’ desire for future business can secure better terms. Kevin expects acquisitions of smaller operators whose delays and financing costs have undermined their economics. Their assets may retain value if a capable operator brings them online. Yan also expects TerraFab’s scale to support strong margins.
  • José pushes back on valuation and downside. In his understanding, cloud contracts can be canceled by either side with three months’ notice, leaving substantial spot-price exposure. He estimates pricing near $50 per watt versus CoreWeave’s $10–15. SpaceX is therefore a leveraged AI bet that could suffer badly if compute prices fall; Yan thinks diversification improves its recovery prospects.
  • A panelist raises Kessler Syndrome as a speculative tail risk: satellite collisions create debris that causes further collisions, potentially rendering low orbit unusable. He connects it to reported military satellite activity and a tweet about buying SpaceX puts. The concern extends beyond one stock to communications infrastructure; he sees little portfolio protection against such a scenario.

12. Familiarity remains the panel’s strongest allocation constraint

  • José wants better exposure to power, grid construction, and infrastructure, already holding the GRID ETF. Commodities might become interesting over the next few years, but he would prefer specialist expertise. Yan thinks commodities call for active trading around events. José ultimately admits little appetite for distributing money across numerous managers.
  • A panelist and Ceteris prefer staying close to crypto, where sustained attention occasionally reveals an unusually obvious opportunity. “I just wish I had more of everything,” Ceteris says. Jake counters that paying less attention sometimes worked better this cycle; group chats still surface opportunities for him. The disagreement is over attention, as much as allocation.

item.title: Franklin Templeton CEO on SpaceX, Anthropic, Circular Deals & the State of the Market
item.description: Johnson favors shorter-term AI financing: today’s cash-generative borrowers differ from internet-bubble firms, but 20- or 30-year data-center debt risks locking in current chip and energy needs. Franklin Templeton’s late-stage SpaceX and Anthropic stakes seek missed IPO returns, but illiquid holdings may stay at 6%, 7% or 8% against a 15% limit.
item.content:encoded:
Sourcery · Jenny Johnson、Molly O'Shea · 2026-10-29 · 42 min · 原语言 EN

Johnson favors shorter-term AI financing: today’s cash-generative borrowers differ from internet-bubble firms, but 20- or 30-year data-center debt risks locking in current chip and energy needs. Franklin Templeton’s late-stage SpaceX and Anthropic stakes seek missed IPO returns, but illiquid holdings may stay at 6%, 7% or 8% against a 15% limit.

TL;DR

  • Jenny Johnson’s constructive market view rests on earnings and cash flow, alongside caution on leverage and sticky inflation. She thinks roughly 70% of companies beat earnings projections and sees markets broadening beyond hyperscalers. The 2% productivity reading, she argues, reflects earlier technologies; meaningful AI contributions to earnings still lie ahead because adoption requires organized data and “change management.”
  • Johnson favors shorter-term AI financing and would personally avoid longer-term data-center financing tied to today’s technology. Extrapolating current chip and energy requirements for 20 or 30 years overlooks the innovation that demand encourages. Today’s borrowers have substantial earnings, but circular financing and unclear revenue recognition require scrutiny: “Know your stuff as you’re making those investments.”
  • Franklin Templeton’s SpaceX and Anthropic positions came through late-stage investing intended to recover the old IPO return opportunity. Companies staying private longer meant portfolio managers were missing their “IPO kickers.” Johnson says mutual funds or ETFs can hold up to 15% illiquid assets, but suggests 6%, 7% or 8% to leave room for market movements.
  • Johnson is enthusiastic about SpaceX’s innovation, citing Starlink’s usefulness and Musk’s work in space and robotics. She says colonizing Mars is quite possible, while emphasizing “a lot of key-man risk with Elon.” She does not directly endorse Musk’s separate claim that SpaceX will become the most profitable company on Earth.
  • Client consolidation underpins the 17 acquisitions in six years cited by O’Shea. The $4.5 billion Legg Mason deal balanced wealth and institutional channels at 50/50; Johnson estimates Canvas grew from about $2.5 billion to $30 billion in roughly four years. She acknowledges Lexington was “fully priced,” but secondary private-equity growth exceeded their models.
  • Tokenization’s clearest benefit in Johnson’s account is lower servicing costs and faster access to earned cash. Franklin’s traditional money-market fund requires $500 to open an account; its blockchain version opens at $20 and probably could reach $5. Second-by-second interest calculation and daily cash payments illustrate why she believes blockchain “will replace the rails in financial services.”
  • AI agents are already producing an early sales result, while their eventual contribution to model-provider revenue remains uncertain. A Microsoft-supported deployment delivered 23% more client visits and 11% higher sales in early results. Johnson says firms will need to consider agent frequency and whether some queries can use free models; O’Shea describes governance that routes requests between models and cites companies shifting to 99% open-weight or open-source usage.

Digest

1. Earnings are holding up before AI lifts productivity

  • Johnson separates “noise” around AI, circular financing and revenue recognition from the broader economy. Inflation is “probably pretty sticky” and rates probably stay higher; today’s level is unusual against the last 25 years, less so historically. Leveraged businesses face pressure, while the US consumer remains strong. She thinks “something like 70%” of companies beat earnings projections and sees markets broadening beyond hyperscalers.
  • Her geopolitical example is the $20,000 drone that can bring a tanker to a halt, make insurance hard to obtain and effectively stop oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz. More oil is getting through than expected, but she sees no quick resolution in the Middle East or Russia–Ukraine. US–China relations look more constructive, though she says each country is heading in its own direction and there are lines neither will cross. The US needs China for rare earths; China needs US consumers for its manufactured goods.
  • AI is her “biggest growth lever,” but Johnson attributes the current 2% productivity reading to earlier digitization and cloud adoption. Running technology taught her that the challenges are data quality and organization—not the system integration people often assume—and “change management,” because “people don’t like change.” Meaningful AI contributions to earnings will take time; that remaining opportunity supports her optimism.
  • Her jobs argument reaches back to a 1997 BusinessWeek cover predicting the internet would eliminate brokers: advisers now provide broader financial planning. Efficiency comes first, then employee creativity. Wearing basic Ray-Ban Meta glasses golfing, she wondered why they could not find her ball; her programmer son is working on an app. “We find new things that we can’t imagine initially.”

2. Long-term AI financing bets on today’s technology

  • O’Shea’s challenge, citing Ken Griffin, is whether chip supply, demand and obsolescence undermine the buildout. Johnson recalls a Gartner curve—she is unsure of its exact name—of excitement, disillusionment and recovery: “So the question is where are we on that curve?” She sees “a frothiness in some areas,” yet distinguishes today’s large, cash-generating borrowers from internet-bubble businesses without revenue.
  • Her financing preference is shorter term; she personally would avoid longer-term data-center financing. Extrapolating today’s chip and energy requirements for 20 or 30 years assumes insufficient innovation precisely when demand encourages breakthroughs. She thinks Griffin is “probably right on that piece of it.” Revenue recognition also leaves company comparisons unclear: “Know your stuff as you’re making those investments.” That supports her preference for active management.

3. Longer paths to IPO drove SpaceX and Anthropic exposure

  • Companies staying private longer deprived portfolio managers of their “IPO kickers,” Johnson explains, prompting late-stage investments including SpaceX and Anthropic. She says mutual funds or ETFs can hold up to 15% illiquid assets but might run at 6%, 7% or 8% to avoid a market-driven breach. Client interest subsequently prompted a venture group that can invest alongside traditional portfolio managers.
  • O’Shea asks whether SpaceX’s Starlink, launch economics and AI positioning support Musk’s extraordinary profitability claim. Johnson does not directly assess that forecast; she first cautions against fashionable labels, noting that Franklin Resources owed its name to the 1970s appeal of gold and “resources.” Her instruction is “stick to your knitting and say what you are.” Her concrete customer endorsement is Starlink, “a game changer” for internet access at her Montana property.
  • Johnson credits Musk with challenging the system around space investment and driving cost efficiency. She says his Mars ambition may not arrive on schedule, but “he often delivers.” She sees colonizing Mars as quite possible and points to robotics as part of that vision, while emphasizing “a lot of key-man risk with Elon.” Her closing choice of Musk as the closest modern Benjamin Franklin carries the qualification that there is “no perfect match.”
  • Johnson traces the pooled-fund idea to giving ordinary investors access to equity-market returns through expert advice, reasonable prices and diversification. Her father took over the Franklin Funds subsidiary with $2.5 million in AUM and $10,000 in revenue in 1955; it took until 1983 or 1984 to reach $1 billion. She sees a parallel in private markets and wants access to be fairer, while recognizing these are “absolutely illiquid vehicles.”

4. Acquisitions buy distribution as clients consolidate managers

  • The $4.5 billion Legg Mason acquisition, which O’Shea says doubled AUM, filled core fixed-income and private-market gaps, including through Clarion Partners. Franklin’s 75% wealth/25% institutional channel mix met Legg Mason’s inverse, producing a 50/50 balance. The deal was announced five days after Johnson became CEO, after a year of work; COVID lockdowns followed three weeks later. She held to the strategic case despite falling markets. Selecting the “best athletes” across teams moved online, and the deal closed 60 days early.
  • O’Shea cites 17 acquisitions in six years; Johnson says the logic is capability and distribution as clients choose fewer managers. Infrastructure is the capability she says remains incomplete. O’Shaughnessy Asset Management’s Canvas platform added tax-efficient separately managed accounts and technology usable over active strategies. She estimates Canvas went from about $2.5 billion at acquisition to $30 billion roughly four years later.
  • Lexington Partners and Clarion Partners have more than doubled since acquisition. Johnson recalls Benefit Street Partners at roughly $26 billion when purchased; private credit now totals just under $100 billion, including subsequent acquisitions. Private credit contains distinct segments requiring origination capabilities. The latest asset-backed team acquisition filled a gap where clients were interested and spreads looked attractive.
  • Deals usually used cash, sometimes with debt; part of the Putnam deal was paid with Franklin stock because Great-West Life wanted broader asset-manager exposure. Johnson estimates Putnam grew from roughly $136 billion to over $220 billion as Franklin opened previously inaccessible platforms. Lexington was “fully priced,” but growth in secondary private equity beat models. Private-market carry creates natural retention through payouts years later, while Franklin’s wealth distribution helps acquired teams reach a different buyer.

5. Tokenization changes servicing costs and cash access

  • Johnson believes blockchain “will replace the rails in financial services,” slowly because it changes business models and transaction-fee economics. Three functions support her claim: one immediately updated source of truth reduces reconciliation; smart contracts embed agreed terms; and the system makes payments. Her example is collateral owed under terms sitting in a document: programming those terms into the transaction makes payment immediate.
  • Franklin’s SEC-approved, natively on-chain tokenized money-market fund initially ran alongside its legacy shareholder-recordkeeping system, allowing a direct cost comparison. Traditional accounts need $500 to avoid other shareholders subsidizing servicing; the blockchain version opens at $20 and probably could reach $5. Johnson expects 24/7 trading, atomic settlement and innovation from programmable transactions, potentially combined with AI.
  • Interest is calculated every second: a hedge fund posting the fund as collateral for 4 hours, 22 minutes and 32 seconds earns interest for that holding period. Cash is paid daily, versus monthly access in a traditional money-market fund. For corporate treasurers and portfolio managers, the benefit is access to earned cash they can redeploy.

6. AI agents lift sales while governance could temper model revenue

  • O’Shea cites more than 1,000 agents for 800-plus investment professionals. Johnson separates the objectives: better research and performance in investing, growth in distribution, and efficiency in operations. Investment-side cost savings are “insignificant” beside better performance. Coding assistance can clear more projects from the backlog; greater capacity need not mean materially fewer people. “I think you just do more.”
  • A Microsoft partnership built coordinating agents combining adviser holdings, product data, ratings and client context to help salespeople “meet the right clients and have the right conversations.” Microsoft supplied free resources because of the technical challenge. Early results showed a market leader visiting 23% more clients and an 11% increase in sales.
  • The revenue uncertainty emerges after experimentation: Johnson says firms will need to ask whether agents need to run, how frequently, and whether some queries can be handled by free models. O’Shea describes a governance layer that could route requests to a top or free model, then cites emerging companies that were overloaded after 14 trillion tokens before shifting to 99% open-weight or open-source models. She suggests frontier models may still be used for biosciences and other frontier projects.

来源：YouTube
