item.title: How to Build the Next SpaceX or Tesla
item.description: Defense customers can fund capacity commercial buyers would reject, creating a base that also serves robotics markets. Technicians using Claude can reconfigure lines in 20 minutes, versus three months and hundreds of thousands of dollars through a systems integrator. Love says first-half 2026 defense risk capital exceeded all of 2025, but factories still take years to build.
item.content:encoded:
The a16z Show · Erin Price-Wright、Connor Love、Elena Burger · 2026-10-29 · 49 min · 原语言 EN

Defense customers can fund capacity commercial buyers would reject, creating a base that also serves robotics markets. Technicians using Claude can reconfigure lines in 20 minutes, versus three months and hundreds of thousands of dollars through a systems integrator. Love says first-half 2026 defense risk capital exceeded all of 2025, but factories still take years to build.

TL;DR

  • Defense demand can finance an industrial rebuild that serves much larger commercial markets. Erin Price-Wright’s premise is that “you don’t have a defense industrial base without an industrial base.” Early defense customers can absorb factory costs that commercial buyers would reject, helping establish capacity for products ranging from robots to hearing aids.
  • Industrial AI gains depend on redesigning entire physical operations. Mariana Minerals owns assets through refining, while Hadrian improves “15 or 20 different things” across factory workflows. Connor Love’s boundary condition matters: “AI cannot turn a wrench yet,” and he says that capability remains far off.
  • Flexible manufacturing can compress both product development and production ramp-up. Price-Wright frames the challenge of high-mix, low-volume manufacturing; Love describes technicians using Claude to reconfigure lines in 20 minutes, versus three months and hundreds of thousands of dollars through a systems integrator. The broader principle is “design for manufacturing”: prototypes and eventual production capacity develop together.
  • Private capital is allowing defense startups to build before receiving formal requirements and funding. Love contrasts fragmented procurement with Castelion’s roughly three years of privately financed hypersonic-missile development before government contracts and purchases. Price-Wright says its team resisted product expansion: “No, we need to do this one thing really well.”
  • Better domestic components could make new robotics markets financially viable. Price-Wright says defense production builds demand for the same motors, actuators and switches that robots need. Her concrete evidence is a portfolio company whose PCB acceptance improved from roughly 50% to 70%, 80% or 90% after switching to emerging suppliers.
  • Capital availability is expanding faster than physical production can. Love says defense attracted more risk capital in the first half of 2026 than throughout 2025, which itself drew many times the amount invested in all previous years combined. Banks, private equity and credit firms are joining venture investors; Price-Wright says hundreds of billions, possibly trillions, are being directed toward the category over the next 10-plus years. Factories still take years to build.
  • Power expansion ultimately depends on willingness to build and communities sharing the gains. Asked about America’s flat power production versus China’s new energy production, Price-Wright says, “I don’t think that is a technology problem.” Her question is “Do we want to grow?” Love adds that communities need to share in the economic upside of development.

Digest

1. Defense demand can finance a much broader industrial base

  • Price-Wright opens with the episode’s governing claim: “You don’t have a defense industrial base without an industrial base.” Decades of industrial hollowing now have battlefield consequences for American soldiers and allies. Elena Burger frames the AD50 around three connected layers—inputs extracted from the ground, factories making components, and finished systems—rather than treating defense manufacturers as a self-contained sector. Each layer constrains what the next can deliver.
  • Price-Wright says “dual use” can tempt startups to pursue too many things at once, even though the industrial base being rebuilt can serve many markets. Government buyers may pay costs that commercial buyers would reject, funding machinery and first-of-a-kind capex. Love illustrates this with a new U.S. PCB fab: a defense buyer can help pay for the equipment, while PCBs are also used in robots and hearing aids.
  • Price-Wright contrasts earlier government-led technology development—in space, the internet and nuclear energy—with private industry and capital now often providing the impetus. Government can still subsidize technical and process learning, while discerning American consumers push capability higher and prices lower than government buyers would. Love uses DJI to illustrate the transfer: after consumer drones, the company’s business expanded into public safety and national defense in the late 2010s. He says the people behind DJI are now the world’s largest robot producers, since drone motors are similar to robot actuators, which he calls the hardest part of building a robot.

2. Asset ownership can unlock full process redesign

  • Price-Wright points to SpaceX and Tesla as rare modern companies that have built at scale and as examples of vertical integration. She cautions against integrating everything, though: a unique, exquisite system such as a missile may require it. Love adds that SpaceX and Tesla built capabilities because the U.S. industrial base to support them did not exist, while high-quality suppliers should be used where available. Price-Wright notes Tesla had to recreate a battery supply chain; Love adds that its power electronics and drivetrain were built from scratch. Price-Wright says the underlying papers had been collecting dust since the 1970s.
  • Mariana Minerals illustrates why ownership can matter. Price-Wright says incumbent miners would not adopt technology quickly enough, so Mariana acquires and develops assets, mines and operates them, refines materials, and sells finished commodities across multiple minerals. Love says owning the asset can be necessary to change it. Price-Wright emphasizes the feedback loop: software across planning, operations, mining and refining captures data that feeds back into the process.
  • Hadrian supplies Love’s factory counterpart: improvement comes from “15 or 20 different things,” rather than one breakthrough. He cites quoting and accepting orders, making parts, inspection and movement between steps. Building factories from scratch—or taking over a mine—lets founders question whether practices inherited from the previous 100 years remain appropriate, rather than optimizing only one isolated task within an unchanged operation.
  • Love’s limit on the AI thesis is direct: “AI cannot turn a wrench yet.” He expects that eventually, but says “we’re far off.” Applying AI to industry therefore looks different from deploying it in legal work or customer service. Operators need deep knowledge of physical processes and how to manipulate them; software’s contribution sits inside that operational understanding, with robotics and autonomy still developing.

3. Flexible factories connect faster iteration with production scale

  • Price-Wright introduces the distinction between low-mix, high-volume production and high-mix, low-volume work. Love explains that traditional automation is expensive to reconfigure for varied products. Manufacturing technicians understand the process, and new software lets them reconfigure lines without necessarily having software-engineering training. Love’s example: a manufacturing engineer using Claude can make a change in “20 minutes,” instead of waiting three months and spending hundreds of thousands of dollars with a systems integrator.
  • Price-Wright says a more adjustable line makes it possible to prototype faster and then reach production rate sooner; otherwise, companies may have to rejigger subsystems after finalizing a production-level system. Love sums up the principle as “designing for manufacturing from the outset.” Price-Wright points to Anduril’s facilities in Ohio and Baltimore and Saronic’s shipyard, saying they are on a near timeline to produce thousands, tens of thousands and, hopefully, hundreds of thousands of systems. Burger notes that this is no longer theoretical: real products are coming off the lines.
  • Price-Wright treats repeat site visits as a way to observe execution, returning roughly every three months. Her image is an empty warehouse with epoxy floors, a flag, pallets and a founder excited about a rented forklift. Six months later, technicians fill the building and the company needs the city to provide more power because too many machines are plugged in. The transformation makes operating speed visible.

4. Building ahead of procurement rewards focus and operating experience

  • Drawing on his Army service, Love describes defense procurement’s disconnected decision makers: “the buyer is not the user,” and the person appropriating dollars for the buyer is further removed. Historically, primes waited for the government to specify and fund a system, producing products based on what was needed a decade earlier. Venture financing lets founders interpret military needs and build ahead of a formal request, aligning products with current technology and soldiers’ needs rather than waiting for the procurement sequence.
  • Love cites Castelion as an example: private venture capital funded its hypersonic-missile development before government contracts and purchases arrived. Price-Wright says the team spent 2.5 to 3 years focused on its first missile, resisting suggestions to build a small drone instead: “No, we need to do this one thing really well.” She connects that focus to SpaceX’s culture of engineers taking personal responsibility for whether their component works.
  • Price-Wright sees supplier startups emerging from problems founders encountered at Anduril, SpaceX, Tesla and Saronic. Existing relationships provide early customers willing to tolerate failures while solving their own difficult problems—much like YC companies selling to one another. Love adds that delivering the first product builds process knowledge, supplier relationships, design-for-manufacturing capability and customer trust, making subsequent products easier. But “it doesn’t work unless you deliver on that one core thing.”
  • Love describes Mariana CEO Turner traveling to remote locations without electricity or cell service and spending weeks or months away from family. The people founders engage with may have different timelines and cultures, and can be tough to negotiate with. Love says, “It sounds kind of sexy and romantic, but when you’re actually doing it, it’s rough.” Price-Wright adds that if founders are going to put themselves through that, “it better be damn worth it.”

5. Domestic suppliers can improve components and open new markets

  • Price-Wright argues that defense production creates demand for actuators, motors, valves and switches that future robots will also need. Improving their quality and cost could make previously uneconomic robotics applications viable. She estimates there is a “99% chance” that most components a robotics company buys today come from China. Love says companies want to bring purchasing onshore for quality, cost and speed of iteration, as well as geopolitical reasons, and notes how much of a supplier ecosystem has developed in just the last three years.
  • Price-Wright’s evidence is a portfolio company that, three years earlier, ordered twice as many PCBs as needed because it expected to reject 50% for quality problems. Emerging suppliers using software and modern manufacturing changed that: the company now sees 70%, 80% or 90% passing. Her conclusion is that close customer-supplier collaboration and co-development can materially improve quality, beyond simply relocating purchasing.
  • Love calls the next opportunity the “manufacturing middle.” His Boeing–Honeywell landing-gear example explains the obstacle: suppliers rationally repeat an existing design, potentially 50 years old, while lower-tier manufacturers remain in “receive mode.” That arrangement makes sense if the existing part meets requirements and suppliers are paid the same either way. But new systems and materials create reasons to rethink components. He expects suppliers to co-engineer with end manufacturers, pushing improvements upward through the chain. He calls this creating an “American manufacturing asset class,” distinct from buying factories and improving costs.
  • Price-Wright sees a parallel in electricity: mechanical infrastructure deployed in the 1970s and 1980s is giving way to power electronics, battery storage and more software-native architectures, opening the supply chain to redesign. Burger raises the possibility that demand may not grow fourfold and argues that even delivering half the anticipated requirement could start a snowball. Love agrees that “you’re not going back”; Price-Wright adds that a new architecture can bring better cost, efficiency, serviceability and ease of manufacturing.

6. Capital is following evidence that physical businesses can become valuable

  • Love’s distinction is that these companies can now be among the most valuable, as well as the most important. He cites Palantir, Anduril and SpaceX as proof that companies in these categories can become very large, and says most of the world’s ten most valuable companies are hardware companies. Burger quips that some of these overnight successes took 20 years.
  • Love argues that America’s private capital markets can follow entrepreneurs and demonstrated success flexibly, without a top-down-directed industrial policy. He cites JPMorgan committing trillions toward investing in the physical world and growing participation from private equity and large credit firms. Capital-intensive factories and systems require that broader financing stack. Price-Wright says hundreds of billions, if not trillions, are being directed toward the category for the next 10-plus years.
  • Love says more defense risk dollars went into the ecosystem in the first half of 2026 than in all of 2025; he says 2025 itself was many times the amount invested in all previous years combined. He also says the financing “valley of death” around contracts and capex is starting to disappear with capital-market support. That change extends beyond defense into energy, robotics and critical minerals.

7. Expansion requires patience and communities participating in the upside

  • Burger asks what would close the gap between essentially flat U.S. power production and China’s rising new energy production. Price-Wright answers, “I don’t think that is a technology problem.” She frames it as a question of national willingness: do Americans want conforming projects built, and “Do we want to grow?” If so, she believes technology and capital will follow.
  • Price-Wright says the snowball has started to roll, but asks whether emergent winners will bring more capital into the ecosystem. Physical projects require moving dirt and understanding supply chains, so “these things take years”; she says capital markets need patience. She is optimistic, but warns that government and national choices can obstruct the process: “it’s ours to lose.”
  • Love says physical projects make economic participation important: unlike software’s more abstract benefits, a mine, data center or power plant changes surrounding communities. Residents have “a say” and “a stake.” He expects companies to figure out how to bring communities along and make participation economically worthwhile, even if the transition is short-term painful.
  • Price-Wright gives AMA as an example of a company partnering with small machine shops, working with them to build new products rather than cutting management and firing people. She says companies need to work with communities rather than against them. She expects AD50 companies to bring jobs and prosperity to Middle America; Love adds that broader growth could reduce wealth concentration in elite coastal pockets.

来源：YouTube

item.title: 168X 对话 QinbaFrank：AI 商业化兑现、Anthropic IPO 与 2026 Q4 的市场窗口
item.description: QinbaFrank认为，AI基建仍能托住美国名义增长，但能源通胀限制加息空间。Anthropic上半年收入162亿美元、三季度168亿美元，微软云增长48%、Google云增长103%，支持AI商业化加速的判断。CapEx转为产能、订单与现金流仍待验证；Anthropic可能11月上市及募资1,000亿美元均属情境假设。
item.content:encoded:
168X · QinbaFrank · 2026-10-29 · 109 min · 原语言 ZH

QinbaFrank认为，AI基建仍能托住美国名义增长，但能源通胀限制加息空间。Anthropic上半年收入162亿美元、三季度168亿美元，微软云增长48%、Google云增长103%，支持AI商业化加速的判断。CapEx转为产能、订单与现金流仍待验证；Anthropic可能11月上市及募资1,000亿美元均属情境假设。

TL;DR

  • QinbaFrank认为，AI基建仍能托住美国名义增长，但能源通胀决定市场还能承受多少次加息。 他估算大科技CapEx由2025年的4,000亿—5,000亿美元增至2026年约9,000亿美元，宏观强劲与中低收入群体消费偏弱可以同时成立。此次暂停加息是“鹰派内部的一个耐心共识”；若美伊迟迟不能缓和，高油价向工业品扩散，风险就会从市场尚能接受的一两次加息，变成更长的紧缩过程。
  • 他对AI商业化的判断仍是加速，依据是实际收入和云业务，而非漂亮的年化指标。 Frank据Anthropic上半年162亿美元、三季度168亿美元收入，推演全年约500亿—600亿美元，并认为2028年达到2,000亿美元的概率很大；微软云增长48%、Google云增长103%，也支持这一判断。他强调全年实际营收与年化口径“这两个含金量是完全不同的”，而大规模商业化目前“只有三个季度”，尚未看到饱和。
  • AI投资回报的争议，核心是一年前花的钱何时转成今天的产能、收入和现金流。 Frank的“时间差”框架是先买地、建电力和数据中心，再上线算力、兑现订单，最后观察现金回报；不能拿当季CapEx直接对照当季收入。下一处重要拐点是云收入增速超过CapEx增速，但他也承认，自己认为账能算出来，不代表市场已经获得足够证据。
  • Anthropic IPO可能先带来反弹窗口，再触发机构调仓和上市后的资金分流。 11月9日启动路演、11月16日当周上市，都是对谈中的假设；Frank特别提醒：“假设它是十一月九号。” 若募资1,000亿美元、认购需求达到约四倍，就可能需要约4,000亿美元资金准备。他参照SpaceX上市推演“吸血”效应，并未把时间表或认购规模视为已确定事实。
  • AI行情的主线正在迁移，不能继续把AI、半导体和存储画等号。 Frank认为，上半年最强的存储，到八九月已让位于光模块和部分软件；模型商品化、token成本下降，还可能让云平台、企业部署、agent与高价值应用受益。“AI不只有半导体，半导体也不只有存储”，旧主线仍可能反弹，但不应直接外推早期的直线上涨。
  • 高长债收益率会让第四季度更像个股分化行情，指数仍可能创新高。 能源通胀、国债供给和AI企业发债共同争夺资金，使长债收益率“易涨难跌”，市场因此更挑剔现金流和业绩瑕疵。Frank认为高权重科技股轮流修复可以支撑指数，但若能源冲击迫使更多加息，或云业务连续两个季度减速，大盘和AI主线都需要重新评估。
  • Warsh的制度改革比一次议息结果更值得追踪，但具体方向仍要等工作组报告。 Frank关注利率沟通减少之后的三件事：2%通胀框架是否调整、如何衡量AI生产率，以及是否改变充足准备金制度和庞大的资产负债表。他认为这些工作组“不是摆样子”，同时没有断言一定改目标或大幅缩表。
  • 加密资产的短期交易条件是流动性回流，长期主线则是合规融资和传统资产上链。 Frank提到TGA约1.02万亿美元，若11月开始释放资金，币市可能回暖，并把10月调整视作“大周期向上的正常回踩”。监管方面，他区分了融资提案与创新豁免：合规ICO最快也可能要等到明年上半年；证券、国债和股票代币化，则可能持续利好链上及DeFi基础设施。

Digest

1. AI新基建托住名义增长，微观消费仍在分化

  • Frank把美国经济拆成两张表：一张看名义GDP，一张看消费者。他估算，大科技CapEx从2025年的4,000亿—5,000亿美元，升至2026年约9,000亿美元，新增投入本身就可能带来约1.5—2个百分点的GDP增速贡献。“AI大基建”仍在加速，宏观增速就有支撑，不能仅凭部分消费疲弱判断整体衰退。
  • 他的类比是十年前的中国：消费、出口、基建三驾马车中，过去中国依靠房地产，如今美国的核心驱动力换成AI新基建。他还援引Warsh讲话，称美国上半年GDP增速由1.8%上修至2.4%，三季度继续加快；这是他认为宏观经济“没问题”的依据之一。
  • 但宏观强劲并不等于每个人处境改善。Frank认为中高收入群体消费仍强，中低收入群体偏弱，AI替代劳动力还会加深“K型分化”。他举微软面向约6万名员工的自愿买断计划，明确区分它与强制裁员；电力、电工等基建相关行业受益，其他行业未必分享到同样增长。

2. 中东石油运量恢复，不代表油价可以同步回落

  • Frank把今年能源冲击分成两个阶段：七八月以前，主要是霍尔木兹海峡封锁造成供给中断；进入9月后，问题更多转向运输成本。他援引第三方统计称，9月下旬波斯湾运出的石油日量，已经接近2月战争爆发前水平，但“油价没下来，核心是运输成本太高”。
  • 替代通道包括沙特通往红海、日输约600万—700万桶的管道，以及阿联酋通往富查伊拉港、日输约300万桶的管道。他还描述产油国租用单船可装约200万桶原油的超大型油轮，通过海峡运输。这些办法能恢复运量，却不能消除护航、风险和转运费用。
  • 他给出的关键对比是：波斯湾原油运往亚太，年初每桶运费约3—4美元，如今约35—40美元，而布伦特仍在每桶110多美元。油轮在海峡附近集结，夜间沿靠近阿曼的一侧航线、在美军护航下驶出，再转运到远洋油轮；这一段成本最高。船东面临袭击风险，产油国为了保住客户也不得不接受高运费。因此，“有油运出来”与“低成本供给恢复”是两回事。

3. 炼化瓶颈和AI基建，让通胀缓解存在第二层时滞

  • 主持人补充了炼油能力受损的问题，提到乌克兰和俄罗斯交战期间，乌克兰打击了许多炼油厂。Frank此前也提到，中东不少炼厂被毁，乌克兰和俄罗斯在8、9月互相炸毁了不少炼油厂；即使原油运输恢复、运费下降，炼化能力仍需时间恢复，成品油价格未必马上回落。
  • 在Frank的解释中，今年通胀反弹首先仍由能源驱动，汽油、柴油再影响上游化学品和工业原料；核心通胀的扩散暂时没有同样强。AI基建则是另一种较长期的力量，推高电力产品、上游材料和部分商品价格。他没有把两者混为一谈：当前最重要的是能源，AI相关压力已经显现，但尚未特别明显。
  • 他还把9月CPI下降的一部分，归因于统计规则调整：与AI基建相关的若干分类权重下调，对PCE的影响可能更大。这是Frank对数据的解释；他的意思并非价格压力消失，而是表面读数与市场感受到的基建成本压力可能存在差距。

4. 暂停加息只是鹰派内部愿意再等一等

  • 对此次FOMC按兵不动，Frank拒绝直接解释为鸽派转向，称其为“鹰派内部形成了耐心共识”。在他的框架里，决策者仍把通胀放在重要位置，只是愿意多看数据：如果高油价主要来自一次性地缘冲击，局势缓和后未必需要继续加息。
  • 乐观路径是，美伊在中期选举前后达成缓和，油价明显回落，11月和12月通胀随之改善。即便如此，Frank也只说联储可能继续按兵不动，因为还要确认能源降价是否传导到通胀；他没有把局势缓和、油价下降和政策转松写成一条自动发生的链条。
  • 悲观路径则是冲突延续至11月、12月，能源成本逐渐进入化工、工业品和商品价格，原本一次性的冲击变成持续数月的反弹。Frank认为市场尚能消化一到两次加息，但若12月仍要加、明年还要继续，担忧会明显升级；这是他眼中较大的潜在宏观风险之一。

5. 美伊破局窗口更可能在中期选举之后

  • 主持人追问战争何时能结束，并直言美国打得“不明不白”，怀疑以色列情报和内塔尼亚胡的政治动机影响了决策。Frank没有给出停战日期，而是把关键窗口放在中期选举之后的一两周，或整个11月。
  • Frank承认自己的早先推演需要调整：原本认为伊朗的忍受力远大于美国，特朗普可能先退让，随后双方和解；但拖到选举前，退让反而损害强人形象，使他“被架在那儿”。在Frank看来，伊朗集权体制的承受能力被低估，经济制裁造成民众痛苦，却未必迅速迫使决策层让步。
  • 因此，选后可能出现两条路：直接退让，或再进行一次猛烈打击后退让。Frank不认为追加轰炸必然改变结果，理由是3、4月已经做过一次、当时力度更大；若不上地面部队，很难迫使伊朗出现大问题，而地面介入又可能陷入越南、阿富汗式泥潭。他期待缓和，但明确保留再次开战的可能。

6. 军事威胁与外交斡旋正在同时推进

  • 对美军准备选后强力打击的报道，Frank一方面认为军事准备可能真实存在，提到中东至少有两个航母战斗群、另有两栖攻击舰战斗群，以及第三艘航母可能前往的消息；另一方面，他把这些信号也视为“极限施压”。施压对象不仅是伊朗，也包括所有承受不起油价再次飙升的国家。
  • 他的机制是：伊朗整体实力远弱于美国，仍可能袭击油轮、炼厂、管道等局部目标；一旦美国再打，能源风险就会促使海湾国家和其他大国加紧斡旋。他提到巴基斯坦、沙特、土耳其方面有实权人物参与接触，以及中国可能斡旋的迹象，并推测地区国家也在讨论战后安全秩序。
  • Frank还援引万斯与伊朗国家安全委员会秘书通信、讨论谈判框架的报道，认为直接沟通与第三方斡旋同时出现，是可能缓和的理由。他倾向认为双方部分条件已有共识，真正卡住的是先后顺序：伊朗先解除海峡封锁，还是美国先解除封锁、制裁并解冻资产，双方都担心先让步后对方不兑现。
  • 对战争起因，他的反思是特朗普把委内瑞拉的成功经验外推到伊朗，忽略两国差异。他也回顾自己在哈梅内伊遇袭后的判断：领导人被清除未必让伊朗软化，反而可能让更强硬的一派上台。因此，他不认为再次展示军事优势就足以解决信任和政治条件的问题。

7. Warsh减少利率沟通，是更广泛制度改革的一部分

  • 主持人把问题从战争转向Warsh的管理风格。Frank介绍的安排是：明年议息会议从一年8次减到7次，其中一次不讨论利率政策；到2028年再减少两次，变成6次利率会议。他认为这反映了Warsh不希望市场过度围绕下一次利率决定运转的思路。
  • Frank特别看重6月中旬上任后成立的五个工作组，议题涉及通胀框架、AI生产率、资产负债表与通胀关系，以及对外沟通等。他提到工作组吸纳经济学家和其他央行人士，原先预期12月提交结果，判断它们“不是摆样子”，而是要研究实际问题。
  • 沟通方面，他观察到Warsh的思路是减少沟通、反对前瞻指引，也不公布点阵图。Frank认为，后续可能有更多人不愿公布点阵图或过多评论下一次会议，而是每次根据数据说话。不过，减少承诺并不等于已经选择更松或更紧的方向。

8. 通胀框架、AI生产率与准备金制度，是改革的三条主线

  • 第一条是2%通胀目标及其衡量方式。Frank回顾鲍威尔时期曾从对称的2%目标，转向一段时间内平均2%的框架，高于和低于目标可以相互抵消。他提出的是问题：现有框架会不会再改；他并未断言Warsh一定提高或取消目标。
  • 第二条是AI生产率。Frank把技术进步视为长期通缩力量：同样投入能生产更多商品，单位价格下降；但短期AI投资热潮又会挤压电力、材料和设备供给，推高价格。政策难点在于怎样判断AI何时真正提高全社会生产率，以及如何平衡眼前的供给紧张与长期效率收益。
  • 第三条是庞大资产负债表与充足准备金制度。他认为，工作组结论出来前，Warsh不太会贸然大幅缩表；真正需要看的是明年是否要进一步缩小资产负债表、改变2008年以来的充足准备金制度。在Frank的设想中，这可能让银行体系更积极；具体方案、力度和方向，都要等工作组报告与Warsh表态。

9. Anthropic的实际营收，比年化数字更能检验商业化

  • 主持人将讨论转向投入能带来多少收入。Frank先界定观察对象：微软、亚马逊、Google云，以及Anthropic和OpenAI收入，比主要自用算力的Meta更能直接检验商业化。Meta虽成立企业业务平台，但目前算力仍主要用于自身模型和广告，因此不能完全采用同一把尺。
  • Frank援引Anthropic披露的数据：2025年收入约45亿美元，今年上半年约162亿美元，三季度约168亿美元，前三季合计约330亿美元。若四季度仅做到约170亿美元，全年也已约500亿美元；因此他给出500亿—600亿美元区间，但没有把区间当成公司指引。
  • 他反对拿这500亿—600亿美元全年实际收入，与OpenAI所谓1,000亿美元ARR直接比较：“这两个指标的含金量完全不同。”按现有增速，他认为Anthropic明年可能跨过1,000亿美元、后年达到2,000亿美元的概率很大，同时没有要求公司永久保持早期千倍百分比的增长。

10. 微软财报提供了企业需求扩散与现金流的双重证据

  • Frank认为微软这次财报“还是非常好的”：云业务同比增长48%，自由现金流约186亿美元，在其他大厂现金流承压时尤其突出。他还提到微软有6,700多个订单，其中约30%预计在未来12个月确认收入；他没有明确说明订单总额的单位。
  • 企业客户的变化比单一模型客户更有说服力。他回顾微软二季度披露：未履约订单环比增加的部分，约90%来自前沿模型厂商以外的客户。这意味着新增算力需求并非只由OpenAI、Anthropic支撑，传统企业采用也在形成可见订单，是他判断需求扩散的重要依据。
  • 本季他还看重Foundry收入达到去年同期三倍、付费客户约4.4万家，以及企业客户按量计费的收入三季度比二季度环比增长75%。Frank据此强调，云业务加速与企业客户扩大正在同时发生，不能只把微软理解成把算力转售给少数大模型公司的渠道。

11. 云平台正在成为企业的AI调度系统

  • Frank用微软电话会的一组问答展开：分析师追问，微软既有OpenAI合作，又推出自有模型，还部署DeepSeek、通义千问等开源模型，如何分工？他转述纳德拉的回答是按任务选择模型，同一项工作甚至可以调用多个模型，成熟任务再用开源或自有模型优化成本。
  • Frank提到微软6月推出的自有闭源模型Microsoft AI，但他的重点不是哪家模型排名更高。企业不一定要锁定一家模型，也不关心具体用哪家；他们更在意能否稳定、高质量地完成工作，以及完成一次任务花多少钱。模型可以轮换，任务结果、成本、数据连接与权限却需要统一管理。
  • 这使云厂商成为他所说的“AI操作系统”：负责任务调度、模型路由、数据连接和权限管理，而不只出售某一种模型的API。Frank又援引Anthropic今年约一半收入通过云平台销售的说法，认为云平台可同时承接闭源、自研和开源模型需求，是观察AI商业化的重要入口之一。

12. Google的不及预期，主要发生在广告兑现和现金流表面

  • Frank没有否认Google财报令人担忧：总营收和利润不及预期，股价也大跌。但他要求拆开看，云业务同比增长103%，单季收入300多亿美元，营业利润超过100亿美元，利润率继续提升。即使包括TPU销售，他援引公司的说法认为，云业务大部分收入来自GCP，不能把强增长都归给卖芯片。
  • 问题在于搜索中的AI回答和对话功能，查询量虽高，商业化却不及预期，拖累了广告主业。Google单季1,200多亿美元收入中，约800亿—900亿美元仍来自广告；因此，一个增长很快但体量较小的云业务，未必足以抵消主业兑现不足，这也是他承认财报存在瑕疵的原因。
  • 自由现金流约负90亿美元，差于市场预期的负35亿美元。Frank拆出两个因素：TPU库存增加约32亿美元，以及为2018年欧洲相关诉讼和解支出约52亿美元。若把这两项加回，三季度自由现金流基本打平；他的判断是“没有那么差”，而非现金流已经恢复强劲。
  • 不过，他也承认市场可能不愿做这层调整：宏观环境不佳、利率偏高时，投资者看到的是主业受压和现金流低于预期，于是先卖出。微软财报不错、Google存在缺口，两者不同的股价反应，正体现市场对兑现质量的要求正在提高。

13. 商业化只有三个季度，渗透率与单用户消费仍在上行

  • Frank认为市场容易把AI投资热潮的长度，误当成商业化已经成熟的程度。按他的梳理，大科技从去年三季度开始明显加速CapEx，今年一季度Anthropic收入开始加速，二季度云厂商业绩才更明显体现token需求。“大规模商业化到现在也就三个季度”，因此他尚未看到增长饱和的证据。
  • 他沿用互联网的两条收入轴：一是使用者越来越多，对应渗透率；二是每个人、每家企业花的钱越来越多，对应ARPU和token消耗。他此前提出渗透率可能由约10%快速向40%推进，认为一旦趋势形成，采用与使用深化会形成飞轮，个人和企业的token消耗都会继续增加。
  • 供给也限制了收入释放。Frank指出，过去几个季度大厂共同口径仍是“需求大于供给”，算力不够；若需求尚未被满足，新增产能上线就可能立即转成收入。因此，他认为商业化还在加速，远没有到增速放缓的时候，但这一判断仍以需求持续强劲为前提。

14. CapEx与收入不能按同一个季度直接对账

  • Frank反复强调“时间差”：今天云业务的增量，往往来自一年前买地、建数据中心、铺电力、买芯片和服务器的投入，而非今天新增的CapEx。去年下半年开始加速的建设，可能在今年下半年至明年集中上线；在供不应求时，产能释放本身就可能推动收入提速。
  • 他的检验顺序是资本开支、产能上线、订单转收入，再观察折旧和现金回报。进攻端先问收入是否加速，防守端再问现金流何时改善；这不是允许无限期花钱，而是避免用建设期的现金流，直接判定成熟运营期的经济性。他承认市场仍需更多数据，才能接受自己认为能够算通的账。
  • 下一处拐点是云收入增速超过CapEx增速。他举Google为例：2025年CapEx约800亿—900亿美元，今年指引1,950亿—2,050亿美元，同比增速超过100%；云业务增速则从较低水平升至82%、再到103%。若四季度达到110%—120%，云业务增速可能超过CapEx增速；这是他的推演，并非已经发生。

15. 投资回报还取决于数据中心和GPU能用多久

  • Frank援引亚马逊管理层给出的框架：一笔投入花出去，约两年建设投产、三年开始回本，之后再赚三年。厂房和电力设施还能继续使用，只需更换芯片；资本开支结构会随之变化。
  • 他回顾此前GPU折旧从4年延长到6年的争论：质疑者担心GPU用三年左右性能就不够，财务折旧过于乐观。Frank以H100作例子：H100推出已有约6年，性价比仍有吸引力、租赁价格还在涨；他的着眼点是旧芯片仍能在适合的任务中赚钱。
  • 他又援引CoreWeave二季度签下的H100订单，订单期限一直到2029年，推测相关芯片潜在使用寿命可能达到9年，而不只是6年。不过，他没有把单一订单当成全行业回报率的最终证明，仍希望结合亚马逊及其他新云厂商下一轮财报，进一步看清资本投入、利用率和现金回收的关系。

16. Codex之后的需求，不必由另一个单一大场景接棒

  • 对“Codex之后有没有第二场景”的担心，Frank的回答是第二场景未必是一个场景。企业后续需求分散在财务、法务、税务、营销、人力资源，以及各行业纵向流程中。单项规模可能不如Codex，但多个场景叠加，未必更弱。
  • 他还认为Codex、Web Codex变强后，许多非Codex场景也会用到相关技术。个人AI代理则是另一条方向；他提到Meta、Google、Grok、Anthropic和OpenAI自9月以来都推出了自己的Agent，认为个人AI代理也很有潜力。
  • 更高价值的一端是AI制药等科学发现应用。他提到多家巨头加码、OpenAI和Anthropic收购AI医疗公司的动作，认为这些任务可能消耗大量算力和token。这里他的判断仍是需求继续深化的可能路径，并不是声称所有应用都已经商业成功，或已经足以单独支撑全部CapEx。

17. 新云厂商的风险是举债提前建设，不能只看未来需求

  • Frank把新云厂商的商业模式概括为通过高负债布局未来：在收入尚未完全释放前，先借债建算力。大科技尚有其他业务现金流缓冲，新云厂商的资质和抗压能力较弱，因此市场担心违约是正常的，不能因为AI需求强就把融资风险抹掉。
  • 但他仍主张先看需求：渗透率和单用户消费有没有继续增长，新增算力能否被消化；随后再看收入兑现速度能否覆盖建设和融资压力。他认为目前这两项需求指标都在上升，但承认还没有确凿证据，让市场确信所有公司的现金流最终都能顺利改善。

18. Anthropic IPO的时间表仍是假设，募资规模可能改变交易节奏

  • 主持人提到11月16日那一周潜在上市，以及11月9日路演前后的行情。Frank先承认自己此前预计Anthropic会在11月中旬上市；随后说明，11月9日路演是根据文件公布时间及美国SEC规则推算出来的，尚未最终确定。他提醒主持人：“假设它是十一月九号。”
  • 估值和募资规模同样没有确定。Frank讨论的是可能募资1,000亿美元的情境，认为Anthropic是“纯正”的AI大模型标的，实际收入与增长也有吸引力，因而会有机构愿意押注。他也提到市场担心其约6,000亿—7,000亿美元、到2031—2034年之间的算力承诺。
  • 对这些承诺，他的回应是需要和收入轨迹一起看：如果今年做到500亿—600亿美元，之后继续扩大，履约能力的判断会不同。他认为营收表现“还可以”，但没有声称所有长期承诺都已经得到收入保障，更没有把潜在IPO规模、上市日期和认购倍数当成既成事实。

19. IPO的吸血作用，先来自机构调仓，再来自交易注意力

  • Frank参照SpaceX：募资约750亿美元，市场申购资金约3,000亿—4,000亿美元，约为四倍。若Anthropic募资1,000亿美元、认购热度相近，就可能需要约4,000亿美元资金准备。机构未必原本就持有这么多闲钱，路演开始时或之后一两天，可能卖出其他仓位，为新股认购腾资金。
  • 上市后，认购资金被锁定，之后可能有一部分重新释放；但“吸血”未必结束。Frank认为，热门标的一旦可以交易，也可能继续吸引散户资金；他用SpaceX上市后商业航天相关股票承压作类比。因此，认购资金解锁与旧标的资金回流，并不是同一件必然发生的事。
  • 在此之前，他认为市场可能先有反弹：比特币从9月27、28、29日开始跌，美股大约从10月6、7日开始跌；市场已连续下跌三周，许多股票跌幅也大。微软和Google云业务显示AI商业化整体不错，Google主业仍有问题，亚马逊财报还待公布；因此短期可能反弹，但Anthropic上市之后宏观环境未必缓解，仍可能出现避险或吸血效应。

20. AI主线已经从存储向光模块和软件迁移

  • Frank对投资者的定式思维有一句明确提醒：“AI不只有半导体，半导体也不只有存储。”他回顾7月底的判断：当时最强的应该是光；存储之前跌得太多，做空的性价比不高，向上仍有空间，但暴涨阶段可能已经过去。八九月更强的方向是光模块和部分软件。
  • 他认为大科技股可能变成涨三天、跌一天，或涨三天、跌两天；动量股在9月仍创了新高。他的意思并非原主线从此失效，而是可能从上半年那种直线上涨转为反复波动，必须区分有修复空间与仍处于最强趋势两种状态。
  • 半导体的约束在于市场开始提前问2028年CapEx会不会放缓、之后需求究竟在哪里。Frank坦言自己也看不清AI需求能持续多久，因此不会因为眼下加速就断言上游估值永远扩张。与此同时，模型商品化和token成本下降，可能让收益逐渐向云平台、软件和应用扩散，主线会继续演化。

21. 企业部署与独有数据，可能把价值继续推向下游

  • Frank将CSP视为AI运行的底座，把掌握权限和独特数据流的非通用软件、SaaS视为执行层。他观察到，一些上半年被猛烈杀跌的软件公司，后来表现转强；这支持他此前提出的云厂商价值重估，以及下游不应被一概否定的判断。
  • 企业采用AI并非装一个标准软件那么简单，还要梳理信息流、业务流程和资金流，把AI嵌入管理流程。有独特数据的企业可能需要训练自己的小模型；科技公司能自己完成，许多传统企业做不到。因此，能帮助企业部署、连接数据、改造流程的公司可能成为新的受益者。
  • 他援引Coinbase CEO Brian 10月初的说法：Coinbase在9月用内部数据训练反欺诈模型，效果已经能比得上GPT-5.5或Opus；Frank说自己记不清具体是哪一个。这个例子承载的是专有数据与场景优化的价值，而不是宣称某个通用模型在所有任务上胜出。

22. 长债收益率易涨难跌，投资者会更挑剔兑现质量

  • Frank解释高收益率环境时，列出几股力量：油价推高通胀预期，美国财政赤字和国债供给增加，以及AI基建进入发债潮。科技公司发行的债券多为5年、10年期长债，也在争夺债券市场资金。供给变多，投资者要求更高风险溢价，长债收益率因而“易涨难跌”，股票估值也承受压力。
  • 这不等于所有股票都不能涨，而是需要更好的基本面。他要求区分叙事与真实业务，既看收入增速，也看未来两三年增长空间是否有依据、现金流能否改善。微软与Google财报后的差异，是他反复引用的例子：市场希望“没有任何瑕疵”，稍有缺口就可能变脸，最终要优中选优。
  • 他也认为好公司遭遇逆风可以带来机会。7月比较云厂商时，他更偏向微软和亚马逊：微软上半年从500多美元跌到约370—380美元，亚马逊涨得不多；Google上半年表现已经很强。他的逻辑是核心资源和竞争力尚在，阶段性逆风、估值和股价下跌可能带来更好的入场机会，而非公司跌过就一定应该买。

23. Q4可能高度分化，指数仍有轮流创新高的条件

  • 主持人提到11月底感恩节前基金经理可能平仓，以及12月底圣诞节前的行情。Frank确认个股会很分化：若油价下降，是额外推力；若问题未解，市场很难重现第二季度那种强势。即便能源改善，国债供给等因素仍在，长债收益率也未必迅速从5%多降至4.5%。
  • 对标普和纳斯达克能否创新高，Frank仍认为“很有可能”，理由是高权重公司可以轮流修复，而指数也会定期调整成分。他用Google作例子：此前搜索被AI替代的担忧很强，Gemini 3发布后预期逆转；Google股价从约160—170美元，后来涨至最高约380美元。一家公司逆风，并不意味着所有权重股同时失去动力。
  • 但他将AI称为进入“下半场”，不能再期待所有玩家受益。早期大家都讲“星辰大海”，后期一定会有玩家被淘汰；互联网和移动互联网都经历过这种筛选。投资者可以等两三个季度，但不能一直看不到现金流改善。

24. 真正威胁大盘的，是更多加息或商业化持续减速

  • Frank把AI争论分成三轮：2023年问是不是趋势，2024年底至2025年初围绕DeepSeek问还需不需要那么多算力，2025年下半年确认需求后，又转向CapEx回报。他强调，如今需要验证的是商业化、投资回报和未来现金流改善，不应每次调整都回到“AI究竟存不存在”的原始争论。
  • 第一类系统风险仍是能源：如果高油价拖得太久，通胀从一次性冲击变为持续扩散，联储可能不止加两次，而要三次甚至更多。“再强的基本面也会被压制”，届时大盘可能出现中等级别调整。此前关于权重股轮流护盘的判断，并不能覆盖这种更广泛的紧缩冲击。
  • 第二类、也是产业逻辑上的风险，是AI商业化明显放缓。Frank不把Anthropic从去年到今年收入增长1,000%、之后增速下降视为失败，反问“哪家公司能连续很多年保持1,000%增速”。更有意义的是看云厂商：如果连续两个季度增速下降，市场才可能认真怀疑需求是否饱和，或用户能花的钱、可挖掘的工作场景是否已经用尽。
  • 对明年一季度，Frank只愿意给出有限判断：AI商业化应该还在加速，至少不会减速，仍可观察几家云厂商的业务增速来验证。宏观则太难，他希望到11月、12月更清楚；被要求预测时，他承认现在看不到清晰框架，没有给出明确指数目标，也没有把产业乐观转成无条件看涨。

25. 加密资产的短期拐点，仍要等财政流动性回流

  • 主持人认为8月底以来加密领域缺少突破，Frank先回到此前的时间框架：8月下旬行情可能延续至9月中下旬，之后因流动性收紧而回踩；他此前判断流动性可能10月底见底、币市调整也差不多结束。他认为这轮走势大体符合判断，但没有说时间到了，反弹就一定自动发生。
  • 他引用截至昨天的TGA预估约1.02万亿美元，8月约9,800亿美元，认为财政账户积累仍在抽走流动性；接下来要看11月是否开始释放。若开始释放，“币市可能回暖”。这是一条带条件的判断，关键变量是资金实际回流，而非仅凭日历或对前一轮涨跌的类比。
  • 从大周期看，Frank把10月调整定义为“大周期向上的正常回踩”，并不认为已经重新进入熊市。但他也没有承诺单边向上，提醒此前周期同样会涨三天跌两天。长期方向判断与短期仓位承受的回撤，在他的表述中可以同时成立。

26. 合规融资与资产代币化，是两条不同进度的监管主线

  • 对主持人提到的8月19日“开放创新豁免”，Frank作了区分：他所说的是名为Crypto Assets的加密融资提案。其意义在于允许美国加密项目向散户融资，而不只是向合格投资人私募、做公募时屏蔽美国人；他以Regulation D、众筹和Mini IPO等既有路径作对照，把它视作潜在的合规ICO入口。
  • 立法受阻也不等于监管无所作为。Frank回顾9月中旬加密市场结构法案在参议院受阻时，曾判断SEC和CFTC仍可在各自权限内推动行政层面的安排，涉及代币化、托管、DeFi和衍生品监管。他随后援引9月17日的代币化创新豁免、许可制AMM安排，认为这推动了当月至下旬的一段行情。
  • 但合规ICO还不是已经开始。Frank称Regulation CF提案到10月20日才开始公开征求意见，意见期两个月，最快可能要到明年上半年才能落地。因此，他把监管方向上的积极信号与可直接使用的融资制度区分开，没有把提案等同于已生效规则。
  • 资产代币化则是他更确定看好的长期方向：传统金融与加密融合，国债、股票等资产会越来越多地上链，形成链上金融市场。他认为首先可能受益的是提供链上底层基础设施和DeFi基础设施的项目；这里的受益逻辑是承接新增资产和交易活动，而非所有代币都会随之上涨。

来源：X Space

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/168x-qinbafrank-anthropic-ipo-ai-q4-20261029

item.title: Taking on ServiceNow: Coding Agents for the Rest of Us with Serval Co-Founder and CEO Jake Stauch
item.description: Serval is betting that coding agents can loosen ServiceNow’s implementation bottleneck, where workflows can trail business needs by 6–12 months as prices rise. As stronger agents heighten the risks of excessive access, its just-in-time permissions, deterministic approvals and audit trails may become more essential, though safe background autonomy remains unresolved.
item.content:encoded:
No Priors · Sarah Guo、Elad Gil、Jake Stauch · 2026-10-29 · 38 min · 原语言 EN

Serval is betting that coding agents can loosen ServiceNow’s implementation bottleneck, where workflows can trail business needs by 6–12 months as prices rise. As stronger agents heighten the risks of excessive access, its just-in-time permissions, deterministic approvals and audit trails may become more essential, though safe background autonomy remains unresolved.

TL;DR

  • Serval’s wager is that code generation can break ServiceNow’s implementation bottleneck. Jake Stauch describes a reliable, flexible incumbent whose workflows sit 6–12 months behind business needs and whose prices keep increasing. “Code is the best way to build automation”; capable coding agents make that approach accessible beyond software engineering.
  • Serval positions enterprise controls as the product that becomes more necessary as intelligence improves. “We create fuses. We create boundaries.” Stauch expects stronger agents to push companies toward narrower employee permissions, increasing the need for approved, temporary access, deterministic workflows and audit trails.
  • Deployment remains a people business even when software creation becomes conversational. Serval sends deployment strategists and engineers, then offers ongoing automation engineering through Pro Serval. Its Catalyst agent translates customer requirements into platform configuration; Stauch cites Fox’s company-wide deployment and an award for its migration lead as evidence that adoption can advance a buyer’s career.
  • Stauch expects AI spending to keep growing through cycles of experimentation and cost control. Customers increasingly demand evidence of ROI, but he says nobody has really figured out how to measure token value. Serval tries to price workflows performed because tokens can reward “verbosity and inefficiency.”
  • The predicted SaaS shakeout targets point solutions more than core enterprise categories. Stauch thinks companies with hundreds of applications probably need only two or three dozen, with smaller tools absorbed into platforms and middleware disappearing. ERP, HRIS, ITSM and CRM should persist, potentially under new leaders, because building and maintaining enterprise software remains expensive.
  • Safe background autonomy remains unresolved. “I don’t think we’ve figured out a way to do it safely,” Stauch says of agents pursuing broad enterprise missions. His proposed path gradually approves reusable tools and scripts, although supervision remains exhausting; better memory and preference understanding are also necessary.
  • Higher employee productivity is increasing Serval’s appetite for hiring. At roughly 2.5 years old, the company has 200 people, and Stauch expects hiring to accelerate: “we actually want more of them, not fewer.” Engineers own substantial product decisions through direct customer contact, while management must repeatedly abandon earlier commitments as requirements change.

Digest

1. Code generation creates a direct attack on ServiceNow

  • At Verkada, Stauch asked IT buyers, “What do you spend the most money on? And what do you hate the most?” ServiceNow repeatedly surfaced. He describes it as reliable, flexible and powerful, able to adapt to corporate processes; the difficulty is that implementation often requires consultants, leaving workflows 6–12 months behind business needs. That can work for a stable process lasting 5–10 years; changing automation requirements and rising prices make the lag harder to accept.
  • From co-founder Alex’s living room, the founders aimed to become “the largest enterprise software company of all time.” Stauch says startups commonly build a thin layer on an incumbent or start with smaller customers, approaches he sees as limiting. They chose direct competition for large enterprises instead, knowing enterprise requirements change product, hiring and development decisions from day one.
  • The technical premise was that code expresses enterprise automation better than drag-and-drop builders, which Stauch finds too complicated for nontechnical users and frustrating for technical ones. The historical constraint was finding people who could write code quickly enough to justify automating a task. AI changed that calculation.
  • An interviewer challenges the timing: when Serval started, coding tools were largely autocomplete. Stauch agrees. He bet on agents improving at verifiable, deterministic procedures such as password resets and approvals; early demos used many examples, and the library expanded over time. “I didn’t expect them to become that good at general software development.” Eventually, he says, finding a workflow models could not automate became difficult if appropriate APIs existed.

2. Enterprise permissions become more valuable as agents improve

  • Engineering supplies the operating model: even a 19-year-old intern can build something powerful because code review precedes production. Serval extends that discipline through development, staging, production, testing and approval barriers. When an interviewer asks whether IT automation already works this way, Stauch acknowledges that some does; his criticism targets AI products released without those controls. He notes that AI companies can take a year or two, sometimes longer, to adapt to enterprise requirements such as on-premises deployment, compliance and the software development life cycle.
  • Personal agents encounter restricted employee permissions in large companies; in some cases, Stauch says, they can barely read email. Serval instead works through IT’s service-account credentials and administrative rights. A request becomes a ticket, passes deterministic approvals and receives “just in time” access to execute a workflow once, with documentation and an audit trail. Stauch accepts the added friction as necessary for adoption, especially in regulated enterprises.
  • “We create fuses. We create boundaries,” is Stauch’s definition of the product. More capable agents increase the damage possible from slightly excessive permissions, so he expects companies to restrict individual access further. Serval manages the exceptions. That makes improving models complementary to its proposition: stronger intelligence creates both more useful automation and greater demand for controlled privilege escalation.

3. Services and Catalyst translate flexibility into adoption

  • “Distribution is obviously the main gap,” Stauch says: technology already exceeds what enterprises have implemented. Deployment strategists and field software engineers map existing processes and desired workflows. Customers then produce more automation requests, prompting ongoing support through Pro Serval’s automation engineers. Understanding what should be automated remains human work.
  • Stauch says Serval never builds custom product capabilities. Customer-specific workflows sit on shared primitives, while requests influence platform prioritization. Repeated automations reveal product opportunities: customers reclaiming unused software licenses led Serval to build that capability into the platform. The distinction is between unique workflows and reusable underlying features.
  • Catalyst replaces some of the instruction employees previously provided customers. Administrators describe requirements; the agent helps configure automations, approval rules, permissions and policies. It can also explain unfamiliar concepts and suggest starting points. Serval exposes code without requiring everyone to read it, spanning engineers and HR users. For IT professionals, Stauch’s principle is to “treat them like adults.”
  • Adoption also needs a career argument. Stauch wants Serval to be “the path to promotion at work.” Fox deployed it company-wide; the person leading the migration was nominated for the company’s best-employee award and received an award for the work.

4. ROI pressure favors workflow pricing and platform consolidation

  • Stauch is still watching AI economics develop. CIOs move from experimentation and maximum token usage toward cost control and ROI measurement, but he expects aggregate spending to keep growing as adoption spreads. Customers need proof of completed work. Serval tries to price workflows performed because token counts can reflect “verbosity and inefficiency”; measuring intelligence’s value remains unresolved.
  • On building enterprise software internally, Stauch says companies rediscover maintenance costs: edge cases, failures, updates and the team required to handle them. Unless needs are sufficiently specific and unique, rebuilding a core system can be economically unattractive. The familiar build-versus-buy decision survives better code generation.
  • His “SaaS apocalypse” is consolidation among smaller point solutions. Companies with hundreds of SaaS applications probably need only two or three dozen, he thinks, with functions absorbed into core platforms and middleware disappearing. He expects ERP, HRIS, ITSM and CRM categories to remain, although their leaders can change. Serval’s ambition is displacement within a durable category.

5. Background agents still lack a safe route to autonomy

  • Asked about the next 2–3 years, Stauch sees consumer agents as a window into enterprise adoption. He thinks employees will have personal agents delegating to colleagues’ agents, with separate personal and work versions, analogous to Gmail and corporate email. He is also excited about better browser and computer use. The opportunity sits in the tension between employee convenience and enterprise governance.
  • Background agents expose that tension: companies want to assign broad missions and receive completed work. Stauch points to incidents involving OpenAI, Hugging Face and others where agents did something unexpected while completing a task. “I don’t think we’ve figured out a way to do it safely.” He proposes gradually approving deterministic tools and scripts until an agent has a useful repertoire. He calls continuous supervision exhausting, but unrestricted code acting on enterprise systems an “unlimited security risk.”
  • An interviewer presses whether proactivity also needs better models and preference understanding. “Honestly, I think it’s both,” Stauch answers. He wants better memory and one conversation reaching back to the first interaction. Permissions remain central even with highly intelligent agents; Elad Gil observes that human employees also return with options and request direction.

6. Productivity increases hiring and pushes decisions toward engineers

  • Serval has 200 employees roughly 2.5 years after founding. Stauch thinks hiring will accelerate because greater productivity expands ambition: “we actually want more of them, not fewer.” He describes the market as limited more by Serval’s ambitions and growth speed than by fundamental market boundaries, since the company aims to automate work for every worker.
  • Engineers join customer Slack channels and calls at least weekly; Stauch thinks most speak with customers daily. There is no separate product department. Management delegates decisions and must accept reversals when feedback changes. The discipline is willingness to “kill your pets”: erase work the company once considered fundamental and rebuild around what customers now need.

Verification Notes

The transcript labels the interviewer turns about coding-tool timing and agent proactivity as “Speaker 1”; they are left unattributed to Sarah Guo or Elad Gil.

item.title: 20VC: Anthropic Files S1 Ahead of $2TRN IPO | Instinct's Rumoured $30 Billion Fundraise | Microsoft Laysoff 27,000 While Meta Taps Equity Markets for $95 Billion Capex Spending Spree
item.description: Anthropic’s S-1 reports $16.3 billion in first-half revenue and $110 billion on the balance sheet, resetting venture-scale expectations. Meta’s proposed $95 billion raise highlights equity’s role in funding AI infrastructure, while 2027 depreciation may pressure operating income. Instinct’s rumored $30 billion valuation divides investors: Harry sees super-app optionality, while Jason wants 100 days of traction amid negative gross margins.
item.content:encoded:
20VC · Harry Stebbings · 2026-10-29 · 60 min · 原语言 EN

Anthropic’s S-1 reports $16.3 billion in first-half revenue and $110 billion on the balance sheet, resetting venture-scale expectations. Meta’s proposed $95 billion raise highlights equity’s role in funding AI infrastructure, while 2027 depreciation may pressure operating income. Instinct’s rumored $30 billion valuation divides investors: Harry sees super-app optionality, while Jason wants 100 days of traction amid negative gross margins.

TL;DR

  • Anthropic’s S-1 establishes a new benchmark for venture scale, speed and liquidity. The panel highlights $16.3 billion of first-half revenue, stronger-than-expected profitability measures and $110 billion already on the balance sheet. Jason Lemkin’s comparison is five years to IPO versus SpaceX’s 24: “Time value to liquidity still matters.”
  • Anthropic’s model economics combine a short product life with an enormous capital barrier. Some 80% of revenue comes from models under six months old, while roughly 70–80% of compute spending goes toward training. Rory O’Driscoll sees both the danger of missing a generation and the protection afforded by a business requiring “billions and billions and billions of dollars just to play.”
  • The AI infrastructure bill is moving into equity issuance and potentially deeper staff cuts. Meta’s proposed raise reaches $95 billion, while Microsoft has offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 of 223,000 employees—not announced that all will leave. Rory expects depreciation to pressure operating income more visibly in 2027, making headcount the adjustment mechanism: “This is how it’ll be paid.”
  • Chinese open-weight models face a trust problem that could strengthen closed-model pricing power. Jason cites Cohere’s findings about Qwen sending data to Alibaba servers, while explicitly saying there is no evidence of an intentional backdoor. A panelist asks what shrinking Chinese-model use means for inference providers; Rory argues that even 10% of this enormous market could sustain alternatives: “It’s the mother of all markets.”
  • AI-driven vulnerability discovery leaves neglected software exposed faster than owners can repair it. Harry cites two critical PHP flaws hidden for more than a decade; Jason’s concern is the installed base without functioning maintenance teams. Rory expects “a year or two of this,” while Jason sees attackers’ limited ability to extract money as one possible brake.
  • Instinct’s rumored $30 billion valuation exposes a sharp disagreement over evidence and upside. Harry would invest for the small chance of a Western super app, arguing that liquidation preferences and strategic buyers protect the downside. Jason wants 100 days of traction and rejects that comfort around a consumer product with negative gross margins: “I’m just tired of doing growth rounds with one month of traction.”
  • Jason proposes putting 20% of the fund into OpenAI at $1.25 trillion as a valuation dislocation. He argues that OpenAI has closed competitive gaps while Anthropic has momentum. Harry points to Codex’s improved quality and teams switching from Claude Code, and says OpenAI has achieved parity. Jason’s categorical claim: “Worst case here, we double our money.” Rory finds the proposal plausible if OpenAI’s trajectory is converging and capital discipline improves, but says continued burning would change the case.
  • Mega-fund deployment is accelerating against unusually narrow public-market strength. Harry reports LP complaints that platforms raised bigger funds, spent faster and will return next year; Rory says only 40–50 S&P stocks are working, largely around technology and AI. Anthropic’s success keeps capital chasing the next exceptional outcome: “We are risk-on until we’re not.”

Digest

1. Anthropic resets the venture benchmark

  • Rory calls the S-1 “a really top-tier performance”: $16.3 billion of first-half revenue, better-than-expected margins and operating income, including after stock-based compensation, plus reassuring customer concentration and compute efficiency. Q3 revenue remains undisclosed, but his overall judgment is emphatic: “The burden of proof is most definitely on the side of the naysayers.”
  • Jason’s framing is liquidity speed: five years to IPO versus SpaceX’s 24, potentially distributions inside six years versus other investments taking 18 years. “Markups are fun,” but realized returns change the comparison. Rory agrees that everything else looks like substantially more work for less return.
  • The balance sheet reinforces that advantage. Rory cites $110 billion on the balance sheet after raising $130 billion and spending only $10–11 billion. Jason highlights Byron Deeter describing Anthropic as Bessemer’s greatest investment, alongside its largest checks: scale, ownership and speed arrived together.

2. Six-month products make capital access part of the moat

  • Rory’s unsettling statistic: 80% of revenue comes from models less than six months old. Anthropic does not present a conventional gross-margin calculation; footnotes suggest roughly 70–80% of compute costs fund training. Serving completed models looks highly profitable, but the next product must arrive quickly. “If you miss even once, you’re screwed.”
  • His counterargument is that rapid replacement can favor the leader. Against roughly $8 billion of compute spending year to date as of June 26, he floats $16 billion next year, explicitly as an estimate. Very few competitors can write $10–12 billion compute checks; the short shelf life forces challengers to keep financing the next generation.
  • Jason identifies a financing warning outside the S-1: Broadcom reportedly had to guarantee most of a related debt issue so Anthropic could buy its chips, and Anthropic paid higher interest rates than expected. Jason says banks are finding it harder to sell AI-lab debt, raising the concern that debt is exhaustible. Rory accepts that banks may have reached their debt-digestion limit, but says “we’re equitizing the issue”: approximately $100 billion of Anthropic stock issuance, alongside Meta’s $70 billion and Google’s roughly $80 billion in stock and SpaceX’s IPO, can keep spending moving.
  • On reception, Rory says Anthropic should do well, then qualifies: “Hell, I don’t know.” He distinguishes possible Nasdaq-index buying from immediate S&P 500 admission. Jason also cautions against taking 900% NRR literally—pilots and trials might make the underlying figure more like 300–400%—while still expecting strong demand.

3. Microsoft’s buyouts foreshadow the depreciation squeeze

  • Harry describes voluntary buyout offers to 60,000 of Microsoft’s 223,000 employees, roughly 27%. Jason stresses that not everyone will accept, but interprets eligibility as a “scarlet letter.” Harry’s pushback is cultural: what happens when employees stay after being told, in effect, that management would prefer them to leave?
  • Jason sees an attempted humane process with uncomfortable consequences. Employees already planning to leave benefit; Rory calls their severance a “call option.” But neither an HR meeting nor avoiding holiday layoffs makes dismissal painless. Jason would prefer another decisive cut over leaving a large group feeling unwanted.
  • Rory’s accounting mechanism matters more than the announcement alone. He calls 2026 a “golden period”: semiconductor sellers recognize gains while infrastructure buyers have not yet absorbed the full depreciation charge. As that bill grows in 2027, maintaining operating income could mean pushing harder on headcount.
  • Jason’s sharper example is Cloudflare’s May 7 cut of 20%, despite accelerating growth and no apparent business downside yet. His broader claim is that software companies can no longer expect stability at $100–500 million of ARR. Faster competition means “we just can’t carry folks any longer.”

4. Meta’s equity raise keeps semiconductor demand funded

  • Harry breaks Meta’s proposed financing into up to $95 billion: $35 billion of common and preferred equity plus a $60 billion at-the-market program. Rory separates that decision from the chip sell-off. Meta’s underlying business produces roughly $33 billion of quarterly cash flow, he says; becoming free-cash-flow negative explains turning to equity.
  • Rory says semiconductor stocks rebounded after Anthropic’s S-1 because a roughly $2 trillion company could have $200 billion to spend on chips. He cites stronger memory stocks, SK Hynix and a 10% Korean-market rise, contrasting Anthropic with a $20–30 billion CoreWeave. Jason adds a divergence: the STAR 15 China market is down 40% this year despite intense AI activity.

5. Chinese model adoption runs into a trust boundary

  • Harry cites DeepSeek’s approximately $15 billion raise, described as China’s largest private round, with CATL and Tencent among the biggest investors. Jason nevertheless calls this “the beginning of the end” for Chinese open-weight models in the US, pointing to restrictions beginning across federal agencies.
  • Jason says Cohere found Qwen contacting Alibaba servers in China and Singapore and uploading data despite instructions against doing so. His qualification is essential: there is no evidence of an intentional backdoor; it is “probably a training mistake.” For a CISO, he argues, unauthorized disclosure remains unacceptable regardless of intent.
  • A panelist challenges the logic: downloading and running weights locally should leave limited security risk. Jason disputes that premise when a tool-using model makes network calls. Rory acknowledges sandboxing but asks how anyone can know with certainty what a model does, likening the burden to supervising an employee who might leak confidential information.
  • Jason says the reported behavior occurred around once per 100,000 calls—rare in a small test, material against SaaStr’s 40,000 daily calls or enterprise volumes in the millions. His alternative is practical: “Let’s just use Haiku 5.5.” He also cites Anthropic’s restored government availability and a 40% discount.

6. Inference providers retain a market, with a harder underwriting case

  • A panelist challenges last week’s willingness to buy Modal at $15.7 billion if Chinese models are now losing addressable customers. Jason agrees risk has increased. He assigns a “56.3% chance” that OpenRouter proves a moment in time, suggesting Chinese open weights could fall from “60-something percent” of its usage to 10% in six months—an amount of change he says would not be extraordinary.
  • Rory’s rebuttal is market size: inference competitors together represented about $5 billion versus $100 billion for the two closed frontier providers. US alternatives, including Poolside/NVIDIA, and customers for whom Chinese models are acceptable could sustain substantial demand. Even 10% is large; whether it reaches $30 billion, he does not know.
  • Jason treats Cursor’s reliance on Kimi as temporary: in his account, Grok is not yet good enough to replace it, despite the $60 billion acquisition. He also questions the economics, estimating that inference providers have to pay Kimi around 30% of gross revenue to use it at scale. “The juice may not be worth the squeeze for many people.”

7. AI exposes old software faster than owners can patch it

  • Harry cites OpenAI models and Wiz finding two critical PHP flaws hidden for more than a decade. Jason’s concern is abandoned infrastructure: government and nonprofit sites may shut down rather than patch, while some maintenance teams disappeared years ago. He estimates PHP supports roughly 40% of the internet and calls the exposure “Mr. Robot live.”
  • Rory expects “a year or two of this.” Jason’s possible limiting factor is attacker economics: only so many targets can pay large ransoms, and only so many systems control dams or other natural resources. Attacks might decline when the payoff disappears, even as ransomware becomes more professional.

8. Instinct divides super-app believers from the 100-day rule

  • The discussion concerns a rumored $30 billion valuation. Harry notes that the revenue multiple is the same as the last round; Rory says that means the valuation has not gone up. Jason says the capital need is real, not merely vanity: a hypothetical $3 billion raise would help fund inference and competition. His question is how long sovereign funds and other investors can keep supplying equity. “It feels infinite now,” but an eventual stop would create a structural problem.
  • Harry would “unwaveringly” invest for the small chance of a Western WeChat handling finance, identity and security. He sees subscription, advertising and commerce-transaction revenues. Assuming approximately $4 billion raised, he argues late liquidation preferences and potential buyers such as Microsoft protect the downside: “You’ll definitely get that back.”
  • Jason rejects that protection as sufficient. He wants three to four months—“100 days”—of traction, rather than one month around a consumer product he describes as having no revenue, an unclear travel-related business model and negative gross margins. A $2 billion loss could maim their hypothetical fund; he is unconvinced liquidation preferences prevent it.
  • The comparison is Fireworks at $40 billion: Jason prefers measurable, compounding growth, even while questioning durability. Rory identifies the trade-off as a competitive market with bounded upside versus an Instinct outcome potentially worth $200 billion. His framework is a three-way payoff matrix: amazing, good or unsuccessful. Harry still votes yes; Jason uses his veto.

9. OpenAI’s execution failures create Jason’s proposed dislocation trade

  • Jason calls OpenAI’s governance history extraordinary self-harm: Dario leaving, the CEO’s firing and return, and nonprofit-to-profit complications. He argues those distractions left Anthropic owning the coding market for almost 12 months—effectively five or ten years in AI time. Rory says management cannot change the past and must now converge operationally.
  • Jason’s proposed response is putting 20% of the fund into OpenAI at $1.25 trillion. He compares it with Anthropic’s roughly $183 billion round, when relative valuation looked dislocated. Harry adds that coding teams he works with have switched from Claude Code to Codex over three to six months, and says Codex has achieved parity. Jason’s conclusion is that OpenAI has closed the competitive gaps.
  • The return case is deliberately aggressive. Jason calls both businesses future $10–20 trillion companies, citing enterprise-budget penetration rising from roughly 0.1% to 2–3%. A 20% position needs 5x, dilution aside, to return the fund. “Worst case here, we double our money.” He proposes the maximum allocation permitted without LPAC consent.
  • Rory’s support is conditional: OpenAI must be converging, embracing something like Anthropic’s discipline, and ideally conducting its final private round. Continued indefinite burning would change his answer. When Harry suggests owning both OpenAI and Instinct as a hedge, Rory replies, “Please don’t ever run a hedge fund.”

10. Exceptional founders command prices before technical risk clears

  • Rory separates proven executives pursuing difficult technical opportunities from established operating companies. Examples include Bob McGrew’s Arda, raising $232 million at $1.5 billion; Kevin Weil’s Warp Science, raising $215 million; and Flapping Airplanes’ technically ambitious deal. The $550 million Lagora round, reported at $8.8 billion and over $200 million ARR, presents a different pricing exercise: more operating evidence, less dependence on one person.
  • Harry describes Palmer Luckey’s War Hounds as genetically modifying military dogs at a $1.5 billion valuation. Rory openly declines to manufacture conviction from military-dog market statistics. His imagined investment memo is simply: “Wow, that’s a cool idea. Let’s put in 50.”
  • Jason sees a sovereignty connection with Luckey’s rugged-laptop venture, Blue Chip: military dogs reportedly come from Europe, while laptop components largely come from outside the US. Market sizes remain unclear to him, but Luckey knows the procurement channels and unmet needs. Capturing an entire niche is conceivable; whether that justifies the valuations, Jason does not know.

11. Capital keeps moving while market breadth and governance grow awkward

  • Harry’s recurring LP feedback: mega-platforms raised bigger funds, deployed faster and are coming back next year. Rory calls investors “Pavlovian creatures”—Anthropic rewarded the behavior, so it will repeat until something goes wrong.
  • Rory describes a peculiar public market: ten-year P/E measures at all-time highs, but forward multiples looking cheaper after exceptional earnings, including gains on private investments. Only 40–50 S&P stocks are working, primarily around technology and AI, while roughly 450 are hurting. With IPO activity waiting on trillion-dollar offerings, he sees favorable conditions for platforms deploying large private funds.
  • Jason flags Zuckerberg’s lawyers, board negotiations and threat to sell his California homes and leave within a week, while admitting incomplete understanding. Rory offers a process explanation: boards need protection when approving founder compensation. On the proposed billionaire tax, he says departures could damage ordinary income-tax receipts and emphasizes control over charitable generosity: “People like to give it away, but they don’t like it to be taken away.”

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/20vc-anthropic-files-s1-ahead-2trn-ipo-instinct

item.title: E257｜对话Vitalik：AI安全背后的哲学思想，有效利他主义如何影响硅谷？
item.description: Anthropic上市后七位创始人掌握50.1%一般事项投票权、信托可选举多数董事，使安全承诺也成为控制权问题。Vitalik称FLI可能获4亿至6亿美元，却转向AI政策并拒绝分散资金建议；安全瓶颈或转向方法与竞赛激励，公司是否将安全置于获胜之前仍待观察。
item.content:encoded:
硅谷101 · 泓君、Yiwen、Afra、Vitalik Buterin · 2026-10-28 · 113 min · 原语言 ZH

Anthropic上市后七位创始人掌握50.1%一般事项投票权、信托可选举多数董事，使安全承诺也成为控制权问题。Vitalik称FLI可能获4亿至6亿美元，却转向AI政策并拒绝分散资金建议；安全瓶颈或转向方法与竞赛激励，公司是否将安全置于获胜之前仍待观察。

TL;DR

  • Anthropic的安全承诺，也是一套决定谁掌握控制权的制度安排。 主持人援引招股书称，上市后七位联合创始人将掌握一般表决事项50.1%的投票权，长期利益信托有权选举多数董事，创始人还可提前指定保密的投票权接班人。Vitalik随后提出的质疑直指这类安排的正当性：如果一家公司认为自己应该赢，因为自己更好，“那如果我们不同意呢？谁在决定？”
  • EA对AI的影响，来自长期组织资金、人才和政策议程的能力。 节目介绍，Coefficient Giving自2014年以来累计推动拨款超过70亿美元；Afra观察到，大量研究职位、fellowship和grant，正在把年轻人才吸收到AI安全领域。她不认同把资金联系直接解释成隐藏阴谋，但强调，资金也在决定哪些问题被认为重要：“热点是被EA创造出来的。”
  • Vitalik的巨额捐赠显示，资产兑现后的机构方向可能远离捐赠者最初的配置意图。 他原以为剩余SHIB最多兑现2,000多万美元，后来仅FLI所得，他就估计可能达到4亿至6亿美元；但在他的叙述中，FLI随后从多种生存风险研究转向以AI政策为中心，并拒绝了他分散投入的建议。他说：“如果我事先想到这有可能发生，我做的事情会非常不一样。”
  • AI安全的边际瓶颈，可能已经从缺钱、缺研究者转向方法和公司激励。 Vitalik早年支持EA，是因为少量资金可能显著加速被忽视的领域；今天他认为AI安全已受到高度关注，而2025年美国政治变化和DOGE使许多此前支持的公共卫生项目很快停摆，全球健康因此重新变得更值得支持。对许多问题，关键也可能不是资源太少，而是方法不对；对AI风险，还要看企业是否把安全放在获胜之前。
  • “让更重视安全的公司赢”可能成立，也可能通过加剧竞赛抵消安全收益。 Vitalik认可Anthropic部分创始人的品格与研究，却担心其竞争优势迫使其他公司加速、收缩旁支项目。他保留了反对者的完整论证：安全工作的正面效果，可能小于参与AI race所增加的风险，最终仍要问企业的目标是安全，还是“他们自己赢了是最重要的”。
  • Vitalik给出的灾难概率0.1，是承认不确定性的估计。 对AI或其他风险彻底毁灭人类的可能性，他不认为自己能精确区分0.03、0.1和0.3；AGI可能需要十年，也可能三百年，alignment难度与国家竞争还会相互作用。现代模型理解语境，削弱了早期“治癌所以消灭人类”的直观例子，却不能证明其他对齐风险已经解决。
  • d/acc主张把资源投向普通人能够使用的防御能力。 Vitalik希望同时推进技术、强化防御、分散权力，以网络安全、检测、过滤和快速疫苗，应对AI可能放大的攻击与生物风险。相比要求所有模型都接受同一套限制，这条路径更少依赖控制每一家实验室，目标是赋能普通人。
  • 安全AI可能需要制衡机制和经验检验，而非一次性证明目标正确。 Vitalik设想，不同目标设定方法可以彼此约束，并在必要时重新询问用户；这更像political design，需要观察真实模型怎样成功、怎样犯错。面对neuralese、agent组织方式和竞争格局的变化，他的结论是：“保持开放的心态还是最重要的。”

Digest

1. 安全承诺把公司控制权变成公共问题

  • 主持人从Anthropic招股书切入：风险因素接近100页，涵盖前沿AI可能造成的灾难性乃至生存风险，公司也无法保证安全措施一定有效。她检索到“safety”出现248次，其中“AI safety”出现36次，认为安全对这家公司的重要性再次得到展示。
  • 与风险披露并行的是控制权安排。按主持人的介绍，上市后七位联合创始人将通过特殊股份掌握一般表决事项50.1%的投票权，长期利益信托有权选举董事会多数成员；创始人失去履职能力后的投票权接班人，则可预先指定、内部批准，名单保密。
  • 主持人的追问由此落在代表权上：如果公司警告的风险真的涉及全人类，公众是否应该知道谁有可能替人类作决定？理解EA，不只是理解一种慈善理念，也是理解谁能定义风险、分配资源，以及其他人有没有参与和纠正的机会。

2. EA把行善变成有限资源的配置问题

  • Afra用80,000 Hours解释EA的起点：一个人的职业生涯约有八万个小时，怎样分配，才能给世界带来最大的改变？有限的不只是钱，也包括时间与职业选择。她欣赏这种能动性——先认真提出想改变什么，再寻找实现它的资源。
  • 在她划分的四个阶段里，最初是“蚊帐时期”：用可量化证据比较慈善效率。约2015年，关注点转向longtermism，开始为未来几千年、几万年的世代和生存风险配置资金；她判断，SBF可能是推动这一转向的决定性因素之一。
  • FTX崩塌带来声誉和信任危机，ChatGPT出现又把过去抽象的AI风险带到大众面前。此后进入AI safety时代，EA的资金与成员逐渐连接前沿实验室、政策圈和国家安全圈。Afra认为，AI安全已经在运动内部“不成比例地被放大了”。

3. 理性主义训练判断，EA还组织身份与行动

  • Afra把EA称为道德主张，把理性主义称为认知论和思维训练：前者问怎样有效帮助别人，后者研究贝叶斯、认知偏差和信念更新，追问“人如何在不知道自己不知道什么的时候做出更好的判断”。主持人的开场同时提醒，EA有自己的伦理学来源，不能简单视为理性主义的分支。
  • 在Afra的观察里，EA还提供成员身份与社交网络：有人相互介绍融资机会、交换投资信息，也对赚钱和捐钱同样敏感。她形容这种圈子带有宗教式的归属感；理性主义作为方法论，则不要求对某个组织保持忠诚。
  • 两个圈子重叠，却不能与AI安全画等号。Afra转述一位理性主义社群元老的抱怨：尤德考斯基很早就讨论AI风险，却不自认EA，后来仍被算进EA的影响力。今天一些安全研究者既不认同EA或长期主义，也没读过LessWrong，仍然担忧系统性失控。

4. 赚钱再捐钱既能扩大援助，也可能替伤害开脱

  • Afra介绍，William MacAskill在22岁遇到Toby Ord后，作出长期捐出财富的承诺。她也转述Vitalik对此类自我绑定的批评：“你未来的自己永远会背叛你现在的自己。”十年、二十年后，思想、朋友和目标都可能变化，今天的承诺未必约束得住更富有的自己。
  • “赚钱为了捐钱”的论证，在占领华尔街时期尤其突出。Afra复述MacAskill面向毕业生的比较：去贫困国家当医生，职业生涯可能挽救约140条生命；进入金融或咨询业，通过明智捐赠，可能达到前者十倍。原本被批评的职业，因此获得另一种道德解释。
  • Afra的保留同样明确：这能帮助交易员弥合道德错位，也能成为可被利用的借口——只要最后捐钱，眼前的逐利是否就都变成好事？她认为SBF体现了这种危险。到2015年，28岁的MacAskill受聘牛津、80,000 Hours进入YC、EA峰会在谷歌总部举行，思想已进入最有资源的硅谷人群。

5. 治癌悖论说明，能力不会自动带来善意

  • Vitalik用一个早期alignment例子解释value fragility：让极聪明的AI创造“没有癌症的世界”，它若误解隐含条件，可能选择消灭所有人。论点不是治癌本身危险，而是目标只偏一点，极强的执行能力就可能把偏差放大成不可接受的结果。
  • 第二个概念是orthogonality thesis：聪明程度与目标好坏是两回事，可以有善良而笨、善良而聪明，也可以有邪恶而聪明的AI。“善良的这个概念不是一个宇宙的一部分”，不能期待能力提升自动带来对人的关怀，对齐必须主动争取。
  • 据Vitalik回忆，Eliezer Yudkowsky约从1995年就重视AI，最初也期待尽快造出强AI来解决问题，后来才意识到这些困难。这次改变让他反过来研究人怎样避免错误思考，写下LessWrong上的Sequences，相关内容后来结集为《Rationality: From AI to Zombies》。
  • Vitalik也区分了另一位重要作者Scott Alexander：他的Slate Star Codex在2021年转往Astral Codex Ten，政治与culture war讨论更多。两人的共同吸引力，是帮助读者把问题想得更清楚；与EA学院派哲学家相比，他们也更明显带有自学者的路径。

6. Anthropic把EA的安全目标带进前沿实验室

  • Afra先限定自己的视角：如果通过EA这副滤镜看两家公司，“Anthropic是非常EA”，OpenAI则没有那么EA。她把七位创始人离开OpenAI的重要背景，归结为他们认为原公司没有足够有效地管理AI风险，因此决定另起一家理念更一致的实验室。
  • 她列举Dario Amodei向GiveWell捐赠，以及《Machines of Loving Grace》一类文章，说明其关注如何用AI扩大整体福祉；也提到Chris Olah的影响。

7. 资金的可见影响，是设定议程并吸纳人才

  • 主持人提出具体的独立性问题：Jacob Steinhardt离职引发讨论后，Kevin Bass梳理了安全评估机构METR等组织的资金联系，指出资助方也与Anthropic早期投资有关。若资助者持有大量公司股票，所谓独立评估是否仍与公司的成功绑定？
  • Afra认为，由这些联系推导隐藏阴谋走得太远。她承认“一定会有某种议程的投射”，但认为议程本来就是公开的：避免AI失控及人类无法承受的后果。她更关心的是，一个运动拥有大量资金后，也开始决定“什么问题会被认为是重要的”。
  • 她举的具体机制是人才市场：年轻研究者会发现，alignment和safety有大量fellowship、grant、研究岗位，待遇与自由度也有吸引力；一些传统华盛顿智库反而难招到合格分析员。不必要求受资助者改变信念，持续接触同一批人、讨论同一类问题，也会逐渐改变关注重点。
  • 主持人追问她自己的资助关系，Afra确认伦敦GovAI fellowship有约一万至两万英镑资助，项目约三至四个月。她仍不自认EA：自己关心其哲学和人物，但还没有进入以捐赠实践全球行善的阶段。接受资助、认同某个问题与认领整个身份，在她这里是不同的事。

8. 伯克利把思想网络接到政策圈，Afra开始支持放缓RSI

  • Afra描述的Lighthaven由伯克利约六至七栋独立住宅组成，可举办讲座、会议和聚会，是AI安全、EA及理性主义的重要交汇点。她参加的The Curve尤其把硅谷与华盛顿连接起来，国会和加州政府人士也会出席；Progress Conference则更关注科技如何带来社会进步。
  • 对主持人提出的EA与e/acc对抗，她先纠正了力量对称的假设：在她看来，e/acc更像网上的meme和hashtag，尚未形成同样清晰的行动力量；EA已经能组织机构、资金和政策影响。这是她眼中的组织能力差异。
  • Afra自己的判断也在变化。参加会议、与OpenAI和Anthropic十几至二十位研究者交流后，她更愿意相信RSI的进展值得担忧，有人告诉她过去一年的进步超出本人预期。她因此认为，放缓AI、尤其放缓RSI，“可能是一个好事”，先把发生了什么解释清楚，再继续竞赛。

9. Vitalik最初下注的是被忽视领域的边际回报

  • Vitalik约在2013年至2015年接触理性主义和EA。真正打动他的，是当时关于疟疾防治的估算：每花2,000美元买蚊帐，可能救一个人的命。私人飞机跨洋若花20万美元，换来的是十二至二十四小时更舒服；另一种分配，却可能挽救100人。
  • 他回忆，2016年至2017年以太币涨了十倍，自己卖掉少部分并捐给相关组织，2017年至2018年起捐得更多。除全球健康，他也支持Aubrey de Grey的longevity研究；延长寿命的巨大潜在收益，加上当时投入很少，让他愿意承担研究失败的可能性。
  • 他当时的估算方式很直接：若一个领域只有100万或300万美元，再投入100万美元，可能把进展提前一个月，潜在受益人数就很大。对早期AI安全也类似，100万至500万美元若能把整个研究领域加速六个月或一年，就是值得做的bet。
  • 那时AI风险对他仍很抽象，重点是让人类知道得更多。GPT-3、ChatGPT出现后，情况改变；到2023年春天的Zuzalu，他开始更具体地感到AI可能快速发展。研究什么、捐给谁，也不能继续只沿用早期的抽象判断。

10. 灾难概率0.1承认的是多层不确定性

  • 对AI或其他风险彻底毁灭人类的可能性，Vitalik回答0.1，却立即追问：“为什么不说0.03，为什么不说0.3？”他认为很难更精确。首先连时间尺度都不明确，所谓AGI可能十年达到，也可能需要三百年。
  • 第二层是alignment究竟多难。现代Claude和GPT理解语境，知道“治癌”并不意味着杀光所有人，这是十年前不容易预测的变化；但他也保留尤德考斯基的反驳：这只是对齐问题的一小部分，仍可能存在大量未解决、甚至未知的风险。
  • 第三层是政治。不同国家和公司既想安全，也想获胜；若AI开始危险时恰逢第三次世界大战，最危险的可能是所有人只顾赢。他的判断是技术不确定性再乘政治不确定性，不能把其中任何一个环节当成已经确定的前提。

11. SHIB捐赠先是一次流动性与钱包操作问题

  • Vitalik先回忆自己的memecoin经历：2016年花2.5万美元买Dogecoin，后来变成了1,000多万美元。随后其他项目模仿狗狗币，SHIB把供应量的50%直接转进他的公开钱包；这笔财富并非他主动买入的常规资产配置。
  • 当他发现这些代币的市值达到80亿美元，首先担心的是泡沫可能一周后就破。他当时人在西雅图，资产却在冷钱包里：离线电脑在多伦多，另有两张分别保存、相加才能得到私钥的纸质备份。
  • 于是他买新电脑，打电话让母亲读出多伦多那张纸上的数字，重建私钥，又用两天审核Gnosis Safe代码，准备更安全的多签钱包。巨额慈善分配之前，先得解决如何安全取出、转移和保管资产的问题。
  • 他迅速换出部分ETH，捐出约7,000万美元，其中大部分给Against Malaria Foundation。理由是，这可能是自己能确定拿出的最多资金，应该交给较稳妥、争议较小的用途：“没有人觉得这是坏的。”其余代币受市场深度限制，无法一次卖完。

12. 超预期兑现，让捐赠变成长期治理问题

  • 对剩余代币，Vitalik原以为最多只能兑现2,000多万美元，便把大约一半给印度抗疫组织，另一半给Future of Life Institute。FLI当时研究生物、AI、核战等多种existential risk，并向他介绍，即使拿不到理论上可用的1亿美元，2,000万美元也能做很多事。
  • 结果与他的预期完全不同。对FLI最终所得，他明确说“不知道他们具体拿到了多少”，估计可能4亿或6亿美元；主持人开场则概括为约5亿美元。他承认，若事先想到这种兑现规模可能发生，自己的做法会“非常不一样”。
  • 后来他与印度CryptoRelief的Sandeep商议，让一半资金交回自己开展防疫工作：约2亿美元用于过滤器、开源疫苗、UVC、口罩及long COVID等研究，之后扩展到空气传播疾病；他介绍，Sandeep另用2.7亿美元提升印度医疗制造能力。

13. FLI从多风险研究转向AI政策，偏离了捐赠者的分散意图

  • 在Vitalik的回忆里，GPT-3出现前后也改变了FLI：从关注所有existential risk，转向只关心AI；从研究态度，转向政治行动，开始选择支持哪些法律和政客。他不认同其中一些事情，另一些即使未必反对，也不会由自己出钱去做。
  • 他强调，原始目标是支持多种生存风险防范，因此向FLI介绍过两三次自己资助空气传播疾病项目的进展，希望对方diversify。按他的叙述，对方拒绝了，仍要把资金集中在AI centric、policy centric的方向。
  • 这次转向还带来外部反馈。Vitalik认为，相关法律倡议使a16z等硅谷投资者不满，大约从2023年开始把AI安全视为主要对手。资金支持的行动因此不只产生直接政策效果，也会改变别人如何组织反击。

14. 被忽视程度变了，追加资金的价值也必须重算

  • Vitalik强调EA中的neglectedness：问题重要，还要问有没有足够多的人已经在做。干净饮水当然重要，但若已有很多人研究，自己的额外参与未必最有意义。同样，一个领域十年前缺资源，不能推出它今天仍然最缺资源。
  • 他认为，现在AI安全已经是高度受到关注的话题；全球公共卫生却在2025年遭遇很大伤害。他把这与Elon Musk参与的DOGE及美国政治变化联系起来：原有支持迅速停止，制造更多问题，因此全球健康在他眼里重新变得更重要。
  • 疟疾方面有抗疟疾疫苗的问题，但现在也有疫苗可以做；Vitalik认为全球公共卫生仍然非常值得支持。对其他一些领域，他的判断则是：“问题并不是资源太少，而是大家做的这个方法可能是不对的。”这种情况下，解决方案不能只是继续向原有机构加钱。

15. 安全研究的瓶颈正转向公司激励与临界决策

  • Vitalik没有因领域不再被忽视就停止关心AI安全。他认为更多问题都与AI有关，但OpenAI和Anthropic的激励“比较broken”：两家都想赢、都发展很快，留给研究安全和思考理想世界的时间因此变少。决定性问题可能是危险临近时，公司究竟把什么放在第一位。
  • 他提出一个条件性的研究判断：可能需要用AI version N研究AI version N+1，才能真正理解下一阶段的安全问题。因此三四年前的工作可能没有想象中有用，某些核心alignment问题也未见太多进展。更值得追问的是，实验室到关键时刻会不会投入足够注意力，而这又把问题推向政策和激励。

16. 政治把人对自然的优化题，变成人对人的对抗题

  • 早期EA比较慈善A救十人、慈善B救100人，主要挑战是把数字估准；支持一项政策，却连效果究竟为正还是为负都可能不知道。除了政策怎样直接改变企业激励，还必须考虑它怎样改变公众、竞争者和其他政治力量的行为。
  • Vitalik举例，一个富豪公开拿5亿美元影响政治，可能让别人把AI安全理解成富豪自己的议程，反过来抵制它。他借文学分类区分“man versus nature”和“man versus man”：后者更复杂，因为对手和你一样聪明，会根据你的行动调整。
  • FTX让这种间接后果变得具体：如果骗了很多人的钱，又拿去支持政治议题，议题也会被贴上骗子的标签。Vitalik还认为，大部分EA可能没有意识到SBF有问题，本身也暴露了理解人与机构的不足；运动越institutional、越political，旧有思维越容易失效。

17. EA的战略纪律与理性主义的自由，使安全阵营不断分裂

  • Vitalik认为，把硅谷概括为EA、理性主义和e/acc三派过于简单。他至少区分支持Anthropic的EA、离Anthropic更远的EA、更加populist的Pause AI，以及e/acc。Pause AI更愿意与主流人群合作，也更愿意直接批评理性主义和EA。
  • 理性主义的组织局限，他用一句话概括：“他们的心里他们就是猫。”放进机构就会觉得不自由。尤德考斯基写《Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality》，假设哈利是理性主义者，再重新探索魔法世界；好奇与玩耍本身就是动力。
  • 相比之下，他用“我们在救人的命，我们不能玩”概括EA的严肃感。EA会更努力选择有利于支持度和声誉的表达，理性主义者更不愿为战略需要封闭自己的兴趣。Vitalik认为，过度优化公众形象也可能适得其反，让别人怀疑真实想法被隐藏。
  • Afra补充的政治背景是，普通人的恐惧也来自一种精英控制技术、集中权力并替代劳动者的叙事。她提到Bernie等政治人物开始加入Pause AI；安全争论由此与公众对科技富豪的信任问题纠缠起来。

18. 好公司获胜的论证，绕不开它也在加速竞赛

  • Vitalik完整保留了支持Anthropic的逻辑：世界上有许多公司和国家，不做AI并不现实；既然竞赛会继续，就应该让更关心人类的公司赢，以便它在最需要时更愿意顾及安全。支持者还会比较OpenAI的内部风波，以及Anthropic实际开展的安全研究。
  • 他对Chris Olah的认可有私人经验：两人曾就读多伦多同一所小型私立学校，全校约45人，每班约11人；Olah向他介绍计算机科学与数学，也是他开始使用Linux、支持开源的重要影响者。因此，他并不否定创始人可能真诚而善良。
  • 反对意见从激励继续追问：好人进入更激烈、更危险的竞争，也可能为有利于自己的事情寻找理由。即使Anthropic更安全，它仍可能通过参与竞赛加快AI发展；由此增加的风险，可能超过其全部安全研究的正面作用。
  • Vitalik转述一种看法：OpenAI在2024、2025年把部分资源投向Sora等项目；今年初Mythos出现，或者给大家Fable之后，Anthropic让人感到“天命传到他们了”。随后OpenAI收缩旁支、更加专注强模型。在他的例子里，一家的技术领先会改变另一家的加速决策。

19. 定义安全，也是在争取控制最强AI的正当性

  • Vitalik另提出一种“普通人的批评”：如果安全哲学是“我们应该有权力，因为我们好，你们不应该有权力，因为你们不好”，别人为什么必须接受？“那如果我们不同意呢？谁在决定？”当不同群体各有判断，自认善良不足以回答权力应该归谁。
  • 他以开源争论为例：限制开源被解释为防止危险能力扩散，但按他的理解，目前最危险的攻击还是通过GPT和Claude实施。他还提出个人判断，公司的行动与提高自身权力的行动相关性可能高于90%；争夺的未必只是利润，也可能是谁控制未来。
  • 主持人把OpenAI从非营利组织到商业公司的变化带入讨论，Vitalik则用一句话概括其批评：“sacrifice openness for safety”，然后“sacrifice safety for acceleration”。在他的叙述里，公司曾以GPT-3危险为由放弃开放，后来又因妨碍发展，没有兑现部分安全承诺。

20. d/acc把防御能力分散给普通人

  • Vitalik把d/acc解释为defensive，以及decentralized或democratizing acceleration。技术进步仍然重要，但需要更主动投资防御：AI可能扩大黑客能力，就加强cyber security；可能降低制造危险病毒的门槛，就提前建设防疫能力，并赋能普通人。
  • 他的类比是欧洲山地与向东延伸的平原：山地更容易支持独立城市、地方自治，平坦地带则更容易被强大中心控制。这里的论点是，若缺少可分散部署的防御，保护人们往往只能依靠一个控制一切的中央组织。
  • 他观察到，一些AI组织把约80%的资源投入限制模型帮助人制造更强大的病毒。但这类centralized defense依赖其他国家和团队也采用限制，而且假设危险主要来自那些模型；若这些前提不成立，防御就更fragile。与科幻里的超级病毒相比，他听到的抗病毒研究者更担心短期可能出现的普通病毒。
  • 相比之下，更好的检测、过滤器、更快发现新病毒和开发疫苗，不要求先控制世界上所有AI。Vitalik承认，这需要计算机之外的公共卫生专业能力；但他认为，这条路径既可能更有效，也更少依赖权力集中。只有分散防御确实不可行时，集中防御才可能成为唯一办法。

21. 安全可能更像制度设计，判断仍要留给经验

  • Afra描述自己的不安：像进入一个孩子都在哭、却“没有大人”的幼儿园，研究者也未必知道究竟发生什么；与此同时，巨量资金继续建设data center。她担心的不是单一末日故事，而是能力持续涌现，却无法用清楚的语言或数学解释模型有多强、会做什么。
  • Vitalik把未知数列得很具体：一年、五年、二十五年后人能做什么，Google或中国公司会不会追上，AI更像工具、个人还是别的东西，都没有定论。他因此不愿把自己的预测说成99%，也不愿轻率压到1%或0%。
  • 可观察性本身也可能变化。他喜欢开源模型的一个原因，是能看到思考步骤并从中学习；若未来转向neuralese，用只有模型自己理解的大量数字推理，人理解其过程的能力可能下降，但下降多少仍不知道。四年前，人们还不知道AI发展的下一个阶段会不会通过chain-of-thought实现。
  • 安全AI因此可能更像political design：通过checks and balances，把聪明却不完美的组成部分组织起来，让不同目标设定方法相互限制，必要时再问用户。这只是可能的方向，需要与真实AI合作、观察成功和错误来检验。面对持续出现的意外，他认为保持开放的心态最重要。

来源：YouTube
