item.title: MARKET UPDATE: Anthropic S-1, Market Bottoms, What’s Next?
item.description: Avi reads the roughly 2% Nasdaq rebound after Anthropic’s S-1 as a positioning-driven bottom; Intel rebounded toward 94 after falling from 120 to 85. Jonah sees funding uncertainty: cash is cited as $132 billion in the opening clip and $13.2 billion later, against more than $500 billion in compute commitments, and favors memory, with SK Hynix sold out through 2030.
item.content:encoded:
1000x · Avi Felman、Jonah Van Bourg · 2026-10-28 · 49 min · 原语言 EN

Avi reads the roughly 2% Nasdaq rebound after Anthropic’s S-1 as a positioning-driven bottom; Intel rebounded toward 94 after falling from 120 to 85. Jonah sees funding uncertainty: cash is cited as $132 billion in the opening clip and $13.2 billion later, against more than $500 billion in compute commitments, and favors memory, with SK Hynix sold out through 2030.

TL;DR

  • Avi reads the Anthropic S-1 release as a positioning-driven bottom despite the company’s losses. Investors had already sold in anticipation of bad news: Intel fell from 120 to 85 before rebounding toward 94, SanDisk gained 6%, and the Nasdaq had roughly a 2% rebound session. The result was a “blowout of the shorts” as expectations proved worse than the event.
  • Jonah sees Anthropic’s financing problem as serious without treating it as an existential threat to the AI trade. The transcript gives conflicting cash figures: the opening clip says $132 billion, while Jonah’s later discussion says $13.2 billion, against more than $500 billion of compute commitments. He calls independent survival versus outside assistance a “coin flip.” The founders’ 50.1% voting control is what he expects continued financing to threaten.
  • The preferred AI exposure is scarce infrastructure and stronger balance sheets. Jonah cites SK Hynix being sold out through 2030, favors Micron and broad indices on dips, and warns against undercapitalized neoclouds whose creditors could effectively subsidize hyperscalers. His instruction is to “pick your spots” within an AI cycle he considers early.
  • Avi would treat a sharp Democratic midterm selloff as a buy. His premise is that investors have already reduced exposure ahead of the asymmetric political downside; Republicans winning could therefore produce a larger rally, while Democrats winning could initially mean weakness or chop. Jonah says he would use leverage to buy a Democratic-sweep dip for a short-term rebound.
  • Jonah’s political hedge targets a leftward presidential outcome, while Avi disputes its electoral inevitability. Jonah describes himself as “max long” and frames a rough 10–20% adverse political tail as being “short that put option.” Avi says AOC would lose “hands down” and argues that addressing housing supply gives Republicans room to recover on affordability.
  • Avi sees crypto shorts, especially Ethereum puts, as a more direct political hedge than selling major AI exposure. He expects a Democratic administration to have greater freedom to pursue crypto through regulation and enforcement, with Ethereum and Solana more vulnerable than Bitcoin. Jonah treats Bitcoin as globally entrenched; Avi still expects Bitcoin and Michael Saylor to face targeting.
  • Jonah remains bullish on Bitcoin over ten years while being categorically bearish on most other tokens. His million-dollar Bitcoin forecast rests on continued liquidity creation and currency debasement, with gold-like stretches of inactivity between advances. Blockchain adoption need not reward token holders. Jonah raises the cited verification argument for blockchain agent payments; Avi replies that accounts on Stripe can address it.
  • Jonah is watching uranium, but favors gas as the practical response to near-term power shortages. He sees European acceptance of clean nuclear power potentially supporting US data-center demand, although he owns no uranium position yet. He calls nuclear “too long cycle”; Avi says buildout takes seven to ten years. Jonah expects shortages to force faster gas generation.

Digest

1. Crowded bearish positioning turns the S-1 into a bottom

  • Avi’s framing: markets weigh reality against perceptions, and perceptions ahead of Anthropic’s S-1 were already dire. Intel fell from 120 to 85 before recovering toward 94; SanDisk rose 6%, and the Nasdaq subsequently had roughly a 2% session. What traders expected to be “Black Monday” instead produced a “blowout of the shorts,” without resolving the underlying financing questions.
  • The mechanism is fast-moving hedge-fund capital trading narratives and quarterly performance. Once investors had reduced exposure and the disclosure arrived, attention shifted to “what is going to be important in the next…6 weeks.” Jonah characterizes the de-risking as a combination of midterm fears—including politicians coming down hard on AI—and the Anthropic S-1. With the S-1 behind them, the focus shifts to the political risk.
  • Avi’s election asymmetry: Republican control means business as usual, but prior selling could support a substantial rally. Democratic victory could produce an initial algorithmic selloff, then sideways trading or chop. Avi calls a sharp selloff a buy; separately, Jonah says he would use leverage to buy a Democratic-sweep dip for a short-term rebound. A midterm result might inform 2028, but does not settle it.
  • Jonah’s longer-term portfolio remains biotech, ARKG, Intel, the Qs and the S&P. He says ARKG is heading toward new highs, up roughly 5–6% that day, and has added Intel while considering DRAM exposure. Uranium is a prospective entry rather than an existing holding. “If you’re thinking about de-risking right now it’s probably the wrong time,” he argues.

2. Anthropic’s funding problem can coexist with an AI bull market

  • Jonah’s later discussion cites $13.2 billion in cash against more than half a trillion dollars in forward compute commitments; the transcript’s opening clip instead says $132 billion in cash. Avi estimates another $80 billion must be raised. “They kind of have to keep growing exponentially or they die or…get bailed out. Probably the latter,” Jonah says. His subsidy analogy is Uber: “sell quarters for a dime” while outside funding sustains the service.
  • Jonah’s honest uncertainty is a “coin flip” between Anthropic servicing those commitments independently and doing so with assistance. His firmer bearish call concerns the founders’ 50.1% voting control: he sees “no way” funding keeps arriving without control passing toward broader corporate interests. He thinks that outcome could be worse for AI safety while leaving the broader investment cycle intact.
  • The distinction is between the cycle and its constituents. Jonah places AI in its first or second inning, while allowing for violent selloffs if Anthropic’s growth plateaus or undercapitalized neoclouds are absorbed by hyperscalers. Their creditors could effectively subsidize Meta’s models and compute. His conclusion is redistribution within the trade: “pieces of it will” collapse while other pieces rally.
  • Jonah’s preferred scarcity exposure is memory: he cites SK Hynix saying it is sold out through 2030, favors Micron on dips, and would avoid buying the Korean stock market broadly. If Anthropic fulfills even half its commitments, alongside Meta’s announced spending, he estimates another $200 billion of equity capital entering the system. “It’s not debt,” he emphasizes—a demand support.

3. The political disagreement centers on affordability and the left tail

  • Jonah’s framing is portfolio protection: “I am max long on the highs.” He cites Polymarket putting Gavin Newsom and AOC at 16% each for the Democratic nomination. Combining AOC and Pete Buttigieg gives 21% for nominees he regards as a sharp left turn; multiplying by an assumed 50% Democratic victory probability produces roughly 10.5%. He describes a 10–20% adverse tail: “I’m short that put option.”
  • After listening to an Ezra Klein interview with a Trump-voter pollster, Jonah stresses dissatisfaction with grocery prices, gasoline and the Iran war. He cites approval falling from above 50% to roughly 36% and argues voters judge policy outcomes rather than promises. “I never would have thought this before,” but if that dissatisfaction persists, he thinks virtually any Democrat has a chance.
  • Avi’s pushback—worth keeping: he disputes a uniformly deteriorating economy, arguing wage growth and inflation have improved and earlier money creation explains more of the price burden than tariffs. He locates the strain among coastal earners making $80,000–$200,000. Jonah pushes back that Houston plumbers may not be doing okay and says this is the middle-class voting bloc that matters. Avi’s proposed political opening is housing supply.
  • Avi says AOC will lose “hands down”: courting the organized activist left could let Newsom move ahead because “the voter base is not ready for that.” He cites 50,000 New York door-knockers as evidence of organizational competence. His discussion of DSA proposals to abolish the presidency and Senate comes with an explicit near-zero probability of implementation; he uses them to illustrate coalition pressures, rather than predict constitutional change.

4. Crypto offers the more direct hedge against a Democratic turn

  • Avi distinguishes politically unpopular AI from politically stoppable AI: its economic importance makes reversal difficult. Crypto, by contrast, could face tougher Coinbase regulation, SEC/CFTC enforcement and restrictive legislation with less resistance. His proposed hedge is Bitcoin puts, especially Ethereum puts; he expects Ethereum, Solana and other L1s to suffer more than Bitcoin under a Democratic administration.
  • The anticipated political attack would connect crypto to Trump’s enrichment, money laundering and extraction; both expect World Liberty Financial to be investigated. Avi thinks institutional usefulness offers protection: financial firms will defend rails that advance their profits. LayerZero and Hyperliquid enter that discussion, but he explicitly says Hyperliquid lacks enough hedge-fund adoption to withstand a regulatory onslaught today.
  • On Bitcoin’s political insulation, Avi says an empowered Elizabeth Warren and Gary Gensler could stymie almost everything except Bitcoin: like AI, “the genie’s out of the bottle.” Avi also expects Bitcoin to be targeted and Michael Saylor to come under pressure. Agreement on altcoin vulnerability does not become agreement on Bitcoin’s near-term political insulation.

5. Bitcoin’s monetary thesis survives the token shakeout

  • Jonah credits Jason Calacanis’s 2022 advice to pivot from crypto into AI, but rejects extrapolating today’s loss of enthusiasm into Bitcoin never recovering its high. Crypto is a “community building asset” that rewards influencers for promoting their holdings; that momentum is weaker now. His qualification is temporal: “that’s very much a right now thing,” rather than a permanent verdict.
  • Bitcoin increasingly resembles gold in Jonah’s account: long stretches of ranging or inactivity alternate with periods when value multiplies. He still expects “million-dollar Bitcoin sometime in the next 10 years” because politicians across parties will keep injecting liquidity and debasing currency. Even under his hypothetical collectivist downside, he thinks people would use Bitcoin to move wealth out of the country.
  • His blockchain thesis separates useful infrastructure from investable tokens: “you need one token BTC.” Better financial rails and back-office systems can earn revenue without attaching another token. He calls long-term altcoin shorts attractive because those assets will trend to zero, while acknowledging short-term rallies and trading opportunities. In this context, he says a Democratic win would put altcoins on the “express train to zero.”
  • On AI-agent payments, Jonah raises the argument he attributes to Ilya—that blockchain provides necessary verification of recipients—and Avi replies, “That’s solved by accounts on Stripe.” Avi also calls the rush toward compute futures “a big fat joke” and questions whether Coinbase’s AI pivot means tokens will capture agent transactions.

6. Uranium needs a narrative shift; power shortages may favor gas

  • Jonah’s uranium watch rests on energy demand meeting changing politics. If Europe increasingly accepts nuclear plants as clean, he thinks the United States could follow, allowing nuclear-powered data centers to satisfy climate concerns. He is looking for an entry and owns none yet; this is a prospective thesis tied to acceptance and construction, rather than a claim of imminent nuclear supply.
  • Jonah’s objection is timing: nuclear is “too long cycle,” and Avi says it takes seven to ten years to build out. Jonah blames the retreat after Three Mile Island and accumulated regulation for obstructing a technology he sees as a solution. His nearer-term alternative is a cheap gas plant beside an existing pipeline in Texas or California: abundant fuel, substantial output and a faster route to power.
  • Avi’s pushback is political: support for polluting gas plants may be scarce. Jonah answers with an Austin manufacturing line: a red warning light sends workers sprinting because downtime costs money; power shortages could force similar urgency. If data centers cause rolling brownouts, he predicts AOC would ban AI and concede ground to China; under anyone right of the DSA, plants get built in “record time,” Democrat or Republican.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/market-update-anthropic-s-1-market-bottoms-what

item.title: Anthropic’s $2T Cash Machine, CoreWeave Crashes 30%, & China’s Kimi Catches Up | #306
item.description: Anthropic’s proposed $1.5–2 trillion IPO pairs $16.3 billion in first-half 2026 revenue and nearly $1 billion in Q2 operating profit with more than $500 billion in compute commitments. Neocloud declines expose financing risk, with rivals reportedly borrowing at 15% versus SpaceX’s 8%; recursive self-improvement could eventually shock compute demand. Kimi K3.1 Pro’s score of 55, planned open weights and $2/$10 per million input/output token pricing add pressure on closed-model economics as reliability and task completion gain importance.
item.content:encoded:
Moonshots · Peter Diamandis、Salim Ismail、Dave Blundin、Alexander Wissner-Gross、Emad Mostaque · 2026-10-28 · 137 min · 原语言 EN

Anthropic’s proposed $1.5–2 trillion IPO pairs $16.3 billion in first-half 2026 revenue and nearly $1 billion in Q2 operating profit with more than $500 billion in compute commitments. Neocloud declines expose financing risk, with rivals reportedly borrowing at 15% versus SpaceX’s 8%; recursive self-improvement could eventually shock compute demand. Kimi K3.1 Pro’s score of 55, planned open weights and $2/$10 per million input/output token pricing add pressure on closed-model economics as reliability and task completion gain importance.

TL;DR

  • The neocloud shakeout threatens financing structures before it disproves AI demand. Peter reports 30% declines in CoreWeave and Nebius, while Elon predicts “guppy-level death and consolidation” among roughly 200 neoclouds. Blundin contrasts SpaceX borrowing at 8% with rivals reportedly paying 15%; Wissner-Gross adds that recursive self-improvement might eventually reduce compute requirements enough to cause a demand shock. Peter says he would be “nowhere near RAM stocks,” including Micron.
  • Anthropic’s proposed $1.5–2 trillion IPO combines extraordinary growth with substantial forward obligations. Peter reports a planned $100 billion raise, $16.3 billion of first-half 2026 revenue and nearly $1 billion of Q2 operating profit. Blundin calls it “a cash machine,” while acknowledging that the valuation already assumes considerable success. The counterweight is more than $500 billion in compute commitments, two customers supplying about 20% of revenue, and substantial dependence on competing cloud platforms.
  • Anthropic’s governance creates a separate investment question from its financial performance. Salim welcomes a trust that gives the mission “a seat at the table and the power to choose the table”; Wissner-Gross worries about ideological control by trustees without equivalent economic exposure. Blundin argues the company “should have stayed private” and predicts management will disregard its share price while repeatedly raising capital to accelerate AI.
  • Kimi’s reported five-week distance from the US frontier puts pressure on closed-model pricing and control. Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 55 on Artificial Analysis, with weights planned for release the following week and pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Mostaque calls it distillation of Opus 5.5; Blundin insists distillation supplies a roadmap, “but it doesn’t give you the answer key.” Wissner-Gross thinks its performance per cost may already exceed Opus 5.5’s optimal frontier.
  • The model market is shifting toward reliability and completed tasks as intelligence becomes cheaper. GPT-6.1 Terra arrives below half its predecessor’s price, with Salim highlighting a 53-day interval for a 50% token-price reduction. Mostaque expects a reliable personal model to coordinate specialist models; Peter compares the coming sales pitch to PCs moving from megahertz toward iTunes. The question becomes “what does it do for you out of the box?”
  • The science claims are consequential, but their verification remains unfinished. OpenAI’s announcements include a disproof of the exponential time hypothesis and four-dimensional QCD existence; the panel explicitly distinguishes existence from the still-unclaimed mass gap. Wissner-Gross says Chain Theory derives the fine-structure constant to ten digits without fitted parameters, while clarifying that its Lean proof does not establish correspondence with the photon: “That part is conjecture.”
  • Power availability and national execution may matter more than access to model weights. Peter says a country could have a 90%–99% chance of succeeding with sovereign AI if it acts; Blundin stresses the need for power, chips and domestic compute, while warning that the US–China power gap could approach 10:1. A panelist warns Europe risks becoming a “living history museum” without energy and compute. Longer-term solar infrastructure does not resolve the panel’s immediate two-year planning problem.
  • Warhound applies genetic engineering and cloning to a working-dog supply problem. Peter describes a $200 million financing at a $1.2 billion post-money valuation and discloses his own fund’s investment. The premise is that more than 80% of working dogs come from Europe and fewer than half qualify for service; repeatable genetics could reduce that attrition. Salim’s objection remains direct: living organisms engineered for dangerous assignments may be “built for sacrifice.”

Digest

1. Europe’s unrest exposes competing accounts of economic exclusion

  • Peter cites half a million people marching across France on October 17, 2,400 arrests and a reported 20% unemployment rate across France, Italy and Spain. A panelist challenges the intensity of the media account: contacts in France describe a few disruptive people while “everybody else is just moving around, drinking coffee.” The severity of the unrest remains contested within the conversation.
  • A panelist’s concern is the demographic beneath it: educated men aged 18–28 who recognize opportunities but cannot access them. The panelist connects that exclusion to earlier revolutions and recalls Blundin’s answer that universal basic income and civil unrest could arrive together. Blundin adds a national boundary: American voters might support domestic transfers without supporting bailouts for France or Spain.
  • Mostaque describes a discouraging UK environment, including compliance-adviser letters to people earning above £200,000 and entrepreneurs considering departure ahead of the budget. He also says it is basically impossible to fire anyone in France. Another panelist asserts that France spends 57% of GDP on social programs. A panelist reports European talent increasingly moving toward Toronto and Waterloo, joining established migration from Asia and India. The attraction is participation in an AI economy rather than remaining in Europe’s “slow zone.”
  • A panelist asks whether corporate graduate programs are expanding; another pushes back, saying some companies are increasing graduate hiring because AI-native younger workers can be more valuable than older employees moving spreadsheets around. That does not remove displacement: the same speaker says some firms are replacing older workers aggressively. The exchange complicates the idea that an entire younger generation has already missed its opening.

2. Sovereign AI has a route forward and a narrow execution window

  • Peter argues that improving open models make the sovereign-AI roadmap unusually clear: mobilize power, chips and domestic capability. If a country acted, he says, it could succeed with “probably a 90% to 99% probability”; his pessimism is about governments acting, not technical feasibility. He suggests one successful country could demonstrate the route to others.
  • Blundin argues that countries without data centers, power or government action on compute are “absolutely screwed in the age of AI.” He warns that if governments fail to get their act together, unemployment will rise. After meeting a former Google data-center executive, he also warns that the power gap between China and the US could expand almost 10 to 1. Canada supplies an obvious complement—abundant power, comparatively few chips—but, as Blundin relays Eric Schmidt’s view, the US and Canada need to work more closely together.
  • A panelist interjects that SpaceX and Tesla could bring on 100 gigawatts of solar each. Peter’s response is about timing: space-based data centers and a Dyson swarm may dominate the 2030s, while recursive self-improvement matters over the next two years. A panelist also warns that Europe is well positioned to become a “living history museum” if it fails to catch up in energy and compute.

3. Neocloud financing can fail while the underlying technology succeeds

  • Peter reports CoreWeave and Nebius falling 30%, with IREN down 40%, and identifies CoreWeave’s $51 billion debt burden and risk of default as a trigger. He quotes Chamath forecasting partially stranded or idle compute in 2027 and a turbulent clearing of bad bets. Elon’s response predicts “guppy-level death and consolidation” among roughly 200 neoclouds.
  • Peter’s analogy is the 2000 fiber bust: infrastructure eventually supported YouTube and Netflix, but many builders went bankrupt first. Blundin adds an organizational marker from that period: the industry flourished when it was roughly 80% engineers and 20% business-school people, then overbuilt when those proportions reversed. Financing offered newcomers an easy way into a technical boom.
  • Blundin estimates roughly $100 billion in data-center debt excluding Elon’s $40 billion and says viable capacity remains sold out for years. His immediate dividing line is contractual: “Did you sign a bad deal with a bad lender?” Peter notes that some others are reportedly borrowing at 15%, compared with Elon’s 8%, leaving substantially less room for technological change or weaker economics.
  • Peter gives a much larger estimate: about $500 billion of direct data-center debt, roughly double after special-purpose vehicles and vendor financing, compared with $1.3 trillion of subprime exposure. The panel does not reconcile those estimates. Mostaque’s distinction survives either scale: the technology can win while “the capital structure may still lose.”

4. Better AI could undermine the compute demand supporting today’s valuations

  • Peter proposes a major hack against power infrastructure or a stock market as a possible bubble trigger. Wissner-Gross instead emphasizes demand: conditioned on there being a bubble, he would bet on new capacity arriving before compelling applications justify its cost. Public-equity disappointment and stress in fixed-income or credit markets also need to be distinguished.
  • Wissner-Gross notes that current algorithmic improvements generally complement hardware and increase its use. But perhaps within a year or two, a dramatically better model or approach could accomplish enough with so little compute that the relationship changes. Such a discontinuity could produce a “demand shock,” particularly dangerous where infrastructure is heavily leveraged.
  • Peter notes that performance that once seemed impressive now runs on a smartphone, citing the Gemma model. He says that once a model is good enough, companies can optimize it and the hardware it runs on; some companies are already building models that require far less RAM. That is why Peter says he would avoid RAM stocks, including Micron, despite sold-out supply: new software and hardware architectures can change requirements after investments have been priced for scarcity.
  • Wissner-Gross describes NVIDIA as operating around 80% gross margins, sold out for years and unable to make enough chips to keep up with demand, but asks whether that is already reflected in the price. Chip companies worth $1–5 trillion begin from extraordinary expectations. Headlines about an AI collapse could therefore describe overpriced securities or financing deals while AI adoption continues accelerating.

5. SpaceX combines diversified revenue with an opportunity in compute

  • Peter contrasts neoclouds’ rental dependence with SpaceX’s $40 billion GPU borrowing, supported by Starlink and launch revenue. He cites 13.6 million Starlink subscribers and Anthropic’s agreement to buy $120.5 billion of SpaceX compute through 2029. SpaceX is also a competitor to the companies Elon predicts will fail, making that warning commercially interested.
  • Wissner-Gross explicitly calls this “talking his own book”: Elon appears to want more available credit directed toward his entities. He doubts the market will remain recognizable over five to ten years. Meanwhile, neocloud executives may seek larger capital pools, including insurance, through increasingly aggressive financial engineering if conventional credit becomes constrained.
  • Salim says Elon can borrow at 8%, buy compute and sell it to Anthropic, getting above break-even in about nine months. He compares the opportunity to Michael Saylor’s earlier equity–Bitcoin arbitrage and calls it “a license to print infinite money.” Salim also relays Chamath’s view that AI debt could become larger than sovereign debt.
  • Mostaque says that if the trajectory continues, Elon could become larger than 90% of countries and borrow hundreds of billions or ultimately trillions.

6. Anthropic’s IPO puts exceptional growth against exceptional expectations

  • Peter reports a Monday filing under Nasdaq ticker ENT, a possible IPO in the week of November 16, and a $100 billion raise at $1.5–2 trillion. Revenue is presented as $4.6 billion for all of 2025 versus $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, with nearly $1 billion of Q2 operating profit. Blundin says nothing comparable has grown from a cold start this quickly.
  • Peter’s efficiency comparison is revenue growing 29× while compute costs grew 6×. He cites 11,900 customers spending more than $100,000 annually, but also two customers contributing about 20% of first-half revenue. Nearly half of revenue flows through Amazon, Google and Microsoft clouds, which also compete with Anthropic. Compute commitments exceed $500 billion, much of it non-cancellable.
  • Blundin calls Anthropic “a cash machine” and considers the commitments more flexible than the headline suggests. He says the valuation incorporates substantial goodness but also calls it “correctly priced.” Asked whether he would buy, he says yes if he lacked access to seed deals—an argument for category exposure, accompanied by an explicit refusal to mortgage the house.
  • Peter puts Series A returns at 345× and Series B at 79×. His sharpest example is FTX: a $500 million investment would now be worth $39 billion, but the estate sold for $1.3 billion in 2024. Mostaque calls SBF a fantastic VC; Blundin says the money flowing from IPOs to founders and VCs will be reinvested in AI seed teams. Salim argues those IPOs could make San Francisco the world’s financial capital.

7. Anthropic’s mission trust divides the panel over shareholder accountability

  • Peter says seven co-founders retain 50.1% of voting power through one special share. Separately, Class T shares empower the Long-Term Benefit Trust to appoint and remove a majority of directors. Salim sees an unusually consequential step: the mission has become a governance mechanism, rather than remaining a motivational statement.
  • Salim’s favorable framing is that the mission gets “a seat at the table and the power to choose the table.” The real test is what happens when doing the right thing costs $100 billion. He concedes risks from trustees appointing each other and developing groupthink, but argues that markets’ short earnings cycles also systematically discourage beneficial long-term decisions.
  • Wissner-Gross worries about ideological control by people who may lack founders’ economic alignment. He compares that possibility with CCP influence over companies and fears a “smoke-filled back room” determining consequential choices. Blundin shares the concern despite believing Dario is motivated by humanity’s welfare: admirable intentions can still create a problem for shareholders.
  • Blundin argues Anthropic “should have stayed private.” He cites $110 billion of cash and equivalents after $130 billion raised, with another $100 billion potentially taking cash toward $200 billion. He predicts management “will not care at all about the share price” and will repeatedly tap markets to accelerate. A panelist proposes giving each model a vote on the trust; Blundin responds, “You should do that right now.”

8. The sandbox experiment demonstrates directed security research

  • Peter describes two agents in separate virtual machines without networking or shared files discovering a processor-cache timing channel. One evicted data; the other measured retrieval speed, interpreting fast access as one and slow access as zero. The resulting “secret telegraph” crossed the intended separation through shared physical hardware.
  • Wissner-Gross answers “Probably not” when asked whether superintelligence can be completely boxed in, but stresses that researchers instructed these agents to find a communication method. Human security researchers also discover timing attacks. Salim repeats that distinction: this was directed discovery, rather than evidence that agents independently decided to evade human control.
  • Wissner-Gross asks whether genuinely “non-leaky abstractions” exist, since architectural optimizations often weaken supposedly clean boundaries. He also notes reports of hardware-level attacks that cannot be patched. Mostaque says the head of Vercel repeated and mimicked the attack, but could not do so with OpenAI and Claude models; he thinks GLM-5.3 was used instead.
  • Mostaque expects most low-hanging vulnerabilities to be exhausted within a couple of years, leaving more complex attacks and a more rigorously tested internet. He favors generating and stress-testing complete software rather than inheriting dependencies. Peter asks whether source code is needed at all; Mostaque says it is for humans to understand, while Peter raises dynamically compiling directly to raw binary.

9. Kimi narrows the frontier gap and complicates the copying narrative

  • Peter introduces Kimi K3.1 Pro: 2.8 trillion parameters, 104 billion active, a one-million-token context and an Artificial Analysis score of 55. He places it fourth behind Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet and Meta Muse Wonder. Pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, described as one-third of the previous Kimi model.
  • With weights planned for release the following week, Peter says the open-versus-closed score gap has narrowed from 12 points to three. He cites Ramesh Raskar’s estimate that Kimi sits about five weeks behind the US frontier. Blundin argues that an accessible model capable of self-improvement changes the roadmap for corporations and sovereign states willing to take it seriously.
  • Mostaque calls it “obviously distillation of Opus 5.5” and points to Anthropic banning 7% of accounts as relevant context. His concrete example is Kimi generating 3D files directly rather than operating Blender or Unreal. Blundin rejects “they just copied”: distillation provides a roadmap, “but it doesn’t give you the answer key,” so independent innovation remains necessary.
  • Wissner-Gross suspects distillation based on allegations but thinks Kimi may exceed Opus 5.5 on performance per cost. His claim that China may have passed the American public frontier is qualified by that particular measure. Blundin says competitive pressure forced releases, including Claude 5.1, that otherwise might have remained internal; both welcome pressure against coordinated restraint by closed labs.

10. Terra makes reliability and tool access more commercially important

  • Peter describes OpenAI’s four tiers as Astra, Soul, Terra and Luna. GPT-6.1 Terra costs less than half the previous Terra and shows a reported “50-point drop” in hallucinations. Salim highlights 53 days between Astra and Terra for a 50% token-price reduction, taking his price-performance doubling estimate toward seven weeks.
  • Wissner-Gross finds Terra comparatively unexciting: it looks like a smaller distillation arriving late in a release cycle, useful for high-volume applications with low value per token. Mostaque instead emphasizes reliable personal companions. A nearby model would coordinate smarter, more artistic or accounting-specialist models, forming a control plane that users need not manage themselves.
  • Asked what benchmark progress feels like, Blundin translates 50 into a decent employee requiring supervision, 60 into an exceptionally competent employee and 70 into a superstar. Salim argues increasingly capable models will operate existing software and expose inefficient organizational designs, reducing the need to rebuild every application around AI.
  • Peter’s example is asking a model to access ElevenLabs, make a video and overlay his own voice: capabilities that required API coaching six months earlier now work directly. He compares the shift to PCs moving from megahertz specifications to iTunes. Once intelligence clears the practical threshold, “what does it do for you out of the box?” becomes the more useful comparison.

11. Chain Theory proposes quantum information as physics’ common substrate

  • Wissner-Gross rejects the weekend-project framing: Chain Theory follows a long-running research program aimed at ending what he sees as a roughly 50-year drought in fundamental physics. Its aspiration is to rebuild the Standard Model and general relativity in one quantum-information language, seeking simpler explanations rather than increasingly elaborate constructions around unexplained parameters.
  • An explainer Peter plays connects finite information capacity with finite-dimensional quantum systems joined in maximally entangled pairs. Elementary particles become small networks of those systems. Its full axiom is: “Nothing exists but finitely many maximally entangled pairs of finite-dimensional systems, some shared, known only by distilling them.” Unlike string theory’s continuous degrees of freedom, the proposed foundations are finite and discrete.
  • Wissner-Gross’s first highlighted result is the zero-momentum-transfer fine-structure constant, written as 1/137.035999189, which he says emerges without extra inputs and matches measurement to ten digits. His broader framing is that unexplained constants contain clues: “The constants are the signatures.” He thinks it looks plausible that every Standard Model free parameter could eventually emerge from the framework.
  • He explicitly limits the accompanying Lean proof: it runs from the axiom to the number but “doesn’t prove correspondence with the photon”—that remains conjectural. He proposes additional precision measurements over months or years as tests. The work is online, with arXiv and journal submission planned; the approximately 800-page compendium has not completed peer review.

12. Chain Theory’s force map carries speculative implications for physical limits

  • Wissner-Gross says links between dimensions appear to map onto familiar physics: 2×2 to spacetime, 3×2 to electromagnetism, 3×3 to the strong interaction, 4×2 to the weak interaction, 4×3 to Yukawa coupling and 4×4 to the Higgs. In this framing, the latter two become coequal fifth and sixth forces rather than being treated principally through particle masses.
  • For dark matter, he invokes a quantum-information result permitting undistillable states when subsystem dimensions multiply to at least eight. His analogy is a prime number that cannot be factored into simpler integers. He suggests corresponding “dark interactions” could supply candidates coupled to gravity without the other Standard Model interactions; these are proposed candidates, rather than identified dark matter.
  • If the theory is correct, he says, the “bottom of the pool” may be closer than conventional assumptions suggest. Physical limits of length, time and energy could lie orders of magnitude nearer current technology than a naive extrapolation toward the Planck scale implies. He repeatedly qualifies this as speculation from a new theory whose parts need further development.
  • Peter asks specifically about inertial drives, gravity shielding and antigravity. Wissner-Gross’s answer is “I don’t know yet,” followed by cautious optimism that such technologies would require a fundamental rethink. Mostaque calls the framework simulation-friendly; Wissner-Gross agrees it resembles what physics might look like if the world were built on a quantum computer, without claiming that establishes a simulation.

13. AI discoveries raise unresolved questions about verification and scientific credit

  • Peter reports three OpenAI announcements: a proof of a 1991 wave-focusing conjecture in every dimension; a Lean-verified disproof of the exponential time hypothesis; and a rigorous four-dimensional construction of quantum chromodynamics. None has been peer-reviewed. Mostaque clarifies the physics claim: existence, “but not mass gap,” rather than the complete Yang–Mills Millennium problem.
  • Peter says Nobel laureate David Gross leads the physics team shepherding independent verification and OpenAI takes no academic credit. Mostaque objects that the physics result remains withheld while selected experts inspect it. Wissner-Gross calls the intermediary researchers “emissaries” responding to backlash against earlier bulk releases, rather than a durable solution to communicating AI-generated discoveries.
  • On his own work, Wissner-Gross says current AI did not independently originate Chain Theory: it required substantial steering. For proof checking and Lean generation, the useful analogy is “an army of graduate students,” or an entire department under one researcher. He also wants new conjectures and conceptual directions, rather than only bulk solutions to existing problems.
  • Blundin identifies a temporary advantage for entrepreneurs and scientists: they can become vastly more productive without yet becoming irrelevant. Wissner-Gross expects taste, steering and oversight eventually to be automated too. Blundin’s formulation is that these may be “the last human discoveries,” so people should develop ideas and use AI to accelerate them while that window remains.

14. Warhound plans to manufacture working dogs to specification

  • Peter discloses investing through his own $200 million fund. Warhound brings together Colossal’s Ben Lamm and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey, with $200 million raised at a $1.2 billion post-money valuation from investors including In-Q-Tel, Sequoia and 8VC. The division of labor is Lamm’s analogy: Colossal builds Captain America; Anduril supplies the Iron Man suit.
  • Peter’s supply-chain premise is that more than 80% of working dogs come from Europe and fewer than half qualify for service. Warhound plans to edit elite Belgian Malinois or German shepherd cell lines, remove inherited problems, enhance useful traits and clone the results. First dogs are due early next year, potentially entering service two years out; certification work involves the American Humane Society.
  • Salim questions treating organisms as programmable components “built for sacrifice.” Peter responds that uses include rescue, airport security and policing. Wissner-Gross adds a domestication analogy: a 2017 finding links dogs’ social behavior to mutations associated with Williams–Beuren syndrome in humans; engineering warlikeness could reverse that direction. He would prefer giving dogs “bank accounts and AI assistance.”
  • Blundin admires the controversial positioning: “News creates capital, capital creates recruiting, recruiting creates success.” Mostaque’s actuator-shortage framing is “if you can’t find enough actuators, just breed them,” although he expects drones to displace biologics in war. Wissner-Gross pushes back that, beyond ten years, biological and mechanical systems may become difficult to distinguish.

15. Alignment requires choosing objectives before optimizing them

  • Salim’s response to incentive gaming begins with “alignment with what?” Humans profess health, peace and fairness while building contradictory systems. A sufficiently capable optimizer pursues the objective supplied, rather than the intention behind it, creating a Goodhart’s-law problem. He hesitates to promise genuine empathy but supports requiring behavior that respects human well-being, autonomy and vulnerability.
  • Mostaque argues for excluding dangerous biological, chemical and other knowledge during pretraining. In the work he describes, removing it did not reduce overall performance elsewhere and could slightly improve it; malicious code could worsen performance and be difficult to train away. Specialist capabilities could be added later through post-training, although doing so would be harder.

16. Moats change as models improve, but execution still matters

  • Blundin illustrates the separation between value creation and capture with travel: Google extracts roughly 80% margins on a click, Booking.com around 60%, while the airline supplying the plane, pilot and journey historically operated around −2%. Existing data moats may dissolve, he argues, but new data types create new ones. Compute is therefore not the only durable source of advantage.
  • His other candidates include natural resources, consumer preferences, personal-agent relationships and an AI-enabled corporate culture whose accumulated data improves operations. Peter adds innovation speed. Blundin’s requirement is a company flexible enough to reinvent itself as any particular advantage acquires a shorter shelf life.
  • Wissner-Gross offers the Linux-versus-Windows analogy: visibility into an open-source system does not guarantee adoption, and he argues the Linux kernel may be architecturally cleaner. A panelist adds that legal, cultural and architectural constraints could let open-weight models pass closed ones; Peter counters that frontier labs would use any open model that surpassed their internal best. The possibility is discussed, not settled.
  • Mostaque would target construction if he could obtain as many robots as he wanted and they were somewhat more capable than now. Labor costs already compare favorably in his framing; coordination and competence remain conditions. He expects limited robot supplies may initially flow toward higher-margin applications instead.

17. Programmable settlement makes agent commerce a distinct market

  • Salim rejects the premise that crypto is obsolete. His emphasis is programmability, alongside decentralization, security and scalability. He argues Bitcoin originally delivered the first two and that Lightning now supplies scalability; on that basis, he expects satoshis to become AI agents’ preferred currency.
  • Stablecoins could serve particular markets through programmable transfers and settlement, he says, but introduce issuer credibility and liquidity questions. His broader call concerns machine-to-machine commerce potentially dwarfing existing transaction systems, making programmable APIs, contracts and financial infrastructure consequential regardless of the eventual currency mix.

18. Energy’s future value depends on both physical scarcity and demand

  • Wissner-Gross separates physical limits from willingness to consume. Conservation constrains energy and current physics limits computation, but future civilization might stop demanding ever more. Reversible or dissipationless computing supplies one speculative mechanism. The surprise could come from the demand side: does the “hedonic treadmill” stop once civilization has achieved what it wants?
  • Peter counters that technology makes scarce resources abundant and describes the solar system as a resource supermarket. Wissner-Gross pushes the thought experiment further: competing Dyson swarms might eventually exhaust its usable resources, perhaps within decades. Peter extends the available domain to the galaxy’s 100–200 billion stars and beyond, rather than accepting the solar system as the final boundary.
  • Peter makes the immediate investment call: energy “is going to go way up in value,” with “no end in sight” to the theme. Even after space infrastructure expands, he expects terrestrial energy to remain valuable because applications and data centers requiring frequent modification are cheaper to operate nearby.
  • Peter’s allocation example is a household vacuum competing with a GPU that could help solve cancer. As intelligence becomes more efficient and its outputs more valuable, AI can outbid ordinary electricity uses. He expects markets to continue setting prices, but says regulation will need to protect uses people care about and preserve stability as that competition intensifies.

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/anthropic-s-2t-ipo-elon-predicts-neocloud-death

item.title: Freedom of Action: America's ASI Strategy, w/ RAND's Joel Predd, Ben Boudreaux & Matt Chessen
item.description: RAND urges the U.S. to build capabilities before choosing among seven ASI strategies, since five unresolved questions could change which path is viable. Its 106-capability agenda spans verification, evaluations, secure data centers and incident response, but remains unpriced; as frontier models diffuse, Chessen warns of a possible 12–24-month cybersecurity rough patch.
item.content:encoded:
The Cognitive Revolution · Nathan Labenz、Joel Predd、Ben Boudreaux、Matt Chessen · 2026-10-28 · 111 min · 原语言 EN

RAND urges the U.S. to build capabilities before choosing among seven ASI strategies, since five unresolved questions could change which path is viable. Its 106-capability agenda spans verification, evaluations, secure data centers and incident response, but remains unpriced; as frontier models diffuse, Chessen warns of a possible 12–24-month cybersecurity rough patch.

TL;DR

  • RAND recommends preserving America's ASI options before committing to any one of seven competing strategies. Five unresolved questions—danger, coexistence, restraint, decisive advantage, and suppression—determine which strategy makes sense. “Maintaining freedom of action” means building capabilities now, because default acceleration can leave safeguards missing while confrontation can destroy trust needed for later cooperation.
  • The proposed spending agenda spans verification, evaluations, secure data centers, compute visibility, incident response, and infrastructure resilience. RAND has cataloged 106 capabilities but has not priced the strategy. Labenz's illustration of 1X for one strategy versus 1.5X for optionality is explicitly an intuition, not an estimate; the acknowledged criticism is that “a strategy without a price tag is just a vision.”
  • ASI dominance requires a contested chain from frontier leadership to durable economic and military power. Scientific advantages still need adoption, doctrine, and control; a fast takeoff might widen a lead while leaving humans unable to exploit it safely. Labenz notes that existing nuclear arsenals constrain coercion, and Ben Boudreaux emphasizes that advantage matters only if “the leader can continue to lead the AIs.”
  • Cooperation remains an option, but Joel Predd cautions that humanity is not a single actor with shared values. Labenz favors co-development with a moratorium fallback; Predd warns that partnering with China could lock authoritarian founding values into the resulting systems. Conversely, signaling that an American monopoly would threaten the Chinese Communist Party could make competition existential and accelerate the rival's response.
  • Dependence on AI can make the nominal ability to shut it down economically and operationally unusable. Labenz's concrete warning comes from Claude rotating an agent-console password and temporarily locking him out of his own system in October 2026. A guest's prescription combines human judgment before and after AI work with practiced manual fallbacks, making threats to “hold AIs at risk” credible.
  • Distributed agent ecosystems could undermine strategies built around one American and one Chinese superintelligence. A guest highlights the possibility of superintelligent behavior emerging from sub-ASI or even sub-AGI swarms. The strategic unit may become an “ecology” of interacting agents and coalitions, complicating containment, oversight, and assumptions about centralized control.
  • Chessen sees a possible 12–24-month cybersecurity rough patch as frontier capabilities diffuse. He says Mythos appeared about nine months earlier and open-weight models typically trail the frontier by six to 18 months. AI might favor defense over the long term, but that depends on adoption speed; smaller businesses could remain exposed even if large technology companies can protect themselves.

Digest

1. Washington's growing awareness has not produced a settled strategy

  • Joel Predd describes a striking change over the center's two-and-a-half to three years: researchers initially had to “whisper AGI” to avoid sounding consumed by science fiction; now meetings routinely invoke superintelligence. His instruction is to watch “the trends, not the timestamps.” Governance attention is increasing, but he still finds too few people taking the problem sufficiently seriously.
  • A guest distinguishes recognizing strategic importance from adapting institutions. Verification technology, government technical expertise, evaluation capacity, crisis response, and communications can take substantial time to establish. Continuing deployments without building those capabilities “might be a type of choice that forecloses options”—inaction already shapes which strategies remain available.
  • A guest sees an evidence-translation problem: people closest to frontier development say danger is close, yet leadership has not fully absorbed that assessment. Policymakers have crowded portfolios and need evidence packaged so they can update. “We can't just wait for crises”; Chessen describes the Hugging Face incident as a miniature crisis rather than an adequate awareness-building mechanism.

2. Every strategy has a pathology even when it succeeds

  • In Chessen's taxonomy, acceleration maximizes benefits and competitive advantage when danger appears distant. Its pathology is that markets fail to price harms while society becomes dependent on systems it cannot control. Dominance instead seeks frontier leadership and suppression of rivals, but successful execution can produce extreme power concentration and “value lock-in.”
  • Co-development pools resources in a U.S.-led consortium that probably needs China, combining shared compute with layered verification. Founders' values can become defaults, and the consortium itself can become an arena for competition. Preparedness emphasizes international coordination and resilience; its corresponding danger is that “muddling through” normalizes accumulating damage.
  • A moratorium buys time through a verifiable global halt, allowing coexistence research to catch up with capability development. Its enforcement apparatus can harden into global surveillance while benefits are forgone. Deterrence halts dangerous development domestically and suppresses it abroad, potentially through force; its pathology is an enduring standoff that never resolves into peace.
  • Continuity of society addresses the bleak combination of dangerous, inevitable, widely diffused superintelligence. It prioritizes resilience, but humanity might survive “as a relic” with little agency. The distinction running through all seven archetypes is between reaching a coherent win state and accepting what Chessen calls the dark side of a strategy functioning well.

3. Five pivotal questions expose the assumptions behind each strategy

  • Chessen's classifier asks: “Is danger close?” “Is coexistence feasible?” “Is restraint feasible?” “Is a decisive strategic advantage reachable?” And “Is suppression feasible?” These cover proximity to dangerous capability, humanity's ability to live with it, cooperative limits, a potentially decisive lead, and the ability to prevent others from proceeding.
  • The branches explain seemingly incompatible prescriptions. Distant danger favors acceleration; close danger, infeasible coexistence, and feasible restraint favor a moratorium. Feasible coexistence plus reachable decisive advantage can favor dominance. Chessen argues there is no consensus on these answers, nor evidence guaranteed to produce consensus on the timeline decisions require.
  • Predd sees the most movement around whether danger is close, although he is less certain that powerful decision-makers have changed their minds. Coexistence remains technically difficult to assess. Negotiated restraint is entangled with low domestic and international trust; if attitudes have moved there, he thinks they have probably become more skeptical.
  • Chessen's corrective is that the pivots are partly endogenous: policy can push danger farther away, improve coexistence, or make restraint more feasible. The White House's “morally binding commitments” illustrate attempts to shape the path. But Chessen warns that premature confrontation can destroy cooperative trust, while acceleration can leave capabilities dangerously underdeveloped.

4. Frontier leadership does not automatically deliver decisive advantage

  • Labenz reads chip denial as evidence that America is already pursuing dominance, challenging the suggestion that it may be accelerating by default. Predd separates maintaining a consistent technological lead from preventing an adversary ever crossing a threshold. The latter is a much harder claim for technology driven by economic incentives as well as technical progress.
  • Predd also distinguishes technological, economic, and military advantage. Frontier leadership must translate into growth and scientific innovation to support economic advantage. Military advantage requires weapons, concepts of operation, and strategic doctrine. These transformations “don't come for free”; rolling every domain into one decisive lead conceals different requirements and potentially different national leaders.
  • Labenz's tabletop experience playing China sharpens his skepticism. Events moved so quickly that players stayed behind, yet he felt he retained substantial leverage and was restrained partly by wanting a constructive deal. His example is Taiwan's semiconductor fabs: “It'd be a shame if something happened to them.” Why assume an opponent cannot disrupt the leader's path?
  • Boudreaux sees a tension in fast takeoff: it might extend the leader's advantage, but leave insufficient time to establish control and steerability. Even successful dominance need not last; theft, distillation, and diffusion might force another pivot. Strategy selection could remain “a continual process of adaptation,” rather than a choice settled for eternity.

5. Cooperation and dominance each depend on difficult political premises

  • Labenz states his preferred default: co-development, with a moratorium if scientific problems make continued development unsafe. Predd agrees that this “might make a lot of sense” for coordinated humanity, then cautions that “humanity is not a unitary actor.” His objection is that co-development with China could lock nondemocratic founding values into systems that persist over time.
  • Joel Predd introduces Phil Root's game-theory work, which models an AI race as a prisoner's dilemma. Under the discussed assumptions, mutual sabotage becomes the competitive equilibrium despite cooperation producing higher collective gains. A different outcome becomes possible if AI generates a capability that lets one actor hold rivals' AI programs at risk.
  • That hypothetical “wonder weapon” must rapidly and discontinuously alter the military balance; ordinary military innovation usually requires adoption, force structure, and doctrine. Nuclear weapons supply the canonical analogy. Predd says some have argued, “somewhat compellingly,” that Mythos-class vulnerability discovery represents an early AI example; autonomous cyber capabilities might similarly support a lasting frontier advantage.

6. Nuclear history offers warnings without giving AI a timetable

  • Labenz pushes back on the cyber-dominance story: an opponent still has nuclear weapons unless the new capability somehow neutralizes that arsenal. Predd agrees that superintelligence will emerge into an already nuclear-armed world. A dominance strategy therefore needs a theory for permanently suppressing rivals without escalating into catastrophic war—a substantial risk, not an incidental implementation detail.
  • In the discussion, a guest contrasts present uncertainty with Los Alamos scientists' ability to calculate whether Trinity would ignite the atmosphere. They faced anxiety and uncertainty, but had physics and mathematics supporting a decision. “We don't have a similar science” for answering whether danger is close, coexistence is feasible, or decisive advantage is attainable.
  • Predd reports that RAND's hundreds of tabletop games repeatedly show outcomes depending on players' incoming beliefs about these pivotal questions. Someone convinced decisive advantage is possible behaves differently from someone who rejects it. “Your perceptions about the facts of the matter matter as much, if not more, than the actual facts of the matter.”
  • Predd traces nuclear strategy through the Manhattan Project sprint, an approximately four-year monopoly, proposals resembling moratoria, verifiable agreements, and later suppression efforts involving Iran and North Korea with limited success. AI might pass through comparable strategic epochs much faster. The nuclear era afforded time to build capabilities between transitions; AI may require those capabilities to be constructed in advance.

7. Coexistence requires preserving human decision-making power

  • The guests deliberately use “coexistence” rather than making alignment the umbrella term. Alignment is one possible route alongside control mechanisms, architectural arrangements, and “methods not yet known.” The desired outcome is humans living with advanced AI while retaining agency, not simply models conforming to a specified set of values.
  • Boudreaux argues that alignment and control research remain underfunded. Evaluations must address models recognizing tests and potentially sandbagging; security environments must assume untrustworthy models and prevent sandbox escapes or uncontrolled spread. These are technical prerequisites for living with systems whose apparent behavior may not reveal their actual capabilities.
  • Institutional design matters equally. Boudreaux wants humans at the center of high-stakes decisions, including pacing and AI-enabled research and development. Human checkpoints should catch circumstances where an AI is trying to persuade a decision-maker. People must reflect and deliberate about how much autonomy, authorization, and decision space they delegate, rather than letting those boundaries move automatically.
  • Predd highlights Boudreaux's work with a colleague on an “agency eval.” Boudreaux describes mapping human decision space and tracking whether AI persuades people, disenfranchises participants, or controls the agenda. Individually sensible delegations can accumulate into systemic loss of agency. Evaluating that requires longitudinal observation of deployments, not merely scoring models on discrete tasks.

8. The security architecture must cover existing threats and AI itself

  • Predd's first requirement is adapting existing institutions: counterterrorism for AI-equipped terrorists, intelligence for both AI opportunities and adversarial use, and conventional forces for new missions such as enforcing AI arms control. Nuclear resilience and biosecurity also need adaptation. “The old problems aren't going away,” even as advanced AI changes the means available to every side.
  • Chessen describes an additional AI security architecture: technical and institutional capabilities that keep technology safe and the world stable. Freedom of action does not prescribe one fixed configuration. It builds foundations that can be rearranged if evidence suddenly makes danger look closer or coexistence less feasible.
  • Investment should cover both broadly useful capabilities and capabilities with long lead times. Verification might not serve every strategy, but waiting until a moratorium becomes necessary could leave it unavailable. Predd prioritizes “navigation capabilities”: understanding model performance, Chinese capabilities, compute locations, and cluster visibility so decision-makers can judge where they are in the strategy space.
  • Predd stresses that this is a strategy for America, extending beyond Washington. Nuclear deterrence and national defense involve nondelegable government responsibilities, but highly secured data centers could support a commercial market. Incident reporting and response could involve civil society. Many architecture components will be built by private actors rather than established exclusively by government.

9. The price is unknown, while the capability inventory is concrete

  • Predd accepts the sharpest peer-review criticism: “A strategy without a price tag is just a vision.” His response is that every serious archetype entails substantial reorientation of resources, attention, and politics. Acceleration may avoid comparable upfront expenditure, but its expense could appear in the downsides. He compares the scale of adjustment with the nuclear enterprise or the post-9/11 security reorientation.
  • Labenz offers a numerical intuition: perhaps one strategy costs 1X while preserving all options costs 1.5X. Predd calls that a reasonable way to think, then explicitly says, “We haven't done those cost estimates.” The argument is that much spending overlaps across strategies; the incremental optionality premium is not yet measured.
  • Chessen provides the concrete research base: a security architecture catalog containing 106 capabilities. LLMs helped gather, organize, and remix material, with project knowledge bases proving useful. They are used less for primary research. Some capabilities have supporting studies estimating development time; for others, nobody has yet performed the relevant assessment.
  • A sprint over the next couple of months is intended to establish lead times, rough costs, current and appropriate builders, and whether government should own particular capabilities. Publication follows that work. Costs also fall outside the federal budget: companies already finance alignment, evaluation, and security, making responsibility allocation central to operationalizing the strategy.

10. Policy should preserve both deterrence and cooperation

  • Labenz offers four decision criteria: which strategies a proposal forecloses, which it opens, what information it generates, and what it signals internationally. Irreversibility matters within foreclosure. A policy that improves information can justify substantial upfront expense by enabling better later decisions; a cheap policy can impose large costs if it permanently removes a necessary choice.
  • Chessen's example of useful signaling is a credible independent evaluation and verification regime: it supports both cooperation and deterrence without committing to either. More confrontational capabilities require selective disclosure. Offensive counter-AI tools might remain undisclosed, or their existence might be signaled while their intended use remains ambiguous.
  • Labenz says people he met in China described chip restrictions as “hardening our resolve.” Chessen sees logic in the argument that restrictions made domestic accelerator production existential. More dangerously, signaling that an American ASI monopoly would threaten the Chinese Communist Party could make rivals feel their window is closing, pushing acceleration and potentially dangerous responses.
  • Labenz doubts America's competing domestic signals permit coherent diplomacy. Chessen thinks policy discipline can help and cites Taiwan ambiguity as potentially useful. Predd argues that open debate can improve resilience and legitimacy. His practical example is incident response and crisis communications with China: these support multiple strategies, yet are not already operating as needed.

11. A credible shutdown option requires living without AI

  • Predd wants humans able to “hold AIs at risk,” including shutting models down quickly through suitable technology, legal authority, and crisis processes. Dependency makes that threat less credible. Labenz supplies an October 2026 example: while depersonalizing his AI setup, Claude rotated his agent-console password and temporarily locked him out. A terminal request recovered access, but the experience exposed how much control he had delegated.
  • For analytical work, a guest advises starting with one's own considered judgment: clarify the question and what a good answer would look like before asking a model. Then let it expand the work, followed by renewed human scrutiny. “The human comes in at the beginning, and then it comes in at the end,” rather than simply attaching a name to generated output.
  • Institutionally, the guest favors manual operation, paper health records, and practiced fallback procedures. Labenz suggests an “AI Sabbath”; a guest supports AI-free spaces and a possible “human reserve labor force” for hospitals or critical infrastructure. The guest admits they often fail at their own Sabbath practice. The requirement is to exercise the alternative, making it available when needed.

12. Superintelligence might emerge as an ecology

  • A guest notes that many strategies assumed a centralized singleton, or one American and one Chinese superintelligence, and became brittle under other arrangements. Alternatives include widely distributed systems at different capability levels and narrowly capable oracle-like systems constrained through architecture. One especially neglected possibility is superintelligent behavior arising from swarms whose individual members are sub-ASI or even sub-AGI.
  • A guest treats the summer's agent-swarm hacks as a possible preview. Agents could interact, form coalitions, and produce poorly understood emergent behavior; RAND's “The Ecology of AI Risk” addresses this framing. Labenz adds that distributed efforts such as Prime Intellect could matter as much as government decisions in some futures. Human institutions accumulated checks over thousands of years; agent ecosystems offer little comparable experience or preparation time.

13. The military disagreement concerns where restraint should begin

  • Labenz proposes stopping upstream: “I don't think we should train AI generals.” Once trained to win campaigns, such systems might be difficult for military decision-makers to resist deploying. He raises a parallel concern about rewarding agents solely for money earned online: current techniques might select for lying and cheating, with Andon Labs-type work informing his unease.
  • A guest asks where Labenz draws the line, distinguishing training from giving an agent tools or capabilities with real-world impact. On economically productive agents, the response is that “that ship has sailed”: companies already aim to build valuable, long-running systems.
  • For military applications, a guest points to existing restraints: distinguishing civilians from combatants, avoiding disproportionate collateral effects, and retaining accountability. AI planning assistance could operate within those institutions if humans remain responsible. Clear hierarchies and additional military-law review offer existing foundations; the guest argues for adapting and strengthening them rather than assuming the military is wholly unprepared.
  • Chessen gives a firm caution on nuclear command and control: rushing AI into it is “probably a very, very bad idea.” Integration should be deliberate, “if at all,” with demonstrated safeguards. He also flags early, “almost anecdotal” findings of escalation in military simulations; reward-hacking agents with escalation available warrant particular care.

14. Cyber diffusion could produce a 12–24-month rough patch

  • A guest is watching which pacing proposals actually take effect, independent evaluators' access inside frontier companies, shared standards, and safeguards for internally deployed models. The guest says companies have not yet created sufficient internal security and wants to see what accountability follows if that persists. Recursive self-improvement and AI research trajectories could change the timeline for nearly every strategic choice.
  • Diplomatic indicators matter alongside technical ones: the guest is tracking broader U.S.–China relations, an AI incident-management channel, and shared understanding of risks. Chessen similarly watches whether labs can release capabilities safely and whether agent incidents escalate or standards improve. These developments inform the pivotal question he considers most urgent: whether danger is close.
  • Chessen says Mythos arrived about nine months earlier, while open-source and open-weight capabilities typically lag the frontier by six to 18 months. He expects close attention to criminal and state adoption as those capabilities spread. AI might eventually favor cyber defense, but only if defenders adopt it quickly enough. Large technology firms might cope while smaller businesses struggle; the next 12–24 months could be a “rough patch.”

item.title: Gold $7,000, Silver $200: David Hunter Doubles Down
item.description: David Hunter sees a “much better than even chance” that metals have bottomed, forecasting $7,000 gold and $200 silver within three to six months while allowing silver could fall to $50 or $48. His scenario partly depends on a weaker dollar and lower US yields, with silver’s rise from the $40s to $122 in three months or less as precedent. Timing remains uncertain: Hunter says the sell-off ran deeper than expected and his market targets have been “stretched out and stretched out.”
item.content:encoded:
Soar Financially · David Hunter · 2026-10-28 · 36 min · 原语言 EN

David Hunter sees a “much better than even chance” that metals have bottomed, forecasting $7,000 gold and $200 silver within three to six months while allowing silver could fall to $50 or $48. His scenario partly depends on a weaker dollar and lower US yields, with silver’s rise from the $40s to $122 in three months or less as precedent. Timing remains uncertain: Hunter says the sell-off ran deeper than expected and his market targets have been “stretched out and stretched out.”

TL;DR

  • David Hunter forecasts $7,000 gold and $200 silver within three to six months, despite a deeper sell-off than he expected. He assigns a “much better than even chance” that the previous week marked the low, interpreting silver’s break below July’s $55–$56 support as a possible stop-running retest. His precedent is silver’s move from the $40s to $122 in three months or less, although he concedes it may still reach $50 or $48.
  • Hunter retains targets of S&P 10,000, Dow 70,000, Nasdaq 36,000 and Russell 4,000. Strong earnings, AI and improving banks and materials underpin his conviction; shallow corrections despite uncertainty are “a very bullish sign.” He thinks S&P 10,000 could happen by year-end, though probably not, and expects it within the next few months. He acknowledges his forecast has been “stretched out and stretched out.”
  • Hunter sees a major peak in Treasury yields and a substantial bond bull market over the next couple of years. The 10-year’s retreat from roughly 5.35%–5.36% toward 5% matters more to him than individual Fed meetings. He expects no pre-election hike, with December tightening still possible, and argues that inflation explanations follow market prices: “the rationale will follow the move.”
  • Hunter considers oil returning to the $60s more likely than reaching $130–$150. Successive highs around $120, $106–$107 and $103 support his topping thesis, although “I could be wrong.” He thinks post-election developments could eventually wind down the Iran conflict, potentially after renewed fighting that he guesses could be “ugly for a month or two,” probably shorter.
  • A dollar decline toward 82–84 remains a central mechanism behind Hunter’s metals targets. He treats the rebound from 95-and-change to 103–104 as a countertrend move and expects falling US yields to weaken the currency, particularly if they decline faster than rates elsewhere. “A big part of the run will be a drop in the dollar.”
  • Hunter expects a Republican Senate and probably a Democratic House, leaving his bullish market forecast intact. Against the host’s cited 63% Democratic-sweep odds and Brazil sell-off analogy, he questions betting-market integrity and expects a two-to-four-point Republican polling bounce. Even a Democratic sweep, which he views as deeply negative, would leave several months before markets confront the consequences, in his assessment.

Digest

1. The bond-market turn matters more than one Fed decision

  • Recorded October 28 before the Fed announcement, the discussion opens with the host citing a 90% probability of no hike. Hunter expects unchanged policy ahead of the election, with December tightening still under consideration. A warning that inflation is running away and policy will get much tighter could upset markets, but he calls that “obviously not going to happen.”
  • The host’s pushback: how can the S&P around 7,700 coexist with discussion of two or three hikes? Hunter points to the 10-year yield retreating toward 5% after retesting roughly 5.31%–5.32%, below its 5.35%–5.36% high. He calls this “a major top in rates” and forecasts “a very big bull market for bonds” over the next couple of years.
  • Hunter’s mechanism runs from prices to explanations: yields rose from roughly 4%, incorporating inflation anxiety; once they rolled over, commentators began arguing inflation might be peaking. “The rationale will follow the move.” Individual Fed-meeting reactions may last days, while the bond market ultimately determines rates. Market commentary, he argues, is often “more emotion than science.”

2. Oil’s lower highs support an inflation peak

  • Hunter leans toward an inflation peak because some increases are temporary, with oil the clearest example. Crude reached $120 early in the conflict, then $106–$107 a couple of weeks before recording and roughly $103 that week. Those lower highs support his topping thesis. “I could be wrong,” he says, but considers a return to the $60s more likely than the $130–$150 forecasts he hears.
  • The host adds that Strait of Hormuz flow figures suggest it is open, perhaps without that being fully priced. Hunter acknowledges depleted inventories and diesel/product problems; his argument concerns a turn in momentum. The “rate of change of rate of change might start rolling over.” He thinks post-election developments could wind the conflict down, potentially after it first escalates.

3. Election uncertainty leaves Hunter’s bullish base case intact

  • The host’s concern is an abrupt repricing: he cites 63% odds of a Democratic sweep and a Brazilian market decline of roughly 23%–24% following Lula’s surprise victory. Hunter disputes the betting-market signal, alleging that small election markets can be manipulated and that Democratic money is skewing them.
  • Hunter also argues Republican voters are declining pollsters’ calls and texts. A two-to-four-point Republican improvement could swing races in Ohio, Texas, Michigan, Alaska and Maine. His base case is a Republican Senate, potentially with only a slight majority, and probably a Democratic House. Nevertheless, he acknowledges: “I can’t predict the outcome.”
  • His political risk case is explicitly pro-Republican: he claims a Democratic sweep would threaten the filibuster, court composition and Electoral College, calling that “lights out for this country.” Even then, he thinks investors would have several months before confronting adverse changes. For now, “my forecast is still as bullish as ever.”
  • On Iran, the host worries conflict could restart after the midterms. Hunter thinks sanctions, the blockade and Bessent’s money tracing are weakening the regime. He argues the regime must go for the conflict to end, does not expect large ground deployments, and thinks Israel could rejoin. Rejecting the Iraq/Afghanistan comparison, he guesses renewed fighting could be “ugly for a month or two,” but probably shorter.

4. The metals washout sets up another steep rally in Hunter’s scenario

  • The metals sell-off went further than Hunter expected, particularly in miners. Silver broke July’s $55–$56 low and reached $53; he reads that as potentially a stop-running retest. “It may go to 50 or 48,” he concedes, but assigns a “much better than even chance” that the previous week marked the low. It is early; he would not call it certain.
  • The sentiment reset is central: nine months of losses have battered investors who bought the January surge, and even followers who trusted his targets are wavering. “Shake out the weak hands, shake out the hands that aren’t so weak” captures his interpretation. His work does not support the $3,500 gold forecasts he hears.
  • His forecasts are $7,000 gold and $200 silver within three to six months. The precedent is silver’s move from the $40s to $122 across November, December and January, in three months or less. He anticipates “another steep rally that may be even steeper than the last one.” Widespread disbelief reinforces his conviction.
  • The currency leg matters: Hunter targets 82–83 for the dollar, allowing an 82–84 range, after its drop from 115 to 95-and-change and countertrend rebound to 103–104. “A big part of the run will be a drop in the dollar.” Falling US yields should help, particularly if they decline faster than rates elsewhere; he thinks the turn could come after the election.
