5. Improving breadth sustains the equity targets as timing stretches

  • Hunter retains “very high conviction” in S&P 10,000, Dow 70,000, Nasdaq 36,000 and Russell 4,000. For the S&P, year-end is possible but probably too soon; he expects the move over the next few months. He cites strong earnings, expects that strength to continue next year, and sees AI as an important contributor.
  • Breadth carries more weight for him than election or Iran uncertainty: banks, financials and materials bottomed a couple of weeks earlier and are turning up while AI has resumed advancing. The Nasdaq corrected only about 6%, the S&P 2.5%–3%. A market given reasons to fall that refuses to do so is, for Hunter, “a very bullish sign.”
  • His admission matters alongside those targets: “my forecast has been stretched out and stretched out.” Some earlier targets were met and subsequently raised because his indicators still showed upside. With the S&P only 1%–2% below its highs, he sees a “huge wall of worry” and investors reluctant even to embrace 8,000. He concedes “forecasts can be wrong”; market moves are “not on a clock.”

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/gold-7-000-silver-200-david-hunter-doubles-down

item.title: Mark Cuban on Why AI Could Turn Solo Founders Into Trillionaires
item.description: Cost Plus Drugs grew from 111 generics in January 2022 to roughly 4,000 SKUs at a fixed 15% markup, with its public API giving buyers a price benchmark. Pre-signing AI review of Dallas’s 1,335-page PBM contract could uncover overcharges; savings may reach millions for organizations above 1,500 employees or members, depending on existing overcharging. Manufacturing pods target roughly 200 annual sales within two years, though 1,000 ANDA applications alone would cost $365 million plus other fees, before manufacturing investment.
item.content:encoded:
The a16z Show · Mark Cuban、Julie Yoo、Erik Torenberg · 2026-10-28 · 60 min · 原语言 EN

Cost Plus Drugs grew from 111 generics in January 2022 to roughly 4,000 SKUs at a fixed 15% markup, with its public API giving buyers a price benchmark. Pre-signing AI review of Dallas’s 1,335-page PBM contract could uncover overcharges; savings may reach millions for organizations above 1,500 employees or members, depending on existing overcharging. Manufacturing pods target roughly 200 annual sales within two years, though 1,000 ANDA applications alone would cost $365 million plus other fees, before manufacturing investment.

TL;DR

  • Cost Plus Drugs is using public prices and consumer trust to introduce competition into an opaque market. Cuban says the business has grown from 111 generic medications in January 2022 to roughly 4,000 SKUs, with a set 15% markup and no advertising spending. Julie Yoo says Cost Plus’s mere presence forced incumbents to change where decades of policy and other pressures had not. Its public pricing API also gives large buyers negotiating leverage: “Trust is still our primary product.”
  • Cuban argues vertical integration lets large carriers raise costs and steer people toward affiliated businesses while obscuring what providers are paid. He cites UnitedHealth’s 3,000-plus subsidiaries and $150 billion in annual intercompany transfers. Yoo sees AI enabling new health plans; Cuban’s counter is that better technology cannot undo unfavorable contracts or eliminate the question of who takes risk.
  • His immediate AI prescription is to audit benefits contracts before signing them. Dallas’s PBM contract runs 1,335 pages, illustrating why manual review struggles. For organizations with more than 1,500 employees or members, he says savings could reach millions, depending on existing overcharging; his suggested prompt is: “Where are they fucking me over, and what should I do about it?”
  • Manufacturing pods are Cuban’s largest commercial ambition, with aggressive volume targets and substantial regulatory costs. At roughly $20 million each, he projects a couple hundred annual pod sales within two years and a couple thousand within five. He says domestic generic production could undercut his Indian suppliers, but puts each generic’s ANDA application at $365,000 plus other fees—$365 million for 1,000 applications, before manufacturing investment.
  • Personalized medicine could become an AI subscription feature, but Cuban leaves the timing wide open. Whether in five, ten or twenty years, he expects personalized drug-design costs to approach zero and suggests including the service in $20 or $200 subscriptions. Yoo expects better drugs to change care delivery; both see substantial demand for doctors, with Cuban’s formulation: “Novel data equals person.”
  • Cuban’s consumer agenda combines access to existing hospital assistance with a proposed alternative to insurance premiums. He says some nonprofit assistance programs extend to 600% of federal poverty levels, potentially above $100,000 for some families in some states. His proposed system would retain premium-equivalent deposits in individually owned accounts, backed by government-guaranteed loans and stop-loss coverage; unused balances and interest would become available at 65.
  • He treats AI adoption as a management and distribution challenge as much as a technical one. Employers need executives who understand the tools and entry-level employees who accumulate organizational context. Frontier labs, meanwhile, need to reach personalized social feeds: Cuban says position papers are “useless” without that distribution, while entrepreneurs should use AI to learn rather than avoid learning.

Digest

1. Transparent prices give Cost Plus leverage beyond its own sales

  • Cuban dates the launch to January 19, 2022, with 111 generic medications; the portfolio now totals roughly 4,000 SKUs. Growing volume attracted additional manufacturers and products. He says the business spends nothing on marketing or advertising, relying on savings to generate referrals. Even if someone offers “cost plus 1%,” his defense is that “Trust is still our primary product,” supported by transparency and a set 15% markup.
  • Local access comes through teamcubancard.com and approximately 17,000 affiliated pharmacies. Its $12 dispensing payment supports independent pharmacies but makes a $5 statin uncompetitive. For expensive specialty generics, biosimilars and insulin, Cuban says local pickup can be cheaper, particularly when it avoids cold shipping. Separately, Cost Plus Marketplace sells hospital injectables at “cost plus ten or cost plus twelve”; purchasing departments sometimes resist despite CEO support.
  • Yoo says Cost Plus’s presence forced incumbents to change, despite policy and other forces having failed to change them for decades. Cuban sees its public API becoming a negotiating benchmark: large buyers can demand, “You have to beat this price.” He also says at least one company told him a big-three carrier had claimed Cost Plus was in its network, although Cost Plus has no agreement with any of the big three.

2. Incumbent control limits what better technology can fix

  • Yoo describes a potential replacement cycle in employer health plans, with some startups facing 60% annual premium increases. Cuban says vertical integration compounds the problem: UnitedHealth has 3,000-plus subsidiaries and $150 billion in annual intercompany transfers, by his account. Employers can face higher premiums and deductibles while patients are steered toward affiliated businesses whose ownership they do not recognize.
  • Cuban says 60% of people receiving employer healthcare are covered by self-insured employers. Carrier-owned administrators can obscure the difference between employer charges and hospital receipts. Employers may lack their own claims or the 835 and 837 files needed to reconcile payments. His contention is that medical spread pricing is worse than pharmacy spread pricing, across a much larger spending pool.
  • Yoo sees AI making full-stack health plans easier to build. Cuban’s pushback: “This all comes down to who takes the risk.” He expects payer-provider coding “bot wars” eventually to net out, although early adopters can gain temporarily. Acquisition-created data silos could nevertheless make the large carriers slow to become AI-native.
  • Asked about EHR disruption, Cuban answers, “Honestly, I don’t know.” Epic dominates, and he focuses on partnering to show drug prices when clinicians prescribe. Yoo welcomes the announcement but objects that availability waits until “May of next year.” Cuban agrees the delay is typical of healthcare.

3. Contract scrutiny comes before operational automation

  • Cuban calls contractual analysis AI’s most important near-term healthcare application. Dallas’s PBM contract runs 1,335 pages: “There’s no group of humans with enough coffee on the planet” to catch everything. Once unfavorable terms are signed, he argues, operational AI cannot protect the employer. Review must happen before commitment.
  • His agents find public-records opportunities, locate contracts and RFPs, and draft requests that he personalizes and sends. Returned documents enter Google Drive, where several models identify favorable terms, problems, remedies and a plain-language explanation. He also checks one model’s conclusions against another: “One of your peers came out and said this about this contract. What do you think?”
  • Cuban gives the condition as “that 67% of employers representing 67% of the 160 million-plus Americans”—an ambiguous formulation—and says the system would collapse if they reviewed and negotiated contracts this way. He recommends a dedicated healthcare CEO or CFO. For organizations above 1,500 employees or members, savings could reach millions, depending on overcharging. Some public companies have acknowledged problems privately but, he says, fear discussing them on earnings calls.
  • His direct-contract offer exchanges administrative simplicity for better prices and publication rights. Generally trust the doctor, avoid prior authorization and denials except extraordinary cases, pay the contracted amount on time, and assume patient-payment responsibility or credit risk. Providers then avoid becoming “subprime lenders.” Contracts published on costpluswellness.com become reusable agreements or negotiating templates for other employers.

4. Manufacturing pods carry the larger revenue ambition

  • Co-founder Dr. Alex Oshmyansky originally proposed manufacturing generics on the FDA shortage list, including hospital and pediatric cancer medications. Cuban says AI and robotics compressed a football-field-scale operation into 5,000 square feet and permit switching drugs every four hours, producing a six-month supply before moving to another product.
  • That equipment has been reduced further into tractor-trailer-sized manufacturing “pods,” configurable for different drugs and deployable to disaster or military settings. Pods can connect together, including separate sterile and tablet operations. Cuban says the government was the first customer, the first pod was shipped recently, and a second was ordered. He defers technical detail to Oshmyansky, but emphasizes research-hospital configurations for N-of-one therapies; Dallas is already making ASO drugs.
  • At about $20 million per pod, Cuban says margins are attractive. His forecasts are a couple hundred sold annually within two years and a couple thousand within five. At $20 million each, 1,000 pods sold per year would represent $20 billion in annual sales: “If we’re selling $20 billion worth of pods a year, watch out, Elon.”
  • Cuban says pods could manufacture generics in Dallas for less than Cost Plus pays its Indian manufacturers. The constraint is approval economics: he puts each ANDA application at $365,000 plus other fees, making 1,000 applications $365 million before pod costs. An American flag identifying its own US-made drugs on the retail site is “probably two years away” because of FDA work.

5. AI adoption still depends on people who understand the business

  • Cuban rejects eliminating entry-level hiring. Models lag new events, so employees must supply context, interpret consequences and accumulate implementation history. His employment framing is categorical: “People who know how to use AI replace the jobs of people who don’t know how to use AI.” Executives must understand models and agents before enabling their organizations.
  • His example is a consumer-food executive discussing GLP-1-driven acquisitions. Cuban asked ChatGPT to design a cheaper, more GLP-1-friendly competitor to the company’s leading cookie, including a full bill of materials, sources and manufacturing. In roughly three minutes, the executive responded, “Oh, shit.” Cuban’s point is that management cannot enable useful experimentation without knowing such questions are possible.
  • Agent commerce also needs information agents can access. Cuban says they struggle to consume social posts and ads. His experimental agentfeeds.dev, “not truly active,” turns post transcripts into feeds people can give their agents. He expects many such services, while acknowledging unresolved trust problems.

6. Consumer agents could reveal financial assistance already available

  • Cuban cites the claim that 40% of Americans cannot afford a $400 emergency bill. His suggested first step is to ask AI for nearby nonprofit hospitals and investigate their financial assistance programs before an emergency. He says some programs reach 600% of federal poverty levels—potentially over $100,000 for some families in some states.
  • His conditional example is someone who thoroughly understands a local hospital’s assistance program considering whether to accumulate premium-equivalent money in a money market fund. He explicitly qualifies this: “I don’t want to make the decisions for people.” The opportunity he emphasizes is helping families understand eligibility, available options and how to obtain assistance.
  • If starting a company here, Cuban would make nonprofit hospitals’ assistance programs accessible through consumer agents. Hospitals, he says, “suck at marketing” and depend excessively on insurer networks to deliver patients. Better contracts and cheaper networks still face adoption barriers until patients understand how to use them. Reducing fear of a medical financial crisis is his proposed route to AI acceptance.

7. Personalized drugs could become subscriptions without replacing doctors

  • Asked about frontier labs’ ultimate impact, Cuban predicts that personalized drug-design costs will approach zero as algorithms improve. His timing remains “five years, ten years, twenty years.” He starts with over-the-counter medicine: instead of experimenting with how standard ibuprofen affects each person, models could tailor doses or mixtures, then progress to other personalized drugs.
  • He has told two frontier models to include this service in $20 or $200 subscriptions once available. DNA collection might require an upfront payment, with participation contingent on willingness to share sensitive information. He acknowledges that initial costs would be enormous before falling. “I’m selling my own book here”: Cost Plus wants its pods positioned to manufacture those individualized treatments.
  • Yoo suggests personalization could shift doctors’ work away from medication troubleshooting and titration, while increasing demand for actual care and moving physicians toward “physician-scientists.” Cuban agrees: “Novel data equals person.” If a personalized medicine makes him vomit, he wants a human observing with all five senses and incorporating family context. He rejects replacing doctors; their training would instead change, and he anticipates work for “AI translators.”
  • Intellectual property complicates the abundance thesis. A clinician could restrict a useful procedure to a proprietary model and charge “$9,999 for every access.” Cuban argues that selecting the cheapest model is insufficient if essential knowledge is unavailable for training, post-training or retrieval. “The information may want to be free, but the person who owns the IP feels differently.”

8. Cuban would redirect premiums into savings and guaranteed credit

  • His policy agenda starts with publishing all taxpayer-funded contracts without redactions, exposing nonprofit hospitals’ detailed general ledgers and procurement records, and crediting cheaper purchases toward insurance deductibles. He says eight states already allow the last measure at some level. He also says 72% of large carriers’ revenue comes from taxpayers and argues that they offload risk. Although he supports universal healthcare, he argues that reliable economic data must come first.
  • His alternative to conventional premiums uses mandatory deposits into individually owned accounts. Illustratively, a Texas family of five would deposit $2,100 at the specified income level. A bank would lend when balances fall short, backed by government guarantees; part of deposits would fund stop-loss coverage, perhaps above $40,000. Payroll deductions repay loans. He argues government already guarantees education, housing and business credit.
  • At 65, participants moving to Medicare would receive unused savings and accrued interest. Spending restrictions would prevent misuse. Separately, Erik Torenberg asks whether healthcare could still consume roughly a fifth of GDP in ten years despite better technology. Cuban says yes: the gain should be healthier, more productive people and better value from spending, rather than necessarily a smaller economic share.

9. AI’s public case must reach individual feeds

  • Cuban’s advice to frontier labs is to use their own tools to understand social algorithms, segment audiences and enter personalized feeds. Conventional ads and position papers miss how people form opinions. His instruction is blunt: “Do it like the Russians do it.” He argues that people no longer share the same information environment, so broad messaging cannot assume a common audience.
  • He describes data-center hostility as a proxy for poor understanding of AI, while also criticizing communities for unfavorable negotiated deals. The connection to healthcare is contractual: communities, like employers, can accept terms they do not understand. He says legislators also underestimate the consequences of everyone receiving a different social feed.
  • Asked for neglected entrepreneurial opportunities, Cuban answers, “All of them.” He distinguishes people using AI “to learn anything” from those using it “so they don’t have to learn anything.” His closing advice is to experiment, verify outputs and tolerate awkwardness: “That uncomfortableness is probably the path to something that is groundbreaking and game-changing.”

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/mark-cuban-s-plan-make-healthcare-affordable

item.title: From a $27,500 Charter Company to a $4 Billion Private Jet Giant | Kenn Ricci, Flexjet
item.description: Fractional ownership raises utilization, but Flexjet still holds roughly 70 of its 365 aircraft as unsold core fleet. Buffett’s June 1998 $750 million NetJets acquisition helped unlock nearly $300 million in debt; Flight Options’ sales reached $400 million the next year, teaching Ricci that free cash flow and balance-sheet strength, not EBITDA, govern growth.
item.content:encoded:
David Senra · David Senra、Kenn Ricci · 2026-10-28 · 71 min · 原语言 EN

Fractional ownership raises utilization, but Flexjet still holds roughly 70 of its 365 aircraft as unsold core fleet. Buffett’s June 1998 $750 million NetJets acquisition helped unlock nearly $300 million in debt; Flight Options’ sales reached $400 million the next year, teaching Ricci that free cash flow and balance-sheet strength, not EBITDA, govern growth.

TL;DR

  • Ricci’s central financial lesson is that private aviation runs on balance-sheet strength and free cash flow. Flight Options generated $100 million in sales in its first three months and $400 million the following year, yet growth created financing problems he did not initially understand. “Forget income, forget EBITDA”: profitability could coexist with insufficient cash.
  • Fractional ownership improves aircraft utilization while requiring substantial spare capacity. Ricci credits Richard Santulli with recognizing that corporate aircraft flying roughly 300 hours annually could support multiple owners and floating dispatch. Flexjet still keeps about 70 of its 365 aircraft as unsold “core fleet” to support customers, especially on peak days.
  • Industry validation unlocked financing that Ricci’s own pitch could not. After probably 35–40 banks largely rejected his borrowing proposal, Buffett’s $750 million NetJets acquisition in June 1998 changed lenders’ willingness to participate. Ricci secured almost $300 million in debt that summer: “Accidentally wealthy” includes benefiting from somebody else legitimizing the market.
  • A lucrative exit did not compensate Ricci for losing the business he loved. Warburg Pincus valued the business at $360 million, and Ricci offered $180 million for Raytheon’s half; Raytheon instead bought him out in 2002. He owned 16% and calls the loss the “worst day of my life.” An intervening FBO investment, bought for $80 million and sold for $615 million, helped finance his return.
  • A merger bought time during cash trouble, while later integrations imposed years of cultural and operational work. Ricci bought Flexjet for $180 million in 2014, then spent four years integrating it with Flight Options. His current objection to acquisitions is explicit: buyers frequently pay for capabilities they could probably build themselves while putting their existing culture at risk.
  • A contractual restriction unexpectedly removed $600 million of unfunded aircraft commitments. Ricci agreed to buy fifteen $40 million Globals without knowing how he would finance them; Bombardier subsequently said its NetJets agreement prohibited the sale. That released the heavy-aircraft commitment and opened the way to Gulfstreams, of which Flexjet now operates 85.
  • Ricci treats early wealth transfer as an opportunity to teach judgment and build trust. He gifted family-partnership interests while his children were young and discusses unequal outcomes openly. The siblings devised their own investment-sharing rule: the originating sibling can fund 60% while offering each other sibling 20%, with participation optional.
  • Trust becomes an operating advantage when employees can resolve expensive failures immediately. An employee earning $80,000 can authorize a $300,000 trip compensation without supervisor approval. Ricci also paid $30 million to exit a proposed public listing; his explanation for remaining private centers on purpose beyond wealth accumulation and serving others.

Digest

1. Wealth transfer works better while the founder can still teach

  • Ricci’s family story makes changing circumstances concrete. Each child spent eighth grade traveling on six three-week trips built around a curriculum. By the youngest child’s turn in 2017, he had never flown commercially. On a flight to Tokyo, his reaction was: “Hey, Dad, there’s people on this plane I don’t know.”
  • For Ricci, parenting depends on demonstrating trust, including discussing money. He sees three forces behind restrictive inheritance arrangements: professionals earning fees, entrepreneurial “lions” wanting continued control, and parents fearing wealth will destroy ambition. His challenge to that last assumption is pointed: “You couldn’t parent through that?” He wants to watch his children enjoy wealth and help them make decisions while alive.
  • He established a family limited partnership in 1990 and gifted interests as his children were born, retaining flexibility over distributions as general partner. Their holdings appreciated differently because the oldest began receiving wealth twelve years before the youngest. Family meetings therefore start with “you’re not equal,” which he separates from how much he loves each child.
  • Senra recalls asking Charlie Munger how wealthy founders should handle children raised in very different circumstances. “You give them the money,” Munger answered; “They’ll hate you if you don’t.” Senra recalls Munger conceding that gifts could reduce ambition when either he or another dinner guest pressed the point. That concession did not change Munger’s answer.

2. The children built their own rules for protecting family relationships

  • Asked whether early transfer had downsides, Ricci answers, “Not one. Not one.” Financial education began around ages five or six with charitable giving, before taxes or compounding. His youngest initially wanted to give to Disney; Ricci had to explain that it was not a nonprofit. Personality assessments later helped the children understand their different approaches before discussing the estate.
  • When the youngest was around sixteen, meetings expanded into spreadsheets covering assets, transfers, control and banking arrangements. The five family members now disclose their estates and spending to one another. The children themselves decided against including spouses in these meetings: each sibling would determine how to share information within their own household, rather than introduce newcomers into a long-established process.
  • Reading about families that dissipated wealth led the siblings to focus on the third generation and jealousy from unequal investment success. Their solution: whoever originates an investment can supply 60% but must offer 20% to each sibling. Nobody must participate. “I gave you the opportunity to come in” becomes the answer to resentment; Ricci emphasizes that this was their idea.

3. A flying career became a business because Ricci needed a job

  • After overhearing that his parents could not afford Notre Dame, Ricci investigated financial aid during a campus visit. The deadline had passed, but ROTC still had openings. He initially sought the Navy because he wanted to fly; an Air Force colonel redirected him. Aviation began as a way to finance college, with early flying in Cessna 152s and 172s.
  • Military flying led to cargo work and briefly Northwest Orient, where a furlough left him unemployed. His father regarded pilots as “airport jockeys” moving between unstable jobs and encouraged a fallback profession. Ricci entered law school, taking part-time flying work with J&J Aviation to support himself.
  • J&J’s promoter was running a fraud, Ricci says: selling nonexistent Citation aircraft for $750,000, attracting investors with a 10% investment tax credit, then fabricating lease statements and payments. One fictional statement showed $90,000 revenue, $78,000 expenses and a $12,000 distribution. When investors finally demanded to see their aircraft, the promoter disappeared.
  • At twenty-six, Ricci bought the remaining charter operation to preserve his flying job. The price was $27,500; the company held $27,000 cash. When his father asked about the remaining $500, Ricci replied, “Well, why do you think I called you?” Renamed Corporate Wings, it began with four remaining aircraft and still exists today.

4. A narrow aviation niche attracted aircraft without requiring his capital

  • Ricci distinguishes people who understand business generally from people whose expertise comes from loving a particular activity. His route was the latter: “I love to fly.” His diversification joke is “cash and airplanes.” Timing also mattered: he counts 5,000 private jets when he entered the industry in 1985 versus 35,000 today, growth he had not predicted.
  • A relationship with Chapman Freeborn, which transported concert equipment, supplied an initial niche flying performers including Elton John, Bruce Springsteen and Barbra Streisand. Ricci remained the pilot. A three-month tour could pay $20,000 monthly against an ordinary pilot’s $7,000, leaving the rest of the year to develop the business.
  • Aircraft owners supplied the assets. Ricci’s proposition for a Gulfstream II was that leasing it for three months could pay its annual cost while preserving the owner’s use otherwise. “There’s no Kenn capital at this point.” International celebrity flying established credibility for managing other aircraft, and the managed fleet eventually reached the low twenties.
  • Geography reinforces his preference for concentrating on the market he knows. Ricci puts the US at 85% of the private-aviation market and contrasts about 800 US flights with three flights a day in Asia. Asked about an Asian strategy, his response is categorical: “Don’t need an Asian strategy.”

5. Fractional ownership combined higher utilization with floating dispatch

  • Ricci traces Santulli’s fractional model to unsold aircraft after the 1991 Gulf War. Manufacturers then built inventory before securing buyers, creating “whitetails.” Santulli offered to take twenty Hawkers on consignment and sell fractional interests. That structure let him establish supply without putting up the aircraft purchase capital himself.
  • The utilization insight was straightforward: a typical company flew its aircraft around 300 hours annually, while an aircraft could fly 1,000–1,200 hours. Ricci adds that sitting idle causes mechanical problems. Santulli initially sold 200-hour quarter shares; Ricci says the “QS” ending on NetJets registrations comes from that original quarter-share proposition.
  • Floating dispatch changed the customer’s bill. A Cleveland charter customer traveling to Florida previously paid to return the aircraft home. Santulli could drop that passenger and serve another customer elsewhere. Watching customers migrate, Ricci developed a competing used-aircraft offering: comparable service and aircraft types, but a purchase buy-in around half the new-aircraft price. His preferred description is “previously enjoyed.”
  • Ricci says Flight Options started with “probably twenty-five” aircraft across three fleets, roughly eight per type to demonstrate availability. These were supporting aircraft; additional customer purchases led him to buy additional planes. The principle persists: about seventy of Flexjet’s 365 aircraft are core fleet, supporting sold ownership interests and absorbing demand when multiple owners want to travel simultaneously.

6. Buffett unlocked the debt, but sales growth exposed the cash problem

  • Ricci’s first institutional funding search reached probably thirty-five or forty banks. He thinks he needed $30 million or $40 million in borrowing, but lenders struggled with collateral consisting of fractional aircraft interests. After twelve or fifteen months, he had perhaps $7 million of opportunities if he pledged an equivalent amount of assets: “The worst financing ever.”
  • Buffett’s June 1998 purchase of NetJets for $750 million “christens the industry,” in Ricci’s telling. Suddenly the same proposition looked credible. Bombardier Capital, Boeing Capital and Fleet Bank supplied credit lines, often $50 million at a time. He obtained almost $300 million in debt financing that summer and launched Flight Options on October 13, 1998.
  • Sales reached $100 million between October and December and $400 million the next year. Customers sometimes sent approximately $800,000 before completing documentation: “Send me the paperwork. I want to fly tomorrow.” The bargain was compelling, but Ricci describes having “a tiger by the tail and no clue” about the complexity accompanying that growth.
  • The lesson arrived through financing pressure: “The balance sheet is the whole game.” In capital-intensive aviation, “forget income, forget EBITDA”; free cash flow and balance-sheet strength drive survival. He brought in equity partners, but the 2000 dot-com downturn strained cash even while volume held up. He stresses that he had not understood these distinctions when launching.

7. A rescue merger ended with Ricci losing his company

  • Flight Options merged 50/50 with Raytheon’s fractional-aircraft business, which Ricci says was losing $30 million annually. Flight Options was around break-even and generating accounting profits without free cash flow. Consolidating back offices and presenting lenders with a new strategy bought time; Ricci describes that as one alternative to closure or a distressed sale.
  • His current assessment of acquisitions is much harsher. Paying ten times cash flow for market share may be inferior to investing directly in winning customers; he thinks companies could probably achieve the objective themselves 90% of the time. Adding 10% to a workforce can permit cultural integration, but adding 30% or 40% is “culturally impossible,” in his view.
  • The joint venture included “shareholder’s roulette”: either side could propose a price and the other could choose to buy or sell at that price. After eighteen months, Warburg Pincus backed Ricci at a $360 million valuation. He offered Raytheon $180 million for its half, expecting gratitude. Raytheon instead thought he was buying cheaply and bought him out in 2002.
  • Ricci owned 16%, but calls the exit the “worst day of my life”: “I lost my throne.” Senra presses the contradiction between becoming wealthy and feeling devastated, challenging the founder prescription “Start, scale, sell.” Ricci describes wanting the company to succeed for his friends and his original idea, while also wanting proof that it needed him.

8. Aviation investing supplied the capital for his return

  • Warburg offered Ricci $250,000 annually as an executive in residence, plus participation in deals. He declined because it would give Warburg approval power over opportunities he sourced. Instead, he established Directional Capital, pursuing transactions before choosing financing partners. Existing industry knowledge and relationships meant entrepreneurs did not have to explain operating metrics such as dispatch availability or cost per hour.
  • With Allied Capital, he bought Mercury Air Centers for $80 million in 2005. The approximately eighteen-location FBO business provided fuel and facilities for private aircraft; its earnings came from the spread between fuel purchase and selling prices. It fitted his expertise and sat outside the operating activities restricted by his noncompete. Allied owned 80%; Ricci held 20%.
  • Mercury expanded through acquisitions of smaller operators, sometimes costing $3 million or $4 million, at around six times EBITDA. After roughly doubling its size, the business sold to Macquarie in 2007 for $615 million and became part of Atlantic Aviation. Ricci contrasts those purchase multiples with the fifteen to twenty times he says FBO businesses command today.
  • He also accepts responsibility for helping create an industry structure he now dislikes. Ricci calls FBO ownership a duopoly and criticizes private equity’s focus on investor returns without the wider disclosures public companies make. His example is discretionary “event fees”: “A lunar eclipse, let’s charge an event fee.” “In many ways I created this monster,” he says.

9. Buying aircraft unexpectedly turned into buying Flexjet

  • Ricci says Raytheon lost $600 million during its ownership before selling Flight Options back to him in December, after the financial crisis erupted in September. The headline price was $135 million; accounting for liabilities and payables, he describes roughly $42 million: $15 million cash and a $27 million personal note, approximately three years long. “A personal guarantee of everything” included his home.
  • Replacing the neglected fleet brought him to Bombardier’s eight-passenger, transcontinental Challenger 300. Twenty aircraft at about $15 million each represented a $300 million order, but Bombardier-owned Flexjet had exclusivity. That prompted discussions about buying the subsidiary instead. Ricci says he acquired Flexjet in 2014 for $180 million, accompanied by aircraft commitments ultimately totaling $1 billion.
  • Those commitments included fifteen Globals costing $40 million each. Ricci signed without knowing how to finance that $600 million. Before closing, he feared a requested meeting meant NetJets had outbid him. Instead, Bombardier claimed it had not known that its NetJets contract prohibited selling him Globals. His outward response—“Oh, that sucks”—concealed relief at an obligation disappearing.
  • Removing Globals also released the requirement to buy Bombardier aircraft in the heavy-jet category. Ricci subsequently bought Gulfstreams in 2017, securing exclusivity according to his account. Flexjet now operates 85, which he says makes it the largest Gulfstream operator globally, ahead of the US government. The competing aircraft commitment had unexpectedly opened that opportunity.

10. Integrating Flexjet took four years, and Ricci chose to keep it private

  • Flight Options had lost half its customer base, damaged its reputation, neglected aircraft interiors and fallen behind on bills, Ricci says. Flexjet offered the stronger name and better aircraft. But combining fleets was difficult: Flexjet customers did not want older Flight Options Hawkers. Ricci acknowledges that integration was “a lot harder” than expected.
  • Each company had around 300 pilots, with competing identities and different attitudes toward union representation. Even distributing new uniforms required a coordinated crossover date. Integration ran through 2018 and included a vote for self-representation, which Ricci calls unique in pilot-union history. Those experiences inform his objections to combining cultures.
  • Ricci says the business has quadrupled since 2018 and retains complete confidence in fractional ownership: comparing operating models, he calls it “the only operationally dynamic model.” He also paid $30 million to leave a proposed public listing, calling that a “Thirty million dollar mistake.” Asked why remaining private mattered, he points to a purpose beyond accumulating wealth.

11. Service gives the business its purpose and its operating rules

  • Ricci told Father Ted Hesburgh that understanding balance sheets felt like “a shitty gift” compared with curing cancer or helping the poor. Hesburgh framed it as a lifelong choice between selfishness and service. His prescription for significance was “be true to your God, be as good as your parents, and champion the causes of underdogs”—with “God” reflecting the individual’s own understanding of existence.
  • In 1992, inspired by reading about a tribal chief required to relinquish his possessions, Ricci says he gave away all his assets. He wanted to prove that wealth accumulation would not run his life. He distinguishes that earlier wealth from today’s scale: his wealth is now forty times its 2006 level, he says, and “the temptation gets greater.”
  • Senra offers Henry Ford’s formulation, “Money comes naturally as a result of service,” and Ricci says it captures his outlook. His own ethic is “be passionate about what you do, compassionate about how you do it.” Friendship concerns what you do for friends; approaching each morning with possibility helps avoid missing “the best five days of your life.”
  • That philosophy becomes concrete in service recovery. “Customer service is about what you do when things go to hell,” Ricci says. The employee answering a customer’s call can compensate the trip without supervisor approval: someone earning $80,000 annually can authorize a $300,000 trip compensation. “There is no approval process.” He treats that authority as a demonstration of organizational trust.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/from-27-500-charter-company-4-billion-private-je

item.title: 168X 对话 Rick：Anthropic IPO 之后，AI 的下一阶段是什么？ #2
item.description: Rick预测头部模型公司可能在半年至一年内从订阅转向交付科学成果，药物配方、新材料等将扩大收入来源。即使变现放慢，他认为递归自我迭代的竞争仍迫使前沿公司全力投入算力；AI发债推高利率的风险，以及收入兑现速度，仍待观察。
item.content:encoded:
168X · Rick · 2026-10-28 · 82 min · 原语言 ZH

Rick预测头部模型公司可能在半年至一年内从订阅转向交付科学成果，药物配方、新材料等将扩大收入来源。即使变现放慢，他认为递归自我迭代的竞争仍迫使前沿公司全力投入算力；AI发债推高利率的风险，以及收入兑现速度，仍待观察。

TL;DR

  • Rick认为Anthropic IPO“严重低估”，但不押注上市后的股价路径。 主持人列出2025年营收46亿美元、2026年上半年162亿美元、GAAP仍亏近7亿美元；Rick认为可转债相关负债解释了很大部分账面成本，同时承认没有逐项研究债务。他的买入前提是口中的“1.5个”估值，单位未说清；是否重演SpaceX上市后先涨后跌，他的回答是“I don't know，but I don't care”。
  • 他的核心预测是，头部模型公司可能在半年至一年内从卖订阅转向“交付结果”。 数学、物理能力若转化为新材料、蛋白质和药物，每月200块的套餐就不再是主要价值来源；新药配方可以直接卖给礼来。更强模型也可能不开放API，让竞争对手难以追上。
  • 变现即使放慢，Rick也不认为前沿模型公司敢放慢算力投入。 在他眼里，这是winner-take-all的递归自我迭代竞赛，“全力以赴也不一定赢”，不全力以赴则大概率出局。他把微软据称面向6万人的voluntary package、两年六轮裁员，解读为不断削减其他开支以保住AIDC CapEx。
  • 他认为AI发债会把“higher for longer”推向更高利率，并冲击房地产和海外市场。 他粗估2026年AI产业链发债约3000亿美元，相当于美国政府发债量约20%的额外资金需求，2027年可能升至30%；数字未经细算。他判断十年期美债收益率迟早超过6%，到7%、8%也不会惊讶；若长期维持6%以上，他担忧美元回流及新一轮区域金融危机。
  • Rick已卖掉大半NVIDIA，转向他认为更难被模型快速替代的制造、设备和光学资产。 他断言CUDA护城河已经消失，并担心模型公司自行设计芯片会侵蚀fabless价值；余下NVIDIA主要因持股未满一年、税负较高而暂留。TSMC、Intel、ASML及部分测试设备的优势，在他看来来自认证和生产体系中“不可缩短的时间”。
  • 存储仍是最大仓位，他宁愿承受回撤，也不愿错过AI行情反转。 美光、海力士、三星都有持仓，正股未动，期权则已亏损不少；他的逻辑是模型越强，同一单位算力能创造的价值越高，旧硬件也可能因此更值钱。“我不知道它什么时候会回来”，但他认为应当“time in the market，不要timing the market”。
  • NeoCloud是他亏损最多的板块，关键赌注是电力合同被低估。 他认为既有固定利率债务、锁定收入和可转嫁电费，与未来高息扩张应分开看；把排队中的电力合同按其估值计入资产后，他让AI算出的市净率约为1.6—1.8倍。这是依赖合同估值的调整口径，他也承认合同价格可能下跌、公司并非绝无破产可能。
  • Rick已清空多年持有的比特币，却仍认为长期agent economy只能建立在crypto上。 他回避的是AI推进数学与量子计算带来的不确定性：既不确定破解椭圆曲线签名需要多少逻辑比特，也不确定是否还要等5—7年，认为可能只有2—3年。即使风险最终没有兑现，恐惧本身也可能引发大幅抛售；他还打算减持部分以太坊，同时保留一些crypto对冲法币风险。

Digest

1. Anthropic的营收跃升与账面亏损需要分开讨论

  • 主持人首先摆出财务反差：Anthropic在2025年全年营收46亿美元，2026年上半年已达162亿美元，但GAAP仍亏损近7亿美元。他的问题是，增长固然快，成本是否同样高得难以忽略？
  • Rick把很大部分账面成本归因于可转债：早期融资对应的股权价值上升，也会推高相关liability。他记得实际spending约为10 billion，认为相对当前ARR体现出罕见的capital efficiency，但明确补充“好像”，也承认没有逐项研究债务组成。
  • 对IPO，他的态度是“严重低估”，若按口中的“1.5个”估值上市就会买，单位未明确。他的判断来自快速阅读和让AI辅助分析，并非一份已经完成细项核对的财务结论。

2. 模型公司的下一步可能是卖科学成果

  • Rick把数学、物理、材料和生命科学连成一条价值链：前沿数学能力增强，可能带来物理问题的突破，再延伸到新材料、蛋白质、抗癌药、量子和核聚变。他因此认为，用每月200块的subscription衡量这些公司的潜力，可能很快失去意义。
  • 他转述Sam Altman在Stanford问答中的电力类比：电最初令人害怕，电力公司向家庭推销的是光明，“卖的是光”。同样，普通人很难理解token，却能理解一种新药或新材料带来的结果。
  • 商业对象也可能改变：新药配方可以卖给礼来，新材料可以卖给Applied Materials，不必逐个争取普通用户。他的时间判断仍带猜测：“maybe再过半年，最多一年”，头部公司可能不再卖套餐，直接卖结果。
  • Rick还以他所称OpenAI在八月底至九月用于解决纳维–斯托克斯方程、却迟迟未向市场开放的模型为例，猜测最强模型会被留在内部。他把头部公司可能形成开放节奏默契的想法，明确称为自己“非常恶毒”的解读。

3. 变现速度的反问没有改变他的CapEx判断

  • 主持人的反问值得保留：面向最前沿科研，变现周期会不会比订阅和API慢得多？Rick承认“有可能”，短期ARR可能下降，甚至不排除影响CapEx；这也是市场担忧上游半导体需求的原因。
  • 但他不认为有野心的frontier lab敢主动放慢compute投入。递归自我迭代是一场winner-take-all竞赛，“全力以赴也不一定赢”；不全力以赴，大概率就输了。
  • 在他的框架里，CFO要在发债、发股、股价和削减成本之间维持balance，同时“尽可能激进”。短期收入兑现较慢，并没有消除争夺下一阶段智能能力的动机。

4. 微软反复裁员被他读成保算力的信号

  • Rick提到微软据称面向6万人的voluntary package，以及过去两年六次自愿或非自愿裁员。他猜测财报前释放这一消息，是Amy Hood先向市场说明会cut cost，以缓冲随后CapEx数字带来的紧张。
  • 他的具体类比是，一次裁20%，通常比四次各裁5%更能让留下的人安心；微软反复行动，说明“计划赶不上变化”，包括最初对CapEx的预算。他强调这是非专业解读；主持人则认为，削减成本可能利好股价，但显然伤害员工。

5. IPO的资金分流与盈利增长是两条不同问题

  • 主持人拿SpaceX上市后先涨约50%—60%、随后跌数月的路径追问，Anthropic是否也会如此。Rick不愿赌：“I don't know，but I don't care。”若跌下来，他会用同样资金买更多股；若不跌，则接受买到的股数较少。
  • 对“最纯AI股”会不会吸走存储、光和其他硬件资金，Rick回答“有可能”。但另一面是，Anthropic融资后最可能做的就是买更多算力，因此对上下游整体仍可能是积极信号，净分流多少则“不好说”。
  • 他认为高利率会压缩估值，下一轮上涨主要靠earnings，包括模型公司和利用智能增强业务的企业。Bio是他已看到的方向，相关股票据他描述过去两个月涨了几倍；不过收入增长可能快于利润，市场仍可能punish模型公司。

6. 开源竞争被他改写成算力闭环竞争

  • 对主持人提出的开源模型落后12—18个月，Rick没有照单全收：“是不是有12到18个月的差距不好说。”他只认为差距可能扩大，并用闭源模型解决前沿科学问题、开源模型仍在刷SWE-bench等分数作对照。
  • 他的第一段论是“模型即应用”：模型最终会吃掉应用。第二段是“算力即模型”：只有持续获得算力，模型公司才能在递归自我迭代中越跑越快；没有足够算力的模型公司，他认为可能连投资价值都没有。
  • 第三段是有条件的“瞬间即永恒”：当模型迭代自身、芯片、fab与能源基础设施形成全闭环，算力领先带来模型领先，模型领先再带来更多算力。他判断反馈的增长幂次“大概率大于3”，领先者此后几乎无法被追上。
  • 他把马斯克的行动理解为，在这个完整闭环形成之前争取弯道超车。开源模型若竞争的是token价格，当然能影响闭源收入；若最强模型不开放API、直接卖成果，争夺同一营收的难度就会不同。

7. 中美AI超跌都可看，但中国标的尚未细研

  • 谈到中国，主持人提及字节、腾讯和阿里。Rick说阿里获得算力的消息只是听说，自己还要找时间研究；对A股半导体上下游，他同样坦言尚未仔细看。
  • 他的条件判断是，只要中国没有放弃AI竞争，就会继续全力投入，跌得多的产业链资产值得看。主持人补充估值已经很低，并认为10月22日离岸税相关期限过去后，套现卖压可能减轻；Rick同时提醒，海外资金流向仍受美元利率约束。

8. AI发债在他的框架里通向6%以上美债收益率

  • Rick粗估2026年AI产业链发债约3000亿美元，相当于美国政府发债量约20%的额外资金需求；2027年若继续增长，可能达到30%。他强调这是原先不存在的增量需求，也承认具体数字记不清、“没具体算”。
  • 因果链是资金需求增加、供给没有同步增加，利率就会被抬高。他判断十年期美债收益率“迟早要到六以上”，6%可能挡不住，7%、8%也不会令他惊讶；“higher for longer”还应加上“much higher”。
  • 他拿中国改革开放及房地产大基建时期作类比：银行利率八点几、民间借贷二十几。他认为，按GDP比例衡量，AIDC建设对新增资金的需求可能比当年的中国基建更大，因此高利率未必很快过去。
  • 若十年期收益率长期在6%以上，他担忧美元从亚洲等市场回流，重现类似1997年东南亚金融风暴、欧猪五国金融风暴或南美金融风暴。“从哪里开始我不知道，但会发生。”房地产还要同时面对高利率与他预期的高失业。

9. 他已减持NVIDIA，并把筛选推进到AI板块内部

  • Rick说自己的观点比以前更extreme：从“K型”走向“I型”，即使同在AI板块，也只愿选择最强资产。Broadcom、Qualcomm这类fabless，是他目前较抵触的方向；他仍提到持有Qualcomm。
  • 他透露约两个月前已经卖掉大半NVIDIA。剩下没卖，主要因为正股持有未满一年、出售税负较高。他的判断很明确：“CUDA的护城河已经不存在了”，至少也认为护城河没有过去那么宽。
  • 逻辑是模型公司都在做芯片，模型下一步还会迭代芯片设计。NVIDIA把芯片做成即插即用的大型系统固然有价值，但Google、Amazon、Anthropic也可能做；若设计周期继续缩短，芯片设计公司会遭遇类似软件公司的价值压力。

10. 制造、设备和光学的护城河在于时间

  • 相比设计，Rick更偏向TSMC、Intel、ASML及核心设备制造商。以测试设备和FORM探针为例，进入某代生产线后，替换供应商往往要重新认证；正在运行的产线承担不起随意切换的成本和事故风险，护城河来自“不可缩短的时间”。
  • 光学方面，他在下跌后买了Coherent，也买了其上游设备供应商Veeco，讨论的是MOCVD与磷化铟生长设备。Lumentum仍在犹豫，并未买入。
  • 按他的比较，Aixtron是这一设备市场的最大玩家，Veeco算老二。客户设备一旦用上，不会轻易更换，何况供应商少、产能仍不足；这类持仓是长线选择，他不期待明天突然出现利好、带来巨大弹性。

11. 存储仍是最大仓位，他不接受周期见顶论

  • Rick直说“我不知道它什么时候会回来”，但认为存储安全边际很高。正股仓位没有动，存储期权已经亏了不少；他还没开始买回存储期权，目前买的是市场最不看好的NeoCloud。
  • 他援引供给已卖到2028、2029年的消息，并以海力士为例；零售端则讲了自己的经历：下单后又取消的两条64G、合计128G内存，没多久涨了约50%。这是他反驳需求见顶的具体观察。
  • 核心机制是模型进步提高单位算力产生的智能及潜在收入。同一张卡以后能跑更强模型，硬件就可能更值钱；内存、GPU以及H100、H200、GB200租金最终在哪里平衡，他回答“I don't know”。
  • 对“周期论”，他的判断是错的：需求增长没有停止，增速也“很可能并没有放缓”。即使某段S曲线的加速度下降，新模型仍可能让需求重新加速；若市场对、自己错，他接受亏损，押的是当前定价低估了这条能力曲线。

12. 测试封装已有配置，AEHR只是条件性小注

  • 在材料、测试和封装中，Rick提到Applied Materials、KLA、AMKR、FORM、Teradyne；台股相对较少，只明确提到联电UMC。他表示这些方向已有仓位，但并非每项都买得很多。
  • AEHR是跟随另一位KOL买的一点小仓位。条件是其wafer-level burn-in若获海力士、美光等接受，成为HBM标准流程，可能出现很大上涨；但他承认自己对技术了解有限，把它定义为高风险、高回报的bet。

13. NeoCloud的争议集中在扩张融资与电力合同估值

  • 主持人转述马斯克可能准备收购陷入资金困境的NeoCloud，涉及“两百多家”的说法。Rick则说NeoCloud是自己亏损最多的板块；Bio曾是第二大亏损来源，但已基本回来。
  • 他以自己称为“Coinbase”的公司为例，区分既有债务和未来扩张。既有融资利率已锁定，收入也锁定，电费上涨可以pass through；新借款变贵会阻碍扩张，但他不认为既有债务本身就足以导致破产：“赚的是地主的生意。”
  • 电力合同是另一块估值。他提到约1.5GW已投产，另有约1.5—2GW签约排队；若卖掉其中约1.5GW合同，他认为可能换回几十亿美元。将这些未投产合同估值计入资产后，他让AI算出的市净率约为1.6—1.8倍，属于其调整后的估算。
  • 他认为约15%的债券利率包含了过高的破产担忧，但也没有排除失败：管理层可能做错事，电力合同也可能贬值，让上述倍数回到2.6、2.8甚至3。他押另一条路径——合同继续涨价、调整后市净率低于1，公司届时反而更容易融资。

14. 清空比特币源于数学与量子风险的不确定性

  • Rick确认已清空多年持有的比特币，还打算减持部分以太坊；同时会保留一些crypto资产，对冲法币风险。这是实际仓位变化，并非仅仅表达担忧。
  • 他仍赞同Arthur Hayes对crypto的长期乐观，认为agent economy只能建立在crypto之上。但“什么资产会受益”还不确定；相对比特币，他更倾向以太坊，因此长期看好技术与持有哪种资产，在他这里是两个判断。
  • 第一层风险来自AI推进数学。他转述Vitalik对加密安全假设被动摇的担忧，并谈及Exponential Time Hypothesis，而非以太坊的ETH；对P与NP，他仍认为大概率最终会证明P不等于NP，但担忧相反结果可能冲击加密基础。
  • 第二层是AI加速量子计算。他既不确定破解椭圆曲线签名是否真要1000—1500个逻辑比特，也不确定实现这些能力还需5—7年，认为可能只有2—3年。这些都是他不愿继续重仓承受的时间表风险。

15. 即使Q day没有兑现，恐惧也可能先影响价格

  • Rick强调，即使技术风险最终不发生，担忧本身也可能造成很大跌幅；比特币流动性相对市值较小，不大的抛盘就可能大幅压价。他愿意先避过“上跳之前要先下蹲”，更怕下蹲时持有的资产，未必是之后上跳的资产。
  • 主持人补充的是条件推演：若公开密钥可以被用于推导私钥，资金控制权就会失守。应对可能涉及不再承认某个区块之前的资产，或全体地址做抗量子升级；据他转述，这类选择可能与比特币社群的去中心化原则发生冲突。
  • 主持人记得孙哥给出的窗口约为一到一年半，也提到TRON升级；但他同时怀疑对方是否想“吓一吓大家，然后抄底”，明确说“我不知道”。Rick对TRON具体安排也不清楚，结论仍是先避开这段高度不确定时期。

16. 他选择留在市场，等待多条技术曲线叠加

  • 被问到11月16日当周IPO、年底及2027年Q1走势，Rick回答“I don't know”，承认此前V形或U形反转的判断已错。他愿承受20%—30%、甚至之后再30%的回撤；按他的回顾，错过NTC涨得最凶的一个月，就错过了70%的涨幅。
  • 他把当前回调类比去年年底：当时美光曾从约240回到190，市场质疑prompt和工作流撑不起CapEx，后来coding提供了场景。现在质疑变成“除了coding还有什么”，而他看到AI for science正在形成下一轮用途；回调也可能更长，他不愿赌自己能踩准。
  • 更长的判断是，AI会压缩原有科技周期，并让生命科学、材料、能源、核聚变和量子的成熟度曲线陆续叠加。他转述Dario“未来7年解决所有癌症”的预期，推论上涨可能更剧烈、等待成本可能更低，强调这仍是他愿意押注的路径。
  • 当前仓位从大到小是存储、芯片、Bio、设备；点名持有美光、海力士、三星，以及NTC、ASML、台积电。“我当年怎么持币，我现在就怎么拿着接下来的AI板块。”他的操作原则是“time in the market，不要timing the market”，前提是基本逻辑没有反转。

来源：X Space

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/168x-rick-anthropic-ipo-ai-next-20261028

item.title: Gavin Baker on Anthropic's S-1, GPU Prices, and SpaceX
item.description: Gavin Baker calls Anthropic’s S-1 an upside surprise: about half the Fortune 500 has adopted it, with encouraging profitability, cash generation and unit economics. Open-weight infrastructure companies outgrow OpenAI and Anthropic as demand broadens, while GPU rental prices rose daily in October and forward capacity remains expensive into 2027. Potential IPOs and higher cloud pricing could ease reliance on external financing for the 2027 build-out, though Baker is unsure whether external financing has peaked.
item.content:encoded:
TBPN · Gavin Baker · 2026-10-27 · 41 min · 原语言 EN

Gavin Baker calls Anthropic’s S-1 an upside surprise: about half the Fortune 500 has adopted it, with encouraging profitability, cash generation and unit economics. Open-weight infrastructure companies outgrow OpenAI and Anthropic as demand broadens, while GPU rental prices rose daily in October and forward capacity remains expensive into 2027. Potential IPOs and higher cloud pricing could ease reliance on external financing for the 2027 build-out, though Baker is unsure whether external financing has peaked.

TL;DR

  • Baker reads Anthropic’s S-1 as an upside surprise with substantial enterprise headroom. He points to $10 billion burned, plus encouraging profitability, cash generation and unit economics. About half the Fortune 500 has adopted Anthropic, yet it represents just 0.1% of their expenses—suggesting diffusion is “maybe earlier than I thought we were.”
  • Anthropic’s disclosed customer mix challenges the concentrated-spending bear case. Baker cites only 250 accounts spending over $10 million, while a host highlights 11,000–12,000 spending over $100,000. Baker sees a “very diversified spending base,” while allowing that Ramp’s concentration data might still describe AI spending overall.
  • Open-weight infrastructure companies are outgrowing OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Baker. Fireworks, Baseten, Together, Modal and Cognition underpin his argument that demand is broadening beyond the major labs. Atreides led Fireworks’ latest round, where growth meant “the multiple was effectively going down” daily. Growth beyond Cursor is particularly notable as SpaceX insources Cursor’s compute.
  • GPU pricing signals tightness through 2027 despite the announced supply pipeline. Baker reports daily rental-price increases during October and expensive forward capacity: portfolio companies seeking another 4,000 Blackwells for September 2027 face sharply higher quotes than for their May–June 2026 clusters. “We’re not in backwardation anymore.”
  • Compute returns increasingly depend on execution and retaining pricing upside. Baker praises CoreWeave’s operations but says substantial capacity was contracted far below today’s market. A host argues that more spot exposure and prepayments can produce paybacks “well under a year.” Running clusters resembles “a Formula 1 team”; Baker says a new Jensen product with preassembled racks could shorten deployment and reduce working capital tied up in idle GPUs.
  • Training demand creates a potential inference-supply risk within Baker’s bullish framework. A bearish argument he considers compelling is that Anthropic dedicates 74% of its compute to training. That suggests room for more inference revenue, but if training needs decline, capacity could enter the inference market.
  • IPOs and repriced cloud contracts could reduce the build-out’s dependence on external financing. SpaceX and Anthropic becoming public and fully unlocked could restore mutual funds’ capacity for private investments. Higher cloud pricing could also lift operating cash flow enough to fund more of 2027’s infrastructure internally; Baker does not know whether external financing has peaked, but says, “I think we’re getting close.”

Digest

1. Anthropic’s S-1 pairs enormous scale with low enterprise penetration

  • Baker calls the S-1 “pretty clearly an upside surprise”: $10 billion burned, with encouraging profitability, cash generation and unit economics. About half the Fortune 500 has adopted Anthropic, yet it represents 0.1% of their expenses. Enterprise diffusion may be “earlier than I thought we were.” Baker also cites roughly $67 billion annualized if the reported third quarter is annualized.
  • A host argues that concentrated AI spending is natural among early obsessives, citing Ramp data suggesting 1% of companies account for 90% of spending. Baker disagrees about Anthropic’s customer mix: only 250 accounts spend over $10 million, while a host cites 11,000–12,000 spending over $100,000. Baker calls the S-1 more authoritative and says it shows a “very diversified spending base,” while allowing that Ramp might still describe AI overall.
  • Baker’s broader demand signal is open-weight infrastructure: Fireworks, Baseten, Together, Modal and Cognition are growing faster than either OpenAI or Anthropic. He says that was true during OpenAI’s summer acceleration and remains true amid Anthropic’s October reacceleration. Baker says Anthropic lost share in summer and is now gaining it. He doubts it would leave the October ARR blank in the S-1 without expecting a strong number, while hoping the market moves beyond monthly ARR figures.
  • A host says private-market investors on the West Coast already know these companies are at scale and growing, while the news is less familiar on the East Coast. Atreides led Fireworks’ latest round, and Baker says growth made pricing difficult: “The multiple was effectively going down” every day. He finds inference-cloud growth beyond Cursor especially striking because SpaceX has been insourcing Cursor’s compute. His assessment is that the ecosystem has accelerated and diversified.

2. Grokbot wins Baker through ease of use and information routing

  • A host asks whether Cursor’s product and distribution can help Grokbot despite xAI models not stunning on a particular benchmark. Baker answers as a user: Grokbot is “the most impactful AI product” for him and his firm, and he has about 17 Grokbots. He had kludged together a setup with Claude Code and says that may have been user error.
  • Baker describes investing as “making sure the right information gets to the right person at the right time,” and says Grokbot is very good at that. A host adds the Sunday-night research example: an agent can spend a million tokens investigating a market-size question without asking an employee to work for six hours.
  • Personal agents have not displaced his assistant Susan. “I guess I have executive assistant privilege,” Baker says; he has downloaded Instinct and played with Muse, but says Grokbot has been transformative for his professional use cases.

3. Compute scarcity extends into 2027, but operators capture different economics

  • Baker says October rental prices for essentially every kind of GPU have risen daily. Silicon Data, in which Atreides is an investor and which Baker calls the most authoritative source, says compute is now in contango: forward capacity is expensive too. Portfolio companies with 4,000 Blackwells for May or June 2026 are shocked by the cost of adding another 4,000 in September 2027. Despite supply coming online, Baker says it is hard for them to find compute well into 2027: “we’re not in backwardation anymore.”
  • Baker takes Sarah Friar’s comments literally: long-term compute commitments signed before May 2026 are “way in the money.” A contract buying compute for perhaps $10 or $15 a watt could be resold at a large premium; Friar described a “3, 4, 5X premium.”
  • Baker says CoreWeave runs GPUs well but locked in substantial compute under long-term contracts now far below market. A host explains that CoreWeave sold at fixed prices and argues that more spot exposure and fewer long-term offtake agreements could improve the economics. The host says selling into the spot market could mean paybacks well under a year and large prepayments.
  • The host compares running a GPU cluster to running a Formula 1 team, requiring experienced operators and coordinated execution. Baker agrees that the key is bringing on GPUs, energizing them and running them well. He names CoreWeave, Crusoe, Nebius, SpaceX and the big hyperscalers as companies with a track record of execution, while saying the future remains uncertain.
  • Baker points to a new Jensen product: seven racks, preassembled, that you “just literally plug in and it works.” He says some operators otherwise take three or six months to energize GPUs; at this scale, six months could leave hundreds of billions of dollars in assets generating no revenue. Shortening deployment would take working capital out of the market.

4. Responsible optimism includes a training-driven supply risk

  • Baker says he treats X as an exercise in “cultivated equanimity,” searching criticism for useful bearish arguments. One he finds compelling is that Anthropic dedicates 74% of its compute to training. That could indicate room for more inference revenue, but if training needs decline, substantial capacity could enter the inference market. “I’m not on X to be right”; he says he is trying to learn and get to the right answer.
  • A host raises the timing concern in biology: infrastructure costs arrive now, while drug revenues may take years. Baker says “we’ll see how long it takes,” and points to Montana’s new-drug program and the possibility of using existing compounds for new diseases. He says AI has helped identify a drug that has existed for 50 or 60 years and can effectively cure a rare disease that devastates 10,000 children a year. A friend did the work, but Baker says it is the friend’s story to tell.
  • Baker says AI’s public-relations effort is “-5 out of 100” and the industry needs to tell more stories. His public case includes lives saved, benefits for blue-collar Americans and small towns, reindustrialization, and increased electrical generation: “You cannot reindustrialize without power.” He recounts a skeptic demanding data centers in America’s wealthiest county, then points to Loudoun County, which Baker says is the wealthiest and has the highest per-capita number of data centers.

5. Commodity research is broader than Atreides’ portfolio exposure

  • Asked how far he follows energy infrastructure and commodities, Baker says he pays close attention. He ran a diversified fund for nine years and previously invested in energy and natural resources. He has not made those areas a large part of the portfolio, but says investors need to cast a wide research net and focus capital where the firm has a competitive advantage.
  • Baker says gold has long had a place in portfolio construction. He finds it amusing how strongly some gold bulls react to asteroid mining, calling it a challenge to their worldview; a host compares the possibility of technological disruption to lab-grown diamonds.
  • His concrete private-market exposure is a company with a chemical process for refining rare earths, rather than acquiring mines. “The problem with rare earths isn’t that they’re rare”; refining them is dirty. Baker also credits DARPA’s efforts and says investors never know where a weak but important signal will come from.

6. IPOs and cloud cash flow could loosen the capital constraint

  • Baker argues that SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs can unlock another pool of private capital. American mutual funds face limits on illiquid holdings; when those companies are public and fully unlocked, funds regain room to buy private assets. Baker names Capital Research, T. Rowe Price, MSAM, GSAM and Franklin Templeton as existing participants.
  • Sovereign funding is already substantial, particularly in the GCC and UAE. Baker singles out MGX and Mubadala, calling the UAE “extremely front-footed” on AI; Atreides and Valor co-led Crusoe with Mubadala.
  • Baker expects aggregate hyperscaler and neocloud revenue growth to keep accelerating as underpriced contracts reset and more compute gets spot exposure. Revenue is dropping through at high margins, lifting operating cash flow and potentially financing more of the 2027 build-out than people expect. His hedge matters: “I don’t know if we’ve seen the peak of external financing,” but “I think we’re getting close.”
  • A host suggests public ownership could moderate polarized AI sentiment as direct holders grow from perhaps 50,000 people to millions. Baker favors direct ownership over a foundation whose board or bureaucrats allocate the money. He says every child in America will have a SpaceX share and encourages more companies and wealthy people, including Michael Dell and Brad Kirshner, to support broad participation: “Give everybody a stake in capitalism.”

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/gavin-baker-anthropic-s-s-1-gpu-prices-spacex

item.title: How Anthropic ships the #1 LLM in the World — with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang
item.description: S-1 figures show revenue per employee rising from $1.4 million to $6.6 million and a first 19% GAAP-profitable quarter. More than 50% of customers above $100,000 in trailing-12-month revenue use Claude Platform; Managed Agents keeps credentials beyond agents’ view. A Claude-assisted Rust port cut CPU use 40–50% and first-token latency 10–20%, while CPU scarcity and personalization remain constraints.
item.content:encoded:
Latent Space · swyx、Katelyn Lesse、Angela Jiang · 2026-10-27 · 107 min · 原语言 EN

S-1 figures show revenue per employee rising from $1.4 million to $6.6 million and a first 19% GAAP-profitable quarter. More than 50% of customers above $100,000 in trailing-12-month revenue use Claude Platform; Managed Agents keeps credentials beyond agents’ view. A Claude-assisted Rust port cut CPU use 40–50% and first-token latency 10–20%, while CPU scarcity and personalization remain constraints.

TL;DR

  • The opening’s IPO case rests on a sharp improvement in employee and capital efficiency. Citing Anthropic’s S-1, the host reports $6.6 million in trailing-12-month revenue per employee versus $1.4 million a year earlier, and a first profitable quarter at 19% on a GAAP basis versus a loss equal to 129% of revenue. The opening also puts lifetime fundraising above $100 billion and burn below $10 billion, with an IPO expected “in two weeks at a $2 trillion valuation.”
  • Claude Platform gives Anthropic a business that extends beyond selling access to model intelligence. The opening says more than 50% of customers with at least $100,000 in trailing-12-month revenue use the platform, whose primitives also underpin Claude Code and Cowork. Managed Agents adds infrastructure and harness management, complementing the host’s framing of Anthropic as a cloud platform.
  • Opus 5.5’s pitch combines stronger economics with a more usable model. Katelyn Lesse highlights price cuts, less convoluted writing than Opus 5, and demand for “good intelligence per dollar.” The guests qualify the host’s “top model” description with “depends who you ask”; the opening’s prediction that Fable 5.5 will probably follow within two weeks comes with an explicit “I don’t have insider information.”
  • Safety engineering has become a major component of the model-release workload. Releases now require decisions about retention, online safeguards, offline review, verification programs, and authorization throughout the stack. Anti-distillation measures preserve thinking blocks while accommodating legitimate compaction. Katelyn explains the safety rationale; the host says safety, rather than commercial impact, is the main concern and notes that distillation usage pays Anthropic.
  • CPU availability is becoming a material constraint alongside accelerator supply. The guests describe APIs, sandboxes, research, and growing CI activity competing for Anthropic’s allocation. A Claude-assisted port of the Messages API from Python to Rust delivered roughly 40–50% CPU savings and a 10–20% improvement in time to first token; the critical human contributions were “the plan” and “the verification.”
  • Separating the agent’s brain from its hands turns security into an infrastructure property. Managed Agents keeps the harness durable, execution isolated, and credentials in a separate vault, with an egress proxy injecting secrets the agent never sees. That architecture also improves startup latency and resilience when sandboxes fail; a guest says a colleague who prioritized security was vindicated.
  • Evaluation and personalization remain unresolved constraints on product quality. Different customers want conflicting levels of initiative, and the guests admit, “We don’t do a great job of it.” Their response combines broader eval suites, adjustable effort, and managed harnesses; Angela Jiang is more bullish on a consistent Claude that dynamically changes effort than on visibly switching users between models.
  • The next workload opportunity is longer autonomous work with stronger verification. Angela sees some tasks approaching intelligence saturation, while difficult engineering and science problems remain open. The closing multi-agent advice is one lead, shared state, and asynchronous workers that do not block each other; throughout, humans retain responsibility for quality, because faster implementation is no excuse to ship “10X more features into prod.”

Digest

1. The IPO framing centers on efficiency and a broader platform business

  • The opening host says Anthropic filed its S-1 that day and frames an IPO expected “in two weeks at a $2 trillion valuation.” He contrasts reported lifetime fundraising above $100 billion with lifetime burn below $10 billion. These figures establish the episode’s opening question: how is Anthropic shipping what he regards as the strongest models while building its business unusually efficiently?
  • The cited operating figures describe a sharp reversal: trailing-12-month revenue per employee rises from $1.4 million to $6.6 million, almost fivefold. The host says Anthropic was “losing half a dollar for every dollar of revenue” in Q2 2025 and now generates $2 of revenue per $1 of cost. Its first profitable quarter shows 19% GAAP profit, versus a prior loss equal to 129% of revenue.
  • The host explains the improvement through two reinforcing loops. Better Claude models unlock use cases, adoption produces feedback, and feedback improves Claude; separately, adoption increases revenue and growth, attracting investment that funds more capability. He presents these as the S-1’s “improvement loop” and “investment loop,” linking product performance with the resources available to keep improving it.
  • More than 50% of customers with at least $100,000 in trailing-12-month revenue reportedly use Claude Platform. The host emphasizes that Claude Code and Cowork use the same exposed primitives. He interprets Anthropic’s positioning as moving from chatbots and copilots toward “virtual collaborators”: systems that own goals, use tools, self-correct, and work alongside people across longer tasks.

2. Opus 5.5 targets intelligence per dollar and clearer communication

  • Asked to celebrate the “top model in the world,” the guests immediately qualify it: “Depends who you ask.” Katelyn is particularly pleased that feedback about Opus 5’s convoluted writing translated into a cleaner successor. Price cuts address a separate demand: customers increasingly care about “good intelligence per dollar,” so the team must improve both intelligence and its cost.
  • The opening was recorded around the Opus 5.5 launch and describes strong reactions from the host’s testers. His additional prediction that Anthropic is sitting on Fable 5.5 and will “probably” release it within two weeks is explicitly speculation: “I don’t have insider information.” He connects that timing to the anticipated IPO rather than presenting a confirmed release schedule.
  • Katelyn describes product’s role as balancing intelligence, safety, cost, and commercial impact; she says engineering emphasizes integration and developer experience. Their technical product managers and product-minded engineers deliberately overlap. Asked whether software engineering being “solved” will merge the roles, Katelyn rejects that strength of language: “Ambitions will continue to elevate,” leaving substantial operating and design work for humans.

3. Anti-distillation changes protect safeguards while preserving legitimate uses

  • The discussion of “Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLMs” starts with responsible disclosure, which both guests welcome. Katelyn says the paper exposed a gap Anthropic already understood: extracting chain of thought is “one of the most powerful ways that you can distill models.” The engineering question was how to close that avenue without making useful API integrations substantially worse.
  • Katelyn’s rationale centers on safeguards: Anthropic classifies generated tokens to reduce harmful outcomes, while a distilled model could run without those protections. The host, not Angela, says the primary concern is safety rather than commercialization and notes that “if you distill from us, you actually pay us.” His concern is a derivative of Claude being used negatively without the surrounding safety systems. Angela separately says distillation has become significantly harder in the areas Anthropic can measure.
  • The team distinguishes two kinds of user-experience damage: an annoying integration migration that preserves capabilities, and a change that makes previously possible work impossible. They especially want to avoid the latter. Preserving thinking blocks across turns, and tightening their treatment across accounts, required separating legitimate workflows from extraction techniques rather than simply banning every manipulation of reasoning traces.
  • Compaction supplied the concrete test. Some customers’ existing strategies would break under preserved-thinking requirements, so Anthropic worked with customers and open-source harness maintainers and shipped an API compaction feature compatible with them. Angela does not claim complete visibility or that extraction has been eliminated.

4. Every model now needs its own safety deployment policy

  • The guest discussing release safety frames it across three dimensions: architecture and infrastructure security, online safeguards operating during generation, and offline classification of stored data. Capability determines the work required. Katelyn adds that specific spikes in biology or cybersecurity can demand different treatment depending on whether capabilities appear offense-dominant or defense-dominant, rather than treating all intelligence improvements as equivalent.
  • Retention addresses behavior that may not be recognized while an individual request streams. Networks of accounts may collectively reveal malicious use or distillation, requiring automated or human review. Angela explicitly distinguishes models: Opus 5.5 does not carry the data-retention requirements Fable has. Those requirements are decisions made for individual releases, with engineering needed to enforce them.
  • Cyber verification and the newer life-science verification program let approved users access dual-use capabilities with reduced safeguards for specified purposes. Legitimate vulnerability research and biological research are the examples. Authorization must follow the request throughout the system; Angela contrasts that with casually issuing a key and flipping a feature flag. Launching these programs is now part of launching the model itself.

5. Generic trust grants make uncertain deployment scenarios manageable

  • Fable’s rollback becomes Angela’s example of a roadmap that cannot rely on confidently forecasting use cases. Something the team would not have predicted nevertheless happened, establishing a nonzero probability. Her response is “deeply probabilistic” product management: build “a portfolio of bets,” including controls that may never be needed but provide options if an unusual situation returns.
  • The access system began with granting particular users particular capabilities, but the team chose more generic primitives than conventional product scoping might favor. Those primitives proved useful for broader model access, trusted programs, and model deployments. Work toward a single-button rollback extends that same foundation. Angela says this generic approach has repeatedly paid dividends, while leaving the value of any particular hedge uncertain.
  • A “trust grant” is ordinary authorization expressed through Anthropic’s own data model, not a fundamentally different security concept. For Fable 5.1’s preserved-thinking rollout, existing customers received a grace period to update integrations; grants tracked those exceptions. A service on the request’s hot path checks whether the requester holds the relevant permission, allowing the same mechanism to support multiple policies.

6. Model feedback is most valuable when external harnesses expose failures

  • Model launches move through candidate versions, evaluation, internal dogfooding, and selected external testing. Customers such as Cognition provide a different harness from Anthropic’s own products, which matters because Claude is intended to generalize. Angela wants both formal results and subjective reactions: “Do you like it? What don’t you like?” Negative feedback is often the most useful input for further improvement.
  • The host’s pushback is that feedback still resembles a Slack channel saying, “Hey, this thing seems weird.” Angela agrees the process can be informal, partly because the team is “racing” to minimize the interval between a testable model and broad availability. Early-access customers therefore tend to have robust eval suites capable of producing actionable evidence quickly, alongside subjective impressions.
  • Laziness versus initiative illustrates why outside testing matters. One customer wants Claude to “just finish my task”; another is still planning when Claude unexpectedly writes code. Katelyn says getting that spectrum exactly right for everyone is “literally impossible.” In one case, excessive laziness led the team to put a candidate “back in the oven,” a problem internal product usage might have missed.

7. Personalization exceeds what today’s parameters can express

  • The host uses a code benchmark to challenge model evaluation: a benchmark can penalize excessive activity or file creation even when a user’s CLAUDE.md instructions could suppress that behavior. Is the benchmark then unfairly penalizing the model? The guests’ candid answer on evaluating personalization is, “We don’t do a great job of it.” A constitution can help, Katelyn says, but does not resolve conflicting preferences about how assistance should behave.
  • Effort provides a limited customization mechanism. The conversation specifically identifies Claude Code’s default as medium, while Katelyn says defaults can differ across free users, prosumers, enterprise, Cowork, and API use. The preference is for “gentle defaults” with user control. Some users want maximum intelligence; others benefit from lower effort and faster responses, making a single aggressive default difficult to justify.
  • Katelyn describes a “funny mishmash” of effort, budgets, and other parameters, with no obvious combination for every task. Choices include whether to expose low/medium/high or a 1-to-100 scale, and which controls to retire. As the number of customers grows, she says relying on judgment calls about conflicting preferences will not scale indefinitely; richer ways for Claude to absorb personalization will be needed, but are not solved today.

8. Managed Agents packages the harness while leaving room for experimentation

  • Angela distinguishes the Messages API’s “raw token access” from Claude Managed Agents, a higher abstraction that lets developers define an agent and start a session. Anthropic supplies infrastructure and a harness, including work to accommodate new model parameters and breaking changes. The value is programmatic access without requiring every customer to repeatedly rediscover how to get the best behavior from each release.
  • Managed Agents shares substantial infrastructure with first-party products, including the sandbox fleet, although shared infrastructure does not mean identical harnesses. Angela says the provided harness is “intentionally simple”: it incorporates useful practices and handles difficult but undifferentiated parts of the agent loop. More opinionated strategies can then sit above that foundation instead of being imposed on every developer.
  • Asked whether memory and dreaming have stalled, Angela acknowledges that some feature work has slowed relative to earlier in the year as safety consumes more attention. That is not an abandonment: “We love skills.” Memory and dreaming still address continuous improvement, while the team increasingly wants developers to extend existing primitives and Anthropic to concentrate on providing safe access to model capabilities.
  • Dreaming is itself a multi-agent construction: another managed agent examines the previous agent and writes memories for it. “It’s managed agents all the way down.” Angela also names best-of-N and verifier agents as possible strategies. An update expected “relatively soon” would expose underlying primitives and templates so developers could construct their own variants, rather than only consuming Anthropic’s particular dreaming implementation.

9. Agent engineering increasingly resembles experimental research

  • Angela’s eval advice is breadth: “You probably need more rather than less.” Static deterministic checks and LLM judges serve different purposes; a small supposedly perfect suite will not answer every question. She also recommends starting simply. Debating an elaborate menu of evaluation methods while having zero actual evals is worse than implementing a basic useful check and improving it.
  • The host proposes treating engineering like research: define the goal, formalize an eval, label results, prototype, and scale runs. Failure diagnosis must consider at least three possibilities: the eval is wrong, the environment is wrong, or the model is wrong. Katelyn agrees that “a lot of the time your eval is wrong.” This imports habits familiar to model researchers into application engineering, where satisfying a conventional product requirements document previously dominated.
  • Claude can help build both evals and the interface for grading them. The hosts contrast intimidating JSONL files with a usable left/right comparison UI, where people add ratings and comments. Those judgments become feedback Claude can consume to improve the system. Katelyn anticipates Managed Agents tooling that feels like working with Claude to create evaluations, rather than requiring a separate unfamiliar workflow.
  • A performance blog supplies an example, but the transcript gives differing figures: the host first says 9 of 12 targets were done in about three days, then later says 12 of 13 targets were hit in three days during a two-week effort. The discussion considers expanding the improvement list rather than treating faster implementation as a reason to invent unrelated products. The guests also enjoy publishing actual prompts because the method is often less exotic than imagined: sometimes it is simply, “Try harder, Claude.”

10. CPU demand now requires the planning once associated with accelerators

  • Katelyn says CPU scarcity is “as much of a problem today as the accelerator layer.” Capacity that teams once expected to obtain on demand, provided they had budget, now requires advance planning. VMs and sandboxes are part of the constraint. Her account is not confined to Anthropic: she says other people she talks to across the industry are encountering similar shortages.
  • Product services, APIs, applications, sandbox execution, research, and CI all draw on CPU. More generated code means more CI runs, adding demand beyond the agents’ immediate work. Research and product sandboxing do not commingle, but CPU allocation across the company remains “a zero-sum game”: Anthropic secures capacity from cloud providers and must divide that supply among competing internal needs.
  • The response combines procurement, more efficient sandbox infrastructure, and application efficiency without compromising tenant isolation or security.
