Scale and quality determine whether another supplier is worth integrating. Anthropic also runs across all three clouds, limiting reliance on a single provider’s specialized compute shape; the guest says the common foundation often has to be the most vanilla capabilities available across environments.

11. A Claude-assisted Rust port cuts the Messages API’s resource cost

  • Katelyn says that when she joined a little over a year earlier, the Messages API was a Python monolith in one GCP region. The team has since expanded across regions and confronted a CPU wall. It chose Rust despite initially having no Rust developer in the room. Claude would write implementation code; humans would design the distributed system and learn what they needed to operate it.
  • The crucial work was “the plan to do the thing, and then the verification of the thing.” The team built an entire Rust counterpart and sent shadow traffic through it, comparing outputs against Python before gradually enabling production traffic. The conversation contrasts that with the incremental, multi-year migration previously expected. A few more experienced Rust developers were hired along the way.
  • The guest describing the port says the Rust Messages API had fully rolled out the previous week. The reported ballpark savings are roughly 40–50% on CPU and approximately 10–20% improvement in time to first token, with greater improvements on longer-running workloads. These are operating results from the port, distinct from the separate blog example about making Claude.ai faster in a few days.
  • Scope discipline mattered: it was a port, while the rest of the organization kept adding API features. The migration team used static analysis and coordination to maintain parity, resisting redesign. Later opportunities include storing conversation state so clients need not repeatedly send the entire history. Prompt caching alone does not remove that transfer; long conversations may be few by user count but substantial by token volume.

12. Separating brain and hands improves durability before it improves security

  • A guest explains that Managed Agents could initially have been Claude Code placed inside a sandbox with an API attached. That was insufficient: callers wait for both sandbox and agent startup before receiving tokens, and a dead sandbox can kill the agent. The eventual design puts the harness on a durable server, keeps state separately, and spawns execution environments when needed.
  • Reliability and latency initially dominated the team’s explanation. A product manager kept insisting, “The most important property of this architecture is security.” The guest says they apologized to that colleague the previous day. The change of mind matters: separating orchestration from execution supplies security properties that were less obvious when the team primarily evaluated the architecture through product performance.
  • Credentials live in a separate vault. The agent sees a placeholder; when it calls a service, an egress proxy retrieves and injects the appropriate secret. This avoids putting raw credentials inside the agent’s execution environment and then trying to scrub or conceal them afterward. The guest calls the separation a “literal infrastructure wall” between the agent and those credentials.
  • Sandboxes add domain allowlists or completely disabled network access, constraining what agent-written code can contact. The guest emphasizes both architecture and configuration when customers ask about containment. Managed Agents packages those controls and subsequent improvements: customers receive evolving protections as Anthropic learns, rather than having to independently reconstruct every credential-handling, networking, and execution decision as the field changes.

13. Training breakouts and production deployments have different conditions

  • Challenged on whether sandbox escapes indicate defective technology or poor implementation, a guest distinguishes training incidents from deployed systems. Training may effectively tell a boxed-in model, “Solve an impossible task. I’m going to stress you out. Ready, set, go,” incentivizing escape attempts. Production can include online safeguards and separated infrastructure absent from that setup. The guest cautions against treating those environments as interchangeable.
  • The host also questions advocating “pacing” while releasing a frontier model 11 days later. The response is that pacing means doing the security and safeguards work needed to feel comfortable releasing; Opus 5.5 met those requirements. The guest still describes long-running agents as nascent, with teams figuring things out and racing to install controls, rather than presenting the surrounding engineering as finished.

14. Safety fallbacks expose the same unresolved problem as model routing

  • False positives can interrupt benign work. The host describes asking Fable to analyze its safety card: it reasoned for about five minutes, reached cybersecurity material, then fell back to Opus. The trigger appeared to involve the evolving reasoning and context rather than just the initial request. A user doing biology homework could likewise encounter a block despite a legitimate purpose.
  • The host’s objection is that a less capable classifier may misjudge work performed by a smarter model. A guest responds that classification and answering are different capabilities: recognizing danger need not require being able to carry it out. A smarter judge could help, but introduces cost and latency. The guests acknowledge the problem without claiming a definitive solution.
  • Angela explains that the API exposes several choices. Customers can opt into server-side fallbacks, use client-side SDK helpers to manage them, or re-prompt and continue with the same model. The apps’ fallback behavior therefore is not the only available integration. Angela would prefer a more unified experience that answers the benign part appropriately while reducing access to the problematic capability.
  • Angela connects this to ordinary cost routing: neither the task nor the model is perfectly understood upfront, and new complexity emerges during execution. Visible switches can make the experience convoluted and personalities inconsistent. She is more bullish on a consistent model that starts cheaply at low effort and scales effort continuously as needed. Across different providers, she says she does not know how to solve that discontinuity.

15. Long-running tasks remain an important source of unsaturated demand

  • Angela says intelligence appears increasingly saturated for some workloads, while other classes remain “very unsaturated”—more than people may anticipate. The emerging return comes from “extremely long-running agentic tasks” on problems that historically resisted brute force but might yield to more intelligence. She sees value both for businesses doing the work themselves and startups building agentic products around it.
  • Existing demand includes coding and enterprise products automating distinct processes. Some of those applications are starting to work; others still are not. Biology and cybersecurity introduce another category of hard science and engineering work, beyond straightforward process automation. Angela describes these as increasingly interesting workloads showing up on the platform, without claiming that capability or reliable execution has become universal.

16. Faster implementation leaves humans responsible for judgment and quality

  • Angela says that for documents and code, people should use Claude but ensure the result is high quality; passing along an unread generated artifact transfers the author’s work to the reader, which she calls unfair. Katelyn emphasizes that humans remain responsible for the quality. Consumers should send actual slop back, but avoid reflexively rejecting good work because an em dash or another “Claude-ism” reveals AI assistance. Quality and stylistic telltales are different questions.
  • In engineering, humans ensure system designs and plans are sound; Claude writes much of the code; verification establishes whether the result meets the bar. Katelyn says some changes need only a quick approval. That does not mean handing the production system to Claude with “Good luck”: operating and evolving large systems still requires human expertise.
  • The host cites the warning that new capabilities should not simply produce “10X more features into prod.” Katelyn argues that foundational product planning does not disappear because agents accelerate part of the process. The host admits the tension: when experimentation is cheap, trying everything feels attractive. The counterargument is to use that speed in service of an intentional goal and better understanding of users.
  • The same tension appears in management. Katelyn can spend an entire day unblocking decisions in Slack and feel she produced nothing; Angela protects time for thinking and writing, at the cost of being harder to reach. The host’s correction is that resolving those problems produces “a functioning team” that is unblocked. Claude assistance does not remove every difficult decision that reaches their inboxes.

17. Developer relations is shifting toward teaching people and their agents

  • Katelyn says the platform business can disappear from Anthropic’s public narrative between research, policy, Claude Code, and Cowork. Separate platform and Claude Code DevRel teams address different developer ecosystems. Platform still needs a manager, with individual contributors reporting directly to her. Its challenge includes finding a voice and identity, alongside the familiar responsibilities of product feedback, content, and community.
  • Lance’s deep technical teaching on memory, costs, and evals exemplifies the approach Katelyn wants; CJ contributes examples and community work. The host adds the “master builder” model, borrowed from Lego: demonstrate something impressive with the platform so developers understand what they could build. The work helps reveal possible applications, rather than merely announcing that another capability exists.
  • Cookbooks increasingly illustrate possibilities rather than serving as code people copy. Katelyn contrasts an elaborate older computer-use implementation with the Claude API skill, built by Lance and owned by DevRel, which helps coding agents create integrations. Angela adds that developers can point Claude at a reference architecture. Best practices increasingly reach users through the agents helping them build.
  • The host challenges whether engineers and product leaders should themselves be the public faces, as Boris is for Claude Code. His proposed separation is a public-facing expert supported by production staff: spend 30–60 minutes on a brain dump, then return to work while others help publish it. Katelyn sees DevRel enabling colleagues to communicate well; the host compares that support to HR helping everyone hire.

18. Multi-agent gains depend on shared state and workers that can progress independently

  • Angela’s closing recommendation is to revisit experiments previously constrained by cost or token efficiency. Opus 5.5’s economics and reduced verbosity might let developers get further by letting it run. She specifically recommends trying a multi-agent setup, while declining to supply a narrow recipe for the most promising application. She wants to see what people build with the additional capability.
  • The closing advice is to have one lead coordinate work that can be parallelized, with shared context and asynchronous sub-agents that do not block each other. The guests’ two architectural priorities are shared state and independent progress. Subject to the problem being suitable, they expect gains; beyond those constraints, the advice is to experiment and “let it rip” rather than overprescribe every role.
  • The hosts distinguish assigning agents fixed jobs from agents assigning work among themselves. A guest expects smarter Claude models to improve at splitting, cloning, and adapting their own arrangements. The guest “wouldn’t be surprised” if experimentation yielded interesting results on problems that previously seemed intractable—perhaps solving something “in maybe one shot or something.” The language remains an invitation to test, not a performance guarantee.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/anthropic-ships-1-llm-world-safely-separating-br

item.title: Ep. 041 - EMERGENCY: Inside the Anthropic’s S-1 (Tokenomics/ Markets)
item.description: S-1 disclosures of two profitable quarters, margins above 10%, 85% inference gross margins and 41% compute margins challenge the subsidy thesis. Joey cites ninefold existing-customer spending growth; Jeremie says prospective resources above $200 billion frame $500–600 billion of compute commitments. Whether revenue can monetize 2027 capacity remains unresolved, alongside 25% revenue concentration among the top five customers.
item.content:encoded:
SemiAnalysis · Jordan Nanos、Doug O'Laughlin、Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros、Joey Brookhart · 2026-10-27 · 55 min · 原语言 EN

S-1 disclosures of two profitable quarters, margins above 10%, 85% inference gross margins and 41% compute margins challenge the subsidy thesis. Joey cites ninefold existing-customer spending growth; Jeremie says prospective resources above $200 billion frame $500–600 billion of compute commitments. Whether revenue can monetize 2027 capacity remains unresolved, alongside 25% revenue concentration among the top five customers.

TL;DR

  • Anthropic’s disclosed economics challenge the idea that frontier inference depends on subsidies. Joey cites two profitable quarters, margins above 10%, 85% inference gross margins and 41% compute margins. Jeremie highlights 90% gross margins and a potential 40% EBIT profile, retaining the condition “if they get there”: “You’re selling a dollar for 10 cents.”
  • The compute commitments look manageable to the panel because liquidity and revenue have grown alongside them. Jeremie contrasts $500–600 billion of commitments with over $100 billion already on the books and prospective funding taking resources above $200 billion. His reassurance—“they’re not going to go under”—does not settle whether revenue will accelerate enough to monetize the 2027 capacity.
  • Customer expansion supports the growth story, but concentration still matters. Joey describes existing-customer spending rising ninefold, versus fivefold in Q1; the discussion ultimately separates the top five customers’ 25% revenue contribution from 48% through cloud marketplaces. Jordan calls purchasing commitments and slow model migration “really sticky”: 20% of Q3 revenue still came from models released before April.
  • SpaceX’s expensive, flexible compute can benefit from financing pressure on competing neoclouds. Doug describes a “liquidity run” on neocloud debt and interprets Musk’s criticism as competitive positioning. Jeremie says $14/hour GB300 pricing could persist or strengthen if demand outgrows even substantial supply additions; short commitments also conserve Anthropic’s balance-sheet capacity despite lower margins.
  • Compute efficiency strengthens Anthropic’s economics, although the panel disputes how much credit belongs to the company. Joey cites inference revenue per megawatt rising from $16 million to over $60 million. Doug asks how much reflects Anthropic versus broader hardware gains; Jordan and Doug emphasize software, accelerator diversity and model-assisted engineering: “the model is the differentiator.”
  • Enterprise budgets offer substantial runway, with Q4 seasonality an unresolved counterweight. Joey puts Anthropic at roughly 0.1% of Fortune 500 operating budgets and expects a strong 2027 as formal AI budgeting expands. But the prior holiday period brought a 20% spending decline over two weeks, and Doug’s market assessment is blunt: “The AI stocks are tired.”
  • The disagreement on OpenAI concerns competitive economics more than survival. Jordan frames OpenAI as caught between rivals; Jeremie argues weaker “best-in-breed” positioning would force price competition, but says he remains bullish on both and finds OpenAI more reliable for some data analysis. A panelist raises OpenAI’s enterprise sales as a countercase, while another notes its improving execution and the burden of supporting a large free consumer base.

Digest

1. Inference margins undermine the subsidy argument

  • Joey opens with two profitable quarters, margins above 10%, 85% inference gross margins and 41% compute margins. His explanation combines inference efficiencies with efficient sales, marketing and partnerships: customers expand usage without requiring an equally large acquisition effort. More revenue can therefore flow through without recreating the selling costs associated with winning the original account.
  • Jeremie describes the incremental economics as 90% gross margins and a potential 40% EBIT profile, “if they get there.” His rebuttal to the subsidy thesis is deliberately simple: “You’re selling a dollar for 10 cents.” The significance is that customers genuinely want the output and pay substantially more than its delivery cost.
  • Joey’s retention example supplies the growth mechanism: a customer spending $1 a year earlier now spends $9; in Q1, the comparable figure was $5. That expansion requires little additional selling. “There’s not much you have to do,” he says of upselling usage, connecting customer behavior directly to the margin story.

2. Large commitments look different against a funded balance sheet

  • Jeremie’s data-center perspective starts with creditworthiness. Developers have wanted to sell Anthropic capacity but could not readily finance projects against its credit; the IPO opportunity remains contingent on investment-grade standing. He cites over $100 billion on the books and expects IPO proceeds and promised funding to take resources above $200 billion, after a period when the company “barely burned any cash.”
  • The $500–600 billion compute headline needs a denominator, Jeremie argues. At roughly $100 billion per gigawatt in the Nscale comparison, half a trillion dollars would purchase only 5 GW. Anthropic has contracted materially more capacity than that, implying a comparatively low commitment burden per gigawatt. Its current footprint is under 5 GW, with a substantial increase expected by the end of next year.
  • His comparison with the earlier OpenAI scare is roughly $80 billion of revenue against half a trillion dollars of commitments, rather than $20 billion annualized against $1.4 trillion. Jeremie forecasts Anthropic reaching “multiple hundreds of billions” in annual revenue next year. He also emphasizes the mix of long contracts and flexible arrangements with hyperscalers and SpaceX, rather than treating every commitment as equally binding.
  • Further funding includes Google’s $40 billion package, with another $20 billion tied to milestones such as going public, and a $42 billion Broadcom arrangement that Jeremie says enables more TPU purchases. He regards much of the 2027 compute roadmap as de-risked. The remaining question is explicit: “Can they actually accelerate the revenue enough?” Funding capacity establishes resilience; monetization still has to follow.

3. Customer concentration and distribution require separate readings

  • Jeremie initially wonders what remains if the top-five and cloud-marketplace revenue shares add together. Jordan explains that the categories can overlap, and Doug probes whether the customer figures are look-through. Joey clarifies that the 48% of revenue from CSP marketplaces excludes the top five customers. The discussion settles on 25% from the top five, 48% through cloud marketplaces and 27% elsewhere.
  • Jordan cites alternative-data panels in which the top 1% of customers account for 70–80% of the panel’s spending. That is panel evidence, not Anthropic’s disclosed customer mix. Jordan also cites 250,000 customers on a trailing-12-month basis and says SemiAnalysis is one of 1,900 in the “million-plus” group. He and Joey note that the top 5% of Claude Code users spend $18,000 annually, while non-Claude Code users spend under $75 monthly.
  • Jordan’s stickiness argument combines purchasing commitments with slow migration: 20% of Q3 revenue came from models released before April. Fortune 500 buyers using Bedrock may need certifications before upgrading, whereas startups can move faster. He treats that lag and AWS-style purchasing agreements as evidence that relationships are “really sticky.” Speculation about the identities of anonymous major customers remains speculation, with several suggestions disputed rather than resolved.

4. Neocloud financing pressure can sustain SpaceX’s premium

  • Doug interprets Musk’s attacks on neoclouds as competitive behavior from someone operating a neocloud himself. A “liquidity run on all the neocloud debt” impairs rivals’ ability to finance capacity and can redirect investors toward SpaceX, lowering its cost of capital. A panelist warns that data centers are more constrained than chips today, but that could reverse by the end of next year as Musk pursues 10–20 GW.
  • Asked whether $14/hour GB300 contracts cancellable monthly can persist, Jeremie makes the answer conditional on demand. Supply growth should be huge, but if revenue and compute demand outperform it, premiums could increase: “Who else has as much capacity available in 2027?” If demand fades, the economics become harder. Financing constraints on smaller suppliers make an unlimited competitive supply response difficult even when attractive prices exist.
  • Contract duration explains why Anthropic might accept those prices. Jeremie compares six-year commitments around $100 billion per gigawatt, potentially rising to $120 billion or more, with SpaceX pricing around $50 million per megawatt annually but a 90-day commitment—roughly $15 billion per gigawatt committed. “Margins go down,” he acknowledges, while the recorded obligation stays much smaller. Jeremie also notes the risks of equity-funding capacity and building without a customer.

5. Better hardware and better software reinforce each other

  • Joey cites inference revenue per megawatt rising from about $16 million last year to over $60 million currently. The Q3 dip reflects new SpaceX capacity, less Meta distillation revenue and additional safety compute. Doug reads another S-1 comparison: revenue grew 1,368% year over year for the three months ended June 30, while compute and infrastructure expenses grew 300%. Their conclusion is that inference scales unusually well.
  • Doug asks how much of the efficiency reflects Anthropic versus broader hardware gains, including a cited 50× GB-versus-Hopper comparison. Jordan answers that newer silicon needs software capable of exploiting it. Anthropic can select among TPUs, Trainium, Nvidia GPUs and AMD GPUs, matching accelerators to workloads rather than depending on one platform. Hardware improvement and software execution therefore work together.
  • Jordan says the team may have “underestimated the models,” particularly their ability to perform difficult engineering work. His example is reverse-engineering game binaries that had supposedly been exceptionally resistant to that process. He thinks Fable 5.5 can probably port things across accelerators, reducing the importance of hardware-specific barriers. Diversifying silicon and suppliers also limits individual vendors’ bargaining power: “the model is the differentiator.”
  • Jordan sees favorable timing: earlier entrants accumulated older H100 fleets, while new labs lack Anthropic’s revenue, compute, research and data flywheels. “I don’t know how anybody catches up from here.” A panelist flags a relative weakness in multimodal vision compared with Astra; the panel also allows that specialized applications could capture niches. The broader software-and-research advantage does not mean every domain is already won.

6. Enterprise expansion faces a holiday test and a tired market

  • Joey sees runway even without turning everyone into an extreme user. The top 5% of Claude enterprise users spend $18,000 annually, while non-Claude Code users spend under $75 monthly. Anthropic represents about 0.1% of Fortune 500 operating budgets. Moving the median employee toward today’s 75th percentile would matter without requiring 90th- or 99th-percentile consumption. “We’re painting the lines,” he says of how early adoption remains.
  • The next catalyst is the first Q4 enterprise IT budgeting cycle seriously incorporating AI, despite the two frontier labs already generating roughly $120 billion in combined ARR. Joey expects a strong 2027 and leaves 2028 for later assessment. Government contributes approximately 1% of Anthropic revenue. Hundreds of millions of Microsoft 365 seats illustrate the broader opportunity, although ordinary office workers will not immediately spend like coders.
  • Jordan flags seasonality: spending fell approximately 20% in the two weeks ended January 2, 2026, versus the two weeks ended December 19—roughly a 10% December impact in the discussion’s shorthand. One panelist expects daily Claude Code habits to soften the next holiday dip; another thinks a shift toward consumption billing could worsen it when users log off. The disagreement remains unresolved rather than becoming a confident Q4 adjustment.
  • Doug finds the market response muted relative to the filing’s strength. Data-center land and buildout companies led, but semiconductor and broader AI beneficiaries did not rally as forcefully as earlier in the year: “The AI trade is exhausted.” Doug also highlights management’s statements about not overextending and not missing expectations; a panelist and Jordan frame that posture as “underpromise and overdeliver.” Jeremie, separately, says Q4 numbers being discussed are “stupidly low” and “not believable.”

7. OpenAI’s position draws a genuine disagreement

  • Jordan asks whether OpenAI is “cooked” and frames it as caught between Gemini and Meta in consumer, and Anthropic and open models in enterprise. He says Opus 5.5’s gains in SemiAnalysis’s spending appear to come at Astra’s expense. Jeremie argues that a leader can charge a premium, while a weaker “best-in-breed” position leaves OpenAI “competing with Anthropic on price.”
  • Jeremie says he remains bullish on both companies and still uses OpenAI models for tasks such as data analysis. Other panelists note that users’ preferences can shift when one model seems better or worse. The disagreement concerns relative positioning and profitability, not whether OpenAI can make a business.
  • An unidentified panelist offers a countercase: OpenAI may currently be better at selling to traditional Fortune 500 enterprises. Another panelist points to a strong Q3, greater enterprise focus since July, expected marketplace expansion through Bedrock and Vertex, and aggressive discounting against Anthropic accounts. One- and three-year contracts could reduce rapid model switching. Better sales execution could therefore matter as spending broadens beyond today’s power users.
  • A panelist also identifies the consumer burden. If only 6% of a billion weekly active users become paying customers, supporting the remainder is costly. OpenAI has had little usage-based API revenue, which the panel associates with monetization above $100 million per megawatt. A panelist says OpenAI’s margins currently look very different from Anthropic’s, but expects them to improve.

item.title: How to Accelerate Learning with 'AI Schools'
item.description: Alpha School says learning science and LLMs deliver twice the learning in two academic hours, supporting a network now at 50 campuses. Liemandt cites an AP course whose participants all scored 5, while Founders School’s $1 million-profit tuition guarantee remains untested months after its August opening.
item.content:encoded:
The a16z Show · Joe Liemandt、Erik Torenberg、Gagan Biyani · 2026-10-27 · 56 min · 原语言 EN

Alpha School says learning science and LLMs deliver twice the learning in two academic hours, supporting a network now at 50 campuses. Liemandt cites an AP course whose participants all scored 5, while Founders School’s $1 million-profit tuition guarantee remains untested months after its August opening.

TL;DR

  • Liemandt says Alpha delivers twice the learning in two academic hours a day. His broader claim is that learning science and LLMs enable instruction “ten times faster,” freeing afternoons for life skills. Alpha has reached 50 campuses, and he argues its operating model improves with scale: “We get better as we get bigger.”
  • Alpha treats motivation and measurable life skills as core product features. Liemandt reports that 50% of students prefer school to vacation and argues that “the key to your child’s happiness is high standards.” Third graders practice teamwork in escape rooms, moving from less than 20% uplifting language toward an 85% passing threshold; he says better teamwork makes them three times faster.
  • The university opportunity is to organize learning around consequential work. Among more than 70 interns from MIT, Stanford and UT, Liemandt says only one expected university to prepare them for the world after graduation. The interns feared AI would eliminate the first- and second-year jobs they expected, then worked 80-hour weeks researching and building an educational language model—combining academic study with something they wanted people to use.
  • Education adoption depends on local proof and committed founding families. Alpha’s New York campus opened with roughly 10–12 students after information sessions struggled to convert interest; Liemandt says it is now full at 150. His approach is “magnet marketing”: attract families who want the model and can tolerate early problems, then let visible student outcomes expand demand.
  • The speakers expect human judgment and agency to become more valuable as AI commoditizes intelligence. Biyani says employers emphasize “people skills, maturity, and systems thinking,” developed through building, rejection and responsibility. Biyani’s academy’s one-year format also makes experimentation easier to reverse, although Liemandt’s claim that there is “no downside” is his assessment of that risk.
  • Liemandt expects students to become major suppliers of learning software within two years. AI accelerates acquiring expertise and building products; he cites a student-built AP curriculum whose participants all scored 5. Biyani’s advice is to choose an interesting field and become AI native, approaching the future “on offense” rather than searching for a supposedly protected profession.
  • Founders School puts a financial guarantee behind entrepreneurship education. Liemandt promises students will build a business earning $1 million in profit during high school or receive all tuition back. The specialized school opened in August and is only a couple of months into operation; his expectation that some students will reach $1 million in their first year is a forecast, not a reported result.

Digest

1. Faster instruction changes the entire school product

  • Liemandt’s starting claim is that cognitive science, learning science and LLMs can make instruction “ten times faster.” Alpha’s operating promise is “twice as much in two hours a day” versus six classroom hours plus homework. Compounding that advantage, he argues, eventually takes children to the top 1%, “no matter where you start, given time.” He also calls Alpha the best academic-performing school on standardized tests.
  • The first commitment is that children love attending. Liemandt reports that “ninety-some percent” say “I love school,” 50% prefer it to vacation, and one campus reaches 65%. Shortening academics does not shorten the school day: parents still need six or seven hours, and children want to stay.
  • Afternoons become a curriculum of leadership, teamwork, entrepreneurship, financial literacy, relationships, storytelling, public speaking, grit and hard work. Students undertake challenging group projects with adults guiding them. His question for every school and university: if traditional instruction becomes ten times faster, “what do you do with the rest of the day?”
  • Since becoming principal four years ago, Liemandt has approached Alpha as a product requiring understandable packaging and repeatable delivery. He spent his first three years working on scaling quality. Alpha added 12 campuses last year and is now at 50; he says test scores, satisfaction, student happiness and workshops improve together. “We get better as we get bigger.”

2. Motivation comes from difficult work with visible progress

  • Gagan Biyani asks what makes children enjoy Alpha and how motivation changes outcomes. Liemandt warns that putting its learning engine into an unchanged school day means “it’ll fail.” The prerequisite is redesigning the day around children’s enthusiasm: are you willing to redesign school so kids love it more than vacation? That means challenge: “The key to your child’s happiness is high standards.” Children want to accomplish difficult things with friends.
  • Teamwork becomes something observable. Alpha microphones third graders in escape rooms, then uses AI to analyze their language. Initially, less than 20% is uplifting; much consists of fighting and insisting on individual ideas. An eight-week workshop requires reaching 85% team-oriented behavior to pass. Students also see themselves finishing escape rooms three times faster when they cooperate.
  • Liemandt contrasts this with conventional group projects, where one child works and everyone else coasts: “You learn like the anti-pattern.” Fourth and fifth graders must subsequently pass the Wharton MBA teamwork challenge, which he says 50% of MBAs fail. Life skills carry assessment requirements comparable to physics or mathematics.
  • Academically, personalization repairs the failure cycle of a time-based classroom. An eighth grader missing a fifth-grade concept receives that lesson without being trapped by age expectations. Alpha targets 80–85% correct answers: 100% suggests material is too easy; excessive difficulty drives disengagement. Scaffolding or faster progression keeps work appropriately demanding. “We engineer wins for the kids in the academics.”

3. University needs to connect serious study with building

  • Biyani draws inspiration from Alpha for the Horowitz and Dreesen Academy, where Liemandt is an investor and adviser. He wants to engineer stronger networks, agency and positive-sum behavior, but stresses that K–8, high school and college require different designs: “You can’t just copy everything over.” He argues university leaders spend 90% of their time attending to adults rather than students.
  • Liemandt recounts hosting more than 70 interns from MIT, Stanford and UT. Asked whether university was preparing them for the world after graduation, only one raised a hand. Others feared AI would eliminate the first- and second-year jobs they expected. Their response was an ambitious project: research and build an educational small language model that could run on a device and be freely available worldwide.
  • Those interns worked 80-hour weeks, including substantial research into learning science and model development. Biyani notes they were studying during those hours and guesses Joe assigned no textbooks; Liemandt says they researched learning science and the Brainlift while building the LLM. Biyani frames learning as “ninety percent motivation,” a point Liemandt affirms, and argues that useful products, revenue and employment can motivate 18-year-olds.
  • Alpha’s first high-school graduates, three years ago, returned from university with 4.0s but called introductory lectures “a complete waste of time”; five wrote newspaper editorials criticizing them. They valued seminars, clubs and activities. University is “a bundle of products,” Liemandt says. Biyani’s counterpoint: much of the attractive bundle is student-created, while formal academics consume roughly half the time for students who attend.

4. Parents must choose a future they have not experienced

  • Liemandt describes a split among parents: some still want a straight path from kindergarten to the Ivy League; an equal number, “maybe even more,” including Stanford and Harvard alumni, explicitly want another route. Younger families look 12 years ahead. Parents of 11th and 12th graders are harder to move: “I’ve been on this route, and I’m at the five-yard line.”
  • His historical analogy is 1910: he says 90% of Americans had an eighth-grade education and more than 30% farmed. Liemandt says the Case tractor ads “literally look[] like an Anthropic ad”: “It does the work of 50 programmers. It does the work of 50 farmhands.” People saw the inherited employment path disappearing. His key detail is that 130,000 towns voted to raise taxes for high schools whose curriculum parents had never experienced. “They knew they had to do something different than their background.”
  • Erik Torenberg raises the objection of a parent who sees an Ivy League school as safer than a new institution. Liemandt’s answer starts with adoption curves: “You don’t need everybody.” He acknowledges his own hesitation. Despite founding a company in a garage, he thought Alpha’s unconventional premises looked unsuitable for a school; moving his daughters from Catholic school took him two years.
  • Interest alone did not produce enrollment. As Alpha was opening 12 campuses, information sessions could attract more than 1,000 people without yielding 25 students. New York opened with approximately 10–12; Liemandt says it is now full at 150. His expectation for the academy is similar: survive the first year, demonstrate students thriving, and make those outcomes the comparison parents use.

5. Founding families are part of the operating model

  • Gagan Biyani describes early adoption as “positive self-selection”: students and parents willing to act on their convictions become part of the value of the community. He says early applicants are courageous and that they can be surrounded by brilliant, committed people. Liemandt agrees, but emphasizes the practical reason to select for commitment: “There will be hiccups.” Founding families who want the product become an important institutional asset.
  • Liemandt calls his approach “magnet marketing”: attract the right families and repel unsuitable ones. Parents fundamentally opposed to AI or screen time are told they should not enroll. A clear product definition helps assemble a coherent community. Biyani takes the corresponding admissions lesson: be strict about who gets in rather than optimizing class size.
  • Biyani presents the academy’s one-year format as a reversible detour: students can return to college. Liemandt goes further, saying “there’s no downside” and that even an unsuccessful experience could be enormously educational. His advice when a student strongly wants to attend is to let them try; Torenberg raises resentment as a risk of blocking that choice, and Liemandt calls that route “much riskier.”

6. Agency can reveal effort that grades fail to capture

  • Liemandt supplies his own counterexample to equating disengagement with laziness. He skipped school, did enough to enter Stanford, then dropped out; his father’s reported reaction was “My son’s a moron.” After seeing him work 100-hour weeks building his company, his father changed his mind two years later: “This was the greatest thing ever.” Doing something he wanted transformed his effort.
  • Torenberg observes the reverse problem: straight-A students can struggle when external structure disappears. Biyani says employers’ main concerns are “people skills, maturity, and systems thinking,” developed by building complex systems, handling rejection and organizing work oneself. Liemandt links that requirement to “AI commoditizing intelligence”: leadership, teamwork, ownership and receiving feedback require practice through projects. Those capabilities should belong in the curriculum, rather than depend on optional clubs.

7. AI-native students can acquire expertise and build with it

  • Asked by Torenberg how an 18-year-old should design an education, Liemandt separates “cognitive onload” from building. AI can fill students’ heads with knowledge ten times faster, he argues, making domain expertise more accessible. He points to high-school students rebuilding the TimeBack software stack he wrote and becoming knowledgeable about learning science, and discusses acquiring master’s-equivalent knowledge in a year.
  • The second capability is applying that knowledge through AI-assisted building. His summer interns researched because they needed to create something. Alpha students, he says, approach AI with confidence: “You adults are cooked,” and “We have superpowers.” He “absolutely” expects that in two years most learning software will be written by students, with peers supplying more engaging experiences.
  • His example is Austin, who built an AP curriculum whose participating students all scored 5. A world-history offering combined a geography-guessing game, historical events, S-tier rankings and a snarky AI. Liemandt admits he does not really understand all the terminology, but students engaged enthusiastically. “Me and the old adult team are never gonna be able to build that.”
  • Biyani rejects choosing a field primarily for future protection: “We want you to be on offense.” He has faith that AI-native mathematicians and coders will create possibilities their predecessors could not. His own commitment to education survived what both call a historically terrible market. Liemandt connects that stance to students reading The Rational Optimist: educators should develop people “optimistically capable with AI.”

8. Founders School makes entrepreneurship a teachable progression

  • Liemandt believes AI will shrink large Fortune 500 companies while producing an explosion of entrepreneurship. Alpha therefore starts financial education in kindergarten, using its “Alphas” currency to teach earning, saving, spending, investing and donating. Entrepreneurship is not “a bolt of lightning”: it is a set of teachable skills, with Founders School providing a specialized high-school path for students who want to build businesses.
  • The promise is explicit: students will start a business earning $1 million in profit while in high school, or receive all tuition back. Liemandt says previous Alpha High students have built businesses over the last four years, supplying examples behind his confidence. The specialized school itself opened in August, however, and is only a couple of months into its operation.
  • Students progress through earning $100, $1,000, $10,000, $100,000 and $1 million, learning skills at each stage. Liemandt says some are “speed running it,” leading him to expect $1 million in their first year: “I’m outta a curriculum.” That is his forecast from early progress. Students’ response, he says, is to plan a larger business afterward.

9. Exposure and feedback raise students’ ambitions

  • Liemandt remembers Stanford’s value in meeting accomplished people and realizing they were “a normal human.” That made comparable achievements feel accessible. He wants high-school students to have those relationships, just as the academy intends for its students. Gagan Biyani connects that goal to a formulation he tentatively attributes to Tyler Cowen: a teacher’s number-one job is to “raise a student’s ambition for themselves.” Biyani says Alpha tries to live that all day.
  • One 14-year-old cold-called Jensen, who returned the call and allowed a 90-second pitch. Liemandt paraphrases the feedback: the student had spent the opportunity asking qualification questions that research or other employees could have answered—“you just used your bullet with me.” The verdict praised initiative but gave an F for preparation. Liemandt calls it the best learning lesson of that student’s life.
  • Real-world exposure also includes Alpha’s World School: a year of service in Africa, with students signing, “I realize this will be the hardest year of my life.” Biyani says the academy has allocated $5,000 per student for travel. Students choose its use; his personal hope is that many travel alone to countries below $20,000 GDP per capita, gaining perspective useful in life and business.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/ai-school-kids-love-more-than-vacation-alpha-sch

item.title: The airline CEO putting Starlink on every plane
item.description: United is using Starlink’s speed—not free Wi-Fi—to attract passengers and convert trial into loyalty through broader technology and service within Kirby’s two-to-three-year window before competitors, potentially including Amazon, catch up. At recording, 48% of flights had Starlink; Boeing 787 certification slowed rollout, while Los Angeles targets full coverage in the first half of next year.
item.content:encoded:
Cheeky Pint · John Collison、Ben Thompson、Scott Kirby · 2026-10-27 · 80 min · 原语言 EN

United is using Starlink’s speed—not free Wi-Fi—to attract passengers and convert trial into loyalty through broader technology and service within Kirby’s two-to-three-year window before competitors, potentially including Amazon, catch up. At recording, 48% of flights had Starlink; Boeing 787 certification slowed rollout, while Los Angeles targets full coverage in the first half of next year.

TL;DR

  • United is using Starlink to turn a temporary connectivity advantage into lasting customer loyalty. Kirby accepts a window of two to three years before competitors catch up with low Earth orbit connectivity, potentially including Amazon. The plan is to make passengers try United for Wi-Fi, then stay for its broader technology and service: “Free was never the value proposition. Fast is the value proposition.”
  • Starlink’s payoff depends on predictable coverage and rapid certification. At recording, 48% of flights had Starlink, approaching 50%, with roughly three aircraft being equipped daily; smaller aircraft came first because they were certified first. Los Angeles is targeted to become the first fully covered hub in the first half of next year, while Boeing’s 787 certification work slows other markets. Kirby says the financial “numbers weren’t that big.”
  • United’s pandemic fleet order rested on shrinking competition as much as recovering demand. Kirby ordered 200 wide-bodies plus several hundred narrow-bodies while other global long-haul airlines permanently retired aircraft. Buying assets with 30-year lives during the downturn secured favorable pricing and positioned United for recovery: “We don’t have to be right. We just have to be not totally wrong.”
  • United’s technology advantage began with infrastructure spending that lacked a conventional payback calculation. A project costing several hundred million dollars, started in 2020, moved systems off mainframes and modernized databases. Kirby’s subsequent AI enthusiasm centers on programming and faster product delivery, rather than document summaries; his constraint on technology investment is now “how much can we manage? It is not money.”
  • Better disruption handling combines clearer communication with attempts to prevent the disruption itself. Kirby thinks a weather-radar messaging experiment moved NPS from negative 60 to positive 60 for passengers delayed an hour. He also says AI-supported routing could probably reduce Denver’s summer weather delays by 50%–75%, subject to FAA cooperation: “You can’t use weather as an excuse.”
  • Air traffic control is the structural ceiling on airline growth in Kirby’s account. He calls it “90% of the issue”: modernization takes five to 10 years, but annual appropriations repeatedly interrupt execution. Despite praising current progress, he expects flight limits to spread as airports reach the capacity the existing system can manage.
  • Kirby sees airline profitability as a route-network discipline problem before a product problem. He expects six of 10 US airlines to lose money this year and estimates American’s Chicago loss at roughly $1.5 billion. Low-cost carriers face their own mismatch: he contrasts New York airport charges of $52 per passenger with Spirit’s former $58 average fare. The rule is to “stick to your knitting,” including accepting limits to growth.
  • Credit-card revenue overstates the loyalty business’s contribution if redemption costs disappear from the analysis. Kirby says more than 50,000 passengers fly United daily using credit-card miles, creating a substantial carrying cost against the disclosed revenue. He calls the popular accounting interpretation “blown way out of proportion”; his preferred loyalty investments include club space, already more than doubled since before COVID and planned to grow another 50%.

Digest

1. United bought long-lived capacity when competitors were shrinking

  • Kirby’s pandemic premise was that COVID would be deep and prolonged, followed by recovering travel demand. While every other global long-haul airline permanently retired some wide-body capacity, he says, United ordered 200 wide-bodies and several hundred narrow-bodies. The wide-bodies list around $400 million each, before substantial discounts. Competitor retrenchment meant “we don’t have to be right. We just have to be not totally wrong.”
  • Thompson compares the decision with Samsung investing through memory downturns. Kirby agrees with the countercyclical logic, while noting that aircraft have 30-year lives and must survive several recessions. Being effectively the only buyer secured particularly good pricing; United’s commitment also gave Boeing evidence it could take to other customers when restarting the market.
  • The forecasting error, in Kirby’s account, combined extrapolating present conditions with believing surveys about future behavior. Frightened respondents genuinely intended never to travel internationally again; that did not make their intentions durable. “Experts live in the world of two standard deviations,” he argues. He likes surveys about completed experiences but ignores them for deciding what to build next.
  • Collison asks what permits these large bets. Kirby credits extensive reading, a supportive board and constant communication, while dismissing Wall Street’s preference for near-term cost control. Airport fees and union contracts leave future investment as an easy budget cut. His bargain is explicit: invest for the long term, but “if it doesn’t work, you ought to lose your job.”

2. Modern infrastructure made AI useful as a programming tool

  • During COVID, United began a project costing several hundred million dollars to leave mainframes, modernize databases and make information accessible. “There was no ROI. There was no payback,” Kirby says. The justification was future execution speed: United can now deliver changes that competitors cannot easily implement because their underlying systems do not support them.
  • Kirby’s AI epiphany came after three one-hour tutoring sessions. During a Saturday workout, with about 2.5 hours of elapsed runtime, he built a website comparing odds across four betting venues, including Kalshi. Dropdowns selected sports, dates and bet types; entering an amount sent the bet to the venue offering the best odds. His reaction to the team: “We’re all in on this.”
  • Owning critical software matters independently of AI. Kirby says United owns its reservation system, also used by Copa, after an inherited arrangement eventually forced United to support it itself. Ownership is now an advantage as more systems come in-house. For one major mainframe replacement, United withheld several hundred flights from the schedule as a precaution; the transition ultimately worked without a hitch.
  • The same logic reaches the seat-back screen. United is taking software control from Panasonic so maps can remember passenger preferences instead of cycling through unwanted views. Kirby also wants a live celebration when a passenger crosses two million miles, with flight attendants knowing the precise moment. “We could have never done that unless we took over the software.”

3. Customer communication must come with better operational choices

  • Thompson’s pushback is personal: after internalizing ConnectionSaver as a United advantage, he expected it to protect a tight Denver connection and was particularly disappointed when the departing flight had already closed. Kirby accepts the disappointment. His answer combines better communication with continued invention: a customer’s “wow” becomes the expected baseline, and “then we owe them another ‘wow.’”
  • A weather experiment illustrates the communication opportunity. On a sunny Chicago day, storms beyond the airport blocked departure routes. Half the affected passengers received the usual delay message; half saw the radar map explaining the obstruction. Kirby thinks the figures for an hour’s delay were negative 60 NPS versus positive 60—a 120-point difference, with the explanatory message outperforming an on-time flight.
  • United already offers alternative flights alongside weather warnings. Kirby wants a more detailed interface ready by Christmas: an illustrative screen would show a 41% weather-impact probability for the booked flight, versus 12% earlier and 3% later. The distinction is actionable information instead of a notification that merely raises anxiety. Integrating seat-back screens with the app should make such communication more consistent.
  • Collison and Thompson call this expectation management; Kirby resists because the phrase can excuse poor outcomes. For Denver’s pop-up storms, United is simulating alternatives to the FAA’s worst-case restrictions across arrival and departure routes. Using unaffected routes could “probably reduce 50%–75%” of summer weather-impacted delays, he says, but FAA help is necessary. The cultural instruction is to overcome weather’s effects, rather than invoke weather as the explanation.

4. Air traffic control determines how much the industry can grow

  • Asked whether aircraft or airports constrain United, Kirby answers: “No, it’s air traffic control. Air traffic control is 90% of the issue.” Once the FAA reaches what its current system can manage, flight caps follow—as in New York and Chicago—even when physical airspace could accommodate more traffic under a different system.
  • The funding mechanism frustrates him: projects requiring five to 10 years face annual appropriations. Delayed budgets, ramp-up and shutdown can leave only four productive months in a year. Kirby believes private enterprise could execute modernization in two to three years, while explicitly declining to advocate FAA privatization because it is politically toxic. He nevertheless praises current FAA and transportation leadership and progress.
  • Kirby’s political diagnosis includes private-jet lobbying, which he says protects essentially free access while airlines fund the system. He also questions maintaining roughly 450 facilities when controllers largely work from screens and could be centralized with backups. Congressional concern about local jobs complicates consolidation. His conclusion is constrained optimism: more progress than during his career, but government remains poorly equipped to move at a technology company’s pace.

5. Chicago shows why duplicate hubs consume scarce capacity

  • Thompson asks why a larger United presence would benefit Chicago. Kirby’s answer is network economics: United operates roughly eight daily Chicago–Milwaukee flights, largely feeding connections, while American duplicates that catchment service. Instead of roughly 16 flights, eight larger aircraft could carry the passengers and release scarce flight capacity for Paris or Tokyo. He attributes Atlanta’s and Dallas’s stronger hub metrics partly to avoiding this duplication.
  • Thompson challenges whether Kirby’s rivalry with his former employer makes the argument personal. Kirby denies it and points to even larger share shifts against other competitors elsewhere. In Chicago, he says United moved from lower market share than American to roughly double its revenue share. He estimates American will lose about $1.5 billion there this year.
  • Collison presses the competitive tension in grandfathered airport slots: incumbents deserve returns on infrastructure, but entrants also need opportunity. Kirby prioritizes preventing schedules that exceed airport capacity, noting he sought effective slot control at Newark. His preferred expansion mechanism is better air traffic control creating additional slots. Chicago’s separate gate-allocation process also mattered: United returned to its pre-COVID schedule, while American, focused on the Sun Belt, did not restore its schedule and lost six gates.

6. Starlink’s proposition is speed, with loyalty as the destination

  • Kirby ranks schedule first in airline choice and now puts Starlink immediately behind it. Free connectivity alone does not solve insufficient bandwidth; he says recent flights on three competitors’ legacy systems were terrible. Thompson agrees that making constrained Wi-Fi free can worsen the experience. Kirby’s categorical framing: “Fast is the value proposition,” and Starlink is currently “the only option.”
  • Collison asks why rivals’ decisions against Starlink might have seemed rational. Kirby describes the industry’s habitual pace: an aircraft modification can be treated as an eight-year project, making a one-year delay appear immaterial. He acknowledges United also underestimated the opportunity. Early passenger reactions changed the scale and urgency of its commitment.
  • Kirby calls the advantage temporary: competitors will eventually have low Earth orbit service, whether Starlink or potentially Amazon. He accepts Collison’s window of two to three years to win customers. “They’re going to try us for Starlink,” then stay for other technology and products. He also acknowledges Asian and Middle Eastern carriers’ strengths in service and physical product; United must keep improving beyond connectivity.

7. Coverage certainty changes the value of the Starlink rollout

  • Starlink costs more, but Kirby says the financial “numbers weren’t that big.” United initially planned installations during heavy maintenance checks and coverage for only 65% of the fleet, excluding retiring aircraft. Then passengers began choosing regional flights specifically for Starlink. That behavioral evidence prompted acceleration, supported by SpaceX, rather than the customary gradual retrofit.
  • At recording, Starlink covered 48% of flights and was approaching 50%, with about three aircraft equipped daily. Thompson notes that seat-mile coverage is lower because small aircraft came first. Kirby says certification dictated that sequence. Boeing’s remaining 787 certification work is a particular obstacle for a hub such as San Francisco, with substantial 787 flying.
  • Thompson argues that guaranteed availability matters much more than a chance of connectivity. United plans flight-specific probabilities in its app; Kirby illustrates a MAX 8 that might have 25% availability now and 36% by Christmas. Los Angeles is planned as the first hub with 100% coverage, sometime in the first half of next year, reflecting both competition and its aircraft mix.

8. Product ambition extends from new airframes to family travel

  • Collison notes that the 737 still flies around Mach 0.78, as in 1967, despite burning 50% less fuel and becoming 30–40 times safer. Kirby finds the pace “maddening.” He believes Boeing and Airbus have informally avoided new-airframe investment because investors resist it. After seeking a 757 replacement for more than 20 years, his answer is blunt: “We need a third aircraft manufacturer.”
  • United is investing in JetZero’s blended-wing-body approach, which Kirby compares with the B-2 bomber’s efficient shape. Thompson raises airport compatibility; Kirby acknowledges larger aircraft would require gate changes. He also sees room for better engines.
  • Relax Row, planned for later this year or next year, would turn three economy seats into a place to lie down. Kirby expects profitability but says the product will barely register financially. Its value is also brand-building. With seven children, he evaluates travel through a parent managing young kids alone; seat-back entertainment and Starlink help make that journey easier.
  • For Kirby, managing 120,000 employees is “99%” creating the right culture. Marketing provides his example of trust producing speed: Maggie Schmerin launched a Starlink campaign without seeking his approval. He learned about it through other people while attending a CVS Health board meeting. Multiple approval layers, he argues, drain work of speed, creativity and fun.

9. Route experimentation works when unsuccessful flights actually stop

  • Collison asks whether airlines have structurally become better businesses. Kirby answers “yes and no”: six of 10 US airlines are expected to lose money this year, while he sees United and Delta as the two winners through brand loyalty. He describes an $8 billion oil-price increase for United this year against $5 billion of profit in its best year, yet still expects solid profitability below last year’s.
  • Kirby credits Patrick Quayle’s team for destinations he would never have selected, including Nuuk. United expects 53 transatlantic destinations next summer versus 23 a decade earlier, with only two failures. Bergen disappointed despite Kirby liking the destination, so United stopped it. “Our assets are fungible”: the ability to redeploy aircraft makes experimentation economical.
  • The sharpest discovery example is pilgrimage travel between cities in Spain and Portugal. Quayle investigated the journeys, then found fragmented itineraries: passengers flew United into one city and another airline home from the other. Adding both endpoints addressed the actual trip. The opportunity began with noticing a behavior, then finding supporting data, rather than demanding historical evidence for a route nobody had operated.

10. Low-cost airlines need low-cost airports and strategic restraint

  • Kirby contrasts New York airport charges of $52 per passenger with Spirit’s former $58 average fare. That leaves almost nothing for fuel, aircraft, employees or maintenance. He says major-airport expenses have risen roughly 70% since before COVID, making these airports particularly difficult for low-cost operators.
  • Thompson pushes back: did United also price low-cost carriers out through basic economy and finer seat segmentation? Kirby acknowledges the competitive mechanism. Basic economy and larger aircraft let United compete profitably on price much of the time. Once the fare advantage disappears, he argues, the low-cost carrier loses its main reason for being chosen.
  • Ryanair supplies his model of discipline: secondary airports rather than Heathrow or Charles de Gaulle. US low-cost airlines moved into expensive major airports, abandoning a foundational advantage. Collison compares the problem with chasing growth beyond a successful operating formula. Kirby’s formulation is broader: “Know who you are, know what your strengths are, and stick to your knitting.”
  • The mistake runs both ways. Legacy airlines failed at creating internal airlines to out-Southwest Southwest; Kirby expects Southwest to struggle at becoming more like United. Allegiant illustrates a bounded model he respects, connecting smaller cities with destinations such as Las Vegas. He counts it among the four US airlines expected to be profitable this year.

11. Network depth makes hub entry exceptionally difficult

  • United’s discipline means flying through its hubs rather than building unrelated point-to-point routes. Kirby explains that on American’s Dallas–Los Angeles service, 75% of passengers connect from elsewhere. A competitor without that feed fights for just 25% of the market. “If you’re not first, you’re last” applies by market, rather than to an airline’s overall size.
  • Kirby has closed three hubs and opened none during his 30-year career. United would like more southeastern presence, but he estimates competing with Atlanta and Charlotte would require 600 daily flights. Raleigh-Durham might have the city size, yet lacks sufficient gates and runways. Expanding an airport takes a decade or more; an attractive vision does not remove those constraints.
  • His advice to new airline CEOs starts with route-level profit and loss. A broken network cannot be rescued by excellence elsewhere. When managers explain persistent losses as “strategic flying,” citing corporate accounts or credit cards, Kirby says to cancel the flying. “If you have bad routes that lose money, you cannot make the airline work. It is impossible.”

12. Loyalty and partnerships must earn their economics through the experience

  • Kirby rejects treating disclosed credit-card revenue as equivalent to profit. More than 50,000 passengers daily fly United using credit-card miles, and carrying them has a cost. Collison recasts the popular “credit card business with airplanes attached” claim as a financial-reading error. Kirby agrees that analysts are “looking at the revenue side and ignoring the cost.”
  • Frequent-flyer changes should be judged by brand loyalty, Kirby says, rather than program mechanics alone. Limited first-class seats require calibrating benefits, while overcrowded clubs call for capacity investment. United more than doubled club square footage from before COVID and plans another 50% increase. Pandemic closures created a rare opportunity to rebuild without inconveniencing normal passenger volumes.
  • Alliances extend the network: Kirby thinks United operates four times as many Frankfurt and Munich flights as American and Delta combined, with about 60% of passengers connecting onward. The problem is consistency across airlines. After years of requests, he threatened to end partnerships without seat assignments for United customers. His aim is for a partner flight to feel like an extension of United.
  • Thompson asks where Kirby’s enthusiasm for consolidation stops. Kirby returns to customer experience, then adds an ambition for an American flag carrier people feel proud of. He says overseas competitors supply two-thirds of long-haul seats into the US although only 40% of customers originate overseas, attributing the imbalance partly to state subsidies. He wants United able to compete with those airlines on every dimension.

item.title: Cliff Sosin - Owning the Complements to Intelligence - [Invest Like the Best, EP.497]
item.description: Cheap intelligence shifts value to complements: data, attention, scale, proximity, and attachment. Meta illustrates the upside: Sosin pairs $250 billion in revenue with equal annual spending treated as intelligence, whose price could fall “by a factor of 100 or something over the next five years.” His “diamond-shaped demand frontier” leaves lab profits uncertain as good-enough intelligence commoditizes.
item.content:encoded:
Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy、Cliff Sosin · 2026-10-27 · 61 min · 原语言 EN

Cheap intelligence shifts value to complements: data, attention, scale, proximity, and attachment. Meta illustrates the upside: Sosin pairs $250 billion in revenue with equal annual spending treated as intelligence, whose price could fall “by a factor of 100 or something over the next five years.” His “diamond-shaped demand frontier” leaves lab profits uncertain as good-enough intelligence commoditizes.

TL;DR

  • The investment question is what remains scarce when intelligence becomes cheap and ubiquitous. Sosin would own “the complements to intelligence” — data, attention, physical proximity, scale, and emotional attachment — while scrutinizing software that packages intelligence and businesses whose margins depend on consumer inertia. The premise is powerful but bounded: more IQ cannot remove the need to “touch reality.”
  • Meta is Sosin’s clearest example of an existing franchise strengthened by cheaper intelligence. His deliberately reductionist model pairs $250 billion of revenue with $250 billion of annual spending treated as intelligence; prices falling by “a factor of 100 or something over the next five years” would improve the economics of “personalized TV.” Better creative, recommendations, and advertising can monetize the same scarce data and attention rather than simply shrink costs.
  • Frontier intelligence can keep improving without guaranteeing durable frontier-lab profits. O’Shaughnessy argues that private models and superior distillation could preserve lab advantages; Sosin grants that uncopyable quality and cost leadership would make a great business. His competing hypothesis is a “diamond-shaped demand frontier”: enormous demand for increasingly commoditized good-enough intelligence, but potentially few uses for elite capability.
  • The AI build-out can transform the economy while remaining extremely difficult to underwrite. Sosin cannot forecast inference supply or demand “within several orders of magnitude,” and both bottlenecks and technology can shift before capital earns its return. He prefers identifying the CPG brands that follow the railroads, while admitting that lasting shortages and overbuilding are stories he can tell “with equal certainty.”
  • Consumer agents could compress inertia-based profits while reinforcing genuine cost advantages. Garbage collection illustrates the loop: a 50-cent monthly saving triggers switching, route density rises, and the winner becomes cheaper still, potentially capturing much more volume at lower margins. “Price is a miracle because it’s a signal wrapped in an incentive”; agents should sharpen that mechanism.
  • Sosin’s roughly 80% Carvana position reflects an explicit trade-off between expected return and unusual risk. He believes its infrastructure and brand leave few scenarios of severe failure. In the portfolio-sizing discussion, he says he is “underweight”; O’Shaughnessy jokes Carvana “should be 90%.” Sosin accepts that AI may eventually outcompete investors, but questions portfolio-sizing evidence without a long verification history.
  • Cheaper intelligence could reduce economic rents without settling the direction of margins or inequality. Full-stack businesses might become more efficient and more profitable, while consumers gain from lower software, banking, and professional-service costs. Against those leveling forces, agents could magnify returns to initiative and ambition: “I seem to very distinctly have two hands on everything.”
  • Education still needs human knowledge even when models can do the work. Sosin wants unaided foundations that let students direct models intelligently, alongside AI-assisted assignments “a hundred times harder and more ambitious.” Students must defend the resulting work and demonstrate that they understand it.

Digest

1. Intelligence cannot outrun missing information

  • Sosin rejects the amoeba-to-Einstein-to-God extrapolation: intelligence resembles “the roundness of a ball,” rather than an unbounded height. It interpolates between sparse facts; eventually, more intelligence exhausts what existing information supports. Mathematics can admit perfect answers, while complex dynamic systems require observations and experiments. “You have to touch reality.”
  • His weather-model example supplies the mechanism: rerunning a forecast after rounding initial conditions by one fewer decimal initially produced similar answers, then entirely different weather by the third, fourth, or fifth day. Errors compound through successive simulation steps. “If you wanna simulate the whole universe, what you actually need is the whole universe.”
  • Automated labs can accelerate learning without abolishing physical timelines. If an experiment requires mice that need a year to grow up and die, it still takes time. A lab might have 5,000 ideas but capacity for 20; a model-selected experiment might have only a 1% success rate, even if that were ten times the average researcher’s odds. “Being smart has limits.”

2. Meta illustrates the value of owning intelligence’s complements

  • The investment test is to assume everyone has excellent intelligence and ask “what’s left.” With “a team of 200 IQ people working full-time in our pocket,” agents can pursue a $400 annual saving consumers currently ignore. Software packaging “crystallized and hardened” intelligence, and businesses monetizing customer lethargy, face pressure. Complements include data, attention, emotional attachment, physical proximity, scale, and regulatory capture.
  • Meta’s core business, in Sosin’s framing, is “personalized TV.” His deliberately reductionist picture puts revenue at $250 billion and annual spending, including CapEx, at $250 billion, treating that spending as intelligence purchased through computing and engineering. If intelligence prices fall “by a factor of 100 or something over the next five years,” costs could fall dramatically; he warns against taking the simplification literally.
  • His upside scenario gives creators intelligence at 1/100 the cost and 10,000 times the effectiveness, alongside better recommendations, ads, and advertiser conversion. Meta might reinvest rather than eliminate spending, sell more ads, and win time from other activities. Its durable assets are “data and attention”: cheap intelligence does not make people stop enjoying funny 20-second videos.
  • Grindr supplies a smaller-company variant: attention and data already exist, but a finite team and budget constrain what it can build. Sosin’s thought experiment supplies 10,000 of Google’s best engineers for five years. More intelligence could unlock more of that franchise. He twice stresses that he does not own Grindr.

3. Frontier labs face both commoditization and uncertain demand

  • O’Shaughnessy’s countercase is that private frontier models may pull away, resist distillation, and let labs dominate cheap tokens too. Sosin concedes the economics if those conditions hold: superior models plus uncopyable, much cheaper adequate intelligence would make “a great business.” But he does not know whether labs can sustain that advantage; their financials are private, and bullish friends may have better information.
  • His observed pattern is a moving frontier: better models unlock tasks, but those tasks commoditize behind them; customer-service chatbots need not use frontier models. He points to rapid commoditization at each step, including the rise of Chinese models, and collapsing costs. Even if labs lead in cheap tokens, the shrinking commodity market may limit the opportunity.
  • Coding was a huge market. Beyond it, he considers a “diamond-shaped demand frontier,” with increasingly rare uses for elite intelligence. “How often do you really need a 300 IQ,” he asks, while remaining unsure that higher IQ alone delivers cancer cures.
  • Against O’Shaughnessy’s Jevons-paradox argument, Sosin describes a market that first grows as a product improves and gets cheaper, then can shrink when further price drops no longer generate enough demand; at zero price, he says, market size goes to zero. Communications is his analogy: traffic growth eventually stopped offsetting price declines, and the market shrank as costs kept falling. He thinks one Cogent Communications division routes 30% or 40% of internet IP traffic, yet the company’s market capitalization is only a few billion dollars. Jevons describes “a particular spot on a curve.”
  • O’Shaughnessy invokes a friend’s maxim, “Intelligence creates its own demand,” and asks whether models could generate new questions. Sosin grants, “Certainly, maybe.” Reading across disconnected papers will unlock discoveries, but eventually new hypotheses require experiments. Physical throughput then constrains progress; he does not assume thought alone supplies unlimited new, valuable applications.
  • Sosin says his own model use has become commoditized: he has a Groqbot route work among his subscriptions on a server, and no longer knows which model is doing the work.

4. An essential build-out can still be difficult to underwrite

  • Sosin cannot forecast inference supply or demand “within several orders of magnitude.” Even getting volumes right leaves questions about falling unit costs, bottlenecks along the value chain, and competition within each segment. His demand example is a five- or ten-minute, 3Blue1Brown-style mathematics explainer for his daughter: wonderful at very low cost, but something he does not think he would buy for $5. He also uses his Muse app to get workout-form pointers for very little money, but says he would not do so at a meaningful price.
  • O’Shaughnessy’s pushback is that the smartest entrepreneurs are dedicating themselves to supply. Sosin reverses the causality: a huge infrastructure project requires strong price signals and extraordinary talent; their participation does not establish where an outside investor earns returns. He would rather identify what follows construction: “once you have railroads,” anticipate the CPG brands.
  • Sosin likens society to a household saving for a house: resources dedicated to AI infrastructure mean less consumption today. The build-out absorbs electricians and plumbers, raising costs elsewhere. Because profits attract investment and projects have lead times, he expects expansion to continue until it overshoots: “the last person to stop will regret it.” Technology changes during construction, further complicating forecasts. He can describe both chronic shortages and overbuilding “with equal certainty.”
  • Even Nvidia’s designs ultimately become “flat files that they send to Taiwan”; Sosin raises the possibility that intelligence could commoditize that work. TSMC’s process knowledge has more physical, tacit, accumulated attributes, though he disclaims expertise. Its difficulty meeting demand also pushes others to replicate its moat: “That’s not a great fact.”

5. Agents can strengthen scale while competing away inertia

  • Delegability matters. For bank deposits, Sosin could almost entirely defer to an agent: given FDIC insurance, seek the highest rate. Choosing a favorite sweater sits at the opposite end; an agent can source options, but personal judgment remains essential. The distinction determines how aggressively optimization can alter customer behavior.
  • Garbage collection shows how switching can reinforce scale. An agent might accept a 50-cent monthly saving after confirming that “the garbage will go away.” A collector with two customers on a street could recruit the rest, gaining route density and lowering costs further. The result could be much more volume at much lower margins: “everyone moves to the low-cost producer, who in turn gets to be the lower-cost producer.”
  • Asked whether intelligence could replace price, Sosin calls it “a signal wrapped in an incentive.” Agents instead sharpen markets by reducing sticky, lazy pricing. A $60 monthly garbage bill followed by an unnoticed 5% increase to $63 could give way to frequently changing prices as providers recalculate marginal costs and customers continuously compare offers.

6. Companies need sustained organizational work to deploy cheap intelligence
