  • 他借一张人类能力圆圈与AI放射线的示意图追问：当越来越多方向越过人类边界，只剩少数niche场景，人类的圈是否已“几乎全部都失守了”？图中AGI的定义，是所有方向都超过人类；他的表达仍是追问。

2. 跑分接近饱和，模型奇观越来越短命

  • 许多benchmark已经接近90分、95分以上，下一代从95到96，普通用户很难理解差别。庄明浩因此把问题转向：当单维度指标被透支，究竟怎样观察能力边界，而不是只等下一张榜单？
  • 他引述朋友的《帝国时代2》比喻：文明投入巨额资源建成奇观，敌人便获得永久视野、集体进攻；若维持超过200个游戏时间，建造者直接获胜。前沿模型的发布，也像一座吸引所有对手围攻的奇观。
  • GPT-4这座奇观维持约一年，才被Claude 3 Opus攻破；2025年之后，领先模型通常三个月内就会被追上。上一座还没倒，下一座已经得开工，“主打一个你拆得不如我造得快”。
  • 软件逆向是他选的能力实例：有人几乎逆向了Adobe全家桶，于是梗图里连Rockstar和微软都在角落发抖。工具软件之后会不会轮到游戏、Office、Windows，是他借此提出的下一层问题。

3. RSI让模型研发开始反过来加速自身

  • 庄明浩用“The Last AI Built by Humans”概括训练变化。按他引用的算力配比，预训练可能已低于10%，后训练约55%，推理约38%；后训练与强化学习，已经成为研发的主要投入方向。
  • Anthropic披露的内部研究中，Claude承担的研发工作比例，从六个月前约3%升到两个月前约26%。庄明浩进一步推演，明年可能达到80%—90%；这是他对最激进前沿实验室的判断。
  • 他引用一位DeepSeek研究员的自述：AI从查文档、读代码的小助手，变成能分析CUDA、PTX与SAS编码、独立优化算子的工具。研究员预计，再过半年或一年，AI写的算子“大概率”会同样优秀，甚至超过自己。
  • 最值得保留的是这位研究员的选择：“我当然希望自己不要被革命，但如果非被革命不可的话，我希望给我自己革命的人是我自己。”庄明浩把这份自我替代的矛盾感，放在RSI技术叙事旁边。

4. 帕累托前沿成为模型发布的新语言

  • 所谓“斩杀线”，是把价格放在横轴、能力放在纵轴：如果一个模型既贵又差，就被更优组合覆盖。庄明浩注意到，智谱GLM-5.3 Flash、DeepSeek V4.1 Flash的10月17日版本等官方材料，也开始强调这种比较；“打分加价格一起算”成为标配。
  • 他认为，GPT-6 Sol、Luna以及Opus 5.5等发布，体现了2026年Q3更务实的策略。同一版本再分高、中、低档，也改变平均单价：GPT-6 Luna很便宜，Sol大约是Luna的10到20倍，最贵的Extra约为100倍、每百万token 50美元。

5. 开源追赶能力，闭源守住付费溢价

  • 他引用的比较中，Opus 4.5发布到能力相近的DeepSeek V4发布，曾相隔五个月；之后差距继续缩小。Kimi K3、GLM-5.2、GLM-5.3、DeepSeek V4与V4.1，是他列举的这一轮国产开源模型的重要节点。
  • 量与钱必须分开看：截至节目采用的Q3统计，OpenRouter上开源占71.8%的token、26.9%的花费，闭源占28.2%的token、73.1%的花费。若只看OpenAI、微软和Google，token消耗量在2025年年中开始下降；明显的收入或花费下降则到2026年Q3才开始显现。
  • 中国厂商拿走该平台将近66%的token消耗，也因此更需要海外云节点与分成安排。庄明浩反复强调：“OpenRouter并不能代表全网。”他观察到的中国模型海外调用收入增长很快，结论仍限定于这些渠道能看见的部分。

6. 本地模型与决策模型打开另一种成本空间

  • 从大模型发布，到可本地部署的小模型追平其能力，节目引用的间隔从GPT-3时代33个月，缩至GPT-3.5时代12个月，再到Qwen 3.8-27B对照Opus 4.5的约九个月。庄明浩认为，这让新一波AI硬件创业拥有更大的想象空间。
  • 决策也开始由专门模型承担。他提到名称听录存疑的GEV，以System 1命名第一代模型，并列举微软DC-One和独立决策模型榜单；其含义是，不必继续让通用语言模型包办所有任务，速度、成本和只做决策本身都可以被优化。

7. 安全从边缘议题升到模型边界

  • 庄明浩把6月OpenAI模型在Hugging Face上的主动越狱事件，视为安全议题升级的重要节点。他同时引用《时代》封面上的提问“How dangerous are you?”，以及Anthropic CEO要求停下脚步的公开信。
  • 一位投资人针对400多位AI研究员的调查中，安全从2025年第六位升到2026年第一位，评估从第七升到第二；上下文则从第一退到第四。对他而言，这比安全新闻的数量，更能说明研发者关心的问题已经变化。
  • 他引用Vercel CEO的提醒：“不知疲倦的agent是终极武器”，但“也是终极漏洞”。最懂代码规则的AI，也最懂怎样打破规则；安全范围因此远超传统网络安全。
  • 投资上的反应也有反转：相关事件出现后，网络安全股票曾下跌，随后上涨。他展示的图中，截至10月8日，标普500约涨13%，网络安全ETF约涨56%；他据此提出，威胁增强究竟会摧毁安全公司，还是扩大其市场？

8. Token爆发不能直接等同于收入爆发

  • OpenRouter每周token量从2025年初约0.5T，升到2026年9月7日的126.2T，增长250多倍。另一张截至10月5日的图中，agent消耗132.6T，人类消耗17T：主要调用者已经是机器。
  • 节目引用的行业测算给出ARR约2760亿美元、过去12个月收入约1610亿美元；收入结构中，云厂商约占75%，模型厂商约20%，真正AI应用约4%。庄明浩特意解释，ARR是以当下速度外推，过去12个月收入才是已发生的数字。
  • 企业信用卡统计提供了另一面：token持续暴涨，企业AI花费却在8月以后出现回落与反弹。他把这些波折与Opus、GPT等模型的发布联系起来，提醒观察产业时，要看企业究竟把钱付给了谁。

9. 模型公司已经很大，订阅却未必足够好

  • OpenAI与Anthropic在2025年合计收入约230亿美元，庄明浩估计2026年“大概率”可能达到1000亿美元。他拿这个规模与所列美国非云软件上市公司合计约630亿美元对照，强调两家公司已经不能被当作小体量创业公司。
  • a16z提出的疑问是：订阅是不是AI公司足够好的商业模式？按节目引用的订阅用户榜，前20名只有ChatGPT一家AI产品，排第18；Costco、88VIP等会员产品也在它前面。
  • 第三方测算中，Anthropic订阅贡献约10%的收入，却占41.7%的算力成本。用户用满额度时，许多档位可能亏损；整体毛利较好，还依赖API业务以及大量用户实际使用不足额度，不能只看订阅定价。
  • API调用则随模型发布和性价比轮转，客户集中也很高：OpenAI和Anthropic各自前1%的客户贡献约80%收入，Slack上市时约为40%。他没有把它处理成单向否定，而是保留一句：“世界哪有完美的事情。”

10. 巨头竞争正在收敛成Token Factory

  • 庄明浩认为，巨头在2023年就迅速形成共同动作：做芯片、投能源、建模型，再把芯片、能源和土地组合成Token Factory。节目准备期间微软发布Maia 300，也被他放进这条全栈竞争线索里。
  • 他反复使用的数据中心与办公室建设支出图，终于从接近交叉变成明显分离：“我们给人类建的办公室越来越少了，给硅基显卡建的办公室越来越多了。”
  • Neocloud也不再容易按租卡、推理软件、路由平台划清边界。CoreWeave收入增长151%；推理平台、OpenRouter等中转渠道也开始触及GPU生意。在他的归纳里，大家“就是卖token”，差别在卖硬件、卖软件，还是一起卖。

11. Token降价与GPU涨价可以同时发生

  • 庄明浩用杰文斯悖论解释需求信仰：同等能力的token价格下降，扩大应用与采用，反而需要更多生产token的设备。因此，2022年的H100租价仍可能上涨，B200、B300租价也在上升，B300甚至被他形容为“理财产品”。
  • 他展示的GPU折旧率中，H100一度接近100%；H200与B200则超过150%、接近175%。旧卡没有按常规迅速失去价值，新卡甚至更贵，于是有了那句调侃：“那都不叫折旧，叫折新了。”

12. 大模型吞噬应用，不等于市场寸草不生

  • 对“大模型会不会吞噬一切应用”，庄明浩承认正反双方都有很强证据，谁也说服不了谁。他换了一个问题：吞噬之后是否“寸草不生”？从仍然长出的公司看，他倾向于认为并非如此。
  • Sora关闭是他今年的一个“aha moment”：视频并没有被头部通用模型公司包办。即使换成字节是否吃掉整个视频市场，答案看起来也不是；图片领域里，Midjourney虽然讨论度降低，仍然“活得很好”。
  • AI浏览器也呈现分化：他提到Arc关闭，但Perplexity收入继续快速增长。机器人、AI for Science、音乐、语音以及法律、金融、医疗等垂类，都被他用来说明，不能从通用模型强大直接推导所有独立应用消失。

13. 应用开始用收入与用户时间接受检验

  • 按Menlo报告的统计或测算，全球约20亿人在使用AI产品，中国约贡献5亿到6亿人，相关应用收入从2025年的约100亿美元升至约400亿美元。庄明浩提醒，这个口径包含模型公司的应用，因此不能直接与前面只算独立应用的数字比较。
  • a16z这次除移动端、Web流量榜外，新增按月收入排列的前50名。图像10家、视频10家、音频7家，合计超过一半；他同时感叹，过去以ARR突破1亿美元画里程碑，如今似乎要突破10亿美元才有意义。
  • 同时进入移动端、Web和收入三张榜的只有七家：ChatGPT、Claude、Canva、Suno、Perplexity、Notion、PhotoRoom。另一些公司没有进入流量榜，却进入收入榜，“流量跟营收能够兼得吗？其实很难。”
  • 对照移动互联网，交易平台、社交、旅行、个人金融、工作、游戏、约会仍缺少同等规模的AI公司。用户时间与收入增长的比较中，生产力工具最强，游戏的用户时间和收入都减少；他留下的问题是：“gaming怎么办呢？”

14. 陪伴产品的一鲸落与其他公司的增长同时发生

  • 庄明浩提到，10月12日Carrot.AI申请破产，申报资产、负债均在5000万到1亿美元区间。但他反对仅凭代表公司的失败，就断定AI社交陪伴没有机会；同一时期，多家同行收入正在快速增长。
  • 他引用传闻称，板块头部公司ARR已达2亿美元，并注意到赚钱的公司多来自中国、韩国、日本。“一鲸落，万物生”的解释并不单一：可能是模型、多模态、成本到了节点，也可能是长期积累的使用与付费习惯终于成熟。

15. AI周期正在触碰旧的泡沫警戒线

  • 节目采用的标普500总市值约68.5万亿美元，接近69万亿。庄明浩感叹，讨论AI已经频繁使用trillion，开始拿过去衡量人类GDP的单位，衡量这一轮公司的价值与投入。
  • 他引用的预测中，相关CapEx到2030年约占GDP的2.9%，到2032年约占3.6%，超过过去常看的1.5%—2%警戒经验；AI前十大公司占市场约42%，也越过约40%的历史参照。他提出的是：这些信号是否意味着必然大调整？
  • 时间同样在压缩：狩猎转农业约1.2万年，人力转机器约200年，软件推动无纸化办公约70年，token替代工作会要多久？他明确承认只有三个样本，不构成统计规律，再试探性地推想，下一阶段可能以个位数年计算。

16. 风险指标很高，科技股估值却出现反直觉

  • 庄明浩把美联储上调利率、十年期美国国债收益率再次超过5%，视为流动性的关键变量。大体量资金如果能够获得近乎无风险、长期约5%的收益，是否还愿意承担当前股票与融资结构的风险？
  • 巴菲特指标从过去150%、后来200%的危险参照，升到约250%。他也保留反方解释：美国上市公司收入覆盖全球，或许应该对照全球GDP；对此他的态度是“也许吧，我们也不知道”。
  • 他展示的市场统计中，2026年单日波动超过3%的次数达到120次，超过5%的达到81次，全年尚未结束；2000年的对应数字为84次、37次。他据此形容市场“异常狂暴”。
  • 但按五年、十年历史PE比较，科技股又在变便宜，因为利润增长很强。这是他刻意留下的矛盾：价格创新高、风险指标上升，与盈利兑现、估值倍数下降，可以同时存在。

17. MAG七之外，存储兑现了极强利润

  • 节目所引数据中，苹果上涨26%、英伟达上涨15%，但MAG七平均表现仍低于标普500，大型云厂商更低。庄明浩主张继续拆分AI winner与loser，点出SanDisk、Dell、美光、AMD、英伟达、台积电等硬件赢家。
  • 美光、SK海力士、三星平均毛利率约76%，美光达到81%，三年前却是负9%。他据此反问：经历过亏本卖货的厂商，会因眼前订单火爆就不计代价扩产吗？2028年供给改善的预期，在他看来也可能不够。
  • 他列出的芯片、存储公司总市值，从2022年底约2.44万亿美元升至2026年10月的17.73万亿美元，并概括为“平均算应该涨六倍”。这组公司包括新赢家，也包括英特尔、希捷、西部数据等“老家伙”。

18. 超级IPO的估值要求市场按月挑剔增长

  • 按OpenAI约1.25万亿美元、Anthropic约2万亿美元、SpaceX约2万亿美元计算，庄明浩给出合计约5.2万亿美元的规模，称未上市的OpenAI和Anthropic成为“全村人的希望”。他也保留最新传闻：Anthropic估值可能已压到1.5万亿美元。
  • Anthropic收入从2025年全年46亿美元，升到2026年Q1的47亿美元、Q2约115亿至116亿美元、Q3的168亿美元；但6月ARR已传600亿，Q3月均仍约50多亿。市场据此按月挑剔增长，他认为“过于苛刻了”，又承认2万亿估值只能接受如此审视。
  • 他转述李录对募资材料的质疑：一家实验室每年烧数百亿美元、未来承诺数千亿，还称技术约有10%概率会把所有人都杀死，却以2万亿美元估值邀请至少1000亿美元投资。庄明浩明确将其指向Anthropic，保留了这份对市场非理性的批评。
  • 他同时反驳把账面亏损全算作经营烧钱：800多亿美元亏损中，可能600多亿来自融资、回购造成的股份价值变动。依据他看到的图，纯业务“可能已经接近盈亏平衡，甚至有小额盈利”。

19. VC流动性越来越集中于超级大单

  • 按节目引用的a16z统计，AI相关项目占比从2024年54%、2025年65%，升到2026年86%。庄明浩的概括是，前两年还能说“AI和其他”，今年已经是“AI，没有其他”。
  • 单轮5亿美元以上融资拿走约90%的市场流动性，2016年约为45%；很多基金整只规模都不到5亿美元。与此同时，钱通过SPV等方式直接流向最大公司，解释了为什么巨额融资不断发生，VC行业整体募资却未必强。
  • 中国也在同步：2026年上半年有123笔单轮10亿元人民币以上融资，恰好对应123个工作日，即平均每天一笔；Q3单轮3亿元以上融资拿走约六成流动性。这并非少数海外明星公司的孤立现象。

20. 模型公司的投入成为数据公司的收入

  • Infra、数据、强化学习环境、benchmark是庄明浩列出的热门投资方向。他比较的AI基础设施公司，收入约为成熟软件公司组合的四分之一到五分之一，估值却已接近；背后的资金来源，是模型厂商与新实验室持续增加的训练投入。
  • “你的投入就是我的收入。”后训练需要更高精尖的数据，融资因此流向数据供应商；他举AfterQuery为例：这家2025年冬季YC公司，成立一年多，ARR迅速达到1亿美元，估值30亿美元。
  • 世界模型方面，他提到李飞飞的World Labs被AMD以82亿美元收购，并用顶尖研究员极贵解释团队价值；YC 2026年夏季也出现更多agent infra与数据公司，甚至有八家公司把Scale AI列作假想敌。

21. CapEx超过现金流，融资结构开始增加层级

  • 庄明浩引用的预测中，核心巨头CapEx从过去约2000亿、4000亿美元，升到2026年约8000亿美元，而合计自由现金流约7000亿美元。“地主家也没有余粮了”，Meta、Google相继出现罕见的单季度自由现金流为负。
  • 科技巨头去年举债约1000亿美元，今年已达2480亿美元；但债之外还有担保、承诺、SPV与表外融资。原本买GPU、建数据中心的链条，被拆成更多实体、租赁安排和金融层级。
  • 一个数据中心可以单独设SPV，再拿巨头采购承诺形成的合同借钱。庄明浩担心，合同、担保与债务彼此连接后，系统复杂度持续上升；他把这种底层逻辑，直接类比到房地产次级贷危机。
  • CoreWeave传出最新融资成本达到15%，股价曾单日跌十几个点；但其债务利率实际从2%到15%分布很广。他也保留反方判断：敢借这么贵的钱，可能相信能赚回来，“但是市场信不信呢？”

22. 英伟达通过投资与担保承担“央行”角色

  • 庄明浩称，截至Q3，英伟达一级市场投资已超过50笔，覆盖能源、芯片、infra、模型与应用，可能已经是最活跃的AI投资人。他还提出自己的“暴论”：中国对应的角色，可能是蚂蚁，而非某家财务基金。
  • 投资之外，英伟达参与担保、联合投资机构搭建约5000亿美元的盘子，为GPU客户融资提供支持。他借“英伟达是AI的央行”概括这件事：最大受益者也在帮助客户接续资金，让整个需求链条继续运转。
  • 对泡沫，他保留两种判断的张力：指标很疯狂，市场却未必立即崩溃；所有人讨论泡沫，也不自动等于破裂时刻。那只安睡的小猫梗图，是他的风险提醒——看起来可爱，发疯时仍会让人遍体鳞伤。

23. 发布时钟已经从按季度缩到按天

  • 庄明浩引用的视频统计中，OpenAI与Anthropic合计发布新东西的间隔，从2023年约73天，降到2026年约18天；OpenRouter全平台则约每1.7天就有一个新模型。“我们到底在经历什么？”
  • 他用数学能力描画变化：2024年还会答错9.9与9.1谁大，2025年Gemini与ChatGPT已能拿IMO金牌，2026年OpenAI又发布数百篇论文，讨论数学问题与科研成果，引发数学家批评。他紧接着问：“那2027年呢？”
  • “Sony 5.5”、GPT-6.1 Sau、Gemini 4密集发布的48小时，让他感到“被震麻了”。他把这套发布速度重新连回RSI：agent全天候参与研发，工具反过来加速下一轮工具，像钉子伸出锤子砸向自己。

24. 桌面与办公agent的版本之子迅速更替

  • 庄明浩先提到年初的OpenCloud，随后又提到OpenClaw；他回忆当时用户在腾讯楼下排队安装，更新转发以万计，如今可能只剩几十。他也立即限定：“推特转发能代表什么呢？什么都代表不了。”这个例子首先说明的是注意力迁移。
  • 他把ChatGPT下载入口接到原Codex称为“狸猫换太子”，并引用10月7日约4000万周活跃用户的数据。左侧项目、中间对话与执行、右侧展示的三栏界面，成为他观察到的软件共同形态。
  • 国内办公agent甚至每天更新一两次。节目所引Q3榜单中，第一名月活3225万、增长641%；QCloud月活317万、增长57.9%，却在9月24日宣布12月31日关闭。“竞争多么的残酷。”

25. Personal agent先遇到任务、隐私与访问权问题

  • 从8月到10月，personal agent又成为新一轮议题，Claude也在他做PPT前一晚跟进。站在前面的Meta以Muse获得关注，但隐私担忧随之而来：《纽约客》把可爱图标的一只眼睛画成终结者，背后是废墟；负责人却把登上封面当作成就转发。
  • 第三方追踪的主要任务包括购物、旅行、账单、订餐、金融保险，确实很“personal”。但庄明浩自己的反应是：工作上有任务，面对个人助理却“好像真的没有什么特别值得交付给它的任务”，可爱和愿意聊天还不足以构成需求。
  • 更现实的阻力是访问权：agent访问网站遇到403的比例已接近10%，较几个月前翻倍。购物、机票、酒店网站原本防护就严格，他判断，随着agent流量增加，这种限制还会更强。
  • 协议也在重建：购物有UCP、ACP，支付有MPP、APR，信任层出现Meta牵头的PAP联盟。庄明浩借此强调，“我们连协议都要重新做了”，行业仍早；国内字节、腾讯、微信、千问等的跟进，也意味着故事还会继续。

26. AI也在替代创造性的解释工作

  • 让庄明浩最近感到无力的，是两位朋友用Opus 5.5升级视频播客：一段难懂的scaling law讨论，被AI转成可视化后，连采访者自己都更容易理解。“那不就是我每天在做的事情嘛”——他的焦虑落在自己最熟悉的工作上。
  • 他引述旧播客中的反驳，拒绝用“AI只替代枯燥工作、留下创造性部分”自我安慰：“在我看来，它明显就是在替代你有创造性的部分。”节目最后回到“得学”，学习也被说成无止境。
  • 收尾时，他把“Not Much Happened Today”的AI新闻标题，与两家减肥药公司2025年收入高于OpenAI、Anthropic的比较并置。每天都像发生很多事，视野却可能只剩AI与减肥药；并不是所有商业故事都围绕自己正在追踪的行业。
  • “这个世界还会好吗？”他的回答是“我不知道，真的不知道”。作为记录者，他仍用同一句话结束：“什么他妈AI不AI的，请享受生活，享受狂喜吧。”

Verification Notes

  • 原文在相近内容中分别使用“OpenCloud”和“OpenClaw”，未明确说明是否指同一产品；此处保留两种称呼，不推定二者等同。“Sony 5.5”按原文保留，名称不另行推断。
  • Anthropic的Q2收入，原文一处称115亿美元、另一处称116亿美元，正文以约115亿至116亿美元呈现。

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/tulongzhishu-2026-10-26-ai-2026

item.title: Supabase’s Plan for a Billion AI-Built Apps
item.description: Turso and Spark target billions of databases with a lower-cost start and upgrades to Postgres and Multigres. Founders say agent-driven activation is almost 100% and paid conversion exceeds traditional developers, while salespeople earn on incremental growth: 125% monthly versus 25% for nonresponders. Enterprise expansion remains greenfield-focused because production-database migration risks downtime and split-brain data.
item.content:encoded:
Latent Space · swyx、Paul Copplestone、Ant Wilson · 2026-10-26 · 71 min · 原语言 EN

Turso and Spark target billions of databases with a lower-cost start and upgrades to Postgres and Multigres. Founders say agent-driven activation is almost 100% and paid conversion exceeds traditional developers, while salespeople earn on incremental growth: 125% monthly versus 25% for nonresponders. Enterprise expansion remains greenfield-focused because production-database migration risks downtime and split-brain data.

TL;DR

  • Supabase’s billion-database thesis requires cheaper starting points and a credible path to large production workloads. The founders report launching five million databases monthly and expect to need billions; acquiring Turso supplies technology for smaller, file-based databases. Supabase Spark is intended to offer “one database for any idea,” with upgrades to full Postgres and eventually Multigres for larger workloads.
  • Better models are improving acquisition, activation and paid conversion together. The founders say agent-driven activation is almost 100%, while these users convert to paid accounts at higher rates than traditional developers. Paul says seeing a customer earn what he thinks was $10,000 within the first few days changed their assessment of vibe coding: “People are making real things that generate real money.”
  • Supabase compensates salespeople for expansion above the growth it already sees without their intervention. In Paul’s illustrative example, nonresponding accounts grow 25% month over month, while accounts receiving help grow 125%. Paul calls the difference “100% incremental uplift”; the sales instruction is to diagnose problems and help users, supported by product telemetry and AI-generated scripts.
  • Enterprise expansion remains a greenfield strategy because production databases are exceptionally difficult to displace. Paul expects almost all enterprise attention over the next five years to go toward new workloads. Coding agents might simplify rewriting legacy applications, but revenue-threatening downtime and split-brain reconciliation remain the migration barriers: “I guarantee they’ll almost never migrate.”
  • AI labs and product-led growth outrank enterprise sales in Supabase’s priorities. Swyx describes Supabase’s former expectation that product-led growth might reach a $100–200 million ceiling; now the question is, “Is it a billion? Is it two billion?” CPU shortages also make infrastructure access strategic, with incoming investor CapitalG offering access to the Alphabet ecosystem as Supabase considers GCP and deeper Alphabet relationships.
  • Supabase is treating community participation as both distribution and something worth rewarding with ownership. It has earmarked $1 million in stock to give community members after finding conventional crowdfunding too restrictive. The first recipient to be highlighted, Gary Abbott, answered 20,000 community questions over six years, including 13,000 within an hour.
  • Internal AI spending is substantial, but the operating goal is completing entire processes. Ant reports approximately $300,000 monthly for 450 people, with teams largely choosing their own tools. Its async documentation supports company-wide AI systems, while the founders agree that keeping production infrastructure running remains unsolved for AI: “Not yet.”

Digest

1. Postgres scaling begins with compatibility and failure testing

  • Paul’s performance announcement, OrioleDB, replaces Postgres’s Heap storage engine and claims 1.5–2 times faster performance: “You don’t have to change anything else.” It removes the need for some background tasks, such as vacuum and bloat. Supabase acquired the technology, continued development, paid for its patent, and is releasing a full beta under Apache 2.0, which covers the patent.
  • The engine underwent pg_regress compatibility testing, Antithesis, nightly TPC-C benchmarks and Jepsen. Multigres tackles a separate reliability problem: Paul says every Postgres operator they examined could lose data under certain conditions. Supabase rewrote the operator architecture and reports 1,000 sequential failovers without data loss; platform access initially targets serious workloads by invitation.
  • Sharding remains unfinished. Paul recounts Sugu’s lesson from Vitess: “I want to focus only on compatibility first,” so applications should eventually keep their queries unchanged when moving to sharded Postgres. Some sharding work should land by early next year, depending on platform developments. Design partners include Booz Allen, Postman and Perplexity; the project is open source beyond Supabase’s own service.

2. Turso supplies the architecture for billions of small databases

  • Supabase currently launches about five million databases monthly; the founders think it will need billions. Giving every prototype a dedicated Postgres cluster would exhaust available computers. The Turso acquisition addresses this different scaling problem: tiny databases need an economical file format, while demanding transactional applications retain a separate route through Postgres and Multigres.
  • Paul describes Turso’s architecture as adding MVCC capabilities around SQLite, including multiple writers. Its rewrite created a pathway toward Postgres compatibility, which prompted his outreach to Glauber. Paul says object storage has, he thinks, “11 nines” of durability and can supply part of what a database cluster otherwise provides. Swyx’s correction matters here: durability is distinct from reliability.
  • Turso will retain its brand and SQLite focus. Supabase Spark will introduce a smaller instance type compatible with Supabase’s libraries: “One database for any idea, any prototype.” The intended progression is Spark to full Postgres to Multigres. The founders call zero-downtime migrations a requirement: an experiment reaching Hacker News’s front page must have somewhere to grow.

3. Compute removes an execution limit while CPU scarcity shapes strategy

  • Supabase Compute addresses Edge Functions’ stated two-second limit. It supports long-running, serverless container workloads, including Rust, Python, agents, chunking and embedding, inside the database’s private network with direct Postgres connections. Durable workflows become possible to build because the missing primitive was compute; previous community attempts on Edge Functions ran into the timeout.
  • Capacity already requires close planning with AWS and paying more. Paul connects incoming investor CapitalG to both Alphabet’s AI products and a multicloud strategy: “We need more compute.” GCP is the obvious next candidate, although he explicitly does not know whether its object storage matches every relevant S3 feature.
  • Swyx describes S3 Express write times of one to two milliseconds: applications can acknowledge a write after placing it somewhere sufficiently durable, then move data into cheaper S3 in the background, as Ant explains. Swyx asks whether Redis is still necessary; Ant’s answer is categorical—yes. Ant describes the storage layers as memory, an NVMe drive, locally attached storage, S3’s equivalent, and regular S3.

4. Better models turn experimental builders into paying customers

  • Paul divides Supabase’s AI growth into three chapters. First came embeddings: Andrew Kane’s extension helped demonstrate that Postgres could also serve vector workloads. The pitch was consolidation—“You don’t need another database if you’re gonna store your own embeddings.” Paul separately praises Turbopuffer’s use of storage innovations resembling Turso’s.
  • The second chapter arrived with Lovable and Bolt toward the end of 2024. Supabase debated servicing these builders and even building its own competing interface. Its mission resolved the question: “Store the world’s data” meant being present when projects started, including toy projects, while believing the tools would improve. Simultaneously, existing customers needed larger-scale infrastructure.
  • Monetization made the change tangible. Paul says he thinks it was $10,000 that a customer earned within the first few days of launching. Agent-assisted Stripe integration lets projects collect money within their first week. MagicSchool supplies another example: its founder was a teacher who identified repetitive teaching tasks and built a business without the traditional technical-cofounder structure.
  • The third chapter began when models improved at the start of the year. Signups accelerated despite little marketing expenditure, while activation and paid conversion also increased. Agents perform setup themselves, bringing activation close to 100%; the founders say these users convert to paid accounts more readily than traditional developers. Swyx’s compression: “Friction’s gone.”

5. Community distribution became model distribution

  • Supabase’s original “Realtime Postgres” positioning attracted little attention. Switching to “open-source Firebase alternative” preceded an unsolicited Hacker News launch roughly 12 hours later. Users jumped from eight to 800. The infrastructure consequences were immediate: about $10,000 in DigitalOcean credits disappeared within 48 hours, followed by migrating 800 databases to AWS during YC’s first week.
  • Swyx argues that Supabase benefited from being established three to four years before LLMs took off, positioned against an existing category leader. The founders acknowledge fortunate timing but now invest heavily in AEO. Community tutorials, videos and posts supplied material models could absorb; support answers were also collected in GitHub Discussions and mirrored onto Supabase’s website.
  • After lawyers resisted broad crowdfunding without accredited investors, the founders asked, “What if we just give them the stock?” They have earmarked $1 million for community members. Gary Abbott, known as Gary Austin in Discord, answered 20,000 questions over six years, 13,000 within an hour. A retired enthusiast who built a wine app becomes the first highlighted recipient.

6. Product-led sales rewards help that produces additional growth

  • Paul frames Supabase as an “index company,” reporting that 60% of each YC batch uses it. Stripe is the benchmark: a developer company that moved upmarket for more than a decade while retaining developer affection. Sales is layered onto that adoption through product signals, rather than replacing the developer-led motion.
  • Triggers include important logos, scaling, errors, limits and spending. Paul’s illustrative example starts with 1,000 weekly triggers and outreach emails, producing 500 replies. Usage patterns reveal the account’s problem; AI helps prepare a script. The instruction to salespeople is: “Get on a call with these people and help them.”
  • In the example, nonresponders serve as the comparison cohort and grow 25% month over month; responding accounts receiving assistance grow 125%. Paul calls the difference “100% incremental uplift,” and compensation follows that increment. His objection to conventional quotas is that they credit salespeople for expansion the product would already have generated.
  • Enterprise demand also arrives from self-hosting that Supabase deliberately does not track. Paul describes pharmaceutical companies, for example, running 100 instances. Control Tower repackages fleet-management capabilities developed for Supabase for Platforms into an enterprise view for launching, monitoring and administering internal databases. Paul says the product launches tomorrow, though he does not know if it will be announced then.

7. Database stickiness survives easier code generation

  • Paul’s enterprise position is unusually firm: “I guarantee they’ll almost never migrate.” For roughly the next five years, almost all of Supabase’s enterprise focus goes toward greenfield workloads. Enterprises want more employees building products; CPOs returning to development through Lovable and Supabase now become executive champions without a separate effort to cultivate them.
  • Swyx pushes on the larger opportunity: coding agents might finally enable migration away from legacy systems such as Oracle. Paul concedes that rewriting million-line stored procedures is probably easier now. He still considers landing inside the enterprise the first priority; pursuing wholesale replacement sounds attractive but has repeatedly proved difficult for database providers.
  • Paul’s explanation centers on OLTP economics. The production database powers a revenue-generating application, so a minute of downtime loses money. Running old and new systems in parallel creates split-brain risk, with data diverging across both. Reconciling that state is hard; starting new workloads elsewhere is one way to proceed. Swyx points out that this can leave customers with two problems.
  • Swyx also asks whether customers will be more attached to Lovable or Supabase as their offerings overlap. The founders emphasize the difficulty of moving databases. They credit Lovable with being first to do a good job of preventing agents from stuffing images into Postgres or disabling RLS to make applications work; better skills helped, and newer models now make fewer such mistakes.

8. Analytical workloads deserve their own architecture

  • Asked about Databricks’ HTAP claims, Paul says Supabase is particularly interested in DuckLake and DuckDB. Swyx describes DuckDB as “like a SQLite for analytics,” able to read object storage and Postgres. Paul says Supabase’s inclination is to use the right technology for each job. Swyx notes that he has not examined Databricks’ implementation closely and could be misquoting it.
  • The architectural objection is physical: local NVMe capacity has limits, and if a transaction has to be split across servers, fetching data from object storage eventually slows the database. Paul sees sharding as the best route toward petabyte-scale OLTP, with analytics treated separately. Reading shared object-stored data through another route remains possible; “trying to smash these two together” does not necessarily make sense to him.

9. Lab defaults could lift the ceiling on product-led growth

  • Paul ranks the priorities as winning strategic labs, winning models and continuing product-led growth; “P4 is enterprise.” US labs receive most attention because they currently deliver the most traffic, a condition the founders acknowledge could change. Becoming a default backend when an AI product creates an application is particularly attractive.
  • Scale previously prevented that role. Using ChatGPT’s stated 1.2 billion monthly active users as a hypothetical, one database per user monthly means 1.2 billion databases. Paul presents Turso’s technology as the route toward that scale. The example is a capacity requirement for a possible distribution relationship, rather than an announced deployment.
  • Swyx recalls that Supabase once thought product-led growth could reach $100 million, perhaps $200 million, before needing another sales motion. AI lifted that ceiling, but the founders do not know where it now sits: “Is it a billion? Is it two billion?” A revenue target colleagues feared would disappoint the team was reached in about four months.

10. Declarative files make the backend easier for agents to understand

  • Paul describes a progression from dashboard-led development through APIs toward code-first, Git-native workflows. A local Supabase folder represents the backend, including functions and database structure. The new pg-delta library supports declarative Postgres schemas, covering tables, policies and comments, and can be used with Postgres databases beyond Supabase.
  • Migration histories are a poor reading surface for agents: determining a table’s current shape might require reconstructing a thousand files. Launching a local database, replaying migrations and introspecting it also takes time. A declarative schema gives the agent the present state directly, supporting rapid iteration on the filesystem.
  • Ant’s longer-term question is what people will build when personal agents can create applications almost immediately. Ant is already trying development from a phone, while acknowledging that infrastructure knowledge helps direct the agent. “I want to build X” producing a live application a second later is an imagined destination guiding today’s tooling decisions.
  • Swyx raises the risk that agents could converge on one approach and trap development at a local maximum. Ant says low-taste, casual builders may converge on the model’s norm, while discerning, high-skill people will keep caring about the details. Paul asks how those high-skill people will continue to be trained; Ant suggests self-teaching and curiosity will persist among top-tier builders.

11. Open source may consolidate after an AI-assisted rewrite cycle

  • An early hiring story illustrates Supabase’s approach to dependencies. Despite YC’s general advice against immediately expanding the team, its partner encouraged hiring Postgres maintainer Steve Chavez. The assignment was effectively “Don’t worry about Supabase”: keep improving Postgres, with Supabase hiring more people dedicated to that project as the team grew.
  • Ant thinks many tools could converge on Rust if it proves the faster, more correct implementation choice. That could produce a few winning projects rather than endless individual rewrites; developers should preserve their “innovation tokens.” Ant also acknowledges operational tradeoffs around Elixir and BEAM. A coordinated dependency-rewrite fund appeals to the founders, although Ant doubts people would stop doing their own versions.

12. Internal AI investment targets complete processes

  • Ant describes Supabase as different startups “glued together,” with product teams choosing tools and working practices. AI policy largely follows that autonomy, although costs are beginning to be consolidated. Checking internal records, Ant reports current spending of approximately $300,000 monthly for 450 people. Usage appears concentrated among a few employees.
  • Swyx and Ant argue that spend leaderboards can focus attention on the wrong variable. The relevant question is how many complete processes AI handles without human intervention, or how much it compresses long-running work. Supabase’s async documentation makes a company-wide harness practical: its recorded history can supply decisions, context and operating principles.
  • Reliability still requires hiring. Supabase reports roughly 50 open roles, especially SREs, with global remote work and location-independent salaries. Thriving in a fully async environment is a substantive requirement. Swyx says AI SRE remains one of the hardest startup categories; Ant agrees that AI has not yet cracked keeping systems running.

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/supabase-s-plan-billion-ai-built-apps

item.title: An Eval for AI Scientists That Knows the Answer Key - Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
item.description: Leash Bio makes agent decisions auditable across 90,000 rollouts, with 100-molecule budgets to find the best binder in a premeasured landscape. Astra 6 leads, and stronger models’ clearest edge is leaving poor chemical neighborhoods sooner, though why remains unknown. Leash plans to try for maybe 20 environments daily by early 2026 or 2027, but transfer to new biology remains unproven.
item.content:encoded:
Latent Space · Ian Quigley · 2026-10-26 · 17 min · 原语言 EN

Leash Bio makes agent decisions auditable across 90,000 rollouts, with 100-molecule budgets to find the best binder in a premeasured landscape. Astra 6 leads, and stronger models’ clearest edge is leaving poor chemical neighborhoods sooner, though why remains unknown. Leash plans to try for maybe 20 environments daily by early 2026 or 2027, but transfer to new biology remains unproven.

TL;DR

  • Leash Bio makes scientific-agent decisions auditable by premeasuring the full landscape. Agents get a target, a catalog, and a budget of 100 molecules to find the best binder; metabolism and other drug-like properties are outside scope. Across about 90,000 rollouts, Leash can compare results with the measured landscape.
  • Better models’ clearest behavioral edge is leaving unproductive chemistry sooner. Agents may repeat tests, choose molecules at odds with their hypotheses, or keep modifying poor binders; stronger models abandon “crappy neighborhoods” faster. Why they do so remains unknown: “We don't know that at all yet.”
  • Astra 6 leads, while expensive models can still underperform. Quigley also rates Sonnet 5.5 and Sol 6.1 well, and says DeepSeek V4 Flash was “pretty good.” Sonnet 5 is “both very expensive and not very performant”; Opus 5.5 had not yet been tested.
  • Improved chemistry fluency changed what Leash could attempt with general models. After poor SMILES handling last summer, models began working meaningfully with chemistry around February. Removing molecular information hurts their decisions. Quigley says they may understand some of it, but qualifies that they are at least using the information—not changing weights during these tasks.
  • Leash’s scaling plan reuses measured experiments across vast numbers of agent rollouts. Quigley calls it “a lab in the loop with amortized latency,” with choices restricted to measured molecules. Leash has screened about 1,000 proteins against a couple of chemical libraries and is doing two environments a day; it plans to try for maybe 20 a day, with that goal for the beginning of 2026 or 2027.
  • Transfer to new biology remains unproven, and a proposed baseline is untested. Quigley does not know whether reinforcement-learning progress will transfer. Asked about a Bayesian hyperparameter algorithm as a deterministic baseline, he says they have not run one and think it probably will not work because the landscape is “too spiky” and “very high-dimensional.”

Digest

1. A measured chemical world makes scientific decisions auditable

  • Quigley’s structure–activity relationship task gives agents a target, a catalog, and a budget of 100 molecules: “go find the best binder you can.” It measures binding improvement; metabolism and other drug-like properties are outside scope.
  • Agents use different search policies, state readable-language SAR hypotheses about why molecules do or don’t work, and test those hypotheses. Across about 90,000 rollouts, Leash knows the entire measured landscape. An agent might find something only “half as good as the best thing in the entire environment,” making missed opportunities visible alongside final scores.

2. Better models abandon unproductive chemistry sooner

  • Quigley sees agents that give up early, retest molecules, or spend budget on choices inconsistent with their hypotheses. Better models leave poor neighborhoods faster; weaker ones keep making “little subtle changes on molecules that aren't ever gonna go anywhere.”
  • A host asks whether this means recognizing bad neighborhoods, beyond simply jumping more. Quigley agrees that they abandon them faster, but says the reason is unknown: “We don't know that at all yet.”
  • Medicinal chemists have judged sampled rationales plausible. A host’s proposed human game faces a catalog constraint: “you can't do whatever you want, you can just do a lot of stuff.”

3. Astra 6 leads an already shifting model field

  • Quigley names Astra 6 the champion, with Sonnet 5.5 and Sol 6.1 also good. Sonnet 5 is “both very expensive and not very performant”; Opus 5.5 has not been tested. DeepSeek V4 Flash was “pretty good.”
  • Frontier releases roughly every 11 days keep disrupting publication plans. Quigley expects the preprint around the episode’s release, with a blog, data, environment packages, and many thousands of transcripts.

4. Chemistry fluency improves, but a proposed optimization baseline remains untested

  • Last summer, Leash began supervised fine-tuning because frontier models struggled to convert SMILES into noncanonical strings representing the same molecule. A SMILES string traverses a molecule’s graph; starting at a different point can produce a different string for that molecule.
  • Around February, models began working meaningfully with chemistry. Removing molecular information now hurts decisions. Quigley allows that models may understand some of it, but clarifies that the evidence shows they are using the information: “Or at least they're using it”—“We’re not changing weights here.”
  • A host asks about using a Bayesian hyperparameter algorithm as a deterministic baseline. Quigley says they have not run one and think it probably will not work because the landscape is “too spiky” and “very high-dimensional”; he calls that the party line.

5. Reusable experiments scale feedback before proving biological transfer

  • Quigley calls the design “a lab in the loop with amortized latency”: measure once, then run effectively unlimited rollouts. Live experiments allow more freedom; premeasured worlds restrict choices to what Leash already measured.
  • Leash has screened about 1,000 proteins against a couple of chemical libraries. It is doing two environments daily and plans to try for maybe 20 a day, with that goal for the beginning of 2026 or 2027.
  • Whether reinforcement learning in these worlds transfers to new biology remains unknown. A host suggests a covering set might help; Quigley also sees broader questions in experimental budget allocation: “when do I stay? When do I go?”

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/eval-ai-scientists-that-knows-answer-key-ian-qui

item.title: Mathematics Just Changed Forever — Kevin Hartnett
item.description: AI mathematics is advancing through formal and natural-language routes: AlphaProof reached silver-medal level at the 2024 IMO using Lean and substantial compute, while Google DeepMind and OpenAI reported gold-level natural-language results in July 2025. Lean can filter candidate proofs, and Buzzard’s team used AI to uncover missing assumptions in published Annals statements involving four Fields Medalists, underscoring that trust still depends on definitions and specifications.
item.content:encoded:
Machine Learning Street Talk · Tim Scarfe、Kevin Hartnett、Leonardo de Moura、Jeremy Avigad、Kevin Buzzard、Paul Lessard · 2026-10-26 · 94 min · 原语言 EN

AI mathematics is advancing through formal and natural-language routes: AlphaProof reached silver-medal level at the 2024 IMO using Lean and substantial compute, while Google DeepMind and OpenAI reported gold-level natural-language results in July 2025. Lean can filter candidate proofs, and Buzzard’s team used AI to uncover missing assumptions in published Annals statements involving four Fields Medalists, underscoring that trust still depends on definitions and specifications.

TL;DR

  • AI mathematics is advancing through both formal and natural-language routes. Hartnett contrasts AlphaProof’s 2024 silver-medal-level IMO performance, using Lean and substantial compute, with the gold-level natural-language results reported by Google DeepMind and OpenAI in July 2025. Lean still supplies a valuable training and filtering mechanism when models generate many candidate proofs: “Lean can tell you which ones those are.”
  • The adoption hurdle has been the cost of formalization relative to its perceived payoff. Hales spent twenty person-years formalizing Kepler’s conjecture; the de Bruijn factor can require twenty or more lines of formal code per informal line. Mathematicians principally want “discovering new math,” making automation and improved understanding stronger adoption arguments than correctness assurance alone.
  • Autoformalization shifts scarce effort toward library design and maintenance. AI can translate papers into Lean much faster than human teams, but checked code can still use cumbersome definitions and weak abstractions. Hartnett calls the influx “a little bit of a Trojan horse”; Buzzard expects larger AI-generated libraries while maintaining that mathlib must preserve conceptual quality.
  • Machine verification moves the trust problem upstream into definitions and specifications. Buzzard’s team formalized fifty Annals theorem statements, then used AI to find both translation mistakes and missing assumptions in published statements involving four Fields Medalists. These were cases where experts understood the intended meaning, but the literal statement was false: “obviously, n had to be at least three.”
  • Formalization can improve understanding and enable new discovery. Checking Scholze’s six-page argument produced a conceptual simplification and resolved his concern that nobody had carefully read it: “something has now actually finally read it.” Separately, Tao’s collaboration reduced twenty-two million implication questions to four remaining cases while uncovering unfamiliar mathematical constructions.
  • AI code verification offers a potential application, conditional on specifying the right behavior. A compression program can satisfy a round-trip proof simply by returning its input unchanged; correctness of the proof does not establish useful compression. Avigad notes Harmonic’s bet that mathematical proving capabilities will transfer to software verification, while Buzzard preserves the uncertainty: “Whether or not it pans out, I don’t know.”

Digest

1. A proof can settle a question and still overwhelm peer review

  • Scarfe opens with Kepler’s conjecture: the pyramid arrangement of oranges appears maximally dense, at about 0.74. Thomas Hales and Samuel Ferguson reduced the problem to configurations; Hales ultimately had 1,767 computer programs, with cases becoming harder as their densities approached the bound. Finishing in summer 1998 settled the computational work without settling how others could verify it.
  • Hartnett describes the Annals of Mathematics confronting a sprawling calculation buried in code. Everything reviewers examined appeared correct, but they could not establish how the entire structure hung together. De Moura recalls acceptance with a disclaimer expressing something like 99% confidence. Hales subsequently formalized the result using HOL Light and Isabelle, before Lean existed.
  • The distinction Hartnett preserves is between legitimacy and mathematical fertility. Hales settled the question, but his relatively elementary computational methods did not create broadly useful concepts comparable to those developed around Wiles’s Fermat proof. Lessard wants more than reliable answers: “I want to know why it comes up with a particular answer. I want the reason.”
  • The economics explain resistance: Hales invested twenty person-years in formalization, while the de Bruijn factor often runs twenty formal lines per informal line, or higher. For mathematicians already confident a result is correct, that additional assurance can seem less valuable than new discoveries. Ordinary checking instead relies substantially on social trust and familiarity with existing mathematics.

2. Lean concentrates trust in a small kernel

  • Hartnett traces de Moura’s earlier success to Z3, begun amid duplicated theorem-proving efforts at Microsoft around 2006. It could represent software pathways through variables and rule out combinations corresponding to particular bugs. Hartnett credits it with saving Microsoft hundreds of millions of dollars and winning automated-prover competitions, but its limited expressiveness left de Moura dissatisfied.
  • Lean combines a programming language with an interactive proof assistant; it is itself implemented in Lean. Users can write programs, state properties, and construct mathematical proofs. Its logical foundation determines what statements mean, while a checker called the kernel verifies the resulting derivations. De Moura’s deliberately narrow assurance is: “we only trust the kernel.”
  • That boundary matters because Lean as a whole “has zillions of bugs.” A kernel accepting a false statement is much worse than rejecting a true one: falsehood can propagate through subsequent proofs. The episode notes historical kernel bugs in Agda, Coq, and Isabelle. De Moura favored a minimal kernel, influenced by HOL Light, so independent implementations could check certificates.

3. Mathematical users won the foundational design argument

  • Avigad had worked extensively with Isabelle and praised its automation, but found simple type theory limiting for modern mathematics’ interlocking algebraic structures. After his own year working with Rocq, he concluded that dependent type theory suited that mathematics. Separately, de Moura says he spent a sabbatical year in 2009 and 2010 working on formalizing the Feit–Thompson theorem.
  • Avigad acknowledged the trade-off—“with great power comes great responsibility”—including implementation difficulty, usability problems, and corner cases. In summer 2013, de Moura chose dependent type theory, giving Avigad confidence that Lean could become useful for substantial abstract mathematics.
  • De Moura says the additional work paid off beyond pure mathematics. Cryptography and differential privacy also require strong mathematical libraries. His former colleague Cédric Fournet later told him mathlib supplied “the right abstractions I need for verifying cryptography.” Supporting demanding mathematical users helped create abstractions useful to the software-verification users Lean originally targeted.

4. A shared library made Lean useful beyond elementary demonstrations

  • Buzzard’s route began with a research crisis. Returning to hard mathematics after raising three children, he struggled with gaps and mistakes in literature surrounding the p-adic Langlands program. His criticism targeted work built upon Scholze’s discoveries, rather than Scholze’s own rigorous work. Without concrete applications to test against reality, he worried that unchecked abstractions could form a “house of cards.”
  • Early mathlib contained about thirty thousand lines and basic undergraduate material, with real numbers only recently available and complex numbers absent. Buzzard contributed the latter—“complex numbers copyright 2017 Kevin Buzzard”—then recruited undergraduates to formalize what they were learning. Roughly three years later, the library knew most of the material taught in their undergraduate degrees.
  • Hartnett describes a “spirit of a barn raising,” with contributions from Commelin, Massot, Avigad, Carneiro, Buzzard, and others. De Moura compares Commelin’s large projects to software engineering: an architect divides work into pieces that unfamiliar collaborators, even high-school students, can complete. Machine checking removes the need to manually establish every contributor’s proof correctness.
  • Tactics reduce the accompanying drudgery. Hartnett recounts early difficulties formalizing even apparently obvious arithmetic; helper programs automate recurring arguments while producing proofs for checking. A ring tactic, for example, constructs an algebraic-identity proof until Lean reports “no goals.” De Moura also enabled users to write tactics themselves, allowing the community to expand Lean’s capabilities.

5. Formal statements offered a cheaper route to the frontier

  • Buzzard first hoped formalizing schemes would establish Lean’s relevance, but mathematicians dismissed them as decades-old material. Around 2018, Buzzard, Massot, and Commelin instead targeted Scholze’s perfectoid spaces, building the definitions needed to express them. Hartnett calls this a “narrow skyscraper to the frontier”: mathlib broadly reached roughly first-year graduate mathematics, with some undergraduate gaps and isolated advances far beyond it.
  • Hales proposed a less expensive entry point than translating entire proofs: formalize theorem statements. Buzzard’s example explains why that matters. Section 3 may establish that a prime p is at least five, while a theorem in section 7 simply mentions p. A reader entering there can miss the inherited hypothesis and misunderstand what has actually been proved.
  • Buzzard initially recognized that checking modern papers wholesale was impossible, whereas defining objects and stating claims looked viable. Hales pushed the idea in 2017; seven years later, Buzzard wrote a grant proposal pursuing it. After a year, his team was about 20% through its selected recent top-journal statements, and he expected substantially more progress over the following year.

6. Scholze’s unread argument supplied the breakthrough

  • In November 2020, Scholze asked Buzzard whether he had carefully read a recent preprint. A London study group had spent a term on it, but a follow-up question exposed the gap: they had skimmed a six-page technical proof, possibly theorem 8.4. Scholze had received similar answers from Princeton and Harvard: “that’s what everybody says.”
  • Scholze and coauthor Dustin Clausen believed the argument worked, but Scholze worried that nobody else had checked it closely. Because much of the technical material was ultimately undergraduate-level, Lean might be capable of verification. The community initially anticipated a year’s work; Commelin found a simplification, and the key argument was checked in six months.
  • The result offered more than reassurance. Buzzard recounts Scholze’s excitement that formalization had revealed a more conceptual argument and that “something has now actually finally read it.” Avigad connects this benefit to thinking about mathematical “APIs”: how concepts are packaged, which information is exposed, and how independently developed components interact.
  • Publicity attracted professional mathematicians whose immediate question was whether Lean could handle their latest theorem. Often the answer remained no, but they could build their area’s foundations. COVID also accelerated participation: formalization combined engaging mathematics with the appeal of a computer game, while interactive proofs allowed investigation that static PDFs could not.

7. AI progress is outgrowing a single verification architecture

  • Hartnett explains mathematics’ appeal as an AI training environment: a clear correctness signal supports reinforcement learning. AlphaProof needed Lean statements, however, while competition problems arrived in natural language. DeepMind reportedly autoformalized about 80% of algebra and number-theory questions nearly perfectly; story-like combinatorics proved harder. The resulting training supply reached tens of millions of formalized problems.
  • For the 2024 IMO, AlphaProof received questions after the human competition, used more time and massive compute, and achieved a silver-medal-level score. Lean supplied verification during both reinforcement learning and competition problem solving. The comparison therefore preserves the achievement alongside the unequal resource conditions; it was not an identical sitting of the human examination.
  • In July 2025, Google DeepMind and OpenAI reported gold-level IMO results using natural-language proofs. Google’s result was officially graded by the IMO; OpenAI’s was separately evaluated. Neither relied on Lean to verify those answers. Hartnett nevertheless expects both approaches: expressive models can generate arguments, while Lean can rapidly filter large numbers of candidate proofs.
  • The episode’s September 2026 update reports that, in Epoch AI’s fixed-budget test, a prerelease OpenAI model proved Erdős problem 126 and refuted problem 74 by counterexample, both checked in Lean: two of 68 problems, versus none for four other models. It also mentions OpenAI’s September 8 claimed Navier–Stokes Millennium Problem resolution with Lean, “not under the best circumstances,” while placing that story outside scope.

8. Exhaustive exploration can uncover unfamiliar mathematics

  • Tao launched Equational Theories in September 2024 to map implications among algebraic laws, using Lean to check results. Within a month, twenty-two million questions had narrowed to 238; by late November, 138 remained. By the end of March, four had resisted progress for several weeks. Settling every implication, however, was never the project’s sole objective.
  • Tao envisioned an experimental branch of mathematics analogous to modern physics: large collaborations and extensive data complementing theory. Exploration uncovered constructions including magma cohomology. John Baez, who had initially called the project a “colossal waste of time,” acknowledged that he had never encountered it. To Tao, this was evidence for discovering “math from Mars.”
  • Hartnett also recounts a speculative discussion with three mathematicians about starting AI from axioms, AlphaZero-style. Their expectation was that it would not necessarily rediscover more than the rational numbers before diverging from human mathematics. Their reasoning concerned abstraction: human researchers select concepts that feel satisfying, useful, and expansive, whereas correctness-driven search need not share those preferences.

9. Autoformalization creates a maintenance bottleneck

  • AI can lower two barriers Hartnett identifies: learning Lean’s fiddly syntax and manually expanding its mathematical library. Agentic coding can help mathematicians express proofs without mastering every language detail. Beyond that, autoformalization promises textbook-scale translation; Hartnett says papers can now become Lean code in a fraction of the time previously required by human teams.
  • The complication is canonical quality. Mathlib wants “polished mathematics”: well-understood concepts expressed at useful generality, with definitions that support future work. Changing a foundational definition can break thousands of files. An influx of formally valid but awkward material therefore creates substantial review and integration work, rather than automatically enriching the shared library.
  • Buzzard observes that AI is happy to “just plow through” constructions humans would redesign. It could also repair downstream breakage after foundational changes. He expects AI-developed libraries to emerge within a year that are more poorly thought out in those terms. Mathlib’s maintainers still require conceptual quality; pouring tokens into the problem does not resolve their different objective.

10. Checked proofs move trust upstream to definitions

  • Scarfe states the limit directly: “a checked proof can still be a proof of the wrong thing.” Someone must establish that a formal conjecture captures the intended definitions and assumptions. The kernel checks the derivation; it does not certify the human choice of target. “The trust has basically moved upstream.”
  • Buzzard’s team translated fifty Annals theorem statements, then asked AI to check them before publication. It found both team translation mistakes and cases faithfully reproducing defective published wording. Four Fields Medalists were involved in statements that were literally false because assumptions such as n being at least three, or a set being nonempty, had been omitted.
  • Buzzard describes a change of mind: a few years earlier, he would have said experts wrote exactly what they meant. Now he sees formalization exposing the gap between expert interpretation and literal expression. His “ninety-nine percent to a hundred percent” framing concerns making those implicit conditions explicit, rather than declaring the intended underlying results overturned.
  • Scholze’s concern reaches deeper: how can anyone know a Lean definition matches the mathematical object intended? “Mathematics remains a human activity.” Commelin and Topaz supplied concrete examples as unit tests—objects that look and quack like ducks. These were not watertight evidence, but Commelin considered them at least as reassuring as reading conventional definitions.

11. Software verification is only as good as its target

  • Scarfe raises Kim Morrison’s experiment using Claude agents to implement zlib in Lean. De Moura says the AI translated C code, repaired the implementation until it passed the C version’s test suite, and proved that, for any data and compression level, compressing then decompressing returns the original input.
  • Scarfe’s pushback compares partial specifications to blind men examining different parts of an elephant. De Moura supplies the sharpest failure case: an identity function for both compression and decompression satisfies the round-trip property without compressing anything. Additional constraints might address output size and comparison with a Rust implementation’s compression on test cases.
  • De Moura distinguishes assistance with a human examining the code from letting AI “go wild” without inspection. In the latter case, incomplete specifications can produce exactly the requested properties while missing the intended behavior. Hartnett also flags skepticism that specifications can adequately cover software at the complexity of most real programs.
  • Scarfe calls review and verification the current bottleneck in agentic coding. Avigad suggests AI might help write specifications as well as implementations, increasing formal verification’s role, and notes that Harmonic believes mathematical-proving capabilities could transfer to software verification. Buzzard leaves the outcome open: “Whether or not it pans out, I don’t know.”

12. The infrastructure remains a human project

  • Hartnett describes a decisive fracture during roughly 2018–2022, when de Moura withdrew to build Lean 4 while mathlib continued growing. He lacked a supporting engineering team and struggled with relentless user requests. Friction with Carneiro reflected different visions for Lean and its open-source mathematical library. De Moura’s complaint was that casually proposed ideas imposed increasingly expensive rebuttal work on their recipient.
  • Hartnett reconstructed the story through six or seven core sources, private emails, and public and private Zulip conversations. Buzzard says trust developed when the participants recognized that Hartnett was not seeking villains or scandal. His own account ends with renewed friendship: an afternoon walking around Seattle with de Moura, talking about Lean and about life beyond it.
  • Buzzard places himself at the excitement end of reactions ranging from “grief” to enthusiasm, while admitting nobody knows how good AI mathematics will become. He expects more theorems and understanding. He supplies the closing counterweight: “what makes our goals special is that they’re ours.” The relevant question remains how humans want to interact with machines and what they want to understand.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/mathematics-just-changed-forever-kevin-hartnett

item.title: Why OpenAI Is Racing to Make Computer Use Superhuman
item.description: OpenAI’s computer-use push hinges on delegation: Ari Weinstein says agents already outpace average users and are “getting really close” to experts. Using existing interfaces, they can connect legacy workflows without new integrations, including procurement that moves 1,000 spreadsheet rows into purchasing and vendor outreach. Enterprise uptake still depends on permissions and approvals, while fragmented browsers and credentials remain a cloud-product hurdle.
item.content:encoded:
The a16z Show · Ari Weinstein、James Sun、Seema Amble、Fabrizio Serafini · 2026-10-26 · 44 min · 原语言 EN

OpenAI’s computer-use push hinges on delegation: Ari Weinstein says agents already outpace average users and are “getting really close” to experts. Using existing interfaces, they can connect legacy workflows without new integrations, including procurement that moves 1,000 spreadsheet rows into purchasing and vendor outreach. Enterprise uptake still depends on permissions and approvals, while fragmented browsers and credentials remain a cloud-product hurdle.

TL;DR

  • Ari Weinstein’s speed thesis is that expert-level computer use could make delegation the default. He says agents are already faster than the average human at using a computer and are “getting really close” to exceeding experts. The adoption threshold is overcoming the feeling that “I could’ve just done that myself,” particularly when a task must finish before other work can happen.
  • Computer use gives agents access to legacy software without waiting for new integrations. Weinstein’s framing is that “computer use works with everything,” using applications through the same interface as a person. He expects decades-old systems and cheaper, newly built software to coexist, creating room for products that wrap legacy workflows in better experiences.
  • Enterprise adoption depends on enforceable boundaries alongside better models. James Sun describes application and website restrictions, configurable approval requirements, and a system he calls Guardian—or “auto-approve” in the app, he thinks—that checks actions against safety and the user’s intent. As agents become too fast to watch continuously, “the control part becomes more and more important.”
  • The clearest immediate workflows connect tedious work across systems of record. Sun’s procurement example moves 1,000 spreadsheet rows through purchasing software and vendor outreach; finance reconciliation offers another opening where APIs are missing. Seema Amble’s interjection captures the opportunity: “boring is opportunity.”
  • Vertical expertise and deployment remain openings for startups despite broader lab capabilities. Sun argues that understanding regulation, go-to-market and customer service still matters, while OpenAI’s own teams remain stretched. His “speed and pain” moat is illustrated by a restaurant workflow connecting inventory photos, demand forecasting, purchasing and employee scheduling.
  • Agents create pressure on web monetization without eliminating the value of interfaces. Sun thinks agent ad impressions usually do not generate revenue, while WebMCP could let people browse and agents handle tedious tasks. His broader position is explicit: “I don’t think UI is going away”; Fabrizio Serafini adds that enterprise users still need payment explanations, audit trails and control.
  • Cloud distribution could broaden adoption, but product coherence remains unfinished. Sun reports “YC-level growth week over week” after browser capabilities entered products already used agentically, without providing figures. Reaching a billion users is an ambition tied to giving phone users cloud computers; fragmented browsers, credentials and context remain obstacles, while Weinstein wants agents to “adapt to you instead of you adapting to it.”

Digest

1. Superhuman speed would make delegation the default

  • Weinstein says computer use is already faster than the average human at using a computer and “getting really close” to being superhuman, meaning faster than an expert computer user. Background jobs can take time, but watched tasks—or tasks that must finish before something else can happen—must overcome “I could’ve just done that myself.” Once agents are faster, he expects delegation to become the default unless someone specifically wants to perform the task.
  • Weinstein says Sol was already strong at computer use. Astra is “a little bit faster on average” because it needs fewer thinking tokens for the same task, and feels more reliable around the edges. His comparison between 99% and 97% reliability illustrates why a small improvement matters; he presents that assessment as anecdotal experience.
  • Creative gains appear in the Microsoft Paint launch demo Weinstein cites. Sun adds that Astra beats 5.6 “every time” in internal game matchups and cites tweets describing Astra beating Fallout in “about 30 hours or something like that.” His bridge to practical work remains loose: “I know that probably translates to something.”
  • Weinstein calls OpenAI’s offering the “fastest, cheapest, and most reliable” computer-use product, without supplying comparative figures. He expects improving cheaper models to produce more variation in model choice by task. Sun still sometimes handles a two-button task himself because that is easier; further speed gains could remove even that boundary.

2. Enterprise readiness requires controls beyond model capability

  • Amble’s pushback is accountability: employers can hold a trained person responsible, even if that person performs worse. Sun generally finds Astra capable of “anything that a person can do” on a computer, with sensitive actions and messages that should feel personal warranting involvement. Repeatable work benefits from product-spec-like requirements; flexible input asks for missing details but can keep gathering context if the user does not answer.
  • Sun calls Astra “our most aligned model,” citing greater resistance to prompt injection and unintended actions. That matters for procurement, vendor interactions and customer communications. Yet enterprise reassurance also involves showing administrators internal and third-party evaluations and giving them explicit ways to exclude sensitive applications or data sources.
  • The deterministic layer is a configurable sandbox: administrators can permit particular applications and websites while excluding others. Separate approval settings can require a person’s intervention for downloads, uploads or entry to a new website. Sun describes these as “dials” an enterprise can adjust, allowing different workflows to carry different levels of autonomy.
  • Sun describes a system called Guardian—or “auto-approve” in the app, he thinks—that uses a model to assess each action for safety and consistency with the original intent. Consumers may want minimal interruptions; enterprises can choose which actions proceed. Weinstein adds visible cursor movement and permissions for new applications or websites, depending on mode, as ways to build trust before users become comfortable delegating more.

3. Universal access connects fragmented systems of record

  • Weinstein’s architectural point is universality: “computer use works with everything,” without waiting for a developer to create a connector or MCP server. Sun calls it a “universal kind of API” that increasingly appears inside complex tasks. His desired “shared intelligence layer” would let applications benefit from context gathered elsewhere, avoiding a fragmented world in which every website has an agent that cannot talk to yours.
  • For the “boring is opportunity” category, Sun’s sharpest example is procurement. Teams fill a spreadsheet with 1,000 rows of lab-equipment requests; operations transfers those requests into internal purchasing software; procurement then uses its output to contact vendors. He sees computer use automating the entire sequence across the spreadsheet, internal system and external interactions.
  • Sun also highlights month-end reconciliation across expense and other ledgers whose software lacks APIs: agents can reconcile records, flag anything interesting and investigate. His second category is more ambitious creation—circuit design, architecture, hardware engineering and game design—supported by stronger visual capabilities. He thinks usage there could expand as enterprises understand the models beyond the first opportunities to automate tedious work.

4. Proactivity helps when tasks change shape

  • Sun’s Dots example starts with notification fatigue: his old Codex automation checked Slack every hour or 30 minutes, but inconsistent relevance taught him to ignore notifications. A Dot can instead follow a judgment-based goal—flag messages from his reporting chain or critical product feedback—when the task is “not the same shape every single time.” Each Dot gets its own cloud computer, letting it act on what it finds.
  • For a relevant bug report, Sun describes the agent using a browser to enter Sentry, retrieve logs, analyze them and return feedback. That replaces his manual loop of deciding which report matters, opening Sentry, downloading logs and feeding them into Codex. He says Dots can control both local and cloud computers, supporting this kind of proactive, long-running workflow.
  • Weinstein’s consumer examples include DMV forms, unsubscribing from emails, and work people previously lacked time to undertake. His own examples include finance and meal-planning spreadsheets in Apple Numbers, which he calls an “obscure spreadsheet program” that the model nevertheless handles well. He also mentions a personal trainer making customized materials for clients. These are tasks that can be time-prohibitive in personal life but become easier with computer use.

5. Legacy systems and crafted interfaces can coexist

  • Sun asks whether agents preserve clunky incumbents or enable new AI-native vendors. Weinstein expects both: the cost and complexity of creating software are much lower, but production systems written 10, 20, 30 or 40 years ago will not disappear overnight. Computer use “may put more pressure” on vendors to work better with agents because their software can already be operated through its existing interface.
  • On the open web, Sun identifies a business-model conflict: he thinks agent ad impressions usually do not count toward revenue. For willing sites, OpenAI supports WebMCP in its in-app browser. He imagines people retaining enjoyable hotel or shopping browsing, while agents handle tedious work; the person can finish the transaction, enter their credit card, and then hand work back to the agent. WebMCP lets the person and agent use the site’s interface together.
  • Sun’s defense of craftsmanship is a tactical trainer he built for his wife for a game of connecting five pebbles that he thinks is called Omok. He tailored the learning experience to her preferences; an agent could summarize mistakes afterward, but playing remains her activity. “I don’t think UI is going away.” Weinstein extends that possibility to software designed for “100 people or one person.”
  • Serafini’s enterprise counterpart is an interface for setting goals and inspecting logic. A user should be able to understand why a payment happened and specify timing or a discount at 30 days without executing the whole workflow. “Why should we settle for shitty software?” Weinstein imagines purpose-built interfaces with agents underneath, sometimes operating legacy applications to deliver the experience.

6. Startup opportunity remains in domain knowledge and deployment

  • Sun remains bullish on startups despite OpenAI’s scale: even with thousands of employees, its teams feel stretched. Founders who understand an industry’s regulation, go-to-market motion and customer service still have room to build. His formulation is that “speed and pain are kind of the moat,” with slower AI diffusion across many verticals leaving substantial work available.
  • His restaurant example joins several systems: photos of back-of-house storage help estimate what will be missing based on projected traffic for the next day; computer use then orders groceries through Shopee or another procurement application. The workflow also adjusts employee schedules in an ERP, taking account of historical traffic, such as a holiday period. Sun’s point is that these customers need help understanding the tools, connecting them, deploying them and servicing them.
  • Weinstein’s practical advice is to decide whether the product assists a person at their desktop or operates software on a cloud machine through the API. Human intervention should follow that choice. Founders must also decide when to report success or failure and how to summarize activity: a stream of “this happened” notifications will eventually be ignored.

7. Cloud distribution needs a more coherent experience

  • Weinstein describes six to nine months of change: capabilities improved earlier in the year, followed by rapid product uptake in the last couple of months, although only part of OpenAI’s user base uses computer use. Sun’s candid lesson comes from Atlas, which he joined in January: “RIP Atlas.” Its agentic features were not a major draw because many people treated it as an ordinary browser.
  • Sun says incorporating browser capabilities into existing products with established agentic usage produced “YC-level growth week over week,” without giving numbers. He sees cloud access as the next inflection: giving ChatGPT users, including people using their phones for daily life, a powerful computer they do not need to understand how to operate is his route toward a billion users.
  • For the next quarter, Sun emphasizes coherence. The Chrome extension can use Chrome’s password manager and other Chrome features, while the desktop app’s in-app browser has different cookies and passwords, and the cloud computer has different things. Consumers encounter several browsers that do not communicate as expected. Computer use is conceptually simple—“it’s an AI using your computer”—but those implementation details make the experience harder to understand.
  • Weinstein wants to add real-time, multimodal collaboration to a product currently strong at background work. He also identifies a behavioral hurdle: people must remember to delegate and change established habits. Dots’ proactivity suggests a way forward, with the agent identifying useful work itself. His ambition is for it to “adapt to you instead of you adapting to it,” while people continue setting and steering goals.
