item.title: Why OpenAI Should Be Scared of Open Source
item.description: Robot Ventures led Nous Research’s $90 million round on Tarun Chitra’s thesis that Hermes can own AI’s user relationship through a packaged harness. Unsolicited forks by Chinese small-robot makers provide product-fit evidence grounded in Nous’s training, inference and context research. Enterprise distribution and token-order-flow rebates offer growth paths, but Tarun says demand is not secured until contracts are signed.
item.content:encoded:
Delphi Digital · Tommy、Tarun Chitra · 2026-10-26 · 76 min · 原语言 EN

Robot Ventures led Nous Research’s $90 million round on Tarun Chitra’s thesis that Hermes can own AI’s user relationship through a packaged harness. Unsolicited forks by Chinese small-robot makers provide product-fit evidence grounded in Nous’s training, inference and context research. Enterprise distribution and token-order-flow rebates offer growth paths, but Tarun says demand is not secured until contracts are signed.

TL;DR

  • Robot Ventures led Nous Research’s $90 million round on a thesis that Hermes can own AI’s user relationship. Tarun Chitra compares the opportunity to investing in Phantom or FOMO: harnesses control preferences, context and access to users, while inference providers supply execution. If AI develops crypto’s market structure, he expects those two layers to capture value while routers and models face pressure.
  • Hermes’s product advantage comes from years of research compounding into better defaults. Tarun argues that Nous’s work on training, inference and context management lets it absorb decisions that OpenClaw leaves to users. His OpenClaw analogy: “Here’s all the parts to this car. Go build the car.” Hermes instead learns preferences, generates skills and supports work across models.
  • The useful inheritance from crypto is resource-conscious engineering, with token-first projects supplying the cautionary history. Tarun credits Chinese model companies with choosing better optimizations than decentralized-training teams, prompting pivots in 2024–2025. Early token agents anticipated demand but delivered weak products—often “meme coins with more steps.”
  • Unsolicited robotics adoption was a stronger diligence signal than another monetization story. Over three to four months, Tarun examined usage and forks, finding Chinese manufacturers embedding Hermes in small robots without Nous knowing. He treats those forks as evidence of product quality and brand attachment; “retention and stickiness” could matter more in a downturn, even when individual forks generate no revenue.
  • Enterprise customization gives Hermes a second distribution path alongside its consumer community. Businesses can add permissions, compliance, privacy and internal data connections. Tarun says Microsoft and NVIDIA participated in the round; he expects Hermes to be among the open-source harnesses available through Microsoft and says NVIDIA installs it by default on DGX Spark machines. Tommy sees an owned AI stack as a business asset, but Tarun checks his enthusiasm about ready-made enterprise demand: “nothing’s in the bag until the contract’s signed.”
  • A low advertised inference price can conceal a higher total agent bill. In Tarun’s GLM 5.2 illustration, a nominal 95% discount becomes $1.05 over 21 queries when caching savings disappear, versus just over $1 from the higher-priced provider with perfect caching. He reports statistical evidence of providers gaming this mechanism: “you’re probably caching, but you’re not passing on the price benefits of caching.”
  • The longer-term opportunity is to supply the harness underneath other companies’ agents. Tarun calls Hermes the “white label harness for anyone,” with security, context management and brand credibility supporting adoption. His categorical belief is that every SaaS company needs a harness or router to participate in token order flow, where aggregated demand can earn rebates and revenue shares.

Digest

1. Crypto’s AI survivors learned to leave tokens behind

  • Tommy introduces Robot Ventures’ lead in Nous Research’s $90 million round and says Delphi is a co-investor. Tarun’s broader claim is that crypto participants’ “fingerprints” are everywhere in the recent open-source and open-weight surge, particularly among teams applying engineering lessons without attaching a token.
  • The initial 2023 pitch often assumed mining infrastructure could become an AI network with minimal adaptation. Tarun argues that language models introduced difficulties image models did not, and that no one seemed to want a decentralized image model. Tokens also let projects attract valuations before demonstrating utility. His description—“meme coins with more steps”—includes well-meaning teams whose ideas simply did not work.
  • Tarun’s own position changed: he once considered decentralized systems scams, then spent four or five years understanding why blockchains worked despite conventional distributed-systems objections. That left room for a roughly “1% chance” that genuine architectural advances could overcome problems in decentralized training. He was more optimistic about inference than training.
  • Nous stood out through specific research: YaRN for longer context, compression-oriented embeddings, and low-bandwidth training through DisTrO. Tommy adds that Nous did synthetic model evaluation early and recalls a distributed training run of “40 billion parameters or something like that”; the number remains uncertain. Tarun’s criterion was disciplined work on bounded problems, with no token and no promise that one invention would solve everything. He also distinguishes Nous from Prime Intellect, which he says was less focused on training and hedged by becoming a GPU reseller.
  • Tarun’s broader reasoning is that distributed systems succeed through many separate optimizations, not one breakthrough. He uses Bitcoin as an example: hash security, difficulty adjustment, inflation and bandwidth each pose distinct technical problems that must work together. He says Nous and, in many ways, Prime Intellect were unusual in bringing that breadth of focus to decentralized AI.

2. Chinese model companies chose the more productive constraints

  • Tarun compares decentralized-training teams with Chinese model developers starting around the same period. Both faced resource constraints, but of different kinds: uncertain participation, bandwidth and payment on one side; weaker chips and infrastructure on the other. Chinese companies also built cheaper, Mercor-style data-collection operations. Out of thousands of possible optimizations, “the Chinese companies’ 100 were just better.”
  • Tommy pushes back that DeepSeek’s work was genuinely innovative. Tarun agrees: his argument concerns which constraints produced competitive results. Once a model becomes good enough, agentic and recursive improvement can accelerate progress, making catch-up harder. That helps explain why decentralized infrastructure teams began pivoting in 2024–2025.
  • Early crypto agents repeated the pattern: directionally right about agents, weak on execution. A year after their peak, Claude Code and Codex were expanding in capability and usage. Tarun points to Nous and, philosophically, OpenRouter as examples of crypto’s optimization ethos finding a place in non-token AI. He says Together AI started as a decentralized inference network, while distinguishing Corby’s approach from teams trying to launch a token.

3. OpenClaw demonstrated demand while exposing an execution gap

  • Tarun calls OpenClaw “the right idea for a product” with the wrong execution. Its Android-like abundance of choices—models, reasoning, context and infrastructure—restricted who could use it. Tommy corroborates the experience: after building a personal agent in n8n, he tried OpenClaw and returned to manually connecting services because it felt so clunky.
  • Tommy insists OpenClaw deserves credit for creating the category; Tarun agrees. The failure was turning personal experiments into transferable products. At an OpenClaw event around December or January, late 2025 or early 2026, Tarun saw unreliable demos whose configurations others could not readily download. One example was a cat-feeder project that would send a USDC payment. His test was blunt: “does this have a market size of one? Yes.”
  • That creates room for second movers. Tarun attributes Claude’s late-2025/early-2026 uptake partly to accessibility and human touches that let nontechnical people build applications, while acknowledging OpenAI subsequently “came back with a vengeance.” He sees a parallel in Z.ai, Kimi and MiniMax learning from DeepSeek and changing reasoning, resource usage and attention designs.

4. Hermes’s advantage starts beneath the interface

  • Hermes began as Teknium’s side project, prompted by liking OpenClaw’s concept while finding it unusable. Tarun argues Nous’s previous work supplied the foundation: training exposed data-collection problems; inference exposed orchestration and context-management problems. Tommy notes that Nous’s models had tens of millions of downloads. Those research years equipped the team to understand failures underneath an agent’s interface.
  • Context portability is central. Tarun recalls expectations that OpenAI and Anthropic would create lock-in through proprietary context formats. He says OpenAI now supports open models in the same context, undermining that expectation. Nous had already concentrated on sharing context across models and agents: “interoperability is here,” in his blockchain terminology.
  • Tarun’s explanation is cumulative rather than dependent on one architectural breakthrough. Successful distributed systems require “1,000 little optimizations”; he also describes the need for “10,000 tricks” that compound. Hermes benefits from understanding the layer below the product. OpenClaw’s contrasting philosophy was to hand users the components: “Here are all the parts to this car. Go build the car.”

5. The harness becomes AI’s wallet and preference engine

  • Tarun’s “Maslow’s hierarchy of compute needs” starts with renting a GPU, which still leaves environment setup, memory management and DevOps. Together, Modal, Baseten and Fireworks move users toward served model endpoints. His crypto mapping is running your own node versus receiving an RPC endpoint: useful abstraction, but still some distance from an accessible consumer product.
  • A harness is closer to a wallet such as Phantom or FOMO: it manages state, history, preferences and sensitive credentials, with defaults that reduce mistakes. Tarun puts OpenClaw nearer MetaMask or MyEtherWallet because setup still demands substantial user judgment. The distinction determines the reachable audience, just as using a wallet differs from manually submitting a transaction through Etherscan.
  • Hermes’s approach includes learning behavior, generating skills from usage and managing model and inference-spending decisions. Tarun says it was built around the idea that a model router would exist. Tommy’s objection is practical: most users cannot distinguish reasoning settings or model choices, but recognize a bad answer—and then conclude the agent itself is broken.
  • The philosophical difference changes architecture: which choices reach the user, which preferences are learned, and when clarification is necessary. Tarun calls this “the difference between product engineering and back-end engineering.” Nous’s design sensibility matters alongside its technical depth; the team once mocked as an expensive merchandise company had already shown attention to its audience’s tastes.

6. Packaged open source expands the reachable market

  • Tommy describes Hermes as the open-source, non-lab-owned alternative within the consumer-agent set. Tarun qualifies the distinction: DIY competitors exist, but Hermes is “open source but packaged.” His analogy is Ubuntu’s defaults, updates and accommodation of closed-source components. Likewise, Hermes accepts Claude and OpenAI API keys rather than requiring ideological purity about the models underneath.
  • Tarun credits Pi with taking over the DIY community and says it “probably has the most forks.” Its simplicity makes it useful for teaching harness design—including in an introductory computer-science class his brother described—but builders must supply adapters themselves. Hermes targets prosumers and progressively broader users while retaining extensibility. Tarun still wanted evidence developers used its source: an open-source label without actual reuse would concern him.

7. Robotics forks supplied the strongest diligence signal

  • During three to four months of diligence, Tarun combined OpenRouter usage data with inspection of Hermes forks. Public application and model leaderboards made analysis resemble blockchain data research. The forks answered another question: did builders value how Hermes was constructed? He treats this as brand sentiment expressed through engineering choices, distinct from revenue or immediate monetization potential.
  • His strongest example was small Chinese robotics manufacturers using Hermes as an embedded interface. They had to keep costs down because hardware consumed their budgets, and wanted to minimize inference costs. A robot approaching a dryer and folding clothes might need separate models for movement, spatial planning and dexterity, with different reasoning and action requirements. Tarun says evaluations have shown that separating tasks across models often performs better than relying on one model.
  • Manufacturers adapted Hermes with device-specific tool calls such as moving a hand or head. Nous had not even known some existed: “We didn’t even know this person forked it.” Tarun saw unsolicited adoption as product and brand fit. Amid what he says is a market where “half of the ARR numbers are fake,” this attachment mattered because “retention and stickiness” could become more important during a downturn.

8. Enterprise expansion adds customization and distribution

  • Tommy’s ownership thesis is that an organization’s architecture, data, memory, hosting and interactions accumulate as an asset, while customization can produce distinctive outcomes. Tarun describes Nous’s enterprise work in concrete terms: businesses can clone Hermes, connect databases, and add privacy, compliance and permissioning layers. They retain a common foundation while adapting it to internal requirements.
  • Tommy argues a large consumer community supplies advocates inside companies and effectively puts go-to-market “in the bag.” Tarun immediately qualifies that: “nothing’s in the bag until the contract’s signed.” He agrees internal champions help, while maintaining the distinction between widespread individual adoption and closed enterprise business. Nous is pursuing enterprise expansion alongside its consumer and open-source community.
  • Tarun reports growing Portal subscriptions and OpenRouter usage, saying Nous had passed 2 trillion tokens across apps on OpenRouter. He also describes tens of millions of users and, “if I remember correctly,” tens of millions of unique GitHub accounts accessing them daily. He acknowledges multiple accounts are possible and presents GitHub identity as an imperfect measure.
  • Tarun says Microsoft and NVIDIA both participated in the round. He expects Hermes to be one of the main open-source harnesses available through Microsoft, and says NVIDIA installs it by default on DGX Spark machines. These relationships support the enterprise push while the community continues supplying adoption from the consumer side.

9. Cheap inference can become expensive when caching is gamed

  • OpenRouter connects applications requesting models with providers quoting input, output and cached-token prices. Tarun maps the application to a wallet, the router to an exchange or DEX aggregator, the model to a protocol, and the provider to a validator or liquidity provider. Cached tokens can be “hundreds or thousands of times cheaper” because they avoid repeated computation.
  • Providers are not selected solely by lowest price. Tarun describes probabilities incorporating quoted prices and a quality score covering factors such as uptime and throughput. His question was whether providers could advertise attractive rates to win allocation, then misrepresent how much they cache. Without cryptographic verification of cache accounting, a provider’s report determines how much of that benefit reaches the customer.
  • In Tarun’s GLM 5.2 illustration, Z.ai quotes $1 per million tokens and cached tokens at 0.001 cents. With perfect caching, 21 queries cost roughly $1, just over $1. A rival advertises 5 cents per million, a 95% discount, but bills every repetition as uncached: 21 × $0.05 = $1.05. Agent follow-ups make the apparent bargain more expensive.
  • Tommy asks whether the harm is worse memory or responses. Tarun clarifies that it is price: “you’re probably caching, but you’re not passing on the price benefits of caching.” He reports statistical evidence from experiments across providers. A provider may lose money on the first query but earn it back on repeated queries. Tarun also limits the analogy: equating this too closely with crypto front-running or MEV would be wrong, although it is marketplace manipulation.

10. Harnesses and inference providers could capture the economics

  • Tarun’s investment thesis follows from that market structure: “All the money goes to the top and the bottom.” In crypto, he argues, wallets and validators or liquidity providers gained leverage while aggregators and protocols were squeezed. Applied to AI, the favored positions are harnesses and inference providers. “Hermes is like investing in Phantom or FOMO,” in his formulation.
  • Models can attempt licensing monetization. Tarun describes BSL-style terms requiring fees above revenue thresholds; Tommy mentions Kimi, and Tarun says GLM added similar provisions with different terms. He says Kimi’s revenue cap is particularly low. But routers face low entry barriers as SaaS companies, including Vercel and Ramp in his examples, introduce marketplaces. They can become successful businesses while still facing margin compression from abundant competition.
  • OpenRouter’s admission controls mean it is not permissionless or fully decentralized, Tarun emphasizes. Once admitted, providers compete in an open market. That differs from bundled services where users cannot see the infrastructure supplier or allocation decisions. Open models allow users to unbundle the harness, model selection, routing and inference provision that centralized coding products package together.

11. Hermes could become infrastructure beneath other companies’ agents

  • A wallet analogy has limits: Hermes need not be the final consumer interface. Tarun’s “guess” is that harnesses become a “security and brand” and context-management layer underneath applications, including consumer bots like Instinct. Companies can build differentiated experiences while inheriting shared infrastructure. His robotics examples already show developers using Hermes as a foundation rather than an endpoint.
  • Token aggregation supplies a possible revenue mechanism. Tarun says inference providers already offer payment-for-order-flow-like rebates: “if you guarantee me X billion tokens a day,” they can return part of the fee. Tommy asks whether individual users control routing. Tarun agrees they can choose providers directly, while Portal and other access paths create different arrangements for managing that demand.
  • Looking a year ahead, Tarun’s belief is categorical: “every SaaS company either has to have a harness or be a router,” because participation in token order flow creates monetization opportunities. Hermes could be the “white label harness for anyone.” Existing companies bring users and data; they avoid starting from zero and depend on a foundation whose security reputation matters much like a wallet’s.
  • His closing analogy is a fintech sharing revenue with the bank underneath it. Tarun says Muse is going to monetize in a crypto-like way by charging transaction fees on in-app purchases and sharing revenue with Stripe, Shopify and others. To Tarun, competing counterparties and shared order flow make these systems resemble crypto markets. Enterprise deployments, consumer use and applications built on Hermes are therefore separate potential growth paths for the same underlying harness.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/why-openai-should-be-scared-open-source

item.title: Vol.239 访问思考者1｜李翔对话陆铭：聊聊AI、内卷、房价和消费抉择
item.description: 陆铭判断，AI会加速人口向大城市集聚，住房需求仍取决于就业流向。制造业标准化岗位易被替代，劳动力转向依赖人口密度的服务业，AI创新也受益于市中心高频、跨界交流。住房供给与消费时间是集聚转化为内需的约束；企业周均工时已达48.6小时，陆铭认为减少加班、增加休假也很关键。
item.content:encoded:
高能量 · 李翔、陆铭 · 2026-10-26 · 141 min · 原语言 ZH

陆铭判断，AI会加速人口向大城市集聚，住房需求仍取决于就业流向。制造业标准化岗位易被替代，劳动力转向依赖人口密度的服务业，AI创新也受益于市中心高频、跨界交流。住房供给与消费时间是集聚转化为内需的约束；企业周均工时已达48.6小时，陆铭认为减少加班、增加休假也很关键。

TL;DR

  • 陆铭判断，AI会加速人口向大城市集聚，城市与住房的长期需求仍要看就业流向。 制造业中标准化、流程化、可编码的岗位被机器替代，劳动力转向更依赖人口密度、规模和流量的服务业；创新又需要高频、跨界、随机的交流，把企业进一步推向市中心。“人工智能时代不是减少集聚，它是加速集聚的。”
  • 高房价要区分繁荣带来的结果与供给受限造成的成本，房价回落也有两面性。 收入和人口增长推高房价，与限制土地供应、住房不足造成的挤出，政策含义完全不同。陆铭认为，在一定家庭收入基础上，房价下降20%到30%，连同住宅、商铺和写字楼租金下降，可能重新吸引居民与企业；代价是短期土地财政受损，这也不等于他已经判断市场触底。
  • 消费的潜力不仅取决于收入，也取决于服务供给和居民有没有时间消费。 京沪1—8月社零下滑，在陆铭看来还涉及以旧换新的跨期替代、平台销售归属和服务消费统计不足，不能直接等同于整体消费萎缩。他特别强调，企业周平均劳动时间已达48.6小时，而服务消费需要时间；“更多放假、限制劳动工时、减少加班”，也是扩大内需的条件。
  • 地方争投资不自动等于全国利益最大化，规模经济需要统一市场和相应的财政激励。 陆铭用“长期、全局和多维的发展”衡量县域竞争：早期缺资本、产业规模较小时的增长方式，到了汽车、大飞机、人工智能时代，可能转化为重复建设、补贴竞争和地方债务。他寄望消费税扩面、征收环节后移、增加地方分享，使地方从争生产转向吸引人口和消费，但强调改革不能一蹴而就。
  • 汽车等行业的低价竞争，会沿供应链传导为利润压缩、拖欠账款和过度加班。 陆铭指出，中国汽车产量已超过3000万辆，部分竞争实际上发生在中国企业之间；若靠补贴维持亏损企业、压上游成本来抢市场，出口增长未必带来企业和员工共同受益。“牺牲了国内的消费者的福利，补贴了国外消费者”，是他对这种生产方式的尖锐概括，解法涉及退出机制、劳动权益、环保和知识产权执法。
  • 产业政策的关键是实施条件和方式，不能把一次地方投资成功直接复制成全国模板。 陆铭支持政府协调早期投资、土地、金融和人才，但反对过早押定技术路线，以及各地不顾比较优势同时上马相同产业。谈到合肥，他要求把长三角区位、中科大人才、京东方成长阶段和投资时点一起纳入归因；地方基金要求“返投本地”，在他看来还可能造成市场分割。
  • AI改变的不只是研究工具，还包括稀缺性、人的能力、企业组织和社会保障的研究对象。 陆铭把记忆、背诵、演算、推导概括为“机能”，主张大学增加通识、实践和对人性与需求的理解。对于AI供给，他判断美国“大概率”走公司投资、公司收费的道路，而中国正在走更普惠的模式；后者仍须回答算力浪费和补贴加速替代就业的问题。
  • 个人的城市选择应服从职业、偏好、社会关系和人生阶段，不能由集聚趋势推出统一答案。 陆铭把市中心房价比作“演唱会的前排座位票”，提醒居民理解自己为便利与丰富生活付出的成本。对于在老家买房、等身体不好再回乡的安排，他特别提醒：医疗、护工和熟悉的人际网络，可能让人年老后更需要已经生活多年的城市；家乡情感与房产投资应分别考虑。

Digest

1. “逃离”与“逃回”同时存在，大城市仍靠机会和同伴吸引人

  • 李翔以“是不是已经很少再有人谈逃离北上广”开场，陆铭并不认同声音已经消失。增长放缓、服务业受冲击、就业机会减少，以及外来人口获得公共服务的障碍，仍会使人觉得大城市生活压力过高。
  • 陆铭认为，回乡者遇到的也不只是收入问题：小城市就业较少，生活丰富度有限，更可能找不到同行、合作伙伴或兴趣相投的朋友。“大家可能生活在不同的世界里，连对话都很难”，于是有人又想“逃回北上广”。
  • 对城市整体而言，人口是在持续替换中集中的：有人留下，有人离开，又有人进入。繁荣时，房价上涨让“城市病”讨论更突出；增长承压时，他更关心中心城市及周边都市圈能否重新创造就业、拉动经济。

2. 高房价究竟是结果还是原因，决定了它的经济含义

  • 陆铭先把房价看成结果：一个地方经济增长较好、收入较高、人口较多，住房需求自然更强。因此，高收入地区房价更高，本身不必然意味着发展出了问题。
  • 另一条逻辑来自建设用地指标。陆铭解释，城市即使存在把农业用地转为住宅或工业用地的需求，也受到指标约束；过去控制大城市人口、把拥堵与面积扩张简单等同的思路，又加强了这种限制。
  • 关键是限制土地并未让人口停止流入，住房供给不足却推高了成本。此时房价从繁荣的结果变成人口进入的障碍：“会导致生活成本提高，对人口形成挤出效应。”

3. 房价回落既损伤土地财政，也可能降低进入大城市的门槛

  • 面对李翔关于2011年调控后京沪房价受控、甚至下滑的提问，陆铭称其为“双刃剑”。地方收入与土地出让高度相关，房价下跌会拖累土地财政；但对具备一定收入实力的家庭，下降20%到30%可能意味着原来买不起、现在买得起。
  • 住宅租金、店铺租金、写字楼租金下降，也可能让居民和企业重新觉得留在上海可行。陆铭观察最近大半年，成本下降成为吸引力的趋势“恐怕正在重新出现”；他同时保留条件：经济如果触底反弹，才会在新的周期中带来机会。

4. 京沪社零下滑，需要拆开基数、统计归属和消费结构

  • 李翔把房价变化与京沪1—8月社零同比下滑联系起来。陆铭承认，家电、装修等需求与住房有关，但不认为这是主要原因；首先应看上一年以旧换新的基数和“跨期替代效应”——提前买过车，今年不会因为再次补贴就再买一辆。
  • 平台经济改变了销售的统计地点。陆铭举例，上海居民在线上购买商品，销售额未必计入上海，因此按销售地观察城市消费，会受到平台和结算归属的影响。
  • 按陆铭的介绍，社零绝大部分是商品，服务主要统计了部分餐饮、住宿，大量其他服务未被覆盖。一线城市收入较高、年轻人较多，消费更偏向服务，实际发生的结构变化便可能没有充分反映在这项指标中。
  • 他仍保留对城市自身问题的批评：产业转型和长期对年轻人不够友好的政策，会削弱消费人口基础。北京出现年轻人持续负增长，上海虽稍好也有相近压力；年轻人增长受限，对消费拉动并不有利。

5. 城市人口上限，要先统一都市圈口径，再讨论承载能力

  • 陆铭提醒，中国通常所说的地级市、直辖市，可能覆盖一两万平方公里，上海也有六千多平方公里。他认为这类行政范围在国外往往更接近县或都市圈，直接拿北京2000万人、上海2500万人与海外“市”的人口比较，会混淆口径。
  • 他以东京都市圈约1.2万平方公里、3700万人作参照，称其面积大致相当于上海加苏州。若真正以上海市中心画圈，范围大致到昆山、太仓，而非苏州市区；按他给出的这个口径，人口约3100万。
  • 因此，扩大容纳能力不只是向现有行政边界内塞人，而是都市圈连片发展，并让土地配置适应产业、基础设施、学校、医院、养老院和住房的需要。增加住房供应，也会增加可以留下的人口。
  • 承载力还会因基础设施改变。上海曾有“水质型缺水”，青草沙水库建设后，按陆铭的说法增加了约800万到1000万人口的自来水供应能力。“城市对人口的承载力是一个变量，不是常数。”

6. 服务业占比提高，使人口继续向大城市乃至市中心集中

  • 陆铭列举，韩国约50%人口集中在首尔周边都市圈，日本约三分之一在东京都市圈，英国约三分之一在伦敦周边。他用日本作更直观的比较：全国约1.2亿人口、面积接近长三角，却有三分之一人口生活在相当于上海加苏州的范围。
  • 这种集中在他看来来自生产和生活便利，而不是经济学家的倡议。“人口不是经济学家主张出来的，而是人民用脚投票出来的。”即使不少国家尝试控制中心城市人口，集聚经济仍持续起作用。
  • 服务业占比越高，见面交流、学习，以及演唱会、电影、体育等线下消费就越重要。较大市场才能支持更丰富、多样、时尚的服务，因此他在《向心城市》中进一步提出：“人会往贵的地方集中，不是往便宜的地方集中。”

7. 大城市地位逆转很少，技术和体制变化是重要例外

  • 李翔追问超大城市是否也会衰退，陆铭回答“非常少”，但首先列出技术变化。美国早期波士顿领先，后来水运和国际贸易发展，纽约凭借哈德逊河入海口、连接内陆航运与海港的条件，取得了新的中心地位。
  • 战争、自然灾害，以及计划经济人为布局工业，也可能改变城市命运。陆铭以十堰这样的工业城市说明，大厂带动形成的城市，在市场化后可能收缩；剔除这些因素，他认为大城市选址和空间分布总体相当稳定。

8. 人口流出地区要顺势调整，景德镇不能被当成普遍模板

  • 陆铭强调，改革开放对城市分工影响极大：只要经济开放、国际贸易主要依靠海运，东海、南海沿岸就有优势。部分地区制造业萎缩或人口外流，可能有深层历史和地理原因，不能仅靠意愿逆转。
  • 对远离沿海、沿江和大城市的地区，他提出集约化发展，向中心城区集中，同时寻找仍有比较优势的农业、旅游和资源行业。他调研西北时看到的具体机会，包括沙漠、戈壁中的光伏，以及利用高盐度盐湖养海鱼。
  • 有些地方人口负增长，他判断可能是长期趋势，甚至“不可避免”。国家扶持仍可用于改善生态、县城生活品质，让低房价、慢节奏成为吸引力，但这与要求每个地方恢复人口增长是不同的目标。
  • 景德镇的机会来自瓷都产业基础：从规模生产转向大量小作坊，再结合人才培养及国内外年轻人进入，形成新产业。陆铭同时强调，这种条件“并不多”，地方政府和当地人士需要寻找自身机会，不能由外部学者坐而论道地复制。

9. 创新高度集中，不等于人均生活差距必然扩大

  • 陆铭肯定大学对城市的带动：四年学习会形成情感、实习机会和留当地工作的可能，但前提是有与专业配套的企业。李翔补充，企业也会因为大学和人才集中而进入，双方存在相互强化。
  • 对李翔提出的“技术是否扩大城市间不平等”，陆铭区分短期与长期。AI可能在短期拉大地区差距，而且创新的集中度超过经济活动本身的集中度，经济活动集中度又超过人口集中度；这并不等于所有差距都在扩大。
  • 他区分总量与人均：人口和经济总量差距可以拉大，人均GDP、扣除生活成本后的实际收入、生活质量差距却可能缩小。大城市收入高，也有房价、物价、通勤和压力；中小城市能回家午休，就是钱之外的差别。按他的研究，中国人均差距正在缩小，但仍然很大。

10. 去大城市不是普遍建议，职业、偏好和关系决定个人选择

  • 李翔提起保罗·格雷厄姆鼓励年轻人去大城市的建议，陆铭没有顺势给统一答案：“我没有建议。”人口流动的总体规律，不能代替每个人对自身条件的判断。
  • 首先看职业：AI等行业更适合大城市，部分文创、艺术工作者则偏爱安静的小地方。他也把选择具体化为：在市中心住小房子、进AI公司工作，或回小城市从事政府数字化服务，各自有不同的收益和代价。
  • 性格和社会关系同样重要。能否接受贵房、小房、长通勤，是否需要丰富的城市生活，有没有朋友与亲属，都影响取舍。“如果你爱钱，就待在大城市”，只是他的通俗比方；他随后补充，很多人留下来只是觉得大城市好玩。

11. AI创新需要高频、跨界、随机的交流，推动企业重返市中心

  • 陆铭观察，互联网时代企业在硅谷集聚，这一轮AI企业进一步进入旧金山市中心。他把现代创新概括为“高频率”“跨界”“随机”：AI从业者可能每天与哲学、伦理、设计等领域的人交流，也可能在一次活动中偶然认识合作对象。
  • 企业回到中心城区还会带动消费。员工喝咖啡、下班喝酒、看戏，会吸引生活服务业跟进；因此，集聚不只影响博士和技术人员，也影响服务员究竟在大城市就业，还是回乡开店的选择。

12. 市中心房价像前排门票，居民应理解自己已经付出的成本

  • 陆铭的比喻是，大城市房价相当于演唱会门票，市中心房价则是“前排座位票”。离演出、展览和各种活动更近，需要付出额外代价；位置的便利性，本身就是住房价格的一部分。
  • 他劝学生多出门时，列了已经付过的“三笔钱”：房租或房价中的城市便利溢价，税收支持的免费博物馆、图书馆，以及为留在竞争激烈的城市而作出的收入和生活质量牺牲。付完这些再长期宅家，就像买了前排票“然后去打瞌睡”。
  • 有学生后来告诉他，听过这段话后，每个周末都会带孩子逛街、看博物馆。陆铭自己也向往有院子、种花的安静生活，但大学教师职业，以及看展、听音乐会的偏好，又让他享受大城市的便利。
  • 选择还可以随人生阶段改变。陆铭举美国人年轻时在纽约工作、退休后到迈阿密等“阳光地带”养老为例，类比中国的海南：“人一辈子不一定待在同一个地方。”

13. “大国”的优势与治理难题，都需要进入经济学研究

  • 陆铭解释自己持续写“大国”系列，是因为国家规模过去被考虑得不够。大语言模型和平台经济既依赖大量语言使用者，也依赖应用迅速进入足够大的市场；中文用户规模，就是他理解中国AI发展的一个因素。
  • 全球化高歌猛进时，人们更相信自由贸易、跨境投资和国际机构协调，国家大小似乎没有那么重要。地缘政治竞争上升后，大国的话语权重新突出；他还提到加拿大提出“中等强国”联合应对大国博弈的思路。
  • 大国治理也不能直接套用美国联邦制。陆铭用地方债举例：美国地方可以关门、让公务员休假，乃至破产；中国单一制下的中央地方责任和地方间关系，具有不同结构。
  • 人口流动让这种结构问题更具体：财政转移支付若仍按户籍所在地配置，人已到沿海工作，教育、住房等资源却留在流出地。结果是一边公共服务不足，一边学校没有学生，形成“空间资源错配”，需要联动土地、户籍和财政改革。

14. AI替代制造岗位，再通过服务就业加强人口集聚

  • 陆铭把二、三产业作为讨论主体，称其合计占中国GDP已超过93%。制造业大量岗位具有“标准化、流程化、可编码”的特征，24小时黑灯工厂、无人工厂说明，其中不少工作已能由机器人和AI承担。
  • 服务业中则有很多岗位仍需要人与人见面。制造就业收缩后，劳动力会向依赖人口规模、密度、流量的服务业转移；他的具体例子是，今天的骑手或专车司机，上一份工作可能就在工厂。
  • 这不是纯粹的技术判断。若认定AI让集聚消失，就可能觉得外来人口公共服务无需继续改善；若集聚会加速，政策决心反而应更大。个人购房同样如此：相信人口离开还是继续进入大城市，会产生完全不同的决策含义。

15. 地方竞争的强度，与土地权力和税收归属有关

  • 陆铭认为，逐底竞争在美国、日本、欧洲也存在，但程度不能直接与中国相比。在中国，中央决定农田和建设用地指标，地方决定住宅、工业、商业用途乃至楼盖多高；土地、财权、户籍等制度共同扩大了地方介入经济的能力。
  • 李翔用亚马逊第二总部竞标反问：中国似乎没有同样公开的总部争夺。陆铭回应，总部通常只有一个，观察范围应扩大到地区总部、分公司，以及能独立结算的子公司，而不能只盯着唯一的总部选址。
  • 他的解释是，结算和税收往往归总部或注册地，因此地方尤其欢迎设立独立法人、独立结算中心。单纯开一个业务分部，税收可能仍归总部；设立当地结算实体，才更容易把税收、产值和就业留在本地。

16. 县域竞争的局部增长，不能自动加总为全国利益

  • 李翔把张五常强调的县域竞争，与陆铭主张的统一大市场放在一起追问。陆铭提出检验标准：“每个地方都想让自己的本地产出最大化，这些产出自动加起来，就等于全国的产出最大化吗？”他的答案是否定的。
  • 他以“长期、全局和多维的发展”拆解矛盾。借债投资能提高当期增长，却可能留下还不起的债；每个地方都建汽车厂，也能增加当地投资，却可能在全国造成重复建设和产能过剩。
  • 早期中国缺资本，争投资有助积累；浙江不同地方分别生产鞋子、珍珠，也不必然冲突。今天汽车、大飞机、AI的规模经济更强，适合少数地区集中，各地却可能同时争人工智能、大数据、云计算、物联网和生物医药，矛盾随之扩大。
  • 陆铭没有把早期概括为只有好处。他强调，市场分割一直存在，只是过去过分强调竞争收益、忽略代价；与上世纪80年代相邻县阻止对方商品进入相比，今天市场整合其实已经改善，但发展阶段变化，使剩余问题更需要解决。

17. 对企业友好的竞争，应体现为营商环境而非无条件补贴

  • 李翔追问，地方竞争至少是否有利于公司和投资者？陆铭仍答“不一定”：湖南某地石化项目有历史产业基础，布局也考虑了环境条件，投资可以有利；若没有这些条件，只为增长引入央企，可能换来环境破坏和长期成本。
  • 陆铭描述一种循环：条件好的地方，企业靠市场发展，不希望被干预，政府也因企业多而管不过来；条件较差的地方更依赖招商、干预和向企业寻求帮助，反而可能让营商环境恶化，外来投资者也不适应凡事找关系的方式。
  • 他不赞成用“投资不过山海关”概括东北，认为这会污名化整个地区，并特别提到辽宁近年改善营商环境的努力。真正值得持续竞争的是对民营企业友好、公平竞争和法治化：“改善营商环境才是真正最好的招商引资方式。”
  • 仅讲道理仍不够。税收基于生产、以企业注册地结算，考核又重GDP和税收，地方便仍有动力争项目。对人口大量流出的地区继续主要考核增长尤其难以持续，因而政绩观、税制和考核体系都需要调整。

18. 汽车内卷沿产业链传导，出口和产量不等于共同赚钱

  • 李翔提到一组数据，称2020年上半年整个汽车产业利润大概两百多亿元，其中一半是比亚迪；这个利润可能和宁德时代上半年两百多亿元利润差不多。他借此追问，行业内卷是否来自过去的地方竞争。
  • 陆铭认为原因复杂，但地方争相招汽车项目确实是一环。他提到中国汽车产量已超过3000万辆，国内市场有限，企业转向出口和压价；若地方继续扶持亏损企业，竞争和扩产就可能被延长，补贴最后也可能打水漂。
  • 另一环是下游把价格压力传给上游：车企压轮胎供应商，供应商再压自己的上游。产量、出口和销售可能都不错，链条上的利润却很薄，甚至没有；加上严重拖欠账款，企业陷入“不做没生意，做了不赚钱”，也不赚钱。
  • 压成本还会变成减员和加班。陆铭引用上一年企业周平均劳动时间48.6小时，认为过长工时在很大程度上违反劳动法，也挤掉服务消费时间。“讲得难听点，实际上是牺牲了国内的消费者的福利，补贴了国外消费者。”

19. 李翔质疑谁敢先涨价，陆铭把问题转向竞争条件与执法

  • 李翔的反驳很直接：主机厂之间已经如此激烈，哪家公司敢先提高价格、把利润分给供应链？陆铭承认，若国外卖100元，中国卖99元，成本提高后必须卖101元，确实会失去竞争力。
  • 但他要求先判断面对的是国际竞争，还是中国企业彼此竞争。他另设一种情形：国外卖100元，中国卖50元，只因另一家卖49元；在这个前提下，他认为中国企业即使卖到60元、70元，也不影响国际竞争力。
  • 因而他强调监管劳动权益、环境和知识产权，提高违规成本。调研中有小企业抱怨“创新就被仿制，企业核心团队也被挖走”；在他看来，不能一边要求创新，一边容忍侵犯知识产权和压低合规标准。
  • 亏损企业的退出也不能被补贴无限推迟。陆铭认为，地方救助濒临破产的企业，会维持恶性竞争和过度产能，并引发海外对公平竞争的质疑；链主企业也应带着上游和员工一起受益，而非只在意自身利润。

20. 消费税改革可能改变地方政府争生产的激励

  • 陆铭解释，当前增值税与生产密切相关，消费税征收面较窄，且往往在生产环节征收，主要属于中央税。他用香烟举例：最终消费者承担税负，但税在烟厂环节已经收取，地方并未因此形成同样强的消费激励。
  • 他提到的改革方向是扩大消费税覆盖面、征收环节后移到消费端，并增加地方分享。这样地方就会更关心扩大消费；而消费离不开人，公共服务、生活质量和吸引居民留下，便更可能成为地方发展的重点。
  • 陆铭强调，大税制改革“不能一蹴而就”，但问题已经紧迫。短期还需要中央协调、公平竞争审查、严格执法和政绩观改变；在没有地区间关税的国内市场，不能改用补贴、廉价土地或容忍违法来保护本地生产，要考虑“国之大者”。

21. 借鉴美国、日本和东南亚，应分别学习长处并避开旧坑

  • 对美国，陆铭看重私人高科技企业参与重大工程，以及科研、教育体系对全球人才的吸引力；但他也用加州高铁论证和诉讼成本的例子，说明跨地区协调、基础设施建设可能受到体制掣肘。
  • 对日本，他肯定技术引进、吸收和消化能力，以及企业社会责任、合规、海外投资时尊重当地法律文化的做法；需要避免的则是持续补贴亏损企业，导致低效率企业无法退出。
  • 他还建议学习部分东南亚国家的社会组织。即使人均收入更低，它们在贫困、少数族裔平等、女性权益等方面的社会参与，也有值得中国借鉴之处，不能只向收入最高的国家寻找答案。
  • 李翔追问，优点是否与自由主义等治理传统高度耦合？陆铭承认历史影响，但强调不能被传统束缚。过去借债补基础设施可能有用，今天人口流出地区却可能留下八车道、十车道和闲置住房；发展阶段改变，所有国家都需要改革。

22. 技术路线尚未清晰时，产业政策的支持范围不宜过窄

  • 陆铭把日本押注氢能理解为政府和企业共同作用，事后看“不是那么成功”。他的提醒不是停止支持新能源，而是不要把新能源提前等同于某一种能源，误以为已知道几年后的技术答案。
  • AI也存在同样问题：具身智能、实体机器人、大语言模型该走哪条路线，连大企业内部都可能有争议，甚至因分歧出现团队离开。若政府此时宣布已经决定唯一方向，他认为风险很大。
  • 因此，他主张保留多元竞争和淘汰机制，把政府支持做得宽一些，也更多考虑事后激励，而非发展前就把企业和技术名单全部选定。“成功了就奖励，没成功就被淘汰”，是他提出的一种调整思路。

23. 产业政策要区分中央与地方，争论重点是如何实施

  • 陆铭的立场很明确：“产业政策不能没有。”早期产业可能缺乏清晰市场前景和投资，还涉及金融、土地、税收、人才培养及跨地区、跨行业协调，尤其初创企业不可能独自完成这些工作。
  • 但在中国，中央产业政策与地方产业政策必须分开讨论。中央鼓励高科技、AI、生物医药，他认为没有问题；更值得反思的是一声号召后各地普遍上马，不因地制宜，最终变成补贴、重复建设、局部过剩和偿债困难。
  • 所以他要求把争论从有没有政策，移到“怎么实施”。中央需要改善法治、公平竞争审查和税制等环境；地方则要按自身条件制定政策，不能把产业政策简单化成招商引资，最后“弄下一堆烂摊子”。

24. 合肥的成功，需要把地利、人才、企业阶段和投资时点一起归因

  • 面对“学习合肥模式”，陆铭首先提醒，过去某些招商手段恰恰属于今天公平竞争审查不再允许使用的范围。他还提到中央政府前段时间出台政策，严禁区县级政府再搞投资基金，反问：如果政府投就能成功，为什么不应当鼓励所有地方都这样做？
  • 他尤其关注基金要求“返投本地”：政府给资金，企业必须在当地投资、设公司、雇人、产生税收。但企业原本应按成本收益决定选址，这种约束可能造成市场分割；他的团队研究认为，这类问题应纳入公平竞争审查。
  • 对合肥本身，陆铭要求把长三角区位、中科大的人才基础，以及京东方处于高成长阶段、恰好需要选址等条件一起考虑。成功究竟来自这些条件与时机，还是单纯来自政府投资？李翔接住这一点：“大家应该仔细做归因。”

25. 服务业已有需求，观念和场景限制可能让潜力发挥不出来

  • 李翔问最担心什么，陆铭回答的不是没有机会，而是机会被观念和传统制度挡住。他指出，服务业增速快于制造业并非今年上半年才出现；商品价格有时负增长，服务价格却在上涨，在他看来说明不少服务需求真实存在。
  • 供给障碍有很具体的形态：河道水上活动、滑板、餐馆外摆等场景受限；演唱会结束后要求半小时内疏散，地铁有的晚上10点半就停运，也会截断二次消费。服务发展不只是增加项目，还涉及日常管理规则。
  • 他反对把生活服务业笼统看成低端：医疗、教育、养老、卫生、幼托和餐饮，都是生活质量的基础。高收入群体也有需求，例如高尔夫供给不足可能让消费流向海外；满足这些需求，同样可以带动国内就业。
  • 对“居民缺钱”，陆铭并不否认，也赞同恢复增长、资本市场成长和房地产修复所带来的收入与财富效应。他强调的是尚未被充分讨论的部分：放开服务供给，同时减少加班、增加休假，让居民有时间把需求变成消费。

26. 人口老龄化的近期解法，也包括让现有劳动力流向更高收入地区

  • 陆铭赞同推迟退休、鼓励生育和提高劳动者素质，但提醒，今天出生的孩子成为劳动力还需要16年。在这段时间内，不能期待鼓励生育立刻增加劳动供给，必须寻找可以更快起效的办法。
  • 他给出的办法是国内自由流动：一个人在老家只能赚2000元，换到另一个地方能赚4000元、5000元，对个人是收入大幅提高，对国家则是劳动力利用更充分，也增强养老资源。他因此特别重视空间布局、城市群和城市化率。
  • 障碍仍在流入地：陆铭认为发达地区更有老龄化、少子化压力，却可能把外来人口视为公共服务负担，还受财政和土地约束。他以约6000平方公里的上海仍有三分之一土地种庄稼为例，追问高房价、高区位价值地区是否需要保留如此大的农业比例。

27. AI时代的教育问题，正在从读多少年转向究竟学什么

  • 陆铭把记忆、背诵、演算、推导称为“机能”，即机器也能承担的能力。他明确补充，这不等于中小学不需要记忆背诵，因为儿童大脑发育仍需要训练；需要重新审视的是大学是否还把大量时间花在这些任务上。
  • 他希望大学增加跨专业选修、通识和实践，培养审美、价值观、政策理解，以及对人类趋势、人性和市场需求的认识。尤其理工科学生不能只会完成作业，还要更接近企业和社会；教师队伍、课程内容也要一起调整。
  • 陆铭认为，高中更普及、少子化让大学更容易考取之后，毕业率不再是唯一重点。他用东北“人人都上大学”的讨论说明教育机会变化，最后把问题落回内容：“真正应该关心的不是大学毕业率，而是学什么。”

28. AI不仅改变经济学的方法，也改变稀缺性、决策和组织本身

  • 李翔提出，若AI创造极大供给，供需关系是否会变？陆铭认为，学界已经较多讨论用AI建模、统计，却较少讨论研究对象本身的变化。AI会在有些领域极大增加供给，让原来稀缺的资源不再稀缺，也让别的东西变得稀缺。
  • 决策主体也发生变化。AI提供信息、参与决策，可能放大情绪、带来幻觉和错误预期；进入agent阶段后，它又不只是执行指令，而成为代理人，组织里出现“多重委托代理关系”，相应制度需要重做。
  • 企业可能更小、更扁平，并出现没有雇主的就业。陆铭指出，OPC有时仍有几个员工，有时确实只有一个人；一旦不存在传统劳动雇佣关系，社会保险与保障体系怎样覆盖，便成为新的经济学问题。

29. 普惠AI与收费AI各有代价，陆铭给出的是模式判断而非定论

  • 陆铭判断，美国由大公司投资、需要收回投资的模式，“大概率”会倾向公司收费；若有钱才能充分使用，就会在人与人、企业与企业之间产生分化。他把这种分化视为该模式需要面对的重要后果。
  • 对中国，他限定为基于目前接收到的信息作判断，并将正在走的普惠、公共方向称为“AI时代的社会主义”。地方补贴一人公司，让更多人用得起AI，是他用来说明这一路径的例子。
  • 他没有只讲普惠的好处：算力便宜后，会不会被浪费，例如拿补贴算力给自己写小说看，如何监管？企业会不会利用补贴算力替代员工，反而扩大就业压力？这些在他看来都是待研究、待回答的问题。

30. 研究方法的成熟，也可能变成回应新现实的负担

  • 陆铭肯定经济学的数学建模、数理统计和因果分析，认为学科因此发展成熟；但在现实剧变时，既有框架也会成为束缚。他反复澄清自己没有否定模型，而是主张“经济学不应该用我们的方法去剪裁我们的问题”。
  • 新问题可能缺理论、文献和数据，也可能具有中国特殊制度背景，暂时很难模型化。陆铭认为不能因此就不研究：“不能因为方法不适用、不能发论文，就不研究”，不应成为回应社会和政府需求的理由。
  • 他以1994年北大中国经济研究中心成立，以及武汉大学引入现代经济学教育为标志，回顾中国经济学国际化。国际差距缩小是成绩，但晋升评价越来越看国际顶刊发表，也可能让缺乏标准数据和模型的中国重要问题被边缘化。
  • 陆铭对同代及更年轻学者的公共参与作了自我批评。他担心同行评价退化为“你评我，我评你”，不再关心外部需求，最终成为“闭门做游戏”；当社会觉得这个学科不再需要，学科本身也会失去生命力。

31. 创新向企业集中，大学必须重新解释自己的价值

  • 李翔指出，生成式AI的前沿研究正从大学实验室转向企业。陆铭解释，这轮创新需要动辄上亿元的大资本，也需要借大公司的算力和应用场景迅速验证效果；大学往往既缺资金，也缺验证场景。
  • 他观察到美国、乃至中国企业开始直接招聘高中生。学生可能比较：读四年大学拿文凭，还是到大厂工作四年学更多东西？陆铭对大学的警告很尖锐：若还教“不痛不痒的东西”，“就等着被大厂取代”。
  • 大学已经出现回应：美国一些顶尖大学把文科与数据计算、AI结合；他在外滩大会听到一位大学副校长强调横向课题，让团队持续与企业实践结合，对自己团队的适应能力因此更有信心。
  • 陆铭认为，不能一概把横向课题看成挣钱、做生意，基础研究与应用如今高度结合。他尤其批评国内社会科学、经济学回应不足：接受采访、回应现实、服务政府项目，仍可能因不计入评价而被视为浪费时间，甚至被质疑“是不是想当网红”。

32. 是否进入AI公司，要把前沿机会与个人责任分别考虑

  • 对经济学研究是否也会迁入企业，陆铭坦言无法判断；但若假设自己是30岁、没有当前团队和学科责任的年轻经济学家，面对AI公司的邀请，他会“毫不犹豫地愿意”。现实中的他已年过半百，须考虑研究院、团队和交大学科，因而会犹豫。
  • 他支持进入企业并非口头表态：团队与平台、AI企业已有不少合作，一位当年毕业的博士正在面试中国大厂研究院。平台企业关心平台消费，但学界的研究角度未必能回应企业真正的问题，这正是他希望缩小的距离。
  • 陆铭欣赏克鲁格曼和《城市的胜利》作者Edward Glaeser，因为两人都重视现实问题。他尤其反对因克鲁格曼写媒体专栏就否定其学术：基于专业研究做科普是在服务社会，也不能抹去其获奖工作的开创性。

33. 参与政策与保持独立并不矛盾，研究应容许提出不同结论

  • 陆铭认为，经济学作为群体应更多参与实践和国家发展，但这不是要求每个人都做同一类应用题。数学建模或研究全人类一般原理同样有价值；他批评的是整个学界对本来属于自身领域的重要问题回应不足。
  • 他的具体例子是货币传导：货币政策宽松，却似乎未充分刺激消费、信贷和投资。国家希望理解机制、获得建议，如果连这样的核心经济学问题都缺乏足够研究支撑，他认为说明学界出了问题。
  • 独立性则意味着不能“先有结论再做研究”，变成迎合。陆铭回顾自己十年前不少主张与当时政策不同，后来又成为改革基础；他参与中央和地方咨询，并自述是国家“十五五”规划专家组成员，不认为这取消了学术上的距离。
  • 这种距离也体现在新研究中：不少出租住房建在郊区，但主要需求者是工作岗位集中于市中心的服务人员，距离太远可能导致需求不足乃至闲置。他主张更多向市中心布局，说明深度参与政策仍可以提出与现行做法不同的结论。

34. 回乡情感与回乡置业应分开，年老后可能更需要城市服务

  • 陆铭警惕把某次大城市受冲击、务工者返乡，当作人口集聚长期逆转的证据。他观察，有人同时在大城市租房、县城买房、农村盖房；这种安排可能建立在将来一定回乡的预期上。
  • 他在珠三角遇到一位17岁便去广州、如今与他年龄相仿的女性，对方说喜欢广州，但老家也建了房，等“哪天动不了了，就回去”。陆铭以假设表达概率判断：若100人中99人如此想，其中很可能超过一半最终不会回去，尤其身体不好时更需要医院、护工和熟悉的关系网络。
  • 他强调，不能由此判定这个人的选择一定错误；但空置住房和人口流出地房产贬值，可能损害个人福利。对家乡有依恋、常回去看亲友，与是否必须在那里买房投资、身体不好后回去，是应分别讨论的问题。

35. 普遍原理与中国特殊制度，可以构成同一项研究的两层解释

  • 对如何兼顾长期有效的研究与快速变化的现实，陆铭把答案放在两层结合：制造业减少就业、收入提高后服务需求增加，具有普遍性；公共服务对外来人口尚未完全开放、土地配置受管制，则是中国特殊性。前者解释规律，后者导向容积率等具体改革。
  • 他承认英文期刊更偏好一般原理，中国制度背景讲细了别人不熟悉，讲粗了又解释不清，发表可能吃亏。但是否因此放弃，是个人价值选择：“我人在中国，是中国培养起来的本土博士”，对他而言，这不是不研究中国问题的理由。

36. AI基础设施与数据统筹需要国家协调，但行政力量也有边界

  • 对李翔转述马斯克建议美国学习集中力量投入AI基建、能源，陆铭认为有道理。大规模基础设施具有“正外部性”，企业可能无法通过市场收费收回投入，还涉及跨行业、跨地区协调；中国中西部光伏与算力、存储中心的布局，是他举出的协调优势。
  • 数据统筹则是共同挑战。平台数据存在企业和行业壁垒，政务数据也未打通；从同一城市跨部门，到同省跨城市，再到全国贯通，难度逐级上升。若再接入民间数据，还要处理对提供数据的企业和个人给予补偿的问题。
  • 技术摩擦是真实存在的：不同部门存储格式不同、时间变量不同，同一个人或企业未必能对应起来。即使愿意共享，也不等于数据可以直接拼接使用。
  • 制度摩擦同样重要：部门负责人未必愿意分享，平级的大数据管理部门也未必有能力协调其他部门。陆铭最后指出，权力按部门和地区划分，解决内部问题可能有效，跨界时却可能成为阻力，仍需要更高层协调；中国能否把统一市场和中央协调优势转化为更好的结果，“要努力”。

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/gaonengliang-2026-10-26-vol-239

item.title: The $2B AI Startup Simulating Human Behavior with 85% Accuracy
item.description: Simile reports 85%-plus accuracy predicting responses from 1,000 people, tested two weeks after interviews. Studies costing hundreds of thousands or millions over years could become “just a query away,” Park says, with CVS and Banco Itaú among customers. Useful decisions still require modeling alternatives and causal effects, a limitation Park highlights.
item.content:encoded:
Sourcery · Joon Sung Park、Molly O'Shea · 2026-10-26 · 56 min · 原语言 EN

Simile reports 85%-plus accuracy predicting responses from 1,000 people, tested two weeks after interviews. Studies costing hundreds of thousands or millions over years could become “just a query away,” Park says, with CVS and Banco Itaú among customers. Useful decisions still require modeling alternatives and causal effects, a limitation Park highlights.

TL;DR

  • Simile’s “85%-plus accuracy” claim comes from a study of 1,000 real people whose agents predicted responses to surveys, behavioral studies and stimuli. Participants supplied life-story interviews, then returned two weeks later for testing; Park dates the result to the end of 2024. His operating principle is that “the simulation has to be grounded” and evaluated alongside people.
  • The commercial wedge is research that becomes fast enough to run whenever a decision arises. Park says concept testing, conjoint analysis and MaxDiff studies costing hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars over years become “just a query away.” Customers include CVS and Banco Itaú, with applications spanning store layouts, messaging and customer understanding.
  • Predictive value depends on modeling alternatives and causation, including the gap between stated intentions and action. Someone may consistently rate likely gym attendance five or six out of seven, yet choose another hour of sleep instead. Randomized experiments matter because customers ultimately ask, “What do we need to do now to shape the future?”
  • Simile’s panel partnerships reach over 40 million people globally, with new population needs usually met within 24 hours. Park says the operation talks to tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, weekly. Participation requires informed consent and the ability to withdraw; excluding underage people leaves “one blind spot that we own.”
  • Simile pairs predictions with confidence estimates to help customers calibrate consequential decisions. A companion model produces a zero-to-100 estimate; Park says customers find confidence above “90% or usually 85%” robust enough for high-stakes decisions. Deployment includes helping users determine when to validate findings or collect more data.
  • With $300 million raised at a reported $2 billion valuation, Park’s defensibility thesis combines behavior models with close customer deployment. He places simulation in its “GPT-4, GPT-4.5 era,” useful today and changing monthly. He expects the industry to reach today’s coding-agent maturity in about a year and a half to two years, with customer relationships becoming “stickier” through forward deployment.
  • Park’s longer-term ambition includes potentially using simulations to evaluate societal interventions. Climate policy involves competing incentives; if AGI is here or imminent, he asks whether simulations could explore where UBI works without waiting for a five-year study. Asked about a $15 billion acquisition offer, he stays conditional: if only Simile can pursue an ambitious idea, “then we’re going to pursue that.”

Digest

1. Smallville made human simulation plausible

  • Park’s opening “I do think we live in a simulation” rests on a civilizational argument: societies want to understand themselves, and “the best way to understand something is to recreate it.” He calls simulation a societal portrait. Construction starts with individual tastes and behaviors; put those people together, and complex outcomes emerge through their interactions.
  • The 2022–2023 Smallville work began with GPT-3 and GPT-3.5, when models were “still fairly janky.” Researchers populated a Pokémon/Sims-like town with 25 agents, each with a name, characteristics and life story, plus memory, planning and reflection. Set the day before Valentine’s Day, the simulation produced party organizing and romantic invitations without preprogramming those interactions.
  • The first test was believability: researchers interviewed agents about their lives, relationships and gift choices. Human evaluators compared responses with the agents’ experiences and human-written alternatives. An agent should want to see someone it cared about, Park argues, rather than whoever it passed most frequently. That was the “illusion of life”; the next challenge was faithfulness to actual people.

2. Real-person validation produced the accuracy claim

  • Researchers recruited 1,000 people sampled to represent the US across gender, race, ethnicity and other characteristics. Voice-to-voice AI interviews elicited life stories, difficult decisions and important relationships, supplying data for agent twins. After two weeks, participants returned for surveys, behavioral studies and responses to stimuli; agents predicted their answers. Park reports “85%-plus accuracy” at the end of 2024, the initial foundation for Simile.
  • Predictability requires translating stated attitudes into behavior. Park describes risk tolerance as “not really known to change,” while intentions and actions follow different curves: respondents may rate likely gym attendance five or six on a seven-point scale every week, but actually exercising requires greater “activation energy.” Learning that gap requires behavioral knowledge, including irrational tendencies.
  • O’Shea presses on what makes someone continue a pattern or act differently. Park’s answer is “the existence of optionality”: exercising competes with sleeping another hour or taking another meeting. An abstract survey’s confined answer set misses the alternatives and opportunity costs governing real decisions.
  • Interviews, transaction data and mobility data help, but Park emphasizes randomized controlled trials that vary a feature or message and observe behavior change. He was surprised that customers cared less about forecasting than intervention. Told their market will crash in two quarters, they ask what to do now. “What do we need to do now to shape the future?” makes causal mechanisms central to the product.

3. Enterprise research is the initial commercial market

  • Concept testing, conjoint analysis and MaxDiff analysis are the starting applications. Park says studies costing hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars over years become “just a query away.” On Simile’s SaaS interface, users specify whom they want to talk to and what they want to ask; question counts currently have no limit. The gain is faster research with fewer resources.
  • Retail is one of the larger verticals. CVS explores store layout, messaging and decor; Brazil’s Banco Itaú examines policies and messaging that communicate its values. Entertainment, CPG and major financial institutions also participate. Internal applications include employee retention and recruiting communication, such as appealing to Stanford or MIT students, with informed consent and autonomy from participating employees.
  • Purchase decisions require modeling the environment. Park’s water example: a sole source could charge $1 million just to provide access to water, but widely available alternatives—and packaging and branding—change the context. Agents need exposure to competing options before answering what they would pay. “It really is about modeling people and their behavior, but it’s also about modeling the environment.”
  • Asked about an expensive mistake avoided, Park cites an automobile study explicitly conducted before Simile. An electric-vehicle launch message looked like “a clear winner,” yet the simulation showed it also shifted perceptions of non-electric vehicles and lowered sales across the market. For Park, the value is examining “the entire field holistically”: useful simulations surface consequences that are “counterintuitive” and “surprising.”

4. Population coverage and confidence depend on data discipline

  • Vertical-specific “agent bank” panels give customers a starting population; bespoke needs trigger additional collection and training. Partnerships reach over 40 million real people globally, with “tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands” contacted weekly. New panel needs can usually be met within 24 hours. Park highlights Gallup’s panel of hundreds of thousands and relationships spanning decades; representative sampling is the critical discipline.
  • O’Shea’s pushback is whether habitual respondents become biased or tell pollsters what they think is useful. Park acknowledges fatigue and gaming for payment: someone may give “some bullshit answer” to participate. Controls include spacing participation, comparing fresh respondents with experienced ones, and attention checks. Asked to recall the interview’s first question, an attentive participant should remember the simulation discussion.
  • O’Shea says the discussion makes her nervous, “like you can read my mind”; Park had simulated the interview and anticipated her opening simulation question. For panel collection, his boundary is informed consent and the ability to withdraw. Underage people are excluded, “one blind spot that we own,” as are others unable to consent. Otherwise, Simile aims to represent all populations, including “the good behaviors but also bad behaviors of people.”
  • Alongside its foundation model, Simile trains a model assigning responses a zero-to-100 confidence estimate based on training data and the question. Park likens its decision role to the inferential-statistics convention of p < 0.05; he says customers find confidence above “90% or usually 85%” sufficient for high-stakes decisions. Deployment includes helping users decide when to trust results, collect more data and validate findings.

5. Funding supports both model development and customer deployment

  • O’Shea puts total funding at $300 million and the reported valuation at $2 billion, naming Greenoaks, Index, Fei-Fei Li and Andrej Karpathy. Park traces the investor base partly to Stanford relationships: co-founder Micah Bernstein worked closely with Fei-Fei; Percy Liang served on Karpathy’s dissertation committee; Karpathy amplified the 2023 generative-agents paper. The underlying pitch is a technology serving an innate need to understand people.
  • Simile has about 100 people. Roughly 20% are lab mates or “academic relatives”; science, modeling, evaluation and methodology account for about 20%–25% of the company. Social-science methodologists work alongside AI researchers, engineers, product staff and deployment teams. Studying people is part of the technical task.
  • Park places simulation in its “GPT-4, GPT-4.5 era”: useful now, changing monthly. He expects it to reach today’s coding-agent industry’s maturity in about a year and a half to two years. Forward deployment is central: coding companies with close customer relationships became “stickier” and “much more defensible over time,” a pattern he believes will repeat in simulation.

6. Park wants the company to keep earning its next problem

  • Inspired by Thomas Schelling’s segregation modeling in the 1970s and 1980s, Park wants to study generational coordination problems. Climate policy involves actors with competing incentives whose interactions create difficult equilibria; repeated simulations could potentially help explore policy outcomes. If AGI is here or imminent, he asks whether simulations could show where UBI works and fails without waiting for a five-year study.
  • The career trait he admires is being “the common denominator of success”: taking ownership and repeatedly reinventing oneself. He also prizes seemingly incompatible strengths, exemplified by Michael Bernstein’s mature scientific discipline and childlike excitement about game demos. The durable motivation is the “greatest prize in winning the current game is gaining the right and invitation to play the next game.”
  • The failure mode is optimizing for one fundraising, customer win or paper, succeeding, then asking “Now what?” and losing interest. Park qualifies that judgment: it could be “an amazing success,” but becomes failure for someone seeking impact across generations. Asked whether he would sell for $15 billion, his answer remains conditional: if he has reason to believe only Simile can pursue an ambitious idea, “then we’re going to pursue that.”

来源：YouTube

item.title: 20VC: Satya Nadella on Open vs Closed Models: Who Wins | Whether to Trust Frontier Model Providers | Why Companies Need to Own Their Own Intelligence | The Importance of Verticalisation: From Chips to Models and More
item.description: Nadella no longer expects scaling to deliver alignment; powerful agents still need engineered zero-trust controls. Most token use may become commodity; Unilever’s trade-claims shift to lower-cost MAI shows the value of control and training on company traces. Private evaluations may become core corporate IP, while apps route tasks across open and closed models and leave the dominant architecture unsettled.
item.content:encoded:
20VC · Harry Stebbings、Satya Nadella · 2026-10-26 · 26 min · 原语言 EN

Nadella no longer expects scaling to deliver alignment; powerful agents still need engineered zero-trust controls. Most token use may become commodity; Unilever’s trade-claims shift to lower-cost MAI shows the value of control and training on company traces. Private evaluations may become core corporate IP, while apps route tasks across open and closed models and leave the dominant architecture unsettled.

TL;DR

  • Nadella's alignment reversal makes external security controls central to deploying powerful agents—but not a substitute for AI safety. He no longer expects alignment to emerge from scaling and says it must show up in training, perhaps pre-training, embedded in the weights from the beginning; he does not think developers can RL their way to it. His prescription for containment is an “engineered zero trust environment” with identities, tamper-proof logs and behavioral monitoring. Closed providers that hide reasoning risk pushing customers toward open weights.
  • Nadella suspects most token usage will become commodity usage, alongside a lasting frontier market. Stable tasks can move to open weights or cheaper closed models, especially when customers train on their own traces; he gives no 24-month market-share forecast. Microsoft's MAI approach is “licensed weights,” making customer control a separate consideration from whether weights are open.
  • Nadella predicts private evaluation benchmarks will become firms' core intellectual property. His “reverse information paradox” is that buyers can leak value through usage feedback as well as data. He wants firms to retain more of the surplus from AI use by accumulating knowledge in weights, context or evaluations, and imagines today's advanced AI practices becoming commonplace in five years.
  • Enterprise AI implementation creates work that combines business consulting with technical delivery. Unilever illustrates the path: after starting with a frontier model, it substituted an MAI model for all trade claims at lower cost, with control and the ability to train on its own traces. FDEs helped establish the business problem, evaluation and architecture; the internal IT team now manages it, while “traditional systems integration will become the new FDE.”
  • Nadella now considers a single vertically integrated AI winner unlikely. He sees “more competition in every layer of the stack” and sketches five or six competing models in each of the closed and open-weight camps, with applications routing to whichever fits the task. He hopes for multiple winners per layer but leaves the dominant design uncertain.
  • The economic case for $100 billion training runs rests on AI expanding revenues and world GDP. Nadella frames training as part of R&D, noting that R&D-heavy companies spend 15% or 20% on R&D; enough revenue makes training spend possible. Power and silicon have long lead times, and supply-demand timing remains unknown: “any one of us sitting here today would just be speculating.”
  • Coding's AI acceleration does not establish equally elastic demand across knowledge work. Nadella says extending its progress beyond verifiable rewards “seems much harder,” although deployments exist in areas such as contact centers and supply chains, and science “may be as elastic.” His broader growth test is practical and conditional—such as NHS Copilot improving patient outcomes while lowering costs—with adoption ideally focused where displacement is lowest and benefits greatest. He hopes diffusion reaches the Global South and “everyone gets lifted.”

Digest

1. Nadella separates agent security from unresolved alignment

  • Models are becoming more capable and scaling laws are working, but Nadella no longer expects alignment to emerge from scaling; mechanistic understanding remains elusive. He says alignment has to show up in training, perhaps pre-training, and be embedded in weights from the beginning. “I don't think you can RL your way to alignment.”
  • Stebbings's claim that the architecture does not exist draws a correction: “No, that architecture exists.” Pointing to Agent 365 and Perception, Nadella describes agent identities, tamper-proof logs covering activity, tool calls, model calls and chain of thought, plus policies and behavioral monitoring. Security containment can be engineered outside the model while AI safety remains unresolved.
  • Stebbings presses chain-of-thought reliability; Nadella concedes, “It's not,” and says hiding unfaithful reasoning makes matters worse. He wants standardized CoT available as-is, at least for trusted partners, so it can be inspected and audited using multiple models. Closed models' greater power may not protect them if opacity pushes customers toward open weights.

2. Commodity token economics do not settle open versus closed

  • Asked for open-versus-closed traffic shares over 24 months, Nadella offers no percentage: “I think predominantly token usage will be commodity token usage.” When tasks saturate, cheaper closed models or open weights can suffice; training on a firm's own traces reduces the need for the latest model if the problem stays unchanged. For continually advancing evaluations, customers may still pay for frontier models.
  • Frontier demand persists: “There will always be some new thing,” potentially science. Stebbings raises predominantly Chinese open models as a safety concern; Nadella argues an unaligned Chinese model could also attack China, while saying he is pleased with Western open-weight progress.
  • Microsoft's MAI models, he says, will be “not open weight” but “licensed weights.” His preferred framing is “a simple, straightforward software business as opposed to a network-effects intelligence business”; customers' ability to use and control models will determine adoption.

3. Private evaluations become the firm's core intellectual property

  • Nadella starts with Hayek's distributed tacit knowledge: firms must accumulate intelligence rather than leak it. His “reverse information paradox” flips Kenneth Arrow's seller problem onto the buyer: even thumbs-up/thumbs-down feedback creates value for the model provider. More of the surplus from AI use needs to remain inside the firm.
  • Ownership need not mean weights: context and evaluations also hold knowledge. Nadella predicts “every firm will have a private eval benchmark, which is its core IP,” with models trying to hill-climb on it. Asked what becomes normal in five years, he says, “I think a firm would be an AI benchmark.”
  • Stebbings challenges whether this extends beyond sophisticated AI companies. Nadella recalls PC-based forecasting taking “maybe 10 years” to spread; he imagines today's AI-native practices becoming “pretty passé” in five years.
  • At Unilever, an agentic system targets order-to-cash automation and trade claims. After starting with a frontier model, Unilever substituted an MAI model for all the trade claims because it costs less and gives them control; they can train on their traces. FDEs helped define the business problem, evaluation and architecture, and Unilever's IT team now manages the system. Nadella expects systems integration to evolve toward FDE work combining business and technical consulting.

4. Nadella favors composition over a single integrated winner

  • Stebbings asks whether ownership from chips through models to applications becomes mandatory. Nadella once thought a single integrated winner might emerge; he now considers it unlikely, seeing more competition across layers. “You never know,” he cautions: the dominant design remains unsettled.
  • He sketches five or six competing closed models and five or six open-weight models, with applications routing tasks to the best option. He also describes agent swarms and multiple sub-agents that can include local models. His hope is “horizontal specialization with multiple winners in each layer,” allowing customers to compose systems.

5. AI spending ultimately needs economic growth

  • Stebbings cites Mustafa Suleyman's $100 billion training runs and asks whether infrastructure can cope. Nadella ties spending to revenues and GDP growth: a training run is part of R&D, and R&D-heavy companies spend 15% or 20% on R&D. Power and silicon shortages involve long lead times; everyone is building, but supply-demand timing is unknown. Ultimately, enough revenue is needed to fund training.
  • Against Stebbings's roughly 2% annual global-growth baseline, Nadella thinks AI can lift growth and hopes it will. His NHS test is conditional: if Copilot improves patient outcomes and reduces healthcare costs, that helps UK GDP. At a stable state, company income statements still come down to revenue, costs and profit.
  • Stebbings calls Factory fifth yet winning, challenging his top-one-or-two venture rule. Nadella credits coding's progress to RL and verifiable rewards but says cracking knowledge work “seems much harder.” He cites contact centers, supply chains, marketing and quote-to-cash as areas where AI deployment is possible; science may match coding's demand elasticity. Silicon development is also changing through faster tape-outs and better simulation.
  • Nadella sees pockets of the economy with little displacement and substantial potential benefit as the best fit for AI. He hopes diffusion across sectors and the Global South will create convergence growth, so “everyone gets lifted.” His father was a development economist; the ambition is growth beyond simply counting winners and losers.

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/20vc-satya-nadella-open-vs-closed-models-who-win

item.title: Mark Cuban: The Brutal Truth About The Next Market Crash!
item.description: Cuban sees bubble-like pricing in Bitcoin, Micron, Google and Apple, where a one-cent earnings difference can coincide with an 18% share-price move, though he cannot identify a crash trigger. He questions whether AI financing needs will outrun returns as hyperscalers compete with government borrowers, and what gets crowded out if 10-year yields rise. He advocates patience and cash for a potential downturn, while timing, trigger and eventual winners remain unknown.
item.content:encoded:
The Diary Of A CEO · Mark Cuban、Steven Bartlett · 2026-10-26 · 92 min · 原语言 EN

Cuban sees bubble-like pricing in Bitcoin, Micron, Google and Apple, where a one-cent earnings difference can coincide with an 18% share-price move, though he cannot identify a crash trigger. He questions whether AI financing needs will outrun returns as hyperscalers compete with government borrowers, and what gets crowded out if 10-year yields rise. He advocates patience and cash for a potential downturn, while timing, trigger and eventual winners remain unknown.

TL;DR

  • Cuban thinks markets are in a bubble, but cannot identify the trigger for a crash. He calls Bitcoin, Micron, Google and Apple “meme stocks,” arguing that an 18% share-price reaction to a one-cent earnings difference reflects trading psychology rather than a comparable change in intrinsic value. His response is patience and liquidity: “Have some cash,” because he believes bear markets create the strongest buying opportunities.
  • His main financial warning concerns whether AI’s funding demands outrun its economic returns. Cuban sees hyperscaler borrowing competing with government financing needs, with the US already paying, by his account, $1 trillion annually in interest. Using a 5.2% 10-year yield as his starting point, he asks what happens at 6%, 8% or 10%: “Something gets crowded out,” although he explicitly declines to identify what.
  • Cuban calls AI an extraordinary productivity tool while rejecting claims that it possesses human intelligence. His objection centers on stale information, latency, inconsistent answers and dependence on enormous computing resources. Bartlett challenges him with exponential improvement and Tesla’s driving capabilities; Cuban concedes that his experience with earlier computing eras might bias his judgment.
  • Agents are already changing Cuban’s operations, but his argument for new jobs remains conditional. At Cost Plus Drugs, agents monitor lawsuits and bids, then help obtain competitors’ contracts—work that previously went undone because hiring and managing someone was cumbersome. He acknowledges replacing tasks an intern might perform for $15–$20 an hour, while suggesting that greater productivity might generate another business: “Maybe it creates a new business idea.”
  • His entrepreneurial model starts with selling, scarce skills and monthly profitability. MicroSolutions was profitable every month throughout its eight years, sold for $5 million and netted him $2 million. He rejects fundraising and headline revenue as the default measures of success: become excellent at one commercially useful activity, learn the customer’s interests, and sell something that helps them.
  • The Mavericks illustrate Cuban’s emphasis on operational improvements over a predetermined investment horizon. He cites a $285 million purchase price and a $4.3 billion sale figure, retaining 27% after selling majority ownership in 2023. Individual player development, analytics and practical support expressed the culture he wanted; he eventually sold as the business shifted toward valuations and real estate.
  • Wealth bought Cuban control over his time, but family changed how he wanted to spend it. He connects leaving Shark Tank and selling the Mavericks with regret over missed childhood events, once rationalized as “They’re too young to remember.” His leadership also changed: after learning that employees feared him, he found he “got a lot further by being nice than by being a dick.”
  • Cost Plus Drugs is now his principal business mission, with employer purchasing decisions central to his strategy. Cuban says 67% of people receiving employer health insurance are covered through self-insured employers, making those employers responsible for the bills and their choice of intermediaries. Patients reporting savings of $1,000 a month motivate a categorical promise: “I will fix it.”

Digest

1. Selling starts with understanding whose problem you solve

  • Cuban describes a blue-collar Pittsburgh upbringing: his father upholstered cars, never made more than $40,000, and lost an eye after a staple broke at work. His father’s friendliness and support mattered as much as the financial circumstances. One recurring lesson was adaptation: “You don’t live in the world you were born into.”
  • At 12, wanting new basketball shoes, Cuban was told to earn the money. His father’s poker friend offered garbage bags at $3 a box, which Cuban could sell for $6. His neighborhood pitch—“Hi, I’m your neighbor Mark. Do you use garbage bags?”—made selling approachable. “If you can go door-to-door and sell, you can do anything.”
  • His sales principle is care, product knowledge and understanding the buyer’s interests. Rejection trains quick responses; helping customers gives the pitch its purpose. The windows example is a $17 monthly payment offset by lower electricity bills. On Shark Tank, he says, he could immediately envisage how he would sell a product—or recognize that he could not.

2. Profitability and excellence offer a broader route than venture funding

  • Starting MicroSolutions felt possible because Cuban had little to lose: he was broke, bartending and sharing a three-bedroom apartment with five other men. Early survival was itself progress; reaching $15,000 in receivables felt meaningful. Across its entire eight-year existence, the company was profitable every month. Cuban clarifies that MicroSolutions sold for $5 million and netted him $2 million.
  • Cuban rejects two assumptions: that starting requires raising money, and that large sales numbers outrank profitability. Zuckerberg-style outcomes obscure the much larger population making a few million, $5 million, $10 million, $25 million, $50 million or $100 million. Those outcomes are difficult but attainable, he argues: “It’s not a Silicon Valley dream, it’s the American dream.”
  • His answer to aspiring entrepreneurs juggling three ideas is blunt: “That’s ridiculous.” Become great at one thing, then find its commercial application. Time allocation is a better clue than professed passion—he wanted to play professional sports without having the ability. Improvement, comparative competence and rising confidence can reinforce one another until a business becomes plausible.
  • For someone trapped in an unsatisfying job, Cuban recommends getting good at the available work and honestly checking that assessment with others. Advancement at McDonald’s or Dairy Queen can demonstrate reliability to the next employer. A strong reference and evidence of progression over two or three years can open doors without requiring that first job to become a lifelong calling.

3. Preparation creates an advantage whenever technology resets

  • Cuban’s software-store job ended after nine months. Pursuing a transaction that would earn him a $1,500 commission, he ignored his boss’s instruction to open the shop and collected the customer’s check instead. He expected the revenue to settle the disagreement; he was fired immediately. Starting his own company followed the realization: “I suck as an employee.”
  • During the early PC era, Cuban reasoned that only a program’s author necessarily understood it better than everyone else. He stayed overnight or took a computer home, repeatedly reading manuals and teaching himself packages such as Lotus 1-2-3. Each new release offered another opening: “There’s the creator and everybody else is tied for second.” He applies that same competitive logic to learning AI.
  • Bobby Knight supplied the formulation that stuck: “Everybody’s got the will to win,” but “it’s only those with the will to prepare that actually do win.” Bartlett’s pushback concerns visibility: audiences see the championship celebration, not years spent studying software in a crowded apartment. Cuban agrees that preparation is the part success imagery routinely leaves out.
  • His 17-year-old son’s feeds illustrated the opposite incentive: dropshipping, shoe drops and other get-rich-quick pitches. Cuban’s strongest objection concerns people selling supposedly exceptional trading methods: “Nobody who has an edge in the stock market is selling it. They’re using it.” He argues that personalized algorithms reinforce attractive promises while making the unglamorous preparatory work harder to see.

4. The Mavericks purchase began with enjoyment, then the business changed

  • Bartlett offers Cuban as an example of thinking 10 or 20 years ahead; Cuban rejects the premise: “That wasn’t me.” Buying the Mavericks began with being a basketball enthusiast who could suddenly afford the team. Playing alongside Dirk Nowitzki, Steve Nash and Michael Finley sounded fun. Turning an awful franchise into a winner became an intellectual challenge, rather than a planned 25-year investment.
  • Cuban gives the purchase price as $285 million and the sale figure as $4.3 billion. He sold majority ownership in 2023 and says he retains 27%. His motivation changed as NBA conversations shifted from improving basketball toward maximizing team values. Competing increasingly required expertise in real estate and other activities beyond the game; children and changing personal priorities also mattered.
  • Success means waking up smiling and looking forward to the day, Cuban says. Even winning the championship brought an internal “now what?” The deeper reward was taking the trophy to schools, restaurants, bars and children’s events and watching people respond. A corporate earnings record produces no equivalent citywide parade: “Just that communal joy, that’s what made it special.”

5. Cuban sees a bubble without claiming to know its breaking point

  • Cuban invokes the old Warren Buffett advice to wait and see. He says he bought aggressively during the COVID sell-off and “crushed it”; today, surging AI-related shares and rising debt make him more cautious. Small investments for enjoyment are compatible with restraint. “Have some cash because at some point it’s going to turn”—his argument for waiting until forced selling creates opportunities.
  • His bubble diagnosis concerns price formation: “Everything’s a meme stock.” He includes Bitcoin, Micron, Google and Apple, describing a company missing or beating earnings by a penny and its shares falling 18%. “The intrinsic value of that company hasn’t changed 18%.” His baseball-card analogy captures buyers responding to anticipated resale demand rather than calculating future cash flows.
  • Asked what bursts the bubble, Cuban answers: “I have no idea.” He distinguishes this episode from 2000–2001 and separates eventual business success from share-price resilience: Dell and Amazon were crushed during the internet bust, while Amazon later became enormously valuable. Bartlett worries AI might be the final technological opportunity; Cuban expects further innovations and cannot identify whether Anthropic, OpenAI or another company will emerge as the winner.

6. AI’s usefulness does not settle the argument about intelligence

  • Cuban says AI dwarfs earlier technological changes “in aggregate,” improves productivity and can democratize access to knowledge. Yet a released model is, in his framing, immediately out of date: this conversation is not already incorporated into it. Different answers across models—or after small changes to a prompt—support his distinction: “It’s predictive. It’s not deterministic.”
  • His categorical formulation is “AI is not smart.” He associates intelligence with finding inputs, identifying the problem and combining information in real time; he says AI lacks inherent ethics and awareness of consequences. At a busy intersection, he would trust a seeing-eye dog before a phone running the best models. He qualifies video limitations with “at least not yet,” while maintaining that latency leaves humans an advantage.
  • Bartlett challenges the static comparison: capabilities appear to improve exponentially, and his Tesla drives itself with, he says, an apparently lower crash rate than human driving. Cuban responds that deployment also creates resistance and vulnerabilities. People might reject pervasive technology, form communities without it, or deliberately exploit adversarial inputs that cause a driving system to react incorrectly.
  • Cuban also expects knowledge to become less universally available. He tells researchers that publication or patenting makes their work accessible to models, while trade secrets and proprietary models preserve control. Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok consequently receive different information and produce different answers. Their usefulness therefore requires users to question several sources and reconcile the responses, rather than assume a single authoritative output.

7. The evidence Cuban wants is intelligence with fewer resources

  • Bartlett asks what could change Cuban’s mind. His proposed test is an AI that finds information and solves problems with minimal resources, analogous to a brilliant 12-year-old from the worst part of the world. Bartlett notes computers also began as large machines; Cuban counters that early programmers achieved results with little computing power. He nevertheless acknowledges possible historical bias: “Maybe that holds me back.”
  • Cuban calls Elon Musk “the best entrepreneur of our lifetimes,” while treating his forecasts about optional work and humanoid robots as part of selling and fundraising. Bartlett reports hearing radically different views from AI researchers, executives and safety specialists. Cuban takes that disagreement as evidence against an obvious, shared destination—not as proof that the technology lacks commercial value.
  • On cybersecurity, Cuban asks whether reported AI attacks invented a new technique. The security people he describes say no: agents exhaust combinations of known methods at a scale humans could not afford. That changes the threat, but the same brute force can search defenders’ systems for weaknesses. “I’m more afraid of what people do because of their concerns and lack of understanding of AI than I am about what AI will do.”

8. Agents eliminate tasks while the employment outcome remains unsettled

  • Cuban expects creative destruction, using Terre Haute, Indiana, and its progression through records, CDs and DVDs. Those production activities disappeared without eliminating the music economy. New technology can support different businesses and jobs, but he does not deny the transition’s cost: “Is the path going to be painful for people? Yeah.” Bartlett presses that AI reaches unusually broadly across intellectual work.
  • Bartlett points out that Cuban’s agents perform tasks he might otherwise have hired someone to do. Cuban agrees: an intern might have earned $15 or $20 an hour. His counterargument is increased capacity and the possibility of another business requiring employees. The hedge matters: “Maybe it creates a new business idea.” He offers a mechanism for new work, not a quantified employment forecast.
  • At Cost Plus Drugs, agents alert him whenever targeted healthcare conglomerates are sued or bid for contracts. They also help draft emails seeking copies of those contracts through open-records processes. Previously, that research often went undone: recruiting, training and managing someone imposed too much overhead. Now he receives the information and employs other people on different, more advanced work.
  • His advice to his children is to learn agents because competitors who do will be more productive. Access alone does not remove effort: users must ask questions, absorb answers and improve their questions. A generated business plan still needs judgment—“This is right, this is wrong”—and someone who can sell the resulting offering or eventually teach agents to sell it.

9. The AI investment race could become a financing problem

  • Cuban’s prediction that some data centers could become “pickleball courts” is explicitly a metaphor for redundant capacity. His desired trajectory is “less power doing more, not more power doing more.” Otherwise, scaling encounters physical and financial constraints. His enthusiasm for AI coexists with doubt that indefinitely adding computing resources provides a sustainable route to its promised capabilities.
  • He connects government deficits with hyperscaler borrowing and private-credit uncertainty. A company carrying $40 billion of debt could eventually lose access to fresh financing if rates keep rising. He praises Nvidia and Jensen Huang but claims Nvidia is effectively subsidizing half the industry. He tentatively singles out Meta when discussing borrowing exceeding cash generation; the comparison is not presented with a completed numerical multiple.
  • The race is whether economic benefits arrive before financing becomes restrictive. Cuban cites a roughly 5.2% 10-year yield and asks about 6%, 8% or 10%, alongside $1 trillion in annual US interest payments. Government and AI borrowers compete for funds: “Something gets crowded out.” He adds, “I’m not enough of a financial expert” to identify precisely which borrower or activity gives way.
  • Cuban invokes Ray Dalio’s warnings about indebtedness but remains optimistic America will eventually adjust, with pain. His own defense is investing substantially less, holding money in more than one country and waiting for clarity. He acknowledges possible losses and incomplete protection. Separately, he sees value in face-to-face interaction, citing a silent-disco investment and buyers who regard sports as “AI-proof,” though sports has other problems.

10. Money bought autonomy while celebrity imposed costs on others

  • Cuban acknowledges insecurity as part of his drive: he remembers being the overweight child with metal dental caps and wanting to prove people wrong. Indiana University offered a fresh start. After selling MicroSolutions, he bought a lifetime American Airlines pass and traveled for enjoyment. Removing his watch symbolized the real prize: no longer living on somebody else’s timetable.
  • Bartlett dates Broadcast.com’s start to Cuban being 37 and its Yahoo sale four years later at $5.7 billion in stock, giving Cuban roughly $1.5–$1.7 billion in paper wealth. Cuban says that changed his available choices enormously. It did not automatically change his personality: “If you’re miserable when you’re poor, good chance you’re going to be miserable when you’re rich.”
  • He takes pride in keeping school friends, rugby teammates and close relationships with his brothers. Celebrity was harder to manage than wealth because it attracted attention and affected relatives who had not chosen it. An unusual surname meant his brothers repeatedly faced comparisons with Mark and insinuations that they lived off him, despite building their own careers.
  • In a letter Bartlett reads, Brian recalls being suicidal in July 2005: “I wouldn’t be here today if not for you both.” Cuban says Jeff called him, he returned from a trip, and they took Brian to rehabilitation; Brian has remained sober since. Their father’s instruction to stay connected survives in a practical detail: all three brothers live within walking distance, 1,200 miles from Pittsburgh.

11. Leadership improved when Cuban admitted his weaknesses

  • Cuban rejects ruthlessness as a requirement. At MicroSolutions he shouted; at Broadcast.com, Todd Wagner told him employees were afraid of him and that it was counterproductive. “I got a lot further by being nice than by being a dick.” Bartlett challenges whether civility invites exploitation; Cuban’s answer is that treating people well does not mean surrendering business judgment or giving away money.
  • Operational detail is another admitted weakness. At MicroSolutions, Martin Woodall’s perfectionism complemented Cuban’s “ready, fire, aim” approach. Cuban frames that partnership as necessary, rather than decorative: someone had to supply the discipline he lacked. He recognizes the same need for a detail-oriented counterpart in later businesses.
  • He separates leadership from recruitment: he thinks he is good at the former and says of hiring, “Suck at it.” His sales instinct made him imagine how almost any candidate could succeed. His “I can make it work” instinct also echoes the way he discussed Shark Tank pitches. Hiring remains critical despite his weakness; the operating principle is “hire slow and fire fast.”
  • Entrepreneurship is consequently not a universal prescription. Customers and employees can exert more control over the founder’s time than a boss once did. In a business with fewer than 100 employees, somebody’s sick child or personal difficulty becomes a responsibility the owner must address. “You have no control of your life as an entrepreneur” is his warning against equating ownership with immediate freedom.

12. Mavericks spending made the promise of winning credible

  • Cuban describes the original organization as a way station for people unable to get jobs with the Lakers or Celtics.
