He announced a different expectation: “We’re going to win.” Players could commit or request a trade. The promise carried an obligation on his side: “I’ll give you the tools you need to win.”
  • His clearest example is development spending. A head coach and roughly three assistants handled player improvement, while the organization spent more on computer training and support than on developing players earning over $1 million. Cuban brought in former Mavericks, matching each with a current player of similar skills. Individual attention improved capability and demonstrated that management intended to support winning.
  • The immediate record, Cuban says, moved from 9–23 when he took over in January 2000 to 31–19 across that season’s remaining 50 games. Bartlett summarizes the broader tenure as a rise from 39% wins to almost 60%, the NBA’s second-highest regular-season winning percentage. The Mavericks lost the 2006 Finals to Miami before winning the championship in 2011.
  • Analytics supplied another edge. Cuban recognized former statistics professor Wayne Winston after seeing him on Jeopardy, then encountered him at an Indiana Pacers game and hired him. Cuban describes Winston as the NBA’s first full-time analytics hire. Statistics complement observation: “The eye test versus the numbers, and you have to do both.” A less impressive-looking player can contribute more to winning than a prolific scorer.

13. Family changed the cost of another business commitment

  • His parents’ deaths, discussed as occurring in 2017 and 2022, sharpened Cuban’s mortality awareness. His father reached 92 and his mother 85: apparently long lives, until “you realize it’s not as long as you hope.” That changed the value of another trip or missed birthday. His children were 13, 16 and 19 when he sold majority ownership of the Mavericks.
  • Asked whether he could have built his businesses and attended equally to family, Cuban says, “Not as well as I did it,” then acknowledges regret. He had justified missing smaller childhood events with “They’re too young to remember.” The regret comes from both his own reassessment and his children’s reminders. Leaving Shark Tank and selling the team were partly responses to that recognition.
  • Fame adds pressure to his children: a mistake by a friend stays local, while theirs could become worldwide news. His priorities are now explicit: “My favorite word in the world is dad.” He keeps his parents’ pictures in his closet and greets them morning and night; he hopes his children will remember him warmly and feel proud of him after he is gone.

14. Cost Plus Drugs targets the employers paying healthcare bills

  • Cuban wants to change American healthcare. The feedback that matters now comes from patients saying Cost Plus Drugs saves them $1,000 a month and makes treatment affordable. Bartlett calls attention to the value of exposing an industry that resists scrutiny; Cuban goes further: “I will fix it. I promise you I will fix it.”
  • His proposed leverage point is employer responsibility. Cuban says 67% of people getting insurance through work receive it through self-insured employers, which bear the bills and choose the organizations administering coverage. He approaches CEOs directly, arguing that changing those arrangements can save their companies money and improve employee and family health. He describes three large companies as dominating the system.
  • Bartlett asks about Cuban appearing alongside Trump despite their difficult relationship. Cuban says cooperation is justified by outcomes: “Anything that makes people healthier and saves them money on their health care, that’s fine by me.” His stated destination is healthcare that is “truly a right,” requiring the dominant companies to lose their grip on the industry.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/mark-cuban-brutal-truth-about-next-market-crash

item.title: AI 时代，PhD 路上的 10 个关键问题｜对谈李磊：港大 PhD、小米 MiMo 研究员
item.description: 李磊认为，数据公司的长期价值在于持续发现模型能力缺口、组织专家并规模交付；模型公司买数据，也是在买推进前沿的时间。模型自产数据能力提升可能压低成本，因此只有持续升级高质量pipeline的供应商才可能扩大优势。
item.content:encoded:
十字路口Crossing · Koji、李磊 · 2026-10-25 · 52 min · 原语言 ZH

李磊认为，数据公司的长期价值在于持续发现模型能力缺口、组织专家并规模交付；模型公司买数据，也是在买推进前沿的时间。模型自产数据能力提升可能压低成本，因此只有持续升级高质量pipeline的供应商才可能扩大优势。

TL;DR

  • 数据公司的长期价值，取决于能否持续补上模型的新短板。 李磊认为，需求会持续存在；如果数据公司不能持续产出高质量数据，模型自身产数能力提升会让成本降得很低、竞争更加激烈。能识别能力缺口、组织专家并规模化交付的pipeline，优势反而可能扩大。模型公司购买数据，也是购买推进智能前沿的时间；他称“时间是不可逆的资源”。
  • 李磊预期RSI在明确任务上的进展会非常迅速，关键缺口仍是决定研究什么。 搜索更好的参数、算法以及生成数据，都可以通过增加compute推进；但“什么问题是重要的”、下一阶段该解决什么，目前仍主要由研究员判断。他尚未看到特别令自己兴奋、形成充分共识的RSI benchmark。
  • 小米的后训练直播把大规模RL的训练动态与成本推到了公众面前。 李磊称，团队早期训练时看到大规模RL能带来“非常全面”的能力提升，希望借MiMo V2.6的Pro、Flash两款模型，给行业做RL的信心。国内反馈集中在费用，海外反馈更关注透明度；近乎公开TensorBoard，也让研究者获得分析训练dynamics的“金矿”。
  • 在李磊参与的招聘中，论文已从重要筛选标准退为“nice to have”。 他更看代码和数据是否开源、issues有没有维护，以及模型是否有人使用；声称SOTA却每月只有数十次下载，“可能”意味着问题没那么重要。Koji追问这些指标能否被hack，他承认可以，评价体系始终存在reward hacking。
  • 论文供给激增后，研究传播本身成为影响力的一部分。 一个会议从几百篇论文扩到四五千篇，读者越来越依赖推荐与社交媒体；李磊把这称为“attention is all you need”的显化。他有2.4万小红书粉丝，但给PhD的建议是利他、坚持、做自己，用持续输出找到相同research taste的人。
  • PhD是否值得读，首先取决于你希望用这段时间回答什么问题。 李磊不认为进入大公司必须先拿学位：“他做得牛，所以他能去。”他看重的是相对完整、可以满足好奇心的研究旅程；选择时，导师和课题组的差异远比Top 30与Top 50的学校标签更值得调查。
  • 研究效率来自充分选题、尽早验证，再快速执行“难而正确”的问题。 李磊曾花半年多调算法，最后发现假设本身错误，如今会先抽出minimal hypothesis做小实验。Koji质疑难题意味着慢，他的回答是：重要问题哪怕只推进一点，也可能获得很大影响力，关键是找到可靠切面。

Digest

1. 读PhD的价值取决于你想回答什么问题

  • 李磊同时是港大在读博士和小米后训练研究员。2023年11月入学两个月时，他参加了自己的第一个会议；他说自己当时有一篇工作，师弟的论文也拿了Best Paper。这让他觉得是“巅峰开局”，同时也担心会不会“出道即巅峰”。
  • 真正推动他读博的，是想到十年后躺在床上，可能仍会后悔没有这段经历。他承认工业界待遇让机会成本变大；到了final year，同学们除了学术，聊得最多的也包括package，但他仍希望留出时间研究自己想做的事情。
  • 对“为了进大公司而读博”，李磊认为没有必要，Jason Wei等研究员的路径说明：“他做得牛，所以他能去。”另一种期待则值得：用相对完整的时间满足好奇心、补知识、训练研究与传播能力。“人活八十岁”，其中五年可以是一段特殊旅程。

2. 选题慢一些，验证和执行要快

  • 李磊把选题拆成difficulty与importance：问题不够难，competitors会很多，也容易被beat掉；问题足够重要，即使只能“make a little bit of the progress”，也很有可能获得很大影响力。他强调的是找到一个切面，给出可靠的部分解释或实验分析。
  • Koji的追问值得保留：难题做得慢，怎么及时得到正反馈？李磊认为两者可以兼容——大家知道问题难，对完整解决的要求反而没那么苛刻，一小段扎实进展就可能成为后来者的重要milestone。
  • 对超过一百位老师、研究员发起的“慢研究”倡议，他理解其重点是：不把发表论文作为唯一筛选标准，要求学生打牢基础，讲清做了什么、为什么做、怎么做。它不是说不要做科研，而是要平衡课业和科研投入，做重要的事并逐步推进。
  • 他曾花半年多调一个算法，最后发现假设错了。现在会先抽出minimal hypothesis，用小实验尽早验证；方向确定前密集读论文、找研究者讨论，确定后则提高GPU利用率、数据处理速度，用AI帮助并行推进。“快和慢是相对的。”

3. 模型的“锯齿状”能力让研究空间继续存在

  • 李磊观察到，PhD的焦虑有三层：先满足publication和毕业要求，再担心发出的工作有没有意义，最后考虑能否顺利进入职场。Astra等系统出现时，一些做具身研究的人会感觉自己的整个domain被颠覆。
  • 他的应对是回到实验：“真的坐在电脑面前”，去coding、设计harness、跑数据，观察模型具体怎么表现。大模型是“锯齿状”的智能，有些地方非常强，也有能力完全缺失；social media容易放大可见成果，剩余问题需要亲手检查。
  • Koji猜测OpenAI持续采购具身数据，可能解释相关能力的来源，李磊只回应“我们猜测可能是这样”。他明确说自己不是具身专家，但能力从哪里泛化而来、simulator与真机之间有没有gap，都仍值得研究。

4. 论文系统承压，录用结果承载不了全部评价

  • 作为审稿人和Area Chair，李磊看到工作量从两三篇增到大约十篇，DDL下判断的随机性可能上升。他提到NeurIPS有三个会场；社区也在尝试限制投稿、增加资深审稿人的责任、引入AI辅助。比如CHAIR-AI要求两位senior SPC讨论后再做决定。
  • 对Koji提出的“用SOTA模型写一百篇、靠概率中稿”，他直接称其为对系统的“DDoS攻击”。论文的目的本来是分享有意思的研究，关键问题是：“他真的把这些东西弄清楚了吗”，有没有实验或理论支撑所提出的hypothesis。
  • 他也保留另一种可能：如果人加AI确实提出一百个有价值的问题，并给出solid答案，投不投稿都无所谓。只是批量产出并没有消除验证成本，仍需要大量human effort确认结果。
  • 在候选人筛选中，paper已经更接近“nice to have”；开源贡献也可能被AI生成的PR包装。因此他会继续检查代码、数据是否开放，issues有没有维护。“大家不要把这个accept or not作为最终的一个reward。”

5. 影响力来自真实使用，也需要主动分发

  • 李磊会看Hugging Face下载量：如果模型自称SOTA，上个月却只有数十次下载，可能没有解决那么重要的问题。Koji追问下载量能不能hack，他承认可以，但认为下载、存储等成本会让操作代价更大。
  • 学术分发方式也在变。过去ACL录用论文只有几百篇，可以按关键词和熟悉的老师筛选；如今一个会议四五千篇，读者不可能逐一浏览，只能更多依赖推荐。在这些系统中获得权重，能够“amplify你工作的价值”。
  • Koji提到他有2.4万小红书粉丝，李磊也分享过citation超过一万的笔记。他认为社交媒体的直接价值是反馈快，并能找到research taste相近的同学；“大粉理论”则把粉丝、点赞超过citation，视为“attention is all you need”的显化。
  • 他的运营建议是“利他”“坚持”“做自己”。早期持续发论文notes，增长很慢，后来一篇讨论引用与粉丝关系的内容才带来跃升；他分享On-Policy Distillation等研究笔记，也是在表达真实兴趣。争议观点容易吸引评论，却未必让人觉得内容和作者本人有关。

6. 博士训练要从独立研究走向带人和产业协作

  • 李磊划出的第一个阶段，是掌握完整研究基本功。即使AI能辅助，也值得自己从头实现基础算法；他提到用NumPy、MATLAB等实现SVM，以及学习吴恩达的Coursera课程，泛化、overfitting等概念至今仍在发挥作用。
  • 独立完成研究还包括写作、设计实验、justify hypothesis，以及把知识传播出去。AI可以充当reviewer或老师，帮助完善假设；开源、博客、软件和分享则帮助maximize impact。能够独立做好paper并获得一定影响力，才算跑通pipeline。
  • 第二阶段是leadership：从“generator”转向“critic”，把方法教给更junior的同学，并case by case调整指导强度；self-motivated的人可能只需少量引导，另一些人需要更密集的supervision。第三阶段是进入工业界，面对更现实、更多维度的竞争，他说自己也还在学习。

7. 冷启动靠作品累积，也靠进入关键网络节点

  • 李磊大二升大三时发过大约十封cold email，只收到一封回复。孙旭老师给了他进组实习的机会，随后才有顶会工作和保研。他认为今天教授邮箱更拥挤，工业界又受算力与HC约束，主动reach out依然必要。
  • 低算力条件下，可以做GitHub项目、harness或有意思的应用；偏研究的路径，则是把fundamental理清，写好research blog，用小实验论证想法。他举苏剑林早期以推导为主的博客、后来提出RoPE并成为Kimi研究员，说明作品可以先于资源。
  • 没有回复会很常见，但输出本身也是学习过程，要把想学、想创造的东西呈现成作品集。他把这个过程比作“冒泡排序”：持续积累，慢慢被看见。自己最早获得的金山实习机会，也来自对方看到了他的博客。
  • 他转述《巴拉巴西成功定律》中的两个发现：诺奖得主也难预测哪篇会成为代表作，因此要持续创造；艺术品进入某些不算著名的市政博物馆后，却更容易被大馆借展，因为它们是关键节点。Koji说“只要一直build就有好事发生”，他补充：“聪明地build。”

8. 导师匹配比学校标签更需要实地验证

  • 李磊把选导师的优先级放得远高于选学校。他认为Top 30与Top 50可能没有本质区别，顶尖名校的名字确实能带来识别度，但组与组之间的variance更大。PhD仍很像师徒制，长期相处方式直接影响成长。
  • Google Scholar、CSRankings和公开演讲，只能提供公开信息。他更建议私下联系在读生和毕业生，同时看成果与精神状态：有人著作等身却非常痛苦，不能只用产出来判断一个组是否适合自己。他举港大NLP和北大计算语言学研究所为氛围轻松愉快的组。
  • 他在上海AI Lab实习时认识现在的co-supervisor孔令鹏，合作大约半年后才觉得风格match。RA因此是推荐路径：既能实际体验合作，也能融入学生群体，了解课题组情况。导师选择是“双向匹配”，一些差异需要半年甚至更久才能看清。
  • 地域判断同样有条件：内地更方便接触工业界，但要筛选能平衡项目压力与学生成长的组；香港与内地联系紧密，老师profile在他看来更有活力，也有生活压力。美国部分他明确说不太了解，只转述朋友对签证、CPT和实习困难的反馈，同时承认更接近硅谷及美国学术圈。

9. 教授创业能放大资源，也会传导出资方的要求

  • 李磊认为，科技导向的融资环境把前沿researcher和professor推到创业前台。公司形式可以更灵活地买卡、招工程师、采购数据，突破部分学校funding限制，让更大的project更快聚齐要素，起到“杠杆加速”的作用。
  • 另一面是拿钱之后会有要求，压力可能层层传给学生，带来学术以外的“dirty work”。他把它视为硬币两面：使用更多资源需要付出代价，学生应按自身阶段权衡需求，不能只看资源增加这一侧。

10. Agent与大规模RL构成他2026年的两次震动

  • 回顾2026年，李磊最看重agent范式走到前台。他最早研究的是句子positive还是negative，后来模型能翻译、写作文，如今加上tools和脚手架，可以自动完成很多事情。他期待这些能力下一步从digital world走向physical world，产生新的火花。
  • 另一个aha moment来自团队早期训练：李磊觉得它有点像R1，并认为大规模RL能带来非常全面的能力提升。把后训练拿出来直播，也是在面对一些不利于中国大模型形象的rumor时，给行业一个正向信号：这件事可以做，效果也很好。
  • Koji提到直播涉及MiMo V2.6的Pro、Flash两款模型。李磊强调RL对infra和数据要求都高，团队希望用透明方式建立信心，配套开放该开源的内容，也通过直播吸收feedback，修正不足、放大做得好的部分。
  • 国内观众最关心费用，页面上直接显示金额，形成“人民币在燃烧”的感受；李磊转述，海外评论更惊讶于透明程度，有人称其为首次工业级直播。近乎展示TensorBoard，使训练dynamics成为外部研究者可以分析的“金矿”。

11. 数据公司的生意要随着模型边界不断升级

  • 对数据公司的高估值，李磊先说明自己并不特别了解估值，但不认为明显过分：算力、数据、人才都贵，数据生产复杂度和质量要求也已上升很多个量级。他把好数据视为智能的源头，同时强调还需要扎实算法与好的infra。
  • 持续需求来自模型“锯齿状”的能力边界。数据公司要找到缝隙，组织专家、设计激励、规模化交付；模型公司也能做，却会分散精力和算力。“时间是不可逆的资源”，所以模型公司愿意花钱购买数据。
  • “高质量”始终相对于特定模型：数据太难，能力不足的模型也学不会。供应方需要判断难度、评估模型，并source expert；还要平衡两种价值——让demo酷炫的PR价值，以及模型真正学会能力后产生的经济价值。
  • 他对可持续性给了明确条件：能持续生产高质量“燃料”的公司，会持续产生新价值；做不到，生意就肯定做不下去。因为模型自身生成数据的能力会提高，成本就会降得很低；拥有持续升级的规模化pipeline，优势才可能被放大。

12. RSI正在推进执行环节，研究方向仍由人把关

  • 李磊认为RSI的信号“越来越强烈”，但提醒定义很宽。广义上，模型生成数据帮助自身改进，已经算self-improvement；更具体的讨论则包括自己训练自己、探索post-training分支，以及寻找更好的参数和算法。
  • 他预期这些环节的progress会非常迅速，因为问题well-defined，模型擅长搜索，还能通过scale compute找到更好的路径。在训练过程中，模型的PPL会不断下降，研究员也能让模型协助数据、训练等环节的改进。
  • 更前面的缺口是：“什么问题是重要的”，下一阶段需要解决什么。只有具备这类能力，研究员才能放心交出端到端研究；目前他还没看到这里有很好的提升。被问最有影响力的RSI benchmark，他也没有给出推荐，认为领域仍早期，尚未形成良好共识。

13. 好的benchmark必须增加一个真实能力维度

  • 李磊用自己参与的Video-MME举例：当大家还在评估六秒视频理解时，他们把时长拉到一个多小时。随着agent变强，看懂电影、长期分析视频会变得重要，因此六秒到一小时测量的是一个“new dimension”，而非简单延长题目。
  • 第二个要求是问题来自use case，数据质量足够高。过于artificial的任务容易被模型捕捉，形成“它知道你在测试它”的表现，最终与真实用户体验拉开很大gap。
  • 第三个要求是impact和易用性：做好“一键启动、一键测评”，适配主流测评套件，并让别人复现分数。生态整合之所以重要，是它直接节省采用者的时间，让别人更有可能adopt这个benchmark。

14. 专业红利会变化，持续学习和身心状态更值得守住

  • Koji提出，MIT大一新生选择机械工程成为最热门专业，美国四年制本科CS入学人数同比下降8.4%。李磊先保留“可能会有很多别的因素”，再判断如此大规模下降，可能包含junior coding需求被AI吃掉一部分的影响：“一代版本一代神。”
  • 他仍认为，人们即使不主修CS，也应通过一两门课建立general理解，并能在AI辅助下coding。面对“给高三弟弟推荐什么专业”的假设，他不选具体专业，建议与自己比较、持续进步，在一行维持相对前20%—30%的水位，不必执着于top 1%。
  • 对AI与非AI人群的分化，他承认自己幸运，也认为鸿沟中有很多“梯子”。ChatGPT、DeepSeek、MiMo提供了丰富知识，各领域的人可以用工具改变效率和工作范式，也能贡献专业能力帮助模型进步；关键是意识到变化并积极拥抱。
  • 漫长博士阶段里，他认为身心健康始终是第一位的，也提到“搏击理论”和换换脑子。最后的祝福很直接：“paper迟早会中的，饭还是得吃，觉还是得睡。”没有什么大不了的。

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/shizilukou-2026-10-25-ai-phd

item.title: AI Bubble Burst? Bitcoin to Zero? Hedge Funds Wrecked? Sounds Like a Bottom is Near
item.description: Visser argues the AI selloff reflects hedge-fund deleveraging nearing its end, potentially opening a three-month entry window if recession is avoided. Crowded positions built over 18 months are unwinding in 75 days, while weak index hedges push funds into stock shorts and raise squeeze risk; corporate profits are still up 20%. Credit stress and widening junk spreads could undermine the bottom call, while Micron’s possible rise to $1,500 by February’s end and tokenization’s growth offer catalysts to watch.
item.content:encoded:
Jordi Visser · Jordi Visser · 2026-10-25 · 57 min · 原语言 EN

Visser argues the AI selloff reflects hedge-fund deleveraging nearing its end, potentially opening a three-month entry window if recession is avoided. Crowded positions built over 18 months are unwinding in 75 days, while weak index hedges push funds into stock shorts and raise squeeze risk; corporate profits are still up 20%. Credit stress and widening junk spreads could undermine the bottom call, while Micron’s possible rise to $1,500 by February’s end and tokenization’s growth offer catalysts to watch.

TL;DR

  • Visser sees the hedge-fund liquidation approaching its end and a potential three-month entry window in AI. “The AI bubble didn’t pop, hedge fund leverage did”: crowded longs have surrendered roughly half their post-ChatGPT relative gains, yet the S&P fell just 0.47% for the week. His entry argument depends on avoiding an economic recession, which he does not expect, and does not promise an immediate rally.
  • Crowding and compressed time horizons make leverage dangerous even when earnings keep improving. Positions accumulated over 18 months are being unwound in 75 days, while ineffective index hedges push funds into stock shorts and possible squeezes. His warning: “If your earnings beat estimates every quarter for the next eight quarters, your stock can still go down.”
  • Credit contagion challenges the bottom call, but corporate profits and employment still support his distinction between financial liquidation and economic deterioration. French ten-year yields stand 173 basis points above Germany’s, and European banks suffered their worst relative week since SVB. Against that, corporate profits are up 20%, claims show no recession signal, and the S&P retains strong year-over-year gains; widening junk spreads are the warning.
  • Visser’s compute-demand thesis survives a 22% SMH drawdown, and he says Micron could reach $1,500 by the end of February. He quotes Musk saying, “We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone,” and sees suppliers still raising guidance. CoreWeave’s financing risk remains real, but “credit market stress does not automatically translate into corporate bankruptcy.”
  • Healthcare is his proposed companion to agentic compute as specialized AI reaches drug discovery. Eli Lilly’s TuneLab pools anonymized work, including failures, from 135 biotech companies—a mechanism he expects to accelerate discovery. He calls pharma, biotech and life sciences the beginning of “a massive bull market,” with healthcare potentially receiving a growth-sector re-rating.
  • Tokenization is his broader crypto bull-market thesis, already extending beyond Bitcoin’s performance. His 46-name index is up 35% year to date despite losing 10% for the month, versus Bitcoin down 7% year to date. He points to more than 360 tokenized equity products, up 200% year to date, and frames the shift as: “Crypto is no longer a separate industry. It is becoming infrastructure.”
  • He rejects Bitcoin-to-zero certainty while predicting that AI cyberattacks will accelerate blockchain adoption. Visser cites Adam Back’s potentially 20–40-year quantum-threat horizon and accepts that Bitcoin’s upgrade process may be too slow; zero remains “a story,” rather than an established outcome. His nearer concern is “AI hacking capitalism,” with severe cyberattacks becoming a major market story over the next three years; he explicitly acknowledges he is talking his book.

Digest

1. Profitable hedge funds are defending their remaining chip stacks

  • Visser describes one of his career’s largest deleveraging events relative to the market. His opening assessment is “either done or in the seventh or eighth inning”; later, he declares, “Deleveraging is over.” The distinction underpinning that confidence: funds entered the unwind with strong first-half gains and are protecting profits, rather than trying to rescue already-losing years.
  • His Goldman Sachs VIP crowded-long measure versus the S&P has suffered a 75-day decline rivaled this century only during the financial crisis. The window begins around June 30 and captures roughly half the relative advance since ChatGPT being surrendered. He stresses that this is not actual hedge-fund performance and assumes Goldman is keeping the basket updated.
  • Much of his positioning evidence runs through October 16: Jefferies flows worse than the DeepSeek panic, Goldman’s second-largest global AI-stock net selling in a year, and AI net buying since 2025 fully reversed. Goldman’s overall hedge-fund net positioning reached levels unseen outside Liberation Day over five years. Put volume also exploded, reinforcing his reading of forced risk reduction.
  • The remaining “chip stack” matters: a long/short cohort was down 3.8% for the month but still up 8.8% for the year; systematic long/short managers lost 1.3% in a day yet retained 19% year-to-date gains. A new month resets behavior even without recovering losses: “You start trading a little differently,” assuming the manager has not been fired.

2. Crowded positions collide with a faster market clock

  • His historical comparison is August 2007’s quant quake, when forced factor liquidation produced large losses followed by an almost complete recovery. Today’s trade carries concentration risk that he distinguishes from that episode. The shared mechanism is a time mismatch: exposures accumulated over 18 months cannot all exit comfortably in 75 days while prime brokers and clients demand risk reduction.
  • Long/short liquidation explains otherwise puzzling breadth. Selling AI longs encounters substantial dollar volume—he cites $187 billion traded that day—but buying back shorts in homebuilders and consumer staples meets thinner liquidity. That helps explain 324 S&P constituents rising while the index fell 1.36%, the second-widest breadth-versus-price divergence since 1990, behind DeepSeek.
  • Index hedges compound the problem because the S&P and Nasdaq do not reliably offset concentrated AI exposures. Funds therefore build individual-stock short baskets; bearish bets approached five-year highs. Trying to hedge losses without selling longs can actually increase gross exposure, creating squeeze risk precisely when managers are attempting to reduce pain. Green screens outside AI can consequently reflect short covering.
  • The deeper warning concerns time itself: “If your earnings beat estimates every quarter for the next eight quarters, your stock can still go down.” AI agents erode funds’ historical information and execution advantages, while weekend tokenized trading means “you don’t get to sleep anymore on the weekends.” Monthly, quarterly and drawdown constraints become harder to reconcile with exponential technological change.

3. Credit contagion is visible, but economic deleveraging is unconfirmed

  • Visser’s caution is that liquidation has spread beyond equity long/short into multi-strategy funds, converts, CoreWeave credit and French bond carry trades. France’s ten-year yield premium over Germany reached 173 basis points; its spread move produced the worst week in 16 years of data. European banks broke their 200-day average and suffered their worst relative week since SVB. Further banking weakness could trigger additional unwinds.
  • His central separation: hedge-fund deleveraging can crash asset prices while earnings, margins and hiring remain healthy. Economic deleveraging starts with deteriorating margins and profits, followed by hiring weakness. Claims currently provide no recession signal and look stronger than a year earlier. Junk spreads, however, have started widening from exceptionally tight levels, resembling an early warning visible around the 2007 quant quake.
  • Corporate profits, currently up 20%, are his strongest reassurance: historically, declining and then negative profit growth preceded recessions. The S&P also retains substantial year-over-year gains and closed above its 20-week moving average. Since ChatGPT, 85% of weeks have closed above that average, against roughly 72–73% over the broader period. He sees no comparable profits breakdown now, while acknowledging market conditions can change rapidly.

4. Compute demand keeps growing through the stock correction

  • Visser emphasizes suppliers’ guidance, rising Taiwan and Korean exports, and expanding capital expenditure rather than falling share prices. He quotes Jon Gray’s distinction: “With AI, you’re building capacity and you’re hoping you can keep up with the demand.” Blackstone illustrates the disconnect: despite trading near yearly lows, it reversed from roughly 4% down before the open to finish Thursday up 8% after earnings.
  • Citing SpaceX, Visser quotes Musk: “We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone.” Against an incremental ten-gigawatt plan for 2027, he cuts the revenue assumption to $20 billion, calculates $200 billion for ten gigawatts, then $100 billion if only five arrive. His timing caveat: “He very seldom lives up to what he says in this.”
  • His reading of All-In preserves CoreWeave’s financial risk without assuming bankruptcy. Ben Horowitz’s neocloud experience highlights a real-estate-like business; David Sacks explains why underwriting multi-trillion-dollar outcomes makes markets “super sensitive” to current data. Visser considers AI borrowing early-stage: $10 trillion of prospective capital needs does not mean $10 trillion has been borrowed. Large, simultaneous financing demands require higher risk premiums.
  • The price correction is substantial: SMH sits 22% below its peak, which he calls normal for semiconductors. Only 38% of his portfolio remains above the 200-day average, yet 85% of those averages still slope upward. He says Micron could reach $1,500 by February’s end. His three-month entry argument fails if economic recession develops; it does not require an immediate rally before the midterms.

5. Specialized AI brings healthcare into the growth thesis

  • In interviews Visser highlights, Eric Schmidt argues hyperscalers will keep spending because they can afford it and refuse to miss a historic technological transition. Sundar Pichai supplies a complementary distinction: frontier models “will always be needed,” while open-source systems perform substantial work. Visser sees separate lanes, with major gains ahead in healthcare, materials discovery and bending cost curves rather than one model serving everything.
  • Eli Lilly’s TuneLab is his concrete example: one model trained on anonymized work from 135 biotech companies, incorporating both wins and failures. Pooling that experience creates collaboration and accelerates specialized intelligence. His framing is “the Manhattan Project for AI-driven discovery”—more than an application that helps researchers. He compares the specialized approach with Harvey Legal AI, while arguing TuneLab itself carries substantial value.
  • His portfolio implication is a barbell combining agentic compute with pharma, biotech and life sciences. “What is happening in pharma, life sciences, and biotech is beginning a massive bull market.” He recalls healthcare rallies during the dot-com period and financial crisis, and expects the country’s largest spending category to re-rate toward growth as AI-driven discovery produces repeated breakthroughs.

6. Tokenization moves crypto into mainstream financial infrastructure

  • Visser reads a16z’s Frontier initiative and discussions featuring Chris Dixon, Ben Horowitz and Marc Andreessen as confirmation that AI and crypto are converging. The framing he endorses: “Crypto is no longer a separate industry. It is becoming infrastructure.” Autonomous agents, stablecoins and tokenized small businesses connect that infrastructure to commerce and competition with incumbents, rather than leaving crypto as an isolated investment category.
  • His 46-name tokenization index, including Bitcoin, is down 10% for the month but up 50% since August and 35% year to date, outperforming his AI trade; Bitcoin is down 7% year to date. He contrasts 126-day volatility near 40 for his AI portfolio with 30 for Bitcoin. He intends to invest in the index but is still arranging a vehicle that can be traded.
  • Adoption is the supporting evidence: more than 360 on-chain tokenized equity products, up 200% year to date; three JPMorgan tokenized products live on Ethereum; and Canton’s connection with DTCC. He also cites Stripe’s John Collison saying agentic commerce “went vertical last week.” Discussions with Glider concern automated token portfolios, potentially providing a way to implement his own index.
  • For Bitcoin, he cites $664 million entering BlackRock’s IBIT and record shares outstanding during a bear market. After roughly two years of consolidation, a move back above approximately $100,000 would, he thinks, bring substantially greater participation. The quarterly refunding announcement “could be a catalyst” for crypto. These are prospective triggers alongside adoption already taking place; he does not claim the breakout has occurred.

7. Bitcoin’s quantum dispute turns on timing and adaptation

  • Visser disputes Chamath’s Bitcoin-to-zero claim and prefers Adam Back’s cryptographic expertise. Back’s horizon, as Visser presents it, is potentially 20–40 years: existing quantum computers cannot break Bitcoin, and the protocol can upgrade to quantum-resistant cryptography. Visser accepts that the upgrade process may be too slow—“that is a fair statement”—but a categorical zero assumes an outcome rather than establishing it.
  • The distinction is hardware versus software: sufficiently powerful fault-tolerant quantum machines do not yet exist, whereas AI already lowers the cost of cyberattacks, identity theft and exploiting vulnerabilities. Visser cites reports of unvetted agents accessing U.S. bank accounts and says 70% of websites using PHP had a break-in. He predicts severe attacks will make cybersecurity a defining market story over the next three years, rather than treating the danger as merely possible.
  • His proposed consequence is accelerated blockchain adoption as banks seek cryptographic protection and simpler identity systems. Chris Perkins argues quantum fears could accelerate Wall Street’s move; Visser expects present-day AI attacks to do it sooner. “They should be worried about AI hacking capitalism,” including disruption of incumbents. He explicitly acknowledges “I’m talking my book,” while arguing growing institutional participation improves the prospects for coordinated adaptation.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/ai-bubble-burst-bitcoin-zero-hedge-funds-wrecked

item.title: Competition, Intensity & Building a $115 Billion Global Bank | Nik Storonsky, Revolut
item.description: Revolut aims to lead in 100 countries with one configurable platform and ledger, adding 10–15 markets every one to two years. Storonsky says the shared system lowers operating costs, while applying for a UK banking license with seven or eight million customers led to an almost five-year process, making licensing central to mass adoption.
item.content:encoded:
David Senra · David Senra、Nik Storonsky · 2026-10-25 · 67 min · 原语言 EN

Revolut aims to lead in 100 countries with one configurable platform and ledger, adding 10–15 markets every one to two years. Storonsky says the shared system lowers operating costs, while applying for a UK banking license with seven or eight million customers led to an almost five-year process, making licensing central to mass adoption.

TL;DR

  • Storonsky wants Revolut to become the number one bank in at least 100 countries, using shared technology to undercut fragmented incumbents. He puts its footprint at “probably thirty-eight” countries, adding 10–15 markets every one to two years. One configurable platform and ledger support lower operating costs across countries; “I’m coming for his dinner” extends the ambition beyond retail into enterprise and potentially investment banking.
  • Bank licensing is central to Storonsky’s mass-market adoption thesis, and postponing it created a costly sequencing problem. Faster e-money licensing brought millions of customers, but applying for a UK banking license with seven or eight million customers made regulatory approval harder; the process took almost five years. He reports 80% adult penetration in Ireland and about 20% in the UK and France, arguing that reaching mass adoption requires customer trust: “you need to be a bank.”
  • Revolut’s product expansion follows portfolio rules designed to override intuition. Teams generally capped at ten build products over nine to 18 months; bottom-quartile bets are sunset, while up to the top 25% receive more teams and resources. After roughly 50 bets over ten years, Storonsky says, “I don’t really trust my intuition” about which products will work.
  • AI is already changing operating costs, while smaller product teams remain an organizational redesign in progress. Storonsky says 90% of customer support is automated, following a support organization of more than 5,000 people, and reports a 30% increase in engineering speed. He thinks product teams should shrink to two or three people and is betting on a “full stack AI employee” with calls, email, Slack and internal-system access.
  • European constraints shaped an efficiency culture that combines tight resource allocation with demanding personnel decisions. Storonsky says Revolut moved from negative gross margins lasting “three, four, five years” to as much as 80% positive gross margin. He argues that abundant funding encourages founders to solve problems with money before developing repeatable systems, and explicitly prioritizes winning over retaining average performers: “likable is not the goal.”
  • Storonsky treats investor control as an operating risk and has built a competing investment business around statistical selection. He says Revolut now has no VCs on its board and compares investors directing operations to “cheerleaders” trying to play the match. Separately, Quantum Light’s fully invested $250 million Series B fund has a reported 56% IRR; a $500 million Series C fund is starting to invest.
  • Physical advertising serves both customer trust and an attempt to buy impressions below digital prices. After seven years of organic growth, Revolut recruited marketing expertise from gaming and expanded into airport advertising and a Barcelona experience store. Storonsky says ads appear in probably 50% of European airports; Senra’s description of a “cocoon of Revolut ads” captures the intended visibility.
  • The eventual destination for banking cash flow includes technology bets beyond financial services. Revolut has built Pragma, a transformer model trained on transaction data, with 30 million transactions generated daily. Storonsky would like to fund deeper model development and data centers, but only hopes Revolut might have sufficient resources in three to five years; those moonshots “might not necessarily produce P&L” for another three to five years.

Digest

1. Revolut’s target is first place in 100 countries

  • Storonsky’s ambition starts with being “number one in at least a hundred countries.” Revolut began roughly twelve years earlier with a card offering interbank foreign-exchange rates, then added credit, investing, crypto, business accounts and nonfinancial services. It now operates in “probably thirty-eight” countries, with banking licenses in the majority, and is adding ten or fifteen markets every one to two years.
  • Senra’s recollection of “I’m coming for his dinner,” directed at Jamie Dimon’s business, gets a concrete explanation: retail is only part of the opportunity. Storonsky also wants enterprise business and potentially investment banking, which he describes as manual and expensive. His competitive discipline is inward: “I don’t really look at competition.” Instead, he asks how he would outcompete himself and demands “almost hundred percent every day.”
  • His claimed opening is incentive alignment: professional CEOs stay “three, four years,” collect bonuses and defend their jobs; he regards himself and Revolut as “one entity.” Founder-led incumbents, he argues, would already have better products. Against regulators’ concern about excessive risk-taking, his answer is that dependence on the company’s survival discourages “stupid excessive risk.” Senra agrees that founders cannot cleanly separate business from personal identity.

2. Licensing becomes harder after customers arrive

  • The initial choice favored speed: an e-money license could take one year, against three or four for a banking license. But applying after acquiring millions of customers changed the regulator’s incentives. A failed startup with no customers creates little exposure; a failed bank with millions invites blame. Revolut applied with seven or eight million UK customers, Storonsky says, and spent almost five years obtaining the license.
  • Senra repeatedly presses why a fintech cannot become very large without banking status. Storonsky’s answer is trust: customers must feel comfortable depositing salaries and wealth, then using investment products. He says he thinks Chime and Cash App made a big mistake by avoiding licenses; he argues unlicensed firms can target niche cohorts, including low-income customers, but cannot reach prime customers or become a prime bank account. Early adopters and their networks might produce 4% penetration, while his ambition is 40%, 50%, 60% or 70%.
  • Ireland supplies his strongest example: “Four out of five adults use Revolut accounts.” He attributes that 80% penetration to four weak incumbent banks, a small country and many people living outside Ireland as well. He puts the UK and France at about 20%, with certain other markets at 30–40%. Ireland demonstrates what he thinks is possible elsewhere, conditional on becoming a bank.
  • Legacy technology reinforces the opening. Replacing an old third-party core requires customer migration and introduces execution risk, so risk-averse managers avoid it. Storonsky argues that weak technical understanding compounds that reluctance: “doing anything is risky” when management lacks the skills. Banking requires building technology alongside regulation and compliance, and he considers incumbent management poor at that work.

3. Product bets survive on measured growth

  • Storonsky describes organization building as repeatedly repairing a machine’s bottlenecks. When headcount growth reduced speed, he created small, independent teams sharing a platform. Regulation then became the constraint, prompting regulatory and government-affairs capabilities; hiring became another, requiring recruitment processes. “You build something, then you hit a bottleneck,” identify it, solve it and repeat. The machine’s output is a product people use.
  • His trading background contributed risk management and quantification. “Metrics and KPIs” kill internal politics, he argues, because individual contributors and managers face visible goals and objective outcomes. The product-bet process added a missing discipline: Revolut had been releasing many features without adequately tracking performance. Proposals can originate from employees or leadership, but receive scrutiny before a team is funded.
  • A funded bet generally receives up to ten people across engineering, design, product and sometimes operations or data science, then takes nine to 18 months to launch. Gross-profit growth determines what happens next. Across roughly 50 bets over ten years, he says the best have grown 10–20% month on month, illustrating their progression with one million, two million and three million of monthly gross profit.
  • A new product landing in the historical bottom 25% is sunset, with weak bets cut within 18 months. Up to the top 25% receive additional resources: one team becomes several, then a department and a major P&L line. The discipline applies to his own ideas: “I don’t really trust my intuition,” because he has been wrong repeatedly. His preferred approach is “completely algorithmic.”

4. AI changes the size and capabilities of a team

  • Storonsky reports that 90% of customer support is automated; the function previously employed more than 5,000 people and now employs substantially fewer. Engineering speed has increased 30%, while LLMs also handle translation and cross-selling. He nevertheless considers this “just in the beginning.” The implication extends beyond making the existing organization faster: its structure needs to be reconsidered.
  • The ten-person product team “should be two people, three people at best,” he argues, because one developer can cover front end, back end and even data science. His larger bet is a “full stack AI employee” that joins calls, has email and Slack accounts, accesses internal back-office systems and performs work. He thinks this is “completely doable” with current technology.
  • His concrete example of spreading innovation comes from design. One team supplied an LLM with Revolut’s design system at code level and prompted it to generate flows. The output was a working, clickable interface on a laptop or simulator, produced three or four times faster than Figma screens. Storonsky is pushing that approach across designers, consistent with his insistence that useful innovations become standard equipment throughout the company.

5. Autonomous people make a wide reporting structure possible

  • Storonsky has about 50–52 direct reports and also reaches individual designers, product owners and developers on important projects. His criticism of some managers is specific: they merely collect information and pass it to stakeholders without improving direction, introducing innovation or finding an easier route. His preferred “self-guided missiles” identify their own goals and reach them, minimizing the management time required.
  • His hierarchy distinguishes excellent people who identify goals, good people who need a goal supplied, and average people who need repeated guidance. Below-average people may still miss the goal despite that extra time. Asked whether he fires average performers, he answers, “I do, yes.” Winning takes priority over empathy in these decisions. He allows that strong executives might be liked, but “likable is not the goal”; achieving the objective with minimal resources is.
  • His counterexample to advice about hiring experienced executives is blunt: probably 50-plus such hires in Revolut’s first five years, only two retained. Past achievement may cease to predict future fit as priorities, capabilities and competition change. He instead looks for career progression in the top 1% of peers, seeking people around 25 or 30 who can continue that trajectory inside Revolut.

6. Constraints teach skills that abundant capital can conceal

  • Storonsky sees California’s weakness as a culture of solving problems with money. His example is a B2B company reaching one million ARR, then hiring an expensive VP of Sales who recruits 50 salespeople. First build a cheap, repeatable selling system with attractive payback, he argues; then add employees. Otherwise, “you’re not really developing yourself as entrepreneur,” and become vulnerable when funding disappears.
  • Revolut’s own economics initially offered little room for waste. Storonsky says gross margins stayed negative for “three, four, five years” before reaching as much as 80% positive gross margin. He contrasts European interchange of “twenty base points” with “one half percent” in the US, alongside European restrictions on credit. His explanation for survival is sustained effort to optimize individual problems rather than spending through them.
  • A European banking license also did not automatically deliver local primary-account functionality. Each country required a local branch, office, connectivity and regulatory work, plus language differences. Tough employment laws demanded care in hiring. He thinks building through those constraints taught Revolut capabilities that would make certain aspects of expansion into the US, Brazil or Mexico easier, where he considers credit and interchange economics more favorable.
  • Senra challenges the claim that America is not especially competitive. Storonsky says Europe is even less competitive and points to China’s 996 schedule and technical education. His weekend-work argument rests on personal experience: of 140 companies in his original coworking space, three survived five years and two survived ten; all five-year survivors worked weekends. He says most of his direct reports also work his long hours.

7. Investor control can become an operating hazard

  • Storonsky’s “cheerleaders” analogy concerns investors directing a game they have not played professionally. Early European fundraising involved liquidation preferences, board seats and reduced founder voting rights. He considers raising LP capital on “two and 20” economics much easier than building an operating business, and argues that board observation does not teach execution. The danger arises when those investors use contractual power to impose incorrect operating advice.
  • His sharpest example is an investor demanding that he fire his best person for being “too hardcore.” Storonsky refused; even a coalition of investors eventually backed down. He says successive financing rounds removed VC influence, leaving no VCs on Revolut’s board. He prefers operators who have built businesses and urges founders to negotiate agreements keeping investors purely financial, without decision-making powers.

8. Quantum Light applies statistical selection to venture investing

  • Quantum Light originated, he thinks, in 2022 or 2023 after conflict with a major investor that entered Revolut at a $33 billion valuation and held rights blocking shareholder-agreement changes. Frustration became competitive motivation: “I also need to compete with VCs in their business.” Its model selects 30–40 companies over two or three years, investing equal amounts. His ambition is something like BlackRock in private markets: “we’ll see” whether it gets there.
  • The first fund was $250 million, focused on Series B, and is fully invested; Storonsky reports 56% IRR. The second is $500 million and is starting to invest in Series C companies. He recalls supplying 20% or 25% of the first fund himself, with other founders supplying the rest; the second includes institutional LPs. He thinks returns rank in the top 5% of funds.
  • Model inputs include investing funds, individual partners, their performance and age; he says the best partner cohorts are 30–40, while stressing age is only one variable. Support adds Revolut’s hiring, performance-management and expansion playbooks, his advice, and potential access to Revolut as an enterprise customer or to its users. Quantum Light is separate from Revolut and run by someone else.

9. Physical visibility helps a branchless bank earn trust

  • Marketing was organic for the first seven years. Recalling 2021, Storonsky says revenue fell, “I think seventy percent,” as COVID eliminated travel and exposed dependence on the travel-card business. When he turned seriously to marketing, he sought expertise from gaming companies with billion-plus budgets and little margin for error. The resulting machine focused on performance advertising, lifetime value and payback; the first marketing hire was fired.
  • A banking license sharpened the trust problem: without branches, customers cannot physically see Revolut as they see HSBC, Lloyds or JPMorgan Chase. Storonsky also saw an impression-price opportunity. He says Revolut now advertises in probably 50% of European airports, calculating travel frequency, impressions and cost against digital alternatives. His explanation of the immersive placements is simple: “Just buying full airport.”
  • Senra pushes beyond the cost-per-impression explanation: entire hallways create ubiquity, a “cocoon of Revolut ads,” rather than a fleeting sign. Storonsky agrees that trust matters too. The first Barcelona Revolut experience store follows similar logic: an Apple-like setting to try products and generate impressions among visitors and passersby. He evaluates its physical visibility against the price of reaching people digitally.

10. Global banking cash flow is intended to finance deeper technology

  • Asked why an American should choose Revolut over JPMorgan, Storonsky pitches domestic functionality plus global accounts, instant international transfers and a cheaper, better interface. US customers would be able to open accounts in Europe or Australia. Revenue leans more toward subscriptions, transactions and commissions than credit. Revolut offers cards and loans, but has not sold that credit off because it remains a small balance-sheet component.
  • The scaling mechanism is “one system, one ledger” across countries. Legacy banks expanded through acquisitions and accumulated incompatible systems; extracting consolidated reports can take months, he says. Revolut changes configurations for onboarding in the UK, US or Mexico instead of rebuilding each bank. Lower maintenance staffing and reusable product and marketing knowledge produce economies of scale. With time, he thinks this can become “an unstoppable machine.”
  • Pragma is an existing move into deeper technology: a foundational transformer model trained on transactions rather than words. Storonsky says Revolut processes 30 million transactions daily, giving it billions of training examples. Potential applications include fraud detection, credit and possibly investing. His broader aspiration includes building data centers and training additional models, but those ambitions require substantially more investment and cash flow.
  • The eventual moonshots would “most likely” extend beyond financial services. He calls the current business “the same old banking but done in a new way”: cheaper, better products connected inside one app. He wants eventually to build things never done before in technology. Those ideas remain in his head; he hopes Revolut might have sufficient resources in three to five years for bets that “might not necessarily produce P&L” for three to five years.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/competition-intensity-building-115-billion-globa

item.title: Surveillor - Trading Small Markets, Zero Leverage, and Calling the Altcoin Bottoms
item.description: Thread Guy targets the lowest-liquidity markets that fit his size, while Surveillor describes 1x exposure with hedges, not net leverage. Surveillor says Pump app fees are near $300,000 daily, roughly matching FOMO, while product upgrades and partnerships could broaden revenue beyond launchpads. Lighter’s US-distribution case rests on Robinhood’s stated plan and possible approvals, though licensing details remain uncertain.
item.content:encoded:
Thread Guy · Thread Guy、Surveillor · 2026-10-25 · 36 min · 原语言 EN

Thread Guy targets the lowest-liquidity markets that fit his size, while Surveillor describes 1x exposure with hedges, not net leverage. Surveillor says Pump app fees are near $300,000 daily, roughly matching FOMO, while product upgrades and partnerships could broaden revenue beyond launchpads. Lighter’s US-distribution case rests on Robinhood’s stated plan and possible approvals, though licensing details remain uncertain.

TL;DR

  • Thread Guy—not Surveillor—sets out the small-market rule. He favors the lowest-liquidity market that can accommodate his size, where he thinks the median participant is less skilled. He started with memecoins, focuses on alts, and avoids Bitcoin until his size forces him toward majors. His bullishness on selected alts rests on regulatory progress through at least the end of the Trump term, flows out of majors, and perps, buybacks, and tokenization; he thinks some good alts could still be priced at “5x or whatever from here.”
  • Their risk and position sizing are different. Thread Guy says he never uses leverage, has a 20–25% full-book drawdown limit that would make him zero his portfolio, and previously sized PUMP and Lighter at 50–70% of his portfolio at their respective bottoms. Surveillor says he avoids net leverage but uses perps for execution, and describes himself as full-port, 1x long with hedges.
  • Surveillor’s Lighter trade combined Robinhood news with technical execution. He began buying around $3.10 and scaled heavily at $2.80–$2.90 after Robinhood’s crypto head said the company still planned to offer Lighter to US customers. His continuing thesis is US distribution and regulation, though he qualifies the licensing details with “I think” and “maybe.”
  • The transcript attributes two position discussions differently. Thread Guy calls “CARTS” his highest-conviction trade and estimates it at 20–25% of his portfolio, limited by pool liquidity. In the later “CARDS” discussion, Surveillor says he first bought around $0.035, traded in and out, and bought most of his current tokens around the $0.10–$0.12 retest. He plans to hold them until next year or at least $1.50.
  • Surveillor’s CARDS buyback thesis includes employee-token alignment and a possible limited commitment. He says the team is working through buybacks and argues a one-year commitment could suffice. Thread Guy rejects permanent or 100% buybacks and suggests 25–50%; Surveillor agrees a real-world business needs money for continuing expenses and investment.
  • Surveillor’s PUMP thesis goes beyond launchpad fees. He says the app is nearing $300,000 a day in fees, roughly on par with FOMO, and sees on-chain social trading as a valuable narrative. Product improvements, partnerships, and his view that the founders already have about $1.5 billion in cash underpin his expectation of further investment and his “no ceiling” framing.

Digest

1. Thread Guy’s small-market edge and his response to market FUD

  • Thread Guy’s rule is to trade the “lowest liquidity market that can accommodate your size,” where he believes the median participant is least skilled. He started with memecoins, which he recommends to people trading smaller amounts, and moved toward alts. He avoids majors—Bitcoin mostly—until his size forces him to trade them more. He says crypto trading does not transfer completely to stocks because there are more sharks in that bigger game.
  • Surveillor asks whether this approach depends on crypto continuing to grow or risks “playing a game that is maybe dying.” Thread Guy says regulatory progress should continue at least through the end of the Trump term, then “we’ll see what happens.” He also sees flows out of BTC, ETH, and SOL into Zcash and, to some extent, Hyperliquid, and is bullish on perps, buyback tokens, tokenization, and intra-crypto rotation. He thinks selected good alts could still be priced at “5x or whatever from here.”
  • Thread Guy says he mostly ignores alarming headlines about AI and Bitcoin encryption and wants to buy dips; he says “buying the FUD has always worked.” Surveillor says he sold CARTS after Justin Drake’s article and sold at the bottom, though he did not lose money.
  • On contrarianism, Surveillor says it is usually dangerous and “an ego thing,” describing Thread Guy’s style as “really early consensus.” Thread Guy says the field is right most of the time and that a correct contrarian call pays more.

2. Separate risk controls, exposure, and hedging

  • Thread Guy says he never uses leverage because alts can move 10% or more in a day. His full-book max drawdown is 20–25%; if hit, he would zero his portfolio, probably log off for a month, and work on trading tools. He says he sized PUMP and Lighter at 50–70% of his portfolio at their respective bottoms, and had mostly exited those positions.
  • Surveillor says he does not run net leverage, but uses perps to get filled and exit normally; most of his current PUMP and Lighter positions are in his perp account. On PUMP’s unlock day, his spot bids at $0.0014 did not fully fill, and the price did not return to that level. He describes his approach as full-port, 1x long, with hedges.
  • Surveillor looks to hedge altcoins when a narrative or fundamentals stop gaining traction, especially former outperformers he thinks can become the biggest losers. His trades typically play out over a couple of weeks. He describes using a custom Surveillor Dash, catalyst and portfolio dashboards, on-chain and perps monitors, and a Grok bot for relevant news.
  • Surveillor says a P&L screenshot he had sent Thread Guy was down by roughly $600,000; he clarifies this was not realized. He avoids a doxxed wallet because public attention would make it harder to regulate his emotions.

3. The CARTS/CARDS discussions: conviction, liquidity, and buybacks

  • In the earlier CARTS discussion, Thread Guy calls it his highest-conviction trade and estimates it at 20–25% of his portfolio, though he says he cannot add more because he already has a large share of the liquidity pool. The transcript later uses “CARDS” for Surveillor’s discussion; it does not establish whether these labels refer to the same holding.
  • Surveillor says he first bought CARDS around $0.035, about six months earlier, but traded in and out; most of his current tokens came after the last retest around $0.10 or $0.12. Thread Guy presses him on enduring months of poor price action and ridicule. Surveillor admits he had been “tweaking about it,” including when it rose 30% on news and then fell 25% the next day.
  • Surveillor says he sent his current tokens to a Ledger and plans to hold them until next year or at least $1.50, where he would de-risk. He argues whales and funds cannot yet allocate meaningful size because there is no CEX spot market or major-exchange perp and liquidity is too low; he expects that to change as the coin gets bigger.
  • His buyback thesis is that systematic buybacks could support the token. He says the SEC has said tokens can buy back and that the team is working through it. Against concerns about the equity side taking priority, he cites public statements that Collector Crypt employees’ grants are entirely in tokens. He says a one-year commitment, as he understands Pump.fun made, could show alignment without promising buybacks forever.
  • Thread Guy calls permanent buybacks “stupid” and suggests 25–50% rather than 100%. Surveillor agrees that a real-world business needs continuing expenses and investment, unlike his characterization of crypto protocols as having less work after the initial product is built.

4. PUMP’s app broadens the revenue and incentive thesis

  • Surveillor says Pump app fees are nearing $300,000 a day, roughly on par with FOMO. He considers this revenue more valuable than launchpad revenue because “different revenue streams aren’t worth the same amount,” and sees on-chain social trading as one of the cycle’s best novel narratives.
  • He likes partnerships including Hyperliquid for perps and Collector Crypt for sports cards, as well as a native bridge, limit orders, and marketing through traders such as Kimchi. He sees the product and engineering improvements, and a shift away from random experiments such as creator content coins, as positive.
  • His incentive argument is that the founders already have “$1.5 billion or whatever” in cash, so they are not desperate for team-token unlock liquidity. He speculates they will invest a low nine figures in the app and partnerships before taking more off the table. Existing revenue supports his view that “there’s no ceiling”; Thread Guy agrees, saying every price makes sense.

5. Lighter’s bottom hinged on a misunderstood Robinhood relationship

  • Surveillor says Lighter fell to about $2.80 after Robinhood announced its own perps. He began buying around $3.10 and scaled in heavily at $2.80–$2.90. Around $2.90, Robinhood’s crypto head said it still planned to offer Lighter to US customers. Surveillor saw the market as missing that Robinhood would integrate Lighter into its US app.
  • Surveillor describes entries and exits as “50% tingle,” with technicals helping precision. He agrees that information can take time to move prices, but says he does not know why. He also recalls a PUMP entry at $0.0039 around TJR’s liquidation on FOMO.
  • His continuing Lighter thesis is US distribution and possible regulation. He thinks Lighter is applying for DCM and DCO approvals, and says there may be separate US perps licenses or equity perps. He sees a strong narrative if Lighter becomes the first fully regulated US perp DEX.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/surveillor-trading-small-markets-zero-leverage-c

item.title: My Conversation with Dylan Patel and Stacy Rasgon
item.description: Financing costs and shortages in substrates, memory, and clean-room capacity could constrain AI infrastructure supply through 2028, while on-site generation may ease power limits. Construction exceeds $60 billion per gigawatt, shifting cost negotiations; Nvidia’s pricing power depends on performance gains outpacing higher costs. Patel expects Nvidia’s CoWoS and HBM share to fall, even as earnings at least double next year; custom silicon and enterprise token demand remain key signals.
item.content:encoded:
Chipstrat · Austin Lyons、Stacy Rasgon、Dylan Patel · 2026-10-24 · 50 min · 原语言 EN

Financing costs and shortages in substrates, memory, and clean-room capacity could constrain AI infrastructure supply through 2028, while on-site generation may ease power limits. Construction exceeds $60 billion per gigawatt, shifting cost negotiations; Nvidia’s pricing power depends on performance gains outpacing higher costs. Patel expects Nvidia’s CoWoS and HBM share to fall, even as earnings at least double next year; custom silicon and enterprise token demand remain key signals.

TL;DR

  • Financing is becoming a supply constraint, but Rasgon thinks the next year or two are probably okay. Patel says neoclouds increasingly need strong offtake or chip-vendor backstops, while even major AI-lab contracts can carry 13–15% debt costs. Rasgon argues those brakes might create “stronger for longer” conditions by preventing overbuilding.
  • Substrates and memory may constrain AI deployment more than power through 2028. Patel calls substrates the “biggest bottleneck of all the bottlenecks” and estimates nearly 50 gigawatts of global data-center construction next year, with on-site generation helping alleviate power constraints. Rasgon thinks 2028 will probably remain tight; 2029 becomes a demand question.
  • Higher infrastructure prices are shifting profits across the AI supply chain. Patel puts construction above $60 billion per gigawatt, versus roughly $40 billion in 2024, while selling ready capacity can command much more than contracting ahead. Rasgon says “inflation saved the industry during COVID”; the current contest is over which suppliers retain margins and which customers absorb rising costs.
  • Nvidia’s margin defense depends on performance improving faster than prices. Rasgon cites Blackwell-to-Rubin reference costs rising from about $25 billion to $40 billion per gigawatt against a claimed 10x performance gain. He would worry if hypothetical Feynman were only 20% better: “You need to keep giving your customer value.”
  • Patel expects Nvidia’s share of CoWoS and HBM to fall while earnings still at least double next year. His team says OpenAI’s first chip beat Blackwell on InferenceX running open-source Chinese models, sharpening the question of whether design becomes “more commodity like software.” Rasgon emphasizes annual releases, scale and financing as defenses; both connect depressed valuations with competitive fears.
  • Enterprise adoption may generate demand primarily through productivity gains and purchased tokens. Rasgon describes Claude completing a week’s modeling work in 80 minutes, although he considers the evidence for returns encouraging and early. Patel expects batching and model-scale economics to favor cloud consumption: “Most people are just going to be buying tokens.”

Digest

1. Capital constraints may stretch the buildout

  • For Rasgon, financing is a leading concern, but “we’re probably okay” for the next year or two. CoreWeave’s roughly 15% unsecured-debt yield reflects secondary-market trading, rather than its current borrowing cost. It signals what fresh unsecured financing might cost; whether revenues catch up depends on the sustainability of today’s compute scarcity.
  • Patel says neoclouds account for nearly half the buildout, yet financing increasingly requires high-grade offtake. Even Anthropic/OpenAI-backed projects face 13–15% debt pricing. Hyperscalers cannot spend north of $2 trillion next year, he argues, while smaller customers struggle to finance capacity outside those channels.
  • Nvidia’s backstop can guarantee a $3.50 rental price, “the cloud making zero money,” with revenue sharing when others rent above it. Patel cites 50% shares for Sharon AI and Fermi, versus 10% for Lambda’s Anthropic cluster. Broadcom stretches Anthropic’s payments over several years, effectively “a rent to own.”
  • Rasgon’s upside is “stronger for longer”: constraints could postpone supply rather than repeat the dark-fiber overbuild. Patel says Meta has $1.4 trillion of compute and data-center commitments; the broader market can finance capacity against those commitments.

2. Materials and clean rooms may bind before power

  • Patel ranks substrates first, followed by memory, then significant optics constraints. Conservative Japanese materials suppliers underinvested, restricting accelerators, CPUs and other components. Even one major company could not satisfy its full 2028 co-packaged-optics volumes, he argues, given constraints in lasers, fiber attachment and related components.
  • Against the emphasis on power, Patel counts nearly 50 gigawatts of data-center construction next year: about 35 in the U.S. and seven or eight in China. On-site turbines, reciprocating engines and fuel cells offer workarounds. Rasgon agrees those exist while admitting uncertainty about turbine lead times.
  • With memory stocks trading at two to four times forward earnings, Rasgon asks what happens if the feared pricing collapse as supply arrives around 2028 fails to materialize. Memory occupies roughly 70–80% of an AI rack’s silicon area; HBM needs three to four times the wafers per gigabyte of DDR5. Continued demand growth could sustain scarcity.
  • This year’s wafer-fabrication-equipment estimates began around $120 billion and will probably finish near $155 billion; one vendor’s preliminary next-year outlook exceeds $200 billion. Rasgon says full clean rooms limit installation. Some new space arrives in 2027, more in 2028–29. He thinks 2028 will “probably still be tight”; on 2029, “I don’t know.”

3. Pricing power is redistributing the profit pool

  • Rasgon’s framing is that “inflation saved the industry during COVID.” Industry units in 2023–24 were flat against 2019, but blended ASPs were 50% higher, even excluding memory. He expects roughly $1.5 trillion of semiconductor revenue this year, maybe more; memory ASPs account for 70–80% of growth, while units rise about 10%.
  • Patel contrasts TSMC’s steady gross-margin climb from 45% to 60% with memory’s negative gross margins just a few years earlier. TSMC preserves long-term partnerships; memory suppliers respond to customers’ cyclical bargaining. If Apple squeezes them in downturns, “they’re going to screw Apple over in the upside of the cycle.”
  • Patel puts construction above $60 billion per gigawatt, versus $40 billion in 2024. Waiting until capacity is ready lets Musk seek $50 billion rather than $15 billion per gigawatt; Patel says Anthropic generates $70–80 billion per gigawatt of inference capacity. Nvidia’s higher prices do not imply expanding margins: those stayed roughly flat or slipped as memory and other inputs became dearer.

4. Nvidia must keep widening the performance-to-price gap

  • Lyons asks when customers finally reject rising costs. Rasgon answers with performance: Ampere-to-Hopper ASPs roughly doubled for about 10x performance; Hopper-to-Blackwell ASPs rose roughly 50% for 3–30x performance, potentially more after optimization. Blackwell-to-Rubin reference costs rise from about $25 billion to $40 billion per gigawatt, but Rasgon cites 10x performance. Customers are also getting more from each gigawatt.
  • Rasgon’s condition is explicit: “as long as that gap is getting bigger,” higher prices remain palatable. If hypothetical Feynman were only 20% better, he would worry about pricing and margins. Slower innovation would force suppliers to absorb costs, producing “a dogfight” over who pays.

5. Custom silicon threatens margins before it stops growth

  • OpenAI’s first chip beat Blackwell on InferenceX running open-source Chinese models, according to Patel, whose team tested it in OpenAI’s lab. AI helped design and program it. Anthropic wants its chip in half OpenAI’s development time: “aggressive goals,” dependent on models accelerating the process.
  • Patel says getting Nvidia running on InferenceX took six months, versus a month and a half for OpenAI. He asks whether design follows software toward commoditization. The incentive is substantial: removing chip-design-house margins brings his roughly $60 billion-per-gigawatt stack toward $20 billion. Fixed mask and EDA costs remain around $50 million, alongside data and scaling challenges.
  • Lyons asks whether Nvidia’s lost share means units; Patel prefers CoWoS wafers, HBM and associated spending because chip sizes differ. He expects further share loss next year despite earnings at least doubling. Startups face a separate hurdle: Cerebras and Groq illustrate his argument that only “really crazy things,” difficult for incumbents to copy, have a shot.
  • Rasgon emphasizes annual releases, ecosystem, installed infrastructure and financing as defenses; Nvidia also uses AI in design. He allows debate over CUDA’s moat. A note nine or ten months earlier found only 13 days in a decade when Nvidia traded cheaper relative to the SOX; it is cheaper now. “It’s a race.”

6. Enterprise returns need not require enterprise-owned hardware

  • Nvidia’s revenue is roughly 50/50 hyperscale and non-hyperscale, Rasgon says, although lab demand cuts across that split; labs contribute about 20% directly and indirectly. “If we don’t have enterprise adoption, there’s no industry.” Coding already supplies one killer application.
  • His team previously tried AI modeling and got “garbage.” More recently, Claude built a model in an hour and 20 minutes, incorporating ten years of history, resegmentations and forecasts informed by CEO commentary. A colleague would have needed a week. Rasgon sees encouraging evidence of productivity returns, while stressing that adoption remains early.
  • Patel expects most enterprises to buy tokens and combine them with their own data. Batching efficiencies and model-scale economics favor that approach over owning hardware and running models themselves. He adds that even pharma companies and hedge funds are likely to direct most compute and AI spending to models rather than buying compute to run open-source models. Enterprise adoption can therefore expand without a corresponding wave of on-premise accelerator purchases.

来源：Chipstrat

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/my-conversation-dylan-patel-stacy-rasgon

item.title: 少有的同时做过 Agent、多模态和具身的人 | 对谈前混元多模态 RL Infra 负责人淏楠
item.description: Astra把大模型视觉理解转为物理动作，商业价值仍待真实场景验证。淏楠设想小模型成功率达50%—60%后由GPT接管失败、沉淀恢复数据，或推至80%，使一人遥操十台机器。创业壁垒在硬件与System协同设计和真机采数，酒店叠被子是落地例子。
item.content:encoded:
42章经 · 曲凯、王淏楠 · 2026-10-24 · 54 min · 原语言 ZH

Astra把大模型视觉理解转为物理动作，商业价值仍待真实场景验证。淏楠设想小模型成功率达50%—60%后由GPT接管失败、沉淀恢复数据，或推至80%，使一人遥操十台机器。创业壁垒在硬件与System协同设计和真机采数，酒店叠被子是落地例子。

TL;DR

  • Agent 的增量机会，在淏楠看来正转向场景覆盖与使用体验。 他认为多数情况下模型的 coding 能力已超过 AI 工程师平均水平，但 game agent 等场景仍开发不足；更强的智力，也需要 GUI、CUA 和产品交互才能被用起来。“agent 确实现在来看是交互的主线”，多模态创作也会沿这条线组织。
  • 视频生成仍更依赖预训练、数据与资本，淏楠所在团队没有等到预想中的“R1 时刻”。 年初认为 RL 能带来高效跃迁，做了半年后改变判断；他限定，问题是后训练的 scaling 不够 efficient，并非堆数据不能提升。他认为约十名有经验的工程师、两个月能把 infrastructure 推到合理水平，难复制的是数据积累与产品回流。
  • 视频应用仍有很大的可控创作与交互缺口。 对曲凯提到的“Kling 2.5”，淏楠给出约六十分、满分一百分的判断，并明确预计未来半年会出现更好的 studio 或 harness。“抽卡”会继续存在，但可能从排除形变、换脸等错误，转向“它都很好，只是你和我的偏好不一样”。
  • 实时视频尚未成熟，具身也未必要等完整世界仿真。 提速容易破坏一致性，而提升质量又往往需要更大、更慢的模型，淏楠无法预测真正实时互动的节点。他更认同先理解当前环境、行动一步、再更新理解：“你没有必要先理解整个世界，再去做一件事。”
  • 淏楠更看好“大模型大脑＋自有硬件与小模型”的具身分工。 他形容具身厂商与大模型厂商的卡量“差俩零”，创业公司更现实的壁垒是硬件与 System 一起 co-design，以 7B—16B 模型控制本体，再接外部大模型。真机数据仍重要，尤其灵巧手要完成的动作细节，很难由粗糙仿真替代。
  • Astra 最重要的潜在价值，是接管失败步骤并推动采数闭环。 淏楠设想，小模型在陌生场景已有 50%—60% 成功率时，由 GPT 接管失败、留下 error recovery 数据，再把成功率从 60% 推到 80%，最终可能让一名遥操员看十台机器。他认可只学习接管步骤的“软蒸馏”；全程依赖大模型输出机械转角，则“太慢了，太费了”。
  • 具身的高估值仍要靠真实场景兑现。 曲凯以最高估值约 200 亿元、账上约 50亿—60亿元的量级追问，淏楠给出的落地例子是酒店叠被子：地面平，可以用轮式机器人，环境又介于标准与非标准之间。他转向 physical AI 是长期职业偏好，但对行业的要求很直接：“真的落地，真的能够有场景。”

Digest

1. Agent 已成交互主线，下一步是让更多场景用起来

  • 王淏楠从 2025 年 7 月做到 2026 年 2、3 月的早期经历，是 language agent，主要接触 SFT、web search 数据构造。到 2025 年底，他判断继续做下去，大概率会“以造数据为主，干一整年”，这与自己的兴趣和积累诉求不够匹配。
  • 两边都做过后，他感受到的是“围城”：做 Agent 的嫌洗数据，做视频的又担心工作不体现智力。但 Agent 是交互主线，公司做不好还可以换一家继续；多模态岗位更受公司路线影响。理解方向则随着 GUI 再起，包括他提到的 WorkBuddy、GPT-6 Extra。
  • 曲凯认为 personal AI 可能已是 Agent 的终点形态，淏楠仍觉得场景覆盖不足，例如 game agent。他判断，大部分情况下 coding 已超过 AI 工程师平均水平，新增能力的体感越来越难描述；接下来更重要的是“怎么让大家用得上”，至于下一个爆点，他坦言想不到。

2. RL 的差距主要在算力与实验积累，工程只是其中一环

  • 在庞天宇邀请下，淏楠加入混元多模态，负责 RL infra，主要推进 UniRL。他强调图片、视频 RL 是 infrastructure、algorithm、reward 的闭环，尤其需要训练好的 reward，三者得一起推进。
  • 谈国内外差距，他的限定是：“最大的 gap 我觉得可能还是没卡。”工程实践没有那么大的代差，算力不足却会减少实验、训练时长和经验积累。若租云资源一个月、目标只是尽快推高分数，SFT 的效率和暴力刷分能力确实更强。
  • 多模态也没有绕开 Agent：团队希望做“多模态里面的 cursor”。例如先生成三段视频，让用户选一段，或提出第四种修改意见，再沿选中的方案迭代；后训练便围绕这种人机交互组织，而非只提升单次生成结果。

3. 视频没有等来预想的 R1，竞争重新落回预训练与数据

  • 淏楠年初曾相信，视频生成也可能出现 language reasoning 那样的 R1 时刻；做了半年后改变判断：“它并不存在比较 efficient 的 scaling law。”这里指团队探索的后训练路径，连同前面的 caption 改写，都没有带来预期中的跃迁。
  • 曲凯追问，头部视频模型为什么仍能做得那么好？淏楠首先归因于数据质量。他也保留例外：据他了解，字节的后训练已经 work，但不少其他团队的 RL 还没 work；即使 work，最重要的能力提升仍来自前面的预训练。
  • 他没有否定 scaling 本身：堆数据仍能往前推，争议在于效率。预训练 infrastructure 的门槛相对低，十来名有经验的人、两个月，可以做到“相对 reasonable 的水平”；开源也降低了工程差距，数据却没有同样的捷径。
  • 数据要么花钱，要么靠产品回流。他回忆 2024 年底、2025 年初还能爬 YouTube，如今反爬已让获取视频困难得多。因此，这条线更吃资本、大团队与公司积累；团队曾尝试靠一波厉害的人突破，“半年没成”。

4. 视频只有六十分，抽卡会从排错变成选择审美

  • 曲凯用 B 站短剧《无敌超人》说明质量进步，同时怀疑其中加入了大量专业创作。淏楠认可人的参与仍重要，也认为做到“接近电影的水平”没有问题；谈到 Kling 2.5，他的评分仍是六十分，远没到能力终点。
  • 人的价值更多是用 taste 影响方向。淏楠认为 coding 相对有共同认可的好标准，影片却存在镜头语言、表达方式等偏好差异；连贯性、可编辑性是共同要求，具体怎样拍，则需要创作者施加影响。
  • “抽卡一定会存在”，但意义会改变：现在选掉的是形变、稳定性差等坏 clip；未来可能每段质量都好，只是审美不同。曲凯把它类比为导演拍多条素材后选一条，淏楠认可这种理解。
  • rich caption 已能精细控制镜头，但让用户手敲大量描述仍很累。更合理的是机器根据前文 propose 几种镜头，让人选择。他也提醒，真正做一条短剧仍“非常痛苦”，context 管理等环节都不到位。

5. 理解生成一体化之后，平台还要跨过创作门槛

  • 对热门视频复制、换人等单点能力是否会被模型吸收，淏楠回答肯定。他的核心判断是“理解一定能帮助生成”：先理解人物和画面细节，才容易改得好；生成是否反过来帮助理解，他没有同样肯定。
  • 消费视频的人远多于创作者，障碍并非完全学不会，而是麻烦、成本高。他和圈内人期待，未来半年到一年先降低门槛与生成成本，再让更多人同时成为生产者和消费者，形成新平台。
  • 产品层面，他偏悲观地说图片“没什么可做的了，主要就是做视频”，并明确判断：“未来半年肯定有更好的交互的 studio 或者交互的 harness 产生”，把模型能力交到更多人手里。

6. 实时视频还在用一致性换速度，成熟时间无法判断

  • 曲凯区分两条路线：一条只是生成快于消费，看起来像实时；另一条能持续回应对话与动作。淏楠认为，大家目前基本还在第一条，而且第一条也不成熟，越往后生成，一致性越容易崩。
  • 淏楠认为它家的水平应是 H3.0，模型能力大概在 2.0 的水平，仍有失败 clip；2.5 更强的地方还包括控制力，能加入人物正背面、发饰、故事线等大量参考图，以及 video、audio，进而支持更好用的商业产品。
  • scheduler、跳层、蒸馏、一步生成都能提速，但往往让结果更容易崩。他给的具体例子是镜头转回来后，后面的东西或人脸已经变了，因此个人更倾向先保质量。
  • 曲凯提醒，这只是阶段取舍，两条线可以一起推进，未来也可能出现舍弃部分能力、换取速度与低成本的方案。淏楠接受这种可能，但无法预测节点：当前仍在攻坚能力，“还没到能力溢出的时期”，模型越大也天然越慢。

7. 世界模型不必先完整重建世界，才能服务具身

  • 对按上下左右行动、再续写画面的 video world model，淏楠举出类似《塞尔达》跑图的 demo：有人在做，但质量和用途仍有疑问。相比巨大模型仿真整个世界，他觉得“像 Astra 这种 VLM 加上更小的 Diffusion 去做渲染”看起来更 promising。
  • 曲凯的反问是，研究者本来就该知道这条路很难，为什么市场忽然从兴奋转向失望？淏楠认为，研究者可能一直不觉得能很快做出来，只是市场情绪把人“架在那了”，要求马上交付，也未必想清楚做成后能干什么。
  • 他强调，李飞飞的 3D 路线与杨立昆的 latent 路线，本来就不是同一种世界模型。具身不需要先建好草、树叶、光线再行动：“我只要理解当前的情况，做一步 Action”，接着观察、再行动，也可能足够。

8. Astra 的震动，是大模型开始把视觉理解变成物理动作

  • 从视频转向 action，在技术上很自然：action 也可以是一种模态，原来视频加音频，如今视频加 action，都可沿 diffusion 推进。具身输入视频或多个角度的视频，输出可能二十多维的 vector，每一维是关节角等物理量，与 4096 维 latent 不同。
  • 过去让 language model 逐 token 写出“0.96”、逗号和下一串数字，再解析成电机转角，既别扭，也不 work。淏楠认为 Astra 的变化是推理能力更强，能依指令给出真正有意义、能够操控的序列。
  • 对非通用硬件仍有困难，尤其灵巧手。他描述的亮点是：模型动一下关节，再看视频，能把变量变化和视觉效果联系起来，在多轮交互中理解自己的输出怎样影响硬件。“这真挺强的。”
  • 淏楠强调，这次确实训了更多具身数据。曲凯问 OpenAI 的专用具身路线与大模型主线，哪条贡献更大，他选择后者；按他的观察，最终“堆到主线里反而是最 work 的”，是更强主线模型的泛化。

9. 仿真能提供训练环境，真机数据仍决定具体操作质量

  • 曲凯追问 reward 是否来自视觉判断“拿到苹果”。淏楠没有给出确定机制，而是推测能力可能从其他领域迁移：例如操作 Blender、观察渲染结果，建立动作与 3D 视觉变化的关系，再迁移到具身。
  • 仿真的价值要看使用者。大模型厂商可以把它当成 game 一样的 environment；具身厂商最终关心自家机器能否落地，因此要围绕确切机型采 trace，包括成功、失败，以及人接管后的轨迹。
  • 灵巧手的例子说明了差距：两根手指把瓶子捏起来，也许算抓取成功，但真正想要的是五根手指贴合瓶身。仿真中的成功，可能并不符合真实产品对动作的要求，仍需拿对应真机数据训练、调整。
  • 他保留了路线反转的条件：如果 simulation 真能做得非常好，real-to-sim-to-real 确实可以 scaling up，具身和大模型厂商都可能走过去。难点在物理、摩擦系数等细节，当前“仿真仿得不够好”。

10. 大脑趋向平台竞争，小厂壁垒在硬件与 System 的 Co-design

  • 淏楠提到过去 System 零、一、二的划分，认为现在可能收敛为两个系统：直接操控本体的一层，以及上面 language thinking 很强的大模型。这也是他认为具身公司应该拥抱 Astra 的原因。
  • 曲凯举出的量级是最高估值约 200 亿元、账上约 50亿—60亿元、不到 10 亿美元；大模型厂商主要五六家分卡，具身却有上百家。淏楠形容双方卡量“差俩零”，初创缺积累、卡与资金，很难沿重训巨大模型的路线竞争。
  • 曲凯提醒，具身公司基本都有本体；淏楠强调壁垒在“谁的硬件做得更好”，以及与 System 绑定得更好。他更认可 co-design：自有产品配 7B—16B 小模型，接外部大模型，把整套系统跑通并尽快落地。
  • 他认为真做具身更适合去具身厂：产业链像汽车、手机一样长，利润率不像软件，大厂对链条的控制也弱。大厂适合做模型研究，但部门边界让训练人员亲自采数、遥操更困难，难以从底层摸清问题。

11. 长期吸引力在物理生产力，估值要靠真实场景兑现

  • 曲凯追问，为什么在估值已高、又受到 Astra 冲击时入行？淏楠说，视频仍有机会，但个人更想做生产力、做 physical AI，投入十几年、二十几年。若只看短期收益，他当年会留在 Agent，也曾拿到美国 TikTok 相当可观的 package。
  • 对 AI for science，他区分用 AI 解 ODE、PDE，例如遮挡场景下的 Wi-Fi 布点，以及 AI 帮助化学实验。后者需要能做湿实验的工厂，与具身的线下采数体系很像；他觉得这一路目前可能仍偏早，具身进步也能帮助它。
  • 酒店是他认为值得尝试的场景：地面平，可以用轮式机器人；叠被子既有固定流程，也有不同程度的凌乱，介于标准化与非标准化之间。能否降成本、替代部分酒店整理工作，才是把高估值继续往上推的实际依据。

12. 大模型接管失败步骤，才可能让采数闭环转起来

  • Astra 算不算具身的 GPT-3 时刻？淏楠觉得“有点算”。他设想，一个模型在没训练过的场景能有 50% 或 60% 成功率，已经很不错；随后让它先操作，出问题时由 GPT 接管，可能替代部分遥操员。
  • 通过实时读视频判断接管时机，把后续操作 route 给 GPT，完成后留下高价值轨迹。尤其失败后如何恢复，也就是 error recovery，本身就是训练中非常重要的数据。
  • 他给出的迭代是假设性的：把数据回流给自己的 7B、8B 模型，成功率从 60% 拉到 80%；小模型继续操作，失败再交给 GPT，连 GPT 都处理不了才找人。这样可能从一名遥操员盯一台，走到一人盯十台。
  • 他把它类比为 speculative decoding：小模型先 draft，大模型 approve 或接管。成功率提高后，GPT 调用量和人的负担一起下降；让 GPT 常态化直接输出机械转角则“不划算”，因为“太慢了，太费了”。

13. 具身更可行的是局部软蒸馏，而非全程大模型示范

  • 曲凯问，Astra 的能力会不会被蒸馏成具身开源模型？淏楠先区分“硬蒸馏”：让大模型 Roll 出 Trace 再训练。他认为这在具身里成本过高，“没必要”，经济上不划算。
  • 他更认可“软蒸馏”：小模型操作到一半失败，大模型只接管一两步，带回正常轨迹后再交还。“你只蒸了这一两步”，量小、价值高，也能覆盖成本；他判断大概率由具身厂商来做，因为它们更容易部署设备、嵌入采数流程。
  • 曲凯保留对未来几年估值与市场的未知，但认为新可能确实被解锁。淏楠则明确称 Astra 是 game changer：第一次感觉“我靠，这东西真的能落地啊，真的能做啊”。他最后的期待仍带着原话里的尺度：“泛化能力这么强，它还都不是 3.5。”

来源：Podcast
