item.title: AI:AM Highlights: Clean Neurons, Black October, the GPU Credit Crunch, and Buying the Supply Chain
item.description: Zvi Mowshowitz sketches a conditional weekly-release path; contacts call 2027 “completely crazy” and say 2028 “might be unrecognizable.” Evan Conrad says GPU financing is constrained “entirely” by credit; three-to-five-year commitments and sometimes 100% upfront payments could force lab sales within one or two years. Cambrian sees memory rerating from five-to-six times earnings to 10–12 times if demand keeps outrunning supply.
item.content:encoded:
The Cognitive Revolution · Nathan Labenz、Prakash Narayanan、Zvi Mowshowitz、Evan Conrad、Lonis Hamaili · 2026-10-24 · 90 min · 原语言 EN

Zvi Mowshowitz sketches a conditional weekly-release path; contacts call 2027 “completely crazy” and say 2028 “might be unrecognizable.” Evan Conrad says GPU financing is constrained “entirely” by credit; three-to-five-year commitments and sometimes 100% upfront payments could force lab sales within one or two years. Cambrian sees memory rerating from five-to-six times earnings to 10–12 times if demand keeps outrunning supply.

TL;DR

  • Recursive improvement could compress model-release cycles from months to weeks. Zvi Mowshowitz accepts that software-only efficiency gains might peter out without new methods, but says this excludes the breakthroughs that matter: “if nobody ever hits a home run.” His conditional trajectory runs from two months to one month, two weeks and a week; trusted contacts expect 2027 to be “completely crazy,” while 2028 “might be unrecognizable.”
  • Cleaner neurons make interpretability more tractable without establishing that models are understood or their behavior can be predicted. Nathan Labenz sees substantive evidence in training experiments that concentrate on strongly activated neurons. Zvi emphasizes unresolved weak activations, attention and prediction, and warns that optimizing models to display reassuring internals is “playing with, like, liquid fire.”
  • GPU financing could force AI startups into consolidation before technical competition determines the winners. SF Compute’s Evan Conrad says the binding constraint is “entirely credit”: lenders cannot confidently value or operate repossessed clusters, so customers face three-to-five-year commitments, large deposits and sometimes 100% upfront payment. He thinks the next year or two could require much larger venture checks or sales to buyers with stronger credit.
  • The apparent hyperscaler price premium largely reflects flexibility rather than a durable neocloud cost advantage. Conrad contrasts reserved contracts with on-demand capacity at $11 or $15 an hour, which must cover idle inventory and customers’ ability to leave. SF Compute wants liquid resale markets to make GPU collateral financeable, but a startup needing 1,000 GPUs must still raise “roughly the same” capital today; lender confidence will take years.
  • Cambrian argues public markets underprice AI-linked physical suppliers. Lonis Hamaili contrasts semiconductor valuations around 16 times earnings with 22 times for the S&P and nearly 40 times for Walmart. Memory at five or six times earnings could, in his view, rerate to 10–12 times without further price increases—but demand must keep outrunning supply, and Nathan discloses a commitment to invest in Cambrian.
  • The bottleneck trade has explicit technical and political failure modes. Hamaili says almost no experts he knows expect DRAM supply to grow more than 2.5x by decade’s end, but unusually fast memory compression or a larger energy constraint could undermine pricing. Prakash Narayanan challenges the durability of bottlenecks themselves; Nathan still sees a narrow path to pausing frontier scaling for a cycle without popping the bubble.
  • Cybersecurity demand may enrich scarce experts while sending most incremental work to agents. Nathan rejects a broad hiring-boom narrative because displaced workers cannot quickly become elite defenders against agent swarms; companies will put “agents on top of agents.” Their banking debate exposes a separate uncertainty: Nathan doubts weekend rescues generalize to corrupted records, while Prakash thinks institutional promises can sustain transactions during reconstruction.
  • Federal preemption could spend Washington’s bargaining leverage before replacement safeguards arrive. Zvi argues that Anthropic’s leaked draft immediately displaces state protections while federal implementation could take six months or more, potentially increasing risk. “You can’t offer it again” captures his objection to granting preemption now and hoping to negotiate stronger legislation later, especially with possible loss of control in 2027.

Digest

1. Self-improvement may turn release cycles into a weekly event

  • Nathan asks whether evidence such as roughly 1.6 experiments per researcher really supports recursive takeoff. Zvi accepts his reading of Ramez’s analysis as “probably true”: existing software methods, without new scaling laws or paradigm shifts, might exhaust their efficiency gains. But he calls that framing irrelevant to the broader forecast—like estimating a game’s score assuming “nobody ever hits a home run.”
  • Zvi points to exponential growth in tokens used and code committed at Anthropic and OpenAI, while conceding that those quantities need not translate proportionately into useful output. His more concrete example is Nvidia’s reported acceleration during 2026 in doubling CUDA efficiency. That is not true recursive self-improvement, he says, but it demonstrates faster technical work resembling important parts of AI R&D.
  • His conditional trajectory compresses release-cycle advances from two months to one month, two weeks and a week—an “AI 2027 style timeline.” Trusted contacts expect 2027 to be “completely crazy”; 2028 “might be unrecognizable.” Prakash expects markets to underprice exponential growth for 20 years because people cannot get emotionally comfortable with it, repeatedly producing bubble-and-collapse episodes like those of the preceding three months.

2. Clean neurons narrow a problem without solving interpretability

  • Nathan’s read of Nick Cammarata’s “Neural Networks Are Already Clean” is that bigger models, modern training and better interpretability tools might make earlier apparent disorder partly a “skill issue.” He sees a real result, while remaining unsure whether it marks a new era; some enthusiasm, he suspects, reflects people being “desperate for hope.”
  • The concrete training implication matters more than the celebration. Backpropagation requires differentiable architectures; alternative guess-and-check methods can explore a broader space but have been prohibitively slow. Nathan describes experiments concentrating checks on strongly activated neurons, sharply reducing the search. Reported updates were “almost exactly the same” as backprop’s, supporting the narrower proposition that weak activations contribute less in those experiments.
  • Zvi calls the essay useful and interesting but says its reception “dramatically oversold” it. Weak activations, the cache and attention remain substantially unexplained. Knowing what individual neurons respond to does not establish how the network performs a task or predict what it will say—the capabilities he considers central to effective mechanistic interpretability.
  • Prakash asks whether a major hurdle has nevertheless fallen. Zvi says its expected difficulty has been reduced, perhaps making the problem roughly 10 times easier. But the featured Colorado neuron reportedly also responded comparably to “tornado systems.” For him, a readily challenged showcase example warrants concern that the broader hypothesis could be “mainly false.”

3. Inspecting and sculpting models can teach them to hide

  • Nathan describes Soares’s experiments training models to recognize internal activation monitoring through numerical differences caused by finite-precision GPU calculations and operation ordering. Zvi distinguishes an existence proof from an out-of-the-box capability: substantial targeted optimization was required. His concern is that, if detecting observation becomes valuable, models will eventually learn to exploit such information leaks.
  • Nathan asks whether identifying a bad-behavior neuron should let developers block updates that strengthen it. Zvi fears that explicitly optimizing how a network looks internally teaches it to route around interventions and present what observers want to see. These methods could also increase capabilities substantially if they work: “you are obviously playing with, like, liquid fire.”
  • His preferred emphasis is understanding observed results. He describes persistent disagreements with Goodfire over aggressive interventions: “I’m not sure it’s good. I just think it’s fire.”

4. A tiny cognitive core may discard what makes intelligence useful

  • Nathan presents the attraction: neural networks are poor databases, so why not separate reasoning from stored facts? Zvi understands Karpathy’s “cognitive core” proposal—a small reasoning system retrieving information as needed—but rejects its practical premise. A compact underlying mechanism may exist; that does not mean a minimally knowledgeable model will reason as effectively.
  • Zvi’s best example is entering an unfamiliar field: an assistant can explain every acronym, yet the newcomer still needs enough knowledge to ask the right questions. What looks like reasoning from five facts may depend on “five million facts” that supplied the intuitions for selecting them. That rich background helps explain “big model smell”; cheaper compute keeps raising the economical amount to memorize.
  • He cites Opus 5.5 as a current model knowing a remarkable amount, and says, “I wouldn’t have it any other way.” Nathan’s separate alignment concern is explicitly tentative: “I’m spitballing for the first time.” A truly stripped-down core would exclude values such as not stealing; users could inject stealing instead. In that sense, Nathan says, the pure core would be “completely amoral.”

5. Black October raises a record-integrity problem beyond insolvency

  • Against two disclosed PHP bugs and Cloudflare’s reported millions of exploit attempts, Nathan questions whether familiar bank-rescue machinery generalizes. Friday-to-Monday intervention normally addresses a balance-sheet problem with trustworthy records. An “OpenFace”-style incident involving 1,200 agent traces, each millions of tokens long, could leave falsified logs and uncertain account balances—something the FDIC might not resolve over a weekend.
  • Prakash agrees that insolvency and destroyed records differ, but disputes Nathan’s conclusion. Authorities could honor checks and withdrawals, identify recipients, reconstruct accounts later and recover excess withdrawals. “We will all honor all promises” is his institutional model: contracts and government backing can sustain activity while data is repaired. He remains “very sanguine” that the government would overcompensate rather than invite another bank run.
  • A compromised certificate authority, Prakash says, can enable bank-page spoofing, key extraction and relaying of the two-factor code. He rejects expecting everyone to safeguard valuable keys, citing crypto holders attacked for theirs. His uncomfortable speculative endgame is that “the network knows everyone”: passwords disappear, but anonymity exists only to the extent the network chooses to preserve it.
  • Nathan also rejects Aaron Levie’s suggestion that cybersecurity illustrates a coming jobs boom. Great defenders may command bidding wars, but displaced content marketers or designers cannot rapidly become specialists capable of confronting near-superintelligent swarms. Organizations confronting immediate threats lack time for hiring processes: “They’re gonna plow everything that they have into agents,” including agents supervising other agents.

6. GPU finance selects which AI startups can exist

  • Conrad’s diagnosis is categorical: the current bottleneck is neither power nor chips but “entirely credit.” A lender repossessing a supercomputer cannot confidently operate it or estimate its future value. Consequently, financing depends on the customer’s credit quality rather than confidence in the collateral—and new AI labs generally lack the credit lenders want.
  • Three-to-five-year contracts therefore originate with lenders. Meta or Google would be desirable investment-grade customers, but an independent cloud usually serves weaker credits. Those customers need large deposits or cash covering the contract. Paying an entire three-year commitment upfront makes a startup acceptable; raising enough to do so becomes a prerequisite for competing.
  • That changes how Conrad interprets enormous early funding rounds: the visible labs are survivors that secured enough capital to exist. Asked which lab investors should fund, his answer is “the one that you fund.” Without better collateral financing, he fears AI startup formation will resemble starting a chip fab, where roughly $50 billion of capital can become the entry barrier.
  • SF Compute is not yet reducing that requirement. For a startup needing 1,000 GPUs, Conrad says today’s fundraising need is “roughly the same.” Making clusters credible collateral requires years of demonstrated resale value and operating history; lenders do not become comfortable quickly.

7. Compute prices buy flexibility, and liquidity must be engineered

  • Nathan asks how long the hyperscaler–neocloud price gap can persist. Conrad rejects the premise: “it’s an illusion.” Neoclouds mostly quote reserved commitments; hyperscalers’ on-demand prices include customer walkaway rights and idle inventory. At $11 or $15 an hour, capacity is available partly because the price supports maintaining that availability.
  • SF Compute tries to create a resale market rather than allow capacity to disappear into hoarding. Conrad describes a Harberger-tax-style arrangement requiring some purchased capacity to remain available for others to buy. The mechanism deliberately puts offers on the order book; customers cannot simply acquire everything and make the market inaccessible.
  • AutoResearch goes further: users pay for queue priority but cannot purchase all of it. Tiny researchers submitting small, occasional jobs receive priority at the front of the queue. Conrad says these mechanisms explain why SF Compute retains availability while “basically every GPU cloud is sold out,” with its ability to keep capacity circulating secured for years.
  • Asked about his earlier prediction of a credit crunch within three months, Conrad points to more expensive CoreWeave debt, while acknowledging complexity, and customers facing 100% upfront payments. For “possibly a year or two,” VCs should prepare larger checks or encourage sales. He expects probable consolidation as labs and inference providers unable to finance growth sell to stronger-credit buyers.

8. Cambrian buys manufacturing moats at cyclical valuations

  • Nathan, who discloses committing to invest in Cambrian, asks why the thesis is not already priced in. Hamaili contrasts semiconductor stocks around 16 times earnings with roughly 22 times for the S&P and almost 40 times for Walmart. Selected wafer, memory, capacitor and foundry businesses trade around three to five times sales.
  • Hamaili thinks private AI markets can be more efficient than public ones: technical former operators bid a small startup universe to 50 or 100 times sales, sometimes rationally. Public-market capital is much larger, with fewer technical, strongly AI-convinced participants as a share of traded money.
  • Nathan asks for the strongest opposing case. Hamaili acknowledges that many favored manufacturers are poor businesses under ordinary conditions: high fixed costs, sometimes substantial debt, and losses below required utilization. His operating-leverage illustration starts at 10% gross margins: a 10% price increase could double earnings; doubling prices could produce “10x earnings.” That requires the particular AI-demand world he anticipates.
  • His preference is “atoms over the bits”: Nvidia, Broadcom, Arm and Marvell design chips, while physical suppliers own fabs and decades of manufacturing knowledge. His categorical claim is that “there will never be a situation where the labs will compete with a silicon wafer maker,” whereas labs already compete with chip designers.

9. Memory upside depends on demand outrunning supply and compression

  • At five or six times earnings, memory need not receive further price increases to support Hamaili’s proposed rerating to 10–12 times; demand must keep outrunning supply. He says almost no experts think DRAM bits can grow more than 2.5x by decade’s end, and no expert with a track record whom he cites expects 3x. His demand assumption is that AI needs will more than triple.
  • Compression is the key offset. Hamaili says bits per token fell roughly 500x between GPT-3 and DeepSeek V4 while DRAM bit prices rose 6–7x. His bear case is superhuman coders improving compression much faster than other economically useful capabilities, temporarily preventing the demand rebound associated with Jevons paradox. He considers that relatively unlikely.
  • Energy becoming the larger bottleneck is another semiconductor bear case, and Hamaili acknowledges periods of that during the year. His rebuttal is substitution: GE Vernova and Siemens frame turbines are sold out until 2030, but builders can use truck engines, aircraft equipment and behind-the-meter natural gas. Semiconductors lack comparable latent supply: “There’s no fat, essentially.”

10. Intelligence and emergencies could overturn today’s bottlenecks

  • Prakash challenges the manufacturing moat with labs’ data purchases: he believes Anthropic has a Micron deal and OpenAI one with “Synopsys or Cadence.” Nathan distinguishes chip design, a core RSI priority, from building a two-million-square-foot fab. He says there are no good RL environments or manuals for fab-building, and that manufacturing knowledge is tacit, held by Japanese engineers with decades of experience. Nathan says superintelligence may eventually figure out how to extract it; the question is timing.
  • Nathan adds that AI capable of solving the hardest engineering problems would also automate email and Excel work currently costing trillions of dollars, creating value that the physical supply chain could capture.
  • For Prakash, Musk’s edge is capital plus willingness to redesign the stack: a $30 million Japanese supplier may reject a $10 million gamble; Musk can risk $100 billion. Nathan asks, “does he take anyone with him”? Prakash allows a semiconductor market with Musk at 90–99%, analogous to his claimed 90% launch share, but expects OpenAI and Anthropic’s eventual superintelligence to enable them to buy or create competing capacity.
  • Prakash’s “adversarial diffusion” says 10%, 20% or 50% annual GDP growth would require emergency-driven adoption people dislike. His example is mRNA’s 20 latent years, followed during COVID by a vaccine six months after the decision to proceed and widespread vaccination a year later. He expects cyber pressure and fears bio pressure. Nathan calls politics the biggest thesis risk, while retaining a narrow path to pausing frontier scaling for a cycle as existing-model adoption continues, without popping the bubble.

11. Help Peer connects agents while rationing access and autonomy

  • Nathan’s Help Peer project asks whether individuals can benefit from cooperating agent swarms. He sees no established protocol connecting his agents with friends’ agents. The proposed network would let agents help peers on behalf of their humans, within human-defined rules.
  • His own architecture splits privileges: the laptop agent sees email, calendar and messages but acts only on instruction—high access, low autonomy. Separate Mac mini agents have their own email accounts and a credit card, work independently for hours and never receive his keys. “My rule is that no agent gets both.”
  • Prakash favors an auto-accept flow. Nathan worries about private information passing through autonomous agents, so sensitive transfers can trigger phone approval. Yet “five of those false positives” already strain his discipline. His agent Ade is available to attempt good-faith assistance, subject to filtering and another model’s review.

12. Preemption spends negotiating leverage before safety is secured

  • Prakash’s good-faith case for Anthropic’s leaked federal draft is to pass something now, build bipartisan consensus and amend it later; COVID and 2008 demonstrate that frightened Congresses can act quickly. Zvi accepts that steelman but says today’s politics support more than June’s Frontier Act. He considers this draft weaker than that compromise and partly tailored to Anthropic’s interests.
  • Zvi’s objection concerns bargaining and timing: “You can’t offer it again” once preemption has been granted, and satisfied supporters have less incentive to support another bill. Worse, the draft immediately nullifies state protections while federal requirements take months to implement, potentially leaving six months or more without either. Against Prakash’s interim-risk-reduction argument, Zvi believes this particular bill increases risk.
  • Emergency powers expose the institutional conflict. Zvi says the draft requires judicial proceedings and demanding proof that limited transparency may make impossible to supply. Another Fable-style model takedown would instead prompt export controls or threats. Anthropic wants federal preemption while distrusting federal discretion, in his telling, so it cripples replacement authority rather than creating bounded, reviewable powers.
  • Zvi’s urgency comes from labs’ own warnings that capabilities are outrunning alignment, potentially forcing commercial viability against catastrophic risk, including possible loss of control in 2027. He still considers Anthropic probably the most responsible lab: stronger safety culture and real sacrifices on selected convictions, but inadequate for the moment and often behaving like an ordinary corporation expanding capacity and use. “Reality doesn’t have a curve” rejects grading safety comparatively.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/ai-am-highlights-clean-neurons-black-october-gpu

item.title: AI Agents Could Drive 10,000x More Web Activity | Former Twitter CEO
item.description: Agrawal estimates agent web use at 10–20% of human levels, implying substantial runway if his 1,000x thesis holds. Parallel plans around 10X growth, but capacity hinges on GPU type, location and deployment within five milliseconds of its index. Higher-signal search is said to halve searches and cut tokens; model-priced publisher payments could help keep agent access open.
item.content:encoded:
Sourcery · Parag Agrawal、Molly O'Shea · 2026-10-24 · 60 min · 原语言 EN

Agrawal estimates agent web use at 10–20% of human levels, implying substantial runway if his 1,000x thesis holds. Parallel plans around 10X growth, but capacity hinges on GPU type, location and deployment within five milliseconds of its index. Higher-signal search is said to halve searches and cut tokens; model-priced publisher payments could help keep agent access open.

TL;DR

  • Agrawal sees 5,000–10,000x further growth in agent web use if his original 1,000x thesis holds. He estimates current agent usage at 10–20% of human usage, distinguishing it from crawler activity and headline bot traffic. His own agents already make several thousand searches daily: “1000x is too low.”
  • Parallel’s growth benchmark is agent inference, with 10X as Agrawal’s current planning approximation. He expects the world to spend one to two GPUs on web search for every 10 GPUs spent on model inference. Capacity involves specific hardware, locations and timing; some GPUs must sit within five milliseconds of Parallel’s web index.
  • Parallel sells search quality, model independence and lower inference costs. The introduction reports a $100 million Series B at a $2 billion valuation, while Agrawal says headcount grew from close to 30 to about 120 during the year. He claims higher-signal search lets models do “half the number of searches,” consume fewer tokens and finish faster.
  • Consumer-agent retention depends on fulfilling an unusually simple product promise. Agrawal expects good retention because messaging an agent requires little onboarding, but acknowledges having no insider retention data. He rejects the suggestion that OpenClaw’s concept failed: setup, continuous maintenance and early model limitations constrained accessibility.
  • Agrawal argues that agent browsing breaks attention-based web economics even when purchases survive. “You can’t monetize attention anymore,” so he calls advertising and per-seat subscriptions non-durable. Parallel is building payments to content owners for agent reads, with models determining compensation—a proposed “AdSense” for this web.
  • Agent access requires commercial alignment as well as identity and security. Agrawal wants useful agents to identify themselves and inherit their owners’ permissions, yet says identification currently invites blocking. Security remains a separate, layered responsibility; he expects consequential cyber events “every few weeks” as attackers and defenders both spend inference.
  • Agrawal’s next demand thesis is that “the web will go from pull to push.” Today’s always-on agents remain mostly reactive; he expects agents to monitor changes and act on users’ explicit and implicit needs. Across a trillion-page web with growing machine-generated noise, the constraint becomes allocating compute to actionable changes.

Digest

1. Agent web use remains early despite the traffic headlines

  • Agrawal’s original pitch was that agents would use the web “1000x more than humans ever have.” Now, “1000x is too low”: an average person makes around 10 or fewer Google searches daily, while his tracked agents make several thousand. He puts himself roughly, but slightly below, 1,000x. Most people are not there; reaching that point might take a few years.
  • O’Shea cites coding agents reaching 60% of traffic observed by Vercel. Agrawal cautions that automated traffic includes pretraining crawlers, and agents search more than humans to accomplish equivalent work. His best estimate puts agent web use at 10–20% of human usage. If his original 1,000x thesis is right, that implies another 5,000–10,000x from here.
  • O’Shea’s pushback—will smarter agents eventually search less? Agrawal agrees, but rejects scaling old search infrastructure 1,000x. His best guess is that Google will do roughly 10 billion searches daily; multiplying that infrastructure a thousandfold is not something he thinks they can build. Parallel instead uses GPUs to underpin search indexes, historically CPU- and memory-bound, and distills ranking intelligence into smaller models.
  • His conviction came from experimenting with BabyAGI and AutoGPT using models such as “GPT-3.5 or whatever.” They did not work, but the direction seemed predictable: better models running longer, with models becoming smaller and cheaper at constant capability. He did not predict coding agents would lead adoption or that the CLI would become their form factor.

2. Inference sets the growth hurdle and the capacity problem

  • The introduction reports a $100 million Series B “last month” at a $2 billion valuation. Agrawal’s benchmark is inference: “for every 10 GPUs the world spends on model inference, we’ll spend one to two on web search.” His current growth approximation is 10X, higher than last year’s answer. He wants Parallel growing alongside or faster than agent inference, while questioning how many years 10X can persist.
  • Parallel rents GPUs and has experienced multiple capacity scrambles over three months. Availability means the right GPU, quantity, location and timing; some must be within five milliseconds of its web index. For certain large clusters, he also asks whether the physical capacity can be committed for long enough. Agrawal calls every hyperscaler and neocloud. Availability gets established partly on iMessage, then finance teams handle paperwork. So far, GPU shortages have not forced Parallel to turn away a customer.
  • Parallel’s BrowserBase integration, which shipped that day, powers search in BrowserBase. It illustrates the distinction between reading and acting: Parallel’s APIs search and access the web before agents use browsers to log in, buy or write. Agrawal’s “cloud for agents” combines inference, perhaps a sandbox, web search, browsers and API actions, personal or company-data connectors, plus observability, feedback loops and security.

3. Retention and enterprise adoption depend on delivering the promise

  • Agrawal expects consumer agents such as Instinct and Muse to retain users well, while acknowledging no insider retention information. Messaging provides natural onboarding; the challenge becomes whether the product delivers. His test: “can it actually deliver on this very simple high level promise often enough to become a part of your life?”
  • Asked whether OpenClaw hit a wall, he disagrees: “OpenClaw was right in all of the ways.” Most people cannot set it up and continuously adapt it as capabilities change. Early performance also depended heavily on a strong model such as Opus. Managed products can improve underneath users without requiring them to understand what changed.
  • Early customers Harvey and Notion pushed quality; voice agents now push latency. Search needs roughly 150–200 milliseconds, versus roughly 600–700 milliseconds for human search. Expectations harden quickly: Agrawal bets disabling ChatGPT’s web search today would disappoint users on 90% of requests, even with a new model. “You will feel like a caveman.”
  • Headcount grew from close to 30 at the year’s start to about 120, largely as Parallel built go-to-market capacity over the last six months. Agrawal gives three buying triggers: bundled search fails demanding work; customers need independence across proprietary and open-weight models; or scaled workloads require better economics. He says high-signal results enable “half the number of searches,” fewer tokens and faster completion.

4. Keeping the web open requires payments and inherited permissions

  • Agrawal’s economic argument starts with humans “random walking the web.” Publishers monetize subscriptions, advertising, referrals or transactions along that journey. With agents, “the buying action still remains. Every other action breaks.” He calls advertising and per-seat subscriptions non-durable, making incentive alignment with content owners part of the infrastructure problem.
  • Parallel has built a system that runs a model to compute what to pay each content owner whenever an agent reads its content, and is establishing content partnerships. Agrawal describes a version of “AdSense” with “easy, automatic differential pricing.” The bet is that compensation for quality content can keep the web open, replacing publishers’ incentive to block agents with a reason to welcome them.
  • Asked whether bot detection still makes sense, he distinguishes crawlers, useful agents and malicious bots. He has “two contradictory feelings”: good agents should declare themselves, yet declarations can trigger blocking before incentives align. His Instinct and Muse cannot access many sites he can. He wants all agents, including those outside large labs, to inherit their owners’ permitted access and actions.

5. Security remains a continuing contest at every layer

  • Agrawal calls cybersecurity risks real: agents help attackers and defenders. He thinks organizations adopting defensive agents early will be fine because attackers seek the weakest link; frontier-model weights present a separate, more sensitive problem. He expects aggressive use of coding agents for security, consequential cyber events “every few weeks,” and substantial inference spending on both attack and defense.
  • His Twitter analogy is a “knife fight”: attacks can be contained, almost never eliminated, and the hardest activity is what defenders cannot distinguish. Web content can flow into agent contexts and enable injection attacks. Models have made real strides over the last two years, but “you can’t say, ‘Oh, models will solve it.’” Parallel, model builders and applications must each defend their layer; occasional failures will still escape.

6. Proactive agents change search and compute allocation

  • Agrawal’s current obsession is that “the web will go from pull to push.” Instinct, Muse and Dot show glimmers, but remain more reactive than proactive despite being always on. He expects agents to understand explicit and implicit needs, set high-signal, high-precision, high-recall alerts across the web and determine when changes require action. Falling intelligence costs could make earlier alerting concepts work.
  • The allocation problem is a trillion-page web, much of it junk, with many pages changing daily. “No matter how cheap you make compute, we don’t have enough compute to process everything.” Resources must prioritize actionable changes. Agent-generated publishing increases the rate of change and potentially the noise, making signal extraction more demanding.
  • O’Shea distinguishes GEO for chat from AEO for agents; Agrawal initially treats them as equivalent, then accepts her distinction. Parallel has offered human and machine website views since its early stealth period. Still, he considers presentation secondary: “we can transform the web” even when publishers have not made their sites agent-friendly.
  • Parallel designs documentation and onboarding around a developer accompanied by a coding agent. Customers can paste a prompt into their agent; the human authorizes access, adds a credit card and accepts terms. The agent can handle the rest. Agrawal sees designing the entire customer journey around agents as fundamental.

7. Internal expectations drive Agrawal’s operating philosophy

  • Agrawal credits his wife, a physician and Andreessen Horowitz investor, with raising his ambition beyond what he thought possible. His childhood peers were children of nuclear scientists in India, surrounded by expectations of becoming the best. He connects that environment to hiring: “If you don’t hire outliers, you don’t get outliers. If you hire only outliers, you get only outliers.”
  • Asked how he withstands pressure, he replies, “What pressure?” His sleep stayed fine through the Twitter acquisition; he distinguishes pressure from performing daily. “I only want jobs which I wouldn’t hire myself for”: insecurity encourages humility, a little paranoia, curiosity, effort and seeking help. Excepting his wife, he says his expectations have always exceeded others’—internal standards drive him more effectively than external ones.
