item.title: 20VC: Why Robotics Will be 100x Bigger than Coding Agents | Inference Will Be a $10TRN Market: What No One Sees | Why Software Investors are F***** Today with Naveen Rao, Unconventional
item.description: Rao sees US spare power becoming scarce within years, tying AI growth to construction. Unconventional co-designs models and hardware for efficiency as falling token prices pressure inference margins, despite a $10 trillion market forecast within 10 years. He sees robotics 100 times larger than agentic coding, with prototypes in two to three years and a market in five to seven.
item.content:encoded:
20VC · Harry Stebbings、Naveen Rao · 2026-10-24 · 69 min · 原语言 EN

Rao sees US spare power becoming scarce within years, tying AI growth to construction. Unconventional co-designs models and hardware for efficiency as falling token prices pressure inference margins, despite a $10 trillion market forecast within 10 years. He sees robotics 100 times larger than agentic coding, with prototypes in two to three years and a market in five to seven.

TL;DR

  • Rao expects spare US power capacity to become scarce within a few years, forcing AI growth toward the slower pace of infrastructure construction. He cites roughly $50 billion per gigawatt: building 10 gigawatts annually would already mean half a trillion dollars, while claims of 40 gigawatts are implausible today. He regards current financing concerns as “a blip,” with his confidence resting on continued demand for AI services.
  • The hardware opportunity is to redesign the model and machine together around energy efficiency. Rao argues that recent gains largely came from smaller data types, while physical efficiency improvements stalled. Unconventional’s premise is that “we don't treat the model as sacrosanct”: changing algorithms, architecture and physical implementation together can unlock gains unavailable through software optimization alone.
  • Rao forecasts a $10 trillion inference market within 10 years, while expecting pressure on inference operators’ margins. Falling token prices squeeze the layer mapping models onto existing hardware; improving energy-to-intelligence conversion offers more room for differentiation. In three years, he expects open models to handle 80% of tokens, but spending to split roughly 50/50 between open and frontier models.
  • AI’s immediate bottleneck is shifting from producing artifacts to judging whether they work. Rao describes reducing a research question from roughly two weeks to an hour, then warns: “I think we've moved the problem from producing to verification.” Specifications and experienced human judgment remain essential, which is why he expects development output to rise faster than spending shifts from people to tools.
  • Rao’s attack on SaaS narrows considerably when Stebbings brings up businesses delivering outcomes through software and people. He endorses that model, including AI-assisted legal work, and says he would send a provider 80% of his legal workloads if he could gain confidence in its results. The unresolved question is whether existing firms retain distribution or vendors eventually sell those outcomes directly.
  • Rao thinks robotics will be 100 times larger than agentic coding. His timetable is working prototypes for some tasks in two to three years and an emerging market in five to seven; Stebbings remains wary of application timing, particularly humanoids. Rao currently favors the technology stack and expects model developers to become integrated robot businesses: “You're not gonna have a separation.”
  • Rao now prioritizes technical progress over market validation when demand for the solved problem appears assured. For trillion-dollar markets, he calls price “almost irrelevant,” while Stebbings presses on fund concentration, LP expectations and limited diligence time. Rao’s underwriting principle is to back “someone to drive the bus,” because the original technical narrative will be wrong and the team must navigate the changes.

Digest

1. Spare electricity is masking a harder construction problem

  • Rao cites estimates of roughly $50 billion to build one gigawatt, versus $20–30 billion for a semiconductor fab. Recent data-center expansion has drawn on existing headroom: he puts average US grid output around 900 gigawatts, against potential peaks of 1.2–1.3 terawatts. Accessing that headroom is faster than constructing new supply.
  • Even conservative AI growth, he argues, makes excess capacity scarce within the next few years. Expansion then converges toward the construction rate. Claims of building 40 gigawatts annually get a categorical rejection today; 10 gigawatts would be “amazing,” and at his cited cost would require half a trillion dollars.
  • Rao thinks China surpassed US capacity in 2023 after building six times faster for 20 years. Central planning helps giant infrastructure rollouts, he says, while the US retains an advantage in opening new technological fields. He also rejects dismissing Chinese AI work as merely distillation: genuine innovation is happening there.
  • On Stebbings’s debt-cycle concerns, Rao calls this “a blip,” resting on continued AI demand. Anecdotally, bespoke behind-the-meter electricity already commands premiums. His illustrative 5x compute-revenue-to-electricity-cost ratio allows 30–40% higher power prices. A Bloom Energy project involving a couple of gigawatts in Arizona might help, but its approach and economics remain unproven.

2. Energy-first computing requires changing the model itself

  • Rao separates computing into physical devices, computing architecture and models. Physical efficiency gains have largely stalled; recent improvements mostly came from moving from 32-bit to 16-bit, 8-bit and 4-bit data. Moving and computing fewer bits helps, but leaves another opportunity: enforcing locality and reducing data movement at the model level.
  • “We don't treat the model as sacrosanct,” Rao says of Unconventional’s approach. Computing historically optimized speed: ENIAC calculated artillery trajectories faster than humans, and successive machines had to beat predecessors. With transistor improvements slowing, he wants every design decision evaluated for an energy advantage.
  • His co-design example is sparsity. Software might deliver an illustrative 5% efficiency gain on a standard GPU, but off-chip random-access memory limits how far sparse connectivity can help. Brains co-evolved their physical and intelligence layers; hardware expressly built to exploit the model’s structure could produce much larger gains.
  • Rao says specialization does not mean the market for horizontal providers like Nvidia will be small: “The market is going to be huge.” He recalls graphics developers resenting Jensen Huang’s AI emphasis at GTC in 2014, when Rao started Nervana. Huang recognized the opportunity and executed well. Rao’s own criterion is now singular: run neural networks “very, very efficiently, very, very scalably.”

3. Verification becomes the constraint after production accelerates

  • Rao’s concrete productivity example comes from coupled oscillators in Unconventional’s first chip. Understanding noise propagation across four or six hops once meant waiting for researchers and simulations, perhaps two weeks altogether. Asking a model, inspecting its code and iterating now gives him an answer in an hour.
  • That speed creates more artifacts requiring inspection. “I think we've moved the problem from producing to verification.” Stebbings suggests owning verification means owning automation; Rao is unconvinced. “You have to own the spec as well,” including whether the problem is useful and whether the finished result actually implements the intended specification.
  • His caution about agents centers on judgment. Neurosurgery requires seven years of training after medical school because choosing the right action takes experience. Models generate possible solutions, but selecting the good one remains poorly understood across tasks; successive decisions can produce results that look robust while being completely wrong.
  • Stebbings predicts people will eventually trust agents more than themselves. Rao agrees that may happen, but says it is not today’s reality. He expects expertise and training provenance to retain value: an intelligent machine’s usefulness will depend on how it was taught, much as a surgeon’s or chef’s does.

4. Data becomes defensible through curricula and specialization

  • Rao expects data businesses to specialize around important problems. Bulk observations initially looked commoditized; curated coding examples and reasoning data are different. He attributes much of current model capability to data selection, loss functions and the curriculum connecting pre-training, reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning. “That curriculum” is the “secret sauce.”
  • He rejects the assumption that reinforcement learning is more efficient. Measured by improvement per unit of compute or dollars, he thinks it is less efficient, although it keeps capabilities advancing and should remain important for several years. Gathering enough pre-training data to solve every task is impractical, and current models do not use that data efficiently enough.
  • The tennis-serve analogy explains RL’s appeal: demonstrate a good serve, let the learner build a target, then judge attempts against it. Speed and whether the ball lands in bounds provide a verifiable reward. Connecting actions to measurable outcomes supplies a learning structure for tasks that cannot simply be covered by collecting more examples.

5. The transformer is an interim architecture, while labs race to ship

  • “I do think we will be in a post-transformer world,” Rao says, a view he only fully understood a couple of years ago. He sees current reasoning as an inefficient combination of contextual retrieval, sampled traces and selecting among outputs. Brains do not reason by producing a huge trace and feeding it into another model; he expects better algorithmic approaches.
  • Frontier labs face a different incentive: being one month late can be disastrous. To Rao, xAI’s rapid arrival at the frontier shows how much progress can come from resources, experienced teams and executing an established paradigm. That differs from taking the risk of inventing a new one.
  • He places deeper architectural bets, including work associated with Yann LeCun and Fei-Fei Li, closer to startups. The analogy is drug development: startups take major risks, incumbents improve incrementally and acquire promising results. For founders, this raises the importance of vision; execution alone was more sufficient in the pre-AI software market.

6. Expanding inference demand does not protect every layer’s margins

  • Rao’s demand thesis begins with competition: organisms, companies and countries benefit from greater intelligence because their environments are adversarial. Energy powers that intelligence, and hardware converts between them. His definition of hardware includes chips, systems, networks and cloud infrastructure; doing that conversion better is where he expects value to accrue.
  • Some intelligence is already commoditizing. Six-month-old models, including Chinese open models, remain useful, and Rao expects the frontier to be available in open models within six months. That can create a huge market with thinner margins. He does not expect model companies to own the stack’s economics; he says Nvidia currently takes the lion’s share.
  • Inference providers earn their place by making existing models reliable, efficient and available with uptime guarantees. But falling willingness to pay per token forces them to extract more from hardware, with less remaining margin in that intermediary layer. “I actually think the hardware is the place to be over the next 10 years.”
  • In three years, Rao expects open models to carry 80% of token traffic and frontier models 20%, with spending roughly 50/50. His analogy is the mobile-phone market: he describes the iPhone as approximately 20% of the total market but 80% of the margin. A small set of difficult tasks should support premium frontier-model pricing.

7. Outcome businesses survive Rao’s critique of classic SaaS

  • “If you're a pure software investor, you're kinda fucked,” Rao says, targeting the classic SaaS model. Stebbings challenges the definition: AI vendors still sell enterprise software. Rao concedes the distinction and endorses businesses combining software and services to deliver outcomes. Harvey illustrates using AI plus human verification to perform legal work faster with fewer people at the same or near the same quality.
  • Stebbings’s pushback is direct: “Aren't you just investing in a law firm?” Rao agrees it is effectively a better version of one. Existing firms provide distribution, but that channel may not endure. If he could gain confidence that a direct provider’s solution works, Rao says he would send it 80% of his legal workloads, including NDAs and contract reviews.
  • Owning proprietary intelligence requires scale, Rao cautions. A large firm such as Cooley can justify customization; a small Nebraska practice wants an out-of-the-box service. He rejects the idea that every company will improve its own models using historical data. Competitive pressure encourages big firms to invest, while smaller firms may remain service customers.

8. Cheaper development raises expectations as well as output

  • Stebbings cites Benioff discussing $300 million of coding-tool spending against a $6 billion developer salary budget: 5%. Does that become 30%, 50% or 1%? Rao thinks the percentages may remain “sort of stable,” because experienced people are still needed to recognize good output and verify it.
  • His example holds annual development spending at $10 million while delivery accelerates. Customers once accepted yearly releases; now they want bugs fixed within a week, eventually an hour. AI plus humans enables that pace. The omitted variable in simple replacement calculations, he argues, is demand changing as supply becomes cheaper.
  • He extends the argument to construction: robots doing 80% of tasks might shorten a skyscraper project from two years to eight months. The result would not simply be the same construction completed faster; he says twice as many skyscrapers would be built, with humans and robots sharing the work.
  • Despite that productivity, Rao would avoid investing in agentic coding outside model providers. He expects value to migrate toward model capabilities, with less accruing to IDEs or harnesses. His evidence is internal switching: employees move fluidly between tools, suggesting limited stickiness.

9. Robotics opens a much larger physical market

  • Stebbings avoids robotics applications because he sees five-plus years of timing risk, especially for humanoids; non-humanoid machines have a clearer path. Rao initially disagrees strongly, then finds their timelines fairly close: working prototypes for some tasks in two to three years, with a market emerging in five to seven. Exponential development, he argues, makes distant-looking capabilities arrive unexpectedly quickly.
  • Rao forecasts AI models becoming a trillion-dollar market within the next few years and inference reaching $10 trillion within 10 years. Reducing token-delivery costs by one order of magnitude could effectively expand the market 10x “in some ways,” with potential applications increasing more than 10x. He invokes Jevons paradox to explain the expanding usage.
  • “I actually think robotics is gonna be 100 times larger than agentic coding.” Existing industrial robots mostly execute rote human-defined tasks; Rao expects dynamic physical problem-solving. Billions of machines could notice something broken, clean it up or replace it. Those services’ costs will fall substantially, he stresses, rather than drop to zero.
  • His investments favor the technology stack over applications today. Rao does not think the value will be in the model alone: companies building models may ultimately sell integrated robots performing particular tasks well. “You're not gonna have a separation.” Asked where he would put all his money outside Unconventional, he chooses Physical Intelligence for tackling the conversion of a specified task into motor output.

10. Technical milestones replace market validation in Rao’s underwriting

  • Rao’s changed mind over the last 12 months concerns progress metrics. Market validation fits products without deep technical roots; curing cancer does not require proving buyers want a cure. For robotics, computing and biology, he wants investors to assess progress toward solving the technical problem when demand for the solution is already evident.
  • Asked whether he cares about price given the market size, Rao says, “Not really.” He wants a portion of his wealth exposed to robotics and regards entry price as “almost irrelevant” against trillion-dollar-plus markets. Stebbings counters that LPs still care deeply about price and ownership; Rao expects attitudes to shift as established firms show similar trends.
  • Stebbings makes concentration concrete: a $20 million space investment from a $400 million fund risks 5% on technology he does not understand. Rao says early technical narratives will be wrong; investors back “someone to drive the bus, not the bus itself.” The team must make the pivots. Both acknowledge that two or three meetings make this difficult.
  • Steve Jurvetson stands out among Rao’s roughly 1,000 investor meetings. During Nervana’s early days, they discussed numeric representations, exchanged papers and debated annotations like technical colleagues. Jurvetson had independently thought about the opportunity. Rao’s broader point: large successful bets require non-consensus thinking because consensus is already old.

11. The endgame is a better machine for scientific discovery

  • With unlimited resources, Rao would build manufacturing and move closer to raw materials. Supply constraints and general-purpose components limit optimization; he would rather make exactly what his computer requires. That ambition extends down to processing and slicing silicon ingots, because he sees the computer’s value as delivering intelligence.
  • His final enthusiasm is scientific reach: AI lets humans approach questions that previously exceeded the available pool of capable researchers. He mentions deeper physics and theoretical constructs such as wormholes as questions to investigate, including whether they are real or exploitable. He rejects human-extinction framing and describes expanding human understanding as the opportunity: “It makes me feel like a kid.”

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/20vc-why-robotics-will-be-100x-bigger-than-codin

item.title: AI Cyber Panic, Ken Griffin’s Bubble Warning, The Fall of France?
item.description: Chamath estimates 90% of AI spending is concentrated in 1% of companies, with 80% from unprofitable VC-backed businesses, leaving genuine demand diffusion the key test. France’s 10-year yield has exceeded 5%; Chamath says bond pressure toward 8% could force a reset, while Jason sees no reasonable endgame.
item.content:encoded:
All-In · Chamath Palihapitiya、Jason Calacanis、David Sacks、David Friedberg、Nikesh Arora · 2026-10-23 · 103 min · 原语言 EN

Chamath estimates 90% of AI spending is concentrated in 1% of companies, with 80% from unprofitable VC-backed businesses, leaving genuine demand diffusion the key test. France’s 10-year yield has exceeded 5%; Chamath says bond pressure toward 8% could force a reset, while Jason sees no reasonable endgame.

TL;DR

  • Chamath sees AI’s bubble risk in concentrated, venture-funded demand rather than in the technology’s usefulness. His estimate puts 90% of AI spending in 1% of companies, with 80% of that coming from unprofitable VC-backed businesses. He describes VC-funded startups circulating spending, showing revenue traction, then raising again from the same investors. “AI has a diffusion problem”; Jason counters that startups’ rush toward the cheapest, fastest competitive advantage is an encouraging adoption signal.
  • Open models could redirect AI spending toward infrastructure, but compute scarcity limits enterprise independence. Nikesh Arora says Palo Alto Networks prefers open weights for customization and auditability, yet cannot easily procure globally resilient inference outside hyperscalers. His likely destination is rented bare metal running open models: buyers remain “a taker of terms,” while profit pools might shift from chips and memory toward available compute.
  • Arora expects AI-discovered vulnerabilities to arrive faster than enterprises can clear their accumulated technical debt. Jason describes PHP exploits rated 9.2/10 affecting software used across roughly 70% of websites; Arora explains how persistent compute unlocked an attack previously considered impractical. More defensive compute alone cannot fix fragmented infrastructure, making the operational priority “how quickly can I find them and how quickly can I eject them?”
  • Banking agents expose an unresolved boundary between user authorization and defective software. Arora and Chamath put responsibility primarily on users who hand over credentials, while Friedberg sees potential provider liability when an agent disregards bank access restrictions. Arora preserves a crucial exception: a “rogue agent” that fails to behave as advertised creates a product-liability issue.
  • France becomes the episode’s sovereign-risk warning, with disagreement over the relative roles of government provision and immigration. Jason reports French 10-year yields above 5%; Chamath ultimately calls for bond vigilantes to push them toward 8% and force a reset. Chamath warns that political actors can capture power during a reset; Jason, doubting AI abundance would be persuasive to France, concludes, “I don’t see a reasonable endgame.”
  • Friedberg’s fiscal proposals include winding down federal student lending, changing housing finance, and transitioning defined-benefit retirement promises into individually owned investments over a decade. David Sacks supplies the more specific proposal to reduce federal home-loan underwriting, warning of a possible 10–20% hit to middle-class net worth. Chamath supports making student debt dischargeable; the retirement transition would still remove guaranteed income.
  • The closing dispute is whether AI-led growth reaches voters without more direct measures on affordability. David Friedberg calls the US economy “entirely and completely levered to and correlated with the AI trade,” while Jason wants equal attention to housing and lower-paid workers. Jason proposes $1 annual minimum-wage increases toward $15; Friedberg argues for tax relief and credits instead, rejecting government intervention in labor prices.

Digest

1. AI’s bubble question is about who pays the bills

  • Jason introduces Ken Griffin’s warning that AI is “almost certainly a bubble,” alongside Griffin’s longer-term optimism: major economic transformations commonly bring bubbles. The immediate concern is businesses examining Anthropic and OpenAI bills and asking where productivity appears. Jason reports Thursday declines of 10% for CoreWeave, 6% for Meta, and 5% for AMD and SpaceX, while noting recent volatility and a generally upward trend.
  • Chamath’s estimate puts 90% of AI spending in 1% of companies, with 80% of that spending coming from unprofitable VC-backed businesses. His causal chain runs from LP capital to venture funds, startups, token purchases, revenue growth, and subsequent fundraising. The danger is “a bunch of money-losing entities just spinning a bunch of money around,” supporting valuations before demand broadens.
  • An unpublished Ramp chart and a call with its chief economist broadly support Chamath’s estimate, according to his researcher. Jason flags Ramp’s concentration in startup financial services; Chamath says its economist also accesses broader data. Chamath contrasts today’s circularity with early AWS adoption: startups initially dominated EC2 and S3 usage, but Amazon’s retail business was roughly break-even on free cash flow.
  • Jason’s pushback — worth keeping: startups adopting a technology aggressively can reveal genuine economic advantage. They seek the “cheapest, best, fastest edge,” unlike slower enterprises. His examples include cloud computing and WeWork as cost-saving advantages, and initially underpriced Facebook advertising, into which startups poured venture dollars because it worked. Concentrated early adoption therefore can be a leading indicator of diffusion rather than evidence that demand lacks substance.

2. Open weights attract enterprises, but infrastructure remains scarce

  • Chamath reads rising GPU-compute spending in Ramp’s chart as evidence that heavy users are moving toward open models. He also reports changed enterprise buying patterns following Alex Karp’s comments about data sovereignty. One unnamed major US bank told his team it had reduced AWS and GCP spending and built six independent, ground-up data centers: “It’s back to the future.”
  • Arora says Palo Alto Networks prefers open-source, open-weight models because it can modify weights, train them, and interrogate their chain of thought. His enterprise requirements are “explainability, auditability, and verifiability.” In regulated financial services or healthcare, telling a boss that an unexplained result came from an AI model will not suffice; he sees open weights as necessary for that scrutiny.
  • Independence becomes harder at production scale. Arora needs global inference with 99.9% reliability, not a startup’s single 10-megawatt deployment that can tolerate several hours offline. He says Jensen cannot supply chips until 2028, while land, power, and buildings also constrain supply. Having closed Palo Alto’s data centers six or eight years earlier, he now finds rebuilding them an impractical negotiating threat.
  • Arora expects a hybrid outcome: hyperscalers or adjacent providers supply bare metal while enterprises run open models. The “profit pool” could move from NVIDIA and memory suppliers toward owners of available compute. He acknowledges slow enterprise diffusion but calls demand “insatiable”: even if every company committed immediately, he argues, there would not be enough compute to serve them all.

3. The PHP panic turns neglected maintenance into an emergency

  • Jason describes two critical exploits nicknamed “PHP2Shell,” discovered using AI in August and rated 9.2/10. He says PHP powers about 70% of websites, including WordPress and Wikipedia. Developers had coordinated an October 22 patch, but information leaked beforehand; PHP advanced the release to October 21. How the information escaped remained unknown during the recording.
  • The release coincided with increased hacking activity, according to Jason’s account of AWS and Cloudflare reports. He describes millions of attempts, precautionary shutdowns across European government websites, systems taken offline at Wikipedia, and NSA/FBI warnings. His question is whether such emergencies will recur every ten days. Arora’s answer is sharper: “I think 10 days is too long.”
  • Arora’s concrete example is a CIO whose websites run different PHP generations. Current versions can accept the patch; older ones require taking sites down and rebuilding them. The organization had tolerated those older versions because upgrading never seemed important enough. AI has changed the urgency of paying technical debt, rather than creating all the underlying weaknesses.
  • There are two defenses in Arora’s account: patch the vulnerable application itself, or deploy a “virtual patch” through a perimeter product such as Palo Alto’s or Cloudflare’s. The latter blocks the recognized attack before it reaches the server. But publication also informs attackers: they inspect what changed, reverse-engineer the vulnerability, and target organizations that have not yet patched.

4. Defensive compute needs coordinated systems to become useful

  • Arora says powerful models can find vulnerabilities and chain several into an attack path when given sufficient compute and persistence. The PHP problem, he explains, had been identified years earlier but seemed too difficult to exploit because of the coordination required. Persistent computation found a workable path. Once disclosed or reverse-engineered, that discovery became usable by many more attackers.
  • Jason asks whether well-funded defenders can simply outcompute hackers. Arora says that is not true today because infrastructure lacks the necessary orchestration. A company with 5,000 websites may still have IT staff cataloging them individually rather than operating from a unified inventory. Without that baseline preparedness, defenders cannot dispatch coordinated agents to patch systems merely because more compute is available.
  • Continuous penetration testing helps, Arora says, but each stronger model may discover additional entry points. His alternative starting assumption is that breaches will happen: “The question becomes less about how I got breached” and more about detection and ejection. Aggregating signals and data makes anomalous behavior visible, allowing superior defensive compute to operate against an intruder rather than an unknown inventory of vulnerabilities.

5. Banking agents blur identity and divide liability

  • Friedberg separates suspicious browser activity from conventional application access through verified APIs and intermediaries such as Plaid. Arora likewise distinguishes two problems: unauthorized access possibly connected to the PHP vulnerability, and personal agents logging in with their users’ credentials. Banks cannot readily distinguish the latter from users themselves. CAPTCHA is an incomplete boundary because AI can solve it or hand the challenge back to a person.
  • Jason asks whether banks are exaggerating danger to prevent agents from routing customers toward better rates and cheaper services. Arora considers that too much strategic credit. His explanation is liability and support costs: a customer says $50,000 disappeared, while the bank must reconstruct actions performed by software holding valid credentials. Repeated requests for explanations could become expensive even before reimbursing disputed transactions.
  • Friedberg’s initial liability view places responsibility on an agent provider if its software ignores a bank’s prohibition on agent access. If the software warns the user and receives an explicit override, he thinks responsibility shifts to the user. Jason supplies an e-commerce parallel: his Grok shopping agent can prepare an Amazon cart, address, and payment choice, but “I won’t hit the buy button.”
  • Arora’s default is user responsibility: “There’s a word in agent, it’s called agency.” Chamath calls that the only scalable arrangement. Jason pushes back on agents that find unauthorized workarounds to satisfy instructions, prompting Arora’s exception: a “rogue agent” that behaves contrary to its advertised purpose creates a product-liability problem for its maker. Their agreement on authorization does not erase that distinction.

6. Removing model guardrails produces the sharpest AI disagreement

  • Jason describes incubated company Obliteration AI as supplying models without built-in constraints for white hats and corporations, with customers responsible for controls and liability. He frames the product as infrastructure for serious testing rather than unrestricted public distribution. Arora asks what this adds beyond taking an open-weight model and training it internally; Jason’s answer centers on serving infrastructure and efficiency.
  • Chamath finds this “unbelievably scary,” calling it an underappreciated risk vector that concerns him more than alignment. Arora argues governance depends on the weakest link: restrictions elsewhere accomplish little if another provider supplies raw capability without guardrails. His analogy is handing a nuclear bomb to anybody who can afford it. Jason maintains that qualified defenders also need powerful tools to strengthen their systems.
  • Arora separately rejects Jason’s theory that frontier labs cause the security problem by withholding their strongest defensive capabilities. He sees researchers struggling to package powerful systems under compute constraints; even his access to recent publicly available models remains rate-limited. Their commercial motive is more basic than a deliberate attack on cybersecurity incumbents: “They just need money, bro,” including money ultimately owed to Jensen.

7. Security spending and management incentives have to change together

  • Chamath explains why technical debt persists: engineers prefer the next product to maintenance, while privately deployed software drifts into many versions with different upgrade schedules. Arora adds the incentive problem: CIOs are rewarded for keeping costs low and systems available. Upgrades cost money, introduce downtime risk, and generate complaints, so the behavior that preserves today’s service can accumulate tomorrow’s security exposure.
  • Arora puts cybersecurity spending at roughly 4–10% of IT budgets. Cloud-oriented businesses can sit around 4–5% because hyperscalers handle infrastructure security; financial services and the federal government are nearer 8–10%. He says customer calls increasingly ask how to stop getting “punched in the face every morning.” Jason expects the transition to raise both security’s importance and its claim on scarce AI talent.
  • Beyond existing defenses, Arora says enterprises still need security systems for AI itself: discovering agents, inspecting their actions, and controlling information leakage. He cites a researcher finding that a shared Muse conversation could expose private information. Yet he also sees opportunity: as finance, HR, and marketing all seek AI expertise, “the CIOs could become the next CEOs.”
  • Asked how he would respond to Bernie Sanders demanding an AI stop, Arora answers, “Why don’t you start? I’m right behind you.” He argues AI’s builders have overemphasized alarming capabilities and created a “race to the bottom” in public messaging. Jason sees the political consequence: predictions of lost jobs and catastrophic risk give populists on both the left and right an attractive campaign issue.

8. France’s unrest is becoming a financing problem

  • Jason reports more than half a million participants, damage to over 3,000 businesses, more than 1,000 injured police, and 2,500 arrests. He describes protests originating in dilapidated schools before becoming broader unrest and looting, including destruction of Limoges’ 143-year-old city hall. His account also includes spillovers into Italy, Spain, and Albania, along with French curfews and conflicting government explanations of the violence.
  • The market figures sharpen the discussion: Jason says France’s 10-year yield exceeded 5%, its highest since 2002, while the US equivalent slipped below 5%. He cites a possible flight from European into US debt. Polymarket prices mentioned on the show imply an 18% chance of a French emergency declaration by year-end and 91% odds of a Moody’s or S&P downgrade by October 31.
  • Chamath condemns the violence as domestic terrorism and argues the government created a “tinderbox” by failing to confront it. Economically, France’s proposed €50 billion austerity package would need to grow, he says, making additional education investment harder even if school conditions were the central grievance. He predicts the government will lose the coming presidential election and face a complicated bureaucratic and economic reset.

9. The hosts disagree over what France’s social contract proves

  • Friedberg resists Jason’s comparison with BLM and January 6, which he sees as tied to more specific political events. France’s complaints seem broader: schools, healthcare, jobs, and Palestine. His diagnosis is a cycle in which citizens demand more state provision, services disappoint, and the disappointment creates demands for still more spending. “The more the government tries to provide to the people, the more the people are let down.”
  • Friedberg calculates US public spending at $12 trillion against $33 trillion of GDP, or roughly 36%, including $7.4 trillion federal and $4.6 trillion state/local spending. He puts both countries near 120% debt/GDP, with deficits of 5.4% in France and 6.2% in the US. Growth of roughly 0.5% versus 2.3%, he argues, explains why France could reach the fiscal cliff first.
  • Chamath’s challenge is that France and Italy already provide roughly free healthcare and education, yet still face unrest. Jason cites French university fees around €300 annually against approximately €12,000 in state cost. Friedberg disputes that low prices mean the problems are solved: weeks-long medical waits and classrooms of 60 students can leave people dissatisfied despite formally available services.
  • A later chart puts French tax revenue at 46% of GDP versus 22% for the US. Jason challenges its persuasiveness: many Americans want the healthcare and education associated with countries above the US on that list. Chamath rejects the claim that most want to live there; Friedberg argues the comparison must include employment and advancement alongside public services.

10. Proposed affordability reforms would redistribute gains and losses

  • On education, Friedberg would end the federal student-loan program while creating a way to discharge existing debt, potentially through bankruptcy. Chamath is “extremely sympathetic” to cancellation and says the debt should always have been dischargeable. Friedberg insists relief must accompany termination of new federal lending, otherwise the price-support mechanism remains. He expects institutions and tuition to adjust over roughly ten years.
  • On housing, Friedberg argues for changing housing loans that inflate home costs. David Sacks later makes the more specific proposal to reduce underwriting in the federal home-loan system, warning that this could cut middle-class net worth by 10–20%. His premise is that financing has supported existing homeowners’ asset values while excluding younger buyers. Maintaining those values preserves current owners’ solvency and sense of wealth, but broader access requires existing middle-class, upper-class, and wealthy owners to accept a hit.
  • Healthcare is Friedberg’s least complete proposal: “Healthcare’s the hardest.” He would put more responsibility on employers purchasing insurance, expecting competition to pressure prices and services. He names HIPAA and state/local housing regulation as barriers in their respective markets. These are multi-year changes in his framing, not immediate fixes; healthcare’s complexity remains explicit even as he argues for reducing government intervention.

11. Retirement reform would replace guarantees with ownership

  • Friedberg proposes making defined-benefit retirement programs, including Social Security, illegal and moving them into defined-contribution accounts over a decade. Each year, 10% of an individual’s promised amount would transfer into an IRA-like or Trump account, with investment allocations chosen according to age and preference. He acknowledges the objection: people lose guaranteed income. Jason points to Australian superannuation, and David Sacks adds Norway as an example.
  • Jason connects the ownership thesis to Elon Musk’s stated plan to give every American child one SpaceX share, then worth roughly $150–170, describing the gift as about $10 billion. He imagines wider participation by wealthy donors and separate accounts for education and retirement. The important feature in Jason’s argument is holding productive assets over time: “forcing people to hold onto it makes them part of capitalism.”

12. Immigration arguments split economic selection from cultural assimilation

  • Jason places much of the blame on immigration and failed integration, while also assigning responsibility to native French society for not integrating newcomers. In the subsequent exchange, a speaker cites annual immigration of 1.5% of the population and argues that inflows should be weighed against growth, employment, and needed skills. Another participant argues for selecting immigrants who can support themselves and share civic principles; the transcript’s speaker labels for these comments are unclear.
  • The latter speaker distinguishes shared civic values from cultural assimilation, naming women’s equality, individual rights, respect for others’ rights, and civil law taking precedence over religious authority. The discussion presents this as a proposed screening criterion, not a claim that ethnicity or first language should determine eligibility.
  • Jason says there were reports that Chinese and Jewish businesses were targeted while Muslim businesses were avoided. Friedberg presents an interview expressing resentment that Chinese immigrants had become prosperous. Jason—not Chamath—says the targeting reminded him of a “bottom-up” version of Kristallnacht. This is his interpretation of alleged ethnic targeting and envy, rather than an established explanation for all the unrest.
  • Friedberg’s most personal example comes from his family’s restaurant: his nurse mother made desserts to save money, and he and his brothers polished silverware and worked from childhood while the family remained financially stretched. That experience underlies his anger at small businesses being destroyed. Both he and Jason argue owners should be able to defend their property with firearms, invoking Korean shopkeepers during the LA riots.

13. Bond vigilantes offer a reset that Chamath also fears

  • Chamath argues bond investors can force a structural bargain by making French debt unfinanceable. When Friedberg asks whether 6–7% yields would suffice, Chamath answers, “I think you need to take France to, like, 8% and just break them.” His desired result is to put pensions, immigration, service quality, and other commitments on the negotiating table before the underlying social tensions compound further.
  • Yet Chamath also describes why forced resets fail: political actors accrue power, assign blame, and preserve influence rather than repair institutions. “In the middle of a reset, what happens is you just give away all your rights.” AI abundance might offer another route, but Jason doubts distressed French citizens would trust promises from Silicon Valley oligarchs. His admission remains unresolved: “I don’t see a reasonable endgame.”
  • David Sacks distinguishes violent social collapse from debt-driven economic restructuring, citing Argentina, Brazil, and Greece. The latter still entails protests, inflation, and lost wealth, but might avoid a deeper social breakdown. Sacks argues US leaders should reduce annual federal spending from roughly $7.5 trillion toward $4 trillion “in a way that doesn’t destroy the economy,” using deliberate reforms rather than waiting for a financing crisis.

14. AI-led growth and voter reassurance are different political tasks

  • Jason turns France’s discontent into a warning about US political communication ahead of November 3. Trump, he argues, should discuss housing as frequently as data centers and visibly address lower-paid workers alongside technology and large businesses. He credits the administration’s economic activity but says voters hear attention to crypto and infrastructure while their own housing, wages, and healthcare remain unresolved.
  • David Friedberg’s defense is that the AI buildout carries an outsized share of economic growth and benefits workers beyond the largest technology companies. He points to skilled-labor wages, investment in local communities, and pressure to build data centers behind the meter while lowering electricity costs. His categorical framing: “The US economy is entirely and completely levered to and correlated with the AI trade.”
  • Jason accepts the growth argument but maintains that its political transmission is weak. He wants explicit commitments to affordable housing and the bottom half of the income distribution, not reassurance that a “golden age” has arrived. The disagreement concerns whether the administration has connected those benefits convincingly to everyday life, alongside the substantive question of what additional policies workers need.

15. Minimum-wage disagreement survives agreement on helping workers

  • Jason proposes adding $1 annually to the federal minimum wage for seven years toward $15, a destination he dates to 2032. He estimates the change would reach roughly 10–15 million people and argues their extra income would be spent back into businesses. His case combines spending velocity with social cohesion: the president should visibly ask employers to do better for their lowest-paid workers.
  • Friedberg invokes California’s AB 1228 and its $20 fast-food wage, citing 18,000 lost jobs. He explains the mechanism through a consumer who can afford a $4 burger but not an $8 one: employers cannot indefinitely pay wages unsupported by customer demand. In his account, closures hurt both willing workers and consumers, and even smaller mandated increases can push marginal transactions beyond viability.
  • Jason rejects the comparison with an abrupt move to $20, says the California policy added about 25 cents per meal, and argues displaced workers found more productive jobs without changing the overall unemployment rate. He challenges Friedberg to reconcile that objection with their usual argument that automation releases labor for better work. Friedberg maintains that Jason is still trying to determine the market’s correct price.
  • David Sacks’s alternative is lower taxes, credits, and other incentives that increase disposable income without setting labor prices. Jason endorses a zero tax rate up to $150,000 and urges presidential support. That agreement does not settle the original dispute: Sacks says intervention has adverse consequences, while Jason closes by noting the country already has a minimum wage, so the question remains what its level should be.

item.title: It's worse than you think w/ Tulip King, Eli Ben-Sasson and Saeed Badreg
item.description: Ansem’s October 22, 2026 risk reduction clashes with Tulip King’s “retirement cycle,” as stablecoin use and scaling challenge ETH/SOL value capture. Sunrise’s roughly $160 trillion tokenization opportunity hinges on market makers, mint-and-redeem arbitrage and distribution, not merely cross-chain transfers. Starknet’s L1 exploration adds a post-quantum catalyst, but Ben-Sasson’s “next two years” is a concern window, not an attack forecast.
item.content:encoded:
Market Bubble · Tulip King、Eli Ben-Sasson、Saeed Badreg · 2026-10-23 · 221 min · 原语言 EN

Ansem’s October 22, 2026 risk reduction clashes with Tulip King’s “retirement cycle,” as stablecoin use and scaling challenge ETH/SOL value capture. Sunrise’s roughly $160 trillion tokenization opportunity hinges on market makers, mint-and-redeem arbitrage and distribution, not merely cross-chain transfers. Starknet’s L1 exploration adds a post-quantum catalyst, but Ben-Sasson’s “next two years” is a concern window, not an attack forecast.

TL;DR

  • Ansem is cutting risk while Tulip King calls this his “retirement cycle,” making asset selection and time horizon the episode’s central disagreement. Ansem’s October 22, 2026 view is that weakening memory and semiconductor stocks could drag crypto into another pullback; he initially expects the summer lows to hold, while later entertaining Bitcoin tests of the mid-$70,000s or mid-$60,000s. Tulip is looking across a decade at businesses that could absorb much larger on-chain markets: “Stop buying shitty coins.”
  • Tulip’s portfolio framework separates coins that are money from coins that make money, leaving ETH and SOL under pressure to justify their valuations. His argument is that stablecoins increasingly supply collateral and trading denominations, while scaling reduces the fees native tokens capture. Ansem disputes the assumption that existing holders will suddenly abandon monetary and ecosystem valuations, but agrees that profitable applications might become money more easily than base layers become better businesses.
  • Hyperliquid and Derive anchor Tulip’s argument that investors can own emerging financial infrastructure without predicting every new winner. His HYPE “100 bagger” case explicitly assumes Hyperliquid wins as assets and trading migrate on chain; his options thesis rests on convex payouts, volatility trading, and Derive’s claimed 90% share of options premiums. He would reconsider competitors when they establish durable share, rather than constantly trade between prospective challengers.
  • Saeed Badreg frames tokenization as a distribution and market-structure opportunity measured against a roughly $160 trillion asset pool. Capturing even 1% would exceed $1 trillion, but moving tokens between chains is insufficient: Sunrise needs market makers, working mint-and-redeem arbitrage, and distribution through wallets, exchanges, and DeFi. “We have 8,000 stocks” is unimpressive if “you have zero markets”; the objective is liquid, programmable assets that unlock uses unavailable through conventional brokerage apps.
  • Eli Ben-Sasson says Starknet’s community has supported exploring an L1 because Ethereum scaling demand and Ethereum-dependent security no longer settle the strategic question. He describes a potential post-quantum “ark,” with programmable privacy and account abstraction, while acknowledging that he cannot predict a quantum breakthrough. Asked when he would worry most, he says “over the next two years”; that is his concern window, not a claim that a practical attack will arrive then.
  • Zcash and Pearl represent different attempts to capture demand for alternatives to Bitcoin’s existing design. Tulip categorically says Zcash reaches a trillion-dollar valuation but offers no timing, while Pearl’s appeal is its proposed substitution of matrix multiplication for SHA-256 to connect mining with AI infrastructure. He qualifies the miner-migration evidence and calls quantum a “pretty bad narrative,” creating a clear disagreement with Ben-Sasson’s emphasis without supplying a detailed rebuttal.
  • Trading media’s commercial opportunity rests on audience distribution and trading activity, while its credibility depends on distinguishing evidence from mythology. Tulip describes sponsorship economics that favor customers who retain capital and keep trading, plus a clipping operation whose reach can far exceed live viewership. Banks sees Kimchi’s mainstream breakout as valuable, but also acknowledges manufacturing an exaggerated story for a viral clip; the hosts’ discussion does not establish the widely repeated $40 million trading-profit claim.
  • The practical research edge described here is persistent investigation beyond headline dashboards, followed by enough patience to let a thesis develop. Tulip uses protocol testing, source-code activity, holder analysis, and AI-assisted data retrieval to ask why revenue should persist; GMX at roughly 1.2 times revenue is a research prompt, not a completed investment case. His largest stated equity exposure is Eli Lilly, and his reluctance to buy AI-stock dips reflects both concentration concerns and a preference for opportunities where he believes he has an edge.

Digest

1. Ansem’s bearish turn begins with equities failing to reward good news

  • Ansem explicitly reverses the view he held two weeks earlier. He expected another advance in AI-related equities, memory stocks, and semiconductors, with crypto extending its Q3 leadership. “I was wrong,” he says about expecting fresh highs. His concern is that stocks which have dominated since late 2022 and 2023 now contain substantial unrealized gains, creating room for sustained profit-taking rather than another shallow interruption.
  • The backdrop adds several pressures simultaneously: continuing war, sharply rising oil, still-high interest rates, and AI discovering software vulnerabilities faster than humans previously could. Ansem cites a significant PHP vulnerability as an example of processes being disrupted. He does not reduce the selloff to that technology story; the central call remains that equities might be approaching the “tail end” of their macro cycle.
  • The uncomfortable detail is that business results can remain strong while stock prices stop advancing. Ansem points to Micron’s substantial Q3 earnings beat, after which the stock failed to extend higher and effectively marked a local high. “The revenues are matching up, but they’re still not making new all-time highs.” He also sees memory stocks forming a second lower high after their parabolic advance.
  • His crypto interpretation remains a question, not a settled diagnosis. Bitcoin weakened in Q1 and Q2 while equities rose, then bottomed around the same late-June week that memory stocks peaked. Q3 strength might therefore reflect an earlier oversold condition rather than a fresh bull market. Tulip’s later challenge—why Bitcoin has remained “pretty damn strong”—gets this answer: relative strength can coexist with vulnerability to another equity-led decline.

2. Taking profit is a different decision from initiating a short

  • Ansem says he is both reducing exposure and shorting, but immediately distinguishes his own trading from what he recommends to viewers. BTC, ETH, and SOL are already near important support, so a new short would be “shorting into support.” Timing matters: getting stopped out before the eventual decline produces the particularly frustrating outcome of losing on the short and then missing the move.
  • For people up 2–3X on positions such as Pump, Zcash, or VVV, he thinks taking some profit makes sense. His initial expectation is a higher low, with the roughly $70,000 Bitcoin area offered as a possibility, and he says he does not think the summer lows break. Later, he entertains mid-$70,000s or mid-$60,000s tests while saying, “I’m not sure.”
  • The cleaner relative-value expression he offers is long Bitcoin against short memory stocks. That separates his belief that Bitcoin can outperform memory equities from the harder question of whether Bitcoin rises outright. He also recalls SOL around $60 near the earlier summer opportunity: someone who bought near those lows can still have substantial gains to protect without needing to declare the entire crypto recovery finished.
  • Banks pushes back with a familiar contrarian rule: widespread CT pessimism usually makes him more bullish. Ansem’s own experience complicates that instinct. He became bearish in September 2025, absorbed criticism, bought Bitcoin after it subsequently reached highs, and then had to sell into a decline. The exchange preserves the distinction between being directionally right, being early, and changing position under social pressure.

3. Paper Trade shifts its rewards from early farmers toward continuing traders

  • Ansem describes Paper Trade, launched by his friend Jez, as a synthetic perpetuals platform offering up to 1,000X leverage using Hyperliquid midpoint pricing for BTC and ETH. Positions are against the house rather than a matched opposing trader. Losses accrue to the house; winners are paid from its funds. When the house does not have ample funds, Ansem describes it as “kind of like a pool that collects over time.”
  • He describes a controversial change to the token distribution. At the beginning, he says, a large majority of the supply would be distributed based on how much the house was making. He recalls the maximum supply as 12.6 billion PAPER, and says it would be reached after a certain amount of time—“something like $500 million in the LP.” He is uncertain about the precise calculations. The supply has since increased; now there is no maximum supply and more PAPER is minted, though he says he does not know the exact calculation.
  • Ansem thinks the change benefits traders who actively use the exchange. “Before, it benefited farmers more than traders,” he says. He farmed early himself, but says the platform has changed how PAPER is distributed and people have been mad about it. His defense is that the revised approach better rewards active exchange use, while acknowledging that farmers benefited more under the previous setup.
  • Transferability has also been delayed: the token will be non-transferable for longer. Ansem says PAPER can currently be staked on the exchange to receive a portion of its revenue. He likes the platform and the changes, while recognizing that the altered distribution and delayed transferability are sources of user frustration.

4. Pump’s missing airdrop is a legitimate grievance; falling coins are another argument

  • Ansem separates two complaints that CT has bundled together. Anger that Pump is paying Kimchi, KOLs, and other promotional rewards before delivering its anticipated airdrop is, in his words, “justified.” Banks agrees that the airdrop was central to earlier expectations discussed on the show. Their defense of Pump’s business does not erase that unresolved distribution promise or the resentment around who has received money first.
  • The complaint that Pump should somehow make launched coins appreciate gets a different response. “Pump cannot make coins go higher. They’re just the launchpad.” Ansem says higher starting market capitalizations might produce different outcomes, but that remains an unproven counterfactual. Comparing today’s market against an imagined design that supposedly fixes everything does not establish that the alternative would actually work better.
  • His explanation for Pump’s resilience is its existing low-cap ecosystem. He says the platform can still make around $1 million daily during a bear market because traders and developers repeatedly use pre-bond and very small-cap markets, even without $500 million runners. Removing that activity to favor a different kind of participant could damage the users and behavior responsible for the platform’s continued revenue.
  • Banks and Ansem reject treating all successful exchange revenue as uniquely objectionable “extraction.” They point to Coinbase, Uniswap, Raydium, and Axiom as businesses that also charge for services. Their argument is competitive: users keep returning, and rival launchpads have failed to displace Pump. That supports their view of product demand, while leaving the airdrop criticism intact rather than answering it through fee comparisons.

5. Kimchi’s attention is observable; the trading fortune remains disputed lore

  • Tulip King repeatedly distinguishes Kimchi’s actual content from stories circulating around it. He says the 22-year-old has not personally confirmed the widely repeated claim that he made $40 million trading Trump. In one vlog encounter, a fan asks about that number; Kimchi laughs, says, “Good to meet you, bro,” and moves on. Banks had earlier summarized the persona as “hit big and logged off,” rather than publicly documenting a trading process.
  • Tulip also describes an on-chain thread presented as proving that Kimchi made “only” $6 million on Trump. He says the wallet was subsequently confirmed as Kenzo’s, Kimchi’s friend who travels with him, and therefore was not Kimchi’s wallet. Tulip says there was no comment from Kimchi and no confirmation one way or another about the $40 million claim.
  • Their strongest positive evidence is cultural reach: the vlog, luxury-brand attention around Bottega, and interactions with major streamers who appear genuinely interested in Kimchi. Banks argues that CT saturation is different from a mainstream ceiling. Someone can already occupy nearly all the conversation inside crypto while still rapidly expanding outside it; criticism within the smaller audience may become progressively less important to the overall business.
  • Banks sees a self-reinforcing commercial opportunity: attention itself could eventually allow Kimchi to make $40 million through partnerships and future projects, regardless of the original rumor. That is a prediction, not confirmation of the earlier trade. He thinks Kimchi’s advantage is having no obligation to debate CT: travel, friends, and compelling vlogs can continue working without turning the brand into a market-commentary service.

6. Tokenization’s market size matters only if assets become usable

  • Saeed Badreg explains Sunrise’s origin through an inadequacy in interoperability alone: “Just bringing an asset over from one blockchain to another doesn’t really solve the problem.” Internet capital markets require healthy, liquid markets and useful financial activity after the bridge transaction. He puts equities at approximately $160 trillion against crypto around $1.5–$2 trillion; even 1% migration would represent more than $1 trillion of value.
  • His stablecoin analogy is about demand invisible to people already well served. An American with easy dollar access can miss the importance of that access elsewhere. Badreg invokes stablecoins’ growth and Tether’s Treasury purchases to argue that making an asset globally accessible reveals demand that incumbents underestimated. The mechanism is distribution: “You completely have no idea how much demand is out there for a particular asset.”
  • Badreg says tokenized equities were below $1 billion “last year” and have expanded roughly 30X over about a year and a half. He describes the growth as a hockey stick and thinks even his own team underestimates the eventual scale. The hosts later loosely restate the $160 trillion figure as broader tradable assets; Badreg initially introduces it as the equity-market opportunity rather than supplying a reconciled market taxonomy.

7. Global access and cheaper capital formation are separate tokenization opportunities

  • Badreg’s response to Americans asking why they need tokenized US stocks is blunt: “It’s not for you then.” Their opportunity might instead be exposure to DeepSeek, Unitree, or SK Hynix. He says Sunrise has been meeting people and regulators internationally, including during a Shanghai visit, and hopes Chinese equities can reach these rails. “Hopefully soon” remains an aspiration, not a launch announcement or guaranteed access timetable.
  • Banks supplies the investment puzzle that made DeepSeek interesting to him: a valuation around $10 billion versus the roughly $300–$500 billion figures being discussed for major American AI companies at the time. Were the latter really worth about 50 times as much? The discussion does not resolve that valuation question; it uses the inaccessible comparison to explain why investors might want distribution beyond their domestic brokerage universe.
  • The second opportunity is companies raising capital without following the conventional IPO route. Badreg estimates that a serious US listing is unlikely to cost less than roughly $30 million and can require 1.5–2 years of organizational change. He qualifies that estimate as based on numbers he has seen, rather than personal IPO experience. A good company earning tens of millions might still find that process economically unattractive.
  • Banks corroborates the burden through his own SPAC experience with B. Riley, including the need to raise a PIPE, and says taking a company private is also expensive. Ansem connects tokenization to Hyperliquid’s distribution of value to users and team members. Badreg sees convergence with broader capital formation, citing a16z’s expansion into frontier businesses: crypto rails could serve operating companies whose businesses are not themselves crypto.

8. MemeFi exposes the cultural component already present in stock markets

  • Badreg says he initially thought pairing memes with stocks made little sense, then changed his mind after watching the activity closely. Traditional finance, he argues, understates how much assets trade on “narratives, community, culture, momentum.” Tesla, GameStop, and Nvidia illustrate his point: they are companies with financial statements, but also communities with identities. Tokenization makes that cultural layer more directly accessible to new trading behavior.
  • Eli Ben-Sasson interprets the experiment as isolating attention and narrative from the conventional asset, while Tulip King supplies the uncomfortable counterexample: the meme could perform well while its paired stock tanks. Badreg accepts that the structure can deliver “the best of both worlds” or “the worst of both worlds.” His enthusiasm is for experimentation and participation, not a claim that attaching an equity automatically improves an investment’s economics.
  • Tulip places the experiment in crypto’s longer history. Many assets traded on Bittrex and Cryptopia in 2017, or during 2020–2021, failed; he thinks those failures helped reveal which mechanisms worked. “They didn’t call them meme coins back in the day. They just called them altcoins.” Badreg also sees tokenization forcing public-company CEOs to take positions, with resistance and eventual acceptance resembling earlier battles around stablecoins.

9. Sunrise’s product is the market around the token

  • Badreg identifies a strong market-maker network as the first requirement for usable tokenized equities. Coming from the trading world, he emphasizes understanding how liquidity providers actually operate rather than assuming they appear after issuance. The goal is an asset that can trade reliably across an ecosystem, not a token whose existence technically proves that an off-chain security has been represented on a blockchain.
  • Mint-and-redeem infrastructure provides the second requirement. If a tokenized stock trades above or below its reference market price, authorized participants need a practical way to arbitrage the discrepancy. That mechanism is what can pull prices back toward one another. Badreg treats it as fundamental plumbing: without working issuance and redemption, an apparent listing may not become an efficient market for ordinary users.
  • Distribution is the third requirement, encompassing centralized exchanges, wallets, DeFi applications, aggregators, routers, and DEXs. Sunrise tries to combine the components into something that looks simple externally but is difficult internally. Badreg’s claim is conditional: solve enough of these connected problems and a team can launch 100 assets on Solana while maintaining functioning markets, then expand from there.
  • Asset selection also requires judgment. The initial heuristic was to bring whatever the community wanted, but Badreg describes that community as highly opinionated and difficult to satisfy consistently. His criticism of indiscriminate catalogs is memorable: “We have 8,000 stocks,” but “you have zero markets.” He prefers listings that capture attention, provoke research, and make a trader ask why this particular asset is arriving now.

10. Programmable equities and social participation create different sources of demand

  • Badreg rejects a simple contest between spot tokenized stocks and stock perpetuals. Spot markets support ownership and composability; perps support hedging and more complicated strategies. “You’re trying to make Apple stock programmable.” The objective is not merely replicating a brokerage position on another screen, but allowing assets to participate in financial operations that other protocols, bots, and agents can execute together.
  • His example is moving collateral through several operations that conventionally might require 2–3 days, 4–5 companies, and repeated reconciliation. On-chain infrastructure could let a user or agent coordinate those steps programmatically. The challenge he leaves to Solana developers is concrete: what can someone do with a tokenized stock that they cannot already do through traditional finance or the applications on their phone?
  • A different source of growth comes from younger people’s willingness to trade and share publicly. Badreg and Tulip King speculate about participation moving from below 1%, perhaps 0.1%, among earlier 18-year-old cohorts toward much larger current numbers; Tulip suggests 10–20%. They do not establish those figures as measured statistics. Their underlying observation is a cultural shift toward active investing, visible portfolios, and earning from capital rather than labor.
  • Ansem offers the darker version: AI could concentrate economic power in a few companies while displacing jobs, leaving ownership of those companies increasingly important. Badreg adds reports of banks restricting AI-agent access and cites the interpretation that bots were moving deposits toward better yields. He frames that interpretation as incumbent resistance to competition; the conversation does not establish it as the banks’ documented reason for restricting access.

11. Starknet’s L1 discussion reflects a changed problem, not an abandoned scaling capability

  • Eli Ben-Sasson introduces himself through academic cryptography, his realization at a 2013 Bitcoin conference that zero-knowledge techniques could help scalability as well as privacy, and subsequent work co-founding Zcash and StarkWare. His description of StarkWare is “the skunk works or the Bell Labs of crypto”: a research organization turning inventions into usable systems. That is his positioning, rather than a neutral ranking of competing technologies.
  • He says a Starknet community vote concerning becoming an L1 concluded that day with substantial support. The next step is to investigate and build toward that direction, rather than claim the migration is already complete. The intended combination includes post-quantum security, programmable privacy, and improved usability. He describes the prospective network as a “safe haven” or high ground if a quantum threat materializes.
  • The strategic change has two parts. Starknet successfully built Ethereum-scaling technology, but Ethereum currently has multiple scaling options and insufficient demand for that capability alone. Separately, Starknet’s security as an L2 depends on Ethereum’s migration speed. Ben-Sasson characterizes the community’s message as: “We’re not confident that Ethereum’s gonna move fast enough for our safety, so we’re gonna move ourselves.”

12. The “quantum tsunami” is a preparedness thesis with an uncertain clock

  • Asked when a quantum threat might arrive, Ben-Sasson first says, “I don’t have the crystal ball. I don’t know.” Pressed for a guess, he identifies “the next two years” as the period when he would be most worried. His reasoning is accelerating innovation across multiple quantum-computing teams and hardware approaches. He does not provide a probability estimate or assert that an attack is certain within that window.
  • The metaphor carries his prioritization: “This is the damn ark that you can board if the flood comes.” Living on an ark is not necessarily the most convenient experience, but convenience becomes secondary if a house and garden sit beneath 100 feet of water. He therefore frames the prospective L1 around safety under a particular threat, rather than primarily as another competition over transaction-speed marketing.
  • Ben-Sasson nevertheless claims Starknet already offers superior efficiency, cost, safety, and usability, and highlights account abstraction and privacy that can compose with DeFi. The interview does not supply comparative benchmarks for those categorical claims. His point is that these capabilities already exist in the technology; the new strategic argument is to make security less dependent on how quickly another chain changes its underlying cryptography.
  • AI enters the same discussion from both sides. StarkWare is exploring hyperscale transactions and micropayments for agent commerce, without announcing a finished product. Ben-Sasson also worries AI could accelerate quantum development or weaken existing cryptographic assumptions. He argues that zk-STARKs’ reliance on hash functions provides a safer foundation against those threats: infrastructure for agents, and infrastructure designed to withstand advances in the tools agents use.

13. A zk-STARK lets an untrusted operator prove that the work was correct

  • Ben-Sasson’s explanation begins with Darth Vader processing a day of Bitcoin transactions and reporting the new system state. Without a proof, the concern is obvious: Vader might simply assign the bitcoin to himself. A zk-STARK changes the acceptance rule. The operator can do the computation, but the result is accepted only after a verifier checks a short cryptographic proof that the required rules were followed.
  • In the example, the proof is smaller than a Bitcoin block, while standing behind the much larger set of transaction updates. Ben-Sasson calls it a kind of cryptographic “cement” enforcing integrity, reliability, and correct execution even when the operator is not being watched. He believes Satoshi would have embraced usable ZK, noting that early discussion recognized its privacy potential before practical implementations could deliver the broader scaling capability.
  • The eventual user experience he wants resembles handing over a $20 bill: a transaction between counterparties without an intermediary observing and controlling everything. He extends that intimacy to lending, borrowing, investing, and perpetuals, with usability comparable to Robinhood. The important addition is self-custody and privacy rather than a central application holding funds and seeing every action: familiar interface quality applied to decentralized financial relationships.

14. Long adoption timelines do not excuse waiting passively for developers

  • Ben-Sasson accepts Ansem’s observation that Zcash spent many years without strong market recognition. He dates the underlying paper he co-authored with six other cryptographers to 2014 and Zcash’s implementation to 2016; meaningful attention took roughly nine years after launch. “It was painful,” he acknowledges. The admission preserves a distinction between believing a technology is important and expecting markets to recognize it quickly.
  • His comparison is monetary adoption: paper money took centuries to become accepted, while ATMs and credit cards required decades of trust-building. On that scale, digital money taking years to establish which properties matter is unsurprising. He applies the same patience to Starknet. Privacy, scarcity, and security may each become salient at different times; his stated commitment is to keep building the properties he believes usable money needs.
  • He is less forgiving about the original ecosystem-development strategy. “Build and they will come” did not produce a great return on the funding deployed. Some strong DeFi and gaming projects emerged, but too few funded teams became durable, self-sustaining businesses. That assessment is an explicit change in approach: excellent infrastructure and grants alone did not reliably generate the applications and users the network needed.
  • StarkWare is consequently building some applications itself while continuing to support external teams. Ben-Sasson names SuperVega, at supervega.app, as a retail options product with a focus on good UX and exposure to assets including Bitcoin, Zcash, and STRK. He hopes internally developed applications can bring users and attention more directly, rather than leaving the entire demand problem to independent developers.

15. Tulip’s bullishness is measured in decades and contingent winners

  • Tulip King enters with the opposite emotional register from Ansem: “I’m, like, so fucking bullish.” He thinks the scale described by Sunrise is directionally right—trillions in assets and potentially quadrillions in trading—and asks who genuinely expects less activity on crypto rails two years from now. Repeated over successive periods, he thinks that migration adds multiple orders of magnitude to today’s markets.
  • His HYPE “100 bagger” statement has a stated premise: “Just presume that Hyperliquid wins.” He accepts that another perpetuals venue could become the better allocation and require a switch. Against the upside he imagines, hypothetical HYPE prices of $60 or $40 do not alter his long-term enthusiasm. “I’ll sell my kidney” is the deliberately extreme expression of that conviction, rather than an articulated risk-management rule.
  • He extends the opportunity to options, lending, spot markets, and other DeFi businesses, with buybacks supplying the link to tokenholders. The horizon is the next decade, not the next week. “This is my retirement cycle.” He says his own portfolio is at highs and criticizes treating a disappointing broad market as proof that no attractive assets exist: the distinction is which projects investors actually own.

16. Options preserve financial exposures that perpetuals cannot replace

  • Tulip’s Derive thesis begins with the payoff structure. A perpetual is a leveraged linear exposure with path risk, which is why liquidation exists to protect protocol solvency. Options can offer convex outcomes. In a market with extreme tails such as crypto, he regards that difference as economically valuable rather than an inconvenient product feature that superior perpetuals interfaces will simply eliminate.
  • Options also permit hedges, spreads, and positions expressing a view on volatility rather than the asset’s direction. Tulip allows that perpetuals might compete with retail zero-day options activity, but says the rest of the options market remains largely untapped. His argument is therefore not that one interface wins all speculative trading; it is that distinct exposures support a separate market as crypto’s financial structure matures.
  • He quotes Derive as having around 90% of options premiums and sees that leadership as a reason not to overcomplicate the selection. His estimates of remaining volume growth are deliberately rough: perhaps 10,000X, perhaps 100,000X, “however many zeros it is,” to reach traditional-finance scale. Those are his order-of-magnitude expressions of the opportunity, with explicit uncertainty about the calculation, rather than a detailed valuation model.
  • Competition does not invalidate owning the present leader. He would consider Lighter or Variational once they show 20–30% share, and names Hyperliquid and Paradex as other potential challengers. If another venue genuinely overtakes Derive, “you’ll see it coming.” He thinks buying after that evidence can still leave substantial upside, because the investment premise is expansion through another order of magnitude or two.

17. The barbell favors distinct exposures over multiplying correlated positions

  • Asked for his largest holdings, Tulip opens with “my entire net worth is Eli Lilly,” then describes Bitcoin, HYPE, and Zcash as roughly similarly sized positions whose relative weights change with prices. He also says early purchases of Pearl and Derive have grown into significant holdings. The conversation conveys strong concentration and several meaningful exposures, rather than a precise, internally reconciled portfolio allocation.
  • His governing categories are “coins that are money” and “coins that make money.” The first basket includes Bitcoin, Zcash, and Pearl, with possible comparisons such as Zcash versus Monero or Pearl versus other AI-linked assets. The second contains operating protocols whose economic activity benefits their tokens.
