item.title: What will computer chips look like in 2045?
item.description: Ranade says available tools may support 2X, not 10X, leading-edge wafer output, while an Intel speaker says AI demand is 40–50% above maximum capacity. With roughly 80% of fab costs fixed, utilization and yield matter; TSMC ships upwards of 3X Intel’s leading-edge wafers, and Ranade says Intel will invest more, though tool limits remain.
item.content:encoded:
Dwarkesh Podcast · Dwarkesh Patel · 2026-10-22 · 69 min · 原语言 EN

Ranade says available tools may support 2X, not 10X, leading-edge wafer output, while an Intel speaker says AI demand is 40–50% above maximum capacity. With roughly 80% of fab costs fixed, utilization and yield matter; TSMC ships upwards of 3X Intel’s leading-edge wafers, and Ranade says Intel will invest more, though tool limits remain.

TL;DR

  • Available equipment may support about 2X leading-edge wafer output, not 10X; 2030 supply depends on broader capacity growth. An opening, unidentified Intel speaker says AI demand is “easily 40–50% above our maximum capacity.” Dwarkesh notes that ASML makes fewer than 100 EUV machines a year and describes limited plans to increase that materially by decade’s end. Asked whether the world has enough tools to 10X leading-edge wafers, Pushkar Ranade answers, “Not 10X, but probably 2X, yes.” Dwarkesh’s later timeline summary puts tool orders placed now into ’28 and a new fab shell near the end of the decade; Ranade does not explicitly confirm that summary. The claim that AI’s decade of 3X annual compute growth “just can’t continue” is Dwarkesh’s framing.
  • AI labs securing fab-scale capacity is a possibility raised by Dwarkesh, not a commitment from Ranade. Dwarkesh’s calculation is that a couple billion dollars of Intel CapEx could support the logic behind roughly $100 billion a year in AI-model revenue; he also notes that memory and other parts of the stack matter. He speculates that AI labs might buy or guarantee supply. Ranade says some model companies could consume an entire fab’s worth of silicon and have the capital to fund it, but the “early signs” of this shift are Dwarkesh’s characterization. Ranade’s closing response to the suggestion that Intel buy more tools: “Had we known what we know today, we would have invested more like a year ago. Knowing what we know now, I think we’ll be investing more.”
  • Ranade argues Intel is within a few percent of TSMC technologically; scale and execution remain important gaps. He says that within a few percent on performance, power, or density, “you’re splitting hairs,” and that on-time delivery and yields supporting rapid ramps matter more. He disputes Dwarkesh’s cited SemiAnalysis benchmarking of 14A against N2. Dwarkesh cites TSMC shipping upwards of 3X Intel’s leading-edge wafers and spending about $50 billion on CapEx versus Intel’s roughly $20 billion. Ranade says about 80% of a fab’s cost structure is fixed, making utilization and yield improvements especially valuable; he notes there are now only three foundries at the advanced node, down from about 20 forty years ago.
  • High-NA EUV is an architecture-dependent choice, not simply a tool race. Chris Auth explains that Intel’s backside power relaxes some front-side pitch requirements, making High-NA useful for Intel; TSMC’s tighter pitches without backside power require double-patterning EUV. “For them, it’s not very helpful. For us, it is very helpful.” Intel’s 10nm experience—originally targeted for 2016, with manufacturing starting in 2018—taught it to limit per-node innovation and use phase-gate maturity metrics. 14A is planned to have a high-quality PDK from the outset, after 18A “started out not having a PDK.”
  • Intel’s memory exits look costly amid today’s shortage, though Ranade says the demand was unforeseeable; Terafab is another response to demand. Ranade says the supply crunch is larger for memory than compute, while noting that nobody could have seen the scale of demand when Intel exited DRAM and flash. He says Intel is working with Elon to help accelerate his fab project. Dwarkesh points out that tool shortages could mean a new fab secures supply without increasing net global silicon; Ranade adds that power, water, and consumables are also required, and says those inputs can be scaled more readily than tools.
  • Long-range 3D structures are a possibility, with thermals a limiter—not a firm 2045 forecast. Auth discusses transistors floating within interconnect and asks what more extensive 3D structures might enable over a 10- or 20-year horizon. He calls heat dissipation a limiter for 3D devices, while saying the system-level analysis and simulation tools are still in their infancy. Separately, Dwarkesh cautions that technology roadmaps often have only about four years of visibility.
  • Hybrid bonding has room to scale, but its densest future uses remain prospective. Tyler Osborn gives the progression from 130–150 µm first-level interconnect pitch 15 years ago, to 25 µm in Foveros high-volume manufacturing today and sub-10 µm in development. He cites a paper presented at this year’s IEEE ECTC with reliability data on a 0.45 µm-pitch device. He says finer bonding could eventually connect lower interconnect layers across chips and reduce power; the potential to approach on-die interconnect is a future possibility, not a current production capability.
  • Rising costs invite radical questions in a risk-averse industry. Ranade says fab costs have been doubling every 4–5 years and puts a High-NA scanner plus associated equipment at around $400 million. He questions whether patterning costs can keep rising at that rate, and asks, “Do you really need a clean room today?” He says no incumbent would willingly test a fab with people eating hamburgers and smoking cigars inside. Kevin Fischer’s operating principle: “If you want to wait for a complete data set, you’ve waited too long.”

Digest

1. Bringing up 14A means fine-tuning 2,000 steps — and learning from 10nm

  • Chris Auth describes 14A as more than three years into development and close to finalizing the process and tool sets. The factory has roughly 2,000 steps, each needing intricate tuning so the process can run thousands of wafers a week repeatably. Defects are found through inline metrology and end-of-line electrical testing; TEM cross-sections can locate a defect between layers and help identify which section of the flow produced it.
  • Auth’s account of 10nm: Intel set aggressive “hyperscaling” targets and developed ideas to reach them without new tools because EUV was not ready. The node eventually achieved world-class yield, performance, and cost, but took longer than intended: its original target was 2016, and manufacturing did not begin until 2018. A news clip in the transcript has Intel’s stock down more than 15% and TSMC up 13%. TSMC used EUV in volume from 2019; Intel’s first EUV process reached products in 2023, leaving TSMC with about four more years of experience with the machines.
  • The institutional response includes phase-gate maturity metrics for yield, defects, and performance, used to decide whether technology can move from pathfinding into development. Auth’s principle is to limit innovation per node so the process can meet the customer’s schedule.

2. High-NA makes sense for Intel and not TSMC — because of backside power

  • Dwarkesh explains the tool economics: High-NA widens numerical aperture from 0.33 to 0.55 and can print features about 1.7 times smaller in a single pass. Standard EUV machines cost around $200 million, while High-NA machines cost about twice as much. The value depends on how many patterning passes the tool can eliminate; extra passes take time and introduce more opportunities for defects.
  • Auth says Intel and TSMC can reach different conclusions from the same tool because their technology architectures differ. Backside power alleviates some front-side pitch requirements, allowing Intel to print some patterns directly with High-NA. TSMC’s tighter pitches without backside power require double-patterning EUV, so the tool is less useful to them. At 14A, High-NA is an option in the PDK and will be discussed with customers individually.
  • On Intel’s foundry learning curve, the transcript says decades as an IDM meant it had not had a formal PDK-type process; 18A “started out not having a PDK.” Customer feedback has informed the process, and 14A is planned to have high-quality PDKs from the outset, with maturity levels such as 0.5, 0.9, and 1.0.

3. From “try to not change anything” to the sledgehammer era

  • Auth contrasts the ’80s and ’90s, when Dennard scaling and lithography drove predictable shrinking, with the “golden age of innovation” that began when scaling alone was no longer enough. Strained silicon, high-k metal gate, FinFETs, gate-all-around, and backside power expanded the process playbook. He estimates the number of materials used has increased about 10X since the ’90s: “Before, it was ‘try to not change anything.’ Now it’s ‘take the sledgehammer and start tearing the thing up.’”
  • Gate-all-around took a long time to reach production partly because other options could deliver performance first. Auth says, “you don’t want to tackle something before you have to”: Intel used strained silicon, high-k metal gate, and FinFETs before taking on gate-all-around. New materials, tools, gases, and heating equipment can require invention by suppliers, and development involves iterating on structures that fail.
  • In a discussion of long-range possibilities, Auth calls gate-all-around “somewhat inevitable,” while describing stripping the substrate and placing wires on the backside as “a little bit out there.” He considers whether future chips could combine transistors and interconnect in more extensive 3D structures, looking at a 10- or 20-year horizon. Dwarkesh adds that technology roadmaps often have only about four years of visibility.
  • Auth describes three limits on compute: switching frequency, power per switch, and heat dissipation. For 3D devices, system-level thermal analysis and simulation are still in their infancy. Thermals are a limiter, he says, but “these are problems that we can go solve.”

4. Inside the Hot Topics meeting: incomplete data, epi tumors, and HotBox 1

  • Kevin Fischer, who helps decide how engineering resources are allocated to 18A problems, says, “You will never have a complete data set. If you want to wait for a complete data set, you’ve waited too long.” His job is to decide how much risk to take: “Do we go now? Do we start risking production?” He says many engineers do not see how the work affects Intel’s bottom line or customers.
  • The example is epi nodules: abnormal epitaxy growth “like a tumor” that grows quickly and can cause one epi to short to the wrong epi, leaving transistors not working. Teams work in parallel on potential fixes, including a special clean to remove nodules and ways to eliminate their source; the first fix that seems promising is not always the one that works.
  • Experiment lots can use a tiered system of “hot boxes.” The highest priority, HotBox 1, gets priority at every tool and races through the factory, but Fischer says it is a drag on factory efficiency. His analogy is reserving a carpool lane for a single experiment.

5. In the research lab: ruthenium, cobalt’s round trip, and CFET’s integration challenges

  • Jack Kavalieros explains why Intel is exploring ruthenium for very fine-pitch interconnects. Copper typically needs a liner to help deposit it and connect it to underlying copper; the liner can occupy a significant part of the conduction path. Ruthenium can be etched without that liner, and Kavalieros says there is a crossover at roughly 20-nanometer pitch where ruthenium can have better conductivity than copper.
  • The cobalt example shows how materials choices can change. Cobalt was the leading option when Intel made its decision, but later solutions brought copper back into contention. Kavalieros says every technology is evaluated against alternatives as the manufacturing time horizon approaches.
  • CFET research uses short-loop vehicles to get faster results than the month or longer required for a full manufacturing flow. Teams can begin with components such as diodes and capacitors, then combine them into transistors. A simplified CFET might use one wire for the NMOS and one for the PMOS, rather than four ribbons stacked on four ribbons. The difficult parts include vertical interconnection, high-aspect-ratio etches, and filling tiny spaces without air gaps.
  • Dwarkesh asks why a lab version does not mean CFET is ready for a phone, and raises a ten-year timescale in his question. The answer is not a firm production timeline: the lab version is simplified and may not outperform side-by-side nanoribbons. The technology must evolve through many steps, including the right metals and dielectrics. Materials can fail because contacts do not adhere or because later processing interacts with a film that is not hermetically sealed.

6. Hybrid bonding is dissolving the boundary between packaging and chip

  • Tyler Osborn contrasts wafer-to-wafer bonding, which is popular in CMOS image sensors, with chip-to-wafer bonding. Wafer-to-wafer requires closely matching dies and sort maps; random differences between good and bad dies can reduce yield. Chip-to-wafer lets manufacturers test and select known-good dies before bonding them to known-good positions. Osborn expects both approaches to be used and says chip-to-wafer makes sense for logic-to-logic.
  • The pitch progression is 130–150 µm for first-level interconnect 15 years ago, 25 µm in Foveros high-volume manufacturing today, and sub-10 µm in development. Osborn cites reliability data on a 0.45 µm-pitch hybrid-bonded device in a paper at this year’s IEEE ECTC; this is not presented as current high-volume production. He sees room for further scaling.
  • Osborn says that if packaging reaches around 0.5 µm or below, it could become possible to connect lower interconnect layers across chips, potentially reducing total IR drop. For non-AI uses, including client devices, he points to interconnect density and lower power per bit, which could mean less heat for the same electrical performance.

7. The supply ceiling: 2X is possible, 10X is not

  • An unidentified Intel speaker at the beginning of the transcript says AI demand is “easily 40–50% above our maximum capacity, which I’ve never seen before.” Later, Dwarkesh notes ASML’s EUV output is fewer than 100 machines a year and says it is not expected to rise significantly by the end of the decade. Ranade calls EUV a limiter, but says shortages extend across equipment: once a process such as 18A is locked to a particular tool, Intel cannot simply substitute another supplier’s tool.
  • Asked whether the world has enough tools to 10X leading-edge wafer production, Ranade answers, “Not 10X, but probably 2X, yes.” Dwarkesh says that means the AI industry’s 3X annual compute growth “just can’t continue” without the supply chain, including sub-suppliers, producing more; that is Dwarkesh’s conclusion.
  • Dwarkesh later offers a timeline summary: marginal output might rise within about 12 months, but 2030 production may not be much higher than forecasts; an 18-month tool lead time puts new orders into ’28, with a new shell pushing out toward the end of the decade. The transcript does not include Ranade explicitly confirming that summary. For 14A, Ranade says Intel tries to preserve fungibility between nodes; perhaps 80% of the 18A tool set can be reused.

8. A couple billion of CapEx and $100B of AI revenue — a capacity-buying scenario

  • Dwarkesh’s calculation is that a couple billion dollars of Intel CapEx could support the logic behind roughly $100 billion a year of AI-model revenue, while noting that memory and other players in the stack also matter. He speculates that AI labs might buy everything or guarantee future supply. Ranade says some model companies have enough demand to consume an entire fab’s worth of silicon and the capital to fund it; the transcript’s “early signs” of this shift are Dwarkesh’s framing, not Ranade’s.
  • On Terafab, Ranade says Elon saw that his businesses would need a lot of silicon and Intel thought it could help accelerate the process of bringing up a fab. Dwarkesh points out that a tool bottleneck could mean a new fab secures guaranteed supply without increasing net global silicon. Ranade adds that a fab also needs power, water, and consumables, and says those inputs can be scaled more readily than tools.
  • After Dwarkesh suggests Intel should commit to more tools, as Nvidia reportedly has for memory and other components, Ranade responds: “Had we known what we know today, we would have invested more like a year ago. Knowing what we know now, I think we’ll be investing more.”

9. Catching TSMC is about scale, not just transistor density — and memory is also constrained

  • Ranade says a gap of a few percent in performance, power, or area is “splitting hairs,” and that being on time with yields supporting rapid ramps matters more. He says a technology includes more than one transistor type: low-leakage and high-performance transistors, SRAM, analog, and RF. He disputes Dwarkesh’s cited benchmarking of 14A against N2 without offering a different density figure in the transcript. Dwarkesh cites TSMC shipping upwards of 3X Intel’s leading-edge wafers and spending around $50 billion on CapEx versus Intel’s roughly $20 billion; Ranade calls the comparison somewhat unfair because TSMC is a foundry for many customers while Intel is largely a foundry for itself.
  • Ranade says about 80% of a fab’s cost structure is fixed, so extra utilization, output, and yield can greatly improve the economics of the same footprint. He says there are three foundries left at the advanced node, compared with about 20 foundries 40 years ago. On Intel’s DRAM and flash exits, he says there were good reasons at the time and nobody could have foreseen the enormous demand; today, he says, the supply crunch is larger for memory than for compute.
  • Ranade says fab costs have been doubling every four to five years, and that a High-NA scanner with associated equipment costs around $400 million. He asks whether the rising cost of patterning can continue at that rate and raises clean-slate questions such as, “Do you really need a clean room today?” He says no incumbent would willingly run the proposed hamburgers-and-cigars experiment. He adds that some CPU-design practices may also be locked into approaches established 30 years ago.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/what-will-computer-chips-look-like-2045

item.title: The Worst Is Behind Us
item.description: Bitcoin’s rebound to $84.4K signals relief, not a confirmed bottom. AI’s roughly $4T CapEx hurdle through 2029 requires $500B in free cash flow at a 12% return, while VC-funded demand and overbuild remain risks. Quantum uncertainty has prompted one speaker to shift some long-term Bitcoin holdings into Zcash, while another is reconsidering his position.
item.content:encoded:
Delphi Digital · Kevin、Jason、José、Yan、Ceteris · 2026-10-22 · 83 min · 原语言 EN

Bitcoin’s rebound to $84.4K signals relief, not a confirmed bottom. AI’s roughly $4T CapEx hurdle through 2029 requires $500B in free cash flow at a 12% return, while VC-funded demand and overbuild remain risks. Quantum uncertainty has prompted one speaker to shift some long-term Bitcoin holdings into Zcash, while another is reconsidering his position.

TL;DR

  • Crypto has bounced, but the desk stops short of calling a bottom. Yan says Bitcoin is back to $84.4K and that the majors are showing strength after a rough month; Jason’s tell is that the daily 10:30 a.m. seller may have run out of coins. A speaker sees Bitcoin at $120K or above next year, after the Saylor-liquidation fears faded.
  • Kevin lays out the AI CapEx hurdle: roughly $4T through 2029 at a 12% return implies about $500B in free cash flow, or $1T of revenue at 50% gross margins. Another speaker argues there are plausible ways to reach the numbers: Anthropic grew from $5B in Q1 to $16B in Q3, while Nvidia is growing rapidly and trades at about 13x forward earnings. His conclusion: “the market is not pricing in AGI.”
  • The near-term AI risk is reflexive demand, not simply debt. New labs trying to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI have raised $40B since 2024, and much of that money may go toward training and model use. A speaker who sold his neocloud holdings says they’re too hard to underwrite; the group expects possible overbuild and spending/revenue timing mismatches, not a perfectly smooth climb.
  • Quantum is affecting allocations, but the risk remains hard to underwrite. Yan’s base case is that most holders will migrate or have coins they can migrate, and that a Chinese or U.S. lab would discover the capability. José says he sold some long-term Bitcoin for Zcash; Jason says he’s seriously reconsidering his own long-term Bitcoin position.
  • Alternative stores of value have regained attention. Yan mentions Zcash, QANX and ORE; a speaker warns that Zcash could reach $5K and later fall below $1K. Pearl draws both interest for its compute-security thesis and skepticism over its roughly $3M in 24-hour volume.
  • The HYPE ecosystem’s loyalty thesis is about giving holders somewhere to use their assets. Jason points to the button for moving funds from Hyperliquid to HyperEVM; Kinetiq’s proposed buybacks are split 50/50 between Kinetiq and HYPE. The discussion treats Elysium’s November 9 mainnet and subsequent user and TVL traction as signposts—not a guaranteed Kinetiq launch date or outcome.
  • Unlocks are concentrated in projects the desk follows, not the whole industry. One speaker sees material weakness in Lighter as a potential buying opportunity, while Jason is watching for teams to cushion supply with buyers or restaking. The closing high-conviction list is Grass, Hyperliquid and probably Lighter; Venice is another possibility, pending an acquisition.
  • The Year Ahead themes are money and better token designs. A speaker argues that value-accruing tokens can build loyalty, while crypto’s unlocks are further along than those in AI equities. Jason has no read on the midterms; another speaker sees a possible pre-event sell-off but doesn’t treat it as a major market factor.

Digest

1. “Imagine being a bear”: a bounce, not a confirmed bottom

  • Yan says Bitcoin is back to $84.4K after a rough month. He says the speculative Robinhood/Solana “trenches” have been hammered, while some majors are showing strength. José objects to using “on-chain” as shorthand for the speculative end of the market.
  • Jason had bids around $73K–$75K: Bitcoin could trade below $75K, $74K or $73K and still look fine in the bigger picture. A three-day rally came before those bids filled. His tell: “The 10:30 a.m. seller who’s been here every day for the last month, just nuking the charts, appears to have run out of coins, maybe.”
  • On the Robinhood ecosystem-fund rumor, one speaker says even a small amount of business could move the needle, but he isn’t banking on it. He bought Pawns and Cash Cat after hearing the rumor.

2. Unlocks and midterms: risks people already see

  • Jason is watching year-end unlocks in projects the group follows, including Lighter, where investors in private rounds are already well up. He wonders whether teams will try to pull unlocks forward or arrange restaking to get through the supply overhang.
  • Another speaker cautions against treating all unlocks equally: the strongest, revenue-generating projects may be able to speak with investors and line up buyers. He says he’d consider material weakness in Lighter a buying opportunity. The reasoning is that widely anticipated events may not unfold as badly as the market expects—like people calling “Black Monday” on Sunday.
  • Jason says he has no read on the midterms and won’t spend more time trying to game them. Another speaker notes that the incumbent party has often lost the House in midterms, and that a Democratic House could be a crypto headwind. But with crypto resilient despite failed legislation, trade concerns, AI worries and hot inflation, he sees the market climbing a wall of worry. He also notes that open interest in many alts has reset toward pre-move levels and that volume deltas show mostly perp selling—a healthier reset that favors concentration in the names most likely to become blue chips.

3. The $4 trillion AI CapEx question

  • Kevin walks through a Venky-from-Menlo post: roughly $4T of AI CapEx through 2029, at a 12% return, would require about $500B of free cash flow by 2029. At 50% gross margins, that implies about $1T in revenue.
  • One path is that the labs fall short, causing a painful unwind. Kevin notes that this is not necessarily a 2001-style debt crisis: the top four AI spenders account for about 70% of spending and fund most of it from operating cash flow, with strong credit ratings. The debt is more concentrated in Oracle, CoreWeave, Meta’s off-balance-sheet financing and private credit, which the post estimates at about $350B.
  • Another path is that the revenues arrive. Kevin cites possible sources: 3% of roughly $15T in U.S. wages, or about $500B; roughly 1.6% of U.S. GDP; and a shift in global software spending toward AI compute. His takeaway is that there is a path, though the timing is uncertain.
  • A participant flags a popular chart, also tweeted by Chamath, that says 1% of spenders account for 80% of spending, much of it AI and VC-backed. The caveat: “VC-backed” is a binary label; the share of the actual capital coming from venture versus credit matters, and both sources have risks.

4. The bull case: unprecedented growth and new demand

  • One speaker argues that the labs need to grow about 70% a year from a roughly $100B base, which has never happened before—but points out that frontier-lab revenue was around $2B three years ago and is now about $100B. Anthropic grew from $5B in Q1 to $16B in Q3.
  • Nvidia was up 106% year over year in the last quarter, with revenue this year projected to be 80% above last year on a roughly $200B base. Analysts had expected flat or lower results, while bullish analysts such as Altimeter had forecast about 20% growth. The stock was up only about 20%, at roughly 13x forward earnings. The speaker’s conclusion is that “the market is not pricing in AGI.” SpaceX was up 161% year over year and had a roughly $1.5B quarter.
  • Demand indicators include spot GPU rental prices rising through October on the Oren Index; OpenRouter token spend up 36% in a month and 35x year over year, mostly on open models; and, according to SemiAnalysis, about $1T in binding data-center leases signed this year.
  • A further source of demand is classical computing moving from CPUs to GPUs. Citing Jensen Huang on a podcast with Gerstner, the speaker says this is about a third of Nvidia’s revenue and growing 30%–40% a year. He also points to potential future demand from robotics, self-driving, surgical robots, medical and satellite imaging.

5. Reflexive VC demand and the difficulty of underwriting neoclouds

  • A framework from Giovanni Cattani, whom the speakers say they are LPs in, divides AI tasks into bounded and unbounded. Bounded tasks—taxes, accounting or basic front ends—have limited token needs and may shift to cheaper models as they improve. Unbounded tasks, such as quant trading, AI R&D and building software, can absorb much more compute; the analogy is Formula 1, where users keep wanting the fastest car.
  • The speaker says frontier revenue is mostly tied to unbounded tasks, but worries that much of the demand is VC-funded. New labs trying to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI have raised $40B since 2024, and much of that funding may go to training and to using existing models. If venture funding slows, demand could become reflexive.
  • Another speaker notes that if Anthropic takes a material valuation markdown, that could affect the wider VC chain and tighten funding.
  • One speaker says he sold his neocloud holdings and has them in the “too hard bucket” because of the businesses’ complexity and off-balance-sheet structures. He is less concerned about debt itself: the widely circulated 15% figure concerns unsecured debt, while secured borrowing is backed by Nvidia GPUs, including older generations that are reportedly selling for more than their original purchase price.

6. Overbuild, timing and the 2000 comparison

  • One speaker uses a solar-system analogy: revenue may move steadily while spending oscillates around it. Spending and revenue won’t line up perfectly; periods of overspending can be offset by positive revenue surprises, such as a model breakthrough or new use case.
  • Another speaker says an overbuild seems very likely. Jevons’ paradox could play out over a longer timeframe, with companies going bust in the meantime. The speaker distinguishes this from 2000: today’s companies have substantial revenue, though investors may not believe it will last. Nvidia and Meta trade below 20x forward earnings; Nvidia at 100x earnings would imply a roughly $40T valuation.
  • Yan argues that bubbles usually have fewer bears and that buyers tend to keep capitulating into the rally; he jokes that Michael Burry would need to go full-port on CoreWeave before a top.
  • The host emphasizes that revenues may be discounted because their sources are correlated: a problem affecting one part of the AI trade could affect the wider system. CoreWeave has said it would be massively cash-flow positive if it stopped building, though the host advises taking that claim with a grain of salt.
  • The host also highlights the gap between spot GPU pricing and take-or-pay contracts. Lenders want longer commitments from creditworthy customers, while many startups may only be able to commit for a week, a few months or six months. If those shorter-term customers provide enough demand, or longer contracts roll over at higher spot prices, neocloud revenue could surprise positively. The host stresses that the compute-market mechanics are more complex than the headlines suggest.

7. Goldilocks for crypto—and a Bitcoin outlook

  • One speaker’s Goldilocks case for crypto is that AI continues grinding higher with enough money to sustain it, but without repeating the biggest public-market outliers. He says speculative capital has shifted after the large moves in neoclouds, memory and other AI names.
  • The same speaker sees a good setup for Bitcoin next year: many people sold, fears around Saylor’s potential liquidation eased, and Saylor is no longer seen as a major market force. He says Bitcoin could return to $120K or above.
  • The caveat is that Bitcoin would likely struggle if the AI trade rolled over sharply and the frontier labs were badly damaged. A joking reply is that quantum won’t crack Bitcoin, so the group will be fine.

8. Quantum risk: migration, old coins and uncertainty

  • Yan’s new base case is that by the time quantum risk becomes actionable, most holders will have migrated or will hold coins in unspent UTXOs that they can migrate. He thinks a Chinese or U.S. lab is most likely to achieve the capability, and says it may not matter which country gets Satoshi’s and other old coins.
  • Yan says those coins are too large a supply to treat as permanently lost: Bitcoin should be priced with the assumption that all coins could become active. He allows that a government might sell some over time. He estimates a 90% chance—possibly as high as 99%—that the breakthrough comes from a Chinese or U.S. lab. If it were a Lazarus/North Korea doomsday scenario, he thinks people would fork their coins out.
  • Another participant ranks “Red US” best, China in the middle and “Blue US” worst, arguing that the latter might use the coins to fund a short-term political agenda. Yan says he agrees with that ranking.
  • Yan says quantum concern has helped renew interest in other stores of value, even though he doesn’t think the risk is disproven. If it does not happen for 10 years, people may start to think it will never happen—but until then, it can remain a headwind for Bitcoin.

9. Alternative stores of value—and real portfolio changes

  • Yan says the industry had largely settled on Bitcoin as the store of value, with little room for alternatives, but that quantum discussions have changed that. He mentions Zcash, QANX and ORE on Solana, which he says is still small at around $50M.
  • José says he sold some long-term Bitcoin holdings and put the money into Zcash, because he is less confident holding Bitcoin for a 10-year horizon if it cannot adapt to a cryptographic threat. Yan says his Zcash position changed partly because of how he expects other people to allocate, not because quantum made him personally afraid of Bitcoin.
  • Jason says he has not sold his own long-term Bitcoin holdings but is seriously considering it: he cannot accurately underwrite the quantum risk and would not “mindlessly shill” Bitcoin to family without acknowledging that uncertainty.
  • A participant recounts being asked about quantum risk on a date; another says his uncle, who owns Bitcoin and ETH for his grandchildren, asked him the same question. The discussion illustrates that the concern has reached beyond crypto specialists.
  • One speaker warns that Zcash could reach $5K but later fall below $1K, as these store-of-value assets can be volatile.

10. Pearl: a small-volume trade and a larger thesis

  • After Yan says people are discussing Pearl, another speaker calls it “a tool to identify who doesn’t have size,” pointing to about $3M in 24-hour volume and the aggressive promotion around it. The host notes that OTC brokers with miner connections are facilitating some trades. Yan is skeptical of buying ahead of a possible Coinbase listing, calling it a potential “classic top.”
  • Another speaker says Pearl has a compelling narrative and that people outside crypto are asking about it, though some misunderstand it as a decentralized inference network. The initial thesis is that compute power could secure the network; if it succeeds, the supply of GPUs might also support decentralized inference.
  • A speaker says he bought a bit but found it hard to buy, and wishes the asset were more liquid.

11. Paper Trade: transferability and attack risk

  • The discussion asks whether making Paper Trade’s token transferable and listing perps would expose the protocol to an oracle-style attack. A participant says he did not see an obvious solution. Paper Trade’s thread gives a rough example: a $10M–$15M Bitcoin short paired with a $10M Paper perp short could be enough to threaten the protocol.
  • Another speaker says exposure should be limited on assets that are cheap to manipulate, while noting that existing risk metrics already try to address manipulation. He cites an ETH exploit on the first night that made roughly $1.5M, with some uncertainty about the amount. A shortable native token adds another profit opportunity if an attack succeeds, but could also increase insolvency risk or force more restrictive risk settings.
  • One participant compares the problem to stablecoins, where shorting can be attractive because the worst case is a return to $1; here, the risk is built into the mechanism.
  • Another speaker explains that Rollbit hedged positions by identifying sharp users and hedging winners, which is harder when users can create wallets freely. Keeping the book more delta-neutral can allow more open interest, but might constrain scaling. Possible risk controls include tranching or automatically closing positions far into profit; these could reduce usability. The speaker thinks it may be solvable with risk controls, but the effect on UX is uncertain.
  • A participant says he had owned some PaperStrategy. He says the strategy controls about 2% of Paper’s supply, stakes it and has buybacks that currently outpace inflation. If the issue blows over in a couple of months, he thinks the situation could turn out well for the strategy. Another speaker jokes about the “farm the Hyperliquid airdrop by getting liquidated” strategy.

12. Kinetiq, HYPE and ecosystem loyalty

  • Jason points to the button that lets users move funds from Hyperliquid to HyperEVM: there are billions of dollars on Hyperliquid, and some users may want to transfer funds and explore on-chain. José says HyperEVM can offer a more performant experience, and that app support could bring more users into its ecosystem.
  • Jason frames the loyalty argument: people tend to spend time in ecosystems where they made money. A speaker calls this “patrons of the chain” and argues that the best way to build loyalty is to make people rich on a protocol. Hyperliquid holders have seen large gains and may welcome more ways to use the ecosystem.
  • Kinetiq’s buybacks are split 50/50 between Kinetiq and HYPE. José says that is more aligned than the Ethereum rollups he is comparing it with, which paid ETH data-availability costs. A participant estimates roughly $250K a year in HYPE buybacks based on testnet activity; others caution that testnet activity is not the same as a live product. Solana is cited as an example of an ecosystem where users did want to speculate in native-chain assets.
  • A participant who says he bought Kinetiq also cautions that “first alt on a chain” theses sometimes fail. The host asks about Elysium’s November 9 mainnet; Jason says the useful signposts are actual users and TVL, and that signs of traction should become visible within 30–60 days. Hypercall is said to be launching there on day one.
  • José criticizes the idea that many rollups offer meaningful technical differentiation, citing an L2BEAT founder’s “zero-proof system”/Gnosis Safe troll and the argument that many rollups remain Stage 0. Another speaker praises Solana’s Alpenglow update and its developer and user community, while saying he is unsure how SOL the asset will perform.

13. Year Ahead themes: money and token design

  • A speaker says the two big themes for the Year Ahead are money and protocols with better token designs. Hyperliquid showed that tokens designed to return value to holders can attract interest. The speaker expects more thoughtful token designs and argues that launching a token avoids some of the regulatory concerns associated with equity.
  • The speaker is bullish on tokens being “unfucked,” noting that many crypto unlocks are behind the industry while AI-equity unlocks are starting. He also points to improving breadth, with Zcash, Fennec, hooks activity and Solana among the examples, after Paper Trade took about $140M of liquidity out of the market.

14. Pump, social trading and the closing conviction list

  • Participants debate Pump’s valuation and revenue. One says he sold the rest of his position but keeps changing his mind about whether it could be worth $2B or $10B. Kevin says the Pump revenue chart befuddles him; Jason agrees. They discuss Robinhood activity, Pump’s relatively stable metrics during that period, and whether Pump’s mobile-app revenue may now exceed FOMO’s.
  • The group discusses a video of traders describing how they created a meme coin, bought 50% of its supply and made money as its market cap rose. Jason calls the behavior social trading that incentivizes bad conduct. One participant argues strong KYC and one-account limits could help make social trading more organic; Jason says KYC can help, while noting that people may still find ways around it.
  • The host recommends Jason’s speculation report, highlighting its “antisocial trading” framing: if people are going to participate, owning the house may be the better strategy.
  • In the closing token discussion, one speaker names Grass, Hyperliquid at its current valuation and probably Lighter as three tokens he thinks could be higher a year from now. He thinks options may become relevant for Lighter, with binary products first and event contracts a year out—not three months out—and says to revisit in October 2027. Venice is another possibility, pending an acquisition.

来源：YouTube

item.title: Hedge Fund Manager David Orr: Investing is 99% Talent
item.description: Orr says exceptional alpha is mostly talent, while a pod-shop process may be teachable: 3% unlevered alpha scales to 18% with sixfold leverage. His multi-manager fund relies on verified live results, independent bets and risk controls; core-manager cross-correlation is 0.15, though the sample remains small. AI tracks correlation drift, while hyperscaler contracts may cushion rental-price declines; capacity and returns after fees remain priorities.
item.content:encoded:
Odds on Open · David Orr · 2026-10-22 · 70 min · 原语言 EN

Orr says exceptional alpha is mostly talent, while a pod-shop process may be teachable: 3% unlevered alpha scales to 18% with sixfold leverage. His multi-manager fund relies on verified live results, independent bets and risk controls; core-manager cross-correlation is 0.15, though the sample remains small. AI tracks correlation drift, while hyperscaler contracts may cushion rental-price declines; capacity and returns after fees remain priorities.

TL;DR

  • Orr sees exceptional alpha as mostly talent, with experience and risk management shaping how it compounds. The host cites 50% annualized returns and a 2.1 Sharpe, but Orr rejects extrapolating 50% after fees: “I think we must have gotten lucky.” He distinguishes rare, high-alpha investors from a potentially teachable pod-shop model that turns 3% unlevered alpha into 18% through sixfold leverage.
  • AI’s biggest contribution is making changing portfolio risk visible across an expanding team. A correlated exposure can grow from 25% to 45% without anyone changing positions; custom baskets update daily to catch that drift. Separately, AI ranks news and filings so Orr reads the top five or 10, saving what he estimates is 90% of his previous news-processing time.
  • Verified results and independent bets outweigh credentials in Orr’s recruiting model. He checks live accounts, rejects cherry-picked records and screens for hidden tail risk before allocating capital. Core-manager cross-correlation is 0.15; including trials at hypothetical equal weights would put it below 0.2, although the sample remains small. “You could be, like, a delivery guy, but if you’re killing the market, I’ll give you a shot.”
  • Fast decisions help Orr avoid turning research effort into stubborn positioning. He holds 500 positions without notes and makes initial decisions within an hour; his Gogo short illustrates the danger of investing 100 research hours and remaining attached while the stock rises toward $20, even though he says it subsequently reached $2. His corrective rule: “The market said I’m wrong, I’m wrong.”
  • The fund’s recruiting proposition combines capital, shared infrastructure and what Orr describes as substantial tax deferral. Compensation averages roughly 15% of P&L above the risk-free rate, with terms tailored to strategy. He also presents continued fund access after a manager loses their edge as “almost like an insurance policy,” allowing accumulated capital to remain in the broader compounding vehicle.
  • Orr prefers hyperscalers’ AI exposure because he believes contracts shift much of the bust risk to customers. His model assumes roughly 35% returns on capital and commitments covering about half the compute; even an 80% rental-price decline could leave the provider around breakeven while hurting locked-in buyers. He favors Google, Amazon and perhaps Microsoft, and cut AI hardware exposure in June as the downside changed: “There’s still a very credible bull case, but just not my game now.”
  • Capacity and returns after fees matter more to Orr than gathering assets. A request for $100 million brought $150 million from existing LPs through one email, yet the fund is closed unless successful new managers create capacity. Internal stock borrowing might save roughly $1 million annually today, potentially $2 million if assets double: “I care about the net-of-fees track record.”

Digest

1. AI makes changing correlations visible

  • Orr identifies the risk system as AI’s biggest contribution. Alongside a purchased professional model, Mike built custom stock baskets with names such as “Banks Done Right” for longs and “Yield Traps” for shorts. These supplement traditional factors and replace some manual grouping into categories such as old media or fiber optics, including judgments about stocks that suddenly start trading as interest-rate-sensitive positions.
  • The important mechanism is daily recalculation: a basket can expand or contract even when holdings remain unchanged. An exposure a manager considered acceptable at 25% might become 45% within a week or two as correlations shift. In a leveraged portfolio, that becomes a materially different bet. Tracking those changes across roughly 10 managers would be impractical manually; even Orr’s own sleeve previously required a substantial safety buffer.
  • Automated monitoring does not mean Orr studies every manager daily. He checks the correlation matrix weekly or perhaps every couple of weeks, reviews positions when someone joins and revisits them after weeks or months. He also examines the largest daily losses across the fund and individual sleeves. A hypothetical 8% loss in one position would warrant investigation; he says that has not happened.

2. Live results beat conventional credentials

  • Roughly 95% of incoming track records are “total junk,” Orr says. The remainder still require verification: live performance rather than backtests, no selection of the best among 30 accounts, and an actual account inspection. He also screens for volatility selling, martingaling and concealed tail risk, although he says those have not been a major problem so far. He wants to know whether a manager’s track record reflects genuinely different bets.
  • One recruit won a television game show and lacks conventional financial credentials, but produced a personal-account Sharpe of two-point-something over several years. Another prospect turned $1 million into $9 million. The host raises adverse selection; Orr acknowledges that one candidate shopped around and chose them, but has yet to ask why. His broader invitation is categorical: a delivery worker with strong verified returns gets considered too.
  • Core-manager cross-correlation is 0.15. Including all trials at hypothetical equal weights would still leave it below 0.2, which Orr calls unexpectedly good. He stresses the limited sample, while expecting longer-run correlation probably below 0.3. Preserving independence matters enough that the managers deliberately avoid discussing their investment processes with each other, even when meeting socially.
  • The host suggests Orr’s own investing success helps support recruitment experiments. Orr says he may understand edge better than someone “trying to play manager.” The host characterizes multi-manager firms as marketing businesses that prioritize institutional appeal; Orr adds that some firms may be satisfied collecting large fees rather than increasing returns, while saying he considers Millennium one of the better multi-managers. He gives $100 billion in assets and $2 billion in annual fees as an example. The host calls the “small-scale Millennium” plan crazy; Orr responds, “Who the fuck wants to work for that?”

3. Allocation grows with evidence, while the platform shares resources

  • Orr, Mike and Rodrigo are the core managers, with seven more on trial. Sizing depends on sample size, risk and correlation. A slower strategy might wait six to nine months before reaching $10–15 million, then another six to nine months before $30–50 million. He calls that later increase particularly risky: the edge looks convincing before the evidence is fully robust. A mid-frequency trader accumulates observations much faster.
  • Compensation is tailored to strategy and volatility, averaging roughly 15% of P&L above the risk-free rate. After approximately a year proving the strategy, managers can receive carried interest, which Orr says allows earnings to remain deferred. The platform also supplies developers and operational support; the mid-frequency recruit requires a separate broker because Interactive Brokers apparently is not fast enough for his system.
  • Orr says the leveraged, high-alpha long-short fund has deferred almost all tax since inception. His explanation: harvest losing shorts and replace them with similar exposures, while leaving winning shorts outstanding. A stock down 90% need not be covered; bankruptcy and share cancellation might take 10 years. He says sacrificing a little edge could even produce an LP tax loss during a profitable period.
  • The recruiting proposition extends beyond current compensation. Poker taught Orr that edges disappear as the game changes. A manager whose edge vanishes would lose the trading role but retain access for their capital, which Orr hopes the remaining managers would compound at high rates. Retired PMs would be the last investors asked to withdraw: “It’s almost like an insurance policy you’re getting for free too.”

4. Quick decisions reduce research attachment

  • With 500 positions in his own sleeve and “No notes,” Orr wants an initial decision within an hour. Experienced investors who have already invested 1,000–2,000 hours in learning should try deciding within one or two hours, then skip what remains unclear. His experience comes from a few hundred independent bets annually since 2019. The practical filter: “There’s something easier out there.”
  • Gogo is his example of research becoming a liability. After putting roughly 100 hours into the in-flight internet company, he remained attached to the fundamental short thesis while the stock climbed toward $20. He says it is now around $2 and he remains short, but being fundamentally right did not excuse mishandling the intervening rise. Short-term developments could have offered a better exit.
  • A successful short may fall 40% before Orr revisits it; he sometimes needs a minute or two to remember the business, confirm the deterioration and add. The dangerous counterpart grinds higher without news, eventually perhaps 250%, while he insists the company is terrible. He has improved at abandoning those fights, but still gets stubborn: “The market said I’m wrong, I’m wrong.”
  • Rodrigo uses 52-week highs and lows to generate ideas, then selects what Orr calls the best 5%; buying the whole bucket does not work. Orr usually follows price too, but the host says his biggest long, Hikari Tsushin, has stalled and may be down year to date. The host calls it incredibly cheap and low risk, sometimes sizing such conviction larger: “Am I making a mistake there? I don’t know.”

5. The host favors business histories over investing formulas

  • The host says most investing books feel dated and questions whether their advertised anomalies worked reliably even when published. He allows that a Peter Lynch book may be useful, but says an investor can succeed for several years, write a book, and then see the strategy struggle. These are the host’s views, not Orr’s.
  • The host describes reading selectively—roughly 10–15 books annually, sometimes in bursts—and abandoning books that fail to engage him in the first chapter. He prefers history and business books, including Shoe Dog and Kitchen Confidential.
  • The host’s example from Shoe Dog is a growth-company CEO’s relentless expansion and refusal to let banks dictate the limits. He suggests looking for similarly resourceful behavior in executives: will they push lenders, find alternatives and shop around to 30 banks? Orr agrees that Shoe Dog is a great book; the operating lessons are supplied by the host.

6. The host and Orr discuss AI as a learning tool

  • Orr says AI has changed his company-by-company workflow. It translates and summarizes filings, ranks the day’s news and lets him focus on the top five or 10 items. He estimates that following the news now takes 90% less time; the new challenge is absorbing information quickly.
  • The host says ChatGPT can summarize a book and support an hour of questioning about relevant ideas, but isn’t sure whether that is better than reading. Orr adds that historical anxieties about new technologies may be misplaced, while agreeing that short-form content can be harmful. The host criticizes TikTok-style videos for optimizing the opening hook rather than substantive content.
  • On personal differentiation, Orr asks about building an edge; the host answers that people should focus on growth rather than trying to predict a durable moat. The host argues that young people who learn to use AI well could gain an advantage over those relying on slower, more analog methods, and speculates that exceptional AI ability might command $5 million annually. These are the host’s views.

7. Hyperscalers have the AI exposure Orr prefers

  • Orr separates hardware producers—Taiwan Semiconductor, NVIDIA and memory companies—from hyperscalers or neoclouds and the software-heavy customer base. He prefers the hyperscaler position, specifically Google, Amazon and perhaps Microsoft. The attraction is downside control rather than maximum upside: running what he describes as a 400%-leveraged portfolio makes the downside on longs particularly important.
  • His contract model assumes roughly 35% returns on capital, with customers committing to about half the compute usage. If excess capacity drives rental prices down 80%, he thinks providers could roughly break even. Customers locked into $5–10 billion of compute would bear the liability while their own businesses might also deteriorate. He likens the arrangements to take-or-pay contracts.
  • If compute instead stays tight for 10 years, the uncommitted half could reprice upward and lift returns on capital toward 50%, applied to hundreds of billions invested. Hardware and memory producers offer greater bullish upside, but Orr says revenue could fall 80–90% in a bust. For an unleveraged investor confident memory stays tight for three years, memory might nevertheless be the better bet.
  • Orr says the fund’s AI-factor correlation is zero, although he owned Taiwan Semiconductor and other AI names during the advance. Before April, Taiwan Semiconductor at roughly 20 times earnings offered a different risk-reward. He cut that exposure in June: earnings had risen while the multiple had not expanded much, and the higher earnings base creates more downside if growth reverses. “There’s still a very credible bull case, but just not my game now.”

8. Capacity and returns after fees govern expansion

  • The host cites roughly 9% in July, which Orr approximately confirms: “Something like that.” He says the fund tends to benefit when things blow up, despite describing the broader environment as a “1999 kind of market” and rapidly rising TIPS as a headwind. He also rejects extrapolating the host’s 50% annualized performance figure: “I’m not claiming that we’re gonna compound at 50% after fees a year.”
  • Asked for fund size, Orr answers “480,” without specifying the unit. The fund is closed, although successful trial managers might require more capital. Earlier, some large brokers wanted the fund to grow its AUM; Orr says a $300 million fund is still small for those global brokers. A single email requesting $100 million from existing LPs brought $150 million. Orr thinks he could raise $1 billion if he focused on fundraising, but prefers optimizing the record.
  • Internal stock borrowing is an incremental opportunity. Hiring someone to source borrow directly might save roughly $1 million annually, Orr guesses; if assets doubled, savings might reach $2 million without the employee’s salary doubling. He stresses the estimate is rough. The employee’s cost would come from the management fee, benefiting LP economics: “I care about the net-of-fees track record.”
  • Capacity ultimately depends on which managers arrive and scale. One new managed-futures-style manager runs at 10 vol and has shown negative correlation so far; Orr expects approximately zero over time. He might eventually ask for twice the exposure. He need not understand cattle or orange-juice fundamentals, but wants historical stress scenarios—including several commodity bets moving adversely together—to show that the risk is manageable.

9. Exceptional alpha is mostly talent, while risk can be taught

  • For “the big alpha people,” Orr attributes success almost entirely to talent, comparing the limits of training to producing Michael Jordan. He distinguishes pod shops’ potentially teachable process: train analysts, constrain risk, generate perhaps 3% unlevered alpha and lever it six times to 18%. His rough contrast is something like one person in 50 succeeding through that route versus one in 10,000 at the exceptional end.
  • His mentor Rob’s most important lessons were sizing, avoiding excessive time on one stock and respecting what drives the price. A business can be terrible while revenue rises and investors keep applying a revenue multiple. Rob’s insistence that this was “great for the company” initially infuriated Orr; he now understands the timing lesson: wait for the growth narrative to break rather than letting the market run him over.
  • Orr would mentor a beginner largely through repetition: produce at least one new idea daily, perhaps two, with occasional correction when a key variable is missing. Seeking constant affirmation is a warning sign of groupthink. Still, he credits pod shops as a potentially worthwhile route to substantial earnings, provided someone rejected after two years can mentally reset and try another approach.
  • Orr says his managers are each passionate about their own investing styles. For personal differentiation, he advises unplugging more and curating insightful people rather than consuming algorithmic feeds. Find something genuinely interesting, then ask how it can make money and help somebody.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/hedge-fund-manager-david-orr-investing-is-99-tal

item.title: The Recommendation Engine for Commodity Traders — Anekha Sokhal, Moshi
item.description: Moshi uses an internally built recommendation system to surface second- and third-order market effects a news stream may miss. Its graph combines futures, fundamentals, news, X, podcasts, and private data; Sokhal says answers that take days can arrive in 30 seconds. Yet swyx questions trading on noisy, potentially manipulated X data, citing about $300,000 monthly for Balyasny's X Firehose; Moshi scores confidence, but any opportunity remains unknown.
item.content:encoded:
Latent Space · Anekha Sokhal、swyx · 2026-10-22 · 27 min · 原语言 EN

Moshi uses an internally built recommendation system to surface second- and third-order market effects a news stream may miss. Its graph combines futures, fundamentals, news, X, podcasts, and private data; Sokhal says answers that take days can arrive in 30 seconds. Yet swyx questions trading on noisy, potentially manipulated X data, citing about $300,000 monthly for Balyasny's X Firehose; Moshi scores confidence, but any opportunity remains unknown.

TL;DR

  • Moshi's positioning is deliberately not “new Bloomberg” — founder Anekha Sokhal's framing is “if Bloomberg and Claude and Netflix had a baby, it would be Moshi.” The Netflix part is literal: an internally built recommendation system that surfaces the “second- and third-order derivatives” of what a trader is watching — e.g., an energy-equities move that indirectly impacts oil — “right now,” which “you're not gonna get from a news stream.”
  • The throughput-and-breadth claim: “it takes me four seconds to say this sentence to you, and in the same amount of time, Moshi has learned 300 new things.” The stack spans futures time series and technicals, fundamentals supply/demand, unstructured news/X/podcast audio, and users' private data (internal analysts, LNG ship counts through the Strait of Hormuz), fused into an “N-dimensional graph” that promises “answers in 30 seconds that would typically take you days.”
  • Sokhal's sharpest product thesis is that AI made it easy to build dashboards but not to get people to use them: “you're no longer dealing with a problem, you're dealing with a UI problem.” Anyone can now build “your brain in a dashboard,” but getting someone else to use it requires push-based hooks à la Spotify/Instagram — and Moshi's internal bet is that “if you solve for one [UI], you're naturally also solving for the other [the recsys].”
  • swyx's buy-side pushback is the episode's best stress test: at Balyasny, he says they were among the first to use the X Firehose; he describes it as costing around $300,000 a month for all the tweets, and questions whether he'd trade on them — “sometimes people just talk random crap, and sometimes people try to manipulate markets.” Sokhal's answer: commodity suppliers and LNG facilities post status updates on X as trusted sources, Moshi attaches confidence scores, and disagreement between Reuters/Bloomberg/WSJ “is a data point” — whether there's an opportunity is unknown.
  • On document AI, Moshi has built its own vision-language model for messy PDFs. Sokhal says data privacy is the first consideration when deciding whether to send client data to a third party, while noting that vendors can be useful with clear agreements and off-the-shelf solutions are a good option for teams without engineers. Her team wants to build models; most of it has, in some capacity, worked with NASA.
  • Demand signals from her first AIE look real: she extended her New York stay three times, filled a week of post-conference meetings, and got requests to meet in Houston about energy. Hiring is a separate challenge: one job posting open four days drew 2,500 applicants. swyx called most of the applications noise; Sokhal pointed to undercover applicants and people not legally allowed to work, including visa issues. Her priority is meeting clients, not necessarily hiring.
  • A recurring buyer persona: AI engineers overwhelmed by management's new default — “We don't need a team. You are the team.” They're being asked to build alone systems “typically done by 10 people,” asking whether they need “a swarm of agents” and what to do when tools they've built go unclicked — a window into the problems they bring to Moshi.

Digest

1. From JPMorgan energy derivatives to a Fulbright in the U.S.

  • Sokhal studied MORSE (mathematics, operational research, statistics, economics) at Warwick — “what everyone now calls AI.” After internships in investment banking and trading, including at JPMorgan, she started on emerging markets and moved to commodities and energy derivatives. Her trading style foreshadowed the product: breaking markets into their parts and building them up from fundamentals, news, and what was physically happening.
  • A founder spark came from a computer-vision startup she side-hustled at university: with her parents in the jewelry business, she explored virtual try-on and wanted to become a founder who could talk about the technology. Around 2020 or 2021, she found Fulbright's data scholarship, which she says was awarded to one person in the whole of the UK. In her interview, she discussed the energy-market crisis and volatile gas prices, which interviewers could relate to through their electricity bills. Fulbright brought her to the U.S., where she did machine-learning research, published at ICLR with Stability AI, and collaborated with NASA before Moshi.

2. What Moshi ingests — and the throughput claim

  • The scale framing: “it takes me four seconds to say this sentence to you, and in the same amount of time, Moshi has learned 300 new things.” Sokhal calls it “the program I wish I'd had when I was trading”: real-time insights for commodity, energy, and macro traders.
  • The taxonomy she geeks out on: futures time series with technical indicators and moving averages; fundamentals time series for supply and demand; unstructured news, X data, and podcast audio; plus the user's private layer — trusted analysts, subscriptions, internal data, and examples such as tracking LNG ships through the Strait of Hormuz. Moshi cleans and transforms the data, applies statistics and machine learning, tags it under an ontology, and puts it into the “Moshi N-dimensional graph.”
  • The output is both push and pull: each time a user opens Moshi, it surfaces something new related to their portfolio, and the LLM can provide answers in 30 seconds that would typically take days.

3. The Bloomberg-Claude-Netflix baby, and why RecSys matters

  • Asked whether she's building the “new Bloomberg,” Sokhal demurs — Bloomberg Chat is a “fantastic” feature — and calls Moshi a different type of software: “if Bloomberg and Claude and Netflix had a baby, it would be Moshi.”
  • The Netflix piece is the recommendation system. A trader watching one thing may care about its “second- and third-order derivatives” — for example, an energy-equities move that indirectly affects oil. Sokhal says a news stream won't surface that link; a connected graph can show it, and making the connection requires either a human or something mimicking a human, such as a recommendation system.
  • swyx says he runs an LLM RecSys track at AIE every year featuring people behind recommendation systems at YouTube, Netflix, Instagram, and TikTok, but engineers often don't appreciate how important RecSys is. Sokhal's diagnosis: “they make it seem so easy.”
  • Her adjacent thesis on the post-AI software glut: everyone can build “claw dashboards,” but getting someone else to incorporate one into their workflow is a UI problem. Platforms that push data can hook users; Moshi's internal bet is that solving UI and solving the recommendation system are linked.

4. swyx's buy-side interrogation: noisy tweets, private data, build-vs-buy

  • The host's credentials frame the pushback: swyx says he traded currency options in London, then rates, before moving to the buy side. At Balyasny, he says they were among the first to use the X Firehose; he describes it as “stupidly expensive,” around $300,000 a month for all the tweets. He says his eyes glaze over at the noisy data and questions whether he'd trade on it: people “talk random crap,” and some try to manipulate markets. His number-one buy-side question for Moshi: “Are you looking at my data?”
  • Sokhal's filter: commodity suppliers and LNG facilities are active on X because it's a quick way to give status updates, and users have people in the industry whose voices they trust. Moshi attaches a confidence score and shows the surrounding conversation. Disagreement between Reuters, Bloomberg, and The Wall Street Journal is itself a data point; whether there's an opportunity is unknown.
  • For messy PDFs, Moshi has built a vision-language model to break down uploaded data and build it into its database. On build-vs-buy, Sokhal says the first consideration is not sending client data to a third party without an agreement on how it will be processed. She also says off-the-shelf systems are a good solution for teams without engineers; her team wants to build models, and most of it has worked with NASA in some capacity.

5. Post-talk inbound as a market read: overwhelmed AI engineers, 2,500 applicants

  • After the talk, Sokhal was meant to leave New York that day but extended her stay for meetings on Thursday, Friday, and Monday. People also asked to meet in Houston about energy; she says the week after the conference filled up with meetings. The inbound included traders at funds or in consulting, AI engineers, and potential partners.
  • The most telling buyer segment: AI engineers “overwhelmed by the pressure from management” because “people now say, ‘We don't need a team. You are the team.’” They're asked to build alone systems “typically done by 10 people,” and some ask whether they need “a swarm of agents” or what to do when a system is in users' email but no one clicks it.
  • One job posting open for four days drew 2,500 applicants. swyx says most of the applications are noise; Sokhal points to people applying undercover and people legally unable to work, including visa issues. She says the priority is meeting clients, not necessarily hiring, and that the team is hosting its first webinar because it can't handle all the inbound one-to-one. swyx suggests on-site group meetings; Sokhal likes the idea of scheduled slots so people can meet without traveling to her or her team.
