item.title: Ep. 039 - [EMERGENCY] Our Numbers Are "Insane." Here's the Proof. (Datacenters) | Jeremie Ontiveros, Reyk Knuhtsen, Jordan Nanos
item.description: SemiAnalysis is raising its 2027 data-center forecast from 43GW to roughly 50GW, citing building-by-building tracking, over $1 trillion in signed leases, and self-build starts rising quarter after quarter. Cited modular builds can compress traditional 18-month timelines to 6–9 months, but the team warns the constraint could flip to data-center oversupply in 2028 as chip supply expands.
item.content:encoded:
SemiAnalysis · Jordan Nanos、Jeremie Ontiveros、Reyk Knuhtsen · 2026-10-20 · 35 min · 原语言 EN

SemiAnalysis is raising its 2027 data-center forecast from 43GW to roughly 50GW, citing building-by-building tracking, over $1 trillion in signed leases, and self-build starts rising quarter after quarter. Cited modular builds can compress traditional 18-month timelines to 6–9 months, but the team warns the constraint could flip to data-center oversupply in 2028 as chip supply expands.

TL;DR

  • SemiAnalysis is raising, not cutting, its 2027 data center forecast—from the 43 gigawatts Brad Gerstner called too aggressive on All-In/BG2 to roughly 50GW in a single year. Gerstner publicly cut the forecast in half, and the episode discussed a roughly 25GW alternative. The team’s response: “There’s a lot of thought and work that went into it,” and they stand by it.
  • The methodology rebuttal is granularity: the model tracks thousands of sites “building by building, permit by permit, power allocation by power allocation,” and uses satellite photos. On moratoriums, Reyk Knuhtsen says they mapped over 400 against data centers in the relevant jurisdictions and found about 10% of the mapped data centers were affected. Behind-the-meter generation can provide an alternative where grid headroom is lacking.
  • External haircuts to the number can amount to double counting, because delays are already built into the estimates. The team adds one to three quarters of delay depending on what they observe, treats sub-12-month timelines as a red flag, and assumes conservative ramps—for example, Oracle New Mexico has over a gigawatt under construction but contributes a “fairly low” share to the ’27 number. The Crusoe Childress critique was wrong: the forecast includes under 200 megawatts, not a full gigawatt.
  • The 2027 number rests on trackable leading indicators: over $1 trillion in signed data center leases, plus self-build construction starts rising quarter after quarter. Jeremie Ontiveros points to a waterfall of signals: they predicted an order surge at early-stage constructor Sterling, and track private operators (QTS, EdgeConneX, Aligned, Vantage) whose contracts public markets may not see, alongside crypto-miner backlogs (Applied Digital, Core Scientific) now in the tens of billions.
  • Modular construction is an important reason the team thinks the build-out can happen, compressing traditional 18-month timelines to roughly 6–9 months in cited examples. A modularized power hall can require much less labor than having “20 electricians” stick-build it. Reyk cites Anthropic reference designs, Meta tents, new Amazon buildings, and Project Houdini, which he thinks has a stated goal of 6GW a year for two or three years. He says developers that don’t follow modular approaches may struggle to get the labor they need.
  • The tradeable risk: chips are oversupplied versus data centers today, but the constraint could flip to data center oversupply in 2028. Jeremie’s hedged call is that it’s currently easier to get GPUs than data center megawatts. He says the key watch item is how fast chip supply expands, which would support CapEx such as new semiconductor fabs and equipment.
  • The meta-critique: bearish forecasts may rest on “not the most solid foundation of information,” including site trackers built by prompting Claude. Jordan Nanos’s direct grievance: Gerstner cited their data to audiences of 330,000 and 265,000, then dismissed it. Jordan’s response: “Cite our data, provide specific critiques to it, great. We can always learn”—but an offhand “this is the forecast; we think it’s wrong” seems strange.

Digest

1. The Gerstner callout — and a three-year track record

  • The episode’s trigger: Brad Gerstner showed SemiAnalysis’s 43GW-in-2027 forecast on the All-In Podcast and his BG2 interview with Jensen, calling it too aggressive. The episode discussed an opposing view of roughly 25GW; the team’s answer isn’t a defense of 43—it’s an increase toward 50GW.
  • Jeremie's history lesson: the data center model launched nearly three years ago, with a March 2024 article, “The AI Energy Dilemma: Race for Data Center Space,” putting out forecasts “materially ahead” of McKinsey and peers—“that has largely, of course, been proven right.” In discussing a chart from “Stop Saying Half of U.S. Data Centers Are Delayed,” Jeremie initially referred to 2027, but Jordan corrected him and Jeremie agreed the chart was for 2026; that forecast had “barely moved” across model revisions.
  • His reaction to the public haircut: “Dear Brad called us out publicly and cut our forecast in half. We’re like, ‘Damn, this is actually at least some number we made up.’” He then emphasized that “a lot of thought and work” went into it and that they stand by it.

2. The FUD list is “broadly true” — but does not apply to every project

  • Reyk’s taxonomy of the bear case: moratoriums, grid connections, labor, equipment supply chains—“all of that is true,” but “being able to measure it accurately is a different story.” He says their granularity means tracking “not even at the campus level, but building by building, permit by permit, power allocation by power allocation,” and buying satellite photos.
  • The moratorium answer with numbers: they mapped over 400 moratoriums against data centers in the relevant jurisdictions and found about 10% of the mapped data centers were affected. On energy, grid headroom is one consideration; behind-the-meter generation can provide an alternative for some projects.
  • The logic: “When I’m physically looking at all of these data centers under construction, I don’t know how I could haircut it.” Reyk’s conclusion is that these issues are real but “don’t apply to every project”; he says the appropriate projects under construction pass their bar.

3. Delays are pre-baked, so an extra haircut can be double counting

  • The model treats timelines shorter than 12 months as a red flag, and Reyk says a developer that “just came out of nowhere,” obfuscated permits or power sources, or no identified tenant raises questions. Possible surprises include a northeastern winter storm during a TeraWulf or Nebius buildout and a transformer blowing up at the Core Scientific site. Reyk preserves the caveat: “It’s not to say that these things don’t catch us off guard. They can... I didn’t predict a winter storm. It’s not my job.”
  • Jeremie says the article’s chart covers about 40 sites, still under half of the global data centers shown as under construction. The relevant question is when a site’s first phase arrives and how quickly it ramps; their assumptions vary by project. Oracle New Mexico, which they say they were first to flag as having issues, has over a gigawatt of IT capacity under construction, but they forecast a “fairly low” share of that campus’s megawatts in 2027.
  • The Crusoe Childress correction: Twitter accounts said the forecast included a whole gigawatt in 2027. Jeremie says that is wrong: “We have under 200 megawatts as of the latest version published.” Reyk says adding another haircut can be “a bit of double counting,” since Jeremie says they purposely add delays of one to three quarters depending on what they observe.

4. Over $1 trillion in signed leases and a waterfall of indicators

  • The two signals emphasized in the article are self-build construction starts—tracking when each building starts, with the count rising quarter after quarter—and pre-leasing, where hyperscalers, neoclouds, and AI labs sign leases with data center operators. Jordan cites over $1 trillion of data center leasing signed; Jeremie says these binding contracts help them understand what is likely to be built.
  • Jeremie's supply-chain waterfall includes early-stage constructor Sterling, whose order surge they predicted through project-level tracking; electrical and cooling equipment downstream; and energy lead times. Gas turbines are multiple years out, while reciprocating engines have shorter lead times. The team uses these signals to check project timelines.
  • The public markets’ blind spot: crypto-miner backlogs at Applied Digital and Core Scientific are visible and in the tens of billions, but public markets don’t have a good view of every contract between private operators such as QTS, EdgeConneX, Aligned, and Vantage and hyperscalers or AI labs. Jeremie says tracking those private companies lets them gather data that other forecasts may miss.

5. Modular construction and the 2028 oversupply risk

  • Reyk’s underappreciated mechanism is modular deployment. He contrasts traditional 18-month timelines with DayOne timelines of about nine months for hundreds of megawatts and BrightRay timelines of about six months in Southeast Asia. He says Anthropic reference designs will employ modular approaches, and points to Meta tents and new Amazon buildings as examples of buildings that can appear quickly. He also cites Project Houdini, which he thinks has a stated goal of 6GW a year for the next two or three years; the transcript does not identify its owner.
  • Reyk’s example of the labor savings: a modularized mechanical/electrical fit-out could use a power hall “like a literal shipping container” slotted into the data center shell, rather than “20 electricians” coordinating to stick-build the hall. He says developers that don’t follow modular design strategies probably won’t be allocated the labor they need. BrightRay is talking to neoclouds about selling entire data center modules, not just one-to-two-megawatt crates.
  • Jeremie's balance call, with the hedge intact: “We’re already in a sort of oversupply of chips today,” and it is easier to get GPUs than data center megawatts. Comparing supply-chain expansion into 2028, he sees a risk of the constraint flipping to data center oversupply. How fast chip supply expands is the key watch item; he calls the resulting CapEx, including new semiconductor fabs and equipment, a strong positive.
  • On Jensen taking Gerstner’s framing in stride, Jeremie sees supply-chain aggression: Jensen secured GPUs for crypto-mining build-outs in 2021, which “obviously crashed,” and is writing “massive checks” to memory and logic suppliers. Jordan says Gerstner presented to audiences of 330,000 and 265,000, citing SemiAnalysis’s data and dismissing it. Jordan’s response: “Cite our data, provide specific critiques to it, great. We can always learn”—but an offhand “this is the forecast; we think it’s wrong” seems strange. Jeremie says the article was intended to address a broader topic that clients and others ask about, not to respond to one person.

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/ep-039-emergency-our-numbers-are-insane-here-s-p

item.title: Should You Trust ChatGPT With Your Health?
item.description: GPT-6 Luna, OpenAI’s cheapest frontier API model, beat 5.6 Sol on HealthBench Professional at 34 times lower cost. Singhal sees a path to commoditized health intelligence, but says it has not yet affected the $5.3T US spend; savings require workflow integration. Epic, UCSF, and AdventHealth offer deployment evidence, including roughly 80% lower administrative workflow costs reported by AdventHealth.
item.content:encoded:
The a16z Show · Karan Singhal、Jay Rughani · 2026-10-20 · 56 min · 原语言 EN

GPT-6 Luna, OpenAI’s cheapest frontier API model, beat 5.6 Sol on HealthBench Professional at 34 times lower cost. Singhal sees a path to commoditized health intelligence, but says it has not yet affected the $5.3T US spend; savings require workflow integration. Epic, UCSF, and AdventHealth offer deployment evidence, including roughly 80% lower administrative workflow costs reported by AdventHealth.

TL;DR

  • OpenAI says more than 300 million people a week use ChatGPT for health questions — the vast majority on the free tier, and most outside the US. Karan Singhal frames the health push as the “make upside happen” leg of the AGI mission: “raise the floor of human health” with “trustworthy, abundant, reliable health intelligence for free or nearly free,” and raise the ceiling with capabilities that didn’t exist before.
  • The cost curve is the tradeable claim: GPT-6 Luna, OpenAI’s cheapest frontier API model, beat 5.6 Sol — “literally our best model a month ago” — on HealthBench Professional “despite being thirty-four times cheaper.” Singhal’s explicit bet is “commoditization of health intelligence” (“we don’t wanna hoard that health intelligence”), while conceding health AI “has not yet had a macro effect” on the $5.3T US spend — compression requires integration and workflow deployment, not just cheap tokens.
  • Singhal makes the case for specialized training inside a general model, based on his experience building specialized models: a healthcare-only model “would fall behind the frontier relatively quickly.” OpenAI adds specialized healthcare data into each phase of training across its ChatGPT models shipped over the past year — “specialized training in a general model... the best of both worlds,” “hitching a ride on that scaling frontier.”
  • Trust is built through expert aggregation: “if you ask five physicians a question, you’ll get, like, eight different answers,” so OpenAI has a global network of hundreds of physicians across dozens of specialties and countries. When user comfort conflicts with clinical reality, “it’s basically a prioritization of safety” — the model must say “you should seek care” even when the user wants reassurance. The system-level opportunity: clinical guidelines can take “five to 17 years” to penetrate practice, and point-of-care AI could help compress that lag to “weeks or days or even hours.”
  • OpenAI says AI can’t provide all of medical care: “I don’t think AI can or will provide all of that.” The strategy is to make “the last mile of actually having impact on patients just look like the last hundred meters for all of our partners” — ChatGPT as “a quarterback for your health,” not a replacement for care providers. His advice to healthcare builders: “bet on the models getting better. That’s probably the most important thing.”
  • Enterprise traction is concrete: Epic integration, UCSF using it for chart review, and AdventHealth reporting “roughly eighty percent reduction” in administrative workflow costs. On agents, Singhal argues healthcare’s legacy stack — EHRs running on VMs, no “MCP connector tomorrow” — is ripe for computer-use agents, predicting traditional barriers “will dissolve in the coming months.” Rughani cites a New York Times article and a Blue Cross Blue Shield Association analysis, saying billing and paperwork bots increased spend by “a billion dollars or something like that”; Singhal calls the arms race “a bit of a short-term distraction.”
  • Singhal’s biggest-impact five-to-ten-year prediction is new treatments from AI-guided target and molecule generation plus AI-guided prioritization and validation of clinical trials, where candidate molecules already outnumber trial slots. Nearer term, he’s looking for a “move thirty-seven for health” — predictions from longitudinal data that may seem brilliant only in hindsight, because “a human can’t integrate all that data in their head.”

Digest

1. Health is OpenAI’s “make upside happen” bet — at 300M users a week

  • Singhal’s decomposition of the mission: build and deploy AGI, prevent downside, and “make upside happen” — health is a concrete upside play, with twin goals of raising the floor (“trustworthy, abundant, reliable health intelligence for free or nearly free”) and raising the ceiling. The scale claim: more than 300M weekly health and wellness users, “the vast majority” free users and most outside the US — deployment to the free tier was deliberate from the start.
  • The gap being filled, per both speakers: weeks-to-months waits for specialist appointments even in the Bay Area, then fifteen minutes with a doctor and “six more questions that I wanted to ask” afterward. AI’s natural home is “in between these visits” — Rughani’s own dermatology follow-up is four months out despite writing down his questions beforehand.
  • The specimen story Singhal returns to: Nathan Labenz (host of The Cognitive Revolution), whose young son had fatigue and irritability. AI helped them navigate testing and repeatedly said, “Hey, take this seriously,” even as doctors were less sure and downplayed it. The son was diagnosed with an aggressive form of leukemia, and Labenz used GPT-5 Pro throughout the care journey to understand lab reports before specialists had time to help interpret them.

2. Specialized training inside a general model

  • Singhal built specialized medical models in a previous role, which informs his view: a healthcare-only model would “fall behind the frontier relatively quickly” because frontier progress is so fast. OpenAI instead adds specialized healthcare data to each phase of training across its ChatGPT models shipped in the last year.
  • The strategic logic in his words: “if you bet on scale... things will get better,” so the health team is “hitching a ride on that scaling frontier” while retaining the ability to integrate health-specific evaluations and training data — “the best of both worlds.”

3. Proactive assistants and agents against a fragmented system

  • The doctor-in-your-pocket vision Rughani sketches — memory, personalization, and behavioral nudges — is one Singhal says OpenAI is excited about: “a proactive personal health assistant,” with the hedge intact: “I don’t think that’s any kind of replacement for actually having a doctor.” Connected health information in ChatGPT is intended to be used securely, not for training data or ad targeting.
  • Rughani’s Greg Brockman anecdote carries the safety-net argument: a friend double-checked a medication in ChatGPT, realized from her medical history she might have an interaction or adverse event, and her doctor agreed they hadn’t had time to review the history. Singhal’s generalization: a “safety net for both patients and clinicians,” studied in clinician-copilot experiments with Penda Health, with a similar patient-side role in view — for example, flagging a medication review if a diabetic user’s A1C rises.
  • On agentic products (Rughani cites Instinct, Muse, GrokBot, and OpenAI’s Dots): healthcare “shouldn’t expect everything to have an MCP connector tomorrow”; primary EHRs often run on virtual machines, which can make some things easier for AI agents. Singhal says healthcare is “absolutely ripe for agents and computer use” and predicts barriers between patients, clinicians, and healthcare data “will dissolve in the coming months.”

4. Trust is built by aggregating experts and prioritizing safety over comfort

  • Singhal’s operating principle — health “moves at the speed of trust” — means evaluation and training are tailored by persona. The original HealthBench evaluation, released in May 2025, examined how models adapt technical language for lay users versus clinicians.
  • Why not rely on a few in-house doctors to adjudicate hard cases? “If you ask five physicians a question, you’ll get, like, eight different answers.” OpenAI built a global physician network of hundreds of experts across dozens of specialties, languages, and countries of practice, to aggregate expert perspectives where there may be disagreement.
  • When a user wants reassurance the clinical picture doesn’t support, the priority is safety: evaluations track cases where the model should say “this is unsafe. You should seek care,” even if the user doesn’t want to hear it or wants an alternative treatment. On politicized gray zones such as unapproved peptides and vaccines, Singhal says to rely on experts to define response standards. If a doctor disagrees with ChatGPT, his advice is to handle it like other disagreements and seek a second opinion.

5. The 5-to-17-year guideline lag, honest hedging, and Mental Health Bench

  • Singhal’s systems claim: biomedical papers inform yearly clinical guidelines, which are roughly “flowcharts”; studies have found it can take five to 17 years for guidelines to reach everyday practice. “You don’t want to be practicing medicine five to 17 years behind.” ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians bring current literature to the point of care, with the aim of helping compress that lag to “weeks, days, or even hours.” His reframe: sometimes “there is medical consensus, but it’s not being practiced.”
  • Where uncertainty is genuine, models should recognize it and say, “Hey, there just isn’t enough information.” Hedging under uncertainty is a public aspect of HealthBench; another response to unsettled science is accelerating the science itself.
  • Mental Health Bench extends the method to a domain where “people definitely disagree even more here than they do in physical health”: a baseline safety floor, including safeguards on Dots, plus measurement of upside — “positive mental health experiences.” OpenAI developed it with licensed experts worldwide, aiming for a “shared ruler or measuring stick” across model developers, the healthcare industry, and mental health experts.

6. Enterprise distribution: Epic, UCSF, AdventHealth, and the Overton window

  • The three-part approach: capable models, products that lower the “activation energy” of using intelligence to improve health, and partnerships and deployment. Singhal cites 1.2B weekly ChatGPT users and says OpenAI wants to make frontier health intelligence free. He also describes security, compliance, HIPAA, and privacy work to support healthcare organizations.
  • The traction evidence: Epic can be used in ChatGPT by providers and ChatGPT can be used in an Epic sidebar; UCSF is an early adopter using it for chart review; and AdventHealth has been a leader in deploying agents, reporting “roughly an 80% reduction” in administrative workflow costs. Retention on ChatGPT for Clinicians has been “a very pleasant surprise.”
  • On seeing ChatGPT open on a doctor’s screen: the Overton window “is shifting in real time,” and Singhal predicts both patients and clinicians may feel safer with AI in their care journey — with the caveat, “I wouldn’t say we’re fully there.”

7. Information, not all of care — and the hunt for a “move thirty-seven for health”

  • Rughani frames medical care as a bundled product — diagnosis, empathy, and legal liability. Singhal says, “I don’t think AI can or will provide all of that.” OpenAI’s role is to make “the last mile of actually having an impact on patients just look like the last hundred meters for all of our partners” — a “quarterback for your health” for navigation and logistics, while relying on partners to deliver care.
  • What remains for the visit once both sides have pre-processed information through AI? “The human aspect of healthcare” — empathy, bedside manner, physical examination, and history-taking. Singhal says, “I don’t think all the information exists for the AI to just figure out what should be done.”
  • On AlphaGo’s move 37 analogy — a prediction a human might not have made, but that seems correct and insightful in hindsight — Singhal says, “we’re very early.” In the clinician-copilot study, a common pattern the models flagged was avoiding antibiotic overuse and considering the global issue of resistance, not just the local case. The future version: models integrating a user’s longitudinal history over ten years and across EHR and chat data to make predictions humans couldn’t easily make by integrating all that information themselves.
  • A third constituency beyond patient and clinician is the scientist. Agents may mine healthcare data “stored in boxes in various places” to generate new insights, and accelerate validation — which Singhal thinks may be a bottleneck, rather than proposing new ideas or treatments.

8. The cost curve, the billing-bot arms race, and what to build

  • The economics centerpiece: GPT-6 Luna, OpenAI’s cheapest frontier API model, outperformed 5.6 Sol — “literally our best model a month ago” — on HealthBench Professional “despite being 34 times cheaper.” Singhal’s bet is that, as models reach a level of intelligence clinicians and patients can trust in the care journey, the cost at that level will fall — toward “commoditization of health intelligence. We don’t want to hoard that health intelligence.”
  • Against Rughani’s macro framing — $5.3T in healthcare spending and a third-largest GDP if healthcare were a country — Singhal’s hedge is that health intelligence “has not yet had a macro effect.” Spend compression requires integration, workflows, and deployment at scale; abundant intelligence is a prerequisite, not the mechanism by itself.
  • Rughani cites a New York Times article and a Blue Cross Blue Shield Association analysis, saying billing and paperwork bots increased spend by “a billion dollars or something like that.” Singhal describes possible short-term pain, but says there is no reason the arms race must continue. His ideal is a shared record of what happened in a visit that an AI can help adjudicate; he calls the arms race “a bit of a short-term distraction.”
  • For builders: healthcare founders sit on a spectrum from betting against the models to betting for them — “bet on the models getting better. That’s probably the most important thing.” Procedural care’s near-term macro factor may be prevention, avoiding procedures through earlier action; robotics is “not a next-few-years kind of thing.” Singhal’s five-to-ten-year prediction is new treatments from AI-guided target and molecule generation, plus AI-guided prioritization and validation of clinical trials, since candidate molecules already exceed available trial slots.

来源：YouTube

item.title: The cavalry isn't coming: UK stocks, relistings, and AI analysts | Ben Isaac, Brizo Capital
item.description: AI may increase demand for strong analysts: commoditized data shifts the premium to on-the-ground judgment and access models lack. Across 30-plus relistings, Isaac cites sustained reratings and UK turnover just a third to a quarter of comparable US stocks, alongside talent and M&A benefits. Selection bias remains unresolved, while UK capital-allocation weaknesses may cap valuations.
item.content:encoded:
Yet Another Value Podcast · Andrew Walker、Ben Isaac · 2026-10-20 · 63 min · 原语言 EN

AI may increase demand for strong analysts: commoditized data shifts the premium to on-the-ground judgment and access models lack. Across 30-plus relistings, Isaac cites sustained reratings and UK turnover just a third to a quarter of comparable US stocks, alongside talent and M&A benefits. Selection bias remains unresolved, while UK capital-allocation weaknesses may cap valuations.

TL;DR

  • Ben Isaac’s hot take is that AI materially expands the need for good analysts rather than replacing them. Pre-chewed information can become commoditized — expert-network databases are “ultimately a quasi-commodity” — so the premium shifts to differentiated, on-the-ground work (trade shows, cold calls, scuttlebutt) requiring “judgment, finesse, people skills, EQ” that models “will never have access to.” Across his 70–75 Columbia students, median work quality has risen sharply with AI. On whether the absolute best pitches are materially better than 4, 5, or 7 years ago, though, he says, “I don’t know”; there was strong work five years ago. “These are still not a substitute for investment judgment.”
  • The episode’s governing thesis on UK stocks: “the cavalry isn’t coming to save us.” Ben says it’s easy to find statistically cheap companies globally, with a meaningful fraction of good businesses at attractive valuations. The US — around 70% of global market cap — and perhaps Australia, India, and the Nordics are the only robust, well-functioning equity markets, in his view. Stewardship issues in disclosure, incentives, and “crucially capital allocation” can cap valuations. Brizo is particularly attracted to the UK: many companies are global businesses, and there’s “a really logical, deep pool of strategic and private-equity buyers.”
  • Isaac defends US relistings as more than multiple arbitrage, with data. Of 30-plus “real businesses” relisted over five years, he says it’s hard to find ones that didn’t rerate on announcement and keep that rerating, while liquidity grew even faster. Average UK turnover is a third to a quarter of that of a similarly sized US stock. Suboptimal listings can have operating costs: one UK company pays its head of North America “multiple times what the CEO is getting paid,” and UK dividend policy is “trapped in amber.” Walker’s pushbacks — “one-time sugar high” versus buybacks, and selection bias — draw Isaac’s candid “I can’t disprove the counterfactual.”
  • The Walmart-of-Kenya trap: demand a spread over local cost of equity, and decompose the risk premium rather than slap on a country number. A Kenyan retailer at 10x earnings with 10% growth implies roughly a 20% return against a low-to-mid-20s cost of equity — “probably kind of expensive.” In Brazil, with the Selic in the low teens, Isaac says you need 20%+ fundamental returns “just to get out of bed.” A Brazilian ag business he likes has mostly dollar-denominated streams, trades at a single-digit earnings multiple, and has historically grown 20–40% nominally. He contrasts a Turkish business owning the Houston Airport operating concession with Almaty Airport, which he argues does not have a Turkish cost of equity.
  • Only 10% of UK PLCs require directors to own equity, which “creates obvious cascading consequences.” Isaac says patient capital and a 1–5% stake can change the contours of engagement, but fixes like buyback mechanics may require “gradual education processes.” A five-year fix for a cash-burning steel mill at 30% of replacement value (sellable at 70% of book) is a different proposition from the same hypothetical mill already generating 7–12% ROE.
  • UK private-equity bids can leave shareholders selling before later value is realized, but Isaac sees opportunistic bids as part of a governance transition. In “year 10 of basically just continuous outflows from active management,” local managers may be incentivized to take a win. Isaac sees early bids as a signal that “the water is warm,” helping bring competitive bids and price discovery. He’s fought bids and “gotten yelled at by some very large-cap CFOs.”
  • South Korea is “a super attractive market” competing with the UK for Brizo’s capital. Reforms are stacking up and valuations are compelling, but Isaac says family-controlled businesses are a bigger part of the market than in Japan, and key decision-makers may be slow to adapt. Japan has fewer complicated holdco structures.

Digest

1. AI in the classroom: pre-chew information, don’t outsource the thinking

  • Isaac teaches Columbia’s Applied Security Analysis (with co-professors Evan and Zach; the course is approaching its 20th anniversary) and has worked with interns at Brizo. His core tension: students want professional-looking output fast, but there’s a gap between Claude “helping them do the initial analysis” and “doing their thinking for them.” His gym metaphor: “If you build a machine to do the leg press for you... it doesn’t make you any stronger.”
  • The house rules: use the tools for clean information-gathering, alternative sources, Python scripts, and big scrapes — diligence that was “incredibly time-consuming and painful” takes far fewer person-hours — disclose where you used them, and have them “focus on pre-chewing information as opposed to digesting information for you.”
  • Across 70–75 students, median work quality is up dramatically. On whether the absolute best pitches are materially better than they were 4, 5, or 7 years ago, Isaac says, “I don’t know”; he recalls strong work five years ago. “These are still not a substitute for investment judgment.”
  • Walker’s corroboration from Substack pitches: the writing reads beautifully until you push back and “they’ve got nothing.”

2. Firm adoption is “all over the map” — and hallucination-talk is a tell

  • What firms want in hires varies by mandate and compliance posture. Big shops without the IT architecture are “still stuck on things like Copilot, which really doesn’t have the same kind of horsepower as Claude” (Walker: “I vomited in my mouth a little bit”). Pod shops have amazing tools and data cleanliness; a Claude account that can’t touch company files is “radically less powerful.”
  • Disconnected from everything but the raw internet, these tools are “only so much better than Google” — their power comes from feeding them incremental context.
  • Walker’s view: a year ago hallucinations topped his own worry list; now if someone’s first concern is hallucinations, he thinks they may not have been playing with the tools much.

3. The hot take: AI expands the need for good analysts

  • Isaac first hedges — “for now, people don’t know,” and near-term pressure comes more from economic constraints at large organizations, including fee compression and AUM challenges. But his “perhaps hot take” is that AI “actually materially expands the need for good-quality analysts,” because the premium shifts to differentiated information requiring “judgment, finesse, people skills, EQ.”
  • Expert-network databases can become “ultimately a quasi-commodity,” particularly as organizations get comfortable feeding that material into a context window. Meanwhile, senior people are tied up in investment committees and administrative work; young, energetic analysts can do on-the-ground scuttlebutt that models “will never have access to.”
  • Brizo hires many international interns to bring different cultural contexts and perspectives. Walker’s job-seeker corollary, inspired by recent Pershing Square Challenge winners: “If you’re a CEO, a hard hat is a short indicator. If you’re an analyst or an aspiring intern and you’ve got a hard hat photo... that’s a job-offer signal.”

4. The student superpower: people will take your call

  • Isaac’s commercial for MBAs: “While you’re a student, you have a superpower: a lot of people actually want to get on the phone with you.” The hit rate on a polite 15–20-minute research ask is “pretty good,” and learning to take doors slammed in your face “without taking it personally” is a durable career skill.
  • Walker’s arithmetic: expert networks run $750–$1,000 an hour, ex-CEOs sometimes charge $5,000, and students can get a few minutes with CEOs for free. “You can get access that is literally priceless.”
  • Isaac’s caveat: know “the load-bearing components of your thesis.” Massive write-ups that reveal “I know the name of the CFO’s cat” can be impressive without driving outcomes. Knowing what’s relevant informs whom to contact and what to ask; sounding prepared “unlocks a totally different level of conversation.”

5. The hunting ground: cheap stocks everywhere, functioning markets almost nowhere

  • Brizo’s global, fundamentals-driven mandate is “pretty agnostic about where” companies are, assuming they can underwrite them and be treated fairly. Isaac says it is easy to find statistically cheap companies globally, and a meaningful fraction are good businesses at attractive valuations. In his view, the US — perhaps alongside Australia, India, and the Nordics — is the only robust, well-functioning equity market. The US is about 70% of global market cap, while the vast majority of roughly 40,000 publicly traded securities are outside it.
  • Why the UK specifically: many companies are large global businesses not tied to the UK domestic economy, with English-language operations and “a really logical, deep pool of strategic and private-equity buyers” if public markets fail to value them. Southeast Asia may offer opportunities, but the rules on the ground and governance evolution are at a different stage.
  • The problem is stewardship, “not necessarily coming from malice”: disclosure, compensation, incentives, and “crucially capital allocation.” Operationally, many businesses “aren’t broken”; these are “fixable problems.” Walker names their shared framing: “the cavalry isn’t coming to save us. We need to save ourselves.”

6. Engagement: push on open doors, accept gradual education

  • Walker’s frustration: he pitches alignment — give management stock, “stock goes up, we all get rich” — and gets treated as “a foreigner sitting in your little shoebox of a closet.” Isaac says patient capital and being a 1–5% shareholder can change the contours of the discussion. He can think of very few cases where an investor simply dictated terms as a “brilliant American” and saw the stock change six months later.
  • The structural root: “only 10% of UK PLCs have a requirement that directors own equity. That creates obvious cascading consequences” — not because the directors are bad people, but because they face different incentives. Blockers can include legacy leverage norms or misunderstandings about buybacks, addressed through “gradual education processes — and that can be a very unsatisfying answer.”
  • Selectivity matters. Isaac finds the metaphorical, cash-burning steel mill at 30% of replacement value (sellable at 70% of book) less attractive than other opportunities. If fixing it takes five years, that is a different economic proposition from the same hypothetical mill already generating 7–12% ROE. Walker jokes that “the bottom-feeder in me” hears the discount and says, “Yeah, I’m in.”

7. Relistings: real operational consequences, not just multiple arbitrage

  • Walker’s skepticism: relisting a UK/Spain-revenue business in the US “feels like financial engineering for financial engineering’s sake.” Isaac pushes back: one large UK company had to pay its head of North America “multiple times what the CEO is getting paid,” because UK CEO compensation is far below the market for American talent. Without well-rated equity and the ability to pay in equity, it can be harder to attract and retain talent; a more liquid, highly valued equity can also be useful for M&A.
  • “The dividend policy in the UK is kind of trapped in amber from a very different set of facts.” One Brizo portfolio company says its view of the optimal margin/growth balance doesn’t suit its UK shareholders’ preferences. A changed shareholder base can affect what the business can do.
  • The data: among 30-plus “real businesses” — with real revenue, profitability, and substance — relisted to the US over five years from the UK, Australia, Scandinavia, and other jurisdictions, Isaac says it’s hard to find ones that didn’t meaningfully rerate on announcement and keep that rerating. Liquidity grew even more: the average UK equity trades, as a percentage of shares outstanding, at about a third to a quarter of a similarly sized US company. He says relisting failures were driven by underlying business problems: GAN got into trouble because of its business, and would have gone to zero in another market too.

8. Walker’s two pushbacks: sugar high, and selection bias

  • Pushback one: isn’t the relisting pop “a one-time sugar high” versus buying back discounted stock? Isaac agrees buybacks are “absolutely a great alternative”; one portfolio company is doing exactly that, and Brizo is happy to “let them cook.” But he can think of few other examples in the markets they’re looking at. For companies constrained by talent or liquidity, relisting can address more than valuation.
  • Pushback two: is the rerating caused by the relisting, or by a biased sample of shareholder-minded managements? Isaac says, “I can’t disprove the counterfactual.” The cohort spans industries, and some companies aren’t meaningfully US businesses. In CRH’s case, Trian pushed for the move when the stock was around 35 or 45, Isaac thinks; before that, it wasn’t meaningfully on the board’s agenda. He’s prepared to believe relistings disproportionately select for companies that care about shareholder outcomes.

9. The Walmart-of-Kenya problem: decompose the premium, demand the spread

  • Walker’s chronic struggle: a Kenyan company may screen cheaper, but mixing African towers and UK distributors at equal 5% weights hides very different risks. Isaac’s method is to break the premium into currency (“far and away the biggest risk”), government risk, and operating risk. He contrasts a business in Turkey that owns the Houston Airport operating concession — which may move with Turkish equity flows — with Almaty Airport, which he argues does not have a Turkish cost of equity. Hard-currency, inflation-linked tower contracts with energy-price pass-throughs can also make the apparent risk premium misleading.
  • The mechanics: a Kenyan retailer at 10x earnings growing 10% nominally implies a roughly 20% fundamental return — against a low-to-mid-20s local cost of equity, “that’s actually not really cheap. In fact, it’s probably kind of expensive.” In Brazil, with real rates in the low teens, he says you need 20%+ fundamental returns “just to get out of bed.”
  • A Brazilian ag-linked business Isaac likes has mostly dollar-denominated streams, trades at a single-digit earnings multiple, and has historically grown organically at 20–40% nominally. “We may wind up getting this one totally wrong,” but its growth plus earnings yield is well above the Selic, which is why he finds it attractive. A US company with a 14–17% fundamental return and a 10–11% cost of equity may beat a Kenyan company returning 30%.

10. “Brokenness is relative”: US dysfunction, UK takeouts, Korea next

  • Walker channels Einhorn’s jelly-donut critique: are passive-distorted US markets, especially the dregs of the Russell 2000, really well-functioning? Isaac says people critical of the US should tour other markets. US governance is “getting worse at the margin, but it’s still the best in the world, or at least for now.” He points to a liquid market for corporate control, a large private-equity bid for cheap businesses, and established activists. He acknowledges pockets of dysfunction, particularly among smaller and less-loved stocks: “Brokenness is relative.”
  • On UK private-equity bids: the UK is “in year 10 of basically just continuous outflows from active management,” which can incentivize local managers to take a win. Isaac’s ecosystem metaphor: “Maybe we’re the deer and they’re the wolves... I’d like to have something where I’m not being eaten.” Early-stage governance renaissances — the US in the ’70s and ’80s, illustrated by Danny DeVito’s liquidation-value chalkboard in Other People’s Money — can start with opportunistic bids signaling “the water is warm.” Isaac has fought bids and “gotten yelled at by some very large-cap CFOs”; he doesn’t like seeing companies bought for less than they’re worth.
  • South Korea: Isaac calls it “a super attractive market,” where reforms are stacking up and valuations are compelling. He says family-controlled businesses make up a larger part of the market than in Japan, and decision-makers may be slow to adapt; Japan also has fewer complicated holdco structures. Walker separately contrasts Japan’s low-ownership managerial class with Korea’s family control. Brizo has owned Korean businesses for years and expects to continue investing there. Korea competes for capital with the UK, whose companies tend to be larger and more international, and where corporate governance is already in place.

来源：YouTube

item.title: How Toto Wolff built the most valuable team in F1
item.description: Mercedes combines F1’s scarce team ownership with roughly $1 billion in revenue and a 30% margin, though Collison’s roughly 15x EBIT framing uses current earnings that Wolff says were considerably higher than at the transaction. Owner control supports a ten-year horizon, but the “$200 million and a bit” cap forces lap-time trade-offs, and DAS’s ban after one year leaves regulatory durability an unresolved risk.
item.content:encoded:
Cheeky Pint · Toto Wolff、John Collison · 2026-10-20 · 71 min · 原语言 EN

Mercedes combines F1’s scarce team ownership with roughly $1 billion in revenue and a 30% margin, though Collison’s roughly 15x EBIT framing uses current earnings that Wolff says were considerably higher than at the transaction. Owner control supports a ten-year horizon, but the “$200 million and a bit” cap forces lap-time trade-offs, and DAS’s ban after one year leaves regulatory durability an unresolved risk.

TL;DR

  • Mercedes now has operating profits to support its valuation alongside the scarcity of owning an F1 team. Wolff reports around $1 billion in revenue and a 30% margin, with dividends and limited stadium-related capital expenditure. Collison’s roughly 15x EBIT framing switches the transaction valuation from £4.6 billion to $4.6 billion and uses current earnings; Wolff says earnings at the transaction were “considerably less.”
  • Owner control lets Wolff make decisions against a ten-year horizon rather than a manager’s contract. Mercedes helped finance his stake and gave him authority to act outside the corporate hierarchy. Wolff invokes Dietrich Mateschitz’s advice to entrepreneurs: “You need to be like a downhill ski racer, but you need to be able to stop and walk back up the hill.”
  • F1’s spending limits exchange some scientific freedom for closer competition. A cost cap of “$200 million and a bit” forces choices between near-term lap time and longer-term research, although Wolff rejects the claim that speculative R&D has disappeared. Regulatory durability is another investment hurdle: Mercedes’ push-pull steering innovation worked, but was banned after a year.
  • Mercedes evaluates engineering against the car’s performance and people against their contribution to the team. Simulations establish expected lap-time gains, but those gains still require a driver who can extract them. Wolff’s answer to engineers becoming attached to projects is “You fall in love with the result”; exceptional ability does not earn an exemption from “No dickheads.”
  • Wolff’s formative investment success depended on selling as well as finding opportunities. After a lucrative SMS-business sale, his CFO challenged valuations disconnected from monetization and compared them with an industrial business producing 30 million in EBIT. They exited all but one of nine investments, beginning in late 1999 and continuing through 2000; Wolff credits luck and the incentive to protect his own life-changing wealth.
  • F1’s audience growth combines entertainment with a sporting outcome viewers believe is real. Wolff initially doubted Netflix and declined the first season, but now describes a year-round reality show whose foundation remains “Entertainment follows sport.” He cites 42% female fans and sees live sport as resilient in an AI-heavy world because “Humans watch humans.”
  • Wolff wants durable private ownership with management that can eventually operate without him. He doubts public markets suit a sport that moves “from mania to depression within a week,” despite Collison’s argument that today’s audience is different. His succession plan would probably divide his responsibilities among two or three people, with any future chairmanship requiring clear limits on intervention.

Digest

1. Driver speed is sensory, while team performance requires character

  • When Collison asks for racing’s equivalent of cycling’s power-to-weight metric, Wolff says there is no single equivalent. An eight-year-old beating ten-year-olds can signal potential, but resilience, technical communication and sponsor relationships also matter. “The stopwatch never lies” when drivers share machinery; it does not explain everything underneath the result.
  • Wolff describes exceptional speed as an unusually fine connection between body, car and road. Hamilton once said, “The car understeers from the front axle to where I sit,” describing a sensation engineers could not readily identify. Collison’s formulation is that great drivers strap the car onto themselves; Wolff calls that underlying sensitivity genetic.
  • Wolff’s own path into racing was late: at 18, an accidental visit to an F3 paddock gave him a sense of identity, but he lacked the karting background that teaches the fundamentals of positioning a car. He nevertheless raced through junior formula and GT, touring-car and sports-car stages with some success.
  • The visible racing operation conceals 2,500 people across engine and chassis hubs; around 150 travel, including marketing, with 90 in technical and operational roles. Wolff insists there are 2,500 potential stars and applies the All Blacks’ “No dickheads” rule. Humility, integrity, honesty and enthusiasm matter: there is “no place for the genius asshole.”

2. A fixed budget makes lap time the investment hurdle

  • With a cost cap of “$200 million and a bit” annually, engineering resources force explicit choices: compute for a front wing arriving in three months competes with longer-term laboratory work. Collison suggests speculative R&D had to disappear; Wolff corrects him. Some remains, but its prospective lap-time contribution must justify diverting resources from current cars.
  • Wolff originally opposed the cap because Mercedes’ resources protected it against smaller competitors. Former F1 chief Chase Carey told him, “We need to protect you from yourselves.” Wolff now acknowledges closer competition, while retaining the tension: unrestricted engineering, even within a budget, could produce a leading car five seconds faster than the next.
  • Technical allocation starts with an expected lap-time contribution, then follows simulation, CFD, wind-tunnel measurements and mathematical models against that expectation. Wolff considers this more measurable than Stripe’s task of predicting customer demand. A theoretical tenth of a second can nevertheless disappear if the driver feels unsafe or cannot extract the modeled benefit.
  • Collison presses on engineers demanding another simulation for a beloved idea. Wolff says forceful advocates who pushed experiments beyond reason are no longer in the organization. Technical management must stop work that fails the overall lap-time objective, regardless of a department’s interests. “You fall in love with the result,” rather than the component.

3. Regulatory defensibility is part of the engineering return

  • Mercedes tests contentious innovations through an internal mock trial: inventors prosecute their own proposal, other engineers defend it, and Wolff and general counsel judge. Dialogue with the FIA should begin early when legality is uncertain. If something is “100% defensible,” however, Mercedes may deploy it first and make its argument afterward.
  • The sharpest example is DAS: pushing and pulling the steering wheel changed front-wheel toe, allowing tire surfaces to heat through dragging. Wolff found the extra steering-wheel movement deeply uncomfortable; the F1 drivers wanted to try it, and it worked. He believes a mechanical driver-operated control helped make the system defensible.
  • DAS was banned after a year. Asked why it did not simply become an accepted capability, Wolff answers, “I don’t know,” suggesting Mercedes might have lost the political argument as rivals objected to replication costs. His experience is that regulators may respect an innovation for a season before banning it, although intervention can arrive earlier.
  • On the compression-ratio dispute, Wolff argues that cold-engine measurement was clearly specified and rivals had misread the rules. He declines to confirm claims that Mercedes deliberately engineered advantageous thermal expansion. A compromise eventually changed measurement, but he says it made no difference for Mercedes: the months-long fight was about “the sheer principle of innovation.”
  • Protecting an edge is imperfect: Wolff says Mercedes firewalls some work, but eventually 20 or 25 people need to know, and personnel can move between teams. Contractual limits vary; he cites up to 12 months in the UK and three months in Switzerland. He says innovations will eventually leak.

4. The dot-com windfall became valuable because Wolff sold

  • Wolff’s early investment activity was a hybrid of sweat equity, small investments and success-linked ownership. Inspired by Netscape, Yahoo! and AOL, he searched German-speaking markets for analogous businesses, then offered financing or listing help for equity. Some prospects were not yet incorporated; his eventual investment vehicle remained a company rather than a conventional fund.
  • His standout example is sms.at, a free SMS portal used by two million people against an Austrian population he puts at roughly nine million. Its teenage operator said he accessed telecom SMS servers, switching countries when shut down. Wolff incorporated the business and approached operators who hated it but wanted an accommodation; he says it sold to T-Mobile for “250 million” within two years.
  • After the deal, his CFO compared its tiny revenue and uncertain monetization with a specialized aluminum business generating 30 million in EBIT. Wolff initially defended the internet’s customer potential; the CFO insisted valuations were unsustainable. Collison’s observation is that investor mythology celebrates early entry and permanent ownership much more readily than the commercial judgment to sell.
  • That challenge prompted a review of nine investments. Beginning in late 1999 and continuing through 2000, they exited everything except an Israeli startup they could not sell. Wolff emphasizes luck and his own incentives: after financial hardship, securing generational wealth mattered. Managing others’ money, with fees and potential carry, might have made him more aggressive.

5. Entrepreneurial ownership changes the decisions a team can make

  • Mercedes had bought Brawn, the 2009 champion, but had only one race win before Wolff’s 2013 arrival. Asked why Williams could match that, he challenged the budget comparison: Mercedes’ additional 100 million went toward Schumacher and Rosberg, while Williams had pay driver Pastor Maldonado. At comparable operating resources, Wolff was targeting the top six, not championships.
  • Mercedes concluded the team needed entrepreneurial authority rather than corporate administration. Wolff initially declined because he was a Williams shareholder and wanted to remain an entrepreneur. Mercedes offered equity and helped finance what he could not conservatively afford. He says the resulting framework lets him make quick decisions and run the team “like a 20-person organization.”
  • Collison compares this freedom with founder-led technology companies. Wolff contrasts his ten-year perspective with managers incentivized over three- or five-year contracts and exposed to dismissal for unapproved decisions. Dietrich Mateschitz’s analogy captures the ability to reverse course: “You need to be like a downhill ski racer, but you need to be able to stop and walk back up the hill.”
  • INEOS entered through sponsorship discussions before COVID, when teams were loss-making and valuations were low. Jim Ratcliffe offered “X hundred million” in sponsorship if he could obtain equity; the arrangement left Mercedes, INEOS and Wolff with one-third each. Wolff values Ratcliffe as an experienced, contrarian resource who does not interfere with operations.

6. Scarcity supports the valuation, but cash generation supports the business

  • Wolff separates ownership motives: scarcity, a lifelong sporting ambition, greater visibility and financial fundamentals. F1 has only 11 teams, with another potentially possible under the rules but little enthusiasm for adding one. Trophy buyers may want prominence or participation; a fundamental investor must examine demographics, league income potential, team earnings and continued growth.
  • Collison first cites a £4.6 billion transaction valuation, up 7x in a few years, then frames it as “$4.6 billion” and approximately 15x EBIT. Wolff reports around $1 billion of revenue and a 30% margin, while stressing that revenue and earnings when he sold were “considerably less.” The exchange does not reconcile the currencies.
  • Unlike the earlier marketing-expense model, some teams now earn more than 30% EBIT margins and distribute dividends. Mercedes has limited capital expenditure because it does not own a stadium, while also missing some associated revenues. Wolff says he could probably generate 30% more than the prior sale valuation, but regards finding the right partner as more important.
  • Wolff favors “fundamental cash flow, and profits” over revenue-based valuations; applying some US sports comparables, he says, would imply 10–12 billion. His long-term optimism also rests on live sport’s resilience to technological change: “Humans watch humans.” The attraction is the individual’s drama and glory, rather than simply discovering how quickly a machine can travel.

7. Entertainment expands the audience because the sport remains credible

  • Wolff admits he did not believe Drive to Survive would work. Mercedes and Ferrari skipped season one while fighting for the championship; he thinks their absence might have helped by giving smaller teams an underdog narrative. COVID then brought multigenerational viewing, while F1’s ability to contain its traveling operation allowed racing to resume.
  • Today’s attraction includes personalities, social media, controversy and politics: a “12-month live reality show.” Wolff insists the foundation is credible competition governed by rules. “Entertainment follows sport, not the other way around.” He cites 42% female fans and identifies young women, roughly 15–25 in his recollection, as the fastest-growing demographic.
  • Collison finds Netflix too focused on soap opera and suggests more technical or racecraft programming; Wolff calls that an idea they had not considered. Audience expansion also remains geographically uneven: F1 is visible in affluent US cities, but much less developed in the middle of the country, where Wolff identifies NASCAR as the established presence.
  • Asked how Mercedes serves these audiences, Wolff broadens the question to stakeholders. His “customer” is someone who makes life better: family, employees, sponsors, shareholders and fans create different priorities. Keeping employees in a good place contributes to a faster car; sponsors need to see a worthwhile investment or platform.

8. Commercial alignment does not eliminate structural tensions

  • Teams receive a substantial share of F1’s profits without owning the league. Liberty and public shareholders own Formula One; the FIA governs and polices the sport, receives payment for services, and granted commercial rights through a 100-year agreement. Wolff describes relations as more aligned today, although profit distribution remains a recurring issue in five-year contract renewals.
  • Wolff doubts a stock-market listing is the right long-term structure. Williams’ listing was unsuccessful, and race results effectively create reporting events around 20 times a year: sentiment goes “from mania to depression within a week.” Collison challenges whether today’s larger sport changes the answer; Wolff remains uncertain about that possibility but prioritizes control.
  • Circuit design exposes another trade-off. Collison argues destinations and good racing can conflict, citing Monaco; Wolff initially resists that framing. On Madrid, he praises the execution but says the layout insufficiently accommodated overtaking with the new cars. Because it is not permanent, he thinks next year’s layout will change to provide more straights.

9. Succession requires distributing authority and limiting interference

  • Wolff rejects legacy-building as the objective: the team must be able to live without him. He believes his role will be divided among two or three people he is currently vetting, already demonstrating different strengths. The structure will lack his particular owner-entrepreneur credibility, but he expects a solid management team can succeed.
  • Continued family ownership probably rules out a clean break; an executive or non-executive chairmanship may follow. Its boundaries must be precise: maintaining relationships is different from interfering in daily operations or criticizing successors from the sidelines. Family members must earn operational responsibility, and his children currently have no interest. For now, he still enjoys running the team too much.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/toto-wolff-built-most-valuable-team-f1

item.title: A World Model of Life: Biohub's Alex Rives on Virtual Cells, Measurement, & the $1.8B Data Push
item.description: Biohub’s $1.8B initiative joins the Department of Energy, NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta to map molecular readouts and imaging. Rives calls observability a fundamental bottleneck; a laser phase plate adds phase contrast in cryo-electron tomography, but virtual cells still cannot meaningfully simulate cells. Atlas drafts target one or two years, with a comprehensive map within five.
item.content:encoded:
The Cognitive Revolution · Alex Rives、Nathan Labenz · 2026-10-20 · 65 min · 原语言 EN

Biohub’s $1.8B initiative joins the Department of Energy, NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta to map molecular readouts and imaging. Rives calls observability a fundamental bottleneck; a laser phase plate adds phase contrast in cryo-electron tomography, but virtual cells still cannot meaningfully simulate cells. Atlas drafts target one or two years, with a comprehensive map within five.

TL;DR

  • Biohub just announced a $1.8B expansion of its Virtual Biology Initiative, coordinating the Department of Energy, NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta on data generation for a general model of cellular biology. The effort aims to build contextual maps — spatial biology linking molecular readouts to imaging “at the scale of hundreds of billions or more cells” — with an open call for other funders and the worldwide scientific community to join.
  • Rives sees observability as a particularly fundamental bottleneck for virtual cell models, but not the only one. “There’s so much about the cell that we just can’t measure”; progress requires models, data generation at scale, and observation tools. He says today’s models “just don’t meet the definition of a model that could actually simulate the cell in a meaningful way and serve as an oracle for experimental biology.”
  • The attainable five-year target is an “information-theoretic model of the cell” — a probabilistic transition function from cell state plus inputs to a distribution of next states — building toward “a world model of life.” In “the limit of infinite data and compute,” architectures probably end up the same; cellular biology is far from that limit, so inductive bias still matters.
  • Measurement hardware is where Biohub’s thesis gets expressed: the laser phase plate — “the most powerful standing-wave laser in the world” — brings phase contrast to cryo-electron tomography, helping scientists make out individual molecules and how they interact in the living cell. Biohub also uses whole-organism zebrafish imaging to track every cell from embryo to fully developed organism.
  • The LLM playbook transfers to biology: pretraining on statistical patterns, elicitation, then “RLVR for biology” with lab verification — “empirical AI” that asks a question, performs the experiment, learns, and proposes a better one in a recursive loop. Unlike math and coding, verification must happen in the laboratory, not through fast computation.
  • Timeline and payoff: first drafts of health-and-disease cell atlases within one or two years, a “pretty comprehensive map” within five — then the question becomes “How do I intervene to reverse a state that’s pathologic?” Rives says he has thought less about EHR data; he worries that without a causal basis, models could learn “a bunch of correlations,” while acknowledging that health records could help get existing drugs and care to the right patients.
  • The man building toward curing all disease tracks little about his own health: “I have a watch that tracks my sleep. That’s about as far as it gets.” On fusing language and biology latent spaces, he is unsure; the biological facts we most want to know may not be represented in text and can require experiments to discover.

Digest

1. “Curing all disease” means a world without disease — not a promise of immortality — and medicines you can program

  • Pressed by Nathan on whether the mission implies living forever, Rives calls himself “a practical person” and sets his sights on a world without cancer, infectious disease, or chronic and degenerative conditions, rather than promising immortality.
  • The therapeutic ambition goes beyond the “current medical paradigm, the therapeutic paradigm of pills and molecules” toward “far more programmable medicines” grounded in “reading and writing the programs of biology.” Disease is part of the program and “often unfolds in very regular ways,” which could provide new tools for understanding and intervening.
  • Nathan’s two-part taxonomy — learn the causal structure, then design the intervention — Rives accepts as “the classic framework of drug development,” but argues the information-theoretic view of cells as systems of rules and code “opens up a wider aperture” than target-then-molecule.

2. Why virtual cells fall short: you can’t model what you can’t measure

  • Rives says the cell is “maybe the right mesoscale” for thinking about biology, spanning molecular events and the larger context of tissue, physiology, and the organism — and notes that the transformer does not have the multiscale structure to represent all those levels.
  • More fundamental than architecture is observability: “There’s so much about the cell that we just can’t measure. Sometimes we can’t see it at all.” He points to new measurement and observation technologies as a source of many advances in biology.
  • Three legs must advance together — modeling, data generation at scale that reveals “the information architecture and programs of the cell in their statistical structure,” and observation tools. Rives says today’s so-called virtual cells do not meet the definition of a model that could meaningfully simulate the cell and serve as an oracle for experimental biology.

3. The five-year object: an information-theoretic cell model, en route to “a world model of life”

  • Architecture agnosticism, properly hedged: in the limit of infinite data and compute, models are “just function approximators” and probably end up the same. Cellular biology is far from that limit; protein biology, with sequencing at scale, is an area where researchers can get closer. Away from the limit, inductive bias matters.
  • Of biology’s two ways of thinking — bottom-up from chemical and physical principles versus the emergent informational view of “the cell as an information-processing machine with a genome that encodes the programs that run life” — Rives says the latter could be attainable via AI in the next five years.
  • The first concrete target, aligned with Nathan’s input/output framing, is a transition function from state and inputs to the next state — probabilistic, since the cell transitions “to a distribution of possible downstream states.” The eventual model would represent molecular complexity and cell programs, allowing development and interactions to unfold: “a world model of life.”

4. The $1.8B push: DOE, NIH, DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta coordinate on data

  • The Virtual Biology Initiative was announced in April; the flagship partnership — Department of Energy, NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta — was announced “the day before yesterday,” with an open call for other funders and the worldwide scientific community to join.
  • The effort aims to dramatically expand contextual maps of cellular biology: spatial biology showing cells in tissue, linking molecular-level measurements to imaging “at the scale of hundreds of billions or more cells,” and producing the first datasets for training contextual information-theoretic models.

5. Measurement is the moat: a laser phase plate and transparent fish

  • The laser phase plate, imagined by Holger Müller at Berkeley decades ago and supported by Biohub’s investment for years, uses “the most powerful standing-wave laser in the world” to shift the electron beam’s phase and provide phase contrast in cryo-electron tomography. That contrast helps scientists make out individual molecules in their living context and understand what they are and how they interact.
  • Biohub’s program includes increasing the parameters measured per cell, expanding the field of view and number of cells observed simultaneously, and opening up the temporal and molecular dimensions.
  • On Nathan’s scale-bridging concern — “a single point mutation in a gene can cause disease” — Rives says identifying an entire system down to the molecular level is not possible in the near future. The answer is to learn at the mesoscale and build models that integrate across biological hierarchies. Cells in culture and transformed cells are imperfect proxies for in-situ tissue, but retain core machinery and can still teach us about cellular biology. Biohub’s imaging institute is developing tools across levels of complexity: zebrafish are transparent, so its microscopes can track every cell from a one-cell embryo to a fully developed organism, or follow labeled immune cells moving through living tissue.

6. “In mice” isn’t the bug — evolution-wide transfer is the feature

  • Nathan asks why treatments that work in mice seem not to work in humans more often, given how much biological machinery is conserved. Rives says over-relying on model organisms can fail both ways: you may think a cancer cure works when “it only works in mice,” or miss a human-relevant mechanism because mice do not provide a good proxy.
  • The precedent from Rives’ ESM background: ESM and AlphaFold were not trained just on human proteins. Information across evolution is essential; a model trained only on human proteins would not be accurate.
  • Across life, and especially vertebrates, much core molecular machinery is conserved, while “the programs are completely rewired, but they’re built with the same building blocks.” Organoids are a newer experimental proxy for human biology, but Rives argues that rather than seeking a perfect proxy, models can learn from information across different systems.

7. Pretraining, elicitation, then RLVR with lab verification — “empirical AI”

  • Rives expects biology to follow shared AI principles: pretraining learns the underlying system from statistical patterns, then elicitation brings out “the part of that model which is relevant to the problem.” He connects this to the Hinton, LeCun, and Bengio vision of learning variables and parameters rather than encoding them by hand, with scaling laws as a clear expression of that progress.
  • The hoped-for next step is “RLVR for biology” and “empirical AI”: systems that ask a question, perform an experiment, learn from it, propose a better experiment, and repeat the cycle. Unlike math and coding, biology requires systems that can verify predictions in the laboratory.
  • Timelines, as hedged: atlases of cellular biology across health and disease are “a scaling challenge” addressable with today’s technology — first drafts within one or two years, and a “pretty comprehensive map” within five with a focused, coordinated effort. Such maps could support classical analysis as well as models that identify disease-relevant cell states and help answer: “How do I intervene to reverse a state that’s pathologic and bring it into a healthy state?”

8. Open questions: EHRs, latent fusion — and Rives’ own biomarkers

  • Rives says he has not thought as much about health records. His concern is that patient-history models could produce “a bunch of correlations” without linking them to deeper causal factors in biology. He also sees potential for records to improve care by getting existing drugs and mechanisms to the right people, while arguing that this alone would not reach the biological fundamentals required for a step change.
  • On co-training language and biology into one latent space, he is genuinely uncertain. Language can draw on centuries of empirical knowledge, but the biological facts we most want to know are not represented in text, cannot be derived from first principles or existing knowledge, and may only be discovered through experiments. Fusion may be hard at first because bridging data is scarce, though he says it could be interesting eventually. Protein language models already develop features for unknown biology — “novel concepts that we don’t have words or names for yet” — amid billions of sequenced proteins whose functions are mostly unknown.
  • Nathan’s million-Bryan-Johnsons proposal — longitudinal human phenotyping with micro-biopsies and sensors — gets a qualified yes: Rives says the data would be “immensely valuable” and likely to happen over time. Biohub focuses on its technology layer, including continuous monitoring that measures more parameters, including molecular ones, to link bottom-up and top-down views.
  • Asked for personal health advice, Rives says, “I’m not the right person to ask for that kind of advice” and barely thinks about it: “I have a watch that tracks my sleep. That’s about as far as it gets.”

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/world-model-life-biohub-s-alex-rives-virtual-cel

item.title: 168X 对话 Frank Trading：AI Trade 结束之后，下一笔大交易在哪里？
item.description: Frank 认为四年 AI 牛市可能接近尾声，OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 不及预期，云厂商 free cash flow 转负。供给追上需求后，外溢订单可能回流龙头；他的英伟达／AMD 配对交易押注相对强弱，开源也可能分流 token 计费收入。SOXX 收回并站稳 515 才是他尝试翻多的门槛，11月3日中期选举与衰退或滞胀风险仍可能改变方向。
item.content:encoded:
168X · Frank Trading · 2026-10-20 · 49 min · 原语言 ZH

Frank 认为四年 AI 牛市可能接近尾声，OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 不及预期，云厂商 free cash flow 转负。供给追上需求后，外溢订单可能回流龙头；他的英伟达／AMD 配对交易押注相对强弱，开源也可能分流 token 计费收入。SOXX 收回并站稳 515 才是他尝试翻多的门槛，11月3日中期选举与衰退或滞胀风险仍可能改变方向。

TL;DR

  • Frank 认为四年 AI 牛市可能已到尾声，但长期看空不妨碍短线翻多。 他把 OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 不及预期视为增长与融资信心的拐点。云厂商 free cash flow 已转负，若投资意愿和融资放缓，维持同等规模的基建会更困难。“不要跟股票谈恋爱”，相信 AI 是产业革命，不等于相信 AI 股票还能继续涨。
  • 指数空头最顺的一段可能已经过去，后续更依赖小仓位与关键价位。 他披露在纳指 31,250 附近重仓做空、SOXX 跌破 555 左右后加仓，如今认为最流畅的一段下跌可能已经过去。SOXX 的 500、515、530 是逐级反弹观察位；要收回 515 并站稳、包括在韩国交易时段站稳，他才认为有尝试做多的理由。
  • 他的 reverse bottleneck 瞄准订单外溢退潮后的弱者，而非无差别空掉 AI。 大小厂同时扩产后，供给迟早追上需求，客户会回到龙头；英伟达／AMD 等 pair trade 交易的是相对强弱。“半导体和猪有什么区别呢？没有区别，都是一样的。”
  • 11月3日中期选举是政策分叉，不能预设选后 AI 会获救。 Frank 认为民主党“一定会打 anti-AI 的牌”，若横扫两院，会卡数据中心建设，提高债务上限的谈判和放宽金融公司、大银行监管的政策也可能回撤；长债可能是最优标的。若两党分控两院，他反而认为对股票更友好。
  • 他的明年基准是衰退熊市，比特币能否接棒则没有确定答案。 他认为 AI CapEx 一降，美国经济可能“立刻就衰退”；油价、服务业通胀若不退，则可能走向滞胀。降息且金融条件不紧时，黄金、比特币可能承接资金，但若演变为信用危机，比特币也难独善其身。
  • 非 AI 多头里，他已经买入印度，DIA 则已结束短线任务。 他认为印度基本面“并没有变差”，油价与卢比冲击下仍有强劲内资承接；亚洲 long-short 交易平仓也可能带来买盘。Jio IPO 与 Oil Dollar Window 是额外催化；DIA 只是长债利率回落后的估值修复仓，现已离场。
  • 消费端的新配对是多 ROST、空 XLY，押注财富效应退潮后的消费降级。 他近期新开 XLY 空头，并点名希尔顿、RCL、Starbucks：这些公司仍在前高附近，但股市下跌可能削弱消费能力。对低价零售商 ROST 的多头保留居民仍有购买力的前提；对空腿则说：“下周只要加息，这些公司全都会死。”
  • 开源削弱模型能力的稀缺性，长线机会仍可能留在龙头与端侧。 他所谓“token 计费必然走向终结”，指收入大头从目前可能 80%—90% 的 token 收费分流，而非彻底消失。模型缩小、成本下降，让他看好 Qcom、ARM 等端侧方向；对真正长期投资者，他仍认可英伟达、台积电的龙头地位与估值。

Digest

1. 看空四年牛市，不等于放弃任何一段反弹

  • Frank 开场先划清长期观点与中短期操作：他认为持续四年的 AI 牛市可能已经结束，但若美联储、沃什、特朗普、伊朗或 AI 内部出现大利好，仍可以平空翻多。做交易不能因为自己的 ego，错过与长期判断方向不同的行情。
  • 他举 9 月中旬的交易为例：当时已经非常看空，但看到纳指 100 跌不破，又认为 9 月 FOMC 倾向于 double cut，仍抄底 SMH、SOXX 等半导体股票，做了一轮反弹后在高点附近退出。在他看来，这与长期看空“并不冲突”。
  • 对刚出现的反弹，他的解释却是集中空头回补，而非趋势翻多。“不要接 falling knife”：他判断这轮内生性暴跌不会立刻出现 V 型反转，盘前或盘中看到涨得好就买，更接近上当，而不是抄底。

2. ARR 不及预期，先击穿的是继续融资的信心

  • Frank 把 OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 双双不及预期视作 AI growth 的拐点。低于 3,000 亿美元估值进场的早期投资者或许不慌；但今年 6 月按约 1.5 万亿美元估值买入 Anthropic、现在回到成本线甚至被套的人，再被问要不要新份额，未必愿意继续加码。融资意愿减弱，可能进一步影响后续融资和扩建。
  • 他提到 AI 公司的 CapEx：9 月大约只有 8 月的 40% 多、6 月的 10%—20%。他的逻辑是，云厂 free cash flow 早已转负，不借钱就很难维持相同甚至更大规模的基建；ARR 不及预期会削弱投资者继续投入的“信心和决心”。
  • 主持人追问：下个月的 Anthropic、以及包含 2027 年 OpenAI IPO 在内的事情，谁来兜底？他的回答是“没有人兜底”，并称 OpenAI 去年 10 月试探特朗普时，对方明确说不会兜底。市场里还有其他 AI 公司，并不存在必须拯救某一家模型厂的最终买家。
  • 尚待验证的分叉是：ARR 不及预期究竟因为有订单却产能跟不上，还是因为客户改用千问、DeepSeek、Gemini？他列出的跟踪项包括付费需求、收入增速、新增收入、企业客户换模型、多模型分流与私有部署，以及云厂是否愿意提前向美光等公司锁定产能、交付周期是否缩短。

3. Beta 空头转向小仓位，515 是尝试翻多的门槛

  • 他披露在纳指 31,250 附近开始重仓做空，SOXX 跌破约 555 后再次加仓。如今最流畅的一段下跌可能已经过去，而 AI 泡沫结束尚未成为市场共识；后续消息可能把多空来回打，因此倾向保持小仓位空头，再按技术位置调整。
  • 他给多头的门槛是 SOXX 收回 500、515，尤其 515 须站稳，在韩国交易时段也能站稳；500、515、530 是逐级反弹参考。套牢者不必等三个位置全部走完：反弹失败就减一点，失守关键位再退一步，而不是等到无法回头才处理。
  • 这次下跌的速度、幅度和六七月份那波相近甚至更快，但 VXN 距 7 月高点仍差将近 10 点。Frank 的解读是，这一波很多人根本没有买 put；暴跌是因为真的有人在出货。他把六七月份的回调看作杠杆破灭、基本面未坏，而现在认为基本面坏了，市场上很多人也在出货。
  • 当主持人问什么信号才算真正的转折，他说已经看到了：ARR 不及预期，SOXX 两周跌了快 20%，韩国市场已经跌崩。多头应该反过来问，出现什么转折点之后才值得做多，而不是继续追问何时才算进入熊市。

4. 现金是可选项，保住利润比证明信仰重要

  • 对看不懂的行情，他的反问是：“这个钱我一定要赚吗？”他提到在 Robinhood 存美元、年化 7% 的做法，称自己也存了不少；“一年 7% 也不少”，没有必要每一局都参与。
  • 他自报年内收益 440% 多，账户基本没有特别大的回撤；一些朋友年中曾赚 10 倍、20 倍，后来 YTD 收益却归零、转负，甚至有人爆仓。他惋惜的不是他们不够相信 AI，而是没有保住已经赚到的钱。
  • 主持人据此推断，未来 6—9 个月他是否都会留现金，Frank 随即回应：“明年看不了那么远。”他确认的只是明年走衰退路径的基本预期，并没有把当前仓位外推成未来半年不变的配置。

5. Reverse bottleneck 交易的是短缺红利消退

  • Frank 用生猪解释半导体周期：短缺时所有人一起养猪，等供给同时出来，猪价反而暴跌。“半导体和猪有什么区别？没有区别，都是一样的。”他认定供需不会恰好相等后静止，扩产最终一定会把紧缺推向过剩。
  • 在他的观察中，2025 年后涨得较少的反而是英伟达、台积电；Intel、AAOI、GSS、TTMI 等公司因龙头产能不足，拿到外溢订单、收取高价，才出现基本面反转。等供给够了，客户既然买英伟达就能满足需求，为什么还要把多余预算分给 AMD？
  • “当供给追上需求，过去的赢家就会变成输家。”他用英伟达／AMD，以及 Lumentum／AAOI 的股价比值说明相对强弱：Lumentum 自身一直暴跌，但比值近期在上升。他认为这种 pair trade 合理。
  • 模型会越做越小、越便宜，可能不再需要那么多半导体；美国即便需要很多半导体，也没有电。Frank 预期需求减弱与供给放量会产生错配，而“市场交易的是预期”，所以现在就开始做这件事；至少可以把这个想法放在心上，不一定要做。

6. 民主党若横扫两院，长债可能比股票更有利

  • 以 11 月 3 日中期选举为分界，Frank 当时的估计是：民主党拿下众院近乎确定，拿下参院的概率六成多。因此他列出三种可能：民主党横扫两院、两党五五开、共和党横扫两院；他认为共和党横扫的概率非常小，暂不考虑。
  • 他的政策逻辑来自地方反对：居民觉得数据中心抢电，且在当地没有很强的正外部性，甚至有很强的负外部性；就业者也担心 AI 抢工作。民主党在野时“一定会打 anti-AI 的牌”，若横扫两院，他认为会在地方政府层面卡数据中心建设，理由包括就业、居民电费、土地和水资源。
  • 风险不限于 AI。提高债务上限的谈判，以及放宽金融公司和大银行监管的政策限制，也可能面临回撤。在民主党横扫的情景下，他认为最优标的是长债，其他板块可能都会跌；若两党五五开，他反而觉得对股票来说可能是比较好的环境。

7. 和平协议也不能立即修复炼油瓶颈

  • 主持人提出另一种剧本：未来两周会不会突然出现俄乌战争平息、伊朗达成和平协议，让局势平息？Frank 不认同：“他要是想达成协议，早就达成了。”只剩不到两周，他判断特朗普搞不定了。
  • 他区分原油与成品油：原油有一定出口量、供应够，不代表汽柴油问题解决；炼油厂被炸后，crack（裂解价差）持续扩大，汽油、柴油价格仍在攀升。炼厂恢复需要相当长时间，即使伊朗投降、美国投降或原油供给恢复，也不可能立即改善居民与工业的用油情况。

8. 基准是衰退或滞胀，比特币要看资金如何定义它

  • Frank 把美国描述为 K 型经济，提到 2024 年第三季度曾触发 Sahm Rule；在他的判断里，这几年的美国经济增长完全靠 AI CapEx 支撑，因此 CapEx 一降就可能“立刻衰退”。他的明年基本预期是衰退路径，甚至可能出现“史无前例的衰退型大熊市”。
  • 若衰退促使联储停止加息或降息，黄金与比特币可能承接热钱；但比特币盘子小，能接多少他也“不好说”。若油价与服务业通胀不退、联储仍很强硬，则可能走向更坏的滞胀；他认为软着陆或“金发女郎”剧本的概率非常低。
  • 主持人凭记忆提到比特币与纳指的相关系数约 0.3—0.4，对它能否独强保留看法。Frank 承认“看得不是特别清楚”：股票受连续财报 miss、下调预期的盈利压力约束，币则更像筹码游戏；若大资金按“数字黄金”交易，经济变差、利率下降后持有成本变低，比特币反而可能走牛。
  • 极端情况则是另一回事：若 CoreWeave 暴雷或破产、Oracle 也破产，出现类似金融危机的场景，“所有东西都要跌，包括比特币”。他也澄清，以前说比特币“看归零”只是情绪上的反应，“不代表我的真实想法”，不能当作他目前的确定判断。

9. DIA 多单只是利率回落后的估值修复

  • 谈到主持人看到的 DIA 多单，Frank 先更正：已经走了。他把 DIA 当作成熟公司占主导的仓位：此前 AI 高增长预期推高实际与名义利率，压缩这些公司的估值；OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 不及预期后，AI 增长预期破裂、美国长债利率下降，才给了估值修复机会。
  • 他并不把 DIA 当作衰退或滞胀中的避风港：大银行持有企业债，CAT 的相当一部分增长来自 AI 相关采购，GS 的并购、做市收入也可能受影响。若 AI 投资和股市活动继续冷却，这些公司的盈利同样有问题；“DIA 只是短线的一个打野仓位”。

10. 印度多头押的是基本面与资金流背离

  • Frank 认为印度基本面没变差：上半年增速很快，银行坏账率接近历史低位。下跌来自缺油、采购中东原油消耗美元，继而压低卢比、吓跑外资。按他的估计，外资每月大概卖出 500 亿美元；股市却只跌十几个百分点，而非他设想的 30%，说明内资承接很强。
