item.title: Jeffrey Quesnelle on Nous Research, large language models, and the human mind
item.description: Nous Research’s bet is that open AI needs the capacity to train foundation models independently, with Psyche coordinating distributed GPU participation. Quesnelle says DisTrO cuts training communication requirements by roughly 1,000:1, though each node still needs substantial fast memory and local interconnect. The approach could make frontier research less dependent on a few model publishers, while verification bottlenecks and unresolved safety risks remain.
item.content:encoded:
Sina Habibian Podcast · Sina Habibian、Jeffrey Quesnelle · 2025-10-28 · 126 min · 原语言 EN

Nous Research’s bet is that open AI needs the capacity to train foundation models independently, with Psyche coordinating distributed GPU participation. Quesnelle says DisTrO cuts training communication requirements by roughly 1,000:1, though each node still needs substantial fast memory and local interconnect. The approach could make frontier research less dependent on a few model publishers, while verification bottlenecks and unresolved safety risks remain.

TL;DR

  • Nous Research’s central bet is that open AI needs its own capacity to train foundation models. Quesnelle argues that an ecosystem dependent on a “benevolent third party” releasing models cannot reliably keep pace with closed labs. Psyche is intended to coordinate distributed GPU training, making participation in frontier research less dependent on one company’s willingness to publish its work.
  • Quesnelle says DisTrO reduces training communication requirements by roughly 1,000:1, opening a path to training across ordinary internet connections. His analogy is JPEG: transmit the important components of an update instead of its complete representation. The constraint remains material—each participating node still needs enough fast memory and local interconnect to run the model, so compression does not eliminate demand for substantial GPU infrastructure.
  • Reinforcement learning adds another dimension of AI scaling by turning successful reasoning attempts into training data. Quesnelle describes models searching for solutions, receiving rewards for verifiably correct answers, and feeding those successes back into their weights: “dynamically generating the training data.” Math and programming provide clean starting points; he sees hints of benefits elsewhere, while Habibian presses on the difficulty of verifying scientific discoveries and subjective work.
  • Quesnelle thinks today’s limits on coding agents are “very likely” to disappear within two to three years. His forecast includes agents running experiments and reasoning about code better than the best humans, even though he currently uses AI sparingly because his hardest problems concern subtle bugs and infrastructure. Habibian’s response is to prioritize fundamentals, taste, and judgment; Quesnelle’s distinction is that “AI can’t understand something for you because it is not you.”
  • Decentralization is Nous’s proposed answer to the concentration of power that increasingly capable AI could create. Quesnelle describes a race in which the first organization to enter a self-improvement loop might gain an overwhelming advantage. His argument for broad access starts from irreversibility—“you can’t control matrix multiplication”—and aims to give individuals access to comparable intelligence without relying on a single company or nation-state.
  • Quesnelle favors liability for deployed AI over centralized control of what models may learn, but leaves long-term superintelligence safety unresolved. His near-term proposal is the “dog rule”: the organization deploying an AI bears responsibility for its actions, creating an incentive to constrain harmful behavior. Habibian supports distributing power while emphasizing that more individual leverage also means more capacity for damage; neither offers a settled answer to the ASI problem.
  • The conversation treats AI as both an economic transformation and an experiment in what intelligence actually is. Quesnelle calls the coming decade a “Second Industrial Revolution of thought and intelligence,” while carefully distinguishing similar cognitive phenomena from proof that brains and models work identically. His Catholic faith and Habibian’s meditation practice frame the remaining questions about consciousness, meaning, and human identity.

Digest

1. AI can replace output without supplying personal understanding

  • Despite spending his working life on AI, Quesnelle describes himself as a light user, especially for coding. After roughly 20 years programming, the problems he cannot solve tend to involve nuanced failures, hallucination-prone edge cases, or the organization of servers and infrastructure. Current models, in his experience, struggle to leave their box and investigate those systems directly.
  • That assessment comes with a forceful expiration warning: every AI “it can’t” has “fallen mercilessly in the last five years.” He thinks it is “very likely” that within two to three years agents will run experiments, interact with the world, and reason about code better than the best humans. He leaves open how he will work once that happens.
  • Habibian’s response is to focus on the fundamentals needed to choose worthwhile problems and judge generated work. Quesnelle agrees, but separates economic output from understanding: “AI can’t understand something for you because it is not you.” Always having an answer available creates the temptation of a textbook where “every answer is right in the back of the book.”

2. A creative constraint became a context-length experiment

  • Nous’s origin story begins with Quesnelle building a Choose Your Own Adventure project. He loved science fiction and fantasy but considered himself a poor creative writer and artist. AI offered a way to express ideas through capabilities he lacked, complementing his strength in programming rather than simply making his existing work faster.
  • The immediate constraint was context: his T5 model had 512 tokens, Llama offered 2K, and ChatGPT offered 4K. Longer stories required longer memory. Rather than accept the limit, he stepped through the Python code and experimented with positional embeddings—the information that lets attention distinguish where tokens occur within a sequence.
  • His discovery was that rescaling positional values could extend usable context. Dividing positions by two let the model accommodate roughly 4K within the positional range previously used for 2K: positions became 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2. What had looked like a fundamental barrier could, in this case, be changed through a small intervention after training.
  • Quesnelle’s framing is that the model had treated its training boundary almost like a law of nature: it had never encountered a sequence beyond 2,048, so position 2,049 was outside its world. The experiment also illustrates his broader fascination with AI’s plasticity: floating-point representations can accommodate changes that would seem nonsensical in ordinary integer-based program logic.

3. A private Discord became a lab with an open-access mission

  • Posting the context-length experiment on the LocalLLaMA subreddit brought Quesnelle into contact with Bowen, now Nous’s chief scientist, who had been exploring related ideas. A subsequent Twitter post led to an invitation from Teknium to a private Discord of roughly 30 researchers. Quesnelle recognized the participants and felt he had “broken into the club.”
  • That group became the Nous Research Discord. His deliberately informal account is that they were “homies on the Discord” who grew into something larger. The shared principle was practical openness: being able to run a model on a 4090, step through its code, inspect its behavior, and remove barriers preventing other people from doing the same.
  • Nous described its mission as an “open AI accelerator.” The next barrier was dependence on foundation models released by Meta and a small number of other organizations. Before Llama 3 arrived, the team asked what would happen if there were no Llama 3—or no Llama 4. Open research needed a credible way to remain in the race independently.

4. Heavy investment has not exhausted the research frontier

  • Habibian’s pushback is an efficient-market argument: with so much capital, talent, and attention directed at AI, why assume accessible discoveries remain? Quesnelle sees the opposite—a “vast, unexplored field of science.” His claim is that promising ideas often remain untested, rather than having already been disproved, and meaningful advances in architecture and data continue to appear every few months.
  • His example is Multi-Head Latent Attention in DeepSeek V2. He describes projecting attention queries and keys into lower dimensions, performing the operation there, and scaling back up, claiming roughly 90% lower memory use with the same results. Small code changes matter because they operate at enormous scale; greater data and compute also keep producing improvements, making part of progress a “throw more money at it problem.”

5. The software abstraction quietly dictated the physical infrastructure

  • For Quesnelle, access to text data was not the central obstacle to independent foundation-model training: the relevant material was largely the internet. The harder problems were obtaining GPUs and coordinating them. Habibian frames the practical barrier as raising money and procuring H100s before a researcher can even test an architectural idea.
  • Training software grew around a “single device paradigm”: developers write as though one enormous GPU holds the model. This keeps the research code remarkably compact—Quesnelle says a GPT implementation can be around 40 lines—while layers beneath it distribute computation. A single matrix-multiplication line can therefore conceal a vast physical operation and substantial energy consumption.
  • Preserving that abstraction across many GPUs encouraged homogeneous clusters in one data center, with matching hardware, memory, and predictable connections. Quesnelle cites 400- or 800-gigabit-per-second networking and cables costing around $1,000 a foot. The arrangement makes moving data sufficiently fast that researchers can largely ignore where individual pieces of the model actually reside.
  • Internet training breaks those assumptions through heterogeneous machines, uneven latency, and far less bandwidth. Quesnelle compares the internal connectivity of a 72-chip Nvidia GB200 rack with the capacity of the entire internet. His point is the scale of the mismatch: decentralized training required orders-of-magnitude less communication, not merely a better scheduler for the existing approach.

6. DisTrO treats gradient communication like image compression

  • Nous spent about a year investigating whether training fundamentally required sharing so much information, or whether that requirement reflected how tooling had developed. Quesnelle’s analogy is that unlimited bandwidth would have left everyone sharing bitmap images and uncompressed video. JPEG became necessary because useful communication had to fit a constrained channel; gradients presented a similar opportunity.
  • A gradient describes how each model parameter should change to reduce prediction error, producing an update representation comparable in size to the model itself. DisTrO transforms that information into the frequency domain using a discrete cosine transform. Instead of exchanging the entire gradient, nodes communicate selected components and use the inverse transform to reconstruct updates.
  • The selection rule is top-K: transmit the largest accumulated frequency components. Strong signals can travel immediately, while smaller signals remain and accumulate until they become large enough to communicate. Quesnelle says sharing this small fraction is sufficient to get the same results in the model, delivering an approximately 1,000:1 reduction in required bandwidth.
  • Asked what those frequencies actually mean, he gives an honest non-answer: “That we don’t know.” The method identifies a useful mathematical representation without establishing what each component means conceptually. Bowen’s signal-processing background supplied the connection; getting it to work still required sustained experimentation and, Quesnelle says, enough faith to continue before convincing evidence arrived.

7. Psyche adds coordination without removing every hardware constraint

  • Once communication became tractable, the remaining problem was coordinating participants without a central server or trusted middleman, including in an adversarial environment. Quesnelle’s answer is decentralized consensus with economic security—“crypto rails.” Psyche combines that coordination layer with the training techniques, aiming to support permissionless participation in training one large model or multiple models.
  • Habibian asks why conventional data centers would not simply adopt DisTrO too. Quesnelle agrees that they could: two facilities owned by one operator are an obvious hybrid application. However, DisTrO operates after backpropagation, so each node still needs to execute the model using fast memory. A node might therefore comprise multiple tightly connected HGX systems rather than one individual GPU.
  • Mixture-of-experts models expose another research frontier: distributing experts across separate nodes instead of requiring the whole model within each node. Quesnelle wants Psyche to incentivize work on that problem. At the recording, he says the testnet will arrive “very soon,” enabling compute contributions, alongside an announced model intended to demonstrate where the network is heading.

8. Deep learning advanced when architectures became less task-specific

  • Quesnelle starts his technical history with AlexNet defeating hand-engineered approaches in the ImageNet competition. Earlier AI had tried to encode expert knowledge into rules; the neural-network result showed that learning could outperform sophisticated instructions written by people. It also provided a reason to commit more effort to neural networks rather than the many competing approaches researchers might pursue.
  • His autonomous-driving experience belongs to the next phase: networks assembled for specific tasks such as lane detection. They worked better than conventional code but remained brittle. Researchers combined convolutions, normalization layers, and other components like Lego, then tuned hyperparameters until the arrangement worked. A different task could require a substantially different architecture and another round of engineering.
  • The Transformer’s importance, in his telling, was generality and resilience. “Attention Is All You Need” introduced an attention operation that learned which relationships to emphasize, rather than requiring a bespoke structure for every application. Quesnelle describes attention as a particular arrangement of matrix multiplications whose usefulness extends across tasks and modalities.
  • He distinguishes the original encoder-decoder design, which transformed one sequence into another for applications such as translation, from today’s predominantly decoder-only models. Those generate a sequence autoregressively, one token at a time. His historical reference point for translation is around 2016–2017; next-token generation is a subsequent step in the account, not the Transformer’s original task.

9. Foundation models made intuitive reasoning experimentally accessible

  • The foundation-model idea was to exploit the enormous supply of text by modeling the internet itself. Quesnelle characterizes the ambition as compressing human knowledge and understanding into one model. This pretraining stage accounts for the bulk of the work and supplies the underlying capability that later instruction-following and other refinements build upon.
  • Another crucial discovery was in-context learning: a trained model could follow instructions expressed in text it had never previously encountered. It was not merely replaying a fixed task learned during training. New directions inside the prompt could influence how it represented the problem and generated its response, making the general foundation model useful for many subsequent purposes.
  • The deeper claim is that next-token prediction, matrix multiplication, and backpropagation can elicit what Quesnelle calls intuitive reasoning. Humanity now has at least one procedure that produces the phenomenon and can experiment with it. He suggests that something about the process may be isomorphic to human cognition, while stopping short of establishing the same underlying biological mechanism.

10. Language compresses a richer internal representation

  • Quesnelle’s proposed parallel with the mind is a high-dimensional representation space. “Blue” can activate associations involving cold, water, and other properties; the word is a compact way to invoke that richer internal state. Many underlying dimensions may have no corresponding word at all. Language therefore communicates a compressed account of understanding rather than containing the whole understanding itself.
  • In his evolutionary account, organisms needed to respond quickly to unfamiliar situations to obtain energy and survive. Catching a ball is his concrete example: people act immediately without explicitly calculating the trajectories and muscle dynamics. He describes this intuitive pattern recognition as operating within an internal representation shaped by survival pressures—his analogy for the human training objective.
  • Speech then enabled cooperation by allowing people to exchange pieces of those internal representations. Quesnelle connects this to DisTrO: “We’re creating words for the gradients.” The important difference is that two humans do not share identical internal models. Hearing the same word can therefore produce different interpretations and changes in understanding, even when communication appears straightforward.
  • Habibian sees nested parallels between a training node, an individual mind, and communication between people. Quesnelle tightens the claim: models and minds give rise to “apparently equivalent phenomena.” That does not establish that they are the same thing. Human cognition likely involves multiple interacting systems rather than one monolithic model.

11. Chain-of-thought gives intuition more time to work

  • Habibian describes writing as external memory: a document lets him hold, rearrange, and revisit more than working memory alone permits. He connects this to Ted Chiang’s “The Truth of Fact, the Truth of Feeling” and the possibility that language itself adds external state to cognition. Quesnelle’s provocative formulation is that humanity’s “original sin was the written word.”
  • For Quesnelle, reasoning is the “ordered application of intuition.” Earlier efforts tried to build the structured part before supplying the underlying intuitive capabilities. Once language models possessed those capabilities, the instruction “let’s think about this step by step” substantially improved performance by making them generate intermediate work before giving an answer.
  • The strawberry counting problem illustrates the difference. Producing an immediate answer requires fitting the task into one forward pass; deliberate counting requires intermediate operations. Quesnelle challenges human superiority here by asking how many instances of a letter occur in a much longer spoken passage. People also lose immediate access to the answer once the task exceeds their intuitive capacity.
  • The computational point is explicit: one forward pass contains a fixed amount of matrix multiplication. Generating additional tokens allows additional computation before the final answer. A token is, in his metaphor, the model’s basic unit of experienced time. Chain-of-thought initially supplied a practical way to buy more thinking by making the model say more words.

12. Reinforcement learning turns successful searches into new training data

  • Quesnelle presents DeepSeek’s reasoning approach as applying reinforcement learning after intuitive capability already exists. For a verifiable problem, the trainer need not know the correct next token in the reasoning process. The model can explore different paths, while the reward asks whether the eventual answer is correct: “The only thing that matters is whether you get the answer right or not.”
  • That changes the objective from matching supplied text to earning an outcome-based reward. Quesnelle describes reinforcement learning as converting a nondifferentiable score into an objective that can produce gradients through backpropagation. He names GRPO as the method DeepSeek uses. The successful reasoning process then feeds back into the model’s capabilities, rather than remaining only a temporary sequence of generated words.
  • Habibian’s interpretation is that something initially requiring conscious, discursive effort becomes intuitive through practice. Quesnelle agrees, comparing it with mathematicians who immediately see structure in equations and his own experience of “feeling” code. Decades of feedback have made some programming judgments automatic; he describes himself as having undergone manual reinforcement learning.
  • AI changes the scale of that loop. Instead of one person working through an experience once, training can explore thousands or millions of attempts in parallel. Quesnelle calls this “dynamically generating the training data”: search for a reasoning path that earns a correct result, then use that newly discovered example to improve subsequent performance.

13. Verifiable outcomes extend beyond math, but verification remains a bottleneck

  • Habibian presses on where this approach can travel next. Math and programming have comparatively clear correctness checks; biology and other sciences involve heuristics, incomplete models, and experiments. He asks whether models might need access to virtualized laboratories. Subjective fields pose another problem because the desired result depends on taste rather than a single objectively correct answer.
  • Quesnelle says reasoning reinforcement learning is at “day one,” with substantial room before saturation. He also sees hints of transfer: models trained on verifiable tasks can become better writers. If the underlying intuition is sufficiently grounded, he argues, increasingly complex objectives could extend the approach beyond the cleanest technical domains.
  • His example is gaining a million Twitter followers: a verifiable outcome with many possible strategies, from becoming a social-media sensation to becoming president. That flexibility also raises safety concerns. Aesthetics remains less settled: models have absorbed human judgments of beauty, making it difficult to ask what preferences they would have developed independently. “The jury’s still out” on that question.

14. AI combines an industrial transition with a struggle over power

  • Quesnelle compares the coming decade with the Industrial Revolution, which displaced work previously requiring human bodies. He cites, approximately, 60% of Americans and 90% of the world engaged in agrarian activity before around 1880, followed by a dramatic reversal. His forecast is a “Second Industrial Revolution of thought and intelligence,” automating large categories of work previously reserved for humans.
  • The social question is where people fit after those capabilities become widely reproducible. Habibian calls it a difficult transformation on a collective “hero’s journey”; Quesnelle argues it should be treated as an opportunity to take on another class of challenges. Neither presents the transition as frictionless, and Quesnelle links earlier industrial reordering with major conflict.
  • He expects AI to figure in future geopolitical struggles over chips, materials, and access. The alternative he wants is discovery that alleviates problems rather than conflict over the technology; his example is AI helping solve “room-temperature semiconductors.” Psyche’s decentralization is partly intended to preserve access through political turbulence without dependence on one nation-state.
  • The concentration risk becomes sharper if a model can improve itself: Quesnelle describes the first successful loop as potentially creating overwhelming asymmetric power. He likens that prospect to the advantage conferred by atomic weapons and invokes fundraising figures ranging from $500 billion to $5 trillion as an indication of the stakes surrounding the race.

15. Broad access is Nous’s safety strategy, while liability constrains deployment

  • Quesnelle’s starting point is irreversibility: the necessary operations are elementary mathematics, and “you can’t control matrix multiplication” as one can restrict physical nuclear materials. Given that world, Nous aims for comparable access to frontier intelligence across individuals. He rejects the characterization that this position means indifference to safety; he sees distribution as the best available route to broad benefit.
  • Habibian agrees with distributing power but adds the central objection: technology increases individual leverage in both directions, including the capacity to cause damage. His reference to Michael Nielsen’s writing on wise technological optimism is a reminder that this problem does not require a speculative paperclip-maximizing ASI. Ordinary people with increasingly powerful tools already create a serious governance challenge.
  • Quesnelle’s near-term proposal is the “dog rule”: responsibility passes through to the organization deploying an AI into the world. If operators bear the consequences of what their systems do, they have an incentive to build safeguards. He prefers that outcome-based pressure to assuming a central authority can foresee every failure and prescribe the right technical intervention.
  • He is skeptical of safety arguments that culminate in giving their proponents exclusive control. Habibian adds that even a benevolent leader can die or be replaced, so institutional design cannot depend on personal virtue. Quesnelle’s preferred framework uses existing social enforcement, incentives, and penalties, while acknowledging that harmful deployments would still occur and require investigation.

16. Superintelligence remains an unresolved question for both speakers

  • On medium- and long-term ASI risk, Quesnelle says the “jury’s still out.” If a system truly exceeds humans at everything, simply unplugging it is not a complete answer: it could anticipate the attempt and manipulate circumstances beforehand. Designing an objective that reliably prevents domination also risks the familiar genie problem—getting exactly the wrong consequence from an apparently reasonable instruction.
  • His confidence that things will ultimately be okay rests partly on being a devout Catholic, which he explicitly presents as a prior belief. From a wholly materialist, reductionist perspective, he says he would be concerned about ASI. The philosophical reassurance therefore does not amount to a technical resolution of the problem.
  • Asked why continue without solving it, Quesnelle returns to the world already at hand: the technology exists, and his task is to improve what he can within the time and circumstances available. Habibian also declines a confident answer. He is still testing his own first-principles reasoning against others’ arguments and does not yet have a worked-through position.

17. Quesnelle locates human distinctiveness in relationship, not intelligence

  • Quesnelle says he studied philosophy before deeply entering AI because he could not avoid the questions it raised. His theological starting point is Genesis: being made in God’s image has often been associated with reasoning and intelligence. He emphasizes another interpretation, in which humanity’s distinctive calling is a relationship with God, something superior machine reasoning would not remove.
  • Within that framework, studying intelligence, mathematics, and nature brings him closer to understanding creation. He describes discovery as successive layers unfolding: fire, planetary understanding, Newtonian physics, quantum physics, and now intelligence. Each new explanation reveals another question beneath it. For him, that pattern expresses divine creation rather than undermining religious belief.
  • His illustration of cosmic fine-tuning uses a fine-structure constant of “one over 138.” He says changing it to 1/135 or 1/142 would prevent familiar material structures from forming. The question he draws from this example is why reality permits ordered matter, life, intelligence, and eventually minds capable of examining the chain that produced them.
  • Quoting Augustine, Quesnelle says things are real insofar as “they have their being from you.” He uses that distinction to resist treating touchable matter as the final stopping point of inquiry. Identifying particles still leaves questions about what those particles are, why reality exists, and toward what end it might be understood.

18. Habibian approaches the same questions through meditation and criticism

  • Habibian describes a different personal trajectory: growing up in religious Iran helped push him toward strong atheism and materialism. Curiosity about being alone with his mind eventually led to meditation, including more than six months on silent retreats in total and a longest continuous retreat of six weeks. He stresses that the exploration is ongoing rather than a completed conversion to a settled explanation.
  • His standard remains questioning and critical thinking, particularly because spiritual inquiry also contains people whose claims do not make sense. He describes what he has encountered as coherent and testable while deeply mysterious: “There is a there there.” His background makes him cautious about organized religion, while a personal relationship with questions of mind and reality has proved productive.
  • Habibian frames science as “conjecture and criticism,” not a requirement to assume materialism beyond question. He finds it striking that inquiry can unravel its own starting assumptions and expose deeper mysteries. Quesnelle welcomes an AI research culture in which different worldviews can be discussed openly; both see studying intelligence as making questions about human existence harder to set aside.

item.title: Teknium (Nous Research) on Post-Training, Hermes and Open Models: Delphi AMA
item.description: Nous says 90%+ of its data is synthetic, and Atropos generates reasoning data across more than 1,200 tasks. Teknium sees post-training RL as barely explored and argues open research can pool domain expertise large companies cannot staff internally. He claims Hermes 4 leads Meta’s instruct variant by “something like 60 points” on MATH and 21 points on MMLU-Pro, while urging downstream testing as Psyche’s RL infrastructure is still being built.
item.content:encoded:
Delphi Intelligence AMA · Teknium、Tommy Shaughnessy · 2025-10-09 · 60 min · 原语言 EN

Nous says 90%+ of its data is synthetic, and Atropos generates reasoning data across more than 1,200 tasks. Teknium sees post-training RL as barely explored and argues open research can pool domain expertise large companies cannot staff internally. He claims Hermes 4 leads Meta’s instruct variant by “something like 60 points” on MATH and 21 points on MMLU-Pro, while urging downstream testing as Psyche’s RL infrastructure is still being built.

TL;DR

  • Post-training lets Nous shape models for downstream uses. Teknium says data scarcity is mainly a pre-training concern; post-training RL is “just barely scratching the surface.” Nous’s data is 90%+ synthetic, and Atropos generates reasoning data across more than 1,200 tasks.
  • Nous’s competitive thesis is open research and shared expertise. Teknium argues open contributions can help cover domains that even giant companies cannot staff internally. The transcript’s response also says RL environments may be more efficient than sourcing human prompt-response samples. Teknium sees value in both open and closed models, with differentiated choices.
  • Hermes 4’s pitch is broader user control, with explicit refusal boundaries. Shaughnessy cites 60% non-refusals versus GPT-OSS at 5%; Teknium argues restrictions obstruct uses such as sales automation and produce “the mode collapse of the world.” Nous’s disallowed RefusalBench categories are CSAM and suicide.
  • Teknium argues alignment matters alongside integrations. He calls integrations “quite easy” and points to demand for private assistants handling legal questions and strategy. Memory is in a limited beta for personalization; learning tasks from ongoing feedback is a future capability.
  • Nous’s agent roadmap combines general tools with infrastructure still under construction. Teknium favors CLI access, GUI computer use and ultimately robots, with outcome-based RL teaching effective tool use. Psyche starts with pre-training and SFT; RL comes next and requires coordinating training nodes, inference nodes and environments.
  • Benchmark gains support Hermes’s pitch, but Teknium rejects optimizing for benchmarks alone. He claims Hermes 4 outperforms Meta’s instruct variant by “something like 60 points” on MATH and 21 points on MMLU-Pro. He recommends downstream testing or broader evaluation: “We need way more evals, not fewer.”

Digest

1. Post-training value comes from task design and synthetic data

  • Teknium’s “clay” metaphor explains post-training: shape a pre-trained model for downstream products. Diverse data supports generalization, while known tasks and agent harnesses deserve specific attention. Coordination with pre-training covers data ratios, coding-data allocation, context length, modalities and inference speed. Testing, evaluations and documentation can take as long as training.
  • Data scarcity belongs mainly to pre-training, in Teknium’s view; post-training RL is “just barely scratching the surface.” He says models can generate many problems from a “tiny slice of information.” Nous’s data is 90%+ synthetic, drawing on DataForge’s generation and validation, Atropos’s more than 1,200 tasks, and filters for open datasets.
  • Changing the base generally requires retraining unless it continues the previous base’s pre-training. Teknium’s conditional exception: Llama 3.1 to 3.3 could be merged “for basically free” if both base variants had been released. Cross-architecture merging is “currently not possible.”

2. Open research is Nous’s answer to hyperscaler scale

  • Teknium argues that “open research compounds on itself.” A response to the question about RL environments argues that they rely more on domain expertise than ML engineering, making open contributions useful for fields giant companies cannot cover internally. It adds that labs previously spent hundreds of millions of dollars sourcing human prompt-response samples, and says environments may be more efficient.
  • Teknium describes Nous’s RL expertise in rubric-based and LLM-as-a-judge rewards, including RLAIF, citing Generative Reward Models. He contrasts these fuzzier rewards with hard verifiers used for math. On dataset collection, he names three sources: DataForge’s synthetic data creation and distillation; rejection sampling and RL through Atropos; and filters and curation tools for open-source datasets. The transcript does not directly explain how Nous proves provenance or data quality.
  • Teknium favors open models but sees value in closed-source models too, saying the range of options keeps models differentiated. He argues that a world with only one model and no choice would be undesirable.

3. Hermes competes on control against entrenched distribution

  • Shaughnessy frames Hermes 4 around 60% non-refusals versus GPT-OSS at 5%. Teknium’s concrete example is sales automation breaking when a model detects pressure on a buyer; he also cites creative writing and white-hat vulnerability discovery. He calls restrictions on expression “the mode collapse of the world.”
  • On whether alignment can beat ChatGPT’s integrations and user habit, Teknium says alignment is crucial long term and “Integrations are quite easy,” pointing to existing harnesses and the possibility of Nous building its own. He sees demand for private, at-home assistants handling legal questions and strategy.
  • Asked how Nous stays essential if Meta releases a stronger Llama, Teknium says Nous has kept pace with and often outperformed Llama instruct models since Llama 1. He claims Hermes 4 beats Meta’s instruct variant on MATH by “something like 60 points” and MMLU-Pro by 21 points. He says more open-access models are beneficial because the field builds on them.
  • RefusalBench measures overall refusals and refusals within categories users choose to disallow; Nous chooses CSAM and suicide. Asked about hosting or takedown hurdles, Teknium says synthetic post-training data generally carries less risk of matching copyrighted data.

4. General tools and memory anchor Nous’s agent plans

  • Asked whether models and apps will specialize or agentic capabilities will be built into larger models, Teknium answers “both”: product-specific training can unlock value, and those capabilities may later return to primary models.
  • Teknium names Linux CLI, GUI computer use and robots as three general-purpose harnesses, with robots “the ultimate harness.” He says Nous’s internal agent has a strong focus on CLI and terminal use, which will be part of its RL efforts.
  • Asked whether planning tool order and parameters becomes the central challenge, Teknium agrees “in some ways.” He says outcome-based RL can teach efficient tool sequences, including when not to use tools. General tools can let agents work across environments without being designed for each specific toolset.
  • Memory is currently a limited-access personalization beta. Teknium says it could become a path to online learning; future agents could learn tasks and information through work and user feedback, retaining them permanently or as long as the user wants.

5. Psyche’s rollout requires more than new models

  • Psyche’s sequence is traditional pre-training and SFT first, RL next. Teknium says RL requires coordinating training nodes, inference nodes and environments—the data-creation and validation servers. He closes by saying the team is focused on the “final infrastructure push,” new models and architecture experiments.
  • Teknium credits DiSTRO with enabling large-scale distributed training coordination. Any-to-any architectures remain under research, with a Psyche-powered model possibly coming soon. He says Nous pioneered YaRN around two years earlier, helping expand context from 2,000–4,000 tokens to 128,000; agents and reasoning will need longer contexts.
  • His evaluation stance rejects both benchmark-only optimization and abandoning evals: preserve base-model qualities for creativity, judge models on downstream tasks or a wider suite, and avoid treating LMSYS as the sole arbiter. “We need way more evals, not fewer.” His admitted mistake was underestimating the work beyond the model, especially papers, documentation and blogs. Asked which company or network might be most valuable in 2030, he says he is unsure but Nvidia might be near the top.

Verification Notes

The RL-environment response is labeled “Speaker 3” in the transcript, so its speaker is left unspecified.
